In the first stage, we construct a diverse pool of candidate workflows via evolutionary search. In the second stage, we formulate workflow selection as a Contextual Bandit problem, which enables sample-efficient learning by balancing exploration and exploitation, thereby significantly reducing the feedback required for training. During inference, the model adaptively selects the optimal workflow tailored to each query. Evaluations across five diverse benchmarks demonstrate that CB-Orchestrator consistently outperforms all baselines. Notably, on the MATH dataset, CB-Orchestrator achieves better performance than strong recent baselines while reducing training-phase API token overhead by no less than 40.55% and total end-to-end training (including workflow pool generation) token overhead by no less than 29.73%.

title: TestSuiteBench: Coding Agents Struggle to Generate Strong Test Suites from Specifications
abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used to create large software projects. While code-generation benchmarks have scaled accordingly to full applications, test-generation benchmarks remain limited to individual functions or bug fixes. In particular, generating complete test suites for complex software from scratch remains unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce TestSuiteBench, a benchmark of 165 open-source applications, each with a structured and detailed specification of intended behavior, a reference implementation, a reference test suite, and on average 74 mutants. Each mutant is generated from a single requirement of the specification and refined to isolate that behavior: 73\% are killed by exactly one reference test and, on average, by only 0.2\% of the remaining tests. We find that even frontier coding agents struggle to generate strong test suites given our specifications, achieving mutation scores below 60\%, despite their suites being largely valid and 88\% of their tests passing on the reference implementation. We observe that generated test suites often lack relevant input combinations and are smaller than reference test suites. Meanwhile, implementations generated for the same specifications pass 82\% of the reference tests. These results show agents can build software they cannot verify, a gap that directly limits fully autonomous software development.

title: Evolving Creatives with Clicks: CTR-Driven Advertising image Editing via Attribute Disentanglement and Preference Alignment
abstract: The optimization objective for e-commerce advertising creatives has shifted from aesthetic quality to online business metrics like click-through rate (CTR). Recent methods generate appealing ad images from product images by constructing CTR-based reward signals and refining prompt generation via Reinforcement Learning. Such paradigms equally penalize all attributes within an underperforming image, even though some are actually beneficial to clicks. In this work, we propose Evolving Creatives with Clicks (ECC), which reformulates creative optimization as fine-grained editing rather than generation from scratch. ECC selectively refines attributes that hurt CTR while preserving those that contribute positively. Specifically, faced with a rich attribute space across massive images, ECC first identifies 28 attributes significantly correlated with CTR via ANOVA and Random Forest regression. Based on attribute contrasts between images with disparate CTRs, we instruction-tune a prompt model to generate editing suggestions, then refine it with real click preferences since reference-derived suggestions are not uniformly beneficial. Furthermore, we introduce Consistent Preference Optimization (CPO) as ECC's preference optimization strategy, which enforces consistency across semantically equivalent shuffled suggestions to mitigate DPO overfitting and improve preference generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ECC significantly improves the CTR of ad images, outperforming state-of-the-art models by a substantial margin. The complete data pipeline, including attribute extraction and analysis, the resulting dataset, and source code will be released upon acceptance.

title: TPCS: A Cycle-Level Simulation Paradigm with Native Execution Semantics for RTL Modeling and Generation
abstract: The growing diversity of domain-specific architectures and microarchitectural designs demands fast and accurate evaluation methods during early design stages. However, existing approaches suffer from a fundamental trade-off: high-level simulators offer speed but lack fidelity, while RTL-based tools provide accuracy at the cost of significant simulation overhead. This gap limits efficient pre-RTL microarchitecture exploration. Therefore, we propose Transaction-Pruned Cycle Simulation (TPCS), a novel modeling and simulation framework. It serves as a unified intermediate abstraction spanning microarchitecture modeling, cycle-accurate simulation, and synthesizable RTL implementation. TPCS organizes combinational logic as transaction-based function invocations and leverages host CPU control flow to naturally prune inactive logic, eliminating the need for explicit event scheduling or signal tracking. This enables cycle-accurate simulation with significantly improved performance. TPCS preserves structural correspondence with RTL and supports automatic generation of synthesizable designs. TPCS achieves 36$\times$-42$\times$ speedups over parallel Verilator on SMP systems and 3.4$\times$-7.2$\times$ over single-threaded Verilator on accelerators, with cycle-level waveform agreement on the evaluated traces. The generated RTL demonstrates comparable timing and area to handcrafted implementations, with relative changes of -4.7\% to +2.6\% in clock period and -3.3\% to +4.0\% in standard-cell area. By bridging the abstraction gap between high-level modeling and RTL design, TPCS enables a unified and agile pre-RTL workflow, allowing efficient microarchitecture exploration with both high performance and implementation fidelity.

title: Uniform Exponential Attractors for Non-Autonomous Dynamical Systems and an Application to the damped hyperbolic equation with sub-quintic growth
abstract: In this paper, we develop an abstract framework for the theory of uniform exponential attractors in non-autonomous dynamical systems. Our construction employs time-dependent absorbing sets while ensuring exponential attraction among the constructed sets. Moreover, we show that the resulting exponential attractors are uniform-that is, they remain stable under perturbations. As an application of this abstract theory, we study the weakly damped hyperbolic equation with sub-quintic nonlinearity. Using the proposed approach, we construct exponential attractors for the process generated by the Shatah-Struwe solution, which satisfies both energy and Strichartz estimates. Furthermore, we establish the Holder continuity of these exponential attractors with respect to the external forcing term.

title: Penalizations of Two-Dimensional Simple Random Walk by Direction-Dependent Excursion Counts and Edge-Crossing Counts
abstract: We study penalizations of the two-dimensional simple random walk by functions of direction-dependent excursion counts and edge-crossing counts. The former record completed excursions with prescribed pairs of departure and return directions at the origin, whereas the latter record crossings of a prescribed set of unoriented edges incident to the origin. We determine the distributions of their almost surely finite terminal values and derive explicit path decomposition formulas involving the random walk conditioned to avoid the origin. Moreover, both families of penalized measures can be represented by weighting and normalizing the same universal $σ$-finite measure associated with local-time penalization at the origin. Thus, direction-dependent excursion counts, edge-crossing counts, and local time at the origin give rise to penalizations belonging to a common universality class.

title: A Palais-Smale type condition for optimal control problems
abstract: We consider an optimal control problem with a general control constraint and a fixed initial state, for which convexity assumptions are absent. To establish the existence of optimal pairs, we introduce a control version of the Palais-Smale type condition adapted from critical point theory and prove that optimal pairs exist under this condition (see Theorem 2.1). Subsequently, we verify that a specific class of optimal control problems satisfies our Palais-Smale type condition (see Proposition 2.1). Furthermore, as an application, we present an example (Example 3.1) and show that, to the best of our knowledge, no existing result can be applied to establish the existence of an optimal pair in this case (see Section 3.1.1). Example 3.2 shows that finitely many Pontryagin maximum principle candidates do not guarantee the existence of an optimal control. Finally, Example 3.3 demonstrates that the proposed Palais-Smale type condition is sufficient, but not necessary, for the existence of optimal controls.

title: CAPE - Context-Aware Prioritization Engine for Vulnerability Scoring and Management
abstract: Vulnerability patching is critical for safeguarding an enterprise's software ecosystem from cyber attacks. However, patching requires adequate preparation for potential system downtime and for unforeseen effects of the patched software on a live system. Thus, effective risk mitigation requires prioritization strategies that explicitly account for the operational context of the affected software. While vulnerability prioritization based on Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, can help, their differing goals and methodologies often lead to inconsistent, context-unaware decisions resulting in mis-allocated remediation efforts. In this work, we present the Context-Aware Prioritization Engine (CAPE), a vulnerability analysis framework that enriches each vulnerability scanner report of vulnerabilities (CVEs) with deployment-specific evidence. This evidence is used to perform vulnerability reachability, centrality, and exploitability analysis, producing a ranked priority score for the effective distribution of remediation effort. We evaluate CAPE on 30 open-source agentic applications comprising 6,138 scanner-reported CVEs. Our evaluation shows that a significant majority of CVEs are not reachable and exploitable which results in significant disparities between CAPE and context-free baselines - the CVSS, EPSS, and KEV. It also shows that CAPE consistently surfaces confirmed-exploitable CVEs at higher priority than all baselines, demonstrating that context-aware analysis provides substantially more accurate remediation guidance than context-free severity scoring alone.

title: AV-FlowEdit: Training-Free Prompt-Driven Audio-Visual Editing with Event-Aware Spectral Trajectory Preservation
abstract: Joint audio-video diffusion models generate synchronized content, but editing existing clips requires target changes without disrupting non-target structure or cross-modal correspondence. We present AV-FlowEdit, a training-free and inversion-free framework for prompt-driven audio-video editing. Our key insight is that source--target flow differences provide both cross-modal editing directions and preservation cues. Under shared perturbations, they jointly update the video and audio branches, supporting visual-only, audio-only, and joint edits while retaining pretrained cross-modal interactions. To suppress drift accumulated during sampling, Cross-Modal Event-Aware Spectral Trajectory Preservation combines flow saliency, aligned audio activity, multiscale low-frequency displacement, and diffusion-stage scheduling. This adaptively preserves unsupported regions while allowing intended audio-visual events. AV-FlowEdit requires no model training, external masks, or optimization-based inversion. Experiments show strong prompt alignment and temporal consistency, together with competitive audio quality and cross-modal coherence.

title: Double-Take: Improving Capacity, Binding, and Selectivity In Long-Context Within Bidirectional Memory
abstract: Processing a long sequence does not guarantee that distant information remains usable. As context grows, a fixed-size memory must retain many associations, connect information across positions, and preserve relevant structure without being overwhelmed by everything it observes. These are distinct requirements: a memory may store more information without representing the relationships needed for retrieval, and it may transport those relationships without preserving the ones that matter. Thus, the challenge is not simply extending context length, but constructing a memory that remains usable as context grows. We study this problem in large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identify two basic failures: single-step writes accumulate interference, limiting capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. We introduce Double-Take (DT), which repairs these failures with multi-step unpinned updates and cross-position mixing, and adds bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves end-to-end recall at the $0.10$ chance floor; adding binding raises it to $0.92$. Trained only on $32\,\mathrm{kb}$ genomic contexts, DT reaches $0.927$ AUROC at $131\,\mathrm{kb}$ and $0.856$ near $1\,\mathrm{Mb}$, while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse. Together, these results identify capacity, binding, and selectivity as three requirements for usable long-range memory.

title: All-optical deconvolution via quantum cross-correlation spectroscopy with bright twin beams
abstract: The resolution of spectroscopic measurements is fundamentally limited by the convolution between a system's intrinsic response and the instrument response function, creating an ill-posed inverse problem. While entangled photons can theoretically bypass these limits, low photon flux has hindered their experimental realization. Here, we propose quantum cross-correlation spectroscopy (QCCS), utilizing macroscopic twin beams (signal and idler beams) to physically circumvent this convolution limit in coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering. Employing the signal beam as a broadband probe, QCCS achieves all-optical deconvolution through a correlation-enhanced sum-frequency generation channel between the convoluted anti-Stokes and idler beams. By subtracting the uncorrelated background using a 500-femtosecond temporal window, we successfully retrieve narrow Raman bands (8 cm^{-1} and 15 cm^{-1}) completely obscured by a 75 cm^{-1} probe bandwidth without numerical deconvolution or prior knowledge. Our results establish macroscopic quantum correlations as a robust resource for high-fidelity spectroscopy, paving the way for ultrashort-pulse-free operando studies under natural, incoherent excitation conditions.

title: LongHarness: Advancing Agentic Reasoning over 100M-Token Corpora via Stateful Evidence Management
abstract: Corpus-level long-context reasoning requires agents to acquire and integrate evidence across document collections that exceed their context windows. Existing agent harnesses enable incremental access to these corpora, but acquired evidence and evolving conclusions often remain entangled in a growing interaction history. This implicit state management can lead to two coupled failure modes: unbounded exploration, where retrieval expands the interaction history without resolving decision-relevant information gaps, and evidence-state drift, where previously acquired evidence or subsequent corrections fail to inform the current conclusion. We present LongHarness, a model-agnostic harness that makes the interaction between acquired evidence and evolving conclusions explicit. Its core mechanism, Evidence-Conclusion Coevolution, uses unresolved conclusions to guide exploration toward missing information, while newly acquired evidence strengthens or revises the conclusions that directed the search. LongHarness couples this process with Evidence Lifecycle Management, which keeps accumulated evidence current and traceable throughout the interaction. Together, these mechanisms focus retrieval on remaining information needs and keep conclusions aligned with current evidence. We evaluate LongHarness on OfficeQA Pro V1 and V2, AA-LCR, and LongBench v2 using GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash. Compared with direct reasoning using the same backbone, LongHarness improves GLM-5.3-Flash exact match on OfficeQA Pro from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and from 4.4% to 61.1% on V2. Against state-of-the-art agent harnesses, it surpasses Claude Code by 12.0 percentage points on V1 and Codex by 18.9 points on V2. With Qwen3.8-Flash, LongHarness reaches 61.7% on V1, outperforming Claude Code by 8.3 points and Codex by 12.0 points.

title: Classes of Subgroups of a finite group with isomorphic quotient groups
abstract: In this paper, we study the poset QIso(G) of classes of subgroups of a finite group G having isomorphic quotients. Particularly, we study it for finite abelian groups and for some classes of non-abelian metacyclic groups, namely dihedral groups Dn, the group U2np and affine groups Aff(F) over finite field F. In the case of abelian groups G, we show that there exists a duality from QIso(G) to Iso(G). We show that cyclic groups are the only groups for which QIso(G), up to duality is isomorphic to its subgroup lattice. We also show that cyclic groups are the only nilpotent groups for which QIso(G), up to duality is isomorphic to its lattice of normal subgroups. We characterize finite 2-groups all of whose subgroups are q-self dual with QIso(G) being a chain. We also characterize all p-groups G of order at most p4 whose QIso(G) is a chain.

title: Towards Safer Cities: A Design Process for Perception Datasets in Urban Driving Scenarios
abstract: Urban environments present significant challenges for the perception systems of automated driving due to their high complexity, characterized by dense traffic, diverse obstacles, or a wide range of possible scenarios. While numerous automotive datasets exist, few focus on urban settings, and the majority are acquired exclusively on passenger cars and overlook other transport modalities such as heavy-duty trucks, busses and trams. In contrast to passenger vehicles, these platforms operate under different geographical and operational constraints; including traversing pedestrian zones or platform-specific tasks such as movement of trailer or winter service. In this work a method is proposed for a guided dataset creation based on an analysis of existing datasets using user-generated map data. Furthermore, representative truck-specific use cases are identified and exemplified to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed methodology and to support targeted acquisition planning.

title: Attention Sees, MLP Refuses: Tracing the Attention-to-MLP Safety Pathway in LLMs
abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and can over-refuse benign requests. Understanding these failures requires distinguishing harmfulness recognition from the computation that writes refusal. We reframe this as a pathway question and make it measurable on residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, separating the harmfulness information a module update exposes from the change it produces in readable refusal evidence. Across 18 Base-Instruct pairs spanning Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, harmfulness is decoded more readily from attention updates, particularly in early layers, whereas MLP updates contribute more strongly to harm-selective refusal writing in aligned models. Post-training strengthens MLP refusal writing in all 18 pairs without systematically improving harmfulness decodability, while positive MLP writing becomes more concentrated in deeper layers after post-training. Across six reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains decodable during reasoning while strong refusal writing concentrates at answer onset, a pattern that persists with reasoning disabled. Causal interventions further support this pathway: resetting downstream MLP updates to their clean values substantially reduces the refusal shift caused by upstream attention interventions. Building on these findings, we introduce Sentinel, which combines an attention-derived perception score P with an MLP-derived decision score D. Their joint profiles characterize jailbreaks and over-refusals, and conditional routing with both signals achieves a lower aggregate error rate than single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.

title: VICAR: Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting for Humanoid Interactive Skills
abstract: Third-person human videos offer a scalable alternative to task-specific reward engineering, teleoperation, and manually scripted demonstrations for humanoid loco-manipulation. Recent video-to-humanoid systems have shown that noisy human motion, object trajectories, and contacts can be extracted from unstructured videos and refined into deployable skills. However, a key gap remains for contact-rich imitation: the task is often defined by world-frame contacts whose poses, timing, and speed must survive embodiment mismatch and runtime scene changes. Towards this, we present VICAR (Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting), a pipeline for learning humanoid interactive skills from third-person human videos. The system first recovers human motion, reconstructs task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, and then retargets the motion to a humanoid while preserving global contact poses, motion speed, and collision clearance. Unlike retargeting methods that only remove penetration or preserve local interaction geometry, our formulation represents user-specified contact poses and collision clearance as high-priority Lagrangian penalty terms and optimizes the full motion to remain smooth through contact-rich transitions. The resulting motions are used to train a contact-conditioned motion generator whose inputs include movable contact points enabling runtime adaptation to new contact positions. We demonstrate the framework on ten diverse third-person video skills, including six table-tennis serves, three object-pickup tasks, and ladder climbing, and deploy the learned skills on hardware. These results suggest that contact-preserving retargeting is a practical step toward humanoids that learn useful interactive behavior by watching humans.

title: Limit cycles of slow-fast quintic Lienard systems
abstract: For every fixed real quintic polynomial $F$, we prove that the slow--fast Liénard system $\dot{x}=y-F(x),\quad \dot{y}=-\varepsilon x$ admits at most two limit cycles whenever $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0(F)$ for a suitable $\varepsilon_0(F)>0$. Using scalar comparison near the equilibrium and a logarithmic fold-passage correction, we exclude \rev{canard singular limits}. Every sequence of limit cycles with $\varepsilon\to0^+$ has a subsequence converging in the Hausdorff metric to a common slow--fast path, whose regular slow arcs are either all normally attracting or all normally repelling. We also establish uniform Floquet separation for fixed $F$. The global counting argument uses shared regular arcs, nesting, and stability alternation. These results give a global small-parameter bound and describe the singular-limit structure, complementing the local cyclicity analysis of Li and Lu(J. Differential Equations, 2014).

title: SWEAR: Section-Wise Efficient Audio Reasoning via Self-Rated Difficulty
abstract: Recent work on large audio-language models (LALMs) explores adaptive reasoning to balance accuracy and efficiency. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, overlooking the diverse factors that determine reasoning effort. We address this limitation by deriving five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments. Based on this characterization, we propose SWEAR, a difficulty-aware reasoning framework that learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning allocation across reasoning stages. Experiments on MMAU-test-mini and MMAR show that SWEAR improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens, shortening reasoning for easy instances without sacrificing performance on difficult ones.

title: Human and LLM Facilitation in Collaborative Design Meetings: A Computational Behavioral Comparison
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored as facilitators of group discussion and collaborative work, but the behavioral differences between LLM-generated and human facilitation remain insufficiently characterized. We compare human Project Manager facilitation turns from scenario-based collaborative design meetings with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct responses across 199 paired contexts from the AMI Meeting Corpus. The analysis covers five confirmatory dimensions: contextual semantic distance, a lexical elaboration proxy, empathyand-hedge lexical density, topic divergence, and phase-vocabulary alignment. An exploratory directiveness measure failed domain validation and is not interpreted. The sampled human Project Manager turns were higher on contextual semantic distance (r = 0.644) and on empathyand-hedge lexical density (r = 0.203). The second contrast is carried mainly by hedge terms, so we read it as lexical hedging rather than psychological empathy. Llama-generated facilitation was higher on topic divergence (r = 0.703), the lexical elaboration proxy (r = 0.288; lengthconfounded), and instruction-conditioned phase-vocabulary alignment (r = 0.382). A secondary no-phase check left the Llama-higher phase contrast in place. The system prompt still requested a facilitation move, so that check is not evidence of spontaneous phase awareness. These differences should not be interpreted as a ranking of facilitation quality. The resulting behavioral profile provides a reference point for later comparisons of LLM facilitators, human facilitators, prompts, models, and collaborative settings.

title: The Limits of Query Monitoring against Distributed Model Extraction
abstract: Model providers now face distillation campaigns run through thousands of accounts, each of which looks like an ordinary user. When network and payment metadata cannot link those accounts, the only evidence left is what they ask. We study what a provider can and cannot learn from those queries alone, using one million real chat turns for development and 17 later weeks that no design choice touched for a single frozen evaluation. The answer is set less by anything specific to extraction than by benign coordination: a campaign is visible only if it is more distinctive than the most distinctive group of ordinary users in the same week. We make this precise, show that a small but positive difference between campaign and users buys a detection time rather than detectability, and identify the campaign that is hardest to detect. Empirically, a calibrated monitor catches naive distributed extraction that per-account monitors miss (0.86-1.00 of weeks), and one variant - selecting accounts that move together after discounting how topical each one is - still catches campaigns padded with natural text (0.50-0.96 of weeks) where the other two spectral detectors catch none. Distilling each campaign into a small student shows that, in our testbed, campaigns that evaded every detector kept at most 42% of the capability of a detectable one. The limits are equally concrete: a campaign that ramps up slowly poisons every detector's calibration, benign evaluation pipelines look exactly like distillation, we found no deployable detector at colluder shares of 2.5% or below, and campaigns that relay real users' requests may be invisible to any query-only monitor.

title: Evolution and breakdown of chiral anomaly in Weyl semiconductor tellurium
abstract: Chiral anomaly in topological materials manifests as negative longitudinal magnetoresistance, yet the tunability and evolution of this effect remain elusive. Here we show that doped tellurium serves as a versatile platform to realize a giant negative longitudinal magnetoresistance that is highly tunable via the Fermi level and magnetic field. By moving the Fermi level towards the Weyl point, we observe a pronounced enhancement of negative magnetoresistance, which arises from chiral anomaly and robustly persists up to ambient temperature. Beyond the quantum limit, the system exhibits positive linear magnetoconductance, serving as a compelling transport signature of the chiral anomaly in the lowest Landau level. Notably, in the extreme quantum limit at cryogenic temperatures, the magnetoresistance undergoes a dramatic reversal from negative to positive. This reversal points to a potential field-induced phase transition into a collective electronic state driven by enhanced electron-electron interactions. Our findings provide valuable insights into the unconventional chiral transport and emergent correlated quantum states under extreme magnetic fields.

title: Resolving Pisanski's Conjecture
abstract: We prove Pisanski's conjecture on quadrilateral embeddings of regular bipartite graphs. For integers $m\geq d\geq4$ with $4\mid md$, we construct both a connected simple $d$-regular bipartite graph $G$ with $m$ vertices in each bipartition class and an orientable quadrangulation. This graph's genus is \[ \ga(G)=1+\frac{m(d-4)}4. \] These quadrangulations attain the lower bound on the genus from Euler's formula. We give dihedral constructions for even $m$ and a cyclic construction for every $m\geq d$ with $4\mid d$. In each case, two cyclic permutations of a connection set of size $d$ determine all of the local rotations.

title: Safety Graph: When Safety Responses Become Attack Surfaces in Cyber-Physical Systems
abstract: Modern industrial control systems (ICS) are susceptible to cyber attacks triggering safety failures in the operational technology (OT) layer. The traditional way to mitigate any failure in OT is to implement safety responses. However, we show in this work that these responses can open up new attack surfaces, thereby vastly expanding the scope of lateral movement. Existing frameworks model cyber-to-physical escalation but provide no mechanism to reason about how these safety responses to OT-failures can trigger new cascading cyber attacks in the Information Technology (IT) layer. To enable such reasoning, we introduce Safety Graph (SG), a formal framework unifying three paradigms - Attack Graphs (AG), Fault Trees (FT), and Event Trees (ET) - over a shared propositional state space, capturing the full bidirectional IT-OT cascade. We provide a sound and complete compilation of SG to a classical AI planning problem, performing plan search using A* to find cross-layer cascade paths. Through a Web3D modeling and simulation of the Tennessee Eastman chemical process plant, which is a widely used chemical engineering benchmark serving as a standard for testing control, monitoring and fault propagation, we demonstrate that the planning compilation of SG automatically discovers safety-response-induced lateral movements, and identifies the responsible barriers that are unidentifiable under existing models. A complexity and scalability analysis characterizes how the planning compilation of SG scales with model size and cascade depth. To the best of our knowledge, SG is the first framework to formally model IT-OT attacks and enable operators to explore the problem of cyber attacks triggering cascading failures in ICS.

title: Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion: Object-Centric Flow Replanning for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
abstract: People often learn how an unfamiliar object moves through a small exploratory push, using its response to guide their next motion. Inspired by this behavior, we study humanoids pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are initially unknown. Our object-centric framework closes online estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control into a loop, creating a tension: replacing the plan whenever the belief shifts disrupts the maneuver under way, while keeping it strands the robot on a path its evidence has ruled out. Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) scales revision to agreement, inverting the flow under the old belief only as far as the beliefs disagree before reconstructing under the new one. Across 18 simulated goals it lowers pooled final position and yaw error by roughly 33% and 47% against fixed-depth replanning, and on hardware it translates and turns a non-holonomic cart.

title: Volume Rendering with Metric--Phase Fields for Thin Structures and Sign-Ambiguous Geometry
abstract: Neural implicit surface methods that couple volume rendering with signed distance functions (SDFs), such as VolSDF and NeuS, achieve high-quality multi-view reconstruction for watertight objects. However, these approaches rely on a globally consistent inside-outside partition of space. This assumption becomes fragile for thin structures (e.g., sheets, tubes, and thin walls) and can break down for sign-ambiguous geometry (e.g., surfaces with boundary, non-manifold junctions, and closely spaced surface components), often resulting in spurious closures or loss of fine structures. Unsigned distance field (UDF) formulations relax the global sign requirement and better support non-watertight geometry, but are substantially harder to optimize. We propose PhaseSurf, a neural volume rendering framework built on Metric-Phase Fields (MPFs). MPFs decompose geometry into a nonnegative metric field capturing unsigned proximity and a continuous phase field providing a soft sign cue. By coupling the two through residual phase injection, MPFs yield a signed composite implicit function with stable near-surface gradients while retaining UDF-like robustness in sign-ambiguous regions. This design enables direct iso-surface extraction using standard Marching Cubes and avoids the failure modes of both pure SDF- and UDF-based formulations. We further introduce MPF-specific training losses that enforce metric consistency, stabilize phase transitions near the interface, and suppress spurious geometry in free space. Experiments on multi-view datasets with thin structures and sign-ambiguous geometry show that PhaseSurf produces more stable reconstructions and higher-quality geometry than UDF-based methods and recent 3DGS pipelines, while avoiding artifacts typical of SDF-based approaches.

title: Tight Guarantees for Static Policies in Vehicle Sharing Networks
abstract: We study pricing in a vehicle sharing network with $N$ locations and $C$ vehicles, motivated by on-demand bike, scooter, and car sharing, as well as robotaxi and ride sharing services. Customers request directed trips between locations, with travel times following general distributions, and leave without service if no vehicle is available. Pricing affects both demand for trips and the distribution of vehicles across locations. Computing an optimal dynamic pricing policy is challenging because the system state depends on the number of vehicles available at each location and in transit (including how long they have been traveling), motivating the use of simple static policies that offer a fixed price for each trip. For any number of vehicles and locations, we establish a tight performance guarantee for static pricing relative to optimal dynamic pricing. The guarantee holds for any concave objective functions (including revenue rate) and general travel time distributions. Our tight guarantee is bounded below by $ \frac{C}{C + \min \{ C -1, \sqrt{ CN} \} }$ (over 50%), achieving the first universal, non-asymptotic constant factor guarantee. We also prove that the optimal static policy can be efficiently computed by solving a convex optimization problem. Finally, we extend our performance guarantee to the setting with supply redirection.

title: A robust digital receiver architecture for continuous-variable quantum key distribution
abstract: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution utilizes advanced digital signal processing techniques to mitigate channel impairments, driving the progress of high-performance quantum secure communications. Specifically, digital heterodyne receivers are commonly implemented using down-conversion algorithms to detect both components simultaneously where the signal is modulated onto an intermediate frequency to avoid low-frequency noise and bypass stringent optical phase-locking requirements. However, a rigorous analysis of the quantum security implications of the digital down-conversion algorithm remains absent. In this paper, we investigate the algorithm process from the perspective of quantum operator evolution, revealing that the frequency folding effect inherent in down-conversion inevitably mixes the image-frequency information into the baseband signal. To address this issue, we propose a novel operator reconstruction detection scheme based on dual-path digital heterodyne receiver. By performing a non-equal weighted combination of the output operators along two optical paths in the digital domain, this scheme perfectly cancels out the image-frequency operator physically. The robust receiver architecture preserves the baseband noise-suppression advantages, inherently achieves perfect mode balancing for asymmetric optical detection losses, and fundamentally closes the image-frequency crosstalk. Practical experiments have validated the feasibility of the proposed architecture and its effective suppression of image-frequency noise, achieving a performance of 11.4 Mbps @ 42 km. This work lays a solid theoretical and algorithmic foundation for future high-performance, highly secure digital continuous-variable quantum key distribution systems.

title: A Lipschitz refinement of the Bebutov-Kakutani dynamical embedding theorem for connected Lie group actions
abstract: Let $G$ be a connected Lie group equipped with a compatible right-invariant metric and let $G$ act continuously on a compact metrizable space $X$. We prove that $X$ admits a $G$-equivariant embedding into the right argument shift action on the space of one-Lipschitz maps from $G$ to $[0,1]$ if and only if the set of fixed points topologically embeds into $[0,1]$. This generalizes a theorem proved by Gutman, Huo and Tsukamoto for $\mathbb{R}^k$-flows.

title: When Faster Decisions Do Not Make Better Agents: An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows
abstract: AI agents depend on repeated decisions to accomplish tasks, with large language models (LLMs) commonly serving as their core decision makers. The recent emergence of Jev offers an opportunity to make these decisions faster and at lower cost. However, it remains unclear whether such local savings can be translated into efficient and reliable task completion. In this paper, we investigate this efficiency transfer across five agents in two representative application settings, embodied tasks in ALFWorld and mobile app use in AndroidWorld. Across 4,500 task executions, we jointly evaluate task effectiveness, decision-level and task-level resource use, and execution behavior. Experimental results show that Jev integration substantially reduces decision cost and latency across all five agents, with task-level gains varying by workflow. Task success remains close to baseline levels on ALFWorld and declines more substantially in two mobile agents. Auxiliary reasoning and additional interactions absorb decision savings, while failed recovery and premature completion limit successful delivery. Mean cost per successful outcome increases in one agent even as spending per attempt falls. These findings highlight the importance of preserving progress, supporting recovery, and verifying completion when integrating efficient decision models into agent workflows. Their practical value should be assessed through successful task delivery, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered outcome.

title: ReAT: Residual Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Robot Policies
abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.

title: Certified Outage Dimensioning of Fluid Antenna Receivers: Required SNR, Aperture, and Port Count
abstract: We study the SNR, aperture, and port count needed to meet a target outage in a single-user downlink with a fixed transmit antenna and a single-RF fluid antenna receiver. For known spatially correlated Rayleigh channels and ideal port selection, a sampling-free residual certificate controls reduced-rank outage error over a continuous SNR interval. Positive Bessel features support large arrays, and bounded importance sampling converts the certificate into simultaneous design intervals. At 1 bit/s/Hz and outage $10^{-5}$, a four-wavelength, ten-port receiver requires 4.40--4.55 dB. Reducing its port count from 256 to ten costs 0.70--1.25 dB under a joint 95\% probability statement. At 3.5 wavelengths, ten ports require 4.90--5.05 dB. Integer-port screening across 3--8 dB shows how aperture and port requirements change with available SNR; an effective-SNR transformation extends these decisions to other rates. The reported intervals include model and sampling uncertainty under checked Gaussian covariance inputs. A constructive slow-growth rank bound and a 16--1024-port study support compact evaluation as port count grows.

title: Stochastic Finite-Transition Learning and Exploration for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
abstract: Generative MRI reconstruction maps an initial source distribution to the target image distribution along a learned recovery trajectory. Common generative methods, such as diffusion and flow, typically learn fine-grained local dynamics whose integration defines this global mapping, hence requiring many network evaluations at inference. Existing few-step sampling approaches can lower computational burden by approximating large transformations from local dynamics, albeit at the expense of reconstruction fidelity. FLEX-MRI instead partitions recovery into a small number of finite intervals between retained states defined by progressive changes in k-space support, and directly learns the reconstruction change across each interval. Because such finite transitions can admit multiple plausible outcomes, FLEX-MRI combines support-relaxed finite-transition learning with stochastic exploration. During training, randomized k-space sampling masks define finite-transition targets with varying support, while the prediction loss remains unrestricted by each individual mask. At inference, FLEX-MRI perturbs a random subset of currently estimated k-space coefficients, allowing the learned predictor to stochastically explore alternative transition paths. Each predicted state is then reconciled with the acquired measurements through data consistency. We theoretically show that this stochastic exploration induces nonzero transition-level variation through the learned recovery map and data consistency without requiring an auxiliary generative sampler. Experiments on multi-coil MRI datasets show that FLEX-MRI outperforms competing methods while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to few-step baselines.

title: Detection and Construction of Small Blocking Sets via Critical Independent Sets and Matching Decomposition
abstract: The small blocking set detection and construction problem asks whether a given connected simple graph contains a nonempty independent set whose cardinality equals the size of its neighborhood and is strictly less than half the number of vertices, and, if so, how to construct such a set. Previous work characterized restless explorability in vertex-permuted temporal graphs using small blocking sets, but left the computational complexity of detecting their existence as an open problem. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for detection and construction. Specifically, we first compute a maximum-cardinality critical independent set and use its difference and cardinality to handle the cases that admit an immediate solution. In the remaining boundary case, where the critical difference is zero and the selected independent set contains exactly half the vertices, we establish a projection theorem using a perfect matching and neighborhood counting: the graph contains a small blocking set if and only if the selected independent set contains a nonempty proper tight subset. We then use matching contraction to translate the tight-subset condition into the absence of arcs leaving a vertex subset in an auxiliary digraph. This yields a strong-connectivity test for the existence of a small blocking set and, when one exists, a construction based on a sink strongly connected component. The result resolves the open complexity question for small blocking set detection and provides an explicit construction algorithm.

title: Observation of a Threshold Enhancement in the $π^0π^0$ Mass Spectrum in $ψ(3686) \rightarrow π^{0}π^{0}J/ψ$ Decays
abstract: Using a data sample of $(2712.4\pm14.4)\times 10^{6}$ $ψ(3686)$ events collected with the BESIII detector, we report a high-precision study of the $π^{0}π^{0}$ mass spectrum from $ψ(3686)\rightarrowπ^{0}π^{0}J/ψ$ decays. The enhancement previously observed near the $ππ$ mass threshold in the $π^+π^-$ channel is confirmed, with a statistical significance exceeding 10$σ$. A fit with a Breit-Wigner function yields a mass of $M = 274.3\pm 2.1_{\rm stat.}\pm0.6_{\rm syst.}~{\rm MeV}/c^2$ and a width of $Γ= 17.1\pm 1.5_{\rm stat.}\pm0.5_{\rm syst.}~{\rm MeV}$, consistent with those from the $π^{+}π^{-}$ channel. By including final-state interactions, we analyze the data using both chiral perturbation theory (ChPT) and QCD multipole expansion (QCDME). While the ChPT model describes the higher-mass region above 0.3 GeV/$c^2$ well, it fails to reproduce the significant threshold enhancement. In contrast, the QCDME model, which incorporates the $S$- and $D$-wave admixture structure of $ψ(3686)$, provides a better description of the full $π^{0}π^{0}$ mass spectrum.

title: VETR: Execution-Grounded Self-Improving Agent for Symbolic Graphics Reasoning
abstract: Visual agents for symbolic graphics reasoning depend on executable world representations, yet continued improvement remains bottlenecked by ambiguous supervision from final renders. Recent agentic systems refine scenes through repeated interaction, but they lack mechanisms to recursively extract actionable evidence from execution traces, overlooking which proposed symbolic edits survived, disappeared, or interfered during program execution. To address this, we propose VETR (Verified Execution Trajectories for Refinement), a framework that enables agentic recursive self-improvement over executable world representations for symbolic graphics reasoning. Within each task, VETR retains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and introduces an execution refiner that compiles observed writes and state changes into constrained alternative programs. The refiner validates their endpoints and preservation conditions against captured runtime state; the ordinary visual verifier then assesses goal relevance. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls, but can require additional executions. Evaluations on BlenderGym (280 tasks) and BlenderBench (27 released tasks) with GPT-5.6-luna and Qwen3.8-27B show that VETR consistently outperforms existing refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA. Controlled ablations evaluate the contributions of execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction caps.

title: Khintchine dichotomy for images of self-similar measures and almost random walks
abstract: Following the celebrated breakthrough in Bénard-He-Zhang, we prove Khintchine dichotomy for push-forwards of self-similar measures on $\mathbb{R}^d$ under uniform $C^{1+α}$ maps. For this, we also study almost random walks on $\mathrm{SL}(d+1,\mathbb{R})/\mathrm{SL}(d+1,\mathbb{Z})$ and prove their effective equidistribution.

title: Smale's sixth problem for five bodies in the plane, with a proof formalized in Lean
abstract: We prove that for every choice of five positive masses the planar five-body problem has finitely many central configurations up to similarity. This settles Smale's sixth problem for five bodies in the plane. Albouy and Kaloshin proved it for masses outside a closed algebraic subset of codimension two. We follow their method. Infinitely many central configurations would give an algebraic curve of complex solutions. At the places at infinity of the curve the valuations of the mutual distances must balance. We determine the possible valuation vectors at all positive masses, together with the mass conditions under which each can occur. We treat limits in which four bodies form a cluster of zero potential energy by expanding the potential, which is constant along the curve, at a place. This excludes, at every positive mass, one of the two diagrams in which such clusters occur, and part of the other. The same expansion excludes one further diagram at every positive mass. What remains is an exact analysis, by computer algebra, of the sets of mass conditions that can hold together at positive masses. Exact rational certificates show that the balance fails under each of them, except on a few one-parameter families of masses, which we treat separately. On the rays through $(1,4,4,4,4)$ and $(1,1,4,4,4)$ the certificates do not apply. On the first ray they cannot apply: there the complex equations have a continuum of solutions, as Albouy and Kaloshin observed. On these rays we count the real central configurations: there are 306 and 294 up to orientation-preserving similarity. The certificates, the programs that check them and a proof of the theorem in the Lean proof assistant are available.

title: Determination of $U$-spin breaking parameters with an amplitude analysis of the decay $D^{0}\to K_{\text{S},\text{L}}^{0}π^{+}π^{-}$
abstract: We perform a simultaneous amplitude analysis of the decays $D^0 \to K_{\text{S}}^{0}π^{+}π^{-}$ and $D^0 \to K_{\text{L}}^{0}π^{+}π^{-}$ using an $e^+e^-$ collision data sample, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $20.3\,\text{fb}^{-1}$, collected at the centre-of-mass energy of $3.773\,\text{GeV}$ with the BESIII detector. This study, based on a significantly larger dataset than that used in previous work, presents an updated measurement of the complex $U$-spin breaking parameters ($\hatρ$) associated with various $CP$ eigenstate resonant modes mediating the three-body decays. The magnitudes of the $\hatρ$ parameters range from $0.62$ to $4.45$, indicating substantial $U$-spin symmetry breaking. We also report the resonant fit fraction and obtain a model prediction for the average strong-phase parameters over regions of phase space for both decay modes.

title: From 2.1M Hours of Raw Broadcast Audio to Finnish Speech SSL: Confidence Filtering and Architectural Analysis at Scale
abstract: Broadcast archives offer scale and diversity for self-supervised learning (SSL) but contain substantial noisy, non-speech, and multilingual content. Prior work typically relies on voice activity detection or language identification (LID) to extract speech, ensuring presence rather than quality. Whether and how to filter unlabeled speech by quality for SSL, particularly from noisy broadcasts, remains underexplored. We present a large-scale Finnish SSL study starting from 2.1M hours of unconstrained broadcast audio. We propose automatic speech recognition (ASR) confidence as a proxy for pretraining data quality and show 3-7% relative WER improvements over LID-based filtering despite a smaller training set. We further address the lack of controlled architectural comparisons in speech SSL by evaluating Transformer, Macaron-Net, Conformer, and E-Branchformer at matched parameter budgets. Our models improve upon prior Finnish SSL baselines, particularly at Base scale and out-of-domain.

title: Additive bases and the zero-sum invariant $\mathsf{N}(G)$ for groups $C_p\oplus C_{np}$
abstract: Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, and let $c_0(G)$ be the least integer such that every regular sequence over $G$ of at least this length is an additive basis. Let $\mathsf N(G)$ be the least integer $l$ such that every weak-regular sequence $S$ over $G$ with $|S|\ge l$ has a nonempty zero-sum subsequence $T$ satisfying $\mathsf v_g(T)=\mathsf v_g(S)$ for some $g\mid S$. We obtain a common upper bound for $c_0(C_q\oplus C_{nq})$ for groups of odd order, where $q$ is prime, and prove $\mathsf N(G)\ge r(n_r-1)+1$ when $G=C_{n_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus C_{n_r}$ with $1<n_1\mid\cdots\mid n_r$. If $n\ge1$ and $p\ge3$ is the smallest prime divisor of $np$, we obtain $\mathsf N(C_p\oplus C_{np^2})=2np^2-1$ and give upper bounds for $\mathsf N(C_p\oplus C_{np})$ when $p\nmid n$. We also determine $\mathsf N(C_n)$ for two infinite families of cyclic groups arising in earlier work.

title: Robust Vision-Language Navigation with Awareness of Instruction-Execution Progress
abstract: In Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) tasks involving multi-step instructions as guidance, an agent must associate its observations with the relevant instruction content at each decision point. Most graph-based methods commonly match candidate trajectories with the entire instruction, allowing already executed content to interfere with subsequent decisions. Although instruction-execution progress provides a direct cue for separating executed and pending content, existing progress estimation approaches often rely on explicit progress supervision, sophisticated progress-learning stages, or costly online reasoning with LLMs. In this paper, we propose a robust VLN framework with Awareness of Instruction-Execution Progress (VLN-AIEP), which couples progress estimation with navigation decision-making. VLN-AIEP associates the visited trajectory with the instruction to suppress embeddings corresponding to executed content, and then matches candidate locations with the pending content. This coupling makes correct navigation decisions depend on accurate progress estimation, allowing the progress estimator to learn directly from navigation decision labels without explicit progress annotations. To support progress estimation, we construct a landmark-anchored trajectory representation that encodes the semantic labels and viewpoint-relative geometry of instruction-referred landmarks. These landmarks serve as spatial references for associating the visited trajectory with executed instruction content. Extensive experiments on R2R, RxR, CVDN, and R2R-CE demonstrate that the proposed method achieves favorable performance across multiple metrics.

title: Can Failed Trajectories Reveal Where Agents Go Wrong? Agentic Failure Attribution Without Step-Level Labels
abstract: Failure attribution for LLM agents aims to identify decisive steps responsible for task failure, which is critical for debugging and improving agentic systems. Existing methods rely on costly LLM prompting, step-level error annotations, or verified successful trajectories that lack failure signals for assistance. In this paper, we study failure attribution from step-unlabeled failure trajectories, where each trajectory is known to have failed but its decisive step is unknown. We propose SOAP (Spectral scOring with Attention-guided Propagation), an effective framework requiring neither step-level training labels nor a separate success-only reference set. SOAP first constructs a spectral reference space from LLM representations and assigns each step a base error score according to its projection behavior. Importantly, later steps may exhibit stronger failure signals because they inherit an earlier mistake, causing independent scorers to favor downstream consequences over the decisive error. To address this downstream contamination, SOAP derives soft step dependencies from attention patterns and propagates downstream error evidence toward its likely upstream sources. Extensive experiments show that SOAP consistently improves attribution performance over competitive baselines.

title: Scaling RNA Foundation Models through Iterative Refinement
abstract: Biological function in RNA is encoded across scales, from local sequence motifs to long-range structural dependencies. Conventional RNA foundation models couple parameter capacity and inference depth within a fixed architecture, prescribing a fixed computation graph for each inference. Here we present Eco-RNA, an 80M-parameter RNA foundation model that makes inference depth adjustable through learned iterative refinement. Its shared, input-conditioned Transformer core refines sequence representations through repeated application. The iteration count is selected after training and controls effective depth at fixed model parameters. We train across recurrent depths with masked reconstruction, state regularization, and a one-sided loss that anchors deeper reconstruction to a shallow reference. On the 70-assay RNAGym fitness benchmark, increasing refinement from one to four iterations raises aggregate absolute Spearman correlation from 0.242 to 0.286, with the gain retained through eight iterations. At four iterations, Eco-RNA surpasses the current SOTA Evo 2 40B on all three aggregate fitness metrics despite 500x fewer parameters. Its iteration configurations advance the compute-performance Pareto frontier among the evaluated models. It also outperforms the evaluated baselines in non-coding RNA family classification, RNA secondary-structure prediction, and chemical probing profile prediction. These results establish internal inference computation as an effective scaling dimension for RNA foundation models.

title: Role of composition-tuned disorder on magnetic exchange interactions in NiRuMnGa
abstract: We report the experimental investigation of the quaternary Heusler alloy NiRuMnGa, complemented by first-principles calculations. The energetically favorable crystal structure was identified from first-principles calculations and subsequently used as the structural model for refinement of the powder X-ray diffraction data. The refinement shows good agreement with the experimental pattern and reveals substantial B2-type disorder involving Ni/Ru and Mn/Ga site intermixing. The dc magnetic response exhibits pronounced ZFC--FC irreversibility near $\sim 48$ K, with the irreversibility temperature shifting toward lower temperatures under increasing magnetic field, indicating a field-sensitive glassy state. The isothermal magnetization remains unsaturated up to 7 T, reaching only $\sim 0.4\,μ_{\mathrm{B}}$/f.u., accompanied by pronounced hysteresis, suggesting competing exchange interactions and frustrated magnetic moments. AC susceptibility, together with magnetic relaxation and memory measurements, confirms slow spin dynamics characteristic of a cluster glass state. The lack of a discernible heat-capacity anomaly near the irreversibility temperature further supports the absence of conventional long-range magnetic order. Collectively, these results demonstrate that competition between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions in NiRuMnGa leads to magnetic frustration and stabilizes a cluster glass state.

title: LLM-Assisted Hierarchical Interference Control for Satellite-Terrestrial Integrated Networks
abstract: Time-varying aggregate interference from low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites challenges terrestrial-network (TN) protection, whereas conservative control degrades LEO quality of service (QoS). This letter proposes a hierarchical framework combining geometry-based interference estimation, QoS-constrained power control, adaptive energy detection, large language model (LLM)-assisted candidate ranking, stay-or-switch decisions, and target-band selection, with deterministic verification. The current band is retained only when both spectrum-hole and power-feasibility conditions hold, with periodic reevaluation. Over a 300-s horizon with 0.5-s sampling, the proposed method keeps the aggregate INR from exceeding the $-12.2$~dB threshold and achieves a time-averaged mean LEO-link rate of $320.97$~Mbps with $100\%$ QoS satisfaction. It markedly outperforms power-only and satellite-muting in jointly protecting the TN and preserving LEO QoS.

title: Causality, Redshift, and Matching-Scale Cancellation for Reflective Black-Hole Horizons
abstract: The Boltzmann flux reflectivity used in quantum-horizon models does not by itself define a causal black-hole boundary response. We study two related questions for stationary Schwarzschild scattering. First, a classical Hardy-space condition excludes an exact Boltzmann modulus on the entire positive frequency axis for any nonzero bounded causal reflection amplitude at a fixed matching plane. We construct causal completions that preserve the modulus on any prescribed finite band. Second, we prove a low-frequency outer-phase expansion for a class of completions with fixed profiles and a common Boltzmann slope, including an exact-band completion and a smooth crossover completion. The logarithmic coefficient is common to this class, while the linear constant is an explicit functional of the completion. When the fixed proper-frame cutoff is redshifted to the matching surface and the local temperature is the Tolman redshift of the Hawking temperature, the outer phase cancels the leading logarithmic dependence of the propagation phase on the matching distance. The geometric remainder is quadratic in the proper distance, while a separate dispersive remainder depends on the completion. This is a low-energy comparison of specified response families, not an exact matching invariance or a phase fixed by causality alone. In an axial Schwarzschild example at a fixed matching plane, accounting for the predicted linear-delay difference reduces the maximum relative cavity-factor difference between two cutoffs from about $21\%$ to $0.11\%$ on the sampled frequency band. A passive quantum completion supplies the associated absorption-noise relation and checks the consistency of the asymptotic output.

title: Temporal-Access Resource Theory for Continuous Process Tensors
abstract: The uncontrolled endpoint channel can conceal how well a quantum process can protect a logical task under time-resolved control. We formulate a fixed-task resource theory of continuous process tensors with physical access interfaces, entrance-erasing free objects, and budgeted free conversions. Complete-record total-variation error measures performance; the calibrated capability is monotone under conversions that preserve a common free baseline. For unknown-state transmission the baseline is exactly $1-d^{-2}$. Two qubit processes with the same endpoint channel have optimal errors $0$ and $p=\sin^2(2gh)$ at the same finite pulse budget in an ideal-transparent system-only window architecture, forcing any endpoint-only predictor to err by at least $p/2$ on one of them. An exactly solvable family shows how the allocation of a fixed interaction phase around a control window sets the attainable error, and a nontrivial perfect echo requires and attains total control action $π$ in that architecture. The separation extends directly to every qubit unitary target at a budget that includes its boundary gate, while unitary tasks in any dimension have baseline $1-d^{-2}$ whenever a budget-feasible free realization gives the depolarizing output. Complete-record implementation bounds quantify coherent and dissipative control imperfections. Continuous-process randomized compilation supplies physical instrument pullbacks; compatible completion conditions extend their action, and certified dynamical bounds yield achievable task-error and capability guarantees. The resulting theory identifies temporal structure and control investment that endpoint characterization alone cannot resolve.

title: What Do Visual-Head Discovery Scores Actually Find? Attention Source, Necessity, and Random-Control Pitfalls in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Attention heads that attend to image regions relevant to a question are increasingly used to steer, ground and interpret vision-language models (VLMs) and to reduce their hallucinations. They are mostly found by ranking heads with an attention- pattern score and validated by steering or masking them. We ask how the choices inside such a discovery score shape the heads it returns, and which of the two validations identifies them. On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct we vary the query type, the discovery corpus and the token positions whose attention is read (the attention source) in a full 2 x 3 x 2 design, and test all 12 head-sets for steerability (CERS: Contrastive Evidence-Region Steering score) and necessity (NCS: Necessity Con- trast Score) against layer-matched random head-sets. (1) The attention source and the query type reshape the selected heads far more than the corpus: changing the source keeps a median of 49 of the top-100 heads, the query 55 and the cor- pus 84, while two halves of the same data share 96-99. (2) Necessity follows the attention source: head-sets discovered from query-span attention are more nec- essary than last-token ones (difference 0.083, p=6 x 10^-10), and the two re- ferring + query-span sets lie 17-19 standard deviations above 250 layer-matched random sets (Holm-adjusted p=0.048). The referring + query-span effect re- plicates on several recent VLMs. (3) Steerability is not specific to the discovered heads: no discovered head-set steers better than its layer-matched random sets (rank p >= 0.14), and random sets drawn from the same or from any layer span the discovered sets' scores. Necessity therefore separates the discovery settings, while steering at this strength does not. We turn these findings into a protocol for reporting visual-head discoveries.

title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all-zero "blank" waveform, flagged by prior review as out-of-distribution. We introduce a black-box causal test that isolates the claimed evidence itself: localize a claim's evidence region via CLAP similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random-window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B, localized ablation's raw AUROC trails blank's (0.613 vs. 0.721); this is a duration confound, not a localization failure, since blank removes the entire clip versus the grid's 2-4 s. Holding duration fixed, localization beats random removal at every cell on both models. Raw detection value remains model-dependent, especially on Audio Flamingo 3. The same evidence corrects decoding: contrastive decoding combining blank and language-prior contrasts, gated and ensembled, raises Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, beating AAD alone. A unified causal-grounding profile does not transfer between models, indicating different grounding regimes. The source code and a detailed report of our findings, including identified limitations, are available at https://github.com/khalooei/causa.

title: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation
abstract: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.

title: Degree Adjacency Diametrical Matrix of Graphs Spectral Properties and Energy Bounds
abstract: Graph matrices that combine structural and metric information have attracted considerable attention in spectral graph theory. In this paper, we introduce the \emph{Degree--Adjacency--Diametrical (DAD) matrix} of a connected graph $G$. The DAD matrix is defined by \[ (DAD(G))_{ij}= \begin{cases} d(v_i), & \text{if } i=j, 1, & \text{if } v_i\sim v_j, \operatorname{diam}(G), & \text{if } d(v_i,v_j)=\operatorname{diam}(G), 0, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases} \] where $d(v_i)$ denotes the degree of the vertex $v_i$. We establish fundamental spectral properties of the DAD matrix by deriving trace identities, characteristic polynomials, and spectra for several classes of graphs. Furthermore, we obtain a spectral expression for the Wiener index of graphs with diameter two, derive upper bounds for the largest DAD eigenvalue, and establish lower bounds for the DAD energy. Explicit spectral characterizations are also obtained for complete multipartite graphs. The proposed matrix provides a unified spectral framework that simultaneously incorporates degree, adjacency, and diametrical information, thereby enriching the study of graph spectra and introducing a new graph matrix for spectral graph theory.

title: Assessing quantitative phase reliability in electron ptychography using a twisted trilayer WS2 thickness staircase
abstract: The phase of an electron wave is sensitive to the local electrostatic environment and can therefore provide information about atomic-scale structural variations. In electron ptychography, however, specimen thickness, multiple scattering and projected atomic overlap can complicate the quantitative interpretation of the reconstructed phase. Here, we use a twisted trilayer WS2 thickness staircase containing monolayer, bilayer and trilayer regions as an internal reference, with all regions measured under identical experimental conditions. The mean W-column phase increases by approximately 13.2% from the monolayer to the bilayer region, compared with only 4.7% from the bilayer to the trilayer region, revealing a nonlinear thickness dependence. W-S overlap has little effect on the W-column phase, whereas short-range projected W-W overlap increases it by approximately 8-9%. These results provide a benchmark for evaluating quantitative phase measurement in multilayer WS2 and for assessing phase-based mapping of local electrostatic potential, charge-density and three-dimensional atomic-scale polarization.

title: DRYLAB-Bench: Benchmarking the Biosecurity Risk of Agentic LLM Mutation Design
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) acquire advanced biological design capabilities, they offer substantial research benefits but simultaneously introduce severe dual-use risks, such as engineering enhanced pathogens or drug-resistant bacteria. While biosecurity frameworks recognize these threats, the actual risk of LLMs executing dangerous biological modifications remains unquantified, particularly when augmented with specialized biological design tools (BDTs). Existing evaluations primarily assess hazardous knowledge possession rather than practical application, overlook risk amplification from BDTs, and rely on unreliable, expensive, or hazardous validation methods. To address these gaps, we introduce DRYLAB-Bench (Design Risk Yielded by LLM Agent in Biodesign), the first comprehensive benchmark evaluating the high-risk biological mutation design capabilities of LLM agents. Moving beyond basic question-answering, DRYLAB-Bench tasks agents with 30 genuinely hazardous mutation-design scenarios distilled from biosecurity guidelines. It evaluates models in a multi-round, tool-augmented environment where LLMs orchestrate BDTs to iteratively refine candidates. Crucially, it scores designs directly against 187,695 empirical wet-lab measurements from ProteinGym and ViroGym using our proposed Biosecurity Risk Score (BRS), quantifying risk-associated effects while enabling scalable and safe ground-truth verification. Evaluations of 15 frontier models reveal substantial baseline threats: without tools, 67.6% of one-shot designs exceed the average measured variant, and 21.4% reach the highest-risk decile. Equipping models with BDTs significantly amplifies this risk, raising the pooled risk by \(ΔBRS=+0.116\) and the top-decile share to 23.5%. Code: https://github.com/drylab-bio/DRYLAB-Bench

title: Forward Dynamics Models
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively. Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions. We present Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world-state prediction through an action-to-future paradigm. Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end-to-end training lets ground-truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions. At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost. The paradigm is backbone-agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.

title: The value of information and the emergence of communication in evolved e-puck robots
abstract: We study when communication emerges between autonomous agents and what role an innate action selection architecture plays. Two e-puck robots, reconstructed in PyBullet from their Webots model and validated against it, must find a feeding zone that can only be detected when a robot passes over it. Each robot can emit a one-bit signal whose direction is detected by the receiver. Control is provided by a GRU recurrent network with a residual path, either operating alone or as a channel within an Embedded Action Selection Architecture (EASA). Fitness measures only the time the robots spend over the food. When the robots receive a compass pointing to the food, use of the signal disappears completely. Without a compass, in a small arena, three independent runs achieved similar performance using different strategies: a referential signal, a permanent beacon, or no use of the signal. As the arena expands, the strategy based on a referential signal generalizes best. In contrast, evolving directly in the large arena does not increase the frequency of communication, but it does separate the strategies, and the referential signal clearly outperforms solitary searching. Within EASA, innate reflexes constrain the network and reduce performance. As its priorities evolve, evolution consistently weakens those reflexes. The results suggest that communication emerges in proportion to the value of the information it transmits, and that an innate scaffolding designed for isolated agents can be an impediment in a social task.

title: Human2Dex: Dexterous Robot Learning from Wrist-Centric Human Demonstrations
abstract: Collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations for each robot hand requires repeated task-specific data acquisition. We ask whether one shared corpus of natural human demonstrations can instead serve as a reusable data interface for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot. We present Human2Dex, a wrist-centric human demonstration interface that separates shared human observation and motion semantics from embodiment-specific execution. It aligns observations through local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation with consistent structural semantics across human and robot observations. It constructs executable supervision by retargeting fused human hand motion to each target hand, and introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation (GPIR) to express tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket. The corpus is converted into separate training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, while action labels, normalization, training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain hand-specific. Across six real-world tasks, Human2Dex achieves 109/120 (90.8%) successes on Linker O6 and 97/120 (80.8%) on Wuji. Across both hands, Human-Raw achieves 63/240 (26.3%) successes, whereas the complete Human2Dex configuration achieves 206/240 (85.8%). These results support the use of wrist-centric human demonstrations as a reusable interface across calibrated dexterous hands while retaining embodiment-specific policy learning. The project website is publicly available at https://human2dex.pages.dev/.

title: Replaying the Movie in Your Mind Decoding Dynamic Visual Perception and Recall from EEG
abstract: Decoding dynamic visual content from EEG has advanced rapidly for visual perception, yet it remains unclear which aspects of neural representations are preserved when people internally replay dynamic scenes. We introduce PAIR, an EEG benchmark collected from 20 participants using an interleaved, clip-wise paradigm that pairs naturalistic video viewing with immediate visual recall. This design enables a comparison between externally driven perception and internally generated recall for the same stimulus content within a fixed trial sequence.
