Across image, point-cloud, molecular, and action generation, PFM improves generation quality and provides endpoint-posterior readouts throughout generation.

title: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games
abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement learning with CRAB, an advantage estimator that credits each decision against a shrinkage estimate of the expected return of its position and is defined on every variant. On Qwen3-4B-Base, distillation raises the 13-benchmark mean pass@1 from 45.5 to 62.5, above the three SPIRAL games at the same budget, and self-play with CRAB reaches 64.9. The ordering holds across models, and transfer grows with the number of game families.

title: Splicing Hints into Reasoning Traces: Learning from Demonstrator Failures
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves mathematical reasoning when a final answer can be checked, but a correct answer does not certify the derivation behind it, and proof problems offer no answer to check. Replacing the check with a reasoning model as an in-loop verifier faces a fundamental obstacle: the policy must already produce occasional correct attempts for any reward to exist, which it may never do at olympiad level. We instead move verification and repair out of the training loop and into offline data generation with SPLICE, a workflow in which a second model, given only a reference solution, edits a reasoning model's traces as they are generated: it verifies progress, truncates a failed trace at its last verified step, and splices in an adaptively strengthened hint until progress resumes. The resulting dataset includes repaired examples whose sampled unaided trajectory failed, with failed continuations removed and progress repeatedly checked against the reference solution. A model finetuned on SPLICE traces outperforms the same model distilled from the reasoning model's unedited traces on AIME and, under a grading protocol validated against human grades, on olympiad proofs. The trained model's own traces show a corresponding behavioral signature: at difficult points it announces a branch in the style of the spliced hints and takes riskier steps, with predictive entropy rising there and just after, a pattern absent from the model trained on unedited traces.

title: SharedSAE: a unified sparse dictionary across u-net blocks and denoising time for diffusion models
abstract: Concept representations in diffusion models drift across network depth and denoising time, yet existing sparse autoencoders offer only per-block or per-timestep dictionaries, leaving no single feature dictionary for localization and intervention in the network. We present Shared Sparse Autoencoder (SharedSAE), which learns one sparse dictionary shared across four U-Net attention blocks and all 50 denoising steps of SDXL 1.0. A block-specific low-rank input adapter aligns the residual distribution of each block before the shared encoder, and a temporal conditioning module with a shared timestep branch and a block-timestep correction branch absorbs temporal non-stationarity. Despite spanning both axes, Shared SAE preserves a coherent dictionary structure. Built on the shared dictionary, localized feature suppression reduces the number of NudeNet-positive generations in the I2P detector-positive subset from 139 to 1. Tracing sparse features across the trajectory further reveals that concept representations are redistributed across U-Net blocks during generation, shifting from the earliest downsampling block toward intermediate and later blocks as denoising proceeds. SharedSAE thus provides a unified, interpretable, and intervention-ready representation space for diffusion models, enabling concept analysis and erasure at any covered block and denoising step.

title: Enhanced Trading Systems with Intelligent Market Analysis
abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid reinforcement learning trading framework integrating intraday market data with transformer-based financial sentiment signals. The system extracts sentiment dynamics and semantic event clusters from financial news and incorporates them into a PPO-based trading agent. Experiments on intraday NSE data demonstrate improved risk-adjusted returns compared to price-only baselines.

title: SemTree: Judge-Aware Semantic Decision Trees for Inspectable and Repairable Rule Decisions
abstract: Rule decisions such as content moderation, advertising compliance, and eligibility checks combine several conditions, exemptions, and missing-information cases, and an error can be fixed only once the failing condition is known. We introduce SemTree, a framework that represents a rule decision as a semantic decision tree: each node is a natural-language question with explicit Yes/No/Unknown criteria, a pluggable semantic judge answers it, and the branching structure is compiled on the answers that this judge actually gives. The executed path is the reasoning behind every decision, so errors are repaired where they occur: a reviewer corrects a single node and replays the rule, corrected nodes become training labels for the judge, and a tool-using LLM editor revises questions and subtrees while observing execution results. On all 8,276 ShARC test cases, a tree executed by a hosted judge reaches 67.70% accuracy with 2.99 questions per case, on par with asking the same judge for the final label (68.23%); an earlier tree compiled for a different judge scores 47.87% when executed by this judge, while a new tree compiled on this judge's answers to a 12-question initial pool already scores 64.39%. Node-level repair raises BANKING77 accuracy from 82.04% to 86.16%, an explicit exemption node cuts the false positives of a Chinese e-commerce moderation clause from 24 to 5, and a trained editor raises the development accuracy of edited trees from 64.47% to 73.35%.

title: VH-GPO: Verified Handoff for LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Group-relative reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO train large language model (LLM) agents by comparing rollouts for the same task. When every trajectory in a group fails with the same reward, relative advantages collapse toward zero, leaving no useful learning signal. A frozen teacher can recover from a student-visited state, but letting it complete the task makes the recovered suffix entirely teacher-generated. We ask: after repairing a student failure, when should control return to the student? We propose outcome-verified teacher-student handoff, instantiated in Verified Handoff for Group Policy Optimization (VH-GPO). The teacher provides enough support to reach a state from which the student can succeed, then returns control so that successful experience is again student-generated. Given an environment-verified teacher recovery, VH-GPO selects the earliest independently confirmed handoff point found within a bounded search budget. With Qwen2.5-1.5B, VH-GPO increases success rates over GRPO from 59.38% to 94.79% on ALFWorld and from 71.62% to 77.34% on WebShop. Improvements also hold with the 7B student, for which additional teacher and student output tokens amount to 1.77% and 2.61% of regular student rollout output tokens on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the key components. These results support using verified teacher assistance to repair failures while reinforcing the student's ability to complete tasks independently.

title: PreSO: Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses a self-teacher conditioned on privileged information to turn the sparse outcome signal of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) into dense token-level supervision. Yet the teacher's advantage may depend on information unavailable to the student at inference, raising a central question: which privileged changes are worth distilling? We use cross-problem recurrence as an empirical cue for potentially reusable guidance. Comparing the representation shifts induced by full solutions and compact hints, we find that hint-induced shifts are more concentrated and directionally consistent across problems, and yield more sustained downstream gains despite revealing less information. Motivated by this association, we propose Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation (PreSO). At the source, PreSO uses compact hints to limit the solution-specific detail entering the privileged shift. At the target, it estimates a leading low-rank subspace from shifts pooled across related problems, projects the privilege-induced correction onto this subspace, and adds it to the student's unprivileged representation to form the representation-level distillation target. The selected subspace serves as an operational proxy for recurring structure, rather than a guaranteed separation of transferable and instance-specific information. On five competition-level mathematics benchmarks, PreSO consistently outperforms strong baselines across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B, improving average accuracy over the base model by 6.8, 9.0, and 10.0 points. Beyond peak accuracy, PreSO attains the highest final-checkpoint average at every model scale, with improvements that persist through the end of training.

title: Upper Bounds on the Comon Rank Gap of Real Symmetric Third-Order Tensors
abstract: Let $T$ be a nonzero real symmetric third-order tensor. Denote by $r(T)$ its CP rank, by $s(T)$ its symmetric rank, by $d(T)$ its essential dimension, and put $e(T)=r(T)-d(T)$. We establish two complementary upper bounds for the Comon rank gap $$Δ(T):= s(T)-r(T)\leq\min\{C_{ec}(e(T)),\ C_{dc}(d(T))\}.$$ The excess-controlled function $C_{ec}(e)$ is zero for $0\leq e\leq3$ and equals $9e-3$ for $e\geq4$. In particular, the equality $C_{ec}(e(T))=0$ for $0\leq e\leq3$ extends Friedland's flattening-rank criterion for real symmetric third-order tensors by two additional rank layers. The dimension-controlled function $C_{dc}(d)$ is zero for $d=0$, equals $(d^2-4d+10)/3$ for $1\leq d\leq18$, and equals $d^2/4+d/4+3/2$ for $d\geq19$. The excess estimate follows from the alternating equations and decomposable-bivector support geometry; a low-wedge descent gives the vanishing range $e\leq3$. The dimension estimate combines a transverse polar-completion bound with a shifted estimate for the maximum real Waring rank. Thus the two bounds measure different features of the same tensor and remain effective in complementary regimes.

title: Multiplicity-One Structure in Graded Zero-Divisor Graphs
abstract: Let \(H\) be a multiplicative group, \(R\) a commutative \(H\)-graded ring, and \(M\) a nonzero finitely generated gr-semisimple \(H\)-graded \(R\)-module. We assume that \(M\) admits a fixed decomposition into powers of gr-simple modules with pairwise distinct annihilators, each repeated block carrying the componentwise grading. For a nonzero homogeneous element \(x\), we compute the colon ideal \((Rx:M)\) and show that it is determined by the multiplicity-one blocks on which \(x\) has a nonzero component. This leads to the criterion \( x\leftrightarrow y \text{ if and only if } σ(x)\capσ(y)=\varnothing, \) where \(x\leftrightarrow y\) means that \(x\) and \(y\) are adjacent in \(Γ_H(M)\). Thus adjacency is governed by disjointness of multiplicity-one obstruction supports. The corresponding obstruction classes form a weighted disjointness structure: higher multiplicities affect the sizes of the classes, but not the adjacency relation between their supports. We use this description to study graph invariants, reconstruction, and Kneser-type layers, and, in the finite case, to obtain formulas for the obstruction-class sizes and a reduction of the adjacency spectrum.

title: Showing versus Doing: Teaching by Demonstration
abstract: People often learn from others' demonstrations, and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) techniques have realized this capacity in machines. In contrast, teaching by demonstration has been less well studied computationally. Here, we develop a Bayesian model for teaching by demonstration. Stark differences arise when demonstrators are intentionally teaching (i.e. showing) a task versus simply performing (i.e. doing) a task. In two experiments, we show that human participants modify their teaching behavior consistent with the predictions of our model. Further, we show that even standard IRL algorithms benefit when learning from showing versus doing.

title: Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
abstract: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

title: Coding LLMs Can Be Harnessed to Learn Interpretable Models from Data
abstract: Since compact, interpretable classifiers correspond to simple programs, it is natural to ask if LLM-based coding agents can be used to learn interpretable models from data. In this paper we present a simple harness that repeatedly prompts a coding LLM to produce the next rule in a rule set, given a sample of labeled examples. We show that this approach is competitive with, and often superior to, state-of-the-art rule-learning methods on tabular data, especially with small training sets, and wins by large margins on text, including against another LLM-based rule learner; that this approach outperforms standard harnesses, and that the approach immediately leads to new kinds of interpretable models, since coding agents are not restricted to search a highly restricted hypothesis space. In addition to the advances made in learning interpretable models, these results are of interest because they introduce a new class of coding benchmarks - construction of interpretable classifiers - which includes quantitative measurements of output quality (i.e., test-set error) and existing mature ``specialist coding algorithms'' (i.e., existing learning methods).

title: What Can Language Models Inherit from Solomonoff Induction? Limits, Attainable Properties, and What Served Conditionals Reveal
abstract: A familiar line of reasoning runs as follows: language models are flexible approximators trained under a strictly proper loss, so scale brings them closer to Solomonoff induction, and their predictive success is evidence of that approach. We apply known results from algorithmic information theory, universal prediction and Bayesian consistency. In its uniform form the conclusion holds for no computable model: each has cheap environments it never learns, and every uniformly computable family of total predictors shares one on which each member fails beyond a horizon growing with its index, so ``closer'' can hold only pointwise, one environment at a time. Nor could the offered routes certify even that: finite evaluation cannot certify agreement on rarely reached contexts, perfect corpus fit selects the corpus law as prior, and asymptotic criteria cannot see the constants that carry Solomonoff's guarantee. Our lens is the Kraft inequality read for predictors. Every model has at most the same budget of predictive success, so Solomonoff's predictor, which leaves part of it unspent, differs from a language model not in having more of it but in where it spends it; on mutually singular families this is exact, and only full-mass Bayes mixtures reach the frontier. We then discuss what is inheritable, including in-context learning as amortised Bayesian inference; what survives within a context window; which Solomonoff-like properties a deployed system should have or avoid; and what served conditionals determine. A closing table states what common practices certify and what to report. Tests are developed in a companion paper.

title: Generalized PINN-Based Inverse Estimation of Spatially Varying Heat Transfer Coefficients with Transfer Learning
abstract: This study investigates generalized boundary representations and transfer learning for physics-informed neural-network (PINN) estimation of spatially varying convective heat transfer coefficients (HTCs) in jet impingement cooling. Piecewise-linear (PWL) and neural-network boundary estimators are inferred from transient interior-temperature measurements and evaluated against CFD-CHT reference HTC profiles at Reynolds numbers of 5000, 10000 and 15000. A discrete Adjoint-FEM formulation with gradient regularization based on the $H^1$-seminorm provides an independent inverse-method comparison. Transfer learning is investigated under two source-target conditions: transfer between noise levels at the same Reynolds number, and transfer from a controlled Gaussian-profile problem to CFD-CHT-derived target problems at different Reynolds numbers. For the representative Re = 5000 target with 5% measurement noise, quadratic, PWL, and neural-network PINNs achieve relative HTC-profile errors of 5.08, 5.31 and 5.19%, respectively, while generalized representations reduce the error for the Re = 15000 target from 16.76% for the quadratic PINN to 14.41% and 14.46%. Transfer learning reduces target-training time by 57.86-81.71% for fixed-Reynolds-number transfer and by 50.59-84.94% for Gaussian-to-CHT transfer. Its effect on reconstruction accuracy is target dependent: fixed-profile PWL transfer remains within 0.30 percentage points of scratch training, whereas Gaussian-to-CHT transfer produces differences of 0.10-1.52 percentage points across targets and representations. These results demonstrate that generalized PINN representations can accommodate spatially varying HTC profiles without a prescribed quadratic form, while transfer learning can substantially reduce target-training cost for repeated inverse estimation, with the resulting reconstruction accuracy depending on source-target compatibility.

title: When Log Parsing Removes What Matters: Detecting Failures in Distributed GPU Workloads
abstract: Large AI models increasingly rely on distributed GPU execution, yet it remains unclear whether established failure analysis methods transfer effectively to this setting. We introduce GF-Bench, a PyTorch-based framework and dataset for generating diverse failures in distributed GPU workloads. The framework supports extensible workload and fault-injection logic; based on this design, the current release targets failures visible in multi-GPU communication logs and provides 220 labeled two-GPU executions covering normal runs, CUDA out-of-memory fail-stop failures, and persistent straggler fail-slow failures. Using GF-Bench, we evaluate three sequence-based methods (DeepLog, LogAnomaly, and LogBERT) and the LLM-based LogPrompt on parsed logs, and additionally evaluate LogPrompt on raw logs. On parsed inputs, no method reliably detects both failure classes, and the highest overall F1 score is 0.667. Raw inputs raise the overall F1 score of in-context LogPrompt to 0.983, at 9.0x its average input-token usage and 8.7x its per-run cost. These results expose a substantial trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency: generic log parsing lowers operational cost but discards the distributed execution context required for accurate failure detection. GF-Bench provides a reproducible basis for studying cost-efficient analysis methods and can be extended to additional GPU workloads and failure types.

title: The geometric classification of Novikov-Poisson and Gelfand-Dorfman algebras
abstract: We give the geometric classification of complex 3-dimensional Novikov-Poisson and Gelfand-Dorfman algebras. In particular, we prove that the variety of complex 3-dimensional Novikov-Poisson algebras is 12-dimensional; it has 4 irreducible components and has no rigid algebras; the variety of complex 3-dimensional Gelfand-Dorfman algebras is 11-dimensional; it has 10 irreducible components and has 3 rigid algebras. As an additional result, we have the geometric classification of complex 3-dimensional Novikov algebras: it is 9-dimensional, and it has $4$ irreducible components with one rigid algebra.

title: SIRNET: Causal Adaptation of Pretrained Embeddings for Semiparametric Treatment-Effect Estimation Under Surrogacy
abstract: Modern experiments increasingly produce rich post-treatment objects---such as text, images, and video---that may provide early surrogate signals for outcomes that are delayed, expensive, or observed only for a subset of participants. A pretrained encoder can turn such an object into a strong generic embedding, but the embedding is not trained for the estimation tasks required by a causal estimator and may emphasize information irrelevant to the causal target. We propose SIRNET, a Surrogate-Informed Representation adaptation framework for neural-NETwork-based causal estimation in the presence of unstructured post-treatment surrogates. Starting from pretrained surrogate embeddings, SIRNET learns a shared adapter jointly for outcome prediction, treatment propensity, and arm-specific surrogate marginalization, beyond the generic pretraining objective. The resulting covariate and surrogate representations provide a common interface for these nuisance tasks. The final treatment-effect estimate and confidence interval are obtained from cross-fitted orthogonal scores that attain the semiparametric efficiency bound under the stated nuisance-rate conditions. We also validate SIRNET's performance in synthetic and semisynthetic experiments, as well as the Anti-Amyloid in Asymptomatic Alzheimer's Disease (A4) trial, using frozen pretrained brain-MRI embeddings as surrogates for a long-term outcome.

title: Perfect Reconstruction Cannot Show Whether Two Codebooks on a VAE's Latent Space Agree
abstract: Many systems read the latent space of a variational autoencoder (VAE) as discrete codes, and rely on each latent being read back as the code it was written as. Shannon (1948) took such a shared codebook as given; inside a VAE nothing enforces it. We prove that no item of a standard training report can reveal whether the written and read codes agree on encoded data. We construct two VAEs that reconstruct every input perfectly, infer exactly, and match on every per-example ELBO and every code histogram, yet agreement is one in the first and zero in the second. We then show that the ELBO's own terms bound how far a measured agreement can move: the variational gap bounds the shift to exact inference, and the rate bounds the shift to generation from the prior. For Gaussian posteriors, a mean-field encoder pays an exact price in the gap that depends on its choice of axes. On probabilistic PCA the gap certifies a trained encoder in all 75 settings we test, at agreement between 0.76 and 0.97. On 240 trained VAEs, a floor set by the rate and the dataset size rules out rate-side certification in advance for 66 models, and none of them certifies. The results yield a simple protocol, Certify-or-Measure, for any pipeline that reads a VAE as codes.

title: Disease-level drug approval forecasting from trial-agnostic public data
abstract: Drug development is an expensive and lengthy process requiring developers to select drugs for human trials and diseases to target. Computational tools that can estimate before testing which drug-disease candidates are most likely to reach FDA approval could reduce development time and costs through early program advancement and disease prioritization. Yet existing approaches predict outcomes at a single level or stage or do not distinguish between disease outcomes for the same drug. We ask (1) whether FDA approval can be forecast for a drug-disease pair using only pre-clinical trial information, and (2) whether these forecasts can help prioritize diseases for the same drug. We built a cohort of 14,134 drug-disease pairs by reconstructing programs from ClinicalTrials.gov, extracting disease-level approvals from FDA label documentation, and enriching each pair with molecular, disease, ADMET, target, and pathway features. We divided the cohort into pre- and post-2019 programs and trained a classifier on pre-2019 data to predict FDA approval. On the post-2019 cohort (2,637 programs), the model would have prioritized a program that ultimately gained approval over one that did not approximately three out of four times. For drugs tested across multiple diseases, selecting the model's highest-ranked disease would have identified an ultimately approved disease 61.3% of the time, compared with 40.7% under random selection. These results show that public pre-trial information contains signal for forecasting FDA approval at the drug-disease level and can help prioritize diseases for the same drug. We provide a public web tool for SMILES- and ICD-10-based drug-disease approval forecasting.

title: Physics-Informed State Space Models for Day-Ahead Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
abstract: Accurate day-ahead photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting requires both strong temporal modeling and adherence to physical PV system constraints. Purely data-driven models often ignore the underlying PV conversion process and may produce predictions that are outside the operational range of a PV system. In this paper, we propose a physics-informed state space framework that combines a differentiable PV conversion model with a selective state space backbone (PowerMamba). Our approach follows a physics-residual decomposition. The physics module provides a structured baseline based on solar geometry, irradiance, temperature effects, and inverter limits, while the state space model learns residual corrections from numerical weather prediction (NWP) inputs over a 24-hour horizon. Experiments on one year of utility-scale PV data show that the proposed method significantly improves forecasting accuracy, reducing RMSE by 38.5% and MAE by 45.8% compared to a physics-only baseline, and outperforming a purely data-driven model. Results further show that incorporating system-level physics provides the largest performance gains, while additional refinements offer only marginal improvements. Beyond accuracy, the model improves robustness by constraining predictions toward physical feasibility, reducing unrealistic predictions under corrupted measurements.

title: Bias Robustness of Genetic Multi-Criteria Sorting versus Learned Rankers under Proxy Skew and Label Contamination
abstract: Learning-to-rank (LTR) models can align rankings with undesignated signals when those signals appear as features or leak into training labels. We compare label-free genetic multi-criteria sorting (open Pikaia strategy variants), which reranks fixed candidate pools using an explicit criteria vector C, to label-trained LTR (LightGBM, XGBoost, RankSVM) under two controlled protocols on MSLR-WEB10K, Baidu-ULTR, WANDS, and Expedia. In the main proxy-skew study, labels remain clean while a calibrated proxy P is available as a feature: Genetic AI rankings show lower Spearman rank-proxy correlation than the LTR peers (e.g. about 0.15-0.16 vs. 0.59-0.87 on WANDS), with both families evaluated jointly on clean nDCG@10 on a bias-utility frontier. In a supporting label-contamination study, training labels are mixed with contaminant B: because Genetic AI methods do not use labels, their bias and utility curves stay flat, whereas LightGBM and XGBoost increase rank-B correlation as contamination rises (OLS bias_slope about 0.58-0.65 on WANDS/Baidu). The results support genetic sorting as an architectural option for optimizing declared attributes on a fixed pool when undesignated proxies or label contaminants must be refused.

title: DShuttleNet: A Badminton Doubles Dataset for Evaluating Team Coordination
abstract: Most existing sports datasets are individual-centric or ball-centric, focusing on individual player actions while ignoring interactions among teammates. In badminton doubles, tactical success is governed by rapid team formation and coordination, yet standard resources for modeling these player interactions are scarce. To bridge this gap, we present DShuttleNet, a comprehensive dataset for badminton doubles curated from elite BWF World Tour tournaments. Beyond trajectory data, DShuttleNet uniquely incorporates expert-labeled "Loss Reasons," transforming the dataset into a diagnostic tool for causal tactical evaluation. We formally define two geometry-driven representations, Teammate-Relative Angle (TRA) and Vertical Shot Angle (VSA), to characterize coordination and shot aggressiveness. To quantify interpersonal synergy, we introduce novel metrics, Court Coverage Efficacy Index (CCEI) and Threat Load Asymmetry Index (TLAI), which evaluate the often-overlooked non-hitting partner's role and defensive coordination. Experimental results demonstrate that conventional models suffer from underfitting when failing to incorporate these coordination-centric features, highlighting the critical importance and potential impact of releasing DShuttleNet. Dataset is available at: https://doi.org/10.34740/kaggle/dsv/16097938.

title: Barycentric Anchored Weight Search for Robust Model Merging
abstract: We propose Barycentric Anchored Search, a post-hoc weight-space procedure for improving fine-tuned vision models under distribution shift without additional gradient training or increased inference cost. Given a pre-trained initialization and two checkpoints fine-tuned on a source dataset, the method constructs barycentric candidate weights and performs a small derivative-free search along directions connecting each candidate to the pre-trained model. Candidate weights are selected using a small validation subset of one or more out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets; the selected model is then evaluated on the held-out portions of those datasets, on additional OOD benchmarks, and on the ImageNet validation set to quantify the robustness-accuracy trade-off. The method is inspired by simplex-based derivative-free optimization, including Nelder-Mead and Torczon multidirectional search, but is specialized to the geometry of neural network weight merging. Unlike Model Soup, which typically benefits from many fine-tuned checkpoints, and unlike Model Stock, which applies a fixed geometric merge, our approach uses only two fine-tuned checkpoints and iteratively adapts the merge using validation feedback from OOD data. Experiments with CLIP ViT-B/32 show that the proposed search substantially improves performance on held-out OOD data, including ImageNet-A, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-Sketch, while keeping ImageNet accuracy competitive. The resulting weights also improve transfer to OOD datasets not used during candidate selection, outperforming the original fine-tuned checkpoints, naive model soups, and Model Stock in our evaluations. These results suggest that lightweight optimization in anchored weight space provides a practical alternative to fixed weight-averaging rules, geometric merging, or single-model selection.

title: RoboHarness: A Simple Harness Outperforms VLA and World Action Models
abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has opened a path toward generalist embodied AI, raising the question of how LLMs can act in the physical world. One straightforward approach is training the model to generate actions: collect robot-action data and video demonstration, refine LLM architecture with an action head, and train a vision-language-action (VLA) model at scale. However, we argue that coding agents have the potential to realize generalist embodied manipulation. All they need is a simple yet effective robot harness. We present RoboHarness: a robotic harness that gives LLM agents a visual-geometric control panel so that they can directly understand and invoke embodied tasks. With RoboHarness, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks. The implementation is open source.

title: Argos: A Multi-Tenant SaaS Architecture for Distributed Edge Security Orchestration
abstract: The growing adoption of distributed edge devices for security auditing and operational monitoring exposes limitations in lightweight control mechanisms traditionally used to manage such nodes. While commercial Command-and-Control (C2) platforms offer advanced orchestration features, their licensing constraints, operational complexity, and proprietary nature limit accessibility for small and medium-sized enterprises and research environments. This paper presents Argos, a multi-tenant SaaS C2 architecture designed for transparent, automated, and long-term orchestration of distributed edge devices. The framework implements a structured control plane with role-based access control (RBAC), tenant isolation, persistent task management, and cron-based workflow automation. Unlike operator-driven or stateless execution models, Argos enables scheduled and autonomous coordination of security tasks across heterogeneous environments. To formally substantiate its isolation guarantees, the platform is modeled through a set-theoretic authorization framework, and a tenant non-interference property is proven. The proposed architecture was evaluated across three geographically distributed edge devices, executing 810 automated tasks mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Results demonstrate a global failure rate of 3.33% (95% Wilson confidence interval: [2.30%, 4.81%]) with no statistically significant difference across ARM and x86 architectures (\c{hi} 2 = 1.55, p = 0.21), and stable operation under heterogeneous latency conditions, including intercontinental deployments. To ensure scientific transparency and reproducibility, the evaluation methodology, sanitized datasets, and statistical scripts have been made publicly available in an open-source repository.

title: LabInstruct: Benchmarking Situated Instructional Video Generation for Lab Procedures
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate the full experimental loop, from scientific decision-making to physical execution. Ideally, AI-generated plans could be carried out directly by robotic systems, but reliable automation remains difficult in complex, open-world laboratory environments, where experiments often involve fine-grained manipulation, long-horizon procedures, and substantial variation across tasks and setups. Humans therefore remain an important execution interface between AI-generated plans and physical experiments, creating a need for clear and effective human-facing experimental guidance. Because laboratory procedures are inherently visual, spatial, and dynamic, video is particularly well suited to communicating apparatus configurations, manipulation actions, temporal dependencies, and state changes. Recent advances in video generation now make it possible to synthesize experimental demonstrations directly from an initial workspace image and a natural-language instruction. However, whether such models can reliably communicate real laboratory procedures has not been systematically studied. We introduce LabInstruct, a benchmark for situated instructional video generation in real laboratories. LabInstruct contains 204 tasks across 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions. Evaluating 8 frontier image-to-video models, we find that visually plausible generations frequently remain procedurally incorrect, revealing a substantial gap between visual realism and the reliability required for experimental instruction.

title: CoEvoke: Evoking Multi-Agent Collaboration for Trajectory Collection
abstract: Training multi-agent collaboration requires trajectories of checking, feedback, and repair, yet task-solving rollouts may end in immediate approval or repeat unsuccessful attempts without useful correction. We introduce CoEvoke, a cross-domain framework that evokes these interactions during trajectory collection. Controlled perturbations create recoverable difficulties, while restricted reference-based guidance directs investigation. The resulting dataset contains 4,567 reconstructable trajectories over 4,130 software-engineering and reasoning tasks, linking public interactions to evidence, decisions, and task-native outcomes. Separate experiments over 2,287 same-task pairs show feedback increases of 47.72-100 percentage points across seven perturbation groups; guidance has smaller, model-dependent effects. With identical training tasks, decision-record counts, and updates, perturbation-enriched judge training improves ACPBench-Hard success from 35.38% to 42.12% (+6.73 points). SWE verifier training gains 7.60-9.40 points over interface-matched untrained references. Workflow and post-training evaluations preserve task-solving topology with unperturbed inputs and no private-reference guidance. These results support designing collection conditions to obtain corrective supervision that improves collaborative decisions with frozen solving agents.

title: OPMD: On-Policy Mechanism Distillation Beyond Output Supervision
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model by supervising a student on prefixes sampled from its own policy, but its supervision remains confined to the output space. Consequently, OPD transfers what a teacher predicts without supervising the intermediate computation that produces those predictions. Simply distilling intermediate representations like representation matching is insufficient since teacher and student representations may differ geometrically, and even well-aligned hidden states need not be usable by the student's subsequent computation. We introduce On-Policy Mechanism Distillation (OPMD), which transfers teacher-derived intermediate computation while explicitly accounting for its compatibility with the student. OPMD first constructs a student-compatible teacher that transforms teacher representations into intermediate states usable by the student's downstream computation, then it internalizes these states from on-policy trajectories. OPMD achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation baselines in all three teacher--student settings, and generalizes to multi-teacher distillation and cross-family supervised fine-tuning. Further analyses show that mechanism supervision yields more effective reasoning and meaningfully alters the student's intermediate computation and solution strategies, supporting that it transfers information beyond output supervision alone. Together, these results establish mechanism-level supervision as an effective way to move on-policy distillation beyond output supervision, enabling students to learn inner mechanisms they can use and internalize.

title: Historical Anchors for Scientific Forecasting on Human-Aware Knowledge Graphs
abstract: Predicting which scientific connections will form next can point researchers toward the most promising leads. One successful approach learns representations by sampling paths through publication networks, represented by a hypergraph, that connect scientific entities, concepts, and researchers, approximating how knowledge and expertise move through the literature. Sampled paths are then used to train an embedding model to forecast scientific connections such as a property of a material. Performance, however, depends strongly on how many paths are sampled: too little sampling yields incomplete representations, while further sampling can eventually weaken prediction quality. The best sampling budget is therefore often identifiable only after future discoveries are known. We introduce Query--Anchor Agreement (QAA), a diagnostic requiring no future labels or separately trained model. QAA can be used to select a sampling budget, and refine or re-rank the resulting forecast to improve forecasting scientific connections. QAA compares the candidates a model predicts for a target with those most similar to the target's known historical examples, and identifies when these two views converge. Across thermoelectric-material and COVID-19 drug-repurposing benchmarks, repeated random-seed runs, and three sampling policies, QAA-selected budgets fall on average 1.86 percentage points below hindsight-optimal selection for broad candidate recovery. Further, promoting candidates supported by both views, under a capped fusion that bounds the anchor contribution, improves broad recovery across all six benchmark-policy settings, which define the types of network walks used for sampling.

title: Beyond a Better Score: Long-Horizon Agentic ML Development and Evaluation Protocol for Physics Time Series
abstract: Physics time-series data are central to fundamental discoveries involving dark matter, neutrinos, and gravitational waves. Machine learning has shown strong potential to recover weak scientific signals buried in complex noise. Recent LLM-agent systems further automate ML development, but existing approaches are often driven primarily by one or a few numerical scores. In pursuit of a better score, agents may exploit shortcuts, trigger mode collapse, or game the evaluation procedure, producing models that achieve high scores but are scientifically invalid. We introduce SIDERIUS, an LLM agent system designed to move beyond a better score toward scientifically valid, long-horizon ML development. SIDERIUS combines contract-defined composable capabilities for flexible orchestration and human-in-the-loop, a multi-layer scientific evaluation protocol that distinguishes valid models from unhealthy or gaming models, and resource-aware exploration for computationally expensive scientific ML. In our TIDMAD benchmark, SIDERIUS with a GPT-based orchestrator achieves the highest Valid-model proposal rate of 63.8% and the best valid denoising score of 2.744, compared with 1.6% and -0.647, respectively, for the same GPT model using the general-purpose Codex coding agent. We further benchmark SIDERIUS on three additional physics time-series datasets, demonstrating its reuse and performance across different tasks. Together, these results suggest that progress in agentic scientific ML should be measured beyond a better score, by how an agent explores and by whether the models it produces can be trusted as science.

title: Contrastive Covariance Subspaces for Activation Steering
abstract: Activation steering controls large language model behavior by adding a direction to hidden activations during inference. For steering to work well, that direction must be a pure signal for the target concept: any confound entangled with it, such as an incidental topic or writing style, is injected into the residual stream alongside the concept itself and degrades the generated text. We introduce Contrastive Covariance Steering (CCS), a training-free method that eliminates this confound variation. CCS projects steering vectors to a low-dimensional subspace obtained in closed form by solving a contrastive variance objective, which retains the directions along which the target concept varies while suppressing directions shared with the other classes. Across three LLMs and four steering domains, CCS consistently beats all baseline steering methods in all $12$ model-domain settings. The largest relative improvement occurs on AxBench and Emotion where we outperform the next strongest steering baseline by $48$ to $70\%$ and $13$ to $27\%$, respectively. Furthermore, CCS outperforms naive difference-of-means steering by up to $151\%$, showcasing the importance of deconfounding concepts. A toy experiment verifies our motivation on why: planting a topic nuisance into the training data reduces unprojected steering by $46\%$, whereas CCS loses only $12\%$ and recovers most of the gap to an oracle that explicitly deletes the planted direction. A human study with $23$ raters on $296$ generations reproduces the LLM judge's ranking. Our extensive ablation verifies the importance of our method's components and robustness to the number of nuisance classes. Finally, we extend our method to multi-turn conversations, where CCS sustains both concept expression and fluency, matching system prompt performance as other steering methods drift.

title: Towards New Parity Rules with Asynchronous Updating Inspired by Fatès's Rule
abstract: The parity problem in 1D Cellular Automata is a classifier based on a local rule. If the number of ones in a ring of binary cells is odd then the automaton shall converge to all-one (11...11) else to all-zero (00...00). The objective is to find rules that are related to Fatès's Balanced Rule F but use less active neighborhoods (actions). The method is to analyze the effect of each actions and to find a functioning subset of the 12 actions used in rule F. New rules called HA, HB, HC, HF are defined with 10, 6, 4, 8 actions. Rule HC and HF need only three inputs whereas all others need four. The classification time of the rules was determined by averaging over many simulation runs with random initial configurations. It is almost the same for the rules HA and F, and is longer for the rules HB, HC, HF. In addition, the rule HD is defined, which updates three cells in parallel and works faster. In future work, the functioning and performance of the proposed rules should be treated in a more formal way, and related rules (also with different update schemes) could be considered.

title: SIREN: A nonlinear Rankine-source boundary element solver for the stationary motion of a marine vehicle in calm water
abstract: SIREN (Ship Inviscid Resistance and Elevation eNgine) is a Rankine-source panel solver for the steady wave resistance of a ship, in the tradition of Dawson's method. The free-surface condition is linearised about a base flow, and the linearisation is iterated. In the present formulation the base flow is the solution of a Neumann problem on the actual boundary: sources on the entire hull, wet and dry, and on the free surface panels, with impermeability imposed on both, so that the free surface acts as a rigid lid at the position it currently occupies. This replaces the classical double-body flow, whose image about z=0 is meaningful only for a flat surface and a hull cut at z=0, and it removes the need for desingularised free-surface panels. In the non-linear iteration the free-surface panels are moved rigidly in the vertical to the relaxed wave elevation at their centroid, the hull panels are marked wet or dry against the moved surface, and the base flow is recomputed on the moved geometry; impermeability applies to the whole hull regardless of this marking, which is used only to select which panels enter the force integral, and under-relaxation is confined to the passes where the non-linear correction accumulates without being reset. The radiation condition is imposed by a one-row upstream shift of the collocation points, and the wave resistance is obtained by pressure integration and, independently, by transverse wave-cut analysis.

title: Pick the Mixture, Not the Samples: Combinatorial Data Selection for LLMs
abstract: Data selection for LLM fine-tuning faces two facts about real training: data pools draw from many distinct domains, and evaluation spans diverse tasks. As a result, the same sample helps different tasks differently, and samples interact during training so that a subset's value is not the sum of its parts. Current data-selection methods leave these realities largely unaddressed. We formalize them as Combinatorial Data Selection (CDS), a framework that separates attribution (how samples are scored) from selection (which subset to pick) and models the non-additive interactions among samples. On a real instruction-tuning data pool, we find substantial cross-domain complementarity (joint utility exceeds the sum of singletons), alongside redundancy within domains. Inspired by this, we propose Mixture-then-Select, a two-stage algorithm that first decides how many samples to take from each domain, then ranks samples within each domain by attribution score. Theoretically, the gap to the optimal subset is linear in the selection size and independent of data pool size. Empirically, Mixture-then-Select outperforms strong baselines by 20 to 54%, is robust across attribution methods, and works across different models and data pool sizes. The framework also extends to the data purchasing problem under a budget constraint when sample prices vary. Our findings suggest that allocating selection across domains offers a promising path toward more efficient and effective data selection for modern LLMs.

title: Can We Trust This Evaluation? Instance-Level Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge
abstract: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation commonly aggregates multiple judges' decisions into a majority vote, yet this panel decision process does not guarantee that the evaluation of an individual item is reliable. We propose Structured Cross-fitted Uncertainty Risk (SCUR), a label-free approach for estimating instance-level evaluation reliability based on the judge panel's behavior. A latent measurement model serves as the backbone for measurement system analysis, from which SCUR derives three complementary signals capturing panel uncertainty, measurement cross-entropy, and perturbation sensitivity. These three sources of evidence are combined into a risk score. We evaluate the SCUR approach on five real-world benchmarks using majority-vote error ranking, selective trust, and risk stratification. Furthermore, we show our approach to be more effective at detecting high-consensus risk items, which are the blind spots for many other LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methods.

title: Rotate the Loop: Blockwise Conformality for Looped Transformers
abstract: Looped transformers reuse one shared block across many recurrent steps, so depth becomes a quantity that can be spent at runtime rather than a stack of distinct layers. Those extra steps help only if a write made on one recurrent step is still readable on later ones, and that depends on the linear map applied to the residual between recurrent steps. We show that whether the loop learns to track state is a geometric question about the form of this map, and we propose blockwise conformal injections: the residual splits into coordinate-aligned groups and rotates inside each one, so every group has its own timescale while the geometry stays exact within it. Our experiments show a performance increase on a demanding form of state tracking - last-token accuracy when the rest of the prefix is already correct - and on language modelling, where a signal written earlier has to be retrieved at the end of the sequence.

title: PLDiv: Measuring Dataset Diversity and Semantic Collapse via Persistence Landscapes
abstract: Modern data pipelines increasingly combine human-created and human-curated data with AI-generated data for model training and evaluation. As datasets grow, they often add semantically redundant samples rather than expanding semantic coverage, which deteriorates the quality of the whole dataset. Existing diversity metrics primarily summarize lexical variation, entropy, or pairwise similarity, but provide limited characterization of the shape of the underlying data distribution. In this paper, we propose PLDiv, a diversity metric derived from persistence landscapes that quantifies the structural organization of a dataset from its geometric representation. PLDiv summarizes how data neighborhoods evolve as nearby samples progressively connect, producing an interpretable scalar measure of structural diversity without requiring task-specific supervision. Whether measuring intrinsic diversity in text generations or image embeddings, or detecting semantic collapse in instruction datasets and reasoning trajectories, PLDiv performs competitively against evaluated baselines and aligns strongly with diversity labels during semantic collapse. Consequently, it effectively supports applications in synthetic data monitoring, dataset construction, data augmentation, and generative model evaluation.

title: Polygons and coplanar points on submanifolds of codimension 2
abstract: Problem 73 on Green's list of open problems asks whether a smooth submanifold of codimension two in $\mathbb{R}^n$ must meet some affine two-plane in five points when $n$ is large. In this paper, we answer this question for every $n \geq 6$. Every nonempty relatively open subset of such a submanifold contains the vertices of an affinely regular pentagon, and the bound $n \geq 6$ is sharp for affinely regular pentagons. More generally, for every prime $p \geq 5$, the graph of a continuous map from a ball in $\mathbb{R}^{p-1}$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$ contains an affinely regular $p$-gon. A second argument gives six coplanar points when $n \geq 7$. Both proofs find the points by making the low Fourier modes of the graph map vanish along a circle.

title: OIL: An Object Interaction Layer for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
abstract: Recent progress in learned whole-body controllers for humanoid robots has enabled robust free-space motion by tracking kinematic targets such as joint or end-effector trajectories. This interface provides a useful abstraction for upstream systems, including motion capture, teleoperation, or generative models, which can specify desired motion without reasoning about forces or balance. However, this abstraction has largely been limited to robot motion, requiring task-specific controllers or retraining for object interaction. We introduce OIL, an Object Interaction Layer that extends the kinematic command interface of whole-body control to include desired object motion and contact. OIL augments a standard controller with object-centric commands and translates them into coordinated whole-body behavior while preserving locomotion and balance. This design enables a single learned policy to execute non-prehensile interactions, including pushing, pulling, two-arm pick-and-place, and locomotion-coupled transport, directly from object-level kinematic targets without task-specific retraining. In simulation, we demonstrate that object-level commands improve performance over robot-centric controllers while matching task-specific policies across variations in object properties such as mass and size. We further demonstrate zero-shot generalization to novel behavior combinations and sim-to-real transfer on the Digit humanoid robot.

title: Building Trustworthy Household Robots through Open-World Safety
abstract: Foundation models are expanding robot capabilities, enabling robots to handle more diverse objects, follow sophisticated instructions, and operate in complex environments. These advances bring us to a future in which robots become part of everyday household life. However, cluttered, dynamic household environments also expose robots to unfamiliar objects, tasks, and interactions, making reliable zero-shot task completion an ongoing challenge for robotics research. From a security perspective, we argue for open-world safety: household robots should preserve specified safety requirements in unseen situations, including when they cannot complete the requested task. Safety protections must account for context and interactions that persist across actions and tasks. In this position paper, we examine why existing safety methods can fail to provide this protection. Protection can fail through misinterpreted context, overlooked past interactions, or stopping and recovery strategies that become unsafe under unfamiliar conditions. We therefore propose a research agenda to specify, learn, and ground safety requirements, enforce them with reliable recovery, and evaluate the generalization of such protections. We call for household robots whose safety protections remain reliable beyond the situations, context, and history used to train and develop them, to achieve open-world safety.

title: Residual Compliant Policy: Learning Compliant Policies from Few Demonstrations
abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to be precise in free space to establish the intended contacts, and compliant once in contact to avoid excessive forces. Imitation learning has proven effective for simpler manipulation tasks, but the compliance underlying a demonstration is not directly observable and is therefore difficult to infer from demonstration data alone. We present a framework that makes compliance explicit at every stage. During data collection, the operator teleoperates the real robot while a synchronized digital twin visualizes the error between the commanded reference and the achieved pose, making the current compliance visible, and selects between two discrete compliance modes. To generalize across object poses, we combine Laplacian editing, which retargets trajectories efficiently but is not physics-consistent during contact, with simulation-based trajectory optimization, which enforces physical plausibility but offers no manual guidance. Finally, a residual reinforcement learning policy refines the interaction forces by adjusting the reference pose of the underlying admittance controller. We evaluate on three flipping and pushing tasks on a Franka FR3 based on a total of 7 demonstrations across tasks. Our method is successful on all 40 out-of-distribution trials, compared to 33/40 and 24/40 for two baselines, with our base policy alone reaching 35/40.

title: AI Advice Reinforces Traditional Gender Roles
abstract: Professionals are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) for career advice. We tested whether large language models (LLMs) provide different advice to female and male job candidates in the context of career negotiations. Across two large-scale audit experiments, including four leading models, the LLMs not only recommended lower salary targets for female than male personas, but also constructed distinct negotiation agendas, prioritizing flexibility, caregiving, and well-being more highly for female candidates, and financial rewards, mobility, and advancement more highly for male candidates. These differences closely tracked independent human ratings of employment terms associated with primary caregiver and breadwinner roles, respectively. Our findings identify a subtle pathway through which personalized AI advice may reinforce gender inequality at work: steering otherwise equivalent users toward traditional gender roles.

title: Sharp Antipode-Neighbor Bounds in Every Dimension
abstract: Let $P\subset\mathbb R^d$ be finite with $\operatorname{diam}(P)\le1$. For $0<\varepsilon<1$, let $\mathcal N_\varepsilon(P)$ denote the number of ordered pairs at distance at most $\varepsilon$, including the diagonal, and let $\mathcal A_\varepsilon(P)$ denote the number of ordered pairs at distance at least $1-\varepsilon$. We prove the sharp bound \[ \mathcal N_\varepsilon(P)\gtrsim_d \varepsilon^{(d-1)/2}\mathcal A_\varepsilon(P) \] conjectured by Steinerberger (2025). More generally, the same inequality holds for finite positive Borel measures. The main input is a uniform $L^2$ estimate, at cap thickness comparable to lattice spacing, for a supporting-direction incidence operator. In gnomonic coordinates, this operator is controlled by an incidence estimate for small Fenchel--Young gaps.

title: From bits to atoms: A survey of cross-layer safety in Embodied AI
abstract: Embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) introduces cyber-physical risks because digital failures and attacks can cause physical harm. This survey organizes embodied AI safety through a four-layer reference architecture -- comprising the physical interaction, system and middleware, algorithm and decision, and cloud-edge and data layers -- and uses it to connect vulnerabilities, propagation paths, and safeguards across the system stack. It traces the evolution of safety paradigms and examines how faults and attacks cross architectural boundaries to produce physical consequences. Furthermore, the survey systematizes composite attack chains, outlines multi-layered defense strategies, and reviews representative embodied safety benchmarks. Ultimately, we advocate for unifying software alignment with rigorous hardware constraints to build trustworthy systems capable of operating safely within human-centric environments.

title: RAIN: Robotic Task Generalization with Region-Aware Interaction Networks
abstract: Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from large-scale vision-language pretraining, but tend to memorize training trajectories, limiting their ability to adapt learned interactions to new task and scene configurations. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{Region-Aware Interaction Networks (RAIN)}, which formulates a task as a sequence of goal-conditioned subtasks, each specified by an action type and a target-region mask. This formulation allows learned skills to be reused across different objects and scene layouts and composed into task sequences not seen during training. Its Target-adaptive Cross-View Encoder (TCE) conditions multi-view features on target masks and exchanges information across views, while PlanDiT predicts target-directed trajectories and actions. A Transition Head estimates subtask completion to enable automatic transitions. We also introduce a \textbf{Reference-based Retargeting Strategy (RRS)}, which uses recorded trajectories to synthesize smooth approaches to reference interactions with alternative target regions, without collecting additional data. Experiments on \textbf{LIBERO-Analogy}, our new benchmark for robotic task generalization, and real-world tabletop tasks demonstrate that RAIN generalizes more robustly than existing VLA baselines.

title: Symmetric Cryptography via Dirichlet Convolution
abstract: We discuss a new symmetric-key cipher for digital data encryption. Its implementation is fast, memory efficient, and resilient against classical, AI-assisted, and quantum attacks. Let $x$, $k$, and $c$ be elements of a finite abelian group $G$ with operation $+$ and neutral element $0$. Suppose one is given ciphertext $c=x+k$. Retrieving the plaintext $x=c-k$ from the ciphertext is trivial when the key $k$ is known. Without the key, however, recovering $x$ amounts to a blind search. Even if an efficient criterion were available for identifying the plaintext among all group elements, the average number of trials would remain prohibitively large when the group is sufficiently large. The challenge in constructing a practical cryptosystem is therefore to identify a sufficiently rich group $G$, together with efficient algorithms that enable an immersion of \emph{real digital data} into $G$ and efficient evaluation of the group operations. The proposed cipher is based on generalized Dirichlet convolution over finite fields. We investigate its security against plaintext attacks from an information-theoretic perspective. The nonlocal structure of Dirichlet convolution naturally permits plaintext salting, providing protection against plaintext attacks while allowing controlled key reuse. We establish perfect masking properties over finite fields and prove that the resulting cipher achieves information-theoretic security under key reuse when the underlying arithmetic is carried out in $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p>2$. For arithmetic over $\mathbb{F}_2$, some information leakage remains, leading to a finite key-reuse budget.

title: A Geometric Perspective on Reward Function Updates in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is classically solved using Lagrangian optimisation, by jointly optimising a primal-dual problem with gradient descent to obtain the optimal reward function parameters and corresponding optimal policy. While this algorithmic view of IRL has been highly influential, gradient-based reward updates only paint a partial picture, largely ignoring the geometry of the problem in occupancy space. In this paper, we present an occupancy-space view of reward updates in IRL. We leverage the insight that both the optimal solution and its geometry in occupancy space are known, and show that the geometry along the e-geodesic (straight line in occupancy space) toward the optimal occupancy directly affects the gradient of the IRL dual problem in reward parameter space. This perspective naturally suggests preconditioning the dual gradient with the average Fisher information along the occupancy trajectory. We show that this preconditioned gradient is just a convex interpolation of the old reward and a new target reward, yielding efficient natural-gradient-style updates with little additional computational overhead. We then analyse these occupancy-space reward updates from a Mirror Descent (MD) perspective, and show that policy search over the resulting rewards induces approximate entropic MD on the policy. Finally, we conclude with convergence results of such geometry-aware IRL algorithms.

title: Reinforcement Learning from Real-Robot Interaction without High-Quality State Estimates
abstract: A longstanding goal for robot reinforcement learning (RL) is that robots learn from their own physical experience, as humans and animals do. A key obstacle to learning directly from physical experience, especially outside instrumented lab environments, is that the state of the world is usually unobservable to the learner and must be estimated from on-board sensing. Errors in that estimate corrupt both the policy input and potentially the reward signal. We study this challenge using the contact-rich task of a bipedal robot learning to score soccer goals. We estimate all key state variables on-board with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) and no external instrumentation (e.g., motion capture or overhead cameras). Because the UKF may incorrectly estimate state when the ball is unobserved, we learn a new state representation with a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) that, critically, only corrects the RSSM's latent state when the ball is observed. Building on RLPD, we introduce RSSM-RLPD and apply it to the task of a NAO robot learning to dribble a soccer ball into a goal. We show that the robot learns to score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction, reaching 100% success against 0% for a feed-forward policy under the same training budget. We complement our physical robot experiments with a simulation study and show that RSSM-RLPD learns policies that achieve a higher success rate than behavior cloning, a feed-forward, and GRU baseline. Taken together, our results show that the addition of a learned state representation to existing on-robot learning methods enables RL from real-robot data even with a high degree of partial observability.

title: Refuses in Chat, Complies with Arms: LLM Refusal Does Not Survive Robot Control
abstract: Frontier language models reliably refuse to explain how to cause physical harm. We ask whether this refusal survives when the same models control a robot. We introduce RoboHarm, a physical AI safety benchmark of harmful robot instructions, and test seven frontier models on it. We hold each model fixed and vary only the interface, from text to Code as Policies to vision agents that command end-effector poses or joint angles. In a MuJoCo simulation twin of a bimanual YAM arm robot, refusal falls from 73% of text requests to 18-25% once the model controls the robot, even when it is told what the objects are. On the physical robot, six models with end-effector control refused 18% of 612 trials against 19% in sim, and three with joint control refused 41% of 252 against 31%. GPT-5.6 Sol refused every text request and none of its trials on the real robot. Case studies of the robot transcripts show that models miss the hazard, name it without inferring its consequences, or act despite recognizing it, and their refusals often hinge on uncertainty about what an object is rather than on the harm of the action. Safety alignment learned in text thus fails to generalize to action, leaving current models with a poorly understood safety gap in the physical world.

title: $n$-Valued Analogue of Abel's Theorem
abstract: Abel's classical theorem shows that a continuously differentiable one-dimensional associative law with a two-sided unit is locally equivalent to addition under a change of coordinate. We prove an $n$-valued analogue in the algebraic and formal settings. Over a field of characteristic zero, every associative algebraic $n$-valued monoid on $\mathbb P^1$ with a strong two-sided unit is commutative. Over a reduced commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra, any one-dimensional formal $n$-valued group is commutative. We then classify $n$-valued formal groups over arbitrary $\mathbb Q$-algebras that are integral domains: for any $n$-valued formal group there is a unique divisor $m$ of $n$ such that the law is strongly isomorphic to the $n/m$-fold diagonal of the cyclic elementary $m$-valued law $\mathbb G_m$. This proves Kholodov's classification conjecture over integral domain $\mathbb Q$-algebras.

title: Equivariant Seiberg-Witten equations on Hermitian symmetric spaces
abstract: We formulate and solve a $G$-equivariant analogue of the Seiberg-Witten equations on any irreducible Hermitian symmetric space $G/K$. We use a canonical $K$-invariant form to define a twisted Hodge operator generalising self-duality to higher dimensions. The resulting equivariant Seiberg-Witten equations arise, for a compact $G/K$, as conditions for the absolute minima of an energy functional. Their linear part has a representation theoretic interpretation: the same Weyl group data control the highest-weight realisation of the positive Dirac kernel in the compact case and its discrete-series realisation on the non-compact dual. This space of harmonic spinors collapses almost entirely by the quadratic conditions of the monopole equation. In the compact case, the equivariant moduli set, when non-empty, is a single gauge class, identifying with the $G$-invariant part of Bradlow's trichotomy for vortices, while in the non-compact case, every irreducible solution sits outside the discrete series.

title: An Edge-First Multimodal Asset Management Studio and Retrieval Engine for Heterogeneous AI-Generated Media
abstract: AI-generated image collections combine visual content with heterogeneous provenance such as prompts, model parameters, and workflow graphs. Managing these collections locally requires coordinated metadata extraction, responsive browsing, and retrieval without mandatory remote inference. We present Berry AI Studio, an edge-first asset management system built with Vue, Tauri, Rust, SQLite, and ONNX Runtime. Berry integrates format-specific metadata parsing with raw-payload retention, generation-aware cancellation of queued thumbnail work, a persistent multi-tier thumbnail manifest, cursor pagination, and local image-text retrieval. We evaluate these mechanisms in five independent repetitions on a pinned source revision. With 50,000 catalog records, the median warm first-page database call was 285.3 ms; at offset 40,000, keyset pagination reduced median raw-query latency from 57.9 to 0.46 ms. A controlled browser harness recorded a 0.3 ms median-of-run P95 update time during virtualized scrolling, while cancellation prevented all 1,200 stale speculative decodes in the tested trace. A versioned 10-case corpus produced 53/53 exact metadata-field matches, and controlled retrieval and grouping tests exercised the authentic storage and clustering paths. The implementation, benchmark scripts, raw logs, and checksummed result packages are publicly available.

title: Maximal volumes of pyramids in the unit cube
abstract: Let $Q_n=[0,1]^n$, $n\ge2$. Denote by $M_n$ be the maximal volume of a pyramid in $Q_n$ whose base is a hyperplane section of $Q_n$, and by $M_n^0$ the corresponding maximum when the section contains the center of $Q_n$. We prove that $nM_n<(n+1)M_{n+1}^0$.

title: Real-Space Interference from Quantum Metric
abstract: Real-space interference of wave packets is governed by their central momentum separation and momentum width, which set the oscillation wavelength and spatial envelope, respectively. Here, we show that in crystalline systems, quantum metric distribution in an isolated band can similarly give rise to real-space interference through the evanescent tails of a localized bound state. The location and width of a quantum metric hot spot in the momentum space set a complex wavevector as one evanescent plane wave component of a bound state. Consequently, with multiple quantum metric hot spots, the density distribution of a bound state or the total density of two spatially overlapped bound states exhibits an interference pattern, where the oscillation period and long-range decay length are determined by the momentum-space separation of the hot spots and the width of the narrowest hot spots, respectively. This quantum-geometric interference is particularly pronounced in (nearly) flat bands, where competing scales from band dispersion are suppressed. Furthermore, we demonstrate that using a Josephson STM the real-space interference can be experimentally observed through the tip-position dependence of the Josephson critical current. Our results reveal a direct correspondence between momentum-space quantum geometry and real-space interference, showing how bound-state profiles encode the momentum-resolved quantum metric.

title: A semi-infinite hydraulic fracture propagating in a poroelastic medium
abstract: We solve the near-tip coupled hydromechanical problem of a hydraulic fracture propagating in a permeable poroelastic medium, represented locally as a semi-infinite crack moving at constant velocity. In the moving tip frame, all fracture fields are steady. The porous solid obeys linear poroelasticity, fracture propagation follows LEFM, fluid flow within the tensile fracture is governed by lubrication theory, and the fracturing and pore fluids are treated as identical Newtonian liquids. The primary unknowns are the fracture opening and the fluid displacement function along the fracture, determined from the resulting non-linear system of equations. In a viscosity--toughness scaling, the problem depends on four dimensionless parameters: a dimensionless permeability $\varrho$ (associated with the intensity of fluid leak-in), a dimensionless effective confining stress $Σ_0'$ (measuring the relative importance of fluid leak-off and leak-in), the drained--undrained Poisson's ratio contrast $β$, and the poroelastic stress coefficient $η$. The solution evolves from a drained, toughness-dominated near-tip asymptote with uniform net pressure to an undrained, storage-viscosity-dominated far-field asymptote. Numerical solutions are obtained over parameter ranges representative of various rock types. The fully coupled model is compared with simplified models, namely uncoupled and one-way coupled formulations, over distances from the fracture front spanning laboratory-to-field scales. The resulting relative difference maps in the $(\varrho,Σ_0')$ parameter space identify four characteristic regimes: negligible poroelastic effects, dominance of the direct mechanical poroelastic response, importance of the poroelastic backstress, and a fully coupled regime. The latter occurs mainly at large $\varrho$ and small $Σ_0'$, corresponding to strong leak-in relative to leak-off.

title: An upper bound for the three-dimensional moving sofa problem in a snaky corridor
abstract: Let $K_M \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be the "snaky" corridor with unit-square cross-section: an infinite entry arm parallel to the $x$-axis, a middle arm parallel to the $y$-axis whose clear straight section has length $M$, and an infinite exit arm parallel to the $z$-axis, with the two turns lying in the $x$-$y$ and $y$-$z$ planes. Let $V^*(K_M)$ be the supremum of the volumes of connected bodies that can be moved continuously (by rigid motions) from the entry arm to the exit arm while remaining inside $K_M$. We prove $V^*(K_M) \le 7.8691$ for every $M \ge 3.53$ (Theorem A); by a sharper analysis of the same mechanism, $V^*(K_M) \le 4.2862$ for every $M \ge 2.61$ (Theorem B); and, by replacing the final analytic caps with a certified branch-and-bound computation over the compact family of entry tubes compatible with the forced events, $V^*(K_M) \le 3.4083$ for every $M > 2.2$ (Theorem C; computer-assisted, in double precision with conservative slack). In particular all three bounds apply to the corridor with $M = 4$ used in Problem 6.64 of Georgiev, Gómez-Serrano, Tao and Wagner (arXiv:2511.02864), and uniformly to every "turns far apart" reading of that problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first upper bound for the snaky-corridor 3D moving sofa problem; previously not even finiteness of $V^*$ had been recorded. This note proves upper bounds only; combined with the certified lower bound 1.8558404 from the author's separate certification work via the problem's own evaluation pipeline, the state of the problem becomes $1.8558404 \le V^*(K_4) \le 3.4083$. Theorems A and B are elementary and self-contained: a first-crossing (elbow) event forces a definite tilt of the body's own entry tube, and Fubini-type chord estimates for tilted tubes cap the volume. Theorem C certifies, by the same forced-event skeleton, the largest corridor volume that any admissible entry tube can carry.

title: New certified lower bounds for the moving sofa problem in a three-dimensional snaky corridor
