We use Gaia XP spectra to study Galactic disk mono-abundance populations (MAPs), measuring their scale heights as a function of radius and radial surface-mass-density profiles. We construct a red giant branch (RGB) sample and divide it into MAPs according to $[α/{\rm M}]$ and $[{\rm M/H}]$. The sample covers a $6\times6$ kpc region centered on the Sun in the Galactic plane and extends to $|Z|<3.7$ kpc. We estimate XP completeness using a Gaia photometric parent sample and combine PARSEC isochrones with a Kroupa initial mass function (IMF) to calculate the selection function and convert observed stellar counts into intrinsic stellar mass densities. We fit vertical density profiles with an exponential model to derive scale heights and integrate the fitted profiles to obtain surface mass densities. The resulting profiles are generally consistent with those from APOGEE. All MAPs show flaring, with the high-$α$ population exhibiting the strongest flaring and the metal-poor and sub-solar low-$α$ populations showing the weakest. Surface-mass-density profiles differ significantly among MAPs: the high-$α$ and metal-rich low-$α$ populations show approximately exponential declines, whereas the other low-$α$ populations exhibit plateau-like features, indicating that the Galactic disk cannot be described by a simple single-exponential profile. These differential structures suggest a complex Galactic disk assembly history likely regulated by birth conditions, secular dynamical heating, radial migration, and external perturbations.

title: Can You Trust Your Preference Models? Stackelberg Games for Alignment
abstract: Language models are frequently aligned to human preferences via imperfect evaluators whose errors can be exploited during optimization. We train policies to search for comparisons on which an evaluator may reverse the underlying preference, providing candidates for additional supervision. Since human preferences are unavailable during policy training, we use disagreement among an ensemble of preference models as a proxy for prediction error. We formulate this search as a zero-sum Stackelberg game between two opposing policies, a Leader which tries to minimize disagreement, and a Follower which maximizes it. For a general class of finite contextual Stackelberg games, we establish equilibrium existence and, under regularization, uniqueness and a closed-form characterization. We introduce Stackelberg Mirror Descent-Ascent (SMIDA), a two-timescale algorithm with linear last-iterate convergence in the tabular setting, and develop a neural policy-gradient analogue. Experiments with a synthetic oracle support disagreement as an informative proxy for prediction error. On held out data the trained policies outperform reference policies and increase the fraction of comparisons that exceed a disagreement threshold and reverse the oracle's preference.

title: Anomaly Flow II: Estimates and Long-time Existence for the Coupled Flow
abstract: In this follow-up to \cite{Sua25}, we extend the results to the coupled anomaly flow which incorporates the evolution of a Hermitian metric on a holomorphic vector bundle over a compact complex $3$-fold with general slope parameter $α'$. This yields a similar sufficient smallness condition on the slope parameter $α'$ in order to extend the flow on $[0, τ)$ to $[0, τ+ ε)$. We also augment the argument of \cite{Sua25} slightly to fix the peculiarity of the units in the condition for $α'$ for the $k = 1$ case.

title: On the Complexity Gap Between POMDPs and Multi-Environment POMDPs
abstract: Multi-environment POMDPs (ME-POMDPs) generalize POMDPs by encoding a finite set of possible environments, capturing model uncertainty. The finite-horizon robust reward maximization problem for a ME-POMDP asks for a policy that maximizes reward in the worst environment, and recent work has shown this problem to be $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete. We expand the complexity landscape of ME-POMDPs by identifying which subclasses retain this $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-completeness. In particular, we take subclasses of POMDPs that are tractable in the single-environment case, and investigate the computational complexity of these classes when extended to the multi-environment setting. We first prove the $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness of multi-environment blind MDPs and deterministic POMDPs using a certain closure-under-mixture condition. We then prove $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-completeness for a range of subclasses that do not satisfy that closure condition, yielding new complexity results for multi-observation POMDPs. Finally, we show existential theory of the reals ($\exists \mathbb{R}$)-completeness for numerous ME-POMDP problems under time-dependent Markovian policies or finite-state controllers that are $\mathsf{NP}$-complete for standard POMDPs. These results reveal a subtle relationship between POMDP and ME-POMDP complexity that depends heavily on the subclasses involved.

title: Conformal Sequential Decision Making With Cost and Sublinear Policy Regret Guarantees
abstract: Automated decision makers, such as AI agents that control robots or network devices, must often satisfy hard cost constraints while maintaining competitive performance. In such settings, a cost measure, such as a safety violation rate, energy consumption, or a distortion level, must stay within a given budget in every episode of operation. Furthermore, a cumulative reward metric, accounting for per-step performance, must stay close to the reward of a meaningful reference policy. We formulate this setup as an episodic sequential decision problem in which the state sequence is arbitrary, and the reward and cost may depend on past actions within the same episode. We propose the online conformal episodic agent (OCEA), a policy that selects one candidate action per episode using a regret-controlled algorithm, and switches to a zero-cost action when the remaining budget cannot absorb the maximum cost of one more round. We prove that OCEA satisfies per-episode cost constraints for every state sequence and for every realization of its internal randomness, while achieving a sublinear expected policy regret with respect to the best action sequence in hindsight from a comparator class satisfying the same per-episode cost constraints. We apply OCEA to risk-averse control and online compression with distortion guarantees.

title: CowCare: A Unified Visual Framework for Viewpoint-Robust Cattle Tracking and Spatiotemporal Heat-Stress Analysis
abstract: Reliable individual monitoring is essential for dairy cattle welfare and early heat stress detection in Precision Livestock Farming (PLF). However, translating raw multi-camera videos into automated diagnostics remains challenging due to disconnected tracking and recognition pipelines and complex physical environments. Dense mutual occlusions and cross-camera viewpoint variations fragment identities, while environmental noise, including camera vibrations, and limited agricultural data obscure subtle heat stress cues such as rapid breathing and flank undulations. To bridge low-level visual features and high-level behavioral diagnostics, we propose CowCare, a unified framework combining viewpoint-robust tracking with spatiotemporal heat stress recognition. Its tracking module, CowTrack, maintains cross-camera identity consistency through a View-Decoupled Aggregation Network (VDA-Net). Instead of relying on static global representations, VDA-Net aggregates localized textures under heavy occlusion and uses a Viewpoint Decoupling Transformer (VDT) to suppress transient viewpoint variations. CowTrack further incorporates a causal online self-supervision mechanism for continuous adaptation to dynamic farm scenes. The resulting tracklets are subsequently processed by TSDF-Net, a fine-grained video understanding network. Its Temporal Stabilization and Aggregation Module (TSAM) suppresses high-frequency jitter, while a Diffusion Semantic Prior (DSP) uses frozen pre-trained diffusion semantics to enhance subtle behavioral signals and mitigate overfitting. Extensive evaluations on two real-world farm benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness: CowTrack achieves 83.48% HOTA and 87.72% IDF1 for global multi-object tracking on MVCow, and TSDF-Net achieves 87.72% Top-1 accuracy on HSCow. These results establish CowCare as a robust end-to-end framework for automated livestock health monitoring.

title: Stability in the determination of the coefficients for coupled relativistic Schrödinger system
abstract: In this article, we prove a stability result for the identification of the coefficients appearing in a coupled relativistic Schrödinger system posed on a bounded domain of $\mathbb{R}^{1+n}$, where $n \geq 3$. More precisely, by utilizing input-output operator, where Neumann boundary data are available only on a subset of the boundary, and constructing an appropriate geometric optics solution, we derive a stability estimate of $\log$-$\log$ type for the matrix-valued first-order coefficients. This result is subsequently used to obtain a $\log$-$\log$-$\log$ type stability estimate for the zeroth-order matrix-valued potential.

title: A Half-Space Theorem for the Allen--Cahn Equation in All Dimensions
abstract: We prove that, in every dimension, a bounded, non-constant entire solution of the Allen--Cahn equation whose zero set is contained in a half-space is a one-dimensional heteroclinic solution.

title: Algorithmic Fairness Over Time: Advances & Prospects
abstract: In the presence of feedback loops, algorithmic decisions at one time step can influence observed data in subsequent steps, potentially introducing selection bias or shifts in data distribution. Research has demonstrated that ignoring these effects can lead to unfairness, which may worsen over time as the model remains deployed within society. This raises important questions of how to measure and ensure fairness of algorithmic decision-making models over time. In this short paper, we present a taxonomy that distinguishes between different types of static and temporal fairness notions in recent advancements. We then suggest prospects for future research by identifying common implicit temporal assumptions, open questions to enhance our temporal understanding of fairness, and other open challenges.

title: An Exact Branch-Price-and-Cut Algorithm for a Truck-as-Hub Vehicle Routing Problem with Drones
abstract: Rural last-mile logistics remains challenging because of sparse demand, limited road infrastructure, and long travel distances. We study a Truck-as-Hub Vehicle Routing Problem with Drones in Rural Areas, in which multiple trucks each carry a dedicated fleet of drones. Drone launch and retrieval are restricted to predesignated passive synchronization pads, where a visiting truck temporarily acts as a mobile hub, may dispatch multiple drones simultaneously, and must wait until all launched drones return before continuing its route. We formulate a mixed-integer quadratic programming model that jointly accounts for customer delivery delays, truck return times, and operating costs. To solve the problem exactly, we transform the original truck--drone network so that each feasible route can be represented as a single path and develop a branch-price-and-cut algorithm with tailored pricing, cutting, branching, and parallel-computing procedures. Computational experiments show that the proposed algorithm proves optimality for most large-scale test cases and achieves optimality gaps of no more than 4% for the remaining cases, whereas Gurobi reaches the 1,800-second time limit on all large-scale instances when applied directly to the compact formulation. Sensitivity analyses show that drone operating costs and managerial priorities substantially affect drone utilization and customer delays, providing practical guidance for balancing service quality and operating cost in rural delivery systems.

title: Non-uniqueness for McKean--Vlasov SDEs with Hölder diffusion coefficients
abstract: We show that uniqueness may fail for one-dimensional McKean--Vlasov stochastic differential equations with Hölder continuous diffusion coefficients. More precisely, for every \(α\in(1/2,1)\), we construct an equation with a diffusion coefficient that is \(α\)-Hölder continuous in the state variable, Lipschitz continuous in the measure variable, and of linear growth, for which uniqueness in law and pathwise uniqueness fail. The construction relies on a spreading estimate together with a Schauder fixed-point argument.

title: Nonstandard combinatorial ultrafilters and a new local witness model
abstract: A central object in the theory of proof complexity generators is Krajicek's local witness model. We construct a new such model as a definable ultrapower using a definable version of a selective ultrafilter over a model of arithmetic. We transfer some set theory of combinatorial ultrafilters to the definable nonstandard setting.

title: A counterexample concerning the coefficient formula for de Branges-Rovnyak norms
abstract: Let $\mathcal{H}(b)$ be the de Branges-Rovnyak space associated to a non-extreme point $b$ of the unit ball of $H^\infty$, and let $ϕ=b/a$, where $a$ is the Pythagorean mate of $b$. In an earlier article, the author showed that, if $ϕ\in H^2$, then \[ f\in\mathcal{H}(b) \iff \Bigl(f\in H^2 \text{ and }\sum_{m\ge0}\Bigl|\sum_{n\ge0}\overline{\hatϕ(n)}\hat{f}(m+n)\Bigr|^2<\infty\Bigr), \] in which case we have \[ \|f\|_{\mathcal{H}(b)}^2=\sum_{m\ge0}|\hat{f}(m)|^2 +\sum_{m\ge0}\Bigl|\sum_{n\ge0}\overline{\hatϕ(n)}\hat{f}(m+n)\Bigr|^2. \] It was also shown that there exists a space $\mathcal{H}(b)$ for which $ϕ\in\cap_{p<2}H^p$, yet \[ f\in\mathcal{H}(b)\not\Rightarrow \sum_{m\ge0}\Bigl|\sum_{n\ge0}\overline{\hatϕ(n)}\hat{f}(m+n)\Bigr|^2<\infty. \] Here we complete this circle of ideas by showing that there exists a space $\mathcal{H}(b)$ for which $ϕ\in\cap_{p<1}H^p$, yet \[ \Bigl(f\in H^2\text{ and } \sum_{m\ge0}\Bigl|\sum_{n\ge0}\overline{\hatϕ(n)}\hat{f}(m+n)\Bigr|^2<\infty\Bigr) \not\Rightarrow f\in\mathcal{H}(b). \]

title: PATTERN Can Be Solved from Memory: Generator-Aware Baselines for Synthetic Node Classification
abstract: PATTERN, a synthetic node-classification benchmark still used to rank graph networks, plants a random subgraph in a random host graph and asks which nodes belong to it. Its generator draws 100 patterns once and plants the same ones in every split, so each test graph carries a pattern that also appears in 100 training graphs. A matcher that reads these patterns off the training labels and looks them up in each test graph reaches 99.2 class-weighted accuracy with no trained parameters, against 89.8 for the best published model. Inference under the generator without the patterns reaches 86.8. Two published models, CKGConv and GRIT, score lower on patterns they have not seen: on new graphs with fresh patterns both fall below this pattern-blind predictor, and withholding patterns from CKGConv's training lowers its accuracy on the test graphs that carry them. Training CKGConv with a new pattern in every graph raises its accuracy on fresh patterns by about 2 points, to the level of the pattern-blind predictor, at some cost on the reused patterns. The same kind of inference under the generator matches the best published result on CLUSTER and, without any training, scores above every published result we found on Minesweeper's released board. We recommend that synthetic benchmarks report scores on fresh templates beside reused ones, publish baselines built from their generators, and state how their metric is weighted and pooled.

title: Entanglement detection in dynamical quantum systems
abstract: Quantum science and engineering increasingly target the exploitation and control of large-scale dynamical systems. As system size grows, novel phenomena and quantum advantages emerge, but the resulting many-body dynamics become correspondingly harder to monitor and characterize. In particular, the underlying Hamiltonian often lacks symmetries, and the induced many-body dynamics quickly become hard to track. Focusing on one of the most important quantum features---entanglement---we demonstrate that, for a broad class of common Hamiltonian models, one can design effective witnesses that detect both the presence and structure of entanglement over relatively long evolution times. Inspired by stabilizer-based simulation, we track the evolution of generalized stabilizers of the underlying state and use them to construct linear entanglement witnesses. Through numerical experiments on Heisenberg-type Hamiltonians with up to twelve qubits, we show that the required number of measurement settings can be kept at a modest scale as the system size increases, and entanglement detection remains effective over evolution times that significantly exceed those accessible to naive approaches. The corresponding calculations can be carried out largely symbolically. Furthermore, unlike accurate state simulation, the stabilizer-based design of entanglement witnesses can be performed in a much more coarse-grained, digitized manner. We hope these results will stimulate further exploration of the quantum control of large systems.

title: Graphene-Confined Growth of Few-Layer PtSe2 via One-Step Selenization
abstract: Platinum diselenide (PtSe$_2$), a member of the transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) family, is a promising material for next-generation electronic and optoelectronic applications due to its thickness-dependent properties, transitioning from semimetallic in bulk to semiconducting behavior at the few-layer limit. However, the scalable fabrication of large-area ultrathin PtSe$_2$ films remains challenging, as conventional selenization of pre-deposited Pt layers often leads to undesired three-dimensional clustered growth. This work explores a novel strategy for promoting two-dimensional growth of PtSe$_2$ by employing a graphene-mediated confinement approach. The method involves coating a Pt layer with graphene oxide (GO), followed by annealing in a selenium atmosphere, which results in the simultaneous formation of PtSe$_2$ and the reduction of GO to graphene. The graphene overlayer acts as a physical confinement layer, suppressing vertical growth and enabling the synthesis of graphene-confined PtSe$_2$ heterostructures on centimetre-scale substrates and promoting lateral connectivity of PtSe$_2$ regions observed by STEM. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), including temperature-resolved in situ atomic-resolution measurements, was used to investigate the influence of selenization temperature on the growth mechanism and structural evolution of PtSe$_2$ films. The results show that graphene confinement stabilizes lateral growth and promotes the formation of few-layer films with improved structural ordering. Beyond PtSe$_2$, this graphene-assisted approach provides a general strategy for fabricating and stabilizing ultrathin TMD layers, including those prone to environmental degradation, providing a new outlook for enabling detailed studies of their intrinsic properties.

title: Dynamical Properties of Perturbed Weighted Shifts
abstract: In this paper, sufficient conditions are established for diagonal perturbations of weighted shifts to be supercyclic, hypercyclic, and frequently hypercyclic, extending several classical results for weighted shifts to this more general setting. In addition, a complete analytic characterization of the shadowing property for these operators is obtained. Consequently, examples of frequently hypercyclic perturbed weighted shifts with the shadowing property are constructed.

title: Sharp lower bounds for bisections of graphs with bounded maximum degree
abstract: A bisection of a graph is a partition of its vertex set into two parts whose sizes differ by at most one. We prove that every graph with $m$ edges and maximum degree at most $k$ has a bisection of size at least $\frac{k+1}{2k}m$ when $k$ is odd, and at least $\frac{k+2}{2(k+1)}m$ when $k$ is even. Both bounds are sharp, with equality for complete graphs. This establishes the unweighted case of the bisection conjecture of Gerke, Gutin, Yeo and Zhou (arXiv 2024), removes the additive error from the corresponding bounds of Lee, Loh and Sudakov (JCTB 2013), and extends the odd-degree regular case proved by Bollobás and Scott (JGT 2004) to arbitrary graphs of bounded maximum degree. The proof combines the matching-and-pairing method with the Gallai--Edmonds decomposition. Hall's theorem controls the number of uncovered factor-critical components whose internal degrees are all even. A boundary-edge count bounds this obstruction by the total degree deficiency, while the remaining uncovered components supply the required pairing gain.

title: Mean-Variance Portfolio Selection: Statistical Properties and Distributionally Robust Optimization
abstract: We study Markowitz's mean-variance portfolio optimization problem. When practically using this model, the mean vector and the covariance matrix of the assets returns often need to be estimated from the sample data. The sample errors will be propagated to the optimization output. In this paper, we consider three commonly used mean-variance models and build the asymptotic properties for the conventional sample approximations that are widely adopted and studied, by leveraging the stochastic optimization theory. We show that for all three models, under certain conditions the sample approximations have the desired consistency and achieve a convergence rate of square root of sample size, and the asymptotic variance depends on the first four moments of the returns. To address the variability and the uncertainty in the data driven portfolio optimization, we further consider the distributionally robust optimization (DRO) for the mean-variance model. For the ambiguity sets constructed by the $ϕ$-divergence and the Wasserstein distance, we build the tractable reformulations for the DRO models. We conduct numerical experiments to test the asymptotic properties for the estimation. We also conduct experiments to illustrate that the asymptotic normality might not hold when the fourth moments of the returns do not exist.

title: EnRoute: Iterative Design and Evaluation of a Mobile App for Lower-Carbon Fashion and Transportation Choices
abstract: EnRoute is an iOS application designed to support more sustainable everyday choices in transportation and fast fashion consumption. We describe three design iterations and the user research and field evaluations that shaped each one. Interviews with 15 people from 12 countries informed Version I, which combined errand route planning with basic fashion guidance. A survey of 1,200 people in five countries found much stronger interest in sustainable shopping (78%) than in switching to lower-carbon transport (46%); respondents most often named limited public transport as the main barrier to lower-carbon travel. We therefore narrowed the focus to fashion. Version II added item-level garment scanning with a manual-entry fallback, a Sustainability Coefficient that rates items, and recommendations of more sustainable alternatives; in a two-week evaluation with 3,021 participants in eight countries, participants randomly assigned to receive a short tutorial and educational prompts viewed more recommended alternatives and reported larger gains in purchase intent than those without it. Version III shifted from "buy better" to "buy less," adding a wardrobe inventory, outfit matching, and a "Real Price" that combines cost per wear with estimated environmental and social costs. In a four-week pre/post pilot with 500 participants, self-reported monthly garment purchases fell from 2.9 to 1.9. We report descriptive results, discuss the substantial limitations of these uncontrolled and self-reported measures, and outline what the iterations suggest about designing for sustainable consumption.

title: Recurrent Barycenter Encoder: Prediction, Simulation and Applications to Time Series Analysis
abstract: This dissertation has two parts. In the first part we theoretically develop a framework that extends the optimal transport barycenter problem from independent data with observed covariates to processes whose relevant covariate is their own history. Given a stationary stochastic process, our framework shows there exists an invertible transport map that extracts from it an iid component whose distribution is the barycenter of the conditional distributions of the input process on its own past. This extracted iid sequence thus captures the innovation or noise component of the process that is not explained by the process's own past. In the second part of this thesis we implement an effective algorithm to solve this problem and test it against synthetic data generated with some well-known models in time series analysis for which the solution is known in closed-form. We then show how this method can be applied to build a predictive sampler for such processes, and assess the accuracy of this predictive sampler both with the aforementioned synthetic data and with real-world time series such as the S&P 500 and Bitcoin 4-hour returns, and the daily records of the North Atlantic Oscillation index from the NOAA Physical Sciences Laboratory. Finally, we demonstrate an application of the sampler to path simulation with a well-known time series model.

title: UltraBERT: Beyond the Limit of BERT Pre-Training
abstract: Recent bidirectional encoders have been modernized with innovations from causal large language models (LLMs). However, the pretraining recipe itself remains inherited from small-scale conventions, leaving encoders underoptimized, with no single model performing competitively across both classification and retrieval tasks. In this work, we investigate how far encoder performance can be pushed by revisiting core design choices in training, revealing three key findings: (1) Encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, indicating that additional compute past this point does not help. (2) Across model sizes, lower masking ratios benefit classification while higher ones benefit retrieval, contradicting prior work suggesting larger ratios for larger models. (3) Distillation with pruning improves classification at low masking ratios but degrades retrieval at high ones. Guided by these findings, we present UltraBERT, a single encoder that assigns separate LM heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricts the distillation objective to the low ratio. To our knowledge, UltraBERT is the first encoder to achieve state of the art on both classification and retrieval tasks, reaching 91.0 on GLUE and 47.7 on BEIR. Together, these results show how far encoder performance can be pushed and provide a principled basis for compute allocation, masking ratio design, and knowledge transfer in bidirectional models.

title: Is a 9B Decision Foundation Model Needed for Symptom-to-Disease Classification? Fine-Tuning Clef-Flash Against TF-IDF Baselines
abstract: Disease classification from patient-reported symptom descriptions is usually approached with lightweight discriminative models or with autoregressive large language models (LLMs), which understand language broadly but generate text token by token and require output parsing. We study decision foundation models, which score a closed set of candidate labels in a single forward pass without generating text. We adapt Clef-Flash, a 9-billion parameter decision model built on a Qwen3.5 backbone, to the 24-class Symptom2Disease benchmark using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) on a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases. The fine-tuned model reaches 95.42% accuracy (95% CI 91.98-97.42%) and a macro F1 of 0.9551, up from 65.00% for the unadapted weights (62.92% through the remote API). However, TF-IDF linear SVM and logistic regression baselines trained on the same split reach 98.75% (95% CI 96.39-99.57%) with sub-millisecond CPU inference, so on this benchmark the fine-tuned model offers no accuracy advantage over a well-tuned linear classifier. A Leave-One-Symptom-Out clause-ablation analysis of four illustrative narratives shows predictions depending on distinguishing clauses: in a psoriasis example, removing the clause describing silvery scales lowers the predicted probability from above 99.99% to 0.12% and shifts the prediction to impetigo, while removing other clauses changes it by less than 0.001 percentage points. Decision architectures deliver structured, single-pass predictions from large language backbones, but short, lexically distinctive benchmarks such as Symptom2Disease cannot show an advantage over simple baselines; validation on longer, real clinical text and clinician review are needed.

title: Appearance Compensation in Volume Rendering
abstract: Can a volume that reproduces every external RGB view still have an incorrect density? We study this question in emission-absorption rendering with an independently parameterized, physically bounded effective source. Appearance compensates a density change by replacing the radiance that it removes from the rest of each ray. We characterize the surviving density information with a shared spatial appearance field. Our first result is an optimal density-only gain after finite-degree spherical-harmonic source refitting. A coupled tensor gauge and physical localized packets identify the sharp limiting nonlinear inverse coefficient as its reciprocal. Our second result realizes positive gain at every fixed finite degree for a residual set of isotropic spatial sources at one fixed density. At the same references, growing angular capacity hides a fixed nonzero density error while retaining physicality and any prescribed finite set of smoothness bounds. Local identifiability and the absence of a capacity-uniform recovery modulus therefore coexist. Our third result constructs an exact physical SH2 ambiguity: central density doubles and relative density $L^2$ error exceeds $14.52\%$, yet every external RGB ray is unchanged. We connect these continuum results to shared finite representations, continuous pixel measurements and density-sensitive acquisition. Complete-class certificates separate SH0, SH1 and SH2 fits at one learned density. Finite-camera results expose the distinct role of spatial capacity, and transmission measurements separate otherwise identical RGB fields. Controlled training tests and captured-smoke profiles supply mechanism evidence with explicit observation scopes. The results show why rendering accuracy alone cannot certify density: recovery also depends on appearance capacity, spatial resolution and measurement design.

title: Photometric Identification and Dynamical Purification of Blue Horizontal Branch Stars in DESI MWS DR1
abstract: Blue horizontal-branch (BHB) stars are ideal tracers for mapping the structure of the Galactic stellar halo. However, traditional spectroscopic identification is limited by data quality and sample size, while broad-band photometric methods often achieve only moderate completeness and purity. Building upon the color-space BHB identification method of \citet{2025ApJS..278...62H}, we synthesize SkyMapper $(u,v,g,z)$ photometry from DESI MWS DR1 spectroscopy and identify 9,237 BHB candidates in the $(g-z)_0$--$(u-v)_0$ color space using the HDBSCAN clustering algorithm. We then construct a Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) Bayesian probability model with capture-recapture (C-R) prior to assign posterior membership probabilities, achieving a probability-weighted purity of 88.9\% and completeness of 94.2\%. Applying an escape-velocity cut based on the Galactic gravitational potential, we remove 1,461 contaminants with unphysical kinematic parameters, yielding a clean photometric BHB sample $\mathcal{S}_c$ of 7,776 stars (retention rate $R_{\rm keep} = 84.2\%$). Systematic analysis of the contaminants reveals that they are predominantly faint sources ($g\sim20$~mag) with very low signal-to-noise ratios (median SNR~$<$~5). When the BHB color--luminosity relation is incorrectly applied to these objects, their space velocities are amplified beyond the Galactic escape limit, confirming that the escape-velocity filter essentially acts as a physical detector of low-SNR--driven distance inflation.

title: InCLAD: A Continual Learning Benchmark for Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection
abstract: Industrial anomaly detection benchmarks have advanced rapidly, yet they remain largely static and therefore underrepresent deployment settings in which inspection systems must be extended from one industrial component to another over time. In our setting, continual industrial anomaly detection is framed as a task-incremental problem: each component defines a task, while the learning objective remains semi-supervised. The goal extends beyond conventional anomaly detection, since models should preserve their performance on all components as they are sequentially exposed to new components. This framing is especially relevant because many existing industrial pipelines either assume fully supervised defect labels or study only isolated datasets, leaving open the question of how semi-supervised anomaly detectors behave across a sequence of heterogeneous components. We address this gap by organizing the benchmark as a sequence of related component-level tasks and by defining multiple scenarios, including random, easy-to-hard, and hard-to-easy. In addition to single-dataset continual scenarios, we propose challenging scenarios spanning across multiple datasets. We further evaluate continual performance from two complementary perspectives: image-level anomaly detection and pixel-level anomaly localization. By recasting industrial anomaly detection as a continual benchmark rather than a static train/test problem, our work establishes a concrete path toward studying knowledge retention, adaptation, and generalization in evolving industrial environments.

title: What Drives AI Citations? Content, Retrieval and Model Knowledge in Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)
abstract: Generative search engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity now decide which Web pages users see as sources, and a growing industry of generative engine optimization advises publishers on how to earn these citations. We study what shapes citation in two 90-day collections of answers to commercial questions in contrasting markets: 158,099 answers with 468,037 citations. Comparing pages of the same website, content matters in one way: pages whose title and paragraphs match the questions people ask are cited more, whereas FAQ blocks, structured data, summary boxes and page speed appear effective only across websites. Page properties nevertheless explain little of the variation between pages of a website. Replaying the questions through the engines' APIs shows why. Every page ChatGPT cites is one its own search retrieved, and which pages that search retrieves, for sub-queries the model rewrites on every answer and that rarely coincide with Google's or Bing's results, explains far more of the variation than page properties (32% against 2.8%). Content acts mainly through this step, by matching the engine's queries in meaning. The model's own knowledge shapes it too: ChatGPT writes brands it knows into its searches, prefers websites it knows, and names brands without any supporting page, and controlled experiments show that brand names reorder its rankings of products with identical facts. Pages are thus cited when searched; brands are also named when remembered. The findings replicate in a market of small B2B vendors. We release data and code.

title: Faithful Query Resolution for Conversational Search
abstract: Conversational query rewriting makes context-dependent requests explicit for retrieval, but additional context can introduce an information need the user did not express. This raises a question about the interaction between query fidelity and retrieval breadth. This paper examines that interaction in behavior-adaptive conversational search, using iKAT SCAI 2026 as the evaluation setting. We compare five query-generation configurations within a behavior-adaptive assistant using BM25 and SPLADE retrieval. A minimal-faithful resolver preserves the user's wording and resolves only context-dependent references; weighted reciprocal rank fusion combines its rankings with those from a learned rewriter and the raw utterance. Offline evaluation shows that adding these formulations recovers recall over the faithful query alone, with a slight reduction in nDCG@10. Across our five iKAT SCAI 2026 submissions, the weighted configuration obtains the highest mean retrieval scores, reaching nDCG@5 of 0.534, a 5.3\% relative improvement over the strongest alternative. However, this retrieval advantage does not coincide with the highest conversational satisfaction scores. These findings motivate separating faithful query interpretation from retrieval expansion, while assessing their effects on conversational utility independently.

title: What Really Works for Universal Multimodal Embeddings? A Controlled Study of Contrastive Training Strategies
abstract: Contrastive learning has become the standard paradigm for multimodal representation learning, aligning semantically matched pairs while separating mismatched ones in a shared embedding space. Although various contrastive training strategies have been proposed across negative selection, batch construction, and gradient modulation, their actual effectiveness under controlled, reproducible conditions remains poorly understood. This motivates a fundamental question: Do sophisticated contrastive strategies consistently bring meaningful downstream gains in multimodal embedding learning? To address this, we systematically evaluate representative strategies under a unified benchmarking framework on MMEB. Surprisingly, direct evaluations reveal that most existing strategies offer marginal gains over a standard aligned baseline, with several even degrading overall performance. To uncover the underlying failure modes, we introduce an MLLM-as-a-Judge diagnostic framework that dissects top-1 retrieval behaviors into labeled positives, false negatives (unlabeled valid matches), and hard/easy negative errors. Our systematic analysis yields three key insights: (1) Gradient distortion: Upweighting gradients from high-similarity negatives consistently hurts downstream generalization; (2) Distribution illusion: Wider separation between positive and negative similarity distributions does not necessarily translate to better retrieval performance; and (3) Synergistic training: While false-negative mitigation or hard-batch construction yields limited gains in isolation, integrating hard-negative mining, false-negative mitigation, and hard-batch construction achieves optimal performance, delivering an average improvement of 6.0% on MMEB with Qwen2-VL-2B. Overall, our findings demystify popular contrastive strategies and provide actionable recipes for training universal multimodal embedding models.

title: Detecting photons in radiative Bhabha interaction with Si-strip and LYSO crystals at future e+e- colliders
abstract: Next-generation e+e-colliders have been proposed for the Super Tau Charm Facility covering center-of-mass energies sqrt(s) = 2-7 GeV, and for the Higgs Factories optimized for Z-pole physics and for HZ production. Luminosity can be determined by measuring forward Bhabha scattering. The QED cross-section calculation has reached a precision of better than 10^-3. Detecting radiative photons in Bhabha events provides a tool for validating higher-order corrections in theory. We propose the Forward Detector for detecting Bhabha scattering events at the STCF. The design uses high-resolution silicon detectors and finely segmented LYSO crystals to discriminate radiative photons from closely associated electrons. Bhabha scattering events are simulated with the BHLUMI and BHWIDE programs, and the detector is modeled using GEANT. Systematic uncertainties due to multiple scattering and bremsstrahlung in the beam pipe were evaluated. The potential for achieving precise measurements of radiative processes in Bhabha events is investigated.

title: Tate cohomology of unipotent cuspidal representations of finite groups of Lie type
abstract: Let $p$ be a prime and $k$ be an algebraic closure of the finite field with $p$ elements. Let $G$ be a connected reductive algebraic group over $k$, and let $F:G\rightarrow G$ be a Frobenius morphism, defining an $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational structure on $G$, where $q$ is a power of $p$. Let $\ell$ be a prime different from $p$ and $\ell\ne 2$. Let $Π$ be an $\ell$-adic cuspidal unipotent representation of $G^{F^\ell}$ such that $Π\simeq Π^σ$, where $σ$ is a generator the Galois group ${\rm Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{q^\ell}/\mathbb{F}_q)$. In this paper, we prove the irreducibility of the zeroth Tate cohomology group $\widehat{\rm H}^0(σ,\mathcal{L})$ and vanishing of the first Tate cohomology group $\widehat{\rm H}^1(σ,\mathcal{L})$ for any $G^{F^\ell}\rtimes{\rm Gal}(\mathbb{F}_{q^\ell}/\mathbb{F}_q)$-stable lattice $\mathcal{L}$ in $Π$, using the multiplicity-one property of a progenerator constructed via the generalized Gelfand-Graev representations and Harish-Chandra induction.

title: Training-Free Multi-Agent Cooperative Embodied Search from Uncertain Vision-Language Priors
abstract: Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.

title: Sparsity Saves Compute, Not Samples: Oracle Inequalities for Dense and Sparse Mixture of Experts
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine specialized experts through an input-dependent routing mechanism, and their sparse variants underpin many modern large-scale systems. Yet the statistical cost of adaptive routing remains only partially understood. We study the estimation error of least-squares MoE estimators when both the experts and the gating network are Lipschitz in their parameters. We represent each MoE as a gate--expert pair in a Gated Hilbert Space, whose norm $\|\cdot\|_Δ$ separates the contributions of routing and expert discrepancies. Using its empirical representation, we derive an oracle inequality with a fast rate of order $\tilde{\mathcal O}\big((Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}+d_{\mathrm{pr},g})/n\big)$ for dense MoEs with $K$ experts. For sparse Top-$k$ and Top-$p$ routing, the selection map is discontinuous in the gating parameters. We handle this by partitioning the gating class according to the selection patterns it induces on the sample. The resulting bounds match the dense rate up to an additive routing cost governed by the Natarajan dimension of the selector. We show that such a routing-complexity condition cannot be dropped: Lipschitz continuity in the parameters alone does not suffice. For linear softmax gating, the routing cost is of the same order as the gating term. Finally, for linear experts, we establish a matching minimax lower bound of order $Kd_{\mathrm{pr},e}/n$, showing that the rates are optimal up to logarithmic factors.

title: Homotopy for Rectangular Multiparameter Eigenvalue Problems
abstract: The rectangular multiparameter eigenvalue problem (rMEP) is a recently introduced form of an eigenvalue problem, in which we are looking for the combinations of parameters where the multivariate rectangular matrix loses full column rank. Existing numerical methods for rMEPs typically require substantial memory and are not suitable for problems with a large number of eigenvalues. We propose a novel numerical approach based on the homotopy method that has low memory requirements and can compute all eigenvalues of an rMEP. Moreover, the homotopy method is naturally parallelizable, providing a simple and efficient way to accelerate computations. An implementation, together with a collection of test examples, is available in a public repository.

title: Extreme Localization via a Singular Edge Mode in an Asymmetric Linkage System
abstract: Mechanical localized modes generally retain exponentially decaying tails, whereas confinement to a single structural unit is difficult to achieve without resonators, flat-band lattices or topological design. To address this need, an asymmetric linkage system is introduced in which geometry tunes a boundary mode from finite localization to its extreme limit. Each cell comprises two unequal rigid bars connected by a torsional spring and is described by one generalized coordinate. Linearization and coordinate transformation yield a tridiagonal model and closed-form expressions for the edge mode frequency and spatial decay ratio. The analysis identifies the configurations supporting a singular edge mode at which its decay ratio vanishes, leaving only the boundary cell active in the linear regime. Simulations show near-complete localization under finite-amplitude excitation, and experiments reproduce the configuration-dependent transition from bulk transmission to boundary confinement. These results establish a minimal and analytically tunable platform for mechanical localization

title: Exact Rank of the Largest Good Lattice Point Matrix
abstract: We prove that for every integer $n>2$ the largest good lattice point matrix $U_n=[u_h:h\in H_n]$, whose columns are generated by all integers $h<n$ coprime to $n$, has rank exactly $φ(n)/2+1$. The upper bound follows from the pairing identity $u_h+u_{n-h}=(n,\dots,n,2n)^{\top}$. For the lower bound the columns are centered and the resulting orbit under the multiplicative group $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is analysed by means of odd Dirichlet characters; the essential arithmetic input is the non-vanishing of $\sum_{a}a\,ψ(a)$ for odd primitive characters $ψ$, which is equivalent to Dirichlet's theorem $L(1,ψ)\neq 0$.

title: Information-Theoretic Foundations of Online Temperature Sampling
abstract: Repetitive, degenerate generation is a persistent failure of LLM decoding, and the standard remedies (temperature, nucleus, and top-$k$ sampling) are static heuristics. By Kac's lemma and the AEP, a stationary source takes time exponential in its entropy to repeat a block. We therefore maximize the entropy of the sampling distributions under one cross-entropy budget that keeps the output plausible under the model. Offline, the solution is temperature sampling, with the inverse temperature as the budget's Lagrange multiplier. \emph{Our contribution is the online problem}: the conditionals $p_1, p_2, \dots$ are revealed one at a time, and the sampling distribution $q_t$ must be chosen causally from $p_1, \dots, p_t$ while the budget couples the entire horizon. The optimal temperature is thus a global shadow price that must be estimated from a prefix. We propose Entropic Online Sampling (EOS), which re-solves for the temperature on each prefix. We prove it loses $O(R\log n)$ entropy against the offline optimum while overshooting the budget by $O(R\log n)$, with $R$ an instance-dependent drift parameter. A budget-tightened variant is exactly feasible at the same rate. Conversely, every exactly feasible online algorithm must lose $Ω(R)$, so EOS is optimal up to a $\log n$ factor. When the conditionals are drawn from a finite mixture, $R=\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$. Experiments confirm that EOS tracks the offline temperature and beats fixed-temperature sampling in entropy.

title: PAT: A Personality-Driven Augmentation and Transfer Learning Framework for Depression Detection on Social Media
abstract: Depression is a prevalent mental disorder that affects millions worldwide, with early detection crucial for effective intervention. While exist?ing methods have achieved promising results in automated depression detection, they face two key limitations: (1) noise in post screening: symptom-based semantic screening is easily misled by superficial lexical patterns, thereby introducing false-positive posts; (2) weak op?timization of the post encoder: relying solely on coarse user-level supervision signals pre?vents models from capturing depressive cues within individual posts. To address these limita?tions, we propose PAT, a Personality-driven Augmentation and Transfer learning frame?work. In the first phase, PAT optimizes a post?level encoder via a fine-grained contrastive learning objective, utilizing LLM-based data augmentation driven by classic personality the?ories to alleviate data scarcity. In the second phase, the trained post-level scorer is deployed for high-quality post filtering, while its en?coder parameters are seamlessly transferred for user-level tasks. Extensive experiments demon?strate that PAT significantly outperforms exist?ing methods. Furthermore, PAT delivers multi?granular interpretability by tracing post-level mental-state trajectories and highlighting key symptoms, thereby offering reliable diagnostic evidence for clinical practice.

title: Single-Measurement Hölder Stability for a Spatial Coefficient in a Wave Equation with Principal Memory
abstract: We study the recovery of a spatial coefficient in the principal memory flux of a three-dimensional wave equation with the prescribed exponential relaxation kernel $βe^{-βt}$, where $β>0$ is known. From a single finite-time lateral Cauchy measurement generated by one fixed, coefficient-independent initial displacement that is affine near the unknown region, with zero initial velocity, we establish global uniqueness and conditional $L^2$-Hölder stability. Two difficulties arise in this setting. The affine initial displacement makes the initial acceleration vanish in the unknown region, while the coefficient-difference equation contains a divergence-form source whose direct $L^2$ estimate loses a spatial derivative. We establish an acoustic Carleman estimate that controls the vector source and its time derivative without spatially differentiating the source. The affine condition identifies the relevant initial trace with a directional derivative of the coefficient difference, and the quadratic temporal vanishing of the source permits absorption in the weighted estimate. A transport estimate then yields stability uniformly over a bounded, uniformly coercive $W^{5,\infty}$ coefficient class, without an ordering condition or a smallness assumption near a reference coefficient.

title: Belief Embedding Tree Search
abstract: Beliefs in a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) are posterior distributions over the hidden state given the agent's history of actions and observations. They summarize everything the history says about the state, so planning in a POMDP is planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs. Belief MDPs have continuous state spaces even for finite POMDPs, and exact planning in them is intractable in general. Planners must therefore approximate beliefs and estimate values. Monte Carlo planners do both inside a search tree, with an approximate belief at every node and a value estimate at every leaf. Approximations usually consist of sets of sampled states, with leaf values coming from rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or learned networks. Policies and values computed from these approximations are limited by their quality, and prior methods with learned networks rely on hand-chosen summaries of the sampled states. A belief representation should be computable from the parent node's representation through the POMDP's dynamics, let the search sample from it, and be learned so that it provides the information that policies and value functions need. We present Belief Embedding Tree Search (BETS), a Monte Carlo planner that meets these requirements by representing each node's belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE) while updating it through the POMDP dynamics. BETS trains its belief model alongside its policy and value networks through experience, with the realized hidden state of the POMDP as the belief model's training target. We evaluate BETS on six configurations of RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan against BetaZero and three planners without learned components. BETS is competitive or leading on all six, while every baseline falls far behind on at least one. Where beliefs are highest-dimensional, it outperforms them by a large margin, even without search.

title: Multilevel Monte Carlo for Zeroth-Order Stochastic Bilevel Optimization with Inexact Lower Level Solves
abstract: Variational regularization techniques are dominant in the field of mathematical imaging. The expressiveness of these methods heavily depends on the adopted regularization formulation which usually involves a number of parameters which have to be fine-tuned by the user. To circumvent the heavy computational costs associated with this parameter tuning, data-driven learning strategies have turned out to be a useful strategy. Selecting parameters by learning from data gives rise to a hierarchical (bilevel) optimization problem, which is in general computationally hard to solve. Our aim in this paper is to develop a data-efficient solution strategy for the bilevel learning problem. To that end, we propose a multilevel Monte Carlo derivative-free optimization method that couples Gaussian smoothing of the upper-level objective (parameter selection) with a hierarchy of lower-level (variational regularization) solution accuracies. Being agnostic towards the specific way the lower-level problem is solved, we derive explicit oracle complexity and computational cost statements for approximately solving the entire bilevel learning problem. Our statements are parameterized by the employed lower-level solution method, thus allowing for a direct cost accounting from the variational reconstruction method to the parameter selection problem. This enables us to give a universal end-to-end complexity analysis of bilevel learning, valid for the most important optimization routines in inverse problems, rather than for a specific choice of methods.

title: Nonlinear waves and conservative transport in soluble-surfactant falling films on compliant substrates
abstract: We investigate finite-amplitude waves in a liquid film containing a soluble surfactant as it flows down an inclined compliant substrate. The coupled motion of the liquid and a spring-backed plate is described by a conservative weighted-residual model, which also accounts for surfactant transport in the bulk and at the free surface. The reduction retains viscous terms arising from wall motion, and its pressure closure recovers fluid added mass under uniform translation. Comparison with the coupled Orr-Sommerfeld problem gives a difference of approximately $1\%$ in the peak growth rate of the film mode at $Re=25$. Nonlinear computations are then used to examine travelling states and their dependence on substrate properties and surfactant coupling. Along the prescribed stiffness-damping path, substrate displacement decreases by more than four orders of magnitude, while wave speed changes by less than $1\%$. The extrema of free-surface elevation and liquid thickness vary differently, so surface height alone does not reliably indicate film thinning over a deformable support. In the cases studied, Marangoni coupling reduces surfactant localisation and weakens the wave and substrate response. Moving-frame reconstruction reveals recirculation near the wave crest and distinguishes propagation of the deformation pattern from transverse substrate motion. The load-work budget identifies capillary pressure as the principal net source of substrate work for the two compliant supports considered. A control calculation in which stiffness is varied at fixed damping shows a substantial change in damping loss but a comparatively small change in deformation.

title: Use Of Convolutional Neural Networks In Detection Of Branch Dieback Disease In Pequi Trees
abstract: This study evaluates and compares five convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, AlexNet, Inception, LeNet, VGG16, and MobileNet, for diagnosing branch dieback (seca-dos-ponteiros) in pequi trees (Caryocar brasiliense). This phytopathology represents a severe threat to tree development and fruit yield, causing substantial economic and ecological losses across the Brazilian Cerrado. The methodology implements computer vision techniques using deep learning frameworks to process and evaluate a field dataset expanded to 6,272 multi-scale images, captured via UAV and handheld sensors under uncontrolled illumination. The models were trained to detect pathological visual patterns across leaves, branches, and canopies. The experimental initial results reveal that architectural complexity did not guarantee diagnostic reliability, heavily parameterized networks experienced optimization failures (VGG16 collapsed into majority-class prediction), whereas compact architectures achieved greater stability. MobileNet delivered the most competitive overall performance, obtaining the highest Precision (0.71) and ROC-AUC (0.63), closely followed by LeNet (AUC = 0.62). These findings indicate the viability of lightweight CNNs as foundational tools for automated phytosanitary surveillance of native flora in resource-constrained field environments.

title: Proof of Two Conjectural $q$-Supercongruences Related to Van Hamme's $\mathrm{(G.2)}$ Supercongruence
abstract: In this paper, we prove two conjectures concerning parametric $q$- supercongruences related to Van Hamme's $\mathrm{(G.2)}$ supercongruence. First, we confirm Tang\rq s conjecture \cite[Conjecture $4.1$]{Tang G2} by establishing the corresponding congruences modulo $[m]Φ_m(q)^2$. Second, we prove a conjecture of Wang and Xu \cite[Conjecture $2$]{WangXu24}, extending their $q$-supercongruence modulo $Φ_m(q)^5$ to modulo $[m]Φ_m(q)^4$ when $m\equiv1\pmod4$.

title: Rate-Based Causal Discovery for Heavy-Tailed Models
abstract: In many complex systems, such as river networks and financial markets, extreme events propagate from causes to their effects, and the largest observations carry the most information about the underlying causal structure. Existing methods for causal discovery in extremes, however, are tailored to specific mechanisms, such as linear or max-linear models. This work develops causal discovery for heavy-tailed homogeneous structural causal models, a flexible class that contains linear, max-linear and norm-type mechanisms, which may differ from node to node. In these models, the causal structure is encoded by ancestral impulse responses, which measure how a shock at one node is transmitted to its descendants. We propose the extremal minimum ratio estimator of these responses, which uses only observations in which the potential cause is extreme. The estimator is consistent under regular variation alone, and we derive its exact rates of convergence and limiting distributions, which depend on both the causal relation and the type of mechanism. Building on these rates, we construct consistent estimators of the causal order and of the full set of ancestral relations, using a threshold that adapts to the data and requires no knowledge of the tail index. The method is illustrated on simulated data and on river discharges in the upper Danube basin.

title: On the Structural Optimization of Industrial Control Systems Using Metaheuristic Algorithms
abstract: The paper addresses the synthesis of a cost-optimal hardware architecture of the automated process control system (APCS) for continuous processes. The problem is formalized as the search for a minimum-cost rooted tree of devices subject to constraints on the number of I/O channels, the types and number of communication interfaces, the information capacity of processors, the regulation time and the reliability. The signals are grouped by control rooms. The problem is NP-hard, and a hybrid method is proposed that combines a deterministic hierarchy construction with a modified ant colony optimization (ACO) for device-type selection, enhanced by an adaptive heuristic. On ten instances the method is compared with a genetic algorithm (GA), particle swarm optimization (PSO), simulated annealing (SA) and CP-SAT over 30 runs each. By the best found cost the hybrid ACO outperforms GA, PSO and SA on all instances with more than 100 IOs (by 14-38 %) and runs 9-14 times faster. By the median cost, however, the deterministic-greedy baselines are more reliable (GA attains the best Friedman rank) because the cost of the ACO runs is highly variable. All differences are confirmed by the Friedman and Wilcoxon tests. The method targets the early-design search for the cheapest feasible architecture and synthesizes one within minutes at industrial scale (A up to 1086).

title: Scalar wave dark matter imprints on binary black hole mergers: dependence on field mass and density
abstract: Dark matter environments can modify binary black hole mergers and imprint their gravitational-wave signals. We perform numerical-relativity simulations of nonspinning binary black holes immersed in complex scalar-field clouds, considering mass ratios $q=1,2,3,$ and $4$ and varying both the dimensionless scalar-field mass $\hat m_Φ=m_ΦM_0$ and initial amplitude $Π_0$, which controls the density. Our initial data keep the scalar energy-density profile and binary geometry unchanged when varying $\hat m_Φ$ at fixed $Π_0$, allowing the dynamical effect of the field mass to be isolated. We find that the scalar environment generally accelerates the merger and significantly modifies the gravitational-wave signal. For unequal-mass binaries, differential scalar-field accretion changes the horizon-mass ratio during inspiral, weakly at low density but substantially at high density, thereby increasing the binary asymmetry before merger. Dense scalar environments suppress the energy and angular momentum carried by gravitational waves. Lighter scalar fields propagate more efficiently to large radii, whereas heavier fields remain more localized and show stronger inward energy transport. Scalar angular-momentum transport is more complex, showing nonmonotonic behavior and even direction reversal near the binary. For unequal-mass systems, gravitational and scalar radiation both carry net linear momentum, and their relative orientation determines whether the recoil is enhanced or suppressed. The largest kick is $2063.6~{\rm km,s^{-1}}$ for $q=2$, $\hat m_Φ=0$, and $Π_0=0.0100$, compared with $137.8~{\rm km,s^{-1}}$ in vacuum. These results show that the scalar-field mass and density jointly control the binary asymmetry, dynamics, radiative channels, and momentum balance.

title: Multi-Agent Learning of Reactive Strategies in Iterated Games
abstract: Learning agents, whether humans or algorithms, adapt to one another rather than to a fixed environment. Selfish learning need not produce a good outcome for the group, especially when learners face a social dilemma. The iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) is the classical example, but it is usually studied in populations of agents who imitate successful strategies. Here, we instead study selfish gradient ascent learners on the two-dimensional space of reactive strategies. A reactive strategy is described by two continuous traits: reciprocity, the chance of cooperating after the co-player cooperates, and forgiveness, the chance of cooperating after the co-player defects. Each learner updates its strategy in the direction that most rapidly improves its payoff against all other learners, by an amount governed by its learning rate. We show that heterogeneity in learning rates can qualitatively change the long-term outcome: a population with uniform learning rates converges to always-defect (ALLD), whereas a population with variable learning rates approaches generous-tit-for-tat (GTFT), which produces nearly optimal collective payoffs. In simulations, every population passes through a transient state of minimal forgiveness, in which the distribution of reciprocity determines the outcome. Variable learning rates promote cooperation because slow learners preserve high reciprocity until the population reaches this state. We prove sufficient conditions on the distribution of reciprocity for convergence to ALLD or to tit-for-tat (TFT). Variable learning rates also allow cooperation to recover from perturbation, which is provably impossible under uniform learning. These results suggest that purely selfish and myopic learning can produce persistent cooperation provided the population has intrinsic variability in learning rates.

title: Trace Evolution Bench: Measuring Whether Agents Improve from Their Own Environment Traces
abstract: Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint Gain: held-out success after an update minus success before. That difference can credit a frozen rescore as evolution. We introduce Trace Evolution Bench (TEB), a protocol that separates that rescore from a context or weight update, together with three frozen 80/20/40 packs. An update is accepted only when validation does not fall, held-out identifiers never enter the update, and a text update is not ranked with a weight update. The primary scoreboard is coding, graded by hidden unit tests in a closed workspace. On that pack (40 held-out tasks, one family), DeepSeek v4 Pro under no_evolve never changes its policy yet moves 7.5, 5.0, and 12.5 percentage points across three seeds. Of nine text-update cells inspired by GEPA, ACE, and ExpeL, seven have positive excess above that seed's own band, and one gepa_llm seed moves down by the width of its band (-12.5, regression 0.48). GLM and MiniMax do not reproduce that seven-of-nine pattern. No method stays above its own band on every seed of all three models: GLM has two paired cells above their own bands, and MiniMax expel_llm seed 44 is a third (regression 0.30). The methods were fixed on a validation screen before held-out was read. Office, graded by rule-bounded delivery, and manufacturing table QA are separate packs: office DeepSeek does not exceed its own bands (widest 17.5 points), and manufacturing has no paired positive excess beyond its seed band.

title: Select or Rewrite: Oracle-Guided Fine-Tuning for Generative ASR Post-Editing from N-Best Hypotheses
abstract: Large language models can post-edit ASR by using linguistic context to compare N-best hypotheses and rewrite the transcript when needed, often improving WER without retraining the recognizer. However, prompt-only correction is brittle: it may over-edit when top-1 is correct and hallucinate when the reference is absent, and often needs very large models. We propose oracle-guided fine-tuning that turns N-best lists into supervision via three curated pools: corrections (reference in the list but not top-1) to teach selection, regularizers (top-1 correct) to discourage unnecessary rewrites, and hard negatives (reference absent) to suppress hallucination. Fine-tuning on this data provides more effective supervision than random subset fine-tuning for learning a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy, with the clearest gains from around 3B parameters on the proprietary dataset but less conclusive results on CommonVoice, a divergence suggesting that public read-speech text may overlap with LLM pretraining and mask genuine post-editing gains.

title: Almost every Boolean function has central threshold degree
abstract: The polynomial threshold degree (or threshold degree) of a Boolean function is the least degree of a real polynomial whose sign represents it. We prove that almost every Boolean function has polynomial threshold degree among the central one or two integers. More precisely, a uniformly chosen Boolean function on $n$ variables has threshold degree either $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ or $\lceil n/2\rceil$, except with probability at most $\exp(-c2^{n/2}/n)$, for an absolute constant $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$. The paper proves a 1991 conjecture of Aspnes, Beigel, Furst and Rudich. It also proves a 1991 conjecture of Wang and Williams for even $n$ and its main concentration assertion for odd $n$. A parity example gives a lower bound on the exceptional probability whose exponent differs from ours by a factor of order $n$. The proof relates polynomial sign representation to recovery of Reed--Muller codes from random erasures, and combines sharp-threshold estimates with bounds on generalized Hamming weights and minimum distance.

title: The Optimal Decoder is Tilted Temperature
abstract: Larger sample budgets benefit from higher sampling temperatures in LLMs, but what temperature tuning optimizes and why it works remain poorly understood. We seek to answer these questions: we pose decoding as pass@$k$ maximization subject to two constraints that encode critical decoding failure modes: an entropy floor preventing diversity collapse, and a cross-entropy ceiling preventing implausibility. We prove that this maximization takes the form of a single closed-form conditional sampling rule, the \emph{tilted temperature} $q^\star \propto \bigl(p e^{ηV}\bigr)^{1/T}$. Here, the tilt comes from a verifier potential $V$ that quantifies how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies represent special cases. We further show that, under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with sample size $k$, the resulting optimal temperature increases with $k$, turning empirical choice into a theorem. The optimum still needs the unknown verifier potential, which we estimate using two design approaches. In the online setting, our J-EOS algorithm jointly tracks the two constraint multipliers and learns the verifier potential from binary pass/ fail feedback alone. In the offline setting, we show that when the model is calibrated, its log-probability tracks correctness up to an affine map. Under this condition, the tilt collapses into the exponent and the optimum reduces to ordinary temperature sampling. Calibrated Temperature Decoding (CTD) then fits one scalar offline and samples with zero additional inference-time overhead relative to temperature sampling. Building on these decision rules, we design a practical decoding algorithm for code generation and evaluate it alongside CTD on benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, showing improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines.

title: How Language-Independent Are Emotional Attributes? A Study on Training Data Scaling and Cross-Lingual Generalization
abstract: Current state-of-the-art Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) systems rely on lots of training data, which is available only for a few languages such as English. For low-resource languages, using a cross-lingual model or adapting it to the target language might be an alternative to training a mono-lingual model from scratch. However, it is not clear what constitutes a "low-resource", i.e. where model adaptation loses its edge over the mono-lingual approach. We investigate this topic by training and adapting several SER models on English and Mandarin data, focusing on the emotional attributes of arousal, valence and dominance. Our results show that, for arousal, model adaptation is beneficial even with two hours of data, while for valence 10-20 hours of adaptation material is required to match the performance of a mono-lingual model trained with 100 hours of data. This indicates that task-specific model adaptation may be an effective approach in low-resource speech emotion recognition problems.

title: Probing eV-scale sterile neutrinos with neutrinoless double-beta decay and beta decay
abstract: An eV-scale sterile Majorana neutrino can suppress neutrinoless double-beta decay through destructive interference with the active-neutrino contribution, weakening the resulting constraints on sterile-neutrino parameters. We investigate how complementary beta-decay information restricts this cancellation in the 3+1 framework. Using updated oscillation parameters that include the first JUNO results, we determine the allowed sterile-neutrino mass and mixing regions for both normal and inverted ordering. We show that an upper limit on the effective beta-decay mass $m_β$ of the three light neutrinos strengthens the constraints from neutrinoless double-beta decay alone. The beta-decay bound restricts the light-neutrino masses and hence the cancellation between the active and sterile contributions to $m_{ββ}$. We derive analytic expressions for the resulting boundaries and use complex-plane geometry to explain the allowed values of the sterile Majorana phase $α_4$ for a finite $|m_{ββ}|$ limit. For the mixing considered, normal ordering allows a broad range of $α_4$ at small sterile masses, whereas inverted ordering favors values near $π$. The allowed phase range narrows as the sterile mass approaches its upper bound or the limit on $|m_{ββ}|$ becomes more stringent.

title: Deep Learning-based Semantic Segmentation of Dental Radiographs: Comparative Evaluation of PSPNet, DeepLabv3, UNet, and UNet++
abstract: Accurate and efficient analysis of dental radiographs has become increasingly important for disease diagnosis and clinical decision making. In particular, dental radiographs segmentation plays a critical role as it is challenging due to several reasons, such as low contrast, noise in the images, variations in the image quality, etc. Previous studies have primarily addressed these challenges using convolutional neural networks (CNN)-based models. However, direct comparison of these segmentation models is still challenging due to the variations among the experimental settings. Therefore, we mainly compared four segmentation models, including Pyramid Scene Parsing Network (PSPNet), DeepLabV3, UNet, and UNet++, through a fair, controlled experimentation setting under varying conditions such as image sizes and batch sizes. For this, we used 1269 dental radiography images, and prior to training, we implemented a series of preprocessing techniques. To assess the models, we used several metrics, including Dice coefficient (DICE), Intersection over Union (IoU), accuracy, precision, training and validation losses. According to our results, UNet++ demonstrated the highest IoU score of 0.6719, and a DICE value of 0.7869, showing superior results in terms of segmentation, specifically when configured with an image size of 300x300 and a batch size of 16. In addition, we also explored the effect of image resolutions and batch sizes on model performance and accuracy under different architectures. Therefore, this study provides insights into the strengths of different segmentation models and the potential of deep learning-based semantic segmentation methods for improving automated dental radiograph analysis.

title: Exposing AI Inference as a Telco Network API over the 5G User Plane
abstract: Supporting edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) inference as a network service is challenging because current mobile systems can transport tensors but do not expose or understand the inference context that gives those tensors operational meaning. Prior studies have addressed this gap through dynamic partitioning, collaborative inference, and split pipelines; however, these solutions remain application-bound, network-blind, or context-free. This work proposes Inference on Demand (IoD), an inference-on-demand abstraction that exposes split inference through a CAMARA-like Application Program Interface (API) and carries a split-aware tensor context in-band across the 5G user plane path. We evaluate the IoD on a programmable user plane function (UPF)-based testbed using a partitionable visual AI workload, showing that adaptive split selection can operate as a network-facing service while avoiding the rigid cost profile of static configurations. Including our findings, split inference becomes more than offloading when the service intent, runtime partitioning, and tensor transport are made visible to the mobile data plane. This opens a path toward network-native AI services, in which programmable telco infrastructure coordinates computation, context, and connectivity for user-facing applications.

title: Randomized Experiments with Ambiguous Record Linkage
abstract: Randomized experiments are often linked to administrative data to measure outcomes, but coarse identifiers can leave multiple administrative records consistent with each experimental unit. We show that unbiased estimation of the sample average treatment effect is possible without resolving these ambiguous links or specifying an outcome model. Our key linkage requirement is that the true administrative outcome is contained among the candidate outcomes for each experimental unit. We characterize the precision cost of linkage ambiguity and study two complementary ways to mitigate it: regression adjustment and reweighting based on observed linkage characteristics. We establish finite-sample and asymptotic properties of these estimators and develop valid randomization-based and large-sample inference.

title: Global Disaster Risk Assessment Using World Risk Index Data: A Geospatial and Visual Analytics Approach
abstract: The world has seen several threats that include resource depletion, food security, poverty and inequality, difficulties associated with urbanization, migration, and environmental effects. The World Risk Index (WRI) is a metric that is used to measure the susceptibility of nations against natural disasters and related risks that is reported by the Humanitarian Data Exchange. The WRI is comprised of factors such as susceptibility, vulnerability to natural hazards, and coping mechanisms. The WRI index has allowed to recognize regions in advance in order to face threats and situations beforehand. This study was conducted by analyzing the data that was related to years from 2000 to 2025 using data visualization techniques. Python related libraries of Matplotlib, Seaborn, and Geopandas were used due to their efficiency and usability in analyzing WRI data. As per the analysis, it was identified that countries of Philippines, Mexico, Indonesia, and India were recorded with high WRI index values that showed these nations should be prepared for natural disasters and situations.
