abstract: Under a limited context budget, a long-term agent must recall not merely memories that are individually relevant, but evidence that is collectively sufficient for the current query. Conventional memory access retrieves, scores, and truncates memories, often spending multiple context slots on redundant facts while leaving complementary evidence behind. We cast the read phase of long-term memory as query-conditioned evidence composition: each memory is valued by what it adds beyond the evidence already selected. We instantiate this operation with MemPursuit, a training-free mechanism that uses the residual of a sparse convex query reconstruction as a representation-space proxy for what the current memory set is missing. By reusing the query and candidate embeddings already available from retrieval, MemPursuit progressively composes nested evidence contexts without invoking a language model or cross-encoder to score each query--memory pair. The effectiveness of our method is verified on 3 popular benchmarks in comparison to strong baselines. In fixed-budget LoCoMo experiments, MemPursuit improves end-to-end accuracy by 7.2 percentage points at Top-10 and 5.5 percentage points at Top-20, with consistent gains across multiple memory frameworks, while achieving a 32.9$\times$ speedup in median reranking latency over fully batched BGE-v2-m3. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/FengQi-HITSZ/MemPursuit.

title: A trace lower bound for totally positive units in $\mathbb{Q}(ζ_p)^+$ and its application to fusion category
abstract: Let $p = 4q + 1$ be a prime integer, where $q$ is an odd prime. Let $L = \mathbb{Q}(ζ_p)^+$ denote the maximal totally real subfield of the $p$-th cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(ζ_p)$. In this paper, we prove that if $U_L^+=U_L^2$ (i.e., every totally positive unit is a square in $L$), then for any non-trivial subfield $K \subseteq L$ and any non-trivial totally positive unit $\varepsilon \in U_K^+$, the absolute trace satisfies the sharp lower bound $\Tr_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\varepsilon) \ge p - 4$. As an application, we show that a spherical fusion category $\C$ with global dimension $\dim(\mathcal{C})=p=4q+1$ is pointed, where $2$ is a primitive root modulo $q$, or $p=4q+1<2^{22}$ and $p\neq 29$.

title: New topological phase transitions in $κ$-deformed $ϕ^4$ lattice models
abstract: This paper explores topological phase transitions in the momentum space of the $κ$-deformed $ϕ^4$ lattice model within the mean-field approximation. We show that the double-well structure of the momentum space gives rise to degenerate momentum states at high energies and that this change is marked by a phase transition. We investigate this transition using both numerical and analytical methods, with the analytical approach based primarily on singularity theory. Our numerical analysis shows that the energy at which the topological phase transition occurs is related to the noncommutative parameter by the simple power law $E \sim 1/α^{4}$. By mapping the constant-energy-level surface to the $A_{3}$ singularity, we obtain the same result analytically. We also present results unique to noncommutative systems, showing that the fraction of particles in degenerate momentum states has a nonzero commutative limit. As a nonperturbative effect, this result provides a testable prediction for the existence of noncommutative spacetime.

title: SurgCast: Action-Conditioned Future Skeletons for Controllable Surgical World Models
abstract: Surgical world models must turn prospective robot actions into visually faithful, structurally consistent instrument motion. We introduce SurgCast, which predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and future actions, then uses the forecast to control video generation. Dual-path injection combines skeleton geometry with derived, instrument-specific motion descriptors through geometric residuals and conditioning modulation. Both paths complement native action conditioning and are retained in a four-step causal student. On SutureBot and SRTH-Porcine-Cholei, the teacher and student improve all seven reported quality and instrument-consistency metrics over their respective direct-action baselines; teacher FVD decreases by 37.6% and 67.3%. Ablations show that future actions improve skeleton prediction and that combining both injection paths performs best across all six metrics under predicted skeletons. These results support using predicted articulated structure and its motion semantics as a control interface for surgical video prediction. Project videos and examples are available at https://surgcast.netlify.app/.

title: Weighted Frames and the Douglas-Foias problem
abstract: Let $\mathbf{T}=(T_1,\ldots,T_n)$ be a commuting tuple of bounded linear operators on a separable Hilbert space $\mathcal{K}$, and let $\{a_α\}_{α\in\mathbb{Z}_+^n}$ be strictly positive weights. Under mild assumptions on the weights, we characterize the weighted frame vectors and weighted Parseval frame vectors, that is, those vectors $ξ$ for which $\{a_α\mathbf{T}^αξ\}_{α\in\mathbb{Z}_+^n}$ is a frame or a Parseval frame. We reduce the problem to characterizing surjective module maps from the reproducing analytic Hilbert module associated with the weights onto the module $\mathcal{K}$, equipped with the module structure defined by $\mathbf{T}$. It is shown that weighted Parseval frame vectors differ by a unimodular scalar whenever they exist. If the kernel defined by the weights has the complete Nevanlinna--Pick property, then any two associated weighted frame vectors are similar whenever they exist. We also focus on the case of the Hardy kernel on the polydisc, that is, the case $a_α=1$ for all $α\in\mathbb{Z}^n_+$. This is related to the famous Douglas--Foias problem: whether two similar quotient modules of the Hardy spaces $H^2(\mathbb{D}^n)~(n>1)$ are equal. Our result shows that the answer is negative. This leads to the conclusion that frame vectors for representations of $\mathbb{Z}_+^n$ $(n>1)$ may fail to be similar. It means that, for the case $a_α=1$, there exists a tuple $\mathbf{T}=(T_1,\dots,T_n)$ with $n>1$ on $\mathcal{K}$ and two distinct frame vectors for $\mathbf{T}$ which are not similar.

title: Distributed Economic Dispatch Scheme of A BESS Network with A Switching Utility Grid in Energy Internet Paradigm via Reset Consensus Method
abstract: This article aims to design a distributed economic dispatch (ED) scheme based on marginal cost (MC) consensus for a battery energy storage system (BESS) network considering the utility grid switching. Due to the low control accuracy and slow convergence speed of previous schemes, some important changes have been made in this article. Firstly, the feedback coupling term is introduced into the closed-loop error to further improve the stability and convergence rate of the controller. Then, a proportional integral (PI) controller with a reset mechanism is implemented in the designed scheme, which improves the speed and control accuracy of MC consensus. The performance of a control system with a reset mechanism is well guaranteed by analyzing the eigenvalues of the corresponding matrix. Finally, some tests focus on UG switching, time phased pricing, load switching, a BESS/agent plug and play, and large-scale system applications to illustrate the effectiveness and progressiveness of the design scheme.

title: Post-critically finite polynomials in characteristic $p$
abstract: It follows from the compactness of the connectedness locus that the locus of PCF polynomials in the moduli space of polynomials of degree d (at least 2) over the complex number is a countable union of zero-dimensional subvarieties. Over fields of characteristic p the analogous claim is certainly false, so it is natural to ask how large the components of the PCF locus can be. We show that the components of the PCF locus in the moduli space of polynomials of degree d over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p>0 have dimension at most d/p and that this bound is sharp, in the strong sense that for every p and d there are infinitely many distinct PCF components whose dimension is the greatest integer no greater than this bound (except in the case $p=d=2$).

title: One Goodness-of-Fit Test Is Not Enough: Error-Controlled Localization of Misfit in Logistic Risk Models
abstract: A goodness-of-fit test tells whether a logistic risk model fits, but the analyst also needs to know what is wrong: an overall risk that is too high is repaired by updating the intercept, risks that are too extreme by recalibration, a curved relation between score and risk by a flexible recalibration, and misfit within groups of patients only by revising the model. We split any misfit into these four parts, which are orthogonal and match the calibration hierarchy. Each part gets a group of score tests that sees that part only, and the failing parts are named by closed testing. In external validation, in large samples and for small departures, a part is wrongly named with probability at most the chosen level, and the highest part named points to the lightest update that removes the misfit. Checking a model on its development data never sees an error in the overall risk or the calibration slope, and with binary or skewed covariates it can mistake misfit within patient groups for a curved link. External validation sees all four parts, for any prediction model. In simulations it kept its error rate when the model was right and for small departures, and usually pointed to the right update. On intensive-care data its verdicts for one model differed in-sample, on similar patients and after transport.

title: Transport Polynomial Exactness for Direct ALE-DG Methods with Nonsmooth mesh motion: A Conservative Coefficient-Evolution Framework
abstract: High-order direct arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian discontinuous Galerkin (ALE-DG) methods can suffer severe order reduction under nonsmooth mesh motion despite satisfying the geometric conservation law (GCL). To address this limitation, we propose a new ALE-DG framework applicable to moving triangular and quadrilateral meshes. This framework successfully overcomes the uniform Lipschitz constraint inherent in existing direct ALE-DG methods, retaining high-order accuracy even when the mesh-velocity gradients are unbounded. This capability is driven by transport polynomial exactness (TPE($k$)), which is a structural property stronger than the GCL. TPE($k$) ensures the exact transport of polynomials of degree at most $k$ under arbitrary mesh motion. To incorporate TPE($k$) into a direct ALE-DG method, we introduce a coefficient-evolution (CE) formulation. Reconciling strict local conservation, an indispensable requirement for accurate shock capturing, with the preservation of the TPE(\(k\)) property constitutes the principal technical challenge. We resolve this by evolving the coefficients using the third-order strong-stability-preserving Runge--Kutta method, paired with a conservative correction executed via Simpson's rule integration. Crucially, this correction strictly vanishes for exactly transported quadratic polynomials, thereby ensuring that our third-order scheme rigorously satisfies the TPE($2$) property. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed scheme retains third-order accuracy when the discrete mesh-velocity Lipschitz estimate grows as $\mathcal O(h^{-1})$, whereas a representative existing direct ALE-DG scheme exhibits order reduction under the same mesh motion. Tests with discontinuous solutions further demonstrate robust and high-resolution performance under random and Lagrangian mesh motions.

title: Learned Graph Bases for Neural Operators on Power-System Transients
abstract: Fourier neural operators predict power-system transient trajectories with high accuracy. We extend this line of work by examining the choice of spatial spectral basis, studying both the graph Fourier transform derived from the grid's own coupling network and learnable bases trained from that starting point and from a Fourier control. Evaluated in one controlled pipeline across three protocols spanning unseen fault locations and shifted operating regimes, the learnable bases improve on a parameter- and budget-matched DFT variant by 7-14% in distribution, with per-case significance on both in-distribution protocols and no loss on the third; the gain comes from adaptation rather than from the coordinates alone. We further characterize the regime dependence of this gain, identifying its cause, locus, and continuity, and show that a resolution requires no new model: averaging the learned and frozen variants gives the best shift-robust predictor, while their disagreement provides a label-free alarm that flags every shifted case with no false alarms.

title: Theoretical Investigation of Nonclassical Directional Emission in 1D and 2D Quantum-Dot Antenna Arrays and Quantum DoA Estimation
abstract: A quantum-dot array prepared in a timed Dicke state exhibits directional radiation asymmetry, which has often been interpreted as evidence of reciprocity breaking through quantum-state preparation. We show that this interpretation is incorrect: reciprocity concerns transmit-receive response, not necessarily pattern symmetry. Moreover, the first-order coherence of any single-excitation state is exactly equivalent to the power pattern of a classical phased array driven by conjugate weights, making the observed asymmetry classically reproducible. The genuine quantum signature instead appears in second-order correlations, where a single-excitation state violates the classical lower bound on photon coincidences. We therefore propose a quantum-antenna certificate combining nonzero directional asymmetry with photon antibunching at the beam peak. We further derive a tight asymmetry bound, establish the correct mirror operation for planar arrays, correct the collective decay rate with dipole-dipole coupling, and derive a saturation law for direction-finding precision. All theoretical results are validated through independent numerical implementations.

title: Continuum-many discontinuous actions of $\operatorname{SL}_{n+1}(\mathbb{Q})$ on manifolds
abstract: For any $n\geq 1$, we construct a continuum of non-conjugate actions by homeomorphisms of $\operatorname{SL}_{n+1}(\mathbb{Q})$ on the $n$-sphere $S^{n}$ that do not extend to a continuous action of $\operatorname{SL}_{n+1}(\mathbb{R})$. We do this by adapting a blow-up construction of Bowden and Mann. We motivate studying these actions and note down some related observations.

title: Saving the Queen is hard: Hive is EXPTIME-complete
abstract: Hive is a boardless two-player strategy game in which the pieces form the playing surface. We prove that deciding whether White can force a win in single-Queen $n$-Hive, the generalization with exactly one Queen Bee per player, is EXPTIME-complete, even when all pieces are already placed. Our hardness proof reduces from unbounded two-player Constraint Logic: Grasshoppers encode edge orientations, while the One Hive rule enforces the vertex constraints. We obtain the EXPTIME upper bound by considering positions up to translation. The result answers the single-Queen question raised by Andel and Rin. Keeping the same inventory and movement rules, it also gives EXPTIME-completeness for multi-Queen variants. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first use of unbounded two-player Constraint Logic to prove EXPTIME-completeness for a natural problem.

title: Non-Stationary Quantum Systems Associated with Stationary Scattering in One Dimension
abstract: Stationary scattering admits a dynamical formulation in which the scattering data are extracted from the evolution operator for an effective non-stationary and non-unitary quantum system. This provides a mathematical method of solving scattering problems. We consider the possibility of realizing such a quantum system and relating the scattering information to outcomes of quantum measurements performed on it. To this end, we examine stationary scattering problems in one dimension where the scattering data consist of reflection and transmission amplitudes and the corresponding effective quantum system is a non-unitary two-level system. The states of this system identify points in a Bloch sphere $S^2$ and their evolution yields trajectories in $S^2$. Quantum measurements turn out to be capable of providing information about the reflection amplitudes. We identify configurations displaying reflectionlessness with situations where one or both of the poles of $S^2$ undergo cyclic evolutions. Spectral singularities and coherent perfect absorption correspond to dynamical spin flips which map one of the poles of $S^2$ to the other.

title: Exact Sampling Under Campbell Cost via Rényi Channel Simulation Divergence
abstract: We study the communication cost of exact sampling under Campbell's exponential coding criterion. Given a target distribution $P$ and a proposal distribution $Q$, the sender and receiver share i.i.d. $Q$-distributed samples, and the sender communicates an index so that the selected sample has distribution exactly $P$. We introduce a new information measure Rényi channel simulation divergence $R_α(P\Vert Q)$, a Rényi generalization of the channel simulation divergence. We then show that it lower bounds the Campbell cost of every exact sampler and is achievable, via a new layered sampling scheme, within an additive constant depending only on the Campbell parameter. This yields a tighter one-shot characterization than previous bounds based on Rényi divergences of different orders. For i.i.d. product distributions, under suitable non-degeneracy and moment conditions, we further show that the gap beyond the leading Rényi-divergence term is $\frac{1}{2}\log n+O(1)$.

title: Broadband 600- and 1200-GHz Subharmonically Pumped Schottky Diode Mixers
abstract: A subharmonic mixer topology is introduced that uses quarter-wave stubs to create virtual RF/LO grounds and provide impedance matching in close proximity to the antiparallel Schottky barrier diode pair, thereby reducing the electrical length and enabling broadband operation. The RF/LO matching topology is demonstrated at 600 GHz and 1200 GHz, with good agreement between measured and simulated performance. The 600-GHz mixer demonstrates approximately 20% RF bandwidth with a DSB receiver noise temperature below 1300 K across most of the measured band, while the 1200-GHz implementation achieves DSB receiver noise temperatures below 3000 K over a broad frequency range. Both mixers are characterized at room temperature with approximately 2 mW of LO power. The 600-GHz mixer is used in the Submillimeter Wave Instrument (SWI) onboard ESA's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer. Overall, these results demonstrate state-of-the-art room-temperature performance for broadband receiver front ends targeting atmospheric research and remote-sensing applications.

title: Dynamic Conflict Clustering with Lightweight Learning and Strategic Repair for Distributed Constraint Satisfaction
abstract: Distributed Constraint Satisfaction Problems (DCSPs) model distributed decision-making in multi-agent systems, where agents assign values to local variables while satisfying shared constraints. However, many DCSP solvers still rely on broad, repeated peer-to-peer communication and are largely reactive, with limited support for strategic coordination or learning. This increases communication overhead, can lead to stagnation, and reduces the success of hard instances. Hence, we propose Dynamic Conflict Clustering-Incomplete (DCC-Incomplete), a repair-based solver that combines conflict-centred decomposition, structured coordination, strategic repair, and lightweight learning for stagnation recovery. DCC-Incomplete groups the unsolved part of the problem into conflict clusters and restricts communication via a coordination layer to agents within the same conflict region. It also introduces memory-guided restart, enabling agents and clusters to pause, revise, and adapt repairs based on neighbouring conflict states. A thorough evaluation of DCC-Incomplete on distributed graph-colouring benchmarks with planted satisfying assignments shows that its memory-guided restart improves the success rate from 37.50% to 61.11%, reduces median runtime from 0.565s to 0.367s, and cuts median communication from 12.493 to 6.503 messages per constraint. These results suggest that dynamic conflict clustering, combined with lightweight strategic and learning-guided repair, improves both communication efficiency and robustness in incomplete DCSP solving.

title: Testing Central Structure for Complex Networks
abstract: Centrality measures rank nodes even when the observed differences can be explained by ordinary structural variation. We therefore study a preceding question: whether a network contains a statistically identifiable central structure at all. We formulate this question as a network-level hypothesis testing issue using the adjacency spectral radius as the test statistic and estimate an empirical p-value from randomized networks generated under a specified null model. The framework is evaluated using G(N,M), Chung-Lu, and two implementations of the configuration model on simulated benchmarks and 55 real networks. Controlled experiments further vary the number and connection weights of designated central nodes while holding network size and density fixed. The results show a clear negative association between central-structure strength and the empirical p-value. They also demonstrate that rejection decisions depend substantially on the structural properties preserved by the null model: the detected network sets are not simply nested across models.

title: Sparse All-Layer Connector for Domain Generalised Semantic Segmentation
abstract: Domain generalised semantic segmentation (DGSS) has recently benefited from combining multiple foundation models, such as vision-language and vision foundation models, to leverage their diverse representations for generalisation. Existing multi-model approaches share a common design choice: cross-model fusion is restricted to depth-aligned layers, implicitly assuming that mutually beneficial information resides at the same depth across models. However, foundation models pretrained under different objectives may develop distinct representation hierarchies, making the optimality of depth-aligned fusion questionable. Moreover, we observe that the foundation models exhibit different depth-wise domain sensitivity. Motivated by these observations, we propose a Sparse All-Layer Connector (SALC) that enables each layer to access information from preceding layers of another model. As the number of accessible layers grows with depth, dense aggregation may hurt generalisation. SALC therefore learns to adaptively select a sparse subset of informative layers. We further introduce a candidate dropout regularisation that strengthens sparsity and encourages SALC to explore diverse layers, leading to more robust selection. Across four foundation model combinations and three DGSS evaluation settings, the proposed design demonstrates stronger generalisation than conventional depth-aligned fusion. The code is available at https://github.com/RuoyuGuo/SALC.

title: Feedback as an Interface: Controlling Form and Detail in LLM Translation Refinement
abstract: Feedback presentation shapes how LLMs use evaluator judgments during translation refinement. We introduce a machine translation protocol that keeps the evaluator score, main issue, and recommendation fixed while varying feedback form and supporting detail. Across seven models and six translation directions, low-load feedback outperforms high-load feedback in all 42 translator-direction settings under xCOMET. On the 29,400-record rewriting subset, mean xCOMET scores multiplied by 100 are 83.30 for low-load feedback and 80.67 for high-load feedback; the full-matrix original-translation reference mean is 83.46. MetricX-24 supports the low-load advantage on a stratified subset. A no-feedback second pass yields a small improvement over the original translations, and direct evaluator prompting reproduces the low-load advantage without a separate rewriting stage. These results show that compact feedback limits the quality loss from evaluator-guided refinement in the evaluated high-resource MT settings.

title: Drift, Then Spread: Learning One-Step Generative Policies for Online Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Generative policies offer expressive action distributions for online reinforcement learning (RL), but many diffusion- and flow-based policies require costly iterative sampling. We propose DriftSpread, a one-step generative policy based on Drifting for online maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) RL. To incorporate entropy without a tractable policy density, we build on an energy-based view of Drifting and derive critic-guided Drift and entropy-induced Spread from the negative MaxEnt objective. Our method learns these updates sequentially in the same actor, using action regression for value improvement and distribution matching to capture the effect of entropy. The actor updates require neither direct samples from the critic-defined Boltzmann target nor policy-density or score estimation. Under exact fitting with a fixed critic, we prove convergence to the Boltzmann target in the small-step limit followed by the long-time limit. On MuJoCo, DriftSpread achieves the highest aggregate normalized return among all evaluated methods, while outperforming the diffusion- and flow-based baselines in both training and inference efficiency.

title: A simplified proof of polynomial improvements for 3SUM and APSP
abstract: We give a simplified proof of the polynomial improvements for integer 3SUM and all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) established by Alman and Vassilevska Williams, with weaker exponents. The central ingredient is selected-entry matrix multiplication: computing a prescribed set of entries of a product of dense rectangular matrices. Starting from Schönhage's inner/outer-product identity, we construct a multiplication rule that shares intermediate products among many outputs. We apply this rule recursively and bound the work by counting the requested entries at each level. Applied to incidence matrices, the algorithm solves Offline Set Disjointness over a small universe. Known deterministic reductions then yield truly subquadratic integer 3SUM and truly subcubic APSP for polynomially bounded integer inputs.

title: Separability criteria and lower bounds of entanglement via realignment
abstract: The detection and quantification of quantum entanglement are central problems in quantum information science. Based on the realignment of density matrices and the vectorization of reduced density matrices, we construct a family of enhanced separability criteria for bipartite and multipartite quantum systems. Our criteria recover the previously proposed realignment-based criteria as special cases and detect more entanglement than the earlier ones. Moreover, we derive tighter lower bounds for the concurrence and the convex-roof extended negativity, criteria for detecting the genuine tripartite entanglement, and lower bounds on genuine-multipartite-entanglement concurrence. The advantages of our results are demonstrated with detailed examples.

title: AnyEdit: A Unified Framework for Speech and Singing Voice Editing with Real-World Environmental Consistency
abstract: We present AnyEdit, a unified, separation-free framework for speech and singing voice editing that preserves real-world acoustic environments, including noise, reverberation, and background music. Recent unified generative models already achieve strong speech and singing generation in clean conditions, but real-world vocal editing remains challenging because the model must revise content while simultaneously preserving speaker identity, prosody, and the surrounding acoustic scene. Directly modeling noisy audio end-to-end entangles semantic editing with environmental acoustics, weakening the core vocal generation capability. We therefore adopt a two-stage design that preserves clean-domain editing ability while deferring acoustic rendering to a separate stage: an instruction-guided autoregressive editor first predicts clean prosody and content-style tokens, supported by a teacher-student noise-robust prosody tokenizer that distills clean prosodic tokens from degraded recordings; a flow-matching acoustic model then performs in-context rendering conditioned on the source acoustic context, so the edited segment inherits surrounding noise, reverberation, and background sound while maintaining consistent speaker timbre. To stabilize unedited regions, we introduce unmodified-area-aware supervision; after pre-training, we further apply direct preference optimization on mined real-to-real singing pairs. We also release AnyEditBench, a benchmark covering both speech and singing voice editing under clean, simulated, and in-the-wild acoustic conditions. Experiments on Chinese and English speech and singing datasets showed that AnyEdit consistently outperforms strong baselines in content accuracy, subjective quality, and background consistency under noisy and reverberant conditions. Demo: https://any-edit.github.io/. AnyEditBench: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Ririiiii/anyeditbench.

title: A Persian Vision-Language-Action Dataset and Benchmark for Ambiguity- and Infeasibility-Aware Instruction-to-Plan Grounding
abstract: Converting natural-language instructions into executable action plans conditioned on a scene image is a core capability for embodied human-robot interaction, but existing benchmarks target English, simulated or video-grounded environments, and largely assume instructions are clear and executable. We introduce the first Persian vision-language-action dataset for this task: 258 instances over 230 real household/office photographs, annotated with reference plans, deliberate ambiguity and infeasibility labels, disambiguating question-answer pairs, and an auto-generated chain-of-thought rationale for training. Using this resource, we ablate retrieval-augmentation, chain-of-thought prompting, and an agentic disambiguation step, evaluated with an LLM-as-judge protocol and a new metric, PGOS-FA, extending prior work (PG2S) with step-order sensitivity, an over-generation penalty, and Persian-adapted embeddings. Paired statistical testing across 36 comparisons shows retrieval-augmentation is a large, robustly significant effect, while finer-grained additions are directionally consistent but not statistically distinguishable from noise at this scale, and the LLM-judge metric has near-zero power where PGOS-FA succeeds. A blind human-correlation study on 79 real outputs shows PGOS-FA tracks human judgment at least as closely as the LLM-judge. Testing generalization beyond the ablation's single backbone, we find that most of the gap between an open-weight and a substantially stronger closed planner is attributable to open-weight model generation rather than to the closed model's capability specifically, and that our best configuration significantly outperforms an independently reproduced external baseline despite a weaker backbone. The dataset, PGOS-FA implementation, and evaluation code will be made available upon reasonable request.

title: Rate-Resolved Text Evaluation with Masked Diffusion Language Models
abstract: A single evaluation score can rank generation systems but rarely reveals what failed. We propose rate-resolved text evaluation, which turns the masking rate of masked diffusion language models into a diagnostic axis. By reconstructing text under different fractions of masked tokens, one diffusion score becomes a vector of band-conditioned scores that reflect reconstruction difficulty at varying levels of visible context. On SummEval, preserving this rate structure yields complementary signal: the best masking-rate band improves fusion with autoregressive likelihood over a collapsed diffusion scalar, survives a sample-shuffle control that breaks rate ordering, and adds residual signal to a fixed prompted judge. A second diffusion model reproduces the effect more weakly. On WMT MQM zh-en, roundtrip mask-and-reconstruct probing produces a tunable localization curve in which ranking-oriented AUROC and span-detection F1 peak at different masking rates. Factuality benchmarks bound the interpretation: band semantics are model- and task-dependent, so each application requires empirical validation.

title: Geodesic Models for Loop Spaces on Riemannian Manifolds
abstract: A topological group, defined in terms of ``composable minimal geodesics'' is constructed and shown to be homotopy equivalent to the pointed loop space of a path-connected, simply connected Riemannian manifold $M$ of positive convexity radius. This construction is analogous to John Milnor's free group model for the pointed loop space of a connected simplicial complex. Related models built from composable minimal geodesics are also obtained for the free loop space of $M$ and for the space of maps from any finite two-dimensional CW-complex into $M$.

title: ProtoPur: Prototype-Purity Pseudo-Labeling for Weakly Supervised Instance Learning in Pathology
abstract: Weak bag-level labels are widely available in computational pathology, whereas reliable instance-level annotations for whole-slide images remain expensive and ambiguous. Weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) achieves strong bag-level classification, but instance-level supervision from attention scores, model predictions, negative bags, or spatial refinement may fail to identify class-specific local evidence. We propose ProtoPur, a prototype-purity pseudo-labeling method for weakly supervised instance-level learning in pathology whole-slide images. ProtoPur estimates class-balanced local purity over prototype regions constructed from frozen foundation-model features, and assigns pseudo-labels to high-purity regions strongly associated with a target class. This purity-first design separates class-specific evidence from negative or shared morphology, with coverage used only to ensure sufficient pseudo-label assignment. We provide a PAC-style analysis showing that the risk of an instance classifier trained with ProtoPur pseudo-labels can be decomposed into a standard uniform-convergence term and a ProtoPur-specific pseudo-label noise term, comprising selected-region mismatch and a coverage residual. Experiments on three public whole-slide image datasets with two pathology foundation encoders show that ProtoPur consistently improves instance-level performance across multiple MIL backbones while maintaining competitive bag-level performance. Pseudo-label quality comparisons on two public datasets further demonstrate that prototype-purity selection provides stronger instance supervision. These results suggest that the foundation-model features contain exploitable instance-level supervision signals, and ProtoPur is a way to reveal and use these signals from weak bag labels without requiring dense instance annotations.

title: The entry-exit function and nilpotent corrections in multidimensional slow-fast systems
abstract: We study multidimensional entry-exit phenomena in slow-fast systems whose fast linearization contains a nilpotent component. We show that the classical spectral balance still determines the exit point as $\varepsilon \to 0$, however the nilpotent component induces an algebraic amplification invisible to the spectrum, producing a $\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|$-shift of the exit point for $0 <\varepsilon \ll 1$. We further extend the analysis to systems with several spectral branches and show that mode dominance follows a hierarchical, lexicographic selection principle: accumulated spectral growth determines the leading order, while the nilpotent component resolves degeneracies between spectrally equivalent modes.

title: Synthesizing Ultrasonic Echo Profiles from Text for Open-Vocabulary Silent Speech Recognition
abstract: Eyewear that senses articulation with inaudible ultrasound can now recognize silent speech over an open vocabulary, but its accuracy is limited by the cost of training data. We present SoniGAN, which synthesizes the ultrasonic echo profiles of silent articulation from text and uses them as synthetic supervision. A voice-cloned text-to-speech (TTS) model reads a text corpus, and a two-stage generator synthesizes echo profiles from representations of the spoken content of that audio. Pretraining a recognizer on 104 hours of the synthesized data improves the word error rate (WER) of a public open-vocabulary benchmark by 2.3 points. Adding the sessions the corpus discards for a faulty microphone brings the system to 22.2% without any language model. Lexicon-constrained decoding, LLM rescoring, and ensembling further bring it to 14.9%, the first minimally obtrusive silent speech interface to fall inside the error range in which users report no loss of willingness to use silent speech input.

title: Uncertainty in Compound Decisions
abstract: Researchers and policymakers frequently make a large number of decisions simultaneously over many units using noisy estimates of unit-level effects. Researchers often assume that unit-level effects are drawn from a common effect distribution, allowing for optimal decision-making. In applications, however, this effect distribution is unknown to the econometrician, introducing uncertainty in the ultimate decision-making problem. This paper considers the problem of quantifying this uncertainty. For instance, researchers may seek to understand how an oracle decision maker with knowledge of the effect distribution would compare different feasible decisions, or understand which decisions an oracle would plausibly make. Analyzing these questions from the perspective of an oracle decision maker involves comparing the conditional means of unit-level effects given estimates thereof, suggesting a sufficient inferential objective of uniform coverage of these conditional means. Based on an equivalence between uniform coverage of conditional means and multiple testing, I develop methods that satisfy this coverage. Finally, I consider an application to the problem of identifying high-economic-mobility neighborhoods. My methods sharpen inference relative to existing methods and identify units that can be confidently included in oracle selections.

title: Blow-down and immediate onset of positivity in the Neumann problem for (super-)fast diffusion equations
abstract: For the degenerate parabolic equation $u_t=\nabla\cdot (u^{m-1}\nabla u)$, the homogeneous Neumann problem in smoothly bounded domains $Ω\subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is considered in the (super-fast) diffusion range when $m\in (-\infty,1)$. Upper and lower estimates for solutions are inferred by means of two Moser-type iterations, and optimality properties of these bounds are derived using comparison arguments. On the basis of the accordingly obtained information on regularization into spaces of bounded and uniformly positive functions, a result on global solvability in an associated initial-boundary value problem is achieved for all nonnegative and nontrivial initial data belonging to $L^1(Ω) \cap \bigcup_{s>n(1-m)/2} L^s(Ω)$.

title: Coprime pairs with equal sum of divisors, assuming smooth shifted primes
abstract: Let $h(x)$ be the number of pairs $1\le a<b<x$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$ and $σ(a)=σ(b)$. Erdős Problem #824 asks whether $h(x)>x^{2-o(1)}$. By an argument of Pollack and Pomerance, this follows if for every fixed $δ>0$ there are $y^{1-o(1)}$ primes $p\le5y$ with $p+1$ free of prime factors exceeding $y^δ$. We write this implication out with explicit parameters and formalize it in Lean 4. We then check that the argument of the recent OpenAI preprint "Weighted dilation graphs, smooth shifted primes and totient fibers", which claims the corresponding statement for $p-1$, applies to $p+1$ after a change of sign in two of its sections. Consequently $h(x)=x^{2-o(1)}$, conditionally on the correctness of that preprint, which has not been refereed and whose main new estimates we have not independently verified.

title: Recovering Low-Bit Failures in Vision-Language-Action Policies via Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Quantization lowers deployment costs of vision-language-action (VLA) policies but can compromise task completion. Across five VLA models and 4,050 real-world trials, we systematically reveal that quantization-aware training (QAT) generally improves on post-training quantization (PTQ) but leaves substantial gaps to full precision (FP) on long-horizon tasks and under visual and semantic shifts, while its imitation-based objective does not explicitly use rollout success or partial completion. To exploit these outcome signals, we introduce Quantization-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (QCRL), an offline RL method coupling progress-based advantage estimation with quantization-aware source conditioning. FP rollouts supply reference experience beyond action-level distillation, progress-scaled terminal penalty distinguishes partial completion, and quantization-aware conditioning selects advantageous reference behavior within the quantized policy. We evaluate weight-only INT4 W4A16 on $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.5 and joint weight-activation NVFP4 W4A4 on $π_{0.5}$. Using only in-distribution data, QCRL reaches 99.3% of FP's mean score across three visual-shift conditions for $π_{0.5}$ with INT4 W4A16, alongside 42.9% model-memory savings. With NVFP4 W4A4, it reaches 100.7% of the same FP baseline, alongside a $1.73\times$ speedup using NVFP4/FP8 deployment. Hardware gains are relative to FP16 on Jetson Thor.

title: A greedy double-block nonlinear Bregman-Kaczmarz method for nonlinear equations
abstract: In this paper, we develop a greedy double-block nonlinear Bregman-Kaczmarz method to efficiently find sparse solutions of nonlinear equations. The theoretical convergence rate of the proposed method is established under certain assumptions. Numerical experiments illustrate the competitive performance and superiority of the proposed method.

title: Knowledge Interaction in Hypernetwork-based Continual Learning: Conflict and Composition
abstract: Continual learning aims to adapt pretrained large language models (LLMs) to evolving data while preserving their pretrained capabilities. A central challenge is catastrophic forgetting: adaptation to new data can impair performance on previously learned knowledge. Since continual learning commonly changes model parameters, the model's predictions may draw on knowledge from the base model, the parameter update, and the input context. Understanding how these sources interact is essential: conflicts reveal whether new knowledge can override outdated knowledge, while multi-hop reasoning tests whether new knowledge can be composed with existing knowledge to support generalization. We study these interactions in a hypernetwork-based adaptation framework, where a shared network generates adapters from context, allowing a frozen base model to adapt without task-specific updates. We find that, under knowledge conflict, models preferentially follow the context, and their choices depend more on where knowledge is presented than on its content. We also show that context and adapter knowledge perturb the base model's representations along directions orthogonal to its clean hidden states, enabling us to derive steering vectors that control which source the model follows. In multi-hop reasoning, we find that models fail to reliably compose knowledge across the three sources, with the key breakdown arising from the interaction of the hypernetwork with both the base model and the context. Code and reproduction materials: https://github.com/missswiftie/Knowledge-Interaction-in-CL

title: The Mathematical Collective Unconscious: Jungian Archetypes within the Latent Space
abstract: Carl Jung theorised that the human psyche contains an inherited framework, the collective unconscious, populated by universal archetypes. As large language models (LLMs) are trained on vast corpora of textual data, this paper investigates whether they spontaneously construct distinct archetype-like regions within their high-dimensional latent spaces. The paper proposes that these regions function as spatial constraints that naturally organise semantically related narratives. To evaluate this, we applied cosine similarity and angular distance metrics across thirteen experiments utilising OpenAIs text-embedding-3-small model. The paper contains two experimental sections the first section explores these ideas using synthetically constructed narratives, the results of which act as a baselines for experiments conducted in the second section where the synthetic data is replaced by human-authored literature (Shmoop corpus), unedited dream reports (DreamBank corpus), and culturally distilled folklore (Andrew Langs Fairy Books). The results show that archetypal roles occupy distinct, measurable regions in the latent space. Crucially, these regions remain compact and consistent because of narrative structure rather than simple word overlap. Additionally, text category dictates spatial distribution: dream reports concentrate within Trickster and Shadow regions, while traditional folklore distributes evenly across all tested archetypes. We conclude that transformer latent spaces encode stable regions which appear to correspond to recognised Jungian archetypes.

title: Bipartite edge frustration of nut graphs: proofs and constructions
abstract: The bipartite edge frustration of a graph $G$, $φ(G)$, is the minimum number of edges that must be removed from $G$ to obtain a graph that is bipartite. Core graphs are singular graphs on $2$ or more vertices, for which the kernel of the adjacency matrix contains a full eigenvector. A nut graph is a core graph of nullity one. Nut graphs $G$ are non-bipartite. It is proved here that $φ(G) \geq 2$ if $G$ is a nut graph, i.e. every nut graph requires deletion of at least two edges to produce a bipartite graph. In addition, we give a constructive proof that for every integer $k \geq 2$ there exist infinitely many chemical nut graphs $G$ with $φ(G) = k$. Furthermore, for $3 \leq d \leq 8$, the values $k$, for which a $d$-regular nut graph $G$ with $φ(G) = k$ exists, are characterised. It is shown here that for every integer $k \geq 2$ there exist infinitely many cubic polyhedral nut graphs $G$ with $φ(G) = k$. Two ways of producing larger nut graphs from smaller are described: the cut and frustration constructions. One straightforward consequence is that total double subdivision of a nut graph (i.e. simultaneous insertion of two degree-$2$ vertices into every edge) yields a nut graph.

title: Teams, Truthmakers, Translations
abstract: We present a faithful translation from Aloni's logic BSL into a classical modal logic over semilattices combining ideas from earlier modal translations of truthmaker semantics with algebraic representation theory. We show how our method can also be made to work for other current hyperintensional logics. Finally, we place our results in a broader setting of translating hyperintensional logics into classical modal ones, and discuss applications and new challenges that arise for both areas of philosophical logic connected in this way.

title: Rethinking Human Intent-to-CAD: Parametric CAD Model Generation via Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Parametric Computer-Aided-Design (CAD) modeling from human intent remains challenging, particularly during the conceptual design stage, where design goals are expressed through incomplete and unstructured modalities (e.g., hand-drawn sketches and textual descriptions). In this work, we rethink the human intent-to-CAD pipeline and propose a unified method that directly maps multi-level human intents to executable codes, without assuming the prior existence of target CAD models. To support our study, we construct HiCAD, the first large-scale dataset aligning hand-drawn sketches, textual descriptions, and parametric CAD codes. Based on this, we introduce HiCAD, a two-stage framework comprising Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment to bridge the representational gap between heterogeneous inputs, and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning to enforce geometric and topological consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines across multiple tasks, validating its effectiveness and robustness in transforming heterogeneous human intents into high-fidelity parametric CAD models. Our project page: https://zqwlearning.github.io/HiCAD.

title: Metric Planarity Testing is Hard
abstract: A key milestone in algorithmic graph theory is Hopcroft and Tarjan's 1974 linear-time algorithm for graph planarity testing. At a workshop in 2002, Linial and Rabinovich asked for either a polynomial-time algorithm or an NP-hardness proof for metric planarity testing: given a metric space $(X,d_X)$, determine whether there exists an edge-weighted planar graph $G=(V,E,w)$ with $X\subseteq V$ that realizes the distances in $X$, meaning that $d_G(x,y)=d_X(x,y)$ for every $x,y\in X$. This question arose in the context of research on metric embeddings and their applications in computer science since the mid-1990s. Over the past few decades, polynomial-time algorithms have been developed for several special cases. In this work, we show that metric planarity testing is NP-hard, in sharp contrast to graph planarity testing. Our reduction yields a stronger result: under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), no $2^{o(n)}$-time algorithm for metric planarity testing exists, where $n$ is the number of points in the metric. To complement our ETH lower bound, we give two algorithmic results: (i) an algorithm for computing a metric planar embedding in $2^{\tilde{O}(n^2)}$ time and (ii) a $(1+ε)$-approximation algorithm in $2^{\tilde{O}(n)}$ time for any fixed $ε\in(0,1)$. The second algorithm produces a planar graph that preserves the input metric up to a factor of $(1+ε)$.

title: Indirect prediction and screening of frustrated magnetic materials using machine learning
abstract: Magnetic frustration is commonly quantified by the frustration index, calculated from the Curie-Weiss and Neel temperatures. Because both quantities are not simultaneously available for most materials, direct prediction of the magnetic frustration index remains challenging. Here, we propose a machine learning workflow for indirect prediction of the frustration index and consequent screening of potential frustrated magnetic compounds through independent prediction of Curie-Weiss and Neel temperatures. In our work, composition-based models implemented via the CatBoost algorithm, trained on experimental data were optimized using chemically informed dataset subdivision. The highest predictive accuracy was achieved for the rare earth-oxide model in predicting Neel and for the rare earth model in predicting Curie-Weiss. Ensemble uncertainty was incorporated through a conservative frustration index to improve the reliability of candidate selection. Screening of approximately 67000 Materials Project compounds identified 20 high-confidence frustrated magnetic candidates, including several experimentally known frustrated magnets and previously unexplored oxide systems potential for further investigation.

title: Field Response of the Orbital Moment Probed by Integrated Magnetic Circular Dichroism
abstract: Magnetic circular dichroism (MCD) is an optical probe of orbital time reversal symmetry breaking. Although frequency integrated MCD is related to the self-rotation contribution to orbital magnetization at zero field, its magnetic response generally differs from the thermodynamic orbital susceptibility. Here, we define the MCD susceptibility and derive general expressions for multiband systems using an electromagnetic $U(1)$ gauge invariant approach. For insulators, the response contains contributions from the non-Abelian quantum metric, Berry curvature, and field induced interband mixing. For metals, a finite temperature Green function formulation separates the smooth response into Fermi sea and Fermi surface contributions. An independent Landau level calculation confirms the expressions for the zero-field MCD moment and its linear magnetic response. In a continuum model for twisted bilayer graphene, the MCD susceptibility vanishes within the charge neutrality gap, while the thermodynamic orbital susceptibility remains markedly diamagnetic. Near the gap edges, the orbital moment term dominates the response. Features near the van Hove energies are associated with density of states enhancement. These results clarify how the two susceptibilities reflect different orbital processes even for the same electronic structure and thus establish the MCD susceptibility as a distinct probe of orbital magnetic response.

title: Radioactive Feedback: Tracing Models Trained by Label-Only LLM Supervision
abstract: Conventional distillation transfers capability through teacher-generated demonstrations. LLM-as-a-Judge knowledge distillation offers a distinct and increasingly practical alternative. In the label-only variant studied here, the student generates every response and improves from scalar scores alone. Prior work shows that this non-demonstrative feedback can improve student capability, but it creates a fundamentally different provenance problem. No teacher-generated answer enters the student's training set, so any evaluator-specific trace must pass through a low-bandwidth reward signal rather than copied text. Existing watermarks and distillation detectors do not cover this score-only channel. We introduce Radioactive Feedback, which encodes a registered pattern of behavioral preferences in the rewards themselves. The evaluator applies bounded pointwise adjustments to quality-qualified responses, allowing repeated optimization to transfer the pattern to a student trained by another party. Experiments on code and mathematics show that the registered preferences transfer through scores alone and across datasets, enabling black-box detection against a fixed reference pool.

title: **Winding number forces universal synchronisation**
abstract: We prove that two completely different oscillators synchronise through arbitrarily weak reciprocal impulses. Any two planar oscillators with hyperbolic attracting limit cycles and equal natural periods lock stably one-to-one under translation impulses with generic directions and a suitable range of positive strength ratios, whatever their vector fields, limit cycles and transverse contraction rates. The mechanism is topological: the winding of the asymptotic phase gradient forces phase advances and delays, and the relative winding number of an effective impulse field gives lower bounds on attracting and unstable locked states. Equal periods are not essential: locking persists under small nonzero mismatches, with persistence and loss governed by a shifted phase balance. The analysis covers the full state-dependent impulsive dynamics, including transverse stability. Nearly simultaneous emissions may make the return discontinuous; under an explicit regularity condition the global return has a normally attracting Lipschitz invariant circle with topologically Morse--Smale dynamics.

title: Towards Autopilot Labeling for Short Video Content Governance
abstract: The explosive growth of short videos has presented significant challenges to content governance. Traditional manual labeling is inefficient, slow to iterate, and costly. Therefore, we explore and develop a multi-stage autopilot labeling framework aimed at progressively increasing the level of automation in short video content annotation. To move beyond the heavy reliance on human expert labeling at the initial L0 stage, we first introduce a discriminative MLLM labeler at the L1 stage, which is fine-tuned with supervised data to directly predict labels for short videos. Advancing to the L2 stage, we shift to a domain-adaptive MLLM pretrained on short video data and use it for zero-shot labeling, enabling flexible generalization without task-specific supervision. In the L3 stage, we propose an agentic annotation workflow, and equip the agent with several key tools, which empower the agent to handle complex, unfamiliar, or vaguely defined cases, significantly reducing the need for human intervention. We conduct extensive experiments across various content issues, and results demonstrate that each stage of the autopilot labeling framework progressively improves labeling accuracy, and has significantly reduced manual labor costs in real-world applications by up to 85%.

title: Total Cohomology of Hilbert schemes of Orbisurfaces I: Reduction to Stacky Loci
abstract: We generalize Nakajima's theory of Hilbert schemes of points on surfaces to Hilbert schemes of points on \textit{orbisurfaces}, and obtain initial factorization based on stratification by stabilizers. While the usual formula is retained for the trivial stabilizer stratum and for those strata of codimension $1$, genuine difficulties arise with stacky points strata. In the local picture of an isolated stacky point, the theory reduce to the study of $\Quot^\bfv[\CC^2/G]$ for a \textit{small} finite subgroup of $GL_2(\CC)$. The generating series for their total cohomology is a geometric correction of the generating series for total cohomology of ordinary smooth surface schemes. In addition, we obtain an action of the Borel-Moore homology of the punctual fibre stacks on the total Hilbert cohomology by virtual correspondences, in analogy with the Fock space description in Nakajima's theory. The punctual fibre stacks are genuinely different from the symmetric stack, and has natural realizations via motivic integration.

title: When do explicit penalties improve flow matching?
abstract: Flow matching can learn structure directly from data, raising the question of when additional constraints improve generation. We study penalties that encode such constraints, with physics-informed flow matching as a motivating example. Satisfying a constraint more closely need not make the generated distribution more accurate. We therefore compare penalised and unpenalised generative modelling through their expected squared $2$-Wasserstein error. Our analysis covers both vector-valued and functional data in a Hilbert-space setting. We first derive geometric criteria that account for constraint violations and the distribution of samples after projection onto the constraint set. We then solve the statistical comparison explicitly for specific velocity-field classes and constraints via flow matching. In this model, penalisation improves accuracy exactly when the reduction in estimation variance outweighs the increase in squared bias. The resulting formula shows how this trade-off depends on sample size, the model class, the noise schedule, and the penalty weight.

title: Notes on Uniform Policy Score Bounds and Lipschitz Continuity for Truncated Gaussian, Product Cauchy, Boltzmann, and Softmax Policies
abstract: We establish uniform score bounds and Lipschitz continuity for truncated Gaussian, Cauchy, Boltzmann, and softmax policies under explicitly stated parameterizations.

title: FARL: A Fully Automated Pipeline of RL Interface and Solver Design
abstract: Existing reinforcement learning (RL) largely focuses on optimizing learning algorithms within a pre-defined task formulation, while applying RL to new tasks still relies heavily on human expertise to design the learning pipeline: what an agent observes, how it is rewarded, which algorithm it uses, and how training is configured. Automating these choices is challenging because they are tightly coupled. We introduce FARL (Fully Automated Reinforcement Learning), a framework that automates RL design by jointly searching observation and reward programs, learning algorithms, and training settings. FARL uses training statistics and observed behavior to diagnose failures, propose changes, and test whether they improve learning. Its search preserves diverse candidates and the controls needed for these tests, using a staged budget to screen designs before investing in longer training. Experimental memory records each finding together with its conditions, so an unsuccessful component can be reconsidered in a different combination. Across expert-withheld and expert-available settings, FARL outperforms the evaluated automated baselines on challenging navigation, locomotion, and manipulation tasks. On Adroit Hand Relocate, FARL achieves 97.1% success at 5M training steps per policy, compared with 0% for Eureka and LiMEN and 1.0% for native Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) under the same policy training budget.

title: Do LLM Tutors Actually Teach? A Process-Centered Synthesis of the Tutoring Loop
abstract: Large language models can produce fluent tu- toring dialogue, but whether they actually help students learn remains unclear. We present a process-centered synthesis of LLM tutoring that follows the path from learner-state infer- ence to pedagogical action, tutor training, eval- uation, and student simulation. This view ex- poses a central gap: implementing a tutoring component does not establish that it works or that its outputs meaningfully affect later stages. A structured study-level audit shows that peda- gogical evaluation is common, while evidence becomes much thinner for learner-conditioned intervention, human learning gains, and espe- cially transfer or delayed retention. Human studies nevertheless provide a conditional posi- tive result: LLM tutors can improve learning, but benefits depend on pedagogical structure, learner engagement, and how learning is mea- sured. We argue that progress requires validat- ing the interfaces between tutoring stages, not only improving individual components.

title: Sharp conditions for fully nonlinear equations with $(n-1)$-Hessian matrix: Part I. Monge--Ampère case
abstract: We study positive $(n-1)$-convex entire subsolutions of the normalized real $(n-1)$ Monge--Ampère equation $\operatorname{det}^{\frac1n}\bigl(ΔuI-D^2u\bigr)=f(u)+g(u)|Du|^q$ in $\mathbb R^n$. Under two sets of structural assumptions on the continuous, non-decreasing coefficients $f$ and $g$, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of entire subsolutions when $q<2-\frac1n$. Our results cover the pure-gradient degenerate case $f\equiv0$ with $0<q<1$, the gradient-singular case $q<0$, and the case where $g$ changes sign. For $q=2-\frac1n$, we recover the Keller--Osserman condition for the gradient-independent equation, prove nonexistence when $g$ is eventually positive, and obtain an exponentially weighted condition when $g$ has a nonpositive limit at infinity. This is the first of two companion papers and treats the determinant case.

title: Counting subspaces with prescribed Welch sums
abstract: Let $q=2^n$ with $n=2m+1$ for an integer $m\ge1$, and let ${\mathbb F}_q$ be the finite field with $q$ elements. Let $W_n(x)=x^{2^m+3}$ be the Welch function on ${\mathbb F}_q$. For $1\le k\le n$ and $b\in{\mathbb F}_q$, denote by $N_{n,k}(b)$ the number of $k$-dimensional ${\mathbb F}_2$-subspaces $E$ of $\mathbb F}_q$ such that \[ \sum_{x\in E}W_n(x)=b. \] In this paper, we determine $N_{n,k}(b)$ for all $k$. The only nontrivial case is $k=3$, for which the answer is given in terms of a binary Kloosterman sum. As a consequence, we prove a recent conjecture of Hou and Zhao on the third-order sum-freedom of the Welch function.

title: Developing the Statistical Mechanics of Evolving Assembly Spaces
abstract: A gap exists in connecting biological evolution within the framework of statistical mechanics. It has been hoped that statistical mechanics would provide us with a general predictive principle for the emergence of novelty and complexity. However, the emergence of novel functional features initiated by stochastic processes remains difficult to describe, because these processes commonly arise outside near-equilibrium or linear-response regimes. To understand how environmental influences generate diverse, open-ended, complex objects by driving physical systems to specific regions of phase space over long spatial and temporal scales, a new approach to non-equilibrium thermodynamics is necessary. Here, we present the coupling of assembly theory (AT) with statistical mechanics as a framework that works within the laws of thermodynamics, but can contextualise the processes of novelty, complexity, and evolution within these laws. We map construction processes from physical space to assembly space (AS) and introduce the concept of an assembler, a machine that constructs objects contingent on previous states and is represented by bitwise operations. Using this approach, we apply principles from stochastic thermodynamics with AT to define selection within large combinatorial spaces1 and estimate the work required to create novel and complex objects. This approach allows us to represent complex processes, such as selection, within large combinatorial spaces as a set of rules for a memory-feedback loop followed by the assembler. This framework concretely defines the relationships between thermodynamics and information theory by introducing a novel aspect of physics that uses history and causal contingency to influence the probabilistic time evolution of complex systems.

title: DRanker: A Transformer-Based Multi-Task Ranking Model for the Disney+ Homepage
abstract: We present DRanker (Disney+ Ranker), a transformer-based multitask ranking model serving personalized recommendations on the Disney+ homepage. We describe the encoder-only architecture over enriched engagement-history sequences paired with a lightweight causal debiasing mechanism, and the inference stack that enables transformer-based ranking at scale. Through iterative development, we systematically evaluated more complex alternatives and found that simpler designs consistently outperformed them on offline metrics, qualitative behavioral evaluation, and in production. Deployed globally, DRanker drives over 1% lift in our key engagement metric and 0.5% lift in daily active users across all experiences powered by the ranker. We share practical lessons on data engineering, debiasing, and architectural choices that shaped our ranking system at scale.

title: Sharp conditions for fully nonlinear equations with $(n-1)$-Hessian matrix: Part II. $k$-Hessian case
abstract: We study admissible entire subsolutions and radial boundary blow-up solutions of $S_k^{\frac1k}[ΔuI-D^2u]=f(u)+g(u)|Du|^q$ for $1\leq k<n$, continuing our study of the determinant case $k=n$ in Part I. Under structural assumptions on the continuous, non-decreasing coefficients $f$ and $g$, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of entire subsolutions when $q<2$. Our results cover the non-Lipschitz case $0<q<1$ with a possibly vanishing zero-order term, the gradient-singular case $q<0$, and sign-changing gradient coefficients. We also characterize finite-radius blow-up of radial solutions and derive two-sided estimates for the blow-up radius, as well as pointwise upper bounds for their profiles in terms of inverse Keller--Osserman functions.

title: Symplectic four-manifolds and hyperbolic $π$-orbifolds
abstract: We construct closed symplectic 4-manifolds admitting the structure of hyperbolic $π$-orbifold, addressing LeBrun's conjecture. Our simplest example has Euler characteristic $304$, is tessellated by $64$ copies of the right-angled hyperbolic $120$-cell and admits a four-fold branched covering over a product of two surfaces of genus $4$.

title: TabMosaic: Unified In-Context Diffusion for Tabular Generative Tasks
abstract: Generative modeling for tabular data has advanced to the point where models can synthesize realistic records, recover missing values, and generate samples conditioned on class labels or observed attributes. Despite recent advances, existing approaches either require table-specific training or restrict in-context learning to single-cell prediction. In this work, we formulate these tabular generative tasks as a single problem: modeling the joint conditional distribution of an arbitrary set of target cells given the observed cells of an unseen table. To this end, we turn to diffusion, whose denoising objective is defined jointly over all target cells rather than one cell at a time. Under the pretraining distribution, this objective is minimized by the posterior predictive distribution over the target set. Building on this, we propose TabMosaic, a unified in-context diffusion model for generating mixed-type target cells in unseen, potentially incomplete tables without table-specific training. We further show that its pretraining objective bounds the conditional negative log-likelihood and the divergence from the posterior predictive for arbitrary target sets, extending the Bayesian account of in-context learning from a single-value prediction to joint multi-cell generation. Across 48 real-world tables, TabMosaic ranks first on all evaluated generative tasks against 20 baseline approaches

title: Poissonian Pair Correlation for Bernoulli Orbits
abstract: Let \(α, β\in \mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\), and let \((ξ_n)_{n \ge 1}\) be independent random variables taking the values \(α\) and \(β\) with equal probability. We study the random walk \[X_n = ξ_1 + \cdots + ξ_n \pmod 1\] and present a deterministic Diophantine condition on \((α, β)\) that implies almost sure Poisson pair correlation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result providing explicit examples in this framework where the increment measure is purely discrete. The classical Fourier contraction method fails in this setting; a different approach is required. Our proof uses the parabolic geometry of returns to \(1\) and an exact covariance formula for overlapping blocks.

title: Correcting Burst Errors with Applications to DNA-Based Data Storage
abstract: We introduce the problem of permutation burst error-correction, motivated by applications in molecular data storage with nanopore sequencing read platforms. A permutation burst of length $k$ is an error that affects a substring of length $k$ of a string of length $n$ by permuting its entries. Permutation burst errors can be corrected using classical burst error-correcting codes, such as Fire and Reed-Solomon codes. Here, we study how to reduce the redundancy of these classical codes by taking into account that the burst error preserves the weight of the substring. In addition, we further restrict our model to handle cyclic permutation bursts only, which are of independent practical and mathematical interest. Our main results include proving/establishing the following: a) for $k=o(\sqrt{n}),$ the redundancy of any permutation burst error correcting code is at least $\log n-k+\log \binom{2k-2}{k-2}+o(1).$ This result follows from McDiarmid's concentration bound; b) for $k \geq 9$ and $k=o\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{\log n}}\right)$, the redundancy of any cyclic permutation burst error correcting code is at least $\log n +\log (k(k-1)-56)-\log\,80+o(1).$ c) the asymptotic redundancy upper bounds for the two types of substring errors that are twice the lower bound; d) constructions for both permutation burst and cyclic permutation burst errors that involve Varshamov-Tenegoltz type constraints or represent generalizations and extensions of Fire and other codes. In particular, we exhibit polynomially encodable and decodable codes that can correct cyclic bursts of length $\leq k$ using $\log n + k + 49\log k + O(\log \log k)$ redundant bits.

title: RespFocus: Learning Temporal Evidence for Weakly Supervised Respiratory Sound Classification
abstract: Respiratory auscultation provides a low-cost means of assessing pulmonary function, yet transient crackles and sustained wheezes can be difficult to recognize in noisy clinical recordings. Conventional deep learning classifiers often operate as black boxes, offering limited insight into the temporal acoustic evidence supporting their predictions. We present RespFocus, a weakly supervised framework that uses multiple instance learning (MIL) to learn inspectable temporal evidence from cycle-level labels and integrate it into classification. We also introduce PedResp2026, a multicenter pediatric respiratory sound cohort collected in routine clinical environments with adjudicated cycle-level annotations. In classification experiments, RespFocus achieves four-class Scores of 69.55\% on public ICBHI 2017 and 72.91\% on PedResp2026. Evidence diagnostics and matched temporal interventions support the functional contribution of the learned evidence to model predictions. Together, these findings highlight RespFocus's potential as a tool for automated respiratory sound diagnosis.

title: Revisiting the Multiwavelength Data of GRB 240825A: Implications for a Two-Stage Central Engine and a Dusty Environment
abstract: Reanalyzing the multi-wavelength data of GRB 240825A, we identify two distinct prompt-emission episodes, i.e. an early, spectrally soft plateau and a subsequent bright, spectrally hard gamma-ray pulse. We show that this signature is consistent with a two-stage central engine model, in which the early soft plateau is powered by the dipolar spin-down radiation of a transient proto-magnetar, while the later hard pulse arises from a relativistic jet launched by fallback accretion onto the nascent black hole via the Blandford-Znajek mechanism. Adopting simulation-motivated initial black hole (BH) masses ($M_{\rm BH,0}$) and spins ($a_0$), our fits to the second episode yield total masses supplied to the post-collapse disk of $M_{\rm fb}=0.45$--$0.96 M_\odot$, fallback radii of $r_{\rm fb}=16.9$--$17.6 r_g$, and characteristic fallback timescales of $t_{\rm fb}=0.13$--$0.25$ s. The corresponding maximum inner accretion rates range from $0.18$ to $0.70 M_\odot \mathrm{s}^{-1}$, which is sensitive to $a_0$. Joint spectral fits with optical-X-ray afterglow data reveal a coupled temporal evolution of dust extinction and equivalent hydrogen column density. Incorporating this extinction evolution, an external forward-reverse shock model in a wind-like medium can account for the radio-to-GeV band afterglow data. Although ambient dust and the bright host galaxy may obscure any associated supernova, late-time optical reddening remains compatible with a supernova contribution. Applying the empirical relation between the prompt spectral peak energy and the SN peak bolometric magnitude gives an illustrative estimate of $M_{\rm bol,peak}=-19.46\pm0.35$ mag for a putative associated SN. These results support a two-stage evolution of the central engine and variable dusty environment of GRB 240825A, which provides insights into the nature of its progenitor.

title: DualColl: Throughput-Optimal Bandwidth-Bound Collective Communications via Fractional Tree Packing
abstract: Large-scale distributed training increasingly makes collective communication bandwidth-bound. In modern GPU clusters, communication libraries such as NCCL implement collectives including AllReduce over heterogeneous interconnects such as NVLink, InfiniBand, and Ethernet, making efficient use of available network bandwidth a central systems challenge. ForestColl showed that collective communication on such fabrics can be formulated using fractional tree packing; its scalable polynomial-time construction is developed for AllGather, with AllReduce obtained by composing AllGather and ReduceScatter. We present DualColl, which targets bandwidth-bound AllReduce directly. Under the tree-based AllReduce model, DualColl applies a Garg--Könemann-style multiplicative-weights algorithm and, for any $0<ε<1$, computes a feasible schedule whose throughput is at least $(1-ε)^2$ of the optimal AllReduce throughput. Its key component is an exact minimum-cost collective-tree oracle that projects physical-link dual prices onto a logical graph of participating ranks, reducing each iteration to shortest-path computations followed by a minimum spanning tree. We further extend the framework to local equal-next-hop packet-sprayed routing and to networks without explicit per-tree bandwidth control. For the latter, we introduce a tree-coupled max-min bandwidth-sharing model and show that tree duplication approximates an explicit fractional allocation with a provable accuracy-complexity tradeoff. Finally, we extend the fractional-packing framework to additional collective operations and multiple concurrent collective groups.

title: bharatSetu: a 1M x 22 bridge for indic translation
abstract: India's Eighth Schedule recognises 22 languages, yet parallel data is uneven across them, and many language pairs, especially among lower-resource languages such as Bodo, Dogri, Santali and Kashmiri, lack direct bitext. We present BharatSetu 22-Indic 1M, a row-aligned table of 984,764 English sentences, each paired with machine translations into all 22 scheduled languages (21,664,808 Indic cells), generated with the sarvamai/sarvam-translate model family. Because every Indic cell in a row translates the same English sentence, any two columns form a translation pair: 462 directed Indic-to-Indic pairs, or 506 including English, without direct bitext. We call these pivot-derived pairs and propose a confidence layer that lets users choose how strictly each pair is connected. The corpus is machine-generated and not human-verified; quality is expected to vary by language, domain and sentence style, and pivot-derived pairs can inherit errors from both sides. We therefore release BharatSetu as a machine layer and propose a human-correction layer keyed to the same row identifiers, so that each corrected column upgrades every pair that uses it, together with an evaluation protocol. We report no translation-quality results.

title: Solutions of $x_1^2+x_2^2-x_3^2=D$ with small $x_3$: a spectral approach
abstract: We count the integral solutions of $x_1^2+x_2^2-x_3^2=D$ weighted by $Φ(x_3/M)$, for $M$ smaller than $\sqrt D$. Such solutions correspond to binary quadratic forms of discriminant $D$, and the count becomes a sum, over the geodesics of discriminant $D$, of a function of their distance to the point $i$. We evaluate it by the spectral theory of automorphic forms. Throughout, $θ=7/64$. For square $D=n^2$ the geodesics run from cusp to cusp, and Hecke theory reduces them to the single geodesic from $0$ to $\infty$. For every $n$ and both parities of $x_3$, we obtain an asymptotic formula with error $O(n^{1+θ+\varepsilon}M^{-1/2})$, using the Kim-Sarnak bound and the large sieve of Deshouillers and Iwaniec (and the theta group for the parity of $x_3$). It is non-trivial for $M\ge n^{71/96+\varepsilon}$. This improves the range $n^{5/6+\varepsilon}$ of the elementary method, and confirms the corrected main term of the author's earlier work. For non-square $D=f^2D_0$ the geodesics are closed. A Hecke relation for their traces reduces everything to the fundamental discriminant $D_0$. We obtain an error $O(D^{\varepsilon}f^{1+θ}D_0^{2/3}M^{-1/2})$, using the formulas of Duke-Imamoglu-Toth and Baruch-Mao together with the cubic moment bound of Young and of Andersen-Wu. For $D\equiv 5 \bmod 8$ this counts all solutions, and the range $M\ge D^{1/2-1/1332}$ of Friedlander and Iwaniec improves to $M\ge D^{4/9+\varepsilon}$.
