The formulation reduces to deterministic RoPE when the support collapses to a point. Across layers, the predicted geometry guides cross-view attention, while the updated features refine the geometry used at the next layer. Experiments on novel view synthesis, depth estimation, and 3D geometry reconstruction demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRoPE for multi-view Transformers.

title: SyncReward: Human-Aligned Synchronization Reward for Audio-Visual Generation
abstract: Recent years have witnessed rapid progress in joint audio--visual generation. However, audio--visual synchronization remains a challenge, as generated speech and sound often temporally misalign with visual events. A key bottleneck is the lack of human-annotated data, reliable evaluation benchmarks, and synchronization-aware evaluation models for generated audio--visual outputs. To address these limitations, we conduct a comprehensive study spanning data, benchmarking, and reward modeling. We first introduce SyncReward-Data-80K, a dataset containing 80K professional synchronization ratings for clips from eight audio--visual generators. A taxonomy-guided construction pipeline covers four sound-event families: Speech, Onset, Instrument, and Ambient. We further construct \textbf{SyncReward-Bench}, a held-out benchmark of 1K clips, each independently rated by multiple professionals. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate specialized synchronization metrics and omni-modal models, revealing their substantial misalignment with human judgments. Finally, we develop SyncReward, a reward model that combines semantic--temporal contrastive pretraining on real clips with human supervision on generated clips. As an evaluation metric, SyncReward achieves the strongest agreement with human ratings among the evaluated methods. As a reward, it improves synchronization through inference-time best-of-$N$ selection and reinforcement learning based post-training. We will release the data, benchmark, model, and code at https://github.com/WeChatCV/SyncReward.

title: Distinguishing sets and measures from their planar Brownian images
abstract: Motivated by a question of Hochman, we investigate whether two deterministic time measures or time sets can be distinguished almost surely from a single planar Brownian image. Using rescaled correlation integrals, we give a criterion for mutual singularity of the laws of the image measures, even when the time measures have the same dimension. For self-similar time sets satisfying the open set condition, we also recover the natural occupation measure from the compact image. Together, these results allow us to distinguish lattice and non-lattice self-similar sets and their natural measures within this class. For a naturally parametrised family with two contractions, with fixed dimension, each parameter can be distinguished from all but finitely many others. If the dimension is sufficiently small, every distinct parameter can be distinguished. The results are formalised in Lean.

title: Translational self-affine tiles in $\mathbb{R}^n$
abstract: Two basic problems in the theory of integral self-affine tiles are to characterize the digit sets that generate translational tiles and to understand whether such tiles admit periodic translational tilings. We give a complete solution to the first problem: for an expanding integer matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and a digit set $\mathcal{D}\subset\mathbb{Z}^n$ with $\#\mathcal{D}=|\det\mathbf{A}|$, the self-affine set $T(\mathbf{A},\mathcal{D})$ is a tile if and only if, for some $N\geq1$, the iterated digit set $\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{A},N}$ is of skew-product form with respect to $\mathbf{A}^N$. As a consequence, every integral self-affine tile admits a fully periodic self-replicating $q$-fold tiling. Moreover, $q$ divides $|T(\mathbf{A},\mathcal{D})|$. In dimension two we prove more: every integral self-affine tile admits a fully periodic tiling. In particular, the periodic tiling conjecture holds for integral self-affine tiles in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

title: One-dimensional pressureless flow with a nonlinear velocity law: Bregman variational construction and well-posedness
abstract: We establish global existence, uniqueness and quantitative stability for one-dimensional pressureless flow governed by \[ \partial_tρ+\partial_x\bigl(ρf(u)\bigr)=0, \qquad \partial_t(ρu)+\partial_x\bigl(ρu f(u)\bigr)=0, \] where $ρ$ is the mass density, possibly measure-valued, $u$ is the physical velocity, and $f\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, with $f'>0$, determines the transport velocity $f(u)$. The initial mass has finite positive mass and finite second moment, allowing atoms and unbounded support, and the initial physical velocity is bounded. The difficulty at a cluster collision is that mass and momentum conservation determine a mass-weighted average of physical velocity, whereas transport is governed by the nonlinear law $f$ applied to that average. We construct global entropy solutions by a Bregman variational time discretization whose cost is chosen to reproduce the transport velocity determined by this mass-weighted average, coupled with conditional-expectation updates of physical velocity. For every entropy solution satisfying the Oleinik condition on the transport velocity and initial weak continuity of the kinetic energy measure, we establish a Lagrangian representation and prove uniqueness within this class by comparing flows with possibly different cluster intervals. For two such solutions with the same velocity law and common mass, we obtain a $W_\infty$ estimate for the normalized mass measures in terms of the initial position and physical-velocity discrepancies in mass coordinates, whenever the initial $W_\infty$ distance is finite. The Lagrangian evolution has the semigroup property.

title: Analysis of Integrated Communication and Sensing in Cylindrical Aerial Corridors
abstract: In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) networks, integrated communication and sensing (ISAC) is emerging as a key enabler to support extended and continuous communication and sensing capabilities for sixth-generation (6G) services among UAVs operating in swarms. In this paper, a comprehensive framework is presented to investigate the ISAC coverage probability of a reference UAV-base station (BS) in a UAV network. A fixed number of UAV user equipment (UAVUEs) and UAV-BSs are deployed in an aerial corridor modeled as a finite cylinder. The three-dimensional (3D) binomial point process (BPP) is used to model both the 3D spatial locations of the UAV-UEs and the UAV-BSs. By adopting realistic 3D third generation partnership project (3GPP) antenna patterns for both the UAV-UEs and UAV-BSs, the UAVs' boresight direction of the maximum antenna gain is modeled as a random unit vector. All UAV-BSs have sensing capabilities, so an arbitrary yet fixed reference UAV-BS acts as a monostatic radar to acquire sensing measurements associated with a target UAV-UE at a given time snapshot while the target UAVUE communicates with the reference UAV-BS. Consequently, considering both clutter and communication interference, exact analytical expressions for ISAC coverage probability are derived. Low complexity baseline analytical expressions are also derived by ignoring clutter interference and directional characteristics of the UAV-UEs. Finally, motivated by the vision for intelligent UAV networks, a DeepSets-based model is developed and trained to estimate the optimal location of the reference UAV-BS that maximizes ISAC performance given a spatial deployment of the UAVs. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to rigorously investigate ISAC performance in UAV networks while incorporating the directionality characteristics of the UAV antennas.

title: Efficient Multi-Agent Reasoning via Confidence-Guided Adaptive Debate
abstract: Multi-agent debate has shown promise for improving the reasoning of large language models, yet recent theory suggests its benefits are highly regime-dependent. While interaction can amplify informative signals under corrective conditions, symmetric debate dynamics are neutral in expectation, often making majority voting preferable. We reconcile these views by arguing that debate is effective only when invoked at the right time and with appropriate structure. Based on this insight, we propose LASE: Leader-Adaptive Structured Engagement, a leader-centric multi-agent debate framework that selectively engages interaction only in non-neutral regimes. LASE introduces an asymmetric leader-supporter architecture that enables directed information flow and selective signal amplification, while defaulting to simple aggregation otherwise. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks show that LASE achieves multi-agent-level performance with near single-agent token cost, substantially improving efficiency over static debate and voting baselines.

title: STEPwise: Supporting Teachers in Diagnosing Students' Mathematical Problem-Solving Skills through LLM-Generated Questions and Rubric
abstract: Problem-solving is central to mathematics education. However, diagnosing where students' reasoning breaks down requires individualized probing and consistent criteria that teachers cannot sustain at classroom scale. We introduce STEP (STage-based Evaluation of Problem-solving skills), co-designed with six mathematics education experts, which operationalizes problem-solving as four stages and eight diagnostic sub-skills. By specifying what evidence to elicit and assess at each stage, STEP enables an LLM pipeline to generate stage-specific questions and rubrics for any math word problem, reducing the manual design of diagnostic materials. An expert review (N=8) assessed the pedagogical validity of the generated materials and informed STEPwise, a teacher-in-the-loop system for diagnostic material generation and process-level assessment. In a classroom study with 5 teachers and 64 students, STEPwise helped teachers and students locate reasoning breakdowns and supported students in reflecting on their reasoning. Together, STEP and STEPwise offer a structured approach to fine-grained diagnosis at classroom scale.

title: ChronoScribe: Semantic-Numerical Specialization for Instruction-Driven Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Recent advances in instruction-driven time series forecasting highlight a fundamental tension: systems must simultaneously master natural-language instruction following and precise numerical prediction. Current approaches often force a compromise. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret unstructured requests but may be inaccurate when asked to produce forecast values directly, whereas time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide numerical forecasts but typically require structured inputs specifying the target series, context window, and horizon. We present ChronoScribe, which applies semantic-numerical specialization to this workflow. A LoRA-adapted LLM proposes an execution path and context length; deterministic rules resolve the executable configuration. On the specialist path, a frozen TSFM produces quantile trajectories for the task-specified horizon. Deterministic trajectory summaries condition the response, while the LLM neither generates nor revises predicted values. We evaluate a Qwen3.5-9B--Chronos-2 implementation across 23 evaluation dimensions and 30 public datasets against eleven proprietary direct LLMs and three open TSFMs. ChronoScribe has the lowest error on sMAPE, MASE, WAPE, RMSE, and MAE among all evaluated systems, including fixed-context controls. Across these metrics, even the lowest direct-LLM error remains 2.0--2.7 times the corresponding ChronoScribe error. At the system level, ChronoScribe achieves a Task-Level Score (TLS) of 65.5, 10.6 points above the strongest direct-LLM baseline. The results support ChronoScribe's division of labor, in which the LLM handles interpretation, configuration, and communication while the TSFM handles numerical forecasting.

title: CellChain: Benchmarking Cross-Scale Evidence Use for Perturbation Reasoning
abstract: Recent advances in foundation models and large-scale cellular perturbation datasets have driven growing interest in using LLMs to predict and reason about cellular responses. Biological reasoning in this setting involves relating molecular mechanisms, cellular responses, and functional outcomes across scales. Evaluating foundation models therefore requires assessing not only whether their predictions are correct, but also how those predictions depend on the biological evidence provided. We introduce CellChain, an experimentally grounded benchmark comprising 590 biological cases and 2,360 matched evidence-condition instances across gene-dependency prediction, cytokine-axis identification, and drug-sensitivity ranking. CellChain links perturbation experiments and external biological resources through a provenance-aware evidence graph spanning molecular, pathway, transcriptional, and phenotypic information. Task-specific conditions vary evidence coverage, composition, or assignment while preserving questions, candidate answers, reference targets, and scoring rules. Across 18 foundation models, the highest accuracies under prespecified target-evidence conditions are 57.5%, 75.5%, and 70.8%, respectively, and broader evidence coverage does not consistently improve accuracy. On the drug-sensitivity benchmark cohort, matched reference histories outperform swapped histories by an average of 13.0 percentage points in cluster-weighted accuracy. Decision-transition analysis separates corrections, newly introduced errors, and wrong-answer switches, revealing substantial answer changes hidden by small net accuracy differences. CellChain provides controlled comparisons for attributing changes in model predictions to prespecified expansions of biological context, including changes in evidence coverage, composition, and biological assignment.

title: Rescuing Points Trapped Inside Incorrect Decision Regions: A target for Evaluating and Improving Forward-Forward Learning
abstract: Forward-Forward learning replaces end-to-end backpropagation with local, layer-wise training objectives. Its variants are evaluated primarily by classification accuracy, often measured with linear probes trained on their representations. We show that this evaluation can over-credit the learning method: a linear probe on the representations of an untrained convolutional neural network already reaches accuracy well above chance. Moreover, a single accuracy value does not reveal which datapoints become correctly classified after training and which remain misclassified. To examine what learning contributes beyond the random, untrained baseline, we present an analysis methodology built on the Boundary Proximity Index (BPI), a multiclass margin normalized by a class-centroid reference. We apply our analysis to seven Forward-Forward variants and related layer-local methods and find that initially misclassified points near the probe's decision boundary generally have higher rescue rates than those farther inside incorrect decision regions. Rescue rates vary substantially across methods, with some correcting a substantial fraction of these deeply embedded points. Together, these analyses offer a way to evaluate representation learning beyond accuracy and identify the rescue of points far inside incorrect decision regions as a target for improving local learning methods.

title: DWI Connectome-based Sex Classification in Young using Supervised Variational Autoencoder
abstract: During adolescence, significant changes in brain development are influenced by hormonal changes that impact both the body and the brain. This study presents sex classification in 787 young adults having age range of 15-25 years using Diffusion-weighted (DWI) structural connectome, focusing on 82 Desikan-Killiany atlas ROIs. A supervised variational autoencoder (SVAE) is used to extract latent space features from DWI connectome data. Although several studies explored differences in brain structure and function between sexes, the main contribution of this study lies in incorporating SVAE to learn a compact, regularized latent representation for the task of sex classification. Initial exploratory data analysis shows that these features can capture the differences in sex-specific latent space patterns. Subsequently, the learned latent space SVAE features are fed to different ML models for sex classification. Among the considered ML classifiers, the multi-layer perceptron yields the highest accuracy of 80% in classifying sex. This demonstrates the effectiveness of SVAE in learning compact, informative representations from DWI connectome for sex classification. The present work highlights the potential of using DWI brain connectomics and deep learning to differentiate sex, paving the way for future research on diverse populations that may include transgender individuals, to better understand sex-related variations in brain structure.

title: RIFT: Token Influence Follows the Path of Least Resistance
abstract: Which context tokens drive a language model's answer? Graph-based tools such as attention rollout and attention flow answer this from a single forward pass, yet their faithfulness in decoder-only models is rarely tested against interventions. We view the layers of a decoder as a causal network whose conductances are attention weights, and read a token's influence on the answer from the resistance between them. We propose RIFT (Resistance-based Information Flow in Transformers), which scores a token by the series resistance of its path of least resistance to the answer, found exactly by a classic shortest-path dynamic program. On synthetic in-context retrieval tasks and extractive question answering over Wikipedia paragraphs, RIFT predicts the effect of replacing a token with a Spearman correlation of 0.52-0.68; predicting a single replacement, it reaches 77-96% of the agreement between two different random replacements. It needs no gradients and no extra forward passes, scoring every token of a prompt in 0.9-3.4 ms on one CPU thread, whereas the replacement experiment needs a forward pass per token. On 576 held-out prompts from four models of two families (Qwen3 and Llama 3.2), it outperforms token distance, attention rollout and attention flow in every pre-specified comparison, by 0.23 to 0.88 in mean Spearman correlation, and it is the best or tied-best of all attention-based scores we test. Aggregates that add up all routes (attention flow, effective resistance and rollout) instead mostly encode token position: as a simple proposition shows, early tokens have many more parallel routes to the answer.

title: Generalizing Green's Syzygy Theorems to Symmetric Products of Curves
abstract: Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve of genus $g$, and let $T_{n,L}$ denote the tautological line bundle on its $n$-th symmetric product $C_n$. We prove effective vanishing criteria for Koszul cohomology $K_{p,q}(C_n,T_{n,B};T_{n,L})$, extending two classical theorems of Mark Green. The main ingredient is a weight-one vanishing theorem proved by induction on $n$, using a filtration of the kernel bundle of $T_{n,L}$ to reduce the required cohomological vanishings to lower symmetric products. As a consequence, when $g\geq1$ and $n\geq2$, $T_{n,L}$ satisfies property $(N_p)$ for $\mathrm{deg}(L)\geq(n+1)g+p$. This bound is sharp for elliptic symmetric squares and also gives evidence for a folklore conjecture on adjoint syzygies.

title: Finite-time quantum equilibration from local correlations
abstract: An isolated quantum system evolves reversibly, yet a small subsystem can lose nearly all information about its initial state. Conserved quantities may retain some of this information, depending on how strongly they overlap with local observables. Here we consider a subsystem in an arbitrary initial state coupled to a maximally mixed bath. We show that the worst-input mean-square equilibration error, maximised over window origins, is bounded from above and below by the mean square of a complete local autocorrelation, with the stationary part subtracted. The two mean-square quantities are linearly comparable. A correlation record over a finite interval therefore controls the equilibration error in every interval of the same length, and the result extends to nonnegative observation weights with nonnegative Fourier transform. The result allows arbitrary degeneracies of energies and gaps. We apply it to two static Hamiltonian families. For fixed spin subsystems in the one-particle sector of a bounded-range periodic clock, fixed-accuracy thermalisation is guaranteed on windows that grow only slightly faster than linearly with system size, despite exponentially small positive energies. A random commuting model with logarithmic interaction range retains an extensive set of conserved observables. Its expected mean-square error is bounded by a finite-size term and an inverse-time term. The inverse-time dependence is unavoidable because of the initial transient. These examples show how local relaxation can coexist with exact conservation laws and a finely spaced spectrum.

title: LoongSage: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

title: The $(km,kn)$-square paths theorem
abstract: For positive integers $k,m,n$ with $\gcd(m,n)=1$, we prove a $(km,kn)$-square paths theorem: the symmetric function $(-1)^{k-1}\frac{[km]_q}{[k]_q}p_k[-MX^{m,n}]\cdot1$ is a weighted sum over $(km,kn)$-preference functions. This proves a corrected form of the conjecture of Iraci, Pagaria, Paolini, and Vanden Wyngaerd and generalizes the square paths theorem of Sergel. We encode preference functions by row strict tableaux and closed walks on a set of states, compare them with parking functions for each value of the touch statistic, and apply Mellit's compositional $(km,kn)$-shuffle theorem. Finally, we establish a fall Delta square theorem conjectured by Iraci, Pagaria, and Paolini.

title: Self-Distillation with Verbal Regularization
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a large language model using supervision from a teacher instantiated from the same model as the student. The teacher is conditioned on privileged information (PI), such as verified solutions. The student, which does not observe PI, learns from the teacher's next-token distributions along its own sampled responses. However, PI can bias supervision toward shortcut reasoning with limited verification or reconsideration, accompanied by a sharp drop in the entropy of the output distribution. To address this challenge, we introduce self-distillation with verbal regularization (VRSD), which uses system prompts to regulate how the teacher uses PI, thereby encouraging rethinking and exploration to counteract premature commitment. Theoretically, we model prompting as attenuating the influence of PI on the teacher distribution and derive conditions for entropy preservation. Across three models and four tasks, VRSD improves Pass@1 over OPSD in 11 of 12 model-task settings, by 3.9 percentage points on average, while generally maintaining higher token entropy.

title: PINT: A Unified Model with Shared Predictive Intent for Robot Manipulation
abstract: Generalist robot manipulation can benefit from pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) for semantic reasoning and video generation models (VGMs) for world modeling. However, existing unified models that directly fuse them through shared attention at multiple layers can make it harder to draw on their specialized capabilities. We introduce PINT, a unified model that coordinates semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation through a shared chunk-level Predictive Intent while preserving expert-specific pathways. PINT inserts learnable Intent Tokens into the VLM sequence to form this representation, conditioning both the VGM and an Action Expert (AE). It replaces only the VGM's prompt conditioning and retains the VGM at inference, where the AE reads its representations through one-way attention. Rather than prescribing what Predictive Intent should encode, PINT learns it jointly from the native prediction objectives of the VLM, VGM, and AE, which provide complementary views of the same upcoming task execution. Training uses two stages: Stage 1 freezes the VGM so that future video prediction shapes Predictive Intent with task-relevant future dynamics, while Stage 2 fixes the learned Intent and adapts the VGM and AE. Without embodied pretraining, PINT achieves strong in-distribution (ID) performance and substantially improves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, reaching 15.5% on RoboTwin 2.0-Hard compared with 1.8% for Fast-WAM and 3.2% for StarVLA, and 79.5% on LIBERO-Plus compared with 51.5% and 75.0%, respectively. Across five real-world bimanual tasks, PINT reaches 68% ID and 24% OOD success, compared with 35%/9% for pretrained Motus and 67%/35% for pretrained $π_{0.5}$.

title: naspaclust: A hybridisation of spatial fuzzy clustering with nature-inspired optimisation
abstract: We present an overview of R package called \texttt{naspaclust}, a tool for spatial fuzzy clustering improvement by hybridising the Fuzzy Geographically Weighted Clustering (FGWC) with nature-inspired optimisation algorithms. There are seven optimisation algorithms in general, namely Artificial Bee Colony, Flower Pollination Algorithm, Gravitational Search Algorithm, Harris-Hawk Optimisation, Intelligent Firefly Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimisation, and Teaching-Learning Based optimisation. The optimisation algorithms available do not only use the basic algorithms, but also the modified version of several parts such as randomisation terms and updating rules. Furthermore, we also provide additional options by providing more distance metrics options based on the \texttt{ rdist} package. This study showed the implementation of the \texttt{naspaclust} package in various cases, as well as comparing the performance of the algorithms in the scope of basic algorithms. The \texttt{naspaclust} package allows to improve the performance of fuzzy clustering, mainly in spatial context.

title: VideoSlate: Stateful Commit Control for Temporally Grounded Agentic Video Reasoning
abstract: Agentic video reasoning systems gather and assess video evidence across stages, selecting relevant spans as visual evidence for answering questions. New candidates and observations prompt reassessment of the current span, but revisions can correct localization errors or discard useful evidence already present in the adopted span. Systems therefore need to connect evidence organization across stages with temporal state control, allowing accumulated information to jointly inform revision assessment while explicit adoption decisions govern how assessment outcomes affect downstream visual evidence. We introduce VideoSlate, a stateful commit-control framework built around shared evidence. A typed evidence blackboard links candidate spans, provenance, construction, and verifier observations, enabling an incumbent-relative certifier to assess revision support from the candidate, current span, and related proposals. Based on certification, the controller authorizes a revision or retains the current span, separating evidence accumulation from state updates and recording each decision and its evidence on the blackboard. Extensive evaluations across video grounding and grounded question-answering benchmarks show that VideoSlate can improve temporal localization through selective revision.

title: NP-hardness of additive approximation for generalized Turán problems
abstract: For a fixed graph $T$ and a fixed nonempty family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs, let $\operatorname{ex}(G, T, \mathcal{F})$ denote the maximum number of copies of $T$ in an $\mathcal{F}$-free subgraph of a graph $G$. Alon and Shikhelman~[Algorithmica, 2022] conjectured that if $e(T)> 0$ and no member of $\mathcal{F}$ is a subgraph of a blow-up of $T$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$, approximating $\operatorname{ex}(G, T, \mathcal{F})$ within an additive error $n^{v(T)-\varepsilon}$ is NP-hard for an input graph $G$ on $n$ vertices. The previously established general cases for this conjecture include $\operatorname{ex}(G, K_2, \mathcal{F})$ by Alon, Shapira and Sudakov~[Ann. of Math., 2009], and $\operatorname{ex}(G, K_m, K_k)$ by Alon and Shikhelman. In this paper, we confirm this conjecture for every bipartite graph $T$ and every clique $T$. Our reductions use iterative leaf additions, symmetric rooted extensions and random transversals to encode the maximum number of edges in a $(k-1)$-colorable subgraph of $G$, where $k=\min_{F\in \mathcal{F}}χ(F)$.

title: An algebraic multiscale framework for two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners
abstract: The robustness of two-level overlapping additive Schwarz (OAS) preconditioners for highly heterogeneous elliptic problems hinges on the choice of the coarse space. We propose an algebraic multiscale (AM) coarse space built from the system matrix alone through an algebraic formulation of the multiscale finite element method (MsFEM). The coarse basis functions are energy-minimizing extensions of the solutions of reduced boundary condition (RBC) problems on the subdomain interface, so that coefficient variations along the interface enter the coarse space. By posing the RBC problems on slabs that extend the interface, the construction also applies to general unstructured domain decompositions. Embedding the AM formulation in an energy-minimizing framework extends it to linear elasticity, and we show that existing condition number bounds for OAS with MsFEM coarse spaces carry over to the algebraic setting. For problems with high coefficient inclusions on the coarse nodes, the AM iteration count and condition number are unaffected by increasing the contrast. In 3D scalar diffusion with log-normal coefficients, AM needs about as many iterations as the generalized Dryja--Smith--Widlund (GDSW) coarse space, while solving a coarse problem ten times smaller. For linear elasticity, omitting the coarse basis functions associated with the rotational rigid body modes yields a fully algebraic coarse space that still scales well for homogeneous problems.

title: Shaving Two Logs for Discrete and Continuous Fréchet Distance
abstract: We revisit the classical computational geometry problem of computing the exact (discrete or continuous) Fréchet distance between two given polygonal curves with $n$ vertices in a constant dimension $d$. 1. We present an $O((n^2/\log^2n)\log^2\log n)$-time deterministic algorithm for the discrete Fréchet distance problem, improving the previous $O((n^2/\log n)\log\log n)$ result by Agarwal, Ben Avraham, Kaplan, and Sharir [SODA'13]. 2. We present an $O((n^2/\log^2n)\log^2\log n)$-time deterministic algorithm for the decision version of the continuous Fréchet distance problem, improving the previous $O((n^2/\log n)\log^2\log n)$ result by Buchin, Buchin, Meulemans, and Mulzer [SODA'14] and the recent $O(n^2/\log^{1+μ}n)$ randomized result by Cheng and Huang [SODA'25] for a small unspecified constant $μ>0$ (which converges to 0 as $d$ increases). 3. Finally, we present an $O((n^2/\log^2 n)\log^{O(1)}\log n)$-time Las Vegas randomized algorithm for the continuous Fréchet distance problem, improving the previous $O(n^2\log^2\log n)$ randomized result by Buchin, Buchin, Meulemans, and Mulzer [SODA'14] and the recent $O(n^2/\log^μn)$-time randomized result claimed by Cheng and Huang [SODA'25]. Since these problems have near-quadratic OV-based conditional lower bounds and shaving of two log factors is the best that is known for similar, simpler problems such as longest common subsequence and edit distance, our results reach the natural limit of the current state of the art (up to $\log\log$ factors).

title: HexaBee-4B: Six-Language Translation with Multilingual Answering and Bidirectional Supervision
abstract: Multilingual translation requires a model to preserve meaning while producing text in a requested language. We present HexaBee-4B, a translator adapted from Gemma 3 4B IT through three stages: Wikipedia continued pretraining, joint multilingual answering and answer-text translation, and bidirectional translation specialization. The intermediate stage connects two tasks through shared multilingual answers: answering a question in the requested language and translating an answer into that language. It comprises 19.46 million answering records, including 5.76 million cross-language question-answer pairs, and 10.70 million answer-text translations. The final stage uses 658,274 forward and reverse synthetic translation examples. On 36,572 synthetic test examples spanning all 30 directions among Arabic, Chinese, English, Hebrew, Persian, and Spanish, HexaBee-4B achieves direction-macro chrF++ of 73.75, compared with 57.11 for Gemma 3 4B IT and 66.83 for Gemma 3 12B IT. BLEU, TER, COMET, and a matched model-judged subset support the same overall ranking. These results demonstrate improved translation across the six-language set, with chrF++ gains in every evaluated direction over both baselines.

title: Double Bruhat cells in symmetric spaces
abstract: This paper studies the closures of the double Bruhat cells of symmetric spacess in its equivariant embeddings. We call them large double Bruhat varieties. Our aim is to establish the double Bruhat stratification as a natural setting for extending the geometry of Richardson varieties to symmetric spaces. For the wonderful compactification of the associated adjoint symmetric space, we show their scheme-theoretic intersections with the unique closed orbit are reduced unions of projected Richardson varieties. This connection with Richardson geometry on partial flag varieties supports large double Bruhat varieties as a natural class of subvarieties in symmetric-space embeddings. In positive characteristic, we prove that every equivariant embedding admits a Frobenius splitting compatible with all large double Bruhat varieties and all boundary divisors. These varieties are strongly F-regular, and globally F-regular when the ambient embedding is projective. In characteristic zero, they are of strongly F-regular type, and of globally F-regular type in the projective case; in particular, they are normal, Cohen-Macaulay, and have rational singularities.

title: Log Density Spectrum Based Decoding of Polar Codes for Channels with Strong Phase Noise
abstract: A decoding method is proposed for polar codes under channels with strong phase noise. In contrast to traditional SC decoding, where recursions are performed on scalar soft information such as probabilities, the proposed decoding recurses over probability density functions defined on the phase-noise variable. To make the density-level recursion computationally tractable, we represent each log-density by its spectrum, and derive approximate formulas for the spectrum recursion, therefore, the proposed method is termed log-density spectrum recursion (LDSR). Numerical results are given under strong phase noise and AWGN, showing that a prominent superiority of error performance is achieved by LDSR in comparison with traditional SC and Kalman-based methods.

title: From Sound to Sense: An Anatomy of Semantic Supervision for Speech-Driven Visual Grounding in Remote Sensing Imagery
abstract: Speech-driven visual grounding in remote sensing (RSVG) removes the typing bottleneck of text-based interaction and is intended to preserve prosodic intent, enabling hands-free target acquisition in time-critical missions. The direct-audio paradigm, mapping raw speech straight to a bounding box and bypassing automatic speech recognition (ASR), was recently adopted by RSTalker, but what such grounders actually learn about language remains unmeasured. SemEcho grafts a frozen Whisper speech pathway onto a VLTVG grounding host so that speech and text share one decoder, making the paired text, free by construction since speech corpora in this task are synthesized from DIOR-RSVG expressions, a training-time teacher and a fair, same-host text upper bound. On this instrument we dissect three semantic injection channels (feature-mimicry distillation, word-level CTC supervision, and two-stage ASR pretraining) with linear semantic probes, and release Audio-DIOR-R (80,973 training clips; 10 timbres x K=3; Qwen3-TTS synthesis with online sox noise lambda in [0, 0.4]) and Audio-DIOR-Comp, a re-split holding out 17 attribute-category combinations under a 2x2 acoustic-semantic protocol. Our anatomy yields four findings. (i) Whether direct alignment beats a domain-trained ASR cascade is decided by recognizer quality: against a weak in-domain cascade (CTC 0.53) direct wins by 9.0 Acc@0.5 points with transcription errors concentrated on spatial-relation words, but a strong in-domain cascade (CTC 0.029) reaches the text upper bound (80.8 vs. 81.0) and beats even the strongest direct model by 8.8 points; the anti-ASR premise holds only against weak recognizers.

title: World Models Need a Physical Registry: Learning Internal Predictive States for Physically Plausible World Models
abstract: Video world models must generate physically plausible futures, not just realistic frames. Existing approaches typically use semantic, physical, or predictive information to guide the visual generation stream, leaving a fundamental question: where inside the generator should predictions of scene evolution live? Standard video tokens jointly encode appearance and dynamics, but provide no distinct state for learning and reading predictive dynamics. We answer this question with the Physical Registry: temporally grounded registry slots inside a video DiT that are initialized from an observation-conditioned forecast, co-evolve with video tokens, and receive future-representation supervision, making predictive dynamics an explicit, readable state of the generator. In a controlled comparison of predictive-state interfaces on Physics-IQ Verified, Physical Registry improves vanilla fine-tuning by 9.9/8.7 points on I2V/V2V, the largest gain among the interfaces we compare. Across all Cosmos and WAN backbones, Physical Registry improves Physics-IQ Verified scores. With only 0.45% additional parameters, it enables Cosmos 3 Nano 16B to surpass the published I2V score of Cosmos 3 Super 64B (43.56 vs. 42.7). On WorldModelBench, it also improves physical adherence and the total score for all four evaluated backbones. Because the registry becomes candidate-specific while remaining readable, the Physical Registry Selector (PRS) ranks emerging futures by how far their intermediate registry readouts depart from the shared forecast before full denoising is complete. Across four backbones, this selection improves I2V scores by 5.6-15.9% without completed-video external scoring. Together, these results support a broader principle: dynamics prediction should live as an explicit model state that co-evolves with the video representation. Project page: https://grainsack.github.io/physical-registry/

title: Experiments on an airfoil with adjustable pitch and heave under transonic buffet leading to lock-in coupling
abstract: This paper presents aeroelastic experiments conducted in the ONERA S3Ch transonic wind tunnel using a supercritical OAT15A airfoil mounted on a rig allowing independent control of pitch and heave degrees of freedom (DOF). The study investigates fluid-structure interaction (FSI) mechanisms and lock-in phenomena between transonic buffet and structural modes. Aerodynamic and structural responses were monitored using steady and unsteady pressure sensors, high-speed stereoscopic Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV), accelerometers, and optical sensors. Four configurations were tested: rigid (0 DOF), pitch-only (1 DOF pitch), heave-only (1 DOF heave), and combined pitch-heave (2 DOF). The test campaign spanned selected Mach numbers, angles of attack, and structural natural frequencies for each configuration. Results show that buffet-induced lock-in occurs abruptly when the Mach number increases, but only when the pitch DOF is enabled, in both the 1-DOF pitch or 2-DOF configuration. These findings establish that pitch-buffet frequency proximity is a necessary condition for lock-in. In the 2-DOF configuration, continuous Mach number excursions revealed a three-way coupling involving the buffet, pitch, and bending modes, with the bending mode modulating the coupled dynamics. This coupling generates large-amplitude limit-cycle oscillations (LCO) within seconds, persisting over a narrow Mach range before buffet cessation.

title: Derjaguin-corrected Kelvin equation for finite open slits
abstract: We formulate a Derjaguin-corrected Kelvin equation for phase transitions in finite open slits. In such pores, capillary condensation is modified by the finite wall length because the condensed phase is bounded by two terminal menisci pinned at the slit ends. Starting from the macroscopic generalized Kelvin equation, we introduce a scaling approximation which replaces the implicit edge-contact-angle condition by a closed analytic expression while preserving the exact limiting behaviours. We then incorporate mesoscopic wetting-layer contributions into the finite-slit free-energy balance. The single-wall contribution naturally separates into a planar Derjaguin term and a residual finite-length correction controlled by the competition between the wall length $H$ and the parallel correlation length $ξ_\parallel$. The resulting equation reduces to the standard Derjaguin-Kelvin equation for infinitely long slits and to the macroscopic finite-slit Kelvin equation when adsorbed layers are absent. Explicit forms are derived for long-ranged dispersion forces and for short-ranged forces. The theory is tested using classical density functional theory for finite slits with attractive Lennard-Jones walls and hard walls, corresponding respectively to capillary condensation and its drying analogue, capillary evaporation. The Derjaguin-corrected theory substantially improves on the purely macroscopic prediction, capturing both the correct infinite-slit limit and the observed dependence on wall length. For the short-ranged hard-wall system, the agreement with DFT remains nearly quantitative even for very narrow slits.

title: LoopQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Looped Transformers
abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) improve parameter efficiency by recursively reusing shared Transformer modules, yet their repeated computation over evolving recurrent states poses new challenges for low-bit deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, largely designed for feed-forward Transformers, fail to account for cross-loop activation dynamics, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation, leading to substantial performance degradation at low precision. To address these challenges, we propose LoopQuant, a loop-aware PTQ framework for accurate and efficient low-bit quantization of LoopLMs. LoopQuant is built on three core components: 1) Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization (CLDC) learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while preserving parameter sharing; 2) Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation (ILPA) allocates activation precision under a fixed bit budget by modeling task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions; and 3) Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration (LCTC) further aligns quantized inference with the low-bit recursive trajectory through lightweight task-space calibration. Extensive experiments across LoopLM architectures demonstrate that LoopQuant consistently outperforms existing low-bit PTQ methods. On Ouro-2.6B, LoopQuant under W4A4 surpasses all W4A8 baselines in performance, while reducing model memory by 65.3% with only 3.4% additional storage overhead over naive INT4 and achieving a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16. These results demonstrate a strong balance among accuracy, compression, and inference efficiency, providing a practical and deployment-friendly solution for low-bit LoopLM inference. The code is available at [https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/LoopQuant].

title: RoboBugBench: Benchmarking Automated Repair of Real Robot Software Under an Audited Behavioral Oracle
abstract: Language agents increasingly modify robot software, but whether they can repair it is unmeasured, because the domain supplies no oracle to inherit: a robot bug manifests as behavior, and robot repositories ship almost no tests that capture it. We present RoboBugBench, a benchmark of 33 real, execution-validated defects in a pinned ROS 2 navigation stack, in which a candidate patch is graded by compiling it and driving the robot through a physics simulation rather than by running a unit test. Three frontier models, each given 1 attempt per instance, repair 24.2%-36.4%, with no pairwise difference significant; difficulty tracks the oracle rather than the domain, at 66.7% on instances graded by process survival against 22.2% on those graded by what the robot did (instance-level p = 0.0027). Because the oracle is constructed rather than inherited we audit it adversarially, and report the decomposition that audit yields: counterfeit patches which suppress a failure without repairing the defect are accepted by the shipped rule 11/11, while a distributional rule over the same data rejects 4 at no cost in false rejects. The residual is an observability bound (what the observation channel discards, no predicate over it can recover), so discrimination must be bought with instrumentation rather than stricter criteria, and our repair rates are bounds: inflated by what the oracle cannot distinguish, deflated by unanimity's rejection of correct fixes under run-to-run noise. We release the corpus, criterion batteries, counterfeit suite and cached telemetry.

title: High Sensitivity Transient Holographic Full-Polarization Microscopy
abstract: The polarization state of light provides direct access to ultrafast electronic, magnetic, and structural dynamics in materials. Transient wide-field microscopy with simultaneous amplitude, phase, and polarization sensitivity enables spatially resolved measurements of these dynamics, but its sensitivity is often limited by technical noise and background fluctuations. Here, we demonstrate transient holographic full-polarization microscopy with substantially reduced instrumental noise and sensitivity approaching the shot-noise limit. We compare holographic geometries using one, two, and four reference beams and find that the single-reference configuration provides the most favourable shot-noise-limited sensitivity for the derived polarization observables. Combined with two-camera detection, it simultaneously captures both orthogonal polarization components without distributing reference photons among multiple carriers. A self-referenced noise-reduction framework combining singular value decomposition and background subtraction further suppresses correlated noise. For spatially averaged regions, the baseline noise is reduced by factors of three-sixty, enabling detection of weaker transient responses at lower excitation densities and in weakly absorbing materials.

title: Rule vs.Consequence: Dissociable Internal Representations of Moral Reasoning in LLMs
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in morally and legally sensitive contexts, yet little is known about how they internally represent distinctions between moral reasoning styles. We ask whether a model's differential response to rule-framed and consequence-framed moral questions reflects distinct internal structure or merely surface lexical sensitivity. We construct a 2$\times$2 factorial dataset crossing reasoning style (rule-based vs. consequence-based framing) with judgment polarity (permissive vs. prohibitive), drawn from three established moral reasoning benchmarks and evaluated on a cleanroom test set of novel phrasings that includes conflict pairs where the two framings predict opposite labels. Using linear probing and activation steering, we identify two orthogonal directions in the residual stream: Dir-A tracks reasoning style and Dir-B tracks judgment polarity, each near-blind to the other factor (cross-correlation $|r| < 0.04$). This double dissociation replicates across three instruction-tuned models from different developers at comparable proportional depth, and it is not knife-edged in layer: the directions are recoverable and causally effective throughout an extended band of the network. Dir-A can causally change judgments, and in conflicting scenarios, it selectively corrects errors in rule-based judgments without changing consequence-based judgments, suggesting that it does not simply make the model more likely to accept everything. Generalization beyond the training templates is partial: the direction transfers across benchmark sources, but its advantage over lexical baselines on novel phrasings is modest. We therefore frame the result as moral reasoning style sensitivity, a geometrically dissociable and causally effective structure, rather than internalized normative reasoning.

title: PersonaFactor: Preference Factors with Dynamic Selection for LLM Personalization
abstract: Although users may express different personalization needs across tasks, these task-specific behaviors can reflect shared underlying preference mechanisms. Existing LLM personalization methods often focus on surface-level interactions or undifferentiated histories, overlooking the shared mechanisms underlying these behaviors. We introduce PersonaFactors, a framework that distills reusable and interpretable personalization factors from heterogeneous user interactions. We construct a library of thirteen PersonaFactors by extracting evidence-grounded rationales and clustering recurring patterns across tasks, and develop a dynamic factor-guided generation framework that selects factors relevant to each user's history and current request. Across four personalization benchmarks and four backbone models, Dynamic PersonaFactor achieves the best score on every reported metric. Representation analyses further show that PersonaFactors and user history induce partially overlapping low-dimensional representations, and that their joint use yields complementary shifts. Taken together, these findings suggest that factor-based and history-based personalization can mutually reinforce each other.

title: Resource-constrained Remote Attestation of Smart Meters Using Merkle Trees in a Trusted Execution Environment
abstract: Smart meters are pivotal to the functioning of smart grids, as they measure and transmit energy consumption data that includes sensitive information about household energy usage patterns. While this data offers significant financial benefits, it can also reveal detailed insights into residents' daily routines, making the security of smart meters a critical concern. This paper introduces a novel remote attestation method for smart meters that ensures the integrity and privacy of data exchanged between smart meters and central servers while detecting unauthorized tampering. Our approach structures the communication data into a Merkle Tree-a hash data structure that facilitates efficient data integrity and authenticity verification. All operations involved in constructing the Merkle root and hashing critical data are executed in the secure environment of a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) using OP-TEE, thereby maintaining the integrity and security of the smart meter's data. Comparing our experimental results with the related works highlights the superiority of our method in terms of resource efficiency, security robustness, and the feasibility of implementation on smart meters and resource-constrained devices, thereby enhancing the overall security and reliability of smart grid systems.

title: From Nominal Capacity to Deliverable Compute: Design, Calibration and Validation of the D-PIN SCU Dynamic Metering System
abstract: Nominal chip specifications do not capture the compute deliverable by heterogeneous distributed networks under communication, runtime and verification constraints. We formalize D-PIN Standardized Compute Units (D-PIN SCU) as a dynamic metering system for deliverable compute. The system combines five-dimensional resource normalization with topology-aware and runtime-corrected metering. A cluster-scale Roofline model yields a closed-form communication ridge, while runtime factors describe thermal, fault and load effects. We show that runtime deviations cannot be identified from nominal specifications alone. Uniform re-anchoring preserves relative metering results, and a simplex-constrained calibration algorithm estimates resource weights. The framework couples Proof-of-Physical-Work verification to a no-arbitrage condition for over-claiming and electricity-aware pricing. An end-to-end recomputation on the Zhangjiang Science Gate production node covers ten heterogeneous 8-GPU servers totaling 59.5 D-PIN SCU. Billed throughput of approximately 33,000 D-PIN SCU-hours is consistent with the physical upper bound at 78% utilization over 720 hours. Derived metrics are 3.02 kW per D-PIN SCU at the supply-and-distribution design boundary and 0.26 D-PIN SCU-hours per delivered kWh. Empirically calibrated chip values differ materially from datasheet projections; the published calibration is not independently reproducible from vendor specifications. Validation is limited to one production node, and the originality claim concerns the integrated system rather than the SCU terminology or individual components. The framework provides a basis for scheduling, verification and pricing of deliverable compute in distributed heterogeneous networks.

title: Pathfinder-BP: A Low-Latency Recursive Decoder for Topological Codes
abstract: We propose Pathfinder-BP, a recursive decoder for topological quantum codes that combines belief propagation with controlled bit-flipping. An initial BP pass identifies and permanently fixes high-confidence errors. Upon convergence failure, the decoder recursively explores alternative error patterns by tentatively flipping low-confidence variables. On surface codes, Pathfinder-BP achieves a noise threshold and logical error rate comparable to minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM). A crucial advantage of Pathfinder-BP is its highly parallelizable structure, which yields a worst-case decoding latency quasi-linear in the code distance, making it a suitable candidate for low-latency hardware implementation.

title: Track objects in cubical presheaf automata
abstract: Using the formalism of presheaf automata, we introduce new classes of automata for modelling concurrency that extend higher-dimensional automata and symmetric higher-dimensional automata. We study their languages and characterise these languages in terms of posetal cospans.

title: Four-dimensional almost-Einstein manifolds with circulant structures
abstract: This paper considers a four-dimensional Riemannian manifold with an additional circulant tensor structure $Q$. We prove that such a manifold is almost-Einstein if the curvature tensor preserves the action of the structure on the last two arguments. Additionally, we examine an associated Riemannian product manifold $(M, g, Q)$ where $P=Q^{2}$, deriving explicit expressions for the curvature tensor in terms of the metric and the product structure. The sectional and Ricci curvatures of these manifolds are determined using special bases generated by the images of a given vector under the structure $Q$. Finally, we construct a non-trivial example of a four-dimensional locally product manifold by embedding a four-dimensional hypersurface into a ten-dimensional Euclidean space.

title: Spectral stability of resonant Y-solitons for the KP-II equation
abstract: The KP-II equation was introduced by Kadomtsev and Petviashvili to explain the transverse stability of line solitary waves in shallow water. Using Darboux transformations, we prove the spectral stability of Y-shaped line solitons in an exponentially weighted space that captures the amount of waves receding behind the line solitons. We show that the spectrum of the linearized operator consists of the continuous spectrum of the zero background together with three residual spectral domains whose boundaries contain continuous spectra associated with the constituent line solitons. Exploiting the analytic dependence of the pairings with adjoint eigenfunctions on the spectral parameters, we prove that the orthogonality conditions associated with all adjoint eigenfunctions can be reduced to orthogonality conditions against three families of adjoint continuous eigenfunctions. Moreover, we investigate linear stability of Y-solitons in a subspace satisfying orthogonality conditions against adjoint continuous eigenfunctions associated with outgoing modulations along each line soliton constituting the Y-soliton.

title: Benchmarking a randomized quantum algorithm for estimating expectation values of molecular observables
abstract: Randomized quantum algorithms for the estimation of expectation values of molecular observables offer a promising route to early fault-tolerant quantum advantage by trading circuit depth for an increased number of samples. However, this begs the question whether the resulting measurement overhead remains feasible for industrially relevant molecular systems. In this work, we benchmark the randomized sampling algorithm of Wang et al. [1] through numerical simulations on a hydrogen molecule and resource estimates for various active spaces of the cytochrome P450, an industry-relevant system in the pharmaceutical industry. Our numerical simulations reveal that the analytical error bounds significantly overestimate the actual sampling error, whereas the analytical bound on the required imaginary evolution time is comparatively tight, exceeding a direct DMRG estimate by roughly 44% for the active space where the comparison is feasible. The measurement overhead nevertheless remains prohibitively high: even for the smallest active spaces, the expectation-value estimation alone requires around 1010 samples, scaling to beyond 1015 for the largest active spaces considered. These results suggest that substantial improvements in measurement strategies or algorithmic scaling are necessary before randomized early-fault-tolerant algorithms become competitive for industrial quantum chemistry applications.

title: Fingering instability of thin films with an inclined contact line
abstract: The fingering instability of thin-film flow is a significant obstacle to producing uniform and stable films in industrial processes. In the framework of lubrication theory, we investigate the linear stability of a gravity-driven thin film with an inclined contact line using numerical and asymptotic methods. The contact-line singularity is regularized by imposing the Greenspan slip model. As demonstrated by the results, although the contact-line inclination slightly enhances long-wavelength instability, it significantly suppresses the growth of spanwise finite-wavelength perturbations. Moreover, the most unstable wavenumber shifts toward the long-wave region as the inclination angle increases. The inclination of the contact line introduces complex eigenvalues, leading to traveling-wave modes, in contrast to the standing-wave modes observed for horizontal contact lines. We also performed asymptotic analysis in the limit of small wavenumbers, confirming the enhanced long-wave instability. The physical mechanisms underlying these stability characteristics are elucidated, revealing that the effects of contact-line inclination come from the eigenmode distortion and additional streamwise flux.

title: Large deviation principles for 2D stochastic $g$-Navier--Stokes equations on unbounded channel-like domains
abstract: This paper investigates the large deviation principle for 2D stochastic $g$-Navier--Stokes equations driven by multiplicative noise and defined on an unbounded channel-like domain. We first prove the existence and uniqueness of probabilistically strong solutions for the stochastic equation under small noise perturbations by means of the local monotonicity method. Subsequently, we show the well-posedness of solutions to the corresponding control equation and the convergence in distribution of the solutions for the stochastic equation as the noise intensity tends to zero. Finally, we establish the Freidlin-Wentzell type large deviation principle for the solutions of the stochastic equation by using the weak convergence method. To overcome the lack of compactness of Sobolev embedding on unbounded domains, we employ a scalar stream function together with a truncation technique to derive uniform tail estimates for the solutions of the control equation.

title: Behavior-Conditioned Animal Vocalization Generation: Event-Aware Modeling and Multidimensional Evaluation
abstract: Behavior-conditioned animal vocalization generation aims to synthesize vocalizations from natural-language descriptions of animal behaviors, social interactions, and contexts. This task remains largely unexplored, with limited behavioral text supervision and substantial variation in vocalization duration. We construct the Behavior-Vocalization Dataset (BeVo) by integrating public bioacoustic data from six species with natural-language behavioral conditions derived from species-specific ethological and bioacoustic literature, totaling 31,191 events. We then adapt a rectified-flow-based generator with Event-Aware variable-length modeling, which encodes vocalizations at their actual durations and uses masks to prevent attention to padded latent positions and exclude these positions from the training loss. We evaluate vocalization discriminability, acoustic distribution fidelity, and language-aligned representation fidelity. Experiments show that task-specific adaptation improves all evaluated metrics compared with its zero-shot baseline, while Event-Aware modeling further increases vocalization-anchor macro accuracy from 59.86% to 61.99% and reduces Frechet Audio Distance from 1.40 to 1.22. Conditioning analyses further show that behavioral conditions improve target-anchor discriminability, while swapping behavior shifts generations toward the corresponding vocalization anchors. Demos are available on our project page.

title: Throwing4: Phase-Aware Pose Modeling for Throw-Distance Prediction in Elite Athletics
abstract: Elite athletics throwing provides a structured biomechanical action sequence together with an objective continuous outcome, namely throw distance, making it a suitable setting for performance-oriented sports analytics. In this work, we investigate whether explicit phase alignment of pose dynamics improves throw-distance prediction under realistic broadcast conditions. To support this study, we curate Throwing4, a dataset of 500 elite throwing clips spanning javelin, discus, hammer, and shot put, with corresponding two-dimensional pose sequences, frame-level phase annotations, and official distance labels. We formulate throw-distance prediction from broadcast-derived pose as a regression problem and compare full-sequence modeling against a phase-conditioned approach that partitions each attempt into four technique stages and fuses phase-specific motion representations. Experiments across multiple graph-based pose encoders show a consistent reduction in prediction error when phase structure is incorporated, indicating that phase-aligned modeling provides a more stable representation than treating the entire motion as an unstructured sequence. These findings suggest that explicit biomechanical phase information is a useful inductive prior for pose-based performance modeling in elite athletics throwing. Beyond score prediction, the dataset and protocol provide a basis for future work on fine-grained technique analysis, interpretable sports analytics, and robust modeling from broadcast video.

title: Risk-aware Road-network Trajectory Synthesis under Local Differential Privacy
abstract: Road-network trajectory synthesis under local differential privacy (LDP) enables mobility data analysis without uploading raw trajectories to an untrusted server. Existing locally private trajectory synthesis methods mainly model whole trajectories, point sequences, or grid-level mobility patterns. However, they cannot handle non-uniform privacy risks caused by local road-network and trajectory contexts, such as endpoints, long-stay-associated regions, and low-out-degree branches. They also do not directly protect conditional next-hop choices on road networks, where a user's selected successor may reveal sensitive local movement intentions. To address these challenges, we propose TrajRACE, a locally private synthesis framework for road-network trajectories. TrajRACE uses start, segment-count, and transition reports to represent trajectories. For each transition, it keeps the current road segment as a public aggregation context and perturbs the true successor among legal successors on the client side. It then assigns risk-aware protection strengths to transitions according to local road-network and trajectory contexts. Finally, the server recovers population-level start, segment-count, and conditional transition statistics from heterogeneous privatized reports, and generates synthetic trajectories that follow the public road-network topology. Experiments on three road-network trajectory datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of TrajRACE in improving synthetic-data utility across distributional, query-based, and pattern-level metrics, while providing stronger protection for high-risk local transitions.

title: Nonequilibrium framework for first-order phase transitions
abstract: The first-order phase transition is central to electroweak baryogenesis and gravitational wave generation, yet thermal equilibrium effective potential analyses cannot describe the real-time non-equilibrium dynamics of the phase transition process. We use the Schwinger-Keldysh closed-time-path formalism of real-time finite-temperature field theory to study these effects. For the $ϕ^6$ model, we derive the effective action and the corresponding Langevin equation. We further extend the formalism to the two scalar fields case, obtaining the coupled Langevin equations. These results provide a theoretical framework for the bubble nucleation simulation of the non-equilibrium phase transition process, laying the foundation for reliable predictions of baryogenesis and gravitational wave signals.

title: Persistence diagrams of finite topological spaces
abstract: In this paper, we apply persistent homology to study finite topological spaces by associating persistence diagrams with their elements through the furtherness function. This approach enables us to classify elements according to their topological evolution within the space. We further establish a bottleneck stability theorem showing that the bottleneck distance between the persistence diagrams associated with two elements is bounded above by their mutual furtherness.

title: SP-Allreduce: Symmetric Tree Schedules for Tori and Beyond
abstract: Allreduce is a fundamental communication primitive in large-scale distributed training, and torus interconnects remain widely deployed in high-performance systems. We introduce SP-allreduce, a new allreduce algorithm for $d$-dimensional tori that exploits the symmetry of the topology and routes only along shortest paths. We call an allreduce algorithm \emph{fully bandwidth-optimal} if it incurs no bandwidth overhead, no multihop-induced traffic inflation, and achieves perfect per-round load balance. SP-allreduce is based on a family of carefully symmetrized shortest-path trees that guarantees full bandwidth optimality in the $α$--$β$ model. We prove that it uses the minimum possible number of rounds among all fully bandwidth-optimal allreduce algorithms on $d$-dimensional tori, and therefore the minimum running time in this class. In this sense, SP-allreduce refines Bucket allreduce: it preserves Bucket's key strengths while reducing the number of rounds by a factor of two. We further extend our approach to broader symmetric topologies and to communication trees of prescribed depths. Experimentally, the resulting algorithms improve over the best compared state-of-the-art algorithms for tori by up to $1.19\times$ on square tori and $1.65\times$ on rectangular tori across the tested configurations. On HyperX and spine-leaf networks, we demonstrate gains of up to $14.82\times$ and $1.72\times$, respectively, over the best evaluated baselines.

title: $\mathcal{D}$-Pullback Measure Attractors of McKean-Vlasov Stochastic Lattice Wave Equations
abstract: This paper deals with the pullback measure attractor for a non-autonomous distribution-dependent stochastic lattice wave equation with nonlinear noise on $\mathbb{Z}$. We establish well-posedness in the energy space $\ell^{2}\times\ell^{2}$ and show that the solution generates a continuous non-autonomous dynamical system on $\mathcal{P}_{4}(\ell^{2}\times\ell^{2})$, which possesses a unique pullback measure attractor $\mathcal{A}$. Furthermore, we prove the convergence of the attractor $\mathcal{A}^{\varepsilon}$ as $\varepsilon\to 0^{+}$ to the attractor of the corresponding distribution-independent limit system.

title: Entanglement and parametric resonance in coupled oscillator systems
abstract: We study a system of two quadratically-coupled harmonic oscillators, prepared respectively in the ground state and in a coherent state. This toy model can describe for instance the dynamics of one mode of a quantum field evolving in a harmonically-oscillating classical background. In such situations, it is well-known that, depending on the background oscillation amplitude and coupling strength, the system may exhibit parametric resonance. Using the Feynman-Vernon influence functional, we analyze the interplay between parametric resonance and quantum entanglement by perturbatively computing the purity of the mixed state resulting from tracing over one of the oscillators. We find a runaway behavior of the quantum entanglement between the two oscillators, as well as a rapid breakdown of the validity of perturbation theory, in regions of parametric instability. This provides a quantitative confirmation of various statements in the literature and is highly relevant to questions pertaining to the validity of the semiclassical approximation in coupled quantum-classical systems.

title: QBFF: Deep Quantum Bottleneck for Automatic Speaker Verification Anti-Spoofing
abstract: A central goal of quantum machine learning is to identify applications in which small quantum circuits can improve task performance while remaining executable on real hardware. We investigate deepfake (synthetic) speech detection, a largely unexplored application in this area, where reliable confidence scores are as important as discrimination performance because deployment decisions are made at fixed thresholds and overconfident errors can be costly. We introduce QBFF, which routes a compressed speech representation through a small 8-qubit variational circuit (VQC) used as a drop-in bottleneck, with a matched classical bottleneck as the control. The quantum circuit yields better-calibrated confidence in most matched comparisons, including out-of-distribution evaluation, though the downstream deployment-cost benefit is model-dependent. We then run the same circuit on a real IBM quantum processor. To our knowledge, this is the first anti-spoofing pipeline to run on a QPU; hardware execution demonstrates feasibility, with lower subset EER and $C_{llr}$ but higher mean actDCF than the matched classical reference. Together, these results show that hardware-executable quantum bottlenecks can improve score reliability, with gains that vary by evaluation setting.

title: RetroPlanner: Multi-Route Expansion and Multi-Objective Reasoning for LLM-Based Retrosynthesis Planning
abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis planning is often considered solved once a route to purchasable starting materials is found, but such a route should also be practical in real-world chemistry. Recent LLM-based planners formulate this process as sequential decision-making over an AND-OR graph, yet typically expand a single molecule per turn and are optimized for solvability alone, leaving alternative routes uncompared across the multiple objectives that determine practicality before the search budget is committed. We introduce RetroPlanner, an LLM-based planner that jointly compares multiple routes to steer the search toward higher synthesizability, as measured by reaction plausibility, round-trip consistency, and starting-material price. RetroPlanner is trained to reason over chemical evidence: structural progress from the target molecule, bond changes and reaction classes, where candidate routes diverge from one another, and how they rank across multiple objectives. Experiments on multi-step retrosynthesis benchmarks demonstrate that RetroPlanner recovers more alternative routes than prior LLM-based planners while improving synthetic route quality and maintaining a high success rate.

title: Ramsey Meets Simultaneous Planarity: Vertex Integrity and Pathwidth
abstract: We study the following simultaneous embedding problem: Given k graphs on the same vertex set with the same pairwise intersection, do they admit planar drawings that coincide on their shared graph? We establish fixed-parameter tractability with respect to the vertex integrity of the union graph (that is, the union of the input graphs) plus k, resolving an open question and generalizing the known algorithm parameterized by vertex cover number plus k. Our main technical contribution on the way towards this result is the extension of the recently introduced Ramsey pruning technique beyond ordering problems. Finally, we complement our tractability result with a lower bound that establishes NP-hardness when both k and the pathwidth of the union graph are bounded by constants, ruling out a generalization of our main result to path- or treewidth.

title: Almost invariant subspaces in the topologically non-trivial setting: a pedestrian approach
abstract: We present a self-contained, algorithmic construction of almost invariant subspaces [Panati et al. (2003), De Nittis and Panati (2010), Freund and Teufel (2016)] for Hofstadter-like Hamiltonians $H_b $ acting on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^2,\mathbb{C}^n)$. More precisely, for rational values of $b_0/(2π)$ we describe an iterative procedure that takes a ``locally gapped" projection $P_{0}$ (possibly topologically non-trivial) which commutes with $H_{b_0}$, into a projection $P_{\varepsilon}$ that commutes with $H_{b_0+\varepsilon}$ up to an error of order $\varepsilon^\infty$. Our construction insures that the Chern number of $P_{\varepsilon}$ equals the Chern number of $P_0$ as long as $P_\varepsilon$ exists. Moreover, its integrated density of states varies linearly with $\varepsilon$ (the ``Středa formula"). We also show that any spatially localized Parseval frame of $P_{0}$ can be mapped into to a localized Parseval frame of $P_{\varepsilon}$. We choose to work with a discrete model in order to keep the technicalities to a minimum level, with no need for advanced pseudo-differential calculus. Nevertheless, we are confident that most of our results can be extended to (unbounded) magnetic (pseudo)differential operators, but the technical burden would be much heavier. This is left for future work.

title: Dynamical generalizations of the two-point Chowla conjecture
abstract: In 1965, Chowla conjectured that the values of the Liouville function become asymptotically uncorrelated at consecutive natural numbers. Recently, the two-point case is resolved by OpenAI. In 2026, Charamaras and Richter conjectured a generalization of the Chowla conjecture to the asymptotic independence of the consecutive prime Omega functions. In this article, we prove the two-point case of their conjecture. As a consequence, we obtain a dynamical generalization of the two-point Chowla conjecture.

title: Space AI Infrastructure: Where the Edge Meets the Orbital Cloud
abstract: The fusion of artificial intelligence (AI) and space technologies is extending spaceborne intelligence beyond onboard payloads toward a global infrastructure, here termed Space AI infrastructure (SpaceAI-Infra). Its promise rests on two distinctive advantages of space systems: abundant solar energy in orbit and the global reach of satellite constellations. Realizing this promise hinges on a fundamental systems question: How should satellite constellations be designed and orchestrated to deliver data-center-scale AI services competitive with their terrestrial counterparts? This article develops a roadmap-oriented answer. We first chart the evolution of SpaceAI-Infra through three progressive stages: onboard AI, Space Edge AI, and Space Cloud AI. By revisiting the space-constrained fundamentals for end-to-end token services, we derive enabling design principles and translate them into an integrated space edge--cloud architecture. The communication-centric space edge comprises free-flying LEO constellations that provide user-proximate computing and form the access and backhaul fabric for cloud AI services. Complementing the edge, the computing-centric space cloud comprises formation-flying satellite constellations organized as space data centers in dawn--dusk sun-synchronous orbits. A case study demonstrates that the proposed architecture can support data-center-scale foundation-model inference for millions of concurrent users worldwide.

title: Sampling from Neural Operator Priors to Solve Partial Differential Equations
