DINOv3 features routed through a custom cross-attention matcher supply sub-pixel correspondences on mucosa where classical descriptors fail. Both enter a factor graph alongside a dense constraint from projective iterative closest point (ICP) registration against the system's own running reconstruction, so surface evidence stabilises the directions the visual factors leave weakly observable. On six airways rendered from patient CT scans, the system reaches 26.1 mm mean absolute trajectory error and 77.5% mean surface F-score. Its mean surface accuracy exceeds that of five recent monocular SLAM and feed-forward baselines. MASt3R-SLAM, which fits a free scale to the ground truth, has a lower mean trajectory error (22.0 mm). ORB-SLAM3 completes only two of the six airways, whereas our system completes all six and also reconstructs two ex vivo specimens.

title: The Thousand-Pulsar-Array programme on MeerKAT - XX. Co-existing interacting periodicities and polarization modulation in PSR J1901-0906
abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of the complex subpulse modulation in PSR J1901-0906 using data from the Thousand-Pulsar-Array (TPA) programme. Our analysis reveals the coexistence of three distinct periodicities in the subpulse modulation of both profile components, which obey a beat relation. We also detect additional spectral beat features caused by the modulation of these co-existing periodicities by investigating the Fourier phase correlation in two-dimensional fluctuation spectra. Moreover, the single-pulse polarization states are shown to be modulated and synchronized with the three co-existing periodicities observed in total intensity. Such synchronization has been reported for only a small number of pulsars, but this discovery marks the only one where this synchronization involves multiple co-existing periodicities. The modulation beats are similar to, yet more complex than, the beat system previously identified in PSR J1514-4834 with higher-order harmonics playing a significant role. The coexistence of the observed beat-like periodicities in PSR J1901-0906 implies that they are not independent, but rather originate from an underlying, interconnected physical system within the pulsar magnetosphere. Building upon the same geometric framework previously applied to PSR J1514-4834, we demonstrate that a feedback system with interacting rotating carousels successfully reproduces the complex subpulse modulations observed in PSR J1901-0906 and naturally explains the beat relations.

title: New tools for sparse graph embeddings: Hybrid expanders and application to nested cycles
abstract: We introduce \emph{hybrid expanders}, sparse graphs which combine sublinear expansion across all scales with strong constant-factor expansion on smaller, polylogarithmic sets. We show that every $n$-vertex graph of average degree at least $2^{ω(\log^*n)}$ contains such a subgraph, and use this local expansion to bring into the sparse setting tree-embedding and rollback tools more commonly associated with random or pseudorandom graphs. As an application, for fixed $k\in\mathbb N$, we prove that every graph satisfying this average-degree condition contains $k$ pairwise edge-disjoint cycles with nested vertex sets and compatible cyclic orders, resolving up to a quasi-constant factor a problem of Thomassen, originating in work of Erdős.

title: Parton distribution functions and strong coupling constant: MSHT
abstract: We present an overview of the MSHT family of global PDF fits. We describe the underlying methodology, including parameterisation choice, theoretical inputs and datasets included in the fit. We describe the impact of recent theoretical advances in the inclusion of higher order QCD and EW corrections on the fit and their implications for phenomenology. We discuss recent methodological improvements and ongoing studies relating to closure tests of the parameterisation flexibility and the inclusion of errors on errors for experimental data. We in addition discuss recent results on the determination of the strong coupling from the MSHT fits.

title: $\texttt{NFDiag}$: High-dimensional MCMC Convergence Diagnosis with Normalizing Flows
abstract: Accurately assessing the convergence of Monte Carlo Markov Chains is crucial for ensuring their validity in Bayesian inference problems. However, convergence assessment in high dimensions is known to be difficult, due to most convergence diagnostics becoming insensitive beyond a few dozen parameters. Conventional convergence statistics analyze marginal distributions which in high dimensions neglects increasing levels of information from the joint and conditional probability distributions. Thus we propose $\texttt{NFDiag}$, which taps into the information of the full multivariate joint posterior with a normalizing flow (NF). Our convergence diagnostic thereby also analyzes information from conditional distributions. In other words, by working in the full multivariate space, it is sensitive with respect to the geometry of the chain in high dimensions. Our diagnostic utilizes that NFs assume independent and identically distributed (iid) training samples, which is a testable assumption that will be violated by a non-converged or strongly correlated chain. Our diagnostic trains NFs on separate parts of a chain, and then assesses whether these correspond to the same multivariate target distribution. We test our diagnostic in up to 250 dimensions, and demonstrate it is universal and unbiased, and detects problematic chain quality also when Gelman-Rubin $\hat{R}$ and the multivarite effective sample size do not.

title: Distributed $(Δ+1)$-Coloring in $O(\sqrtΔ+\log^* n)$ Rounds
abstract: We give a deterministic distributed algorithm for $(Δ+1)$-coloring an $n$-node graph of maximum degree $Δ$ in $O(\sqrtΔ+\log^* n)$ rounds in both the LOCAL and CONGEST models. More generally, $(°+1)$-list coloring with lists from a color space of size $C\geqΔ+1$ can be solved in $O(\sqrtΔ\log(1+C/Δ)+\log^* n)$ rounds; in CONGEST, we assume $C\leq n^{O(1)}$. The algorithm combines Barenboim's polynomial coloring procedure with arbdefective decompositions, degree reduction, and a short family of hash functions. Using the polynomial procedure in the degree-reduction framework already gives an $O(\sqrtΔ\logΔ+\log^* n)$-round algorithm when $C=O(Δ)$. Hashing adapts the color space to the current degree and removes the logarithmic factor. We prove the existence of the hash family by the probabilistic method and compute it by deterministic exhaustive search, using unrestricted local computation. We also give an explicit variant based on lossless expanders that avoids this search and achieves $O(\sqrtΔ+\log^* n)$ rounds for $C=O(Δ)$.

title: NANO: A Unified Optimization Framework for Nonlinear Gaussian Filtering
abstract: Conventional Gaussian filtering typically approximates nonlinear models or their statistical moments and retains the Kalman update structure. The resulting approximation errors can affect both state estimates and their uncertainty. This paper presents the Natural Gradient Gaussian Approximation (NANO) framework for nonlinear filtering. Both prediction and measurement update are formulated as optimization problems over Gaussian distributions, with the entire Gaussian distribution serving as the optimization variable. The framework integrates observation losses, distributional discrepancies, natural-gradient optimization, and finite-step update rules, providing a unified formulation for constructing different filters. Natural-gradient iterations account for the geometry of the Gaussian family and jointly update the distribution parameters. The framework incorporates the existing NANO-P method using the Kullback-Leibler divergence and introduces NANO-W using the Wasserstein distance. NANO-P maintains covariance positive definiteness through a positive-semidefinite curvature approximation, while NANO-W uses a covariance transport update that accommodates indefinite curvature. Their update rules and sufficient conditions for covariance positive definiteness are established within the common framework. Through these two realizations, the proposed framework achieves the best estimation accuracy among the evaluated methods on each of six benchmarks. Runtime evaluations further assess its computational feasibility for practical applications.

title: CineRecon: Benchmarking Frontier Models for Agentic Cinematic Reconstruction
abstract: Reconstructing reference videos as editable dynamic 3D scenes is an important path toward controllable video generation for filmmaking: these scenes provide modifiable, renderable visual proxies that enable explicit control over scene layout, subject actions, and camera behavior. To evaluate agents' ability to reconstruct editable dynamic 3D scenes from dynamic reference videos, we introduce CineRecon, a benchmark comprising 50 reference videos and 360 annotated evaluation clips. The reference videos span film, real-world footage, and games. Given a complete video, an agent uses tools to construct, animate, render, and refine its reconstruction. We evaluate this task under three representation settings: Proxy, Simplified, and Detailed. These settings increase geometric and appearance requirements while retaining the same requirements for spatial relations, camera behavior, and subject dynamics. This design tests whether agents can reproduce the events in a video when detailed appearance is unnecessary, and how performance changes as representation requirements increase. For evaluation, we construct checklists that associate observable properties and events with specific entities and times. A vision-language judge compares timestamp-aligned reference and rendered frames across 11 categories, grouped into camera, static, and dynamic consistency dimensions. We evaluate 12 models using their corresponding agent harnesses and find failures across all three dimensions. Subject motions and interactions remain difficult to reproduce even under the Proxy setting.

title: Variational Filtering for Bayesian Last Layers with an Independent Binary Probit Surrogate
abstract: Modern deep classifiers trained by gradient descent need many passes over the data to become accurate, and even then are not always well calibrated; post-hoc temperature scaling corrects calibration after training but cannot influence training-time accuracy or convergence. We propose a variational filtering algorithm for the last layer of deep classifiers, whose parameters are treated as the latent state of a linear-Gaussian state-space model. Each mini-batch is assimilated by an exact prediction step followed by a closed-form variational update, made conjugate by an independent binary probit (IBProbit) surrogate for the categorical likelihood. The filter's process noise stabilises the updates under feature drift and keeps the predictive distribution from collapsing to a point estimate, allowing the same procedure to be used for linear probing on a frozen backbone and for full-network fine-tuning. We evaluate on DINOv3 backbones against two baselines tuned under an identical protocol: AdamW with cross-entropy and post-hoc temperature scaling, and Variational Bayesian Last Layers (VBLL). As a linear probe on frozen features, IBProbit attains the best accuracy and negative log-likelihood on all five downstream tasks at the largest backbone, and on two of the five at the smallest. In out-of-distribution detection with CIFAR probes on the largest backbone, IBProbit reduces the false-positive rate at 95\% true-positive rate by a factor of 1.4 to 3.2 relative to the better of the two baselines, on all three dataset pairs. When the whole network is fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k, IBProbit reaches the final performance of the cross-entropy baseline in half the wall-clock time.

title: LLM-HB: Language-Aware LLM-Guided Hotword Biasing for Code-Switching ASR
abstract: Code-switching (CS) speech, characterized by language alternation within a single utterance, is prevalent in multilingual communities and poses challenges to automatic speech recognition (ASR) due to rapid language transitions. We propose LLM-HB, a language-aware large language model-guided hotword biasing framework for code-switching ASR (CS-ASR). The framework incorporates a mixture-of-experts (MoE) adaptor and an auxiliary language prediction head to better capture and differentiate multilingual representations, while hotwords are injected through LLM-based prompting. Experiments on the ASRU2019 code-switching challenge test set demonstrate that LLM-HB achieves a 20.30% relative reduction in mixed error rate (MER) over the baseline, reaching 5.85% MER under a 15-distractor hotword setting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrate LLM-guided biasing into code-switching ASR. We further release the extracted ASRU2019 hotword list to support future research.

title: Pointwise Ergodic Theorems Along Reiter Sequences on Locally Compact Groups
abstract: Let $G$ be a locally compact, second countable group admitting a Reiter sequence, and suppose that $G$ acts on a von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}$ equipped with a semifinite trace $τ$ via trace-preserving automorphisms. In this paper, we prove a maximal inequality for ergodic averages along such Reiter sequences. Our approach relies on approximating the Reiter sequence by a linear combination of characteristic functions of Følner sequences using the layer-cake representation. Furthermore, we establish the bilateral almost uniform convergence of these ergodic averages. As an application, we deduce a non-commutative Wiener-Wintner type theorem along Reiter sequences.

title: Tailored VxOy Metal--Insulator-Transition Oxides for Temperature-Triggered Smart Insulation in Superconducting Coils
abstract: Smart insulation is a turn-to-turn layer that insulates in normal operation and conducts only near a hot spot. It could combine the fast ramping of insulated coils with the passive energy dump of non-insulated coils. Metal-insulator transition (MIT) oxides are natural candidates, but the only one tested in a coil so far, V2O3, switches at 150-170 K, far above the 30-70 K window useful for REBCO magnets. We explore the vanadium-oxygen system to lower the transition. TGA redox processing produced multi-phase powders with an effective transition near 127 K, about 25 K below V2O3. Hydrothermal V3O7, hydrated or annealed, was far too resistive and showed no usable transition. V2O3-epoxy specimens provided a robust reference and an acceptance criterion. Cryogenic measurements revealed a reproducible thermal hysteresis, and the measured specific heat of V2O3 corrects earlier model inputs by close to two orders of magnitude. A first electro-thermal model reproduces current sharing through the smart-insulation layer. Doped V2O3 and V8O15 are identified as the next targets.

title: Characterizing and Mitigating Distributional Bias in Physics-Informed Generative Models
abstract: Physics-informed generative models augment a data-fitting objective with residual penalties that encourage physical constraints to hold in generated samples. However, improving constraint satisfaction need not improve fidelity to the data distribution. We study this conflict in residual-regularized diffusion models and identify two possible consequences. First, the same prediction error can incur different residual costs near different feasible states, preferring states with lower residual sensitivity (avoidance). Second, this preference can extend to feasible states outside the data support, where the residual also vanishes (leakage). Motivated by this analysis, we propose a data-anchored penalty that weights prediction errors by the residual Jacobian at the clean training sample and normalizes the resulting magnitude. This removes the incentive to relocate to less sensitive states without changing the model architecture or sampling procedure. Experiments on a controlled synthetic system, three PDE systems, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching demonstrate the benefits of anchoring. Code is available at https://github.com/TanjaBien/anchored_diffusion.

title: Fatou Components of Attracting Skew Products: From Polynomial Classification to Transcendental Complexity
abstract: We study the Fatou components of holomorphic skew products $F \colon \mathbb{C}^2 \to \mathbb{C}^2, F(z,w) = (f(z) + r(z,w), g(w))$ near an attracting invariant fiber, introducing a refined classification of components on the fiber: bulging, partial bulging, and nowhere bulging. For polynomial skew products, we give a complete characterization of when the basin at infinity is non-bulging, and show that in this case non-bulging implies nowhere bulging, ruling out partial bulging entirely. In the transcendental setting, the behavior is richer: we construct partially bulging wandering domains and Baker domains, show that any orbitally unbounded Fatou component can be made nowhere bulging by choosing an appropriate function $r$, and prove that for any nonconstant $r$ there exists an entire function $f$ with an escaping wandering domain that fails to be bulging. Bulging thus depends on the interplay between fiber dynamics and perturbation.

title: Identifying Arctic states vulnerable to rapid ice loss with a convolutional neural network
abstract: This work investigates the incidence of rapid ice-loss events in the Arctic, in which a substantial fraction of September sea-ice is lost in only a few years. Such events are seen to occur in climate model simulations forced with increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, but not as yet in the relatively short observational record. We train a convolutional neural network (CNN) using six large climate model ensembles to diagnose vulnerability to rapid ice-loss events. The trained model is shown to separate higher and lower risk states in out-of-sample climate models via a leave-one-out cross-validation. The model emphasises the role of persistently thin sea-ice, remaining sea-ice extent and sustained high upper ocean heat content as predictors of rapid ice-loss. The CNN is applied to observational data over the satelite-era showing a signal for rapid ice-loss prior to a drop around 2007 and an increasing risk from around 2015 to present. Such rapid-ice loss events would likely have dramatic consequences for Arctic ecosystems, coastal communities and global shipping.

title: Onset condition of the ramified-jet regime: an experimental and theoretical study
abstract: This study experimentally and theoretically investigates the electrically induced transition of a gas-focused liquid jet into a rim-emitting sheet. Ultra-high-speed imaging was used to examine the effects of applied voltage, gas and liquid flow rates, and liquid properties on sheet formation and breakup. Fully developed, quasi-stable sheets formed with ethanol, whereas isopropanol exhibited only initial sheet formation. Increasing voltage promoted sheet stretching, finer and more numerous rim jets, and a narrower spray. Higher gas flow rates shifted the transition towards the nozzle and produced finer structures, while higher liquid flow rates generated larger sheets with thicker rims. A first-order theoretical model assumes an equipotential interface and neglects finite charge relaxation, hydrodynamic perturbations, and nonlinear evolution. It balances destabilizing Maxwell-pressure perturbations against restoring capillary-pressure perturbations on a conducting cylindrical jet. The model identifies the elliptic azimuthal mode, m = 2, as the first unstable mode leading to sheet formation and predicts a critical electric Bond number of 3. Predicted onset voltages agree with measurements within 20%, and the threshold was consistent with published ramified-electrospray observations. The agreement with experiments supports electrocapillary symmetry breaking as the mechanism of onset and provides a compact, physically grounded criterion for predicting the transition from electrified jets to rim-emitting sheets.

title: OctMole: Multiscale 3D Molecular Generation with Hierarchical Spatial Flows
abstract: Generating accurate 3D molecules requires jointly determining a variable number of atoms, their identities, and geometry across spatial scales: global shape emerges coarsely, whereas chemical bonds demand fine local precision. Existing atom-based diffusion and flow models operate largely at a single scale, while dense spatial fields become costly at high resolution. We introduce OctMole, a multiscale octree flow framework for 3D molecular generation. A hierarchical occupancy flow progressively resolves sparse molecular support from coarse to fine, and a joint atom flow assigns atom types and continuous in-cell offsets to occupied leaves. This decomposition combines efficient global structure with subcell geometric precision, while cell corruption improves robustness to generated support. On QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, OctMole achieves strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality, with particularly clear gains over Uni-3DAR on GEOM-DRUG and substantial efficiency gains over dense 3D generation. As an additional capability, intermediate occupancy states and selected regions provide spatial conditioning without task-specific retraining, supporting multiscale shape conditioning, regional editing, linker generation, and shape interpolation. Code and pretrained checkpoints are available at https://github.com/octree-nn/octmole and https://huggingface.co/Disembo/octmole, respectively.

title: Code-Interactive Visual Reasoning for Financial Candlestick Understanding
abstract: Financial candlestick understanding requires locating visual elements, aligning them across trading dates and panels, and combining observations through numerical and financial reasoning. Answer accuracy alone does not reveal whether predictions are supported by chart evidence. We introduce Code-Interactive Financial Candlestick Reasoning and present Fin-Thinker, a model based on Qwen3.5-9B that generates and executes code to acquire evidence and perform computations. The model uses the returned observations to guide subsequent reasoning. To train these capabilities, we construct FinKLine-32K with 32,184 replay-verified code-observation trajectories collected through teacher-guided student exploration. These include successful solutions with and without error recovery. Our three-stage training framework combines foundational visual-code fine-tuning, financial process supervision of successful reasoning and corrective continuations, and execution-feedback reinforcement learning. For evaluation, we introduce FinKLineBench with 1,200 questions across 138 financial task types to assess answer correctness, code execution, and evidence grounding separately. On FinKLineBench, Fin-Thinker improves strict accuracy by 13.1 and 33.2 percentage points over the best-performing direct-answer baseline among those evaluated and its base model with sandbox access, respectively. Training-stage ablations further show that financial process supervision and execution-feedback reinforcement learning yield successive improvements in both answer accuracy and GPT-5.6-judged grounded accuracy.

title: Demand Under a Mechanical Price: Elasticity and Welfare in Ethereum's Data-Availability Market
abstract: Ethereum sells data-availability capacity to rollups through "blobs" priced by a controller: the blob fee rises and falls exponentially with cumulative usage above or below a target, and no auction sets it. We measure what this mechanical price costs. The Pectra upgrade of 7 May 2025 doubled blob capacity on a date fixed weeks in advance, while the market was congested, and the blob fee fell from 0.82 mETH per blob (about USD 1.40) to its 1-wei floor. Rollups' blob purchases rose 24%. The 95% interval, built from the same estimator at 516 placebo dates, runs from 8% to 40%, so removing the entire price raised purchases by at most 40%. The implied elasticity at the pre-shock price is -0.19, and no value below -0.31 is consistent with the interval. The estimate includes any rise in L2 activity that coincided with the fork, so it bounds the price response from above. With demand this inelastic, the controller works mainly as a transfer. Rollups paid USD 14.8 million in blob fees under the first blob regime, 67% of it in two quarters when capacity was full and any market-clearing mechanism would have collected comparable scarcity rents. Where capacity was slack, the reserve price introduced in December 2025 cost at most 2.6 ETH (USD 8,039) in deadweight loss under the most elastic demand the data allow. Mempool records for 5.4 million blob transactions show that when the fee sits at its floor, capacity is slack: transactions miss about one block and are almost never priced out.

title: HyBRA-EEG: Hyperbolic Global-Local Brain-Region Aggregation for Self-Supervised EEG Representation Learning
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) representation learning is challenged by noisy signals, inter-subject variability, and heterogeneous electrode montages in different datasets and recording settings. Recent self-supervised EEG pretraining methods improve transferability by converting heterogeneous recordings into unified token or sequence representations, but channel-aware designs may still encode montage- or dataset-specific regularities. We propose HyBRA, a self-supervised framework based on hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation. HyBRA maps heterogeneous channel observations into a fixed regional token space by combining electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances. A channel-evidence injection branch preserves fine-grained discriminative cues during aggregation. The resulting tokens are processed by a Region-Time Transformer and pretrained with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals. HyBRA outperforms the compared methods in average balanced accuracy on six benchmark datasets. Under a controlled six-fold evaluation on OpenBMI-MI, HyBRA matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 percentage points and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, and uses 96.8\% fewer parameters. Matched comparisons on TUAB and TUEV show higher balanced accuracy for hyperbolic matching than for Euclidean distance or cosine similarity.

title: Admittance extraction of quantum dot arrays for charge sensing
abstract: This work demonstrates admittance extraction of quantum dot arrays using a rate equation frame- work matching experimental reflectometry measurements. Using a semiclassical rate equation, we consider a perturbation of the source/drain chemical potential to model reflectometry readout in a quantum dot array. This is a time-dependent extension of the rate equation which has been employed in literature for pumped arrays of quantum dots and capacitance extractions. Here we extend this to a double quantum dot for admittance extraction. The simulations are calibrated us- ing Fermi-Hubbard parameters extracted from experimental data, which it is then shown to closely approximate to.

title: JtT: Rethinking Point Trajectory Diffusion for Diverse and Rigid Motion from an Image
abstract: We study forecasting rigid-body motion from a single image: generating diverse and physically plausible future trajectories for arbitrary points in a scene, without building rigidity into the architecture or relying on geometric inputs such as depth. Like video generators, recent trajectory generators fail at this task, even in simple synthetic Kubric scenes, despite scaling up model size and training on real data. We show how to solve this with the right architecture and parameterization. Our model, JtT, is a simple diffusion transformer that operates directly in coordinate space and decodes arbitrary and dense query patterns, without the trajectory VAEs or fixed grids assumed in prior work. Through a systematic study of the design space of point trajectory diffusion, we find that diffusing per-frame velocities is the only parameterization that captures rigidity, that it must be paired with the right timestep schedule, and that adding full-resolution RGB at the query points resolves the boundary failures of prior methods. However, evaluating such 2D models rigorously is itself non-trivial. To our knowledge, we are the first to observe that physical plausibility and diversity do not improve together during training: larger models, as used in prior work, memorize the single ground-truth future per training image, becoming more rigid while covering fewer possible futures. Yet prior work has paid little attention to this, so we show how model rankings depend on model size, metric, and stopping time, and adopt a stricter, checkpoint-averaged evaluation protocol. Under this protocol, JtT improves over prior methods on both distributional and rigidity metrics and approaches ground-truth rigidity, with only about 50M parameters.

title: Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) is commonly used to enhance the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in solving complex multi-turn tasks. During rollout, agentic RL exhibits a workload pattern distinct from that of traditional RL: multi-turn interactions repeatedly introduce prefill requests, causing prefill and decode workloads to coexist throughout rollout. This workload makes prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation, a design widely used for online LLM serving, promising for speeding up agentic RL rollout. This paper shows that PD disaggregation can improve rollout efficiency by (a) mitigating interference among data-parallel attention modules, (b) enabling stage-specific parallelism, and (c) reducing end-to-end trajectory completion time. However, a fixed prefill-decode allocation may fail to sustain these benefits as workload composition varies across tasks and over time. We therefore present Prorsa, an agentic RL framework for prediction-guided prefill-decode resource allocation. Prorsa observes the lifecycle of every trajectory to forecast short-horizon prefill and decode demand. These forecasts then guide worker allocation decisions and trigger role switching of rollout engines, aligning prefill and decode capacity with anticipated workload demand. Across synchronous and asynchronous agentic RL settings, Prorsa achieves end-to-end rollout speedups of 1.11x-4.05x over prefill-decode colocation.

title: Double-Rollout Reinforcement Learning with Sampling-based Reward Estimation
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) implemented with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has driven substantial progress in training reasoning language models. However, verifiable outcome rewards provide an imperfect measure of reasoning quality: a correct final answer may not be supported by the reasoning trace, whereas an incorrect rollout may contain a nearly correct reasoning trajectory. We present empirical evidence for this mismatch and hypothesize that the resulting reward noise contributes to instability in reinforcement learning for both reasoning accuracy and token efficiency. To address this credit assignment challenge, this paper proposes double-rollout reinforcement learning. For each sampled rollout, we truncate its reasoning trace, sample multiple continuations from the truncated prefix, and replace the original reward with the mean continuation reward, yielding a more robust estimate of reasoning quality. This double-rollout algorithm incurs only a moderate increase in compute cost and yet reaches substantially higher accuracies across math and coding tasks and across Qwen and Nemotron models than baseline algorithms with fewer RL steps. For example, using only DAPO data it trains Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B to reach 95.4% on AIME 2026, versus 91.5% by GRPO and substantially above state of the art for this model size, within 30 RL steps. When combined with length-based rewards, the same algorithm further improves the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier over existing efficiency optimizations. These findings suggest that the double-rollout reward estimation is an effective and cost-efficient way to improve both the accuracy and token efficiency of reasoning RL.

title: Software Testing Meets Bayesian Workflow: A Literature-Driven Artifact Study of Probabilistic Programs
abstract: Automated testing is an effective software quality assurance method, but it is rarely used for probabilistic models. This is despite the heavy use of probabilistic programming for data analytics in research and engineering, where the consequences of errors are dire. A key obstacle is the specification of testable correctness properties for probabilistic models, known as the oracle problem. Like machine learning, probabilistic programming is used precisely where no analytical specification exists: had we been able to write one, we would have written an algorithm instead of fitting a model. An alternative is partial, proxy correctness specifications. The statistics literature already offers many, but as quality guidelines that require human judgment: comparing plots, visually analyzing shapes of distributions, assessing whether parameter values are ''far'' or ''close enough''. These guidelines are not systematically automated. In this work, we elicit, implement, and study testable correctness properties of probabilistic models. We extract 17 broadly applicable properties for probabilistic models from one of the most widely used textbooks in Bayesian data analysis, Statistical Rethinking by McElreath. For each property, we select and implement a test oracle, and study its utility for automatic testing, using a population of 59 probabilistic models from academic and industrial sources. We find realistic use cases (models under test) for all the properties. We observe that the vast majority of tests are not flaky in practice, despite the theoretical potential for flakiness. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to investigate the effectiveness of mutation testing for probabilistic models, showing that standard mutation operators do not capture faults tracked by the probabilistic properties.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Cortical Surface Reconstruction and Spherical Registration for Heterogeneous Brain MRI
abstract: Surface-based cortical analysis is useful in many applications as it is a natural way to model the highly folded structure of the cerebral cortex, allowing quantities such as curvature and thickness to be easily calculated. Existing deep learning (DL) methods have focused on 1x1x1 mm3 T1-weighted (T1w) scans, thus replicating classical pipelines. Here we present a neural network that is trained exclusively on synthetic scans with random contrast and resolution. Consequently, it can be applied to almost any kind of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan. In addition, our model provides vertex-wise uncertainty estimates of the predicted surface as well as a spherical registration to fsaverage space. Our model performs on par with other state-of-the-art DL methods on 1x1x1 mm3 T1w scans and outperforms the only other method capable of estimating cortical surfaces from low resolution, non-T1w scans. The predicted uncertainty, moreover, correlates with overall scan quality on low resolution scans and highlights areas of poor surface reconstruction on 1x1x1 mm3 T1w scans, suggesting that it can be used for quality control. Finally, the predicted spherical registrations prove comparable to other DL and classical registration methods. These qualities, when combined with the fast inference time, will provide the ability to analyze large, existing databases of clinical MRI scans, with the potential for finding disease-specific patterns that would otherwise be infeasible in a research setting.

title: Towards Modality-Agnostic Seizure Classification: A Unified Deep Learning Framework for Heterogeneous EEG and Intracranial EEG Signals
abstract: Seizure prediction and detection, essential for clinical treatment of epilepsy, remain the crucial task of this neurological disease. EEG and iEEG are widely used to analyze epilepsy due to its capability of capturing discriminative brain activities at high time resolution. However, existing works generally analyze either EEG or iEEG seizure activity separately, where EEG analysis has been well-researched, while more and more works consider iEEG for its higher specificity at the spatial level and signal quality. Currently, most of the existing seizure prediction systems are single-modal in nature, which limits its application to a variety of clinical conditions. Therefore, a common framework to analyze seizures with both EEG and iEEG signals needs to be developed. This paper presents a new framework of multimodal seizure classification integrating the heterogeneous EEG and iEEG recordings from different subjects and sources. A specific framework, called Unified Multimodal Signal Harmonization (UMSH), is developed for harmonizing signals with varied sampling rates and recording conditions. Moreover, to handle the extremely class-imbalanced problem in the data sets, we use a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) based data augmentation technique to generate synthetic samples to balance the class distribution. The proposed framework uses the EEGNet-Vision Transformer (EEGNet-ViT) as the feature extraction and classification network to learn the local discriminative patterns as well as global contextual information in the multimodal seizure data. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for robust seizure classification, emphasizing the potential of integrated EEG-iEEG multimodal learning in advancing next-generation epilepsy monitoring and clinical decision-support systems.

title: DEFlow: Deep Equilibrium Flow Maximum-Entropy Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Expressive flow policies can represent multiple high-value actions, but sampling them with few integration steps while retaining tractable action densities remains challenging. We introduce DEFlow, a deep equilibrium flow policy that replaces explicit Euler sampling with implicit Euler integration and solves all intermediate actions jointly as an equilibrium system. We combine implicit differentiation with a discrete change-of-variables formula for the final-action density, enabling off-policy training within soft actor-critic without backpropagating through solver iterations. DEFlow achieves an average relative improvement of approximately 10% in mean successful coverage over the strongest baseline across four Multi-Goal docking variants. It also achieves the highest mean time-averaged return on four of five manipulation tasks, while remaining broadly competitive across five MuJoCo tasks. These results support implicit flow policies for tasks requiring both diversity and precision, at the cost of additional nonlinear and linear solves. Primary

title: Detecting Chain-of-Thought Hijacking in Backdoored Multimodal Large Reasoning Models
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs) to solve complex visual problems, but also exposes them to CoT hijacking: an adversary implants a backdoor through poisoned fine-tuning so that a visual trigger induces a hijacking turn, redirecting an otherwise faithful reasoning chain to an attacker-chosen answer. However, since the hijack acts within the reasoning chain, existing multimodal backdoor defenses designed for MLLMs that answer directly struggle to detect it. Moreover, inspecting the chain itself does not reliably expose the hijack, since the hijacking turn can resemble honest self-correction in form. In this paper, we find that honest reasoning tends to revise its answer at high-entropy "aha moments", whereas a hijack can overturn a confident answer through a near-deterministic turn. To quantify this contrast, we formalize this phenomenon as belief inertia, the cumulative next-token entropy of a reasoning span minus the answer-belief revision it induces, with markedly lower values for hijacked spans than for honest reasoning spans. Since hijacking tokens are also image-dependent, we further improve detection by restricting the measure to image-dependent spans, yielding visual belief inertia (VBI). Building on this, we propose InertiaGuard, a training-free, test-time detector that flags a trace when its VBI falls below a threshold calibrated on a small set of clean traces. Across various attacks and benchmarks, InertiaGuard achieves higher detection performance than existing baselines, while generalizing to different model architectures and trigger types.

title: Solubility of poorly soluble species in bulk and nanopores from grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling
abstract: Poorly soluble species can have mean populations below one in small systems such as nanopores. In this regime, the grand-potential minimum, which identifies the most probable particle number, differs from the ensemble-averaged solute loading. We use grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling (GCWLS) to calculate the density of states $Ω(N_\mathrm{A}, N_\mathrm{B})$ for a binary Lennard-Jones mixture of solute B in solvent A, both in bulk and in slit pores. One set of GCWLS simulations gives ensemble averages over a range of chemical potentials, whereas conventional grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation requires a separate simulation at each state point. Independent GCMC simulations confirm the GCWLS ensemble averages. The solvent number distribution is nearly Gaussian, whereas the dilute solute distribution is skewed and Poisson-like. The most probable solute number therefore lies below the ensemble-averaged loading $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle$ and is zero whenever $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle<1$. Reading the solute loading from the grand-potential minimum underestimates it and can falsely indicate that no solute is present. Defining the oversolubility as $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}=x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{conf}}/x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{bulk}}$, where $x_\mathrm{B}$ is the solute mole fraction, we find $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}\approx12$ in a pore of 3.5 particle diameters width when both wall interactions are repulsive. Adding wall-solute attraction moderately raises it to $\approx13$, whereas wall-solvent attraction lowers it to $\approx3.4$. This comparison shows that the wall-solvent interaction controls most of the enhancement. As the pore widens, $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}$ decreases toward unity. In bulk and in nanopores alike, the solubility of poorly soluble species should be obtained from ensemble averages rather than from grand-potential minima.

title: The symmetry group of Turk's head knots
abstract: For p, q >= 3 with gcd(p,q) = 1 we show that the symmetry group of the Turk's head knot Th(p,q), the closure of the braid (sigma_1 sigma_2^{-1} sigma_3 sigma_4^{-1} ... sigma_{p-1}^{+-1})^q, is the dihedral group of order 4q. This proves Conjecture R of Di Prisa and Şavk for q >= 3; the case p = 3 is due to Sakuma and Weeks. The argument is diagrammatic: by the flyping theorem of Menasco and Thistlethwaite, the symmetries of a knot with a prime, reduced alternating diagram without non-trivial flypes are the symmetries of the diagram (we write out a proof for the diagrams at hand), and we show that the standard diagram of Th(p,q) has no non-trivial flypes and exactly 4q symmetries. The chirality of Th(p,q) for even p, which also follows from a theorem of Murasugi, is visible in the group. We compare the argument with the geometric one of Sakuma and Weeks for p = 3.

title: MixLID: Token-Level Language Identification in Mixed-Language Text
abstract: Processing multilingual text requires both identifying a broad range of languages and distinguishing the language of each token in inputs containing multiple languages. We introduce MixLID, a token-level language identification model supporting 111 language-script combinations. MixLID follows a two-stage training process: it first learns to distinguish individual languages using the language labels of monolingual examples, then continues training on mixed-language data. The second stage uses concatenated examples from existing code-switching data alongside augmented examples created through word substitution based on correspondences between English source words and loanwords. For monolingual identification, MixLID outperforms all baselines in both accuracy and macro F1 on four benchmarks within the language coverage shared with each baseline. For mixed-language identification, it outperforms the baselines in identifying the language of individual tokens on every evaluated language pair. MixLID achieves high performance across a broad range of languages in both monolingual and mixed-language settings. The model is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/nlpai-lab/MixLID.

title: An updated view of Jupiter's UV main auroral emission: large-scale analysis of UV and particle data from Juno's first 60 orbits
abstract: The properties and origins of Jupiter's UV main auroral emission are, at present, not yet fully understood, particularly the extent to which its two distinct zones, the Zone-I and Zone-II aurora, originate from a common source. In this work, remote-sensing and in-situ data from the Juno spacecraft are used to investigate and produce maps of the average properties of the main emission over Juno's first 60 orbits. It is found that the peak in mean energy of electrons precipitating in the main emission is consistently poleward of the energy-flux (or brightness) peak, in both hemispheres and at all local times, and is co-located with the statistical location of the Zone-II aurora. Evidence is presented that the flux-energy relationship of the main emission is adequately characterised by theoretical power laws describing electron acceleration from quasi-static potentials or Alfvénic turbulence and that it shows a modulation with ionospheric electron density consistent with theoretical predictions. Finally, the average energy spectra of precipitating electrons in the Zone-I aurora remain power-law-like between an energy flux of 1 and 100 mW m$^{-2}$, whereas the average Zone-II spectra develop a distinct ``plateau'' or ``flattop'' shape beyond an energy flux of $\sim$5 mW m$^{-2}$. Our results provide some evidence that the Zone-I and Zone-II aurorae are phenomenologically distinct, and the consequences of this interpretation for future investigation of the main emission are discussed.

title: The ring of values of $E$-functions is not a field
abstract: Let $\mathbf{E}$ be the ring of values taken at algebraic points by $E$-functions. The exponential function and the Bessel function $J_0$ are classical examples of $E$-functions. We prove that $\mathbf{E}$ is not a field. More precisely, we prove that it is neither noetherian nor factorial, and construct non-units of $\mathbf{E}$ explicity, including $e+1$, $J_0(1)$, and ${}_1F_1(a;b;1)$ for rational parameters $a$ and $b$ such that $0

title: Design and Analysis of a Nonlinear Parallel Mechanism Coupling for Dynamic Humanoid Legs
abstract: Humanoids increasingly demand lightweight leg mechanisms for agile, dynamic, and energy-efficient locomotion. Reducing distal inertia through proximal actuation has thus become a common design goal. Yet, compact transmissions that preserve torque capability and efficient force transmission remain hard to achieve. This paper presents a novel series-parallel leg design combining a knee parallel mechanism, an ankle parallel mechanism, and a nonlinear knee-ankle coupling where all actuators placed closer to the hip. As the knee flexes, the coupling passively assists ankle dorsiflexion for foot clearance and, as it extends it assists plantarflexion for push-off, redistributing ankle load through the knee transmission. We derive the coupling's nonlinear transmission models and validate them in simulation and on hardware. The design shows that the shared transmission lets both joints draw on each other's actuator capacity by easing the knee's peak torque demand under load and the ankle's peak speed demand during fast motion. With the leg's proximal actuator placement, the leg achieves an effective reflected mass of 0.37 kg at the foot for a 6 kg leg, demonstrating very low distal leg inertia for dynamic humanoid robots.

title: $2$-large sets are sets of nil-Bohr recurrence
abstract: A set $S$ of positive integers is $2$-large if every two-coloring contains arbitrarily long monochromatic arithmetic progressions with common difference in $S$. We prove that every such set meets every nil-Bohr neighborhood of $0$. This proves a conjecture of the first author and gives a sharp answer to a question of Host, Kra, and Maass. We also show that, for every fixed nil-Bohr neighborhood $B$ of $0$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, restricting the common difference to $B$ increases the extremal number for $k$-term arithmetic progressions by at most a factor of $1+\varepsilon$, provided $k$ is sufficiently large.

title: Homotopy Self-Equivalences of $\mathbb{R}P^2\times S^2$ and a Braid for non-orientable $4$-Manifolds
abstract: We compute the group of based homotopy classes of self-homotopy equivalences of the non-orientable $4$-manifold $\RP^2\times S^2$. It is an elementary abelian $2$-group of rank $5$. The subgroup of classes whose based lift to the universal cover $S^2\times S^2$ has degree $+1$ has rank $4$ and is isomorphic to the group of free homotopy classes. The group maps onto the group of self-equivalences of the algebraic $2$-type, which has order $8$, with kernel $π_4(\RP^2\times S^2)\cong(\Z/2)^2$ generated by pinch-fold maps; that these maps are independent is shown by an adjunction argument. We then construct a non-orientable analogue of the Hambleton--Kreck braid of exact sequences in dimension $4$, for non-orientable manifolds with spin universal cover, stated for finite fundamental group. We apply the braid to $\RP^2\times S^2$ and to $\RP^4$, and for the Hambleton--Hillman manifold with fundamental group $(\Z/2)^2$ we determine the normal $1$-type and show that self-equivalences act on $π_2$ through diagonal sign matrices. For $\RP^2\times S^2$ the pinch-fold maps are detected by twisted spin bordism, and, assuming facts from surgery theory stated as hypotheses, exactly one of the three non-trivial pinch-fold maps is homotopic to a homeomorphism.

title: From Earth to Mars and Beyond: AI-Driven Cosmic-Ray Validation and Prediction with CorsikaAgent
abstract: We calculate the sea-level cosmic-ray muon flux with CORSIKA and develop CorsikaAgent, an auditable large-language-model-based system for configuring, executing, and validating air-shower simulations, and for predicting particle fluxes in unexplored environments. The physics calculation uses proton primaries described by the solar-minimum spectrum of Papini et al., with UrQMD at low interaction energies and either Sibyll 2.3e or QGSJET-III at high energies. The predicted momentum spectra at approximately 0 and 75 degrees are compared with experimental measurements of the atmospheric muon flux and with commonly used analytic parametrizations. The two interaction-model configurations give similar spectra and describe the principal momentum and zenith-angle dependences of the data. The agent independently reconstructs the same observable through a different sampling strategy and keeps every steering card, executable, seed, log, and analysis script bound to the result it produced; its output is consistent with the direct calculation at the level resolved by the present comparison. Transferred to Mars, the workflow reproduces the CORSIKA 8 benchmark, and transferred to Venus it produces the first prediction of the surface muon flux, an environment for which no measurement exists. The agent thus extends the workflow from auditable reproduction to first-principles prediction: it autonomously reconfigures the simulation(atmosphere, magnetic field, electric field)for new environments, while the proton-only primary model, limited high-momentum statistics, and an incomplete systematic-uncertainty treatment bound the physical precision that can currently be claimed.

title: How Mobile Oscillators Reshape Dynamical Robustness in Complex Networks
abstract: While the robustness of collective dynamics in static networks is well established, how agent mobility and network topology jointly shape dynamical robustness remains largely unexplored. In this letter, we investigate the robustness of mobile Stuart-Landau oscillators performing random walks on networks and interacting diffusively when co-located. In the rapid-mobility regime, we reduce the dynamics to a mean-field framework linking network degree statistics to an effective global coupling strength. We show analytically that increased degree heterogeneity in the network enhances the effective coupling strength, and strictly lowers the critical threshold of functional degradation for amplitude death. Numerical simulations confirm the predicted heterogeneity-dependent ordering of the transition thresholds, showing an earlier collective collapse in scale-free networks than in random or regular networks. Our results establish mobility and network heterogeneity as key determinants of robustness in mobile oscillator populations, with implications for resilient biological and engineered collectives.

title: Emergent quantum algebras in dissipative time crystals
abstract: Strong dynamical symmetries provide an algebraic description of persistent oscillations in open quantum systems governed by the Lindblad equation. For finite-dimensional systems with a full-rank stationary state, such symmetries are necessary and sufficient for non-decaying oscillatory modes to appear in the Liouvillian's spectrum. These modes can be directly constructed by acting on stationary states with the identified symmetry operators. Here we establish an asymptotic counterpart of this algebra for collective spins. Taking a single spin $S$ in a magnetic field, subject to dissipation through linear jump operators, we identify the exact conditions on the field and dissipative couplings under which non-decaying oscillatory modes emerge as $S \rightarrow \infty$. We then write down a simple, closed form for the corresponding `symmetry' operator which can be applied to the steady state to construct these modes, which are eigenvectors of the Liouvillian, with imaginary eigenvalues, up to $O(1/S)$ corrections. A second operator, an emergent conserved quantity, completes the algebra, and its slow relaxation determines how quantum noise selects the stationary state. The construction can be directly extended to a pair of interacting spins sharing a common reservoir, with the resulting quantum algebra making the entanglement during a quench analytically accessible.

title: Conditional Membership in Regular Languages
abstract: We study a formulation of regular language membership as a promise problem, which we dub conditional membership: we fix a promise language $P$ and a target language $T \subseteq P$, we are given a word $w$ which is promised to belong to $P$, and we must determine whether $w$ belongs to $T$. We study the deterministic worst-case query complexity of this task, when the length $n$ of $w$ is known in advance and where each query examines the $i$-th position of $w$ for some $1 \leq i \leq n$ and returns the $i$-th letter $w_i$ of $w$. Our goal is to characterize the asymptotic complexity as a function of the word length $n$, depending on the fixed languages $P$ and $T$. Our main result is to show that the complexity of this task admits a trichotomy between three regimes: $O(1)$ queries, $Θ(\log n)$ queries, and $Θ(n)$ queries. We further show that the trichotomy criterion is decidable, namely, it is PSPACE-complete to decide which regime applies, given nondeterministic automata $A_P$ and $A_T$ respectively representing $P$ and $T$.

title: The periodic Airy line ensembles
abstract: In this paper we construct a one-parameter family of periodic Airy line ensembles $\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{per},R}$ for $R>0$ as weak scaling limits of Borodin's periodic Schur processes. We establish several properties of $\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{per},R}$, including a determinantal point process structure with an explicit correlation kernel. We also show that, after a parabolic shift and normalization, $\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{per},R}$ satisfies, on its domain $[-R/2,R/2]$, the same Brownian Gibbs property enjoyed by the usual Airy line ensemble. A main technical contribution of the paper is a general tightness criterion for determinantal line ensembles, which extends the argument used by Johansson in [Comm. Math. Phys. 242 (2003), 277-329] to prove a functional limit theorem for the discrete polynuclear growth model.

title: On the singular set of the geodesic flow on nonpositively curved surfaces
abstract: We prove that the singular locus of the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle of a nonpositively curved surface enjoys an additional regularity property: its characteristic function belongs to the geometric anisotropic Sobolev space $H^{5/8-}_xH^{-13/16}_θ$. In particular, this implies that if the geodesic flow is not ergodic with respect to the Liouville measure, then the zero set of the curvature must be thick in the sense that it supports a nonzero, nonnegative function in $H^{5/8-}$. The proof relies on semiclassical analysis and a new radial estimate for parabolic flows.

title: Closed-form construction of exceptional points in a two-parametric PT-symmetric large-matrix model
abstract: Stable bound states living on a discrete one-dimensional N-point lattice are assumed generated by a certain two-parametric PT symmetric potential $V=V(A,B)$. At any $N$, the coordinates $A=A^{(EP)}$ and $B=B^{(EP)}$ of the Kato's exceptional point (marking the phase-transition instant of the loss of stability) are defined, exactly, via roots of a certain elementary quartic polynomial.

title: Bayesian Inversion Beyond the Generator's Range: Reducing Non-physical Constraints from Generative Neural Networks
abstract: To address non-uniqueness in geophysical inversions, Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are often used to parameterise geological or other prior information in a lower-dimensional space (the so-called latent space), thereby reducing the number of inversion parameters. However, the training samples that represent this information are then always incorrect, because Earth structure is not intrinsically low-dimensional, and all GNNs are subject to training errors. Consequently, even when solutions are mapped back to the original higher-dimensional space, they inherit this imperfection and remain restricted to a low-dimensional manifold. From a mathematical point of view, latent space inversion thus fails fundamentally: generally, it can not even reproduce the best, higher-dimensional approximation to the true Earth. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an `escaping prior' distribution, which provides the necessary freedom to find solutions beyond the manifold of GNN-generated solutions, while still using the GNN as a guide. We use a hierarchical Bayesian approach to adapt the strength of prior information to the observed data and synthetic forward function $\textit{a posteriori}$. We illustrate our method on low-dimensional problems where the escaping prior is defined over a 1D manifold in 2D space. We then compare our approach with standard latent space and model space inversions using a uniform prior distribution in synthetic tomography problems, ranging from simple to more geologically realistic cases. Furthermore, we tested scenarios where the true solution is either far from or close to the manifold. In each case, our escaping prior shows significantly better results than the alternatives. It results in solutions beyond each GNN's generative capabilities, solutions which include the best possible model, and clearly demonstrates the limitations of latent space inversion.

title: When 1+1 Backfires: Rethinking Relevance-Diversity Balancing for Sample-Aware Visual Token Reduction
abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.

title: Quickest Change-point Detection in Generalized Linear Models with Variational Estimation
abstract: We consider quickest change-point detection in generalized linear models when the post-change parameter is unknown. Such problems arise, for example, when monitoring whether the relationship between a learned representation and an observed response changes over time. Since detection must occur soon after a change, the post-change parameter must be estimated from a limited number of observations, making finite-sample estimation accuracy particularly important. We propose a window-limited CUSUM procedure that estimates the post-change parameter using a variational-inequality (VI) formulation. For noncanonical links, VI estimation can offer favorable finite-sample accuracy over short windows despite the asymptotic efficiency advantage of maximum likelihood estimation. We characterize how estimation error reduces the effective post-change information rate and affects detection delay, and derive finite-window guarantees accounting for both statistical error and incomplete numerical optimization. The resulting procedure retains false-alarm control and achieves first-order asymptotic optimality under suitable conditions. Numerical experiments compare detection delay and update cost for fixed-budget estimation and benchmark VI-WLCUSUM against alternative detectors.

title: Measurements of lepton-flavour universality in semileptonic $B$ decays at Belle and Belle II
abstract: Tests of lepton-flavour universality in semileptonic \(B\)-meson decays provide sensitive probes of physics beyond the Standard Model. The Belle and Belle II experiments, respectively operating on the KEKB and SuperKEKB colliders in Japan, have collected \(e^+e^-\to B\bar{B}\) collisions at a center-of-mass energy corresponding to the \(Υ(4S)\) resonance in samples with a combined integrated luminosity exceeding \(1\,\mathrm{ab}^{-1}\). These data, with low particle multiplicity, constrained initial-state kinematics, and excellent lepton identification, provide an ideal environment to study lepton-flavour universality in semileptonic decays of \(B\) mesons. New results on the ratios of semitauonic \(B\)-decay rates compared to analogous light-lepton rates are presented. These include new Belle II measurements of branching-fraction ratios \(R(D^{(*)})\) involving exclusive \(B\to D^{(*)}τν\) and \(B\to D^{(*)}\ellν\) decays using semileptonic or hadronic reconstruction of the accompanying \(B\)-meson tag. Belle II and Belle measurements of angular observables in \(B\to D^*\ellν\) modes that test light-lepton universality and the Lorentz structure of the decay are also presented. The measurements are statistically limited and individually consistent with Standard Model expectations. The new \(R(D^{(*)})\) results are also compatible with experimental world averages, which continue to exhibit tension with Standard Model predictions. Belle II has now accumulated an \(Υ(4S)\) data sample exceeding that of Belle, offering substantial opportunities for new analysis approaches and heightened precision.

title: DR-APO: Decoupled-Representation Advantage-Guided Policy Optimization from Continuous Control to Embodied Navigation
abstract: Policy representations in reinforcement learning have expanded beyond Gaussian policies to diffusion and flow-matching based generative policies. However, existing RL methods remain representation-specific, lacking a unified optimization interface for emerging generative policies. In particular, extending likelihood-based objectives to multi-step generative policies couples optimization to their internal generation process, where accumulated likelihood ratios can weaken the update signal. Meanwhile, generative-policy-specific methods often rely on multi-candidate generation and critic-based selection, improving overall return while providing limited improvement to the policy itself. We introduce DR-APO (Decoupled-Representation Advantage-Guided Policy Optimization), which decouples policy improvement from policy representation through advantage-guided target improvement and representation-compatible direct action fitting, providing a shared optimization principle for Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies. Across five MuJoCo-v5 tasks, DR-APO remains competitive with SAC for Gaussian policies and achieves the best aggregate policy-only performance for both diffusion and flow-matching policies. NavDP post-training improves the Success Rate (SR) from 70.33% to 89.55% in simulation and from 25% to 65% in real-world navigation. These results demonstrate a unified policy-improvement principle across Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies, from continuous-control learning to embodied-policy post-training.

title: Sparse Lifts of q-Linearized Permutation Polynomials with Explicit Inverses
abstract: We give a higher unit-torus lift from q-linearized permutation polynomials over Fqn to generally nonlinear sparse permutation polynomials over Fqns. The construction preserves compositional inverses: if a linearized polynomials and its inverse have coefficients (ai) and (Ai), then the lifted polynomial and its inverse have the same coefficients. As a consequence, we obtain nonlinear binomial lifts whose inverses are again binomials in the two-dimensional case, including an explicit inverse for a binomial family over Fq4. The three dimensional specialization yields permutation trinomials whose compositional inverses are again trinomials, together with explicit involution criteria and examples.

title: Weak Segmentation-Guided GAN for~Realistic Color Edition
abstract: Editing the color of images in a realistic way finds many applications such as changing the perception of an image, data augmentation or film post processing. The design of an automatic tool is a complex and long addressed challenge. In particular, two properties are difficult to meet altogether: generating realistic results without artifacts and the possibility to precisely choose the future color. Conventional methods using segmentation and histogram matching maximize the controllability but also introduce a lack of realism or are complex to automate. On the contrary, GANs that specialize in realism are difficult to control. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel GAN architecture leveraging any differentiable segmentation model. We demonstrate the genericness of our framework that presents state of the art results on different use cases. It generates images that look realistic while offering a precise color control.

title: AgentCue: Statistical Summaries for Guiding Decentralized Multi-Agent Self-Organization
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) combine multiple agents to solve complex tasks, and recent MAS scale to more than a thousand agents. At this scale, decentralized MAS remove the central orchestrator that assigns sub-tasks, and the agents, which we call workers, self-organize through their own choices of sub-tasks and collaborators on a shared board. As workers keep adding participation and collaboration records, however, the information explodes: workers spend more and more effort on reading the records of other workers, and self-organization loses efficiency. In the statistical view, we represent the execution history of an MAS by two continually updated networks, a collaboration network among workers and a participation network between workers and task types. We then propose AgentCue, a method built on a new latent space model that places workers and task types in a shared latent space. Each time the networks are updated, the estimated parameters of the latent space model form a compact and interpretable statistical summary, and workers use the statistical summary to choose sub-tasks and collaborators without repeated searches of the shared board. We establish the identifiability of the latent space model and non-asymptotic error bounds for the estimates under network increments, and we show that a fixed number of gradient updates after each network update suffices for the same error rate. Experiments on LongBench v2 Multi-Doc QA show that AgentCue achieves competitive effectiveness, efficiency, and interpretability.

title: Answer It or Not? Towards Prompt-Adapted Adversarial Images on Vision Language Models
abstract: With the advancement in language modeling, research on adversarial images has recently shifted from image classifiers to vision-language models (VLMs). Despite the new, text-prompt-driven nature of VLMs, we find that existing VLM adversaries have largely overlooked the dynamics of text prompts. In a typical use case, adversarial images can protect visual privacy by rejecting VLMs from answering questions about the image. However, existing protections are prompt-agnostic, i.e., indiscriminately rejecting any question, including those for potential legitimate use of the image. To address this limitation, we propose Prompt-Adapted (ProAda) adversarial images, which are optimized to balance the rejection of harmful prompts and the correct response of legitimate prompts. In particular, to achieve a more accurate adversarial direction, the text prompt is also iteratively updated with a simple classifier judging whether the harmfulness of the prompt remains. Extensive experiments on visual-privacy-related datasets validate that ProAda can reject over 90% of harmful prompts while allowing over 90% of legitimate ones, demonstrating superior overall performance compared to existing prompt-agnostic VLM adversaries. In addition, our ProAda achieves competitive overall cross-model transferability and improved robustness against countermeasures.

title: The Effect of Expertise Signaling when Sharing Medical Information in Opinion Dynamics
abstract: Social media heavily influences health decisions, yet few opinion dynamics models account for how information is delivered. This work investigates how signaling source expertise shapes trust and long-term opinion formation. Through an online experiment, we find that adding a professional title to the sender's display name significantly increases a post's perceived credibility. Incorporating these findings to create a data-driven opinion dynamics model, we prove that (1) connecting users through some paths to an expert guarantees consensus with experts' opinion, while (2) higher rates of expertise signaling accelerate reaching consensus. Simulations show that (3) convincing even 20% of users to signal their title reduces consensus time to nearly one-third in Erdos-Renyi networks and (4) higher title adoption brings average opinion much closer to that of experts in scale-free and real-world networks. Altogether, our work highlights expertise signaling as a viable intervention to promote validated medical information online.

title: Adaptive Interaction Network for Human Motion Prediction During Human-Robot Collaboration
abstract: Human motion prediction during human-robot collaboration is critical for achieving safe and efficient interactions in shared environments. Unlike previous studies that have primarily focused on humans and objects, we focus on the robot-aware human motion prediction task, which explicitly models the influence of robots on human motion. This task presents new challenges, such as capturing human-robot heterogeneity and modeling complex spatial interactions. To address these issues, we develop an adaptive interaction network (AINet) model that consists of two branches: a primary branch that predicts future human motion and an auxiliary branch that estimates robot trajectories. The two branches are jointly optimized and coupled via a Local-Global Spatial Interaction (LGSI) Module, which effectively captures fine-grained and global contextual dependencies between human and robot motion sequences. Then, we introduce an Adaptive Weighted Aggregation (AWA) Module to dynamically fuse motion features using context-dependent weights, thereby increasing adaptability across diverse scenarios. Furthermore, we adopt a coarse-to-fine prediction strategy, in which a coarse pseudo-trajectory is first predicted, followed by the refinement of detailed human poses based on that trajectory. Extensive experiments on three challenging datasets reveal that our proposed method achieves superior performance, validating its effectiveness in human-robot collaboration scenarios. Our code is available at: https://github.com/LyTingHub/AINet.

title: LATCH: LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness for Post-Route FPGA Optimisation
abstract: Post-route FPGA timing closure remains expert-dependent and computationally expensive. We present LATCH (LLM-Assisted Timing Closure Harness), a two-layer framework that separates large language model (LLM) orchestration from deterministic FPGA implementation and evaluation. Across sixteen designs and seven LLMs, a single-iteration study compares three agent control granularities - expert-written recipes, direct EDA operations and LLM-constructed procedures - to ask how much control an agent needs per attempt. Functional-pass rates are 98.2%, 71.4% and 17.9%, respectively; yet direct operations give slightly larger 3.4% median Fmax gains when passing, versus 3.2% for recipes. This exposes a trade-off between execution reliability and timing improvement. Informed by this trade-off, a multi-iteration study fixes the action tier at expert recipes to ask how repeated attempts are best organised, comparing a fitted deterministic heuristic with sequential LLM reasoning, branching exploration and knowledge base-guided exploration within 12 checkpoints per run. Branching raises mean maximum-frequency improvement from 10.5% (sequential) to 16.0%, and the knowledge base to 20.3%, improving 15 of 16 designs. Characterisation across 2,421 recipe attempts profiled their gain and validation rates, showing hard-block re-placement gives the largest cumulative mean gain at 41.4MHz.

title: Bosonic Quantum Conditional Mutual Information and Bose-Einstein Condensation
abstract: This article aims to introduce the bosonic asymmetric quantum conditional mutual information (QCMI), $I_{B}(A; B|C)$, as a rigorously defined information-theoretic quantity for continuous-variable (bosonic) systems. After defining $I_{B}(A; B|C)$ through quantum instruments on infinite-dimensional Fock spaces, we prove that Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) induces a logarithmic divergence $ I_{B}(A; B|C) \geq α\log_2 (N_{0}^C+1)$, which further establishes $I_{B}(A; B|C)$ as a quantum-information order parameter for BEC with power-law scaling near the critical point. We provide the complete five-step proof of this result, connecting measurement back-action, off-diagonal long-range order, and Jensen's inequality. In the condensed phase, the effective causal propagation velocity is set by the Bogoliubov sound speed $c_s$ in the long-wavelength limit, and vanishes continuously at the superfluid--Mott-insulator transition. Applications to composite bosons, the BEC--BCS crossover, and a quantum-gas-microscope measurement protocol are presented. Finally, we demonstrate how the reduced bosonic QCMI serves as a finite-size scaling probe analogous to the Binder cumulant.

title: Integrating Feature Understandability into Feature Selection for Human-Centred Tabular Explanations
abstract: Existing human-centred XAI research predominantly evaluates explanations after they have been generated. However, this fails to provide actionable insights into improving accessibility. This study incorporates human-based feature understandability into feature selection to improve the generation of human-centred explanations. Natural language explanations for machine learning models trained on tabular data often cite influential features in the input data to explain a given decision. As a consequence, users' ability to understand the produced explanation hinges on their understanding of the cited features. To quantify this natural-language feature understandability, Rossberg et al. proposed the Feature Understandability Scale, which assigns numerical `understandability scores' to features based on user feedback. To evaluate the degree to which these scores can improve machine learning explanation quality, this study collects understandability scores across two datasets, proposes an understandability-aware feature selection algorithm to select features that are both understandable and informative, and trains a random forest based on these feature subsets. The SHAP-based explanations generated by this model are evaluated using user feedback, and changes in explanation quality are assessed. The individual evaluation of the explanations showed that while the understandability-based explanations scored higher on average, the difference was not statistically significant. In contrast, the comparative evaluation found that participants preferred these explanations significantly more frequently than expected at the chance level. It is concluded that the integration of understandability can yield more understandable explanations at minimal cost to classification performance, although changes to quality require elucidation in larger cohorts.

title: PRB-WM: Physics-Regularized Beta World Models for Predictive Link Adaptation on Real Time-Varying Underwater Acoustic Channels
abstract: Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) improves the spectral efficiency of underwater acoustic (UWA) links, but its feedback is inevitably stale: sound propagates slowly, and by the time channel state information (CSI) arrives, the fast time-varying multipath channel has moved on. Predictive link adaptation therefore needs more than a point forecast: it needs a distribution over each candidate action's consequences. We propose PRB-WM, a physics-regularized Beta world model for predictive per-subcarrier link adaptation on real time-varying UWA channels.
