title: SPLICE: Sparse Physics Library Identification and Compositional Expansion
abstract: Neural operator splitting composes a library of neural operators, one per physical mechanism, into zero-shot simulators of new equations. Existing approaches, however, require these mechanisms and their labels to be specified in advance. We ask whether a pretrained library can instead be adapted and grown from unlabeled trajectories in which multiple mechanisms act simultaneously. We introduce SPLICE, a framework that discovers operators without mechanism labels on mixture data. The contributions of the candidate operators to each trajectory are inferred by solving a convex optimization problem. A calibrated test then assigns each discovered operator the mechanism it implements. Failure cases are also detectable, when the library lacks the required physics or when mechanisms are insufficiently separable. Across one and two dimensional systems, the discovered operators recover mechanisms from unlabeled mixtures and compose into zero-shot simulators of unseen equations; a frozen library can also grow an operator for physics absent from pretraining, without labels and without forgetting. On Navier-Stokes, the discovered operators compose about as accurately as their supervised counterparts.

title: Honeycomb Crystal in a Mass-Asymmetric Electron-Hole Bilayer
abstract: A two-dimensional electron gas in a uniform neutralizing background forms a triangular Wigner crystal at low density. In a strongly mass-asymmetric electron-hole bilayer, localized heavy holes instead provide a nonuniform positive background that supports an electron crystal at densities two orders of magnitude higher than for a homogeneous electron gas in the same material. Here we show that correlated mobile electrons can overturn the preference for triangular order, stabilizing a honeycomb electron-hole crystal. Using the powerful real-space neural-network variational Monte Carlo in the Born-Oppenheimer limit with fixed holes, we find that increasing the density drives a transition from a triangular electron-hole crystal to a honeycomb crystal, which eventually melts into itinerant electrons coexisting with the honeycomb or the triangular hole lattice at fixed interlayer separation. Relative to triangular order, honeycomb order emerges when gains in electronic kinetic energy and electron-hole attraction outweigh its higher intralayer Coulomb repulsion, a threshold never reached in the rigid point-dipole model. Moreover, the honeycomb hole lattice supports paramagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and stripe-ordered spin states. Complex polarization indicates a metal-insulator transition, while the states on the honeycomb hole lattice are consistent with a stripe-ordered Dirac semimetal and paramagnetic or antiferromagnetic Mott insulators via mapping to the half-filled Hubbard model. We further propose a BLG/hBN/WS$_2$-WSe$_2$ heterostructure as a platform for the predicted honeycomb crystal, at an experimentally feasible density $n\sim10^{11}~\text{cm}^{-2}$.

title: A Fully Discrete, Mass-Conservative Adaptive Discontinuous Spectral-Element Method for the One-Dimensional Richards Equation in Mixed Form
abstract: We present and analyze a spatially and temporally adaptive high-order method for the one-dimensional Richards equation describing vertical water transport in unsaturated soil, with an emphasis on resolving sharp wetting fronts while satisfying a fully discrete water mass balance. The spatial discretization uses an arbitrary-order local discontinuous Galerkin spectral-element formulation with collocated Legendre-Gauss-Lobatto quadrature, and the time integration is based on a high-order Rosenbrock-Wanner method. We focus primarily on the mixed formulation of the Richards equation, which advances water content as the conserved variable while evaluating the nonlinear diffusion operator in terms of pressure head; the resulting fully discrete scheme satisfies the water mass balance in exact arithmetic, independent of spatial resolution and time step size, including under spatial and temporal adaptivity. In contrast, the pressure-head formulation advances pressure head through a nonlinear capacity function and satisfies the corresponding conservation identity only at the semi-discrete level. Numerical experiments examine convergence through spatial and temporal refinement studies, with mass conservation assessed under spatial and temporal adaptivity using the solver flux output method (SFOM). The SFOM results confirm machine-precision mass conservation for the mixed formulation, whereas the pressure-head formulation exhibits mass balance errors above roundoff. Moreover, in the temporal refinement studies, the mixed formulation yields more accurate solutions than the pressure-head formulation for a prescribed time step size. The combination of high-order accuracy, spatial and temporal adaptivity, and fully discrete mass conservation makes the proposed mixed-form discontinuous spectral-element method a promising approach for simulating unsaturated flow in next-generation land models.

title: Identifiability and Consistent Recovery for the Unnormalized Graph Laplace Operators
abstract: We study whether an unnormalized graph Laplace operator can determine both the geometry of a manifold and its sampling density. On a fixed compact smooth manifold without boundary, we use a known positive, continuous, strictly decreasing radial kernel at a fixed positive bandwidth. For positive sampling densities, the operator built from geodesic distances determines the Riemannian metric and identifies the density up to equality almost everywhere. When the metric is induced by a Euclidean embedding, the operator built from ambient distances also determines the embedding up to rotations, reflections and translations, and the density. On compact parameter classes with positive continuous densities, minimizing the distance between empirical and popula- tion operators gives estimates that converge to the true parameters under independent, identically distributed sampling. This recovery result assumes that the empirical operator can be evaluated at arbitrary points of the manifold.

title: Cosmic Colliders in Binary Blazars Probing Ultra-High-Energy Particle Physics
abstract: While terrestrial colliders and fixed-target cosmic-ray interactions are bounded at center-of-mass (CM) energies $\sqrt{s} \lesssim \mathcal{O}(10^5)\,\text{GeV}$, we demonstrate that bound sub-parsec binary blazars form broad-band, beam-beam hadronic ``Cosmic Colliders'', overcoming such limitation. Driven by modest jet misalignments ($θ_{\rm mis} \sim 1^\circ - 6^\circ$), co-streaming proton beams collide at CM energies reaching $\sqrt{s} \sim 10^{10}\,\text{GeV}$ - six orders of magnitude above the Large Hadron Collider. Operating in a strictly optically thin regime ($τ_{pp} \ll 1$), the system performs a continuous CM energy scan, probing asymptotic QCD scaling, gluon saturation, and Froissart unitarity, while opening a possible high-sensitivity window into physics beyond the Standard Model. Secondary PeV-EeV neutrinos and sub-TeV $γ$-rays fall directly within reach of current and planned observatories such as LHAASO, CTAO, IceCube, and GRAND, establishing binary blazars as laboratories for physics at the ultimate energy limit.

title: Quasibound states of charged Dirac fields around Einstein-Euler-Heisenberg black holes
abstract: We study quasibound states of a massive charged Dirac field on the Einstein--Euler--Heisenberg (EEH) black hole, the extension of Reissner--Nordström (RN) by the leading weak-field vacuum-polarization term of QED. We derive the background to first order in the Euler--Heisenberg coupling $a$. We show that it admits a nondegenerate horizon at $Q=M$ and an extremal charge $Q_{\rm ext}=M[1+a/(40M^2)+\mathcal{O}(a^2)]>M$, with horizon data that depend on $\sqrt a$ near extremality. From the separated radial equations, we derive an identity that excludes real-frequency quasibound states on any background of this class, so damped branches cannot become unstable. Since the EEH corrections first enter at $\mathcal{O}(r^{-5})$ in the electrostatic potential, the trapping condition $Mμ^2-qQω_R>0$ and the hydrogenic spectrum coincide with RN, and no fine-structure-order splitting arises. Two-sided shooting with a Muller root finder shows that the real frequencies shift only by near-zone amounts that are linear in $a$ and strongly suppressed with angular momentum. The damping rates respond in a branch-dependent way. At $Q/M=0.99$ the $\ell=0$ ground state becomes slightly longer-lived, while the $(n_r,j,\ell,λ)=(0,\tfrac32,1,-2)$ state decays up to $80\%$ faster for $a/M^2\le1$, and near the trapping threshold the damping rate increases by up to $60\%$. Switching on the metric and potential corrections separately, together with a WKB analysis of the inner barrier, identifies the mechanisms: Coulomb screening always increases leakage, while the metric correction controls the sign and size of the $\ell$-dependent effect. Characteristic time-domain evolutions with Richardson-extrapolated matrix-pencil extraction reproduce the frequency-domain shifts.

title: FlashT2S: GPU-Accelerated Tensor-to-Spike Conversion Operators for Heterogeneous Neuromorphic LLM Backends
abstract: Artificial intelligence faces two growing challenges: computational bottlenecks and energy inefficiency inherent to the von Neumann architecture. Neuromorphic computing offers a promising alternative, yet its immature ecosystem still relies on conventional systems for data supply, requiring efficient conversion between tensor and spike dataflow. We observe a clear mismatch, where data conversion is slow while downstream computation is fast. As data size grows quadratically with large language models, this mismatch becomes a major bottleneck. In this work, we examine the data-conversion components that appear on the critical path of training and inference in neuromorphic LLMs. The work presents FlashT2S (Flash Tensor-to-Spike): GPU-Accelerated Tensor-to-Spike Conversion Operators, which applies architecture-aware and data-centric optimizations to reduce conversion latency. Experimental results show that FlashT2S delivers an average speedup of 850.78x over the native operators across individual operators and 802.83x in realistic workloads. Additionally, compared with GPU kernels automatically generated by torch.compile, our kernels achieve 5-11x speedups. Notably, it achieves near-optimal absolute performance: large-scale conversions are reduced to tens of microseconds (10-99 us), while small-scale conversions reach single-digit microsecond levels (less than 10 us). Furthermore, its standardized output enables seamless integration across heterogeneous backends, including diverse neuromorphic hardware.

title: PitchIn: Natural-Language Vocal Coaching from Unstructured Community Feedback
abstract: Effective vocal coaching connects performance issues with corrective advice, but recordings paired with expert diagnoses and advice are scarce. Online singing communities provide a potential source of supervision, but observations and advice are scattered across unstructured comments. We introduce PitchIn, audio-language models for natural-language vocal coaching, and the PeerCoach Dataset: 14,445 instruction examples covering Focused QA, Overall Feedback, and Recognition QA. We compare target combinations on Qwen2.5-Omni and train PitchIn on Focused QA and Overall Feedback using Qwen2.5-Omni and MOSS-Music. On VocalCoachBench, the proportion of requested diagnosis-correction pairs matching an expert issue with valid advice rises from 21.3% to 61.0% for Qwen2.5-Omni and from 31.4% to 51.2% for MOSS-Music. Direct training on source comments yields only 19.8% for Qwen2.5-Omni. For Qwen, Focused QA alone reaches 65.6%, but adding Overall Feedback improves alignment with expert reviews and human preference. Both models improve expert-review alignment over pretrained baselines and are significantly preferred for usefulness (92.0% and 67.3%, respectively). Demo examples are available at https://hayeonbang.github.io/PitchIn.

title: Analysis of a zeroth-order multiscale sampler: strong convergence, convergence of ergodic averages and weak convergence
abstract: In many practical applications of Bayesian inference, it is difficult or undesirable to compute the gradient of the negative log-posterior, motivating the study of derivative-free samplers, also called zeroth-order samplers. The aim of this paper is to generalize and rigorously analyze a multiscale derivative-free sampler recently proposed in the literature by Pavliotis, Stuart and Vaes (2022). In the discrete-time setting, the multiscale sampler we study bears a strong resemblance to other recently proposed methods, such as the so-called zeroth-order perturbed stochastic gradient descent algorithm (Jin et al., 2018) and the zeroth-order Langevin Monte Carlo algorithm by Roy et al. (2022). We present error estimates with respect to all the parameters of the problem, both in the continuous-time and discrete-time settings. The error estimates are in three different metrics: strong convergence, convergence of ergodic averages, and uniform-in-time weak convergence.

title: Entanglement Sudden Death in Gapped Ground States
abstract: Spatial sudden death of entanglement refers to the disappearance of quantum correlations between subsystems after a certain distance called the entanglement length. Specifically, given a density matrix $ρ_{ABC}$ on a tripartite system $ABC$ with $B$ spatially separating $A$ and $C$, the entanglement length is the distance $\ell(A,C)$ after which the reduced density matrix $ρ_{AC}$, given by tracing out the $B$ subsystem, is separable. We show in the case of gapped ground states in any dimension that the entanglement length is finite on finite subsystems. Restricting to one-dimensional systems, we prove that normal matrix product states have a finite entanglement length independent of $A$ and $C$, and that a finite pure state with such uniform entanglement length has a matrix product state representation with bond dimension independent of $A$ and $C$. Consequently, in one dimension, entanglement length distinguishes matrix product states from all other pure states.

title: MENTOR: Procedural Shielding of Tool-Using LLM Agents
abstract: Tool-using LLM agents are increasingly used to automate workflows governed by procedural manuals, such as company rules for booking travel or procuring hardware. These manuals are written in natural language for humans and describe general requirements over such complex workflows. Ensuring compliance of LLM agents with these manuals is difficult, and state-of-the-art techniques use either LLM judges or manually written rules to forbid problematic tool-calls locally at runtime. This is insufficient because (i) only blocking tool calls keeps the agent clueless about how to make correct progress towards fulfilling its task, and (ii) can lead to overly conservative behavior of the agent, as tool calls might only be problematic in certain contexts. To overcome these challenges, we introduce MENTOR, which (i) additionally provides guidance for the agent to make procedural-compliant progress on the task, and (ii) ensures that this compliance is context-aware. We achieve these goals by building a novel history-dependent runtime shield that is obtained from the procedural manual via a multi-step autoformalization pipeline. At its core, MENTOR utilizes a game-based technique to ensure robustness against runtime uncertainty without over-resticting agents' behavior. This yields a formally assisted framework for procedural shielding of LLM agents that improves compliance well beyond existing methods. In particular, MENTOR lifts the compliance of shielded light-weight open-source LLMs above that of non-shielded proprietary models. Since a shield is synthesized once per manual and then serves every task, a MENTOR-shielded agent becomes a viable choice for repeatedly executed workflows, potentially reducing deployment costs when the offline construction cost is amortized over repeated tasks.

title: Beyond Model Bias: Cross-Entropy Based Rankings in Literary and Academic Texts Remain Stable across Small Language Models
abstract: While language models provide powerful mechanisms for evaluating textual predictability, it remains unclear whether the relative extents of LM surprisal remain stable across models. This study presents empirical evidence of the invariance of ranking based on cross-entropy related measures (e.g. mean, variance of each data-point), across four distinct small scale transformer-based models, for a given dataset of text sources. We consider two stylistic environments: a corpus of contemporary poetry and a corpus of academic research papers. We demonstrate that mean and variance of cross-entropy maintain robust cross-model rank correlation ($ρ> 0.90$) across both regimes. To test whether this agreement merely reflects generic differences in textual complexity, we compare it against six parameter-free compression baselines. The extent of agreement among language models is found to be substantially higher than that among model-baselines, for most of the measures. Geometric analysis of the structurally constrained academic regime reveals that higher-order moments are sensitive to specific models, although strong agreement persists. The findings suggest that relative extents of textual unpredictability may be independent of the language model they are computed against.

title: Profinite recognition of uniformity
abstract: Let $G$ be a semisimple Lie group that is not isogenous to the isometry group of real or complex hyperbolic $n$-space. We show that the rational rank is a profinite invariant for irreducible lattices in $G$, unless $G$ has type $D_{2n}$ which forms a genuine exception. In particular, profinitely isomorphic lattices in $G$ of type $D_{2n}$ can have differing virtual cohomological dimension. As another corollary, uniformity is a profinite property for irreducible lattices in $G$ outside type $D_4$. Assuming CSP, the existence of triality symmetries gives uniform and non-uniform profinitely isomorphic lattices in type $D_4$.

title: AD4EDU: Benchmarking University Lecture Audio Description across Accessibility Standards, Metrics, and Learner Preferences
abstract: Audio description (AD) aims to enhance the accessibility of visual media for blind and low-vision (BLV) persons. However, in higher education, where slide-based lectures are a default mode of teaching, lecture AD remains largely underexplored. The main reason is that existing production guidelines, evaluation metrics, and benchmark datasets are oriented toward entertainment content and do not transfer to lectures, where ADs must complement the lecturer's speech, resolve deictic references, and fit within narrow pauses. In this work, we propose AD4Edu, consisting of an AD benchmark, AD4Edu-Bench, and a rule-diagnosable evaluation metric, AD4Edu-Eval, for generating and evaluating ADs in higher education. Specifically, we consolidated established accessibility guidance, including WCAG 2.2, the DCMP Description Key, and NCAM's STEM description practices. We further collected silver reference ADs, judge-ordered preference pairs, and pairwise preferences from four BLV raters, and post-trained models with direct preference optimization (DPO) for detailed analysis. Our findings indicate that while the metric reliably detects violations of the standard, ADs that comply with it do not necessarily fulfill the subjective preferences of BLV persons, most notably on description length, underscoring the necessity of active participation of BLV persons in co-designing inclusive AI solutions.

title: Neos: Learning to Interleave Search and Visual Reasoning
abstract: Recent multimodal deep search agents have advanced tool use and visual content retrieval, yet they still struggle to convert intermediate visual evidence into actionable guidance for subsequent search, limiting their effectiveness in long-horizon settings. To address this gap, we present Neos, a multimodal deep search framework that learns both how to acquire evidence and how to use it to guide subsequent decisions. To make this coupling learnable, Neos constructs training tasks with intermediate visual dependencies while filtering out textual shortcuts, and introduces a lightweight, trainable Multimodal Evidence Interface (MEI) that transforms retrieved content into goal-conditioned observations. At its core, an agent-environment co-evolution procedure treats MEI as a co-adaptive component of this loop. Specifically, reference-guided credit assignment uses verified successful trajectories to localize critical policy errors while preserving credit for useful decisions in failed searches, whereas rollout feedback selects informative local evidence-processing interactions for MEI supervised fine-tuning (SFT). By alternating policy reinforcement learning (RL) with MEI SFT, Neos allows the policy's evolving evidence requests to shape MEI training and the adapted MEI to reshape subsequent observations, closing the loop between evidence acquisition and evidence-conditioned action. Across ten benchmarks, Neos-9B and Neos-35B demonstrate leading performance among specialized multimodal deep-search agents.

title: Oka realizations, fundamental groups, and holomorphic cofibrations
abstract: The homotopy types of Oka manifolds are exactly those of countable finite-dimensional CW complexes. We construct realizations as open subsets of complex Euclidean spaces with explicit dimension bounds. Other realizations have good open covers by sets biholomorphic to $\C^N$, with prescribed finite nerves, or are unions of Fatou--Bieberbach domains whose nonempty finite intersections are again Fatou--Bieberbach domains. Every nonempty Stein manifold admits a proper holomorphic embedding into an Oka open subset of some $\C^N$, and this embedding is a homotopy equivalence. We obtain holomorphic representatives of ordinary and generalized cohomology classes, and realize every countable group as the fundamental group of an Oka domain in $\C^5$. The fundamental groups of algebraically elliptic manifolds are precisely the finite groups, and every virtually abelian Kähler group is the fundamental group of a projective Oka manifold. Finally, we classify holomorphic cofibrations in Lárusson's intermediate model structures and establish factorizations over aspherical targets into proper holomorphic embeddings and holomorphic fibre bundles with Oka fibre.

title: Ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations for Finsler metrics on symmetric spaces
abstract: Ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations are random tessellations that arise as limits of Voronoi diagrams for Poisson point processes as their intensity tends to zero. For the Riemannian metric on a symmetric space of higher rank, Frączyk, Mellick, and Wilkens (arXiv:2307.01194) proved that the corresponding ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellation is almost surely completely connected, with an unbounded side between any two cells. This contrasts sharply with the geometry of ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations in hyperbolic spaces studied by D'Achille, Curien, Enriquez, Lyons, and Ünel (arXiv:2303.16831). In this paper we introduce and study ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations for Finsler metrics on higher rank symmetric spaces. We show that ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations with respect to polyhedral Finsler metrics can exhibit either behavior seen in these previous works: generically they resemble the hyperbolic case, where almost surely all cells have bounded sides. We further introduce the ideal Selberg--Poisson--Voronoi tessellation of the space of positive definite symmetric matrices, which has particularly nice properties.

title: Discrete total variation under the multinomial, Part 2: variance under the uniform null
abstract: For the counts $(X_1,\dots,X_n)\sim\mathrm{Mult}(N;1/n,\dots,1/n)$ of $N$ observations in $n$ ordered bins we study the variance of the discrete total variation $d=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}|X_{i+1}-X_i|$. An exact decomposition splits $\mathrm{Var}(d)$ into per-edge, adjacent-pair and disjoint-pair terms and yields, for fixed $n$ as $N\to\infty$, $\mathrm{Var}(d)/N=α(n)-β(n)/N+γ(n)/N^2+o(N^{-2})$. For every $n\ge 2$, $Nα(n)$ is the classical normal-theory variance (Hoel, Kamat) of the sum of absolute successive differences of $n$ independent $N(0,N/n)$ variables; the correction $β(n)$ is obtained in closed form for $n\ge 3$ (the case $n=2$ is treated separately). Two disjoint edge differences $D_1=X_2-X_1$ and $D_3=X_4-X_3$ are exactly uncorrelated and asymptotically independent, yet $\mathrm{Cov}(|D_1|,|D_3|)=-1/(πn)+O(1/N)$: a correlation of relative order $1/N$, invisible in the Gaussian limit and absent under Poissonized sampling, whose constant is proportional to the exact joint fourth cumulant $κ_{2,2}(D_1,D_3)=-4N/n^2$ and is proved here on the lattice. The adjacent pair contributes the lattice-Edgeworth constant $a_*=-2\sqrt{3}/(9π)$, of which one quarter is a smooth Edgeworth term and three quarters a lattice-corner term; the disjoint skeleton $h(m)$ is closed through a Bessel generating function; and $γ(n)$ ($n\ge 5$) is expressed through a single triangular-lattice constant whose closed form we conjecture. Together with the mean of Part 1, the variance supplies the two moments used by moment-matched approximations to the null law of $d$. This is Part 2 of a series; the cyclic statistic $d^{c}$ will be treated in Part 5.

title: Enhanced Quantum Metrology via Saddle-Point Scrambling in Phase Space
abstract: Nonlinear effects are widely utilized in quantum metrology to enhance measurement precision by leveraging complex dynamical behaviors. Here, we propose a quantum scrambling-integrated scheme that optimizes the selection of initial states and parameter encoding by exploiting the nonlinear dynamical trajectories and their geometric properties in phase space. We consider a two-mode Bose-Einstein condensate as a typical example. Within a certain parameter range, using uncorrelated spin coherent states located at saddle points and separatrices enables the measurement precision to reach the Heisenberg scaling. An analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information under long-time evolution is provided, and our analysis further reveals that the enhancement mechanism is governed by the sensitivity of the energy spectrum to parameter variations. Compared to the criticality-enhanced protocol that requires parameters to approach the critical point, our scheme offers a distinct advantage in its applicability over a broader range of parameters. Moreover, this scheme can also be applied to models that include one- and two-axis countertwisting interactions and chaotic dynamics. This Letter offers a new perspective for advancing the application of nonlinear dynamics to enhance the parameter estimation precision in quantum systems.

title: SpectralBridge: Adding High-Frequency Capability to Large Audio-Language Models
abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have become highly capable on a wide range of tasks spanning speech, music, and environmental sound. However, many modern LALMs resample input audio to 16 kHz mono, making all frequencies above 8 kHz unobservable. We present SpectralBridge, a lightweight extension that gives such a model access to the 8-16 kHz band by joining low- and upper-band representations with time-aligned paired cross-frequency attention. Applied to Audio Flamingo Next, the method trains only a small adapter and rank-8 LoRA modules, while leaving the original audio encoder, audio projector, and base language model frozen. SpectralBridge improves both zero-shot transfer and downstream fine-tuning: it raises zero-shot balanced accuracy on the ESC-50 audio classification dataset from 75.5 to 90.5, and when fine-tuned on Insect-10, a 10-way insect species task we construct from InsectSet459 recordings, under the same budget as a LoRA fine-tuned baseline, it reaches 55.4 balanced accuracy against the baseline's 26.2. On a benchmark where the answer depends only on the 8-16 kHz band, it gains 30 mAP over the frozen model. Erasing the upper-band stream from the trained model removes these gains, showing that they come from the high-frequency signal itself rather than from extra tokens or the adapted prompt format.

title: On the foundations of logic and probability, II. Modal probability spaces
abstract: A class of models which brings to the fore the inner logic of the calculus of probability instead of assigning probabilities to sentences is introduced and investigated.

title: Optical Detection of Coherent Nuclear Spin Control in a Molecular System at Room Temperature
abstract: Molecular systems with optically addressable electron spins are emerging as versatile quantum sensing platforms, offering tunable qubit properties and molecular-scale spatial control. Owing to their longer lifetimes, coupled nuclear spins provide an attractive resource for enhancing sensing performance. For molecular spin systems, the ability to initialise, coherently control and readout nuclear spins at room temperature is crucial for realising such benefits. Here, we present the first optical detection of nuclear magnetic resonance and coherent nuclear spin control with a molecular system at room temperature. Specifically, we demonstrate optically detected Rabi oscillations of $^{14}$N nuclear spins in the photoexcited triplet state of the organic chromophore 6,13-diazapentacene. The strong hyperfine coupling between the electronic spin and $^{14}$N nuclei enhances the nuclear Rabi frequency, enabling fast coherent nuclear-spin rotations. This work lays the foundation for leveraging nuclear spins as memories for enhanced molecular-based quantum sensing.

title: R(V) parameter of the dust extinction curve: mapping based on hot stars and connections to diffuse interstellar bands
abstract: Favored carriers of the Diffuse Interstellar Bands (DIBs) are carbonaceous molecules whose constituents have been presumably expelled by dying stars along with those of dust grains. The parallel evolution of DIB carriers and grains and their potential interplay are unknown. We assembled published R(V) measurements of 505 hot stars. We inverted a catalog of extinction data based on Gaia XP spectra and NIR photometry, and used the resulting new 3D extinction map to locate the opaque areas responsible for R(V) for each star. Using archived spectra, we measured their 5780, 5797 and 8620 A DIBs. In parallel, we compared local and line-of-sight (LOS) R(V)s from recent 3D maps with local and LOS Gaia DIB strengths from our recent map. Results: R(V)s from hot stars reveal variations on large spatial scales, confirming with independent data the published 3D pattern. Gaia DIB strength maps show large spatial scale variations similar to those of R(V) maps, with higher abundance of DIB carriers corresponding to higher R(V). LOS Gaia DIB strengths and R(V)s from 3D maps also correlate positively in the R(V) range 2.3-3.4, but there is no connection for higher R(V), likely due to the disappearance of DIB carriers in dense clouds. Despite averaging effects along the LOS to hot stars, we find differences in R(V)-DIB relationships among the three DIBs, with an evolution from negative to positive correlation from the zeta- to the sigma-type DIBs. This can be understood in the frame of the bimodal evolution of R(V) with the extinction, with the zeta (resp. sigma) DIB carrier disappearance in the decreasing (resp. increasing) phase of R(V). Various combinations of DIB strengths and DIB ratios may allow to define the range of R(V), but the relationship between DIBs and R(V) also appears to depend on the wavelength range used to determine R(V).

title: Bifurcation Structure of Double Hysteresis and Isolated Branches in a Parametric Duffing Nanoresonator
abstract: Direct and parametric driving together generate nonlinear response structures beyond conventional Duffing hysteresis, including multiple switching regions and isolated branches. Understanding how these structures are connected requires identifying the bifurcations that reorganize the response as the parametric excitation is varied. At a phase difference of 45 degrees between the direct and parametric excitations, we experimentally and analytically determine how the steady-state response changes as the parametric excitation is increased. A single resonance peak first splits into two while the response remains single valued. Two successive cusp bifurcations then create two saddle-node pairs and establish a double-hysteretic response. At the parametric-instability threshold, one saddle node of each pair is displaced towards unbounded amplitude and detuning, and an isolated-branch structure emerges above threshold. A parametric representation of the steady state distinguishes amplitude extrema from genuine saddle-node bifurcations and provides analytical conditions for these changes. Measurements on a dielectrically actuated pre-stressed SiN nanostring reproduce the predicted response and associated switching behavior. These results establish the bifurcation pathway connecting the different response structures at this phase configuration, providing a systematic basis for controlling multistability and switching in parametrically driven nonlinear resonators.

title: Measuring Variable Importance Using Proportional Inclusive Marginal Effects
abstract: Shapley-based measures are widely used for measuring variable importance in statistics and machine learning. However, these measures have a serious issue--a nonactive variable can get a positive importance measure when it is correlated with an active variable. Herin et al. recently proposed a measure called proportional marginal effects (PME) that mitigates this spurious effect. However, PME is developed for deterministic models and has high computational cost. In this article, we propose a new measure called proportional inclusive marginal effects (PRIME) that overcomes these two limitations of PME. The key idea in PRIME is to use a novel model-free variable selection technique to identify the active variables and include only them in the computation of the importance measure. Analysis of test functions and real datasets show that PRIME can accurately and reliably quantify variable importance from noisy input-output data.

title: Solar-Blind Ultraviolet Communication: Taxonomy and Experimental Characterization
abstract: Solar-blind ultraviolet communication (UVC) exploits near-zero solar background radiation and strong atmospheric scattering in the 200-280 nm band, enabling photon-level daytime communication and propagation modes beyond conventional line-of-sight (LOS) links. However, existing studies mainly focus on individual channel types, and a unified channel classification is still lacking. This paper presents a taxonomy of all four fundamental solar-blind UVC channels together with representative experimental validations and a comparative performance analysis. The proposed framework provides practical guidelines for selecting appropriate channel architectures for future solar-blind UVC systems.

title: Construction of Regular Fat Linear Sets and Non-Representable q-Matroids
abstract: Let $q$ be a prime power. An $(r, i)$-regular fat $\mathbb F_q$-linear set has exactly $r$ points of weight $i\ge2$, called fat points. All of its remaining points have weight one, and at least one such point occurs. We solve two open problems posed by three of the authors of this paper. First, we derive divisibility constraints on the point weights using the scalar stabilizer of the defining subspace. Consequently, a regular fat linear set of rank $2i$ in $\operatorname {PG}(1,q^n)$ has at most two or exactly $q + 1$ fat points. In the latter case, the fat points form an $\mathbb F_q$-subline. Second, we construct higher-dimensional regular fat linear sets whose fat points do not form an $\mathbb F_q$-subgeometry. In particular, for every $k\geq 3$ we obtain examples of rank $2k$ whose fat locus consists of an $\mathbb F_q$-subgeometry $\operatorname {PG}(k-2,q)$ in $\operatorname {PG}(k-1,q^4)$ together with one external point. This construction is then generalized further. Finally, we apply our projective-line results to $q$-matroid representability and present an infinite family of non-representable rank-two $q$-matroids arising from partial spreads.

title: Capturing Coordination Core Topology in Metal--Organic Frameworks Using Persistent Mayer Homology
abstract: Local coordination cores are critically important in metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and polyoxometalates (POMs), as they govern the fundamental chemical and structural properties of these materials. Existing methods, including element-resolved persistent homology (ERPH), have limited ability to translate local coordination cores into quantitative, scalable, and interpretable information. Here, we introduce persistent Mayer homology (PMH) to enable the detection of the geometric variability invisible by classical topology. By focusing on coordination cores formed by periodic metal-centered heavy-atom, carbon, and donor channels, PMH distinguishes different arrangements of the local coordination environment, linker framework, and potential coordinating atoms. We examine explainable PMH of orders $N=3$ and $N=5$ and separately combine each with ERPH, which characterizes the multiscale organization of chemically defined element groups across the extended framework, to predict eight nitrogen- and oxygen-related adsorption and self-diffusion properties. The resulting coordination-core PMH representations consistently improve predictive performance over ERPH alone, with the third-order Mayer representation providing the strongest overall performance. These results demonstrate that the inner coordination configurations captured by PMH contain essential structural information that is not fully represented by conventional element-resolved topological descriptors. This finding provides a quantitative interpretable topological framework for understanding local coordination environments and may facilitate the rational design of MOFs and POM-based materials.

title: VL-DocIR: A Benchmark for Vision-Based Long Document Information Retrieval
abstract: Vision-based document retrieval has improved rapidly, but current evaluation settings still emphasize short documents and single relevant pages. This leaves an important gap between leaderboard performance and realistic long-document retrieval, where the evidence needed to answer a query may span multiple pages or even multiple documents. We present VL-DocIR, a page-level benchmark for evidence-complete visual long-document retrieval. VL-DocIR is built from 29,641 HTML-born documents rendered into 388,548 page images from Wikipedia, arXiv, PubMed, and SEC proxy statements. It contains 271,760 queries across 23 domains and six evidence structures, covering single-page, within-document multi-page, and cross-document evidence configurations. Evidence annotations are grounded to rendered pages and HTML element identifiers, and queries are filtered with a cleaning pipeline targeting clarity, correctness, closedness, and the absence of explicit layout references. We evaluate leading single-vector and multi-vector visual retrievers together with diagnostic retrieval settings such as document-context scoring, query splitting, reranking, and round-robin ensembles. The strongest evaluated configuration reaches 69.3 nDCGAll@10 and 80.6 RecallAll@10 under structure-balanced Macro evaluation, but source- and evidence-structure breakdowns show that cross-document retrieval remains substantially harder than single-page retrieval, and that document-context scoring is especially helpful for within-document multi-page queries. VL-DocIR exposes these failure modes and provides a more demanding target for visual long-document retrieval. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://yufanchen96.github.io/VL-DocIR.

title: Architecting Instruction Execution for Scalable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
abstract: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) requires orchestrating millions of operations continuously across a tightly coupled classical-quantum control stack. A critical challenge in this orchestration is determining the optimal hardware-software boundary, i.e., the Quantum Instruction Set Architecture (QISA). We focus on cryogenic, fixed-connectivity qubit platforms, such as superconducting and topological Majorana qubits. For these, existing QISA choices either operate at too low a level, violating cryogenic thermal budgets at scale, or at too high a level, imposing unrealizable complexity on the control engine. To reason about these tradeoffs, we introduce the ARIES instruction set hierarchy, which categorizes QISAs into distinct abstraction levels. To systematically evaluate these levels, we develop an end-to-end evaluation toolflow featuring a cycle-accurate classical driver and hardware engine simulator. Using eight quantum applications across superconducting and topological qubit platforms, we measure instruction bandwidth, transceiver power dissipation, and measurement processing overheads. We demonstrate that while physical-level abstractions exceed the thermal limits of dilution refrigerators by orders of magnitude, canonical-level abstractions significantly underestimate hardware routing congestion and execution runtimes. Our Level 4 QISA (local logical operations) offers an optimal architectural balance. As quantum hardware platforms scale toward FTQC in the coming years, our findings provide concrete architectural guidance for the design of their classical control stacks and instruction interfaces.

title: PatientWM: Towards Generalizable Clinical World Models via Unified Patient States
abstract: Clinical decisions depend on anticipating how a patient's condition will evolve as treatment is adjusted and new evidence becomes available. Existing medical world models capture patient-state evolution, but often define the evolving state around a particular modality or task, limiting reuse as inputs or prediction targets change. These models also retain history through observation sequences or recurrent or latent summaries rather than exposing preceding patient states and clinical actions as an ordered transition context. This distinction matters because similar current measurements may follow different recent changes, treatment exposures, and observed responses. To tackle these limitations, we propose PatientWM, a clinical world-model framework built around a unified patient state and sequential latent history. Availability-aware encoders integrate observations available at each decision time into the patient state, while typed decoders produce task-specific clinical readouts without defining the state around any single target. PatientWM further conditions each next-state prediction on the current state and supplied action together with a bounded, ordered history of preceding latent patient states and clinical actions, preserving recent treatment and response context. Experiments across MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and three external clinical datasets show superior performance in clinical prediction, multi-step forecasting, and action-planning evaluation. Transfer experiments further demonstrate the generalizability of PatientWM's patient state. Together, these results establish its ability to forecast clinical evolution and support planning.

title: A higher categorical approach to graded bivariant $K$-theories for Real $C^*$-algebras
abstract: We present an $\infty$-categorical refinement of classical $KK$-theory and $E$-theory for graded, $G$-equivariant for a locally compact second countable group $G$, Real $C^*$-algebras. As a consequence, we obtain a couple of fiber sequences connecting the different $K$-theory spectra, and explicitly analyse the induced endomorphisms on $K_0$-groups. We also answer precisely some folklore questions in the area. Among other things, we show that graded $KK$- and $E$-categories are not a Dwyer-Kan localization of graded $C^*$-algebras.

title: In-context classification: Calibration and noise in linear attention with softmax readout
abstract: We study in-context binary classification in a simple attention model trained to minimise a logistic loss. Each prompt has a latent logistic teacher, and the learner must infer its direction from Bernoulli-labeled context examples. We derive an asymptotic prediction for the test logit in a high-dimensional regime with context length proportional to token dimension, and total training prompts proportional to dimension squared. Our formula cleanly separates calibration, test-time context noise, and non-isotropic parameter-estimation noise as interpretable effects on in-context performance. Our analysis also identifies the ridgeless separability regime and addresses the effects of context length, pretraining-set size, regularisation, and sampling temperature on in-context classification performance. The theory's predictions closely agree with finite-dimensional simulations and fully trained linear-attention models, while experiments with standard softmax attention show qualitatively related behaviour beyond the regime assumed by our analysis.

title: Gradient Routing Localizes and Removes Unintended Behaviors in RL
abstract: We propose a mitigation to reward hacking in reinforcement learning. Our setup involves a misspecified reward function that gives rise to unintended behavior, and a monitor used to detect unintended behavior. As with frontier AI systems, the monitor makes systematic errors. Consequently, using the monitor for data filtering or to apply a reward penalty fails to prevent the model from learning unintended behavior ("reward hacking"). To address this problem, we introduce GRAFT: Gradient Routing Adapter Fine Tuning. Rather than penalizing or filtering flagged samples during training, GRAFT constrains gradient updates on those samples to a sacrificial set of new parameters. This has two benefits: First, because the monitor is not part of the reward function, the model does not learn to hide misbehavior. Second, ablating the sacrificial parameters reduces or entirely stops the unintended behavior while maintaining improved performance on target tasks. We demonstrate these benefits in RL environments where reward penalties cause models to learn to reward hack in undetected ways, training models ranging from 135M to 8B parameters. Additionally, we show a similar effect at a larger scale by distilling frontier LLM trajectories containing reward hacking into Qwen3-32B, without teaching that model to reward hack. Overall, our work suggests GRAFT may be a promising approach for leveraging imperfect monitors during post-training in settings where true performance is difficult to evaluate.

title: An accurate parallel finite difference method for the variable-order fractional Laplacian in heterogeneous media
abstract: Anomalous diffusion in heterogeneous media is ubiquitous across physical and biological systems, where spatially varying microstructures give rise to distinct transport regimes. Variable-order nonlocal operators provide a natural modeling framework for describing heterogeneity and transitions between diffusion regimes. However, the position-dependent long-range interactions inherent in these operators impose prohibitive memory costs and make numerical methods developed for constant-order operators computationally impractical. Consequently, accurate and computationally efficient numerical methods for variable-order nonlocal operators remain scarce. In this paper, we propose accurate finite difference discretizations for the variable-order fractional Laplacian $(-Δ)^{α(\mathbf{x})/2}$ and develop a fast Fourier transform (FFT)-accelerated scheme for their efficient implementation. The computational and memory costs are $O\!\big(MN\log(2N)\big)$ and $O(MN)$, respectively, where $N$ is the total number of spatial points and $M \ll N$. The method is also naturally parallelizable. We establish its consistency and accuracy through a rigorous error analysis that quantifies the local interplay between solution regularity and the spatially varying order $α(\mathbf{x})$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to quantify how these two factors jointly determine convergence rates, with numerical experiments demonstrating this dependence. Extensive numerical experiments confirm the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method. Applications to anomalous diffusion in composite materials further demonstrate its ability to capture the effects of material heterogeneity.

title: Image Priors for Single-Shot Coded Diffraction Phase Retrieval
abstract: Phase retrieval recovers complex-valued objects from intensity-only measurements. In its classical Fourier form, reconstruction suffers from twin-image stagnation. Coded diffraction imaging, which adds a random phase mask before the Fourier transform, has so far required several masks. We show that an image prior makes single-shot coded diffraction imaging possible, with a single random mask followed by a Fourier transform. We validate this claim in simulation and in an optical experiment, in which a spatial light modulator displays the phase object together with the random mask. Our experimental validation covers five test signals and 530 images from the public Brno quantitative phase microscopy dataset of five adherent cell lines. With no image prior or with Fourier-only measurements, reconstruction of complex-valued objects from a single diffraction pattern consistently fails. An out-of-the-box pretrained image denoiser enables accurate reconstruction, in simulation even with fewer measurements than unknowns. Five regularization frameworks built on the same denoiser and one learned weakly convex regularizer all reconstruct the experimental images with peak signal-to-noise ratios within one decibel of each other. A single random phase mask and image priors thus turn coded diffraction imaging into a practical single-shot modality for quantitative phase imaging.

title: TILE: Bridging LLMs and Table Foundation Models for Tabular Learning with Strings
abstract: Real-world tables are often heterogeneous, combining numerical features with free-form string columns. Table foundation models (TFMs) excel on numerical tables but require strings to be encoded numerically, while large language models (LLMs) hold semantic knowledge but are not designed for tabular predictions. Most existing bridges use LLMs as plug-in encoders for cell strings, yet how to extract representations effectively for tabular learning remains underexplored. We show that the interface between LLMs and tables matter as much as the LLM itself. Applied cell-wise, larger LLMs do not give better features. With our interface, the same LLMs improve steadily with size. TILE (Table-Interfaced LLM Embeddings) combines four ingredients: row serialization to provide cross-column context, intermediate-layer extraction to avoid layers specialized for next-token prediction, columnar pooling to remove mean pooling's length bias, and by-pass features to route numbers and categories past the LLM. Paired with TFMs, TILE sets a new state of the art for tables with strings. Across 100 datasets, it beats the strongest baseline on 89% of splits, with gains across 7 LLMs and 10 tabular learners, and ranks first on the 108-dataset STRABLE benchmark.

title: PerturbBridge: Direct Phenotypic Supervision for Cellular Perturbation Generation
abstract: Virtual cell models should capture phenotypes induced by specific perturbations. However, image-based models are typically trained and evaluated to match real-image distributions, which alone does not explicitly prioritize perturbation-specific biological responses. Recent approaches add biological signals through reinforcement-learning post-training or inference-time steering, raising a central question: where should biological response information enter the generative pipeline? We introduce PerturbBridge, a stochastic data-to-data bridge model that directly supervises perturbation-specific phenotypes in predicted perturbed images during training. PerturbBridge jointly optimizes bridge regression and differentiable biological response losses, with biological gradients passing through a frozen image encoder. We further introduce perturbation-response evaluations based on downstream classification and retrieval. Across three microscopy benchmarks for perturbation profiling and subcellular imaging, PerturbBridge surpasses CellFlux in biological fidelity, image quality, and sampling efficiency. On BBBC021, mechanism-of-action classification improves by 5.66 and 7.5 percentage points with morphological and learned visual features, respectively. On JUMP and AllenCell, retrieval Hit@10 and Hit@1 improve by 1.77 and 7.15 percentage points, respectively. On BBBC021 and JUMP, PerturbBridge achieves lower FID with 80% fewer model evaluations than CellFlux. Overall, these results show that directly supervising perturbation responses during training improves phenotypic fidelity while enabling efficient cellular image generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yyc1215lll-creator/PerturbBridge.

title: A unified three-branch deep learning framework for automated detection and counting of wildlife in aerial imagery
abstract: Automating aerial wildlife surveys requires reliable animal detection, consistent delineation of observation strips, and correction for repeated coverage between successive images. We present a unified three-branch deep learning framework that integrates these tasks through WildSeg, WildMatch and WildDet. WildSeg combines rod segmentation with geometric refinement to delineate counting strips from aircraft-mounted markers. WildMatch uses teacher-student distillation to learn dense image correspondences and identify overlapping survey areas without relying on geolocation metadata. WildDet combines dual-scale detection with feature fusion, density supervision and empty-image gating to support animal detection and counting. We evaluated the framework using oblique aerial imagery of four antelope species from the Great Nile Migration Landscape in South Sudan. WildSeg achieved reliable rod extraction, while WildMatch approached teacher-level accuracy with a substantially lighter and faster model. Both modules maintained high accuracy on resized images, improving processing efficiency. WildDet improved detection performance across all four species and reduced detection-based count MAE, RMSE and mean bias by 21.0%, 4.6% and 27.8%, respectively, relative to YOLO11. By connecting spatial survey constraints with animal detection, the framework provides a practical and computationally efficient approach to processing large aerial image collections for wildlife monitoring and population surveys.

title: Fact-check? True!: Tracking Verification Requests and the Absence of Truth Verdicts across Correction Systems
abstract: Misperceptions can run in two directions. Individuals can either believe false information or reject true information, with experimental work finding that debunking efforts are effective at correcting both forms of misperception. Yet despite the efficacy of true corrections, current debunking systems focus almost entirely on the correction of falsehoods, with professional fact-checkers publishing few true verdicts and crowdsourced systems like X's Community Notes program unable, by rule, to display notes verifying true claims. As a result, we do not have a clear understanding of the extent to which overall misperceptions are driven by doubting true information. To answer this question we first draw on a novel dataset of 47,899 queries to X's AI assistant which track users asking for verification on post content. Surprisingly, among questioned posts that received a true or false verdict, Grok judged nearly identical shares as either accurate or inaccurate. Of the questioned posts, more than 83\% were not flagged by Community Notes and only 3.3\% carried a displayed note. Among questioned posts judged accurate by Grok, nearly 90\% received no note at all while fewer than 2\% displayed a note flagging them as misleading. This discrepancy does not seem to have stemmed from a lack of effort, with contributors writing 2,981 notes verifying questioned posts despite there being no way for Community Notes to display them publicly. Alongside further exploration of these findings we discuss both the system- and code-level changes that would be required to effectively address this asymmetric correction paradigm.

title: Task-Space Motion-Force Nonlinear Model Predictive Control for Precise and Compliant Control under Uncertainties
abstract: In Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC), the control law is implicitly determined by the solution of an Optimal Control Problem (OCP). Consequently, OCP design is often tailored to specific platforms and tasks, demanding extensive expert knowledge and tuning effort. To address this, we propose a unified NMPC framework that directly plans and controls the robot joints subject to task-space motion and force requirements and is capable of seamlessly generalizing across multiple robotic platforms and diverse tasks. Furthermore, optimization-based methods often treat interactions as rigid contacts, making the torque solution sensitive to the modeling errors of the robot dynamics and the environment. We study the intrinsic task-space impedance of our proposed controller, its partial contraction for differential stability and differential passivity under unmodeled interactions. As a result, our framework enables closing the force-feedback loop in the high-level planning layer to achieve precise motion-force tracking performance, addressing the long-standing challenge of force-feedback NMPC. Finally, we validate our framework on physical hardware, demonstrating hybrid motion-force control on a redundant manipulator and compliant locomotion on a quadruped, while preserving core NMPC advantages such as hard constraint satisfaction, optimal redundancy exploitation, and real-time planning under unforeseen interactions.

title: $E$-symmetric algebras I
abstract: We study various symmetry conditions related to the Auslander-Reiten formula for finite-dimensional algebras. In particular, we define a new class of algebras which we call $E$-symmetric. A theorem by Derksen-Weyman-Zelevinksy implies that all Jacobian algebras are $E$-symmetric. We prove the converse for the class of monomial algebras.

title: Symmetry-constrained coexistence of charge-three and charge-one Weyl points in nonmagnetic crystals
abstract: High-charge Weyl semimetals (WSMs), particularly those hosting charge-three Weyl point (C-3 WPs), have attracted considerable interest owing to their unconventional topological properties and enhanced boundary phenomena. However, ideal C-3 WSMs remain rare, and the symmetry-constrained coexistence of charge-three and charge-one Weyl point (C-1 WPs) in nonmagnetic crystals remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate a representative eight-node Weyl configuration, consisting of two C-3 WPs and six C-1 WPs with opposite chirality, corresponding to two identical $\{3,-1,-1,-1\}$ irreducible Weyl molecules. By combining topological charge conservation with space-group symmetry analysis, we systematically classify all 230 space groups and identify 12 and 23 candidate groups without and with spin--orbit coupling (SOC), respectively. First-principles calculations without SOC reveal that the boron allotropes TBR-B$_{48}$ and chiral OBD-B$_{48}$ realize this configuration, hosting hourglass-type and non-hourglass-type C-3 WPs, respectively. Surface-state calculations reveal six Fermi-arc branches at the shared projection of the charge-three pair and three at each individual projection. Reversing the structural chirality of OBD-B$_{48}$ reverses the signs of all Weyl charges, establishing a direct correspondence between crystal and momentum-space chirality. Furthermore, breaking the protecting $C_6$ symmetry in TBR-B$_{48}$ splits each C-3 WP into three C-1 WPs and reconstructs the surface Fermi arcs. Our work establishes symmetry-based guidelines for designing and searching for nonmagnetic WSMs hosting charge-three and charge-one Weyl-point coexistence.

title: Think Locally Before Computing Jointly: Efficient Secure Multi-Party Computation via Maximizing Local Processing
abstract: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) lets parties evaluate a function over private inputs without revealing them. In garbled-circuit (GC) protocols, prior optimization has largely treated the number of non-linear gates, especially AND gates, as a proxy for cryptographic cost, and has focused on minimizing multiplicative complexity. We identify an orthogonal source of savings: a gate need not be garbled when one party knows or can locally compute its inputs; that party can evaluate it outside the secure protocol, even when the gate is non-linear. We introduce ownership-aware optimization for GC-based MPC, which minimizes non-linear gates requiring joint evaluation rather than total non-linear gates. We formalize this objective in a cost model and implement a compiler-integrated, gate-level framework that restructures Boolean circuits to increase party-local computation while preserving secure-computation semantics. The method is automated and general-purpose, and composes with existing multiplicative-complexity optimization. Experiments show that it reduces jointly evaluated computation and improves end-to-end GC performance on circuits with party-local structure, revealing protocol-cost savings missed by conventional GC cost models.

title: Non-volatile Orbital magnetoelectric effect in a two-dimensional electron gas
abstract: Electrical control of orbital magnetism is a central goal of orbitronics. While current-induced orbital polarization has recently been demonstrated in inversion-asymmetric systems, nonvolatile electrical control of an equilibrium orbital moment has remained elusive. Here, using x-ray absorption spectroscopy with \textit{in situ} electric-field control of the FE polarization, we demonstrate non-volatile switching of the equilibrium orbital magnetization of the oxide q2DEGs formed at the LaAlO$_3$/EuTiO$_3$/Ca-STO (001) interface. X-ray linear dichroism reveals a reversible modulation, driven by the FE-polarization direction, of the Ti-3$d$ crystal-field splitting and orbital occupancy, establishing a ferroelectric-like metallic state. X-ray magnetic circular dichroism shows a polarization-controlled switching of the Eu$^{2+}$ orbital magnetic moment induced by the orbital magnetization of the q2DEG projected onto Eu-5$d$ states and detected at the Eu-$M_{4,5}$ edge through Eu-5$d$/Eu-4$f$ hybridization in the inversion-symmetry-broken interface. These results provide spectroscopic evidence of ferroelectric control of orbital magnetism in an oxide q2DEG.

title: Matching Randomized First-Order Bounds for Higher-Order Smooth Nonconvex Optimization
abstract: Does randomization improve the worst-case first-order complexity of nonconvex optimization when the objective is very smooth? We prove that, for every fixed finite integer $p\ge3$, finding an $\eps$-stationary point requires $Ω_p(\eps^{-5/3})$ exact value-and-gradient queries, even for $C^\infty$ objectives with initial gap at most one and simultaneous global Lipschitz budgets of one for derivatives of orders $1,\ldots,p$. Together with the known deterministic upper bound, this determines the accuracy exponent up to a single logarithmic factor. The lower bound holds for unrestricted adaptive randomized algorithms, unbounded query locations, and outputs that need not have been queried. One algorithm-independent hard distribution suffices in dimension $O_p(\eps^{-47/3})$. The construction combines a block-chain potential with an exact quartic core, repeated quadratic spectra, and two static Gaussian tensor perturbations. A scheduled Haar argument controls the entire adaptive query span. An innovation-only Gaussian comparison then bounds exact transcript information without assuming finite precision or a minimum query separation. This establishes the $5/3$ randomized accuracy barrier under every prescribed finite smoothness order, extending the previously matched third-order case.

title: Nearest Neighbor Functional Curve Completion for Intraday Probabilistic Revisions of Renewable Generation Forecasts
abstract: We propose a nonparametric approach that fuses deterministic initial forecasts and a partial realization into a probabilistic forecast using the framework of functional curve completion. Our motivation is to construct intra-day forecasts for renewable energy generation, which is a key operational task in modern power grids. The aim is to combine the day-ahead (DA) forecast and the morning realized generation profile to create trajectories for the rest of the day, quantifying operational uncertainty. Starting with a large database of complete forecast-actual pairs across many assets, we adopt a functional point of view and construct a weighted neighborhood based on similarity metrics for the observed partial curve, the DA forecast, the day, and the geographical location. The selected complete nearest-neighbor curves provide a full predictive distribution, including functional focal envelopes and predictive bands based on functional depth. The hyperparameters governing neighborhood size, distances, and fusion rates are tuned across forecast update times and directly target probabilistic calibration in terms of the predictive probability integral transform. Three case studies using synthetic wind and solar assets, as well as real-life regional wind generation, showcase that our algorithm is able to achieve excellent calibration.

title: The Nonlocal Nature of Natural Deduction & the Introduction of Assumptions in Derivations
abstract: This concise manuscript investigates the nonlocal nature of natural deduction, particularly the possibility of introducing assumptions at intermediate stages of a derivation after those stages have already been passed. By examining the structural correspondence between natural deduction and sequent calculus, we demonstrate how the structural rule of left-weakening (LW) permits the enlargement of an antecedent after its corresponding succedent has been derived, without modifying the original inference. Through a number of symmetrical derivations, we establish the proof-theoretic relationship between the introduction of assumptions in natural deduction and antecedent expansion in sequent calculus. On this basis, we formulate the principle of Nonlocal Assumption Introduction (NAI), according to which assumptions may be introduced at any intermediate stage prior to the final conclusion, provided that the corresponding structural expansion is proof-theoretically valid. We further specify the conditions governing this operation, including the preservation of inferential validity, assumption dependencies, and the scope and discharge requirements of the resulting derivation.

title: UZHCL_for_the_win at Touche: Encoder Fine-Tuning, Synthetic Augmentation, and an Underpowered Encoder-LLM Comparison
abstract: Online discussions on platforms like Reddit are a productive testbed for fallacy detection: short texts, broad topical range, and the full inventory of informal fallacies. The Touche 2026 lab at CLEF formalises this as a shared task on a Reddit-derived corpus that combines fallacy detection with argument-scheme classification. This paper describes our participation in all three subtasks (ST1 binary fallacy detection, ST2 eight-way fallacy classification, ST3 four-way argument-scheme classification) and both evaluation tracks. Our submitted systems are fine-tuned RoBERTa-large encoders with task-specific heads, augmented with a small batch of LLM-generated synthetic contrastive pairs; for ST2 and ST3 on the enhanced track we additionally added confidence-filtered pseudo-labelled examples from the unlabelled pool. A wider backbone comparison spanning additional encoders (DeBERTa-v3, ModernBERT) and an LLM track (four Qwen variants from 3B to 32B, zero-shot through CoT-LoRA) showed no validated benefit over RoBERTa-large at this corpus scale, with 5-fold variance wide enough that we call the comparison underpowered rather than settled. We also characterise how much of the enhanced track's lift reflects organiser-rewritten inputs carrying label information rather than genuine argument clarification. On the official Touche 2026 test set our systems ranked first on both base-track classification cells (ST2 and ST3) and second on both binary-detection (ST1) tracks, with the two enhanced-track classification cells topped by cascaded and multitask systems. We close with the rare-class limitation on ST3 and the most useful follow-ups. Code: https://github.com/psychias/fallacy_detection_clef_2026

title: Sustainable trees
abstract: Let $X$ be a connected graph and let $λ_1(X)$ denote the spectral radius of its adjacency matrix. An edge $e$ of $X$ is sustainable if it can be deleted and replaced by a non-edge so that the resulting graph is connected and its spectral radius does not decrease; $X$ is sustainable if every edge is. We study this edgewise notion of spectral robustness for trees, where each replacement is an elementary exchange between trees on the same vertex set. We establish basic properties of sustainability and exhibit infinite families of sustainable and non-sustainable trees. Our main results concern trees with a vertex of large degree: if $T$ is a tree on $n$ vertices with $Δ(T)\geq n/2$, then every vertex of maximum degree is a principal vertex, that is, a vertex at which the Perron vector is maximal. Building on this, we prove that every tree with $Δ(T)\geq n/2+1$ is non-sustainable, and we classify the sustainable trees in the boundary case $Δ(T)=n/2$: for $n\geq 4$, the only such trees are the double broom $B(2,n/2,n/2-1)$ and one exceptional tree on eight vertices. We conclude with open problems on the generalized tree-shift order and the asymptotic proportion of sustainable trees.

title: Rethinking LLM-Guided Visual Question Answering: Does Deeper Knowledge Integration Really Help?
abstract: Some questions about an image need commonsense or factual knowledge that its pixels do not contain. Large Language Models (LLMs) can supply this knowledge to Visual Question Answering (VQA) systems, but the depth at which their guidance should enter a vision-language model remains unclear. We prompt the 70-billion-parameter Llama~3.3 model to describe, for each question, the visual concepts to focus on, the distractors to ignore and the external facts needed. We inject this guidance into a frozen Vision Transformer (ViT) paired with an instruction-tuned Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer (T5) in two ways: decision-level late fusion and attention-matrix injection. On the Outside Knowledge VQA (OK-VQA) benchmark, and contrary to the common view that deeper is better, the shallow route wins: late fusion reaches 39.4% exact match, +10.0 points above an unguided baseline, while attention injection reaches only 31.8% under data-scarce fine-tuning. An LLM paraphrasing pipeline also enlarges the training set more than tenfold. The results suggest that integration depth should be matched to the data regime.

title: Scaling Unified Multimodal Models to Long-Horizon Interleaved Generation
abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) provide an interface for interleaved text-image generation, where generated visual states can directly inform subsequent reasoning and synthesis. However, existing systems are still primarily demonstrated on short trajectories or simplified visual content. We develop a large UMM natively trained on interleaved multimodal data, with strong capabilities in image synthesis, text rendering, complex composition, and multimodal planning, and study how to extend these native capabilities to substantially longer autoregressive trajectories. The main challenge is that generated images continuously accumulate in context: irrelevant or imperfect visual states interfere with future synthesis, while previously established characters and scenes must still be recovered after long intervals. We introduce a visual-memory framework that maintains persistent visual references, selectively retrieves scene-relevant historical states while preserving the complete semantic history, and uses few-step self-rollout to adapt the model to imperfect generated histories. We further introduce LongMIG-Bench for evaluating long-horizon text-to-multi-image and image-to-multi-image generation. Our model achieves high-fidelity long-horizon interleaved generation with strong character and scene consistency, demonstrating how visual memory can scale native interleaved generation to substantially longer trajectories.

title: Extinction by non-spherical particles with the Nanoparticle Transition Matrix Code: perspectives for interstellar medium and exoplanetary atmospheres
abstract: The Transition Matrix formalism (T-matrix) offers an optimal solution to the problem of radiation scattering and absorption by particles characterized by a high degree of chemical and structural complexity. However, its application to particle models composed by large numbers of constituents has been classically limited by the substantial computational burden of the method. As a consequence, the investigation of light scattering and absorption processes, in cases where particle asymmetry and non-homogeneity play an important role, typically need to rely on simplifying assumptions which affect the correct interpretation of transmission spectra and extinction curves. This problem has a huge impact on many fields of scientific application. In particular, it has a critical role in astrophysics, because the ability to model highly non homogeneous particles is a fundamental requirement to understand the role of extinction in different phases of the interstellar medium (ISM), as well as to probe the physics of light transmission in planetary atmospheres within the Solar System and beyond. In this work we describe the application of a new implementation of the T-matrix formalism, based on the framework originally developed by Borghese, Denti & Saija and named Nano-particle Transition Matrix code, which leverages the power of modern hardware architectures to reduce the computational costs related to the solution of relevant particle models for the investigation of dust in the ISM and of hot-Jupyter class planets atmospheric aerosols. This new implementation of the T-matrix formalism can handle calculations of increasing complexity with a direct impact in the interpretation of the transmission spectra of transiting exoplanets produced by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and of those expected from the Atmospheric Remote-sensing Infrared Exoplanet Large survey (ARIEL).

title: DeboRheo v2.0: Improved Robustness for Geometrical VOF Simulations of Viscoelastic Two-Phase Flows
abstract: We present DeboRheo v2.0, an unstructured, geometrically unsplit Volume-of-Fluid framework implemented in OpenFOAM for viscoelastic two-phase flows. Version 2.0 improves numerical robustness when large viscosity contrasts coincide with strongly deformed interfaces and thin viscoelastic lamellae or filaments. The revised interfacial viscosity treatment retains a sharp geometric interface while regularizing the viscous contribution to the momentum equation. The solver combines mass-momentum-consistent phase advection, optional SIMPLEC pressure-velocity coupling, and a modular rheological framework with conformation-tensor stabilization. We assess the method using two-dimensional, axisymmetric, and three-dimensional benchmarks governed by the Oldroyd-B and exponential Phan-Thien-Tanner models. The results agree well with published numerical and experimental data and demonstrate improved robustness for demanding viscoelastic free-surface configurations on unstructured meshes.

title: Declarative Reactive Robot Behaviors from Imperative Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are predominantly trained on imperative programming languages, and existing work on LLM-based robot programming reflects this: it focuses on goal-directed tasks expressed as plans. However, many robotic applications require not tasks but behaviors--open-ended, continuous patterns of sensory-motor engagement with no termination condition (e.g., greeting visitors, patrolling an area). Such behaviors are better served by declarative and reactive programming, on which LLMs have virtually no training. We investigate whether this gap can be bridged. Using Playful, a reactive scripting language, we show that an LLM-based coding agent can generate correct declarative and reactive programs for robotic behaviors. These programs are produced from under-specified natural language descriptions, given suitable context and a set of reusable programming guidelines. The guidelines encode design principles that redirect the agent from imperative defaults toward proper reactive patterns. Developed once by an expert, they generalize across robots and behaviors. Starting from only the generic robot operating system API, the agent jointly designs both the imperative component (Python modules for sensing, acting, and evaluating) and the declarative component (the reactive script that composes them into behavior logic). The declarative nature of reactive programming supports both incremental refinement through conversational turns and one-shot generation of complete behaviors.

title: Decay-Assisted Leptogenesis during Preheating
abstract: We revisit the non-thermal leptogenesis mechanism during preheating using the quantum Boltzmann equations. This framework allows us to study the production and decay of heavy right-handed neutrinos in a consistent manner. Due to their fermionic nature, right-handed neutrino production can saturate after a few inflaton oscillations when their occupation numbers approach unity. Right-handed neutrino decays can deplete their occupation numbers, allowing more particles to be produced and generating a larger lepton asymmetry. Compared with the case where right-handed neutrinos decay only after production has finished, we find that the final baryon asymmetry can be enhanced by two orders of magnitude.

title: Superintelligence and the Triple Risk of an AI Race
abstract: On many estimates, artificial general intelligence (AGI) is likely to emerge within the next few decades or even sooner. Once it does, it may quickly surpass human intelligence, possibly by a huge margin. Some believe that the country that develops AGI first could attain global dominance. This prospect risks setting off intense competition between the United States and China. Indeed, a narrative has already developed that the superpowers are locked in an AI race, with the Trump administration proclaiming its determination to 'dismantle unnecessary regulatory barriers' to winning it. We argue that this approach presents three profound dangers. The first two are familiar from past arms races: being overtaken by a rival or triggering a war.
