The third is new: losing control of human beings' future to agents far more intelligent than we are, which could endanger our very survival. Striving to get to AGI first risks a race to the bottom on safety practices and regulation concerning them. China does not yet appear bent on racing to superintelligence. The United States should prioritise both unilateral and co-operative efforts to improve AI safety and avoid provoking a race that all humanity could lose.

title: An explicit construction of a limit variety of groups
abstract: We construct an explicit countable group \(G_*=N(R)\rtimes A\) whose generated variety is a limit variety of groups: it has no finite identity basis, whereas every proper subvariety is finitely based. Here \(A\) is relatively free in the variety of groups of nilpotency class at most two and exponent dividing four, and \(R\) is an explicitly defined quotient of the group algebra \(\mathbb F_2[A]\). The proof establishes an ascending chain condition for coefficient spaces indexed by six ordered commutator entries and reduces every proper subvariety to a hereditarily finitely based approximation. Non-finite basability is obtained by transferring independent identities from the constructions of Gupta and Krasilnikov. The resulting variety is contained in \(\mathfrak B_4\mathfrak B_2\). This construction provides the first example of such a variety in which both the generators and a basis are explicitly given.

title: The index of conformal Hopf maps
abstract: We compute the index and nullity of any harmonic morphism from $S^3$ to $S^2$.

title: The Right to Be Forgotten under Correlation: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs
abstract: We study privacy-preserving algorithms that redact information from a correlated dataset. The goal is to reduce the information leakage about sensitive parts. We analytically characterize the optimal tradeoff between privacy (leakage through correlation) and utility (number of redactions) for local mechanisms and binary Markovian correlations. Our result shows how to decompose the mechanism design problem into a sequence of local mechanism design problems and reveals their sequential relation. The optimal mechanism is the solution to a Finite-Horizon Deterministic Markov Decision Process.

title: Interactive Navigation Beyond Reachability: Benchmark and Agentic Framework
abstract: Existing embodied navigation tasks commonly assume that traversability and object states remain fixed during an episode. Yet reaching a goal may require opening a door to access a room and then opening a container to reveal a hidden target. We formulate interactive navigation beyond reachability, unifying channel-induced changes in spatial connectivity, container-induced changes in target visibility, and their sequential dependencies. We introduce MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in MolmoSpaces spanning channel, container, and mixed tasks, with interaction-necessity annotations covering required and unnecessary episodes. Its data generation pipeline automates task construction across multiple task types. The evaluation protocol separately measures navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. We further propose MultINav-Agent, a three-stage agentic framework built on a persistent, state-conditioned interaction graph. Semantic interactive perception grounds entities and interaction states; a vision-language model selects task-relevant actions based on expected changes in connectivity and target observability; and post-interaction verification updates the graph to guide subsequent navigation, exploration, or interaction. Experiments on MultINav-Bench show that MultINav-Agent consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks.

title: What the Machine Invented: Mining New Mathematical Instruments from OpenAI's October 2026 Release of AI-Generated Mathematics
abstract: On 6 October 2026 OpenAI published an initial 722 AI-written mathematical manuscripts, organized into 372 problem families, in the public repository github.com/openai/math. The release includes claimed solutions to many prominent open problems. We approach this collection as a treasure mine of mathematical ideas. Our aim is to extract new lemmas, constructions, inequalities and proof mechanisms introduced in the source arguments, and to distinguish them from established tools and new combinations of those tools. We call these mathematical instruments. Extraction comes first; their validity, novelty and possible reuse then become subjects for further study. The resulting descriptions also help readers understand the selected papers without having to reconstruct every argument at the outset. We examine 38 families in two groups of 17 and 21, spanning number theory, geometry, analysis, combinatorics, complexity, algebra, operator algebras, topology and mathematical physics. Each entry records the claim, extracted instruments, antecedents and caveats. Eleven cross-cutting patterns connect the entries, and a scoreboard records formalization status and dependencies. Novelty assessments are provisional and sometimes mixed. Selected source comparisons correct mathematical statements, hypotheses and counts; they do not independently establish priority or certify the underlying proofs. No Lean development was compiled or kernel-checked for this survey. We also briefly describe a subsequent application of the signed restriction lemma from family 112 to circuit lower bounds at every fixed depth.

title: MCCL: Measurement-based Collective Communication Library
abstract: Collective communication is a critical performance bottleneck in large-scale distributed training. Existing libraries and synthesis frameworks compute open-loop schedules once, assuming a static topology and peak link capacities. In production, however, persistent gray failures can silently degrade link throughput and latency for hours, causing pre-computed schedules to lose much of their efficiency during execution. In this paper, we present Measurement-based Collective Communication Library (MCCL), a collective communication library that closes the loop between runtime network measurement and dynamic schedule synthesis. MCCL passively measures GPU-to-GPU throughput, detects persistent degradation, re-synthesizes the affected communication-intensive schedules with warm-started synthesizers, and hot-swaps them without interrupting training. We validate the complete loop on a multi-node hardware prototype and use simulations to evaluate cluster-scale scenarios. In our experiments, MCCL incurs negligible overhead (<2%) while maintaining high measurement accuracy (<1.2% error) and low schedule hot-swap time (about 12 ms). Notably, under gray failures, MCCL reduces training time by up to 4.99x over static schedules on simulated training workloads for state-of-the-art LLMs such as Llama and DeepSeek.

title: Bartnik's splitting conjecture and the cosmological wall: a Cauchy Busemann function approach
abstract: Bartnik's conjecture states that a timelike geodesically complete cosmological spacetime satisfying the timelike convergence condition splits as a static product. We show that any counterexample exhibits a peculiar global causal structure: two disjoint open regions, the future and the past cosmological developments, separated by a non-empty closed causally convex set: the cosmological wall. The developments are bounded by $C^0$ null hypersurfaces, the cosmological horizons, and a component of each horizon contains a lightlike line. These objects are natural and hence carry physical significance, as they do not depend on the choice of Cauchy hypersurface. They can be defined through the Cauchy Busemann functions $b^\pm$ of a compact Cauchy hypersurface $Σ$, the developments being their finiteness domains. Using a product trick we show that $b^+$ is the graph function of a Cauchy horizon in $M\times \mathbb{R}$, and so inherits the regularity and dynamical properties of horizons: $b^+$ is continuous, locally Lipschitz and locally semi-concave on its finiteness domain, and its calibrated curves are timelike rays. We prove that if the two cosmological developments intersect, which happens whenever $b^+$ is $C^1$ on its finiteness domain, then the spacetime contains a timelike line and hence splits, a result which recovers several positive results of the literature. We also obtain a localized rigidity version of Hawking's singularity theorem: if some compact Cauchy hypersurface has non-positive mean curvature on the future development, the spacetime splits. Hence, in a counterexample, every compact Cauchy hypersurface expands somewhere in the future development and contracts somewhere in the past one. If the wall has empty interior, it coincides with both horizons and is ruled by lightlike lines, and under null completeness its components are smooth totally geodesic null hypersurfaces.

title: SFT Leaves a Reproducible Signature in Activation Geometry: Calibrating Post-Training Interpretability Against Run-to-Run Noise
abstract: A model diff credits post-training with whatever separates a base checkpoint from one post-trained descendant, presuming a rerun would land close by. On the sparse co-activation graph of Qwen3-1.7B it does not: two LoRA-SFT reruns sit over half as far apart as either sits from the base. We score each base-to-post contrast against the run-to-run band of its own recipe, and show that $k$ runs certify no better than $p=1/(k+1)$ under run exchangeability, however large the effect, so the band $z$-score is a descriptive scale. SFT leaves a large, reproducible signature: base $\to$ SFT displaces the graph by 17.8 pairwise-distance SDs beyond the mean distance between four independent LoRA-SFT runs, and the pre-registered estimator replicates on Llama-3.1-8B with Llama-Scope. At 29 steps each, four SFT and four DPO runs occupy disjoint displacement ranges, a gap $5.0\times$ and $5.6\times$ the spreads of the two arms, without any band. All bands use graphs built on one GPU architecture. Three other readings stop short of a verdict: DPO band counts (3/4, 1/4, 3/4 contrasts outside at 12, 29, 60 steps) show no consistent dose ordering while its displacement stays flat; light GRPO is a secondary non-detection, not an absence, and we run no equivalence test; and the graph concentration read as an RL signature is already in the zero-RL base. A pre-registered causal sweep at three edge budgets on 4,816 held-out prompts found the displaced sources load-bearing ($12\times$ a matched random control in mean, $3.5\times$ in median at 10,000 edges), but their stage-specificity interaction reversed at two budgets and the third failed its faithfulness gate, so we claim calibrated structural displacement, not a changed mechanism. Scope: one backbone, one SFT recipe and general-text probe states for the full protocol.

title: Particle Selection in Virtual Reality
abstract: Point-cloud representations of 3D data are used in many fields, from astronomical surveys of galaxies to medical imaging and laser scans of buildings. A task common to all of these is interactive selection: picking out a meaningful subset of points for closer analysis. The data is inherently 3D, yet the traditional workflow uses a 2D mouse on a 2D projection and inherits the limitations of a flat screen. This paper compares Virtual Reality (VR) and desktop environments for 3D particle selection, asking whether VR's six-degree-of-freedom hand interaction yields measurable gains in accuracy, speed, usability, workload and flow. In a counterbalanced within-subjects experiment (N = 34), participants selected 90 target galaxies from a catalogue of 16,816 galaxies, using mouse-driven selection with keyboard camera control on the desktop and a hand-held spherical brush that adds or removes particles in VR. We measured task accuracy, completion time, and three standard questionnaires: the System Usability Scale (SUS), the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) and the Flow State Scale (FSS). Accuracy was comparable (91.6% VR vs. 93.1% desktop; p = 0.858), but every other measure favoured VR. Tasks were 23% faster (p = 0.001, d = 0.93), usability was higher (SUS 84.6 vs. 54.0; d = -1.78), workload was lower (NASA-TLX 20.4 vs. 34.7; d = 0.90), and flow was higher (FSS 83.2 vs. 70.2; d = -1.23). Because the underlying problem, making a 3D selection through a 2D interface, is not specific to astronomy, we expect the pattern to carry over to point-cloud selection in other fields.

title: Spin-orbit torque effects in all-electrical spin-wave spectroscopy experiments
abstract: Electrical excitation and detection of propagating spin waves are key elements of magnonic devices. While conventional antennas consisting of non-magnetic metals such as Au or Cu excite spin waves predominantly through radio-frequency (RF) Oersted fields, antennas comprising Pt can additionally generate spin-orbit torques (SOTs) via the spin Hall effect. Recent theoretical work has proposed RF-SOT as an alternative mechanism for coherent spin-wave excitation, predicting distinct characteristics compared with conventional inductive excitation. Here, we investigate Pt antennas for the excitation of coherent spin waves in 105-nm-thick epitaxial $\text{Y}_3\text{Fe}_5\text{O}_{12}$ (YIG) films through two potential mechanisms: an oscillating Oersted field and an oscillating spin current. The raw experimental transmission spectra are strongly affected by fabrication-induced modifications to the YIG film associated with the etching process together with spatially inhomogeneous interface conditions induced by Pt. After removing these contributions, we find the remaining two wave propagation consistent with a combined excitation from Oersted fields and SOTs.

title: Towards Universal Calibration for In-Context Classification
abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) has received a lot of interest recently due to its ability to improve classification accuracy for new tasks without having to fine-tune the model over these tasks. However, the impact of ICL on calibration has been far less studied. Recent work has shown that ICL can have a negative impact on calibration due to biased selection of in-context examples. The existing methods for improving ICL calibration require additional task and model-specific training, detracting from the no-fine-tuning convenience of ICL. In this work, we introduce CALIBFORMER, a universal ICL calibrator for classification tasks, that generalizes to new models and tasks without further fine-tuning on these tasks. Specifically, we design a transformer-based calibrator which uses the model predictions on in-context examples to predict a confidence score for the test input. We show that the calibrator trained on three models and ten tasks, is able to generalize/calibrate ICL predictions on several new tasks and four LLMs unseen during training. Even for frontier models like Gemini, CALIBFORMER is able to obtain over 50% reduction in calibration error.

title: SEAL-DT: An End-to-End Security Engineering and Assurance Framework for Cross-Domain Digital Twins
abstract: Cyber-physical systems connect physical processes, software, networks and organizations. Securing them requires a clear account of what happened, what was observed, which actions were authorized and what evidence supports each decision. Digital Twin (DT) descriptions often fail to explain how these elements stay consistent, blur the distinction between physical events and uncertain observations, or detach simulation results from their requirements and assumptions. This paper presents SEAL-DT (Security Engineering and Assurance Lifecycle for Digital Twins), a structured approach to building and evaluating secure DTs. It brings entity definitions, process models, deterministic simulations, data contracts, evidence records, automated tests and reproducible results into one connected model. The main contribution is an end-to-end DT security framework, spanning scenario definition, entity/process modelling, simulation, security decision logic, evidence handling, validation and reproducible reporting. Security decisions and simulation results thus trace back to their data, assumptions and requirements. A DT is more than a copy of system state: it states what it can observe, how accurate and current its information is, where it came from and which decisions it may support. We demonstrate SEAL-DT in five scenarios: Car2X protection, passive IoT-device detection, an industrial control surrogate, lawful acquisition in a smart home, and medical-IoT monitoring that preserves continuity of care. Each includes formal models, deterministic and negative experiments, uncertainty analyses, schema-valid fixtures, technical reports and verified manifests, testing multiple configurations under normal and adverse conditions. Results show that the framework supports consistent model construction, traceable execution and comparable internal validation, and that security findings link to observable evidence.

title: Contrastive learning for video reuse detection
abstract: The incorporation of footage from other sources has long been a concern from a copyright perspective, as such usage can harm the interests of rights holders. Recent trends in the ``remixing'' of social media content and the development of bespoke stock libraries for specialist causes mean that methods to identify content reuse will have a range of applications. In this paper, we develop a framework based on a Siamese network fine tuned using contrastive learning to identify potential sources for key frames in a given video. This framework makes two contributions to analysis of large video datasets. Firstly, we demonstrate its utility at reducing complex video data to a set of key visuals typically less than 10\% of the size of the full set. Secondly, we show that these reduced sets allow for efficient and effective identification of component footage. We test this method over a set of videos compiled from a stock footage library and demonstrate its effectiveness for constituent video identification with average accuracy greater than 0.95.

title: LocalTrain: Integer-Only Local Learning for Energy-Efficient CNN Training on Edge FPGAs
abstract: Local learning reduces cross-layer training dependencies, but an efficient accelerator must still retain operands, accumulate gradients, and select quantization scales. We present an FPGA system that trains a CNN and its regional auxiliary classifiers using a shared integer matrix engine. Compact errors are expanded on chip, gradients are folded tile by tile, and historical scales permit direct output conversion. At 200 MHz, the KV260 prototype achieves 76.57% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 91.85% on SVHN at approximately 4.20 W mean module power. Effective matrix throughput is 31.22 and 31.57 GMAC/s, respectively. Against the same integer method on Jetson Orin Nano, measured training energy is 40.4% and 42.1% lower, with $1.86\times$ and $1.82\times$ longer runtime; measurements use the respective platform power domains. Selected state checks and matching complete-run prediction counts support functional agreement with the software reference.

title: Block Sensitivity and Certificate Complexity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions
abstract: We study block sensitivity and certificate complexity of rotation symmetric Boolean functions, with particular emphasis on monomial rotation symmetric Boolean functions. We first show that every odd-degree monomial rotation symmetric Boolean function on $n$ variables satisfies $s=bs=C=n$. We then determine sensitivity, block sensitivity, and certificate complexity for every quadratic monomial rotation symmetric Boolean function. For the quadratic function $Q_{n,k}$ generated by $x_0x_k$, we prove, outside the short-orbit case, that \[ C(Q_{n,k})= \begin{cases} n,&4\mid n/\gcd(n,k),\\ n-\gcd(n,k),&4\nmid n/\gcd(n,k). \end{cases} \] Moreover, \(bs(Q_{n,k})=C(Q_{n,k})\) for every quadratic MRS function, and outside the short-orbit case, strict separation \(s<bs=C\) occurs exactly when \[ \frac{n}{\gcd(n,k)}\equiv2\pmod4. \] Finally, for the consecutive quartic family \[ R_n(x)=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z_n}x_ix_{i+1}x_{i+2}x_{i+3}, \] we determine all three measures in every residue class modulo $6$, using the sensitivity formulas and, in one residue class, finite-state results established in our companion preprint~\cite{LiZhangRSBFSensitivity}. In particular, for $r=2,3$ and $6q+r\ge5$ we obtain strict separation, \[ \boxed{s(R_{6q+r})=6q<bs(R_{6q+r})=C(R_{6q+r})=6q+1,\qquad r=2,3.} \] Thus this family gives an infinite collection of rotation symmetric Boolean functions for which sensitivity is strictly smaller than block sensitivity, while block sensitivity and certificate complexity coincide.

title: A Feasible Direction Method with Active-Set Identification for Derivative-Free Optimization
abstract: We propose a model-based trust region method for derivative-free optimization with simulation-based inequality constraints. We are motivated by settings of simulation optimization in which both function evaluations at infeasible points may be unreliable and constraint evaluations are expensive. Our method maintains feasible incumbents and computes steps from a subproblem suitable for a feasible-direction method in order to encourage generation of feasible trial points. To reduce the computational cost of modeling the constraints, we describe an active-set estimation scheme that permits modeling with only a subset of constraints in each subproblem, as opposed to maintaining models of all constraints. We show that every limit point of the incumbents generated by our method is a Fritz-John point, and is additionally a KKT point under the Mangasarian-Fromovitz constraint qualification. Under standard nondegeneracy conditions, the active-set estimate identifies, within finite time, all constraints active at the limit point of the incumbents. Experiments on CUTEst problems show that our method generates feasible trial points far more often than a comparable SQP-based approach and solves more problems within a given budget with fewer function evaluations.

title: Skyrmion gears: translation-to-rotation conversion of skyrmion clusters along periodic substrates
abstract: We investigate how the translational motion of a compact skyrmion cluster can be converted into collective rotation through interactions with a periodic obstacle substrate. Using an effective particle model, we consider a seven-skyrmion cluster driven along a one-dimensional array of repulsive obstacle sites. For suitable obstacle spacings and interaction strengths, repeated interactions with the substrate produce coherent clockwise or counterclockwise rotation, giving rise to gear-like cluster dynamics. We characterize these states using the translational velocity, Hall angle, angular velocity, structural deformation, and a dimensionless gear ratio that relates cluster rotation to motion over the substrate periodicity. Dynamical phase diagrams identify rotating, nonrotating, wall-guided, transverse, and deformed regimes. We further show that coherent rotation persists in the overdamped limit, demonstrating that the conversion mechanism does not require an intrinsic Magnus force and may therefore extend to other driven cluster systems, including colloidal assemblies. These results provide a simple route for controlling collective rotation through structured substrates.

title: Local Turnpike Stability for Two-Population Second-Order Mean-Field Game Systems
abstract: This paper establishes a local turnpike property for a two-population, second-order mean-field game system with a quadratic Hamiltonian, in which the running cost for each population may depend on both population densities. In the case of two populations, imposing a scalar stability condition separately on each species is not sufficient because it neglects cross-interaction effects. The appropriate requirement is instead a matrix-valued coercivity condition on vector perturbations $(μ_1,μ_2)$, which involves the symmetric part of the linearized interaction matrix together with weighted Poincaré inequalities associated with the two stationary measures. Consequently, in the multi-population framework, diffusion still acts independently on each population, but the interactions are controlled by the full coupling matrix. A naive scalar energy functional fails to capture mixed second-variation terms arising from costs that depend on both densities. We prove that matrix coercivity is precisely equivalent to the strict positivity of this second variation, and we provide a spectral characterization in terms of the principal spectral value of the coupled stationary linearized operator. For linear models with cross-interactions, this yields explicit algebraic conditions that separate stable parameter ranges from unstable ones. In the non-potential framework, the skew-symmetric part of the interaction matrix leaves the coercivity threshold unchanged, but it can induce transient oscillatory dynamics. Moreover, the scalar turnpike theory extends in a natural, though nontrivial, manner to multi-population systems, where stability is governed by the positivity of a coupled matrix-valued second variation that encodes both self-interactions and cross-interactions.

title: Dynamic Panel Multinomial Logit Models
abstract: This paper provides moment conditions for dynamic multinomial logit panel data models with individual specific fixed effects. The moment conditions do not depend on the fixed effects and thus form the basis for generalized method of moments estimation. For a leading case, we provide sufficient conditions under which the moment conditions identify the common parameters, and we illustrate their use in an empirical application to household soft drink purchases. The construction of moment conditions is based on transformed models obtained by permuting outcomes across time periods. For any cyclic permutation, the ratio of the transformed model probability to the true model probability is free of the fixed effects, and comparing two such ratios yields restrictions on the common parameters of interest. This construction is not specific to the multinomial logit. It applies to any dynamic panel data model whose static counterpart admits a symmetric sufficient statistic for the fixed effects. This unifies our main result with analogous results for other models.

title: A Composite Representation Theorem for Solution Mappings in Regularized Composite Optimization with Applications to Hausdorff Lipschitz Stability
abstract: We study the geometry and stability of solution mappings in regularized composite optimization, allowing multiple minimizers. We establish a composite representation that separates optimal linear images from their corresponding primal solutions through an image mapping and a generalized basis pursuit mapping. Under a fiber-attainment condition, the image mapping admits a reduced optimization formulation; neither representation requires convexity. For convex regularizers, suitable qualification conditions yield a Fenchel-conjugate representation of the reduced value function and a geometric characterization of the generalized basis pursuit mapping through affine fibers and a fixed lifting set. Using these representations, we establish sufficient conditions for local Hausdorff Lipschitz continuity of possibly set-valued solution mappings. We further show that the primal-space sufficient conditions imply the corresponding image-space conditions, with an additional injectivity requirement arising in the former. The results cover $\ell_1$-type and structured piecewise linear-quadratic regularizers under suitable assumptions. For classical $\ell_1$ regularization, our approach recovers an existing stability result without a finite sign-pattern decomposition. Numerical examples illustrate the recovery of complete solution sets, including a case with a nonpolyhedral graph of the generalized basis pursuit mapping.

title: A Deficiency-Based Approach for Unbalanced Three-Phase Distribution System Expansion Planning
abstract: Distribution planners typically characterize grid needs through power flow studies and fit upgrades to those needs by hand. More principled one-shot optimization methods either do not scale or misrepresent unbalanced three-phase networks. This paper proposes an iterative planning process that alternates between two problem classes with mature off-the-shelf solvers. An optimal power flow (OPF) problem quantifies the deficiency of a candidate portfolio by optimizing the dispatch of controllable devices and measuring thermal and voltage violations on a common scale, with an optimal value of zero exactly at adequate portfolios. The OPF multipliers give a first-order approximation of the relief each investment candidate would provide. We bound the error of this approximation and show that structural properties of the deficiency guard it against overestimation. Building on this property, a heuristic cutting-plane search uses a mixed-integer linear program to propose each next portfolio from these approximations. On six unbalanced three-phase feeders from the SMART-DS dataset, the search outperforms a linearized optimization-based benchmark, and the results agree across five variants of the deficiency.

title: The majority of a cactus is prickly
abstract: We characterise all (undirected) cacti graphs, and forests of cacti, with an edge-preserving near-unanimity operation, by means of forbidden induced subgraphs. Indeed all such graphs also have an edge-preserving majority operation. We show that said majority can be chosen to be symmetric and explicitly construct it for all forests of cacti without the forbidden induced subgraphs.

title: Calibrating AlphaFold confidence scores for interface quality
abstract: AlphaFold confidence scores are widely used to rank protein complex predictions and to select subsets of models for downstream applications. Although these scores provide strong discriminatory power for distinguishing prediction quality, their numerical values were never intended to represent the probability that a prediction satisfies a given structural quality criterion. In this work, we calibrate commonly used confidence scores to estimate the probability that a predicted complex exceeds a chosen threshold of DockQ, an established measure of interface quality. On antibody-antigen and general multimer datasets, post-hoc isotonic calibration consistently improves agreement between predicted probabilities and observed DockQ success rates while preserving the underlying score ordering. The calibrated probabilities also provide more accurate estimates of the fraction of selected models expected to pass a given structural quality threshold. Although the mapping is fitted within a given prediction distribution and therefore transfers imperfectly across prediction domains, we show that reliable estimates are recovered from a small number of labeled target-domain samples. Because the calibration is entirely post hoc and requires no underlying AlphaFold model fine-tuning, it provides a straightforward and customizable way to convert existing model quality rankings into calibrated probabilities of passing a chosen structural quality threshold.

title: Masked Diffusion for Travel Diaries Synthesis
abstract: Because household travel surveys combine household characteristics, variable-length person rosters, vehicle rosters, and trip chains, existing synthesis pipelines split them across separate models or flatten them into cropped fixed-length vectors. Representation, rather than modeling, becomes the bottleneck: splitting severs cross-segment dependence, and cropping truncates the household-structure distribution. We instead tokenize the diary and keep the object whole: each household-day becomes one token sequence with count tokens for vehicles, persons, and trips, and distinct symbols for padded, hidden, unobserved, and inapplicable positions. We introduce DiaryBridge, a masked diffusion model that bridges the fully hidden sequence to the distribution of complete diaries by unmasking positions in any order. One trained model, conditioned on any observed subset, performs synthesis and partial-diary completion alike. Experiments on real data extracted from the 2017/2018 Regional Travel Survey of the Baltimore region show that DiaryBridge generates travel reflecting vehicle availability and employment status, recovers shared trips using other household members' observed diaries, and better reproduces aggregate demand across modes, purposes, and departure periods than the learned baselines.

title: AIPOCH Open-Science: An Open-Source AI Research Workbench with Reproducible .science Packages
abstract: AI-assisted research leaves instructions, computations, artifact revisions and checks whose relationships matter when another researcher receives the work. We present AIPOCH Open-Science, an open-source research workbench with portable .science session packages, and specify an exchange contract for these recorded relationships. Version and assessment targets remain attributable while receiving-workspace identifiers can be remapped, eligible contents can be omitted explicitly, and imported history remains separate from a writable fork. A controlled session tested an incorrect first version, a reviewed correction, an unreviewed revision and a planned but unexecuted step. We compared complete and partial exports with source records extracted independently of the exporter, then inspected imports into separate projects within the same installation. Both conditions retained the tested version and review associations, kept the unreviewed revision distinct from earlier assessments and represented excluded content as unavailable. A documentation-rich ordinary directory also supplied evidence for all seven static inspection questions. A separate registry case connected a table to its recorded task, execution and review; offline execution of its retained script and fixed input reproduced two saved CSV tables byte for byte. The study contributes an implemented exchange contract and a controlled examination of its preservation rules, content-selection constraints and interpretation boundaries.

title: Chiral Vector Beams for Topological Enantio-Sensitive Imaging
abstract: Molecular chiral discrimination is vital across chemistry and life sciences, yet optical approaches remain highly inefficient for small organic molecules. Here we turn vector beams, whose polarization carries a topological charge, into an efficient probe of molecular handedness. We show that the combination of a tightly focused radially polarized beam at the fundamental frequency ω and an azimuthally polarized beam at 2ω creates chiral vector beams, a locally chiral field with structured handedness. Using state-of-the-art computational modeling in the chiral molecule carvone, we show that the nonlinear response (notably sum-frequency generation) of randomly oriented chiral molecules to this chiral vector beam captures the fields' local handedness and is highly enantio-sensitive. The two enantiomers emit light at frequency 3ω with topological ring structures of different divergence, and thus the molecular handedness can be read out directly from the ring radius. The signal inherits the Poincaré index of the driving field, opening up new ways to robust, ultrafast, and and all-optical chiral discrimination.

title: The Rhythm of the Tiles: Narrow and Low Temperature Computation and Simulation in Synchronous Tile Self-Assembly
abstract: In this paper, we prove that the synchronicity provided by the syncTAM can be leveraged to perform two additional feats impossible in the asynchronous aTAM. The aTAM has long been known to be equivalent to finite automata in the one-dimensional case. For our first set of results, we prove that this still holds when a finite, fixed amount of space is available in the second dimension. Yet, surprisingly, in the synchronous setting, a small, fixed, width is enough to simulate a Turing Machine. This holds even in the non-cooperative setting. For our second set of main results we prove that there exists a single set of syncTAM tiles that can be used to simulate any syncTAM system simply by using those tiles to create a scaled version of the seed structure of the original system and then letting the tiles from that set self-assemble from the scaled seed structure. While it has been shown (FOCS 2012) that such a tile set also exists in the aTAM for simulating all aTAM systems, that "intrinsically universal" (IU) tile set requires cooperativity (and is impossible without cooperativity as shown in SODA 2014). We prove there exists an IU tile set in the syncTAM that works without cooperativity. Furthermore, there exists a tile set that is IU for the class of directed systems (i.e. systems which each have a single terminal assembly) while remaining directed during simulation. This was shown to be impossible in the aTAM (FOCS 2016).

title: Calibrated Typed Decisions for Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction
abstract: Information extraction models often perform well on the datasets they are trained on, but transferring to new domains and annotation guidelines remains challenging. Supporting user-specified types alone does not resolve this problem. We present CalOn, a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction across datasets and schemas. The model jointly encodes text and type definitions, then directly identifies entity spans, relations between spans, and event triggers and arguments. Its extraction decisions consider the requested types together, using their combined evidence to identify relevant candidates before assigning a type. This gives all three tasks a common probabilistic formulation while keeping every extracted mention anchored to the input text. We train on diverse sources, and supplement supervised learning with a reward that encourages correct extractions and penalises incorrect ones. Across 40 benchmarks, CalOn outperforms the evaluated baselines on most benchmarks. It leads all reported relation extraction benchmarks and achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments with gold triggers. The same model also performs strongly on aspect sentiment triplet extraction and pronoun resolution through its span-pair formulation. A correction for the probability bias introduced during training improves confidence estimates for entities, relations, and event arguments after calibration, with little change in F1.

title: D-World: An Explicit World-Language-Action Model with Recursive Self-Improvement under Dual Control
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.

title: Machine Learning Models Trained on a Longitudinal Survey Dataset Poorly Predict Hundreds of Life Outcomes
abstract: Understanding the predictability of life outcomes is important for public policy and science, but existing studies focus on a limited number of outcomes and therefore struggle to describe the broad patterns of predictability. We developed a high-throughput approach that uses a single dataset to study the predictability of many future outcomes using past data. We deployed this approach with hundreds of outcomes and thousands of machine learning models per outcome in the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study. Three findings emerged. First, most outcomes were not very predictable, but some were much more predictable than others. Second, even for the most predictable outcomes, our complex prediction procedure typically exhibited little skill relative to a simple procedure. Third, we found modest patterns in how predictability varied across outcomes. We conclude by discussing scope conditions and how future research might address them.

title: Finiteness of Fuchsian equations with unitarizable monodromy on compact Riemann surfaces
abstract: We prove that, on any compact Riemann surface, there are only finitely many meromorphic projective connections with prescribed singular points and real exponent differences whose projective monodromy is unitarizable. We also establish properness and growth estimates for holonomy, including a relative version for smooth marked families, and derive finiteness results for spherical conical metrics and ramification divisors of stable extensions.

title: Gluing Local Contexts into Global Meaning: A Sheaf-Theoretic Decomposition of Transformer Representations
abstract: Existing interpretability tools do not test whether a representation keeps the same content when only the phrasing changes. We treat each paraphrase pair as a local witness that two activations should agree and build a cellular sheaf over the paraphrase graph; its Laplacian $L_\mathcal{F}$ answers the question on a frozen model with no training. The kernel $H^0$ is a content subspace: at 20 dimensions it beats the preserved subspace of the concept eraser LEACE on held-out CounterFact fact retrieval across eight architectures by a mean $+17.1$\,pp, and constraining all paraphrases of a fact jointly adds a further $+6.5$\,pp. The spectral complement concentrates causal influence: ablating the most paraphrase-variable coordinates, a coordinate-wise proxy for it, changes model outputs $5.6$ to $26.5\times$ more than ablating coordinates of matched per-coordinate variability, across nine models from 124M to 13B parameters. Stacking layers into a grid creates $b_1 = N(L-1)$ algebraic 1-cycles, and the resulting model-derived harmonic mass varies by nearly three orders of magnitude across six architectures and ranks them as their steering fragility does (Spearman $ρ= 0.90$, exact one-sided permutation $p = 0.014$). The same paraphrase graph yields the content subspace, the influence directions, and the fragility measure. Project page: https://cwru-aism.github.io/gluing-lc-page/

title: When LLM Agents See a Conflict but Still Proceed: Cross-Domain Dependencies in Network Slicing
abstract: Future AI-native networks are being designed to apply autonomous agents built on large language models (LLMs) in network management through intents. When intents from different domains meet on the same resource, an agent must recognize the cross-domain dependency before taking an irreversible action. We investigate this problem through a smart-grid use case, in which a power utility holds an active intent on a backup slice for protection traffic. This slice appears idle by design, which is precisely the profile targeted by a cost-reduction intent. We built a tool-based environment in which the dependency must be either queried by the agent or read from an inventory annotation, together with a negative control, and evaluated ten models from four different providers in 600 runs. Most models acted against the dependency they had observed: seven of the ten models removed the protection slice at least once after receiving the cross-domain dependency, and in the high-harm tier the slice was removed in 76% of the exposed runs, while four models practically never did. Only one of ten models never removed the slice. We identify two failure modes, not querying the dependency and querying it but proceeding anyway, and show that agents often reported no conflict after observing it. These results indicate that, in AI-native networks, visibility of cross-domain dependencies is not a sufficient safeguard, and that dependency verification should be enforced by the management architecture before irreversible actions rather than delegated to the LLM's judgment.

title: Spatial Partner Markets: Effective Competition, Scale, and Opportunity
abstract: Local partner markets differ not only in population size but in relative partner availability, the scale of opportunity, marriage timing, and population turnover. This paper develops a county-level framework for comparing these conditions across local partner markets. The empirical application focuses on unmarried women ages 25-34 and uses observed partner-age pairings to construct age-specific weights for the relevant unmarried male population. We model absolute opportunity separately, fitting a Michaelis-Menten diminishing-returns transformation to 192 scenarios that vary dating intensity, search horizon, fit, and first-date conversion. The resulting index also incorporates the share of women ages 35-39 who have never married and the inflow rate of adults ages 25-34. Among 320 counties with complete data, the District of Columbia ranks first and New York County second under the baseline specification, and rankings remain highly stable under alternative component weights. An endogenous mobility extension shows that favorable markets attract additional male participants, producing substantial adjustment while leaving the top composite rankings relatively stable over the parameter values considered. The framework is intended as a structural comparison of local partner-market conditions rather than a predictor of individual relationship outcomes.

title: Can Rényi Accountants Beat Lossless Accountants for DP-SGD?
abstract: Recent frameworks in differential privacy (DP), such as privacy loss distributions and $f$-DP, provide lossless representations of the privacy leakage of mechanisms. These approaches are often considered to yield tighter $(\varepsilon, δ)$-DP guarantees than those obtained from relaxed notions such as Rényi DP. But is that always the case? We study this question for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with fixed-size batches under replace adjacency. Our key observation is that in this setting, privacy accounting based on Rényi DP can use a pair of worst-case distributions (i.e., a dominating pair) that differs from the one used in the lossless frameworks. In particular, we characterize the worst-case distributions as two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and derive an improved Rényi DP bound for DP-SGD. Numerical and asymptotic comparisons show that across various hyperparameter settings, a Rényi DP accountant based on the new bound can yield better privacy guarantees than those obtained from the lossless frameworks.

title: Sharp dimension threshold for unique FKPP steady states and BBM recurrence
abstract: We consider the existence and uniqueness of positive, bounded stationary solutions of the Fisher-KPP equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions. We establish that stationary solutions are unique, and exist if and only if the generalised principal eigenvalue is strictly positive (supercriticality), in dimension at most $6$. This is sharp: we exhibit examples both of non-uniqueness and of existence at criticality in dimension $7$ or higher, including for the classical reaction $f(u)=u-u^2$. This proves a conjecture of Berestycki and Graham in the affirmative for dimension at most $6$, and in the negative for dimension at least $7$. We thereby show that branching Brownian motion cannot survive globally without surviving locally in dimension $6$ or lower, but can do so in dimension $7$ or higher, mirroring the classical transition of Brownian motion from recurrence to transience from dimension $2$ to $3$. We further show that relaxing the strong-KPP condition results in a more general sharp dimension threshold for the uniqueness/non-existence result. These results are valid without any regularity assumptions on the domain boundary. As a corollary, we show that solutions of the evolution reaction-diffusion equation are always convergent in the long run in dimension at most $6$, whilst we exhibit non-convergent solutions in dimension larger than $6$.

title: Coordinated Conservation Voltage Reduction and Network Topology Reconfiguration in Active Distribution Networks
abstract: Distribution networks rely on conservation voltage reduction (CVR) and network topology reconfiguration (NTR) to manage demand, distributed energy resources (DERs), and tighter operating margins. Yet these strategies are typically deployed independently, despite coupled effects on feeder voltages, losses, and loading. This paper addresses that gap by developing a day-ahead mixed-integer second order cone programming (MISOCP) framework that jointly optimizes feeder head voltage control and network reconfiguration. The formulation incorporates AC branch flow constraints, ZIP load models, DERs, battery energy storage systems, and multi substation radiality. Using modified IEEE 33 bus and 123 bus systems, four configurations isolate the individual and coordinated effects of CVR and NTR. On the 33-bus system under mixed ZIP loading, NTR reduces active energy loss by 2.50%, while coordinated operation reduces it by 2.91% relative to SDN and produces a 2.46% CVR induced active load reduction relative to SDNTR. Under constant impedance loading, coordinated operation reduces active energy loss by 17.65% relative to SDN, while CVR reduces active load by 14.61% relative to SDNTR. DER portfolio scaling shows a nonmonotonic coordinated load reduction response, strongest at 20% penetration and decreasing at higher levels. On the 123 bus system, NTR reduces losses by 19.3%, while CVR reduces voltage dependent load energy by 2.3 to 2.4%. Under loading stress, SDN becomes infeasible at 120% loading, whereas CEDNTR remains feasible. Overall, the results demonstrate complementary, operating condition dependent benefits shaped by load composition, DER portfolio scaling, feeder topology, voltage margins, and source constraints, highlighting the value of joint optimization.

title: One vertex generates the hard-sphere Boltzmann collision hierarchy
abstract: The Boltzmann equation is the fundamental kinetic bridge between molecular mechanics and fluid behaviour. It converts binary encounters into the evolution of a velocity distribution, underlies rigorous routes from hard-sphere dynamics to Euler and Navier--Stokes--Fourier equations, and remains indispensable when continuum descriptions fail, from hypersonic shock layers and atmospheric re-entry to rarefied multiscale flows. Yet its nonlinear collision term is conventionally represented by an infinite three-index tensor of collisional brackets, with apparently new coefficients at every polynomial order. Here we prove that this entire hard-sphere tensor contains only one primitive collision law: the exact rank-two stress-production vertex $S$. Every polynomial collision vertex is obtained from $S$ by a finite sequence of universal differential and tensor operations, and every conventional bracket follows by differentiation. Thus the interaction physics and its representation separate exactly: all hard-sphere-specific information is concentrated in $S$, whereas the hierarchy above it is universal algebra. A blind eighth-order test in a Mach-5 shock agrees with independent collision sampling and strongly amplifies a weak kinetic precursor. The hard-sphere hierarchy is infinite in dimension, but its primitive collision content consists of a single scalar law.

title: D2: High-Capability Full-Duplex Spoken Language Models from Half-Duplex Backbones
abstract: Full-duplex spoken language models (FD-SLMs) support simultaneous listening and speaking, but often lag behind half-duplex spoken language models (HD-SLMs) in general capabilities. We propose Dialogue-to-Duplex (D2), a framework that converts pretrained HD-SLMs into high-capability FD-SLMs at fine temporal granularity. D2 adapts the original audio encoder to streaming through decoder-free representation distillation and learns full-duplex interaction through supervised fine-tuning. We systematically study the effects of chunk size on full-duplex interaction, general capabilities, and inference computation. We apply D2 to two distinct HD-SLM architectures, Qwen3-Omni and LLaMA-Omni 2. At a 12.5Hz update rate, Qwen3-Omni-D2 achieves 99.2% turn-taking success with 521-ms latency, 99.5% interruption success, and a state-of-the-art VoiceBench score of 70.1.

title: ToolHACE: A Dataset for Detecting Hallucinations in Tool-Based LLM Responses
abstract: Tool-augmented language models ground their responses in external tool outputs, improving reliability beyond parametric knowledge alone. However, even when the correct tool is called and returns accurate information, models may still contradict such outputs, omit critical details, or generate unsupported claims. Existing hallucination benchmarks for tool-augmented dialogue primarily focus on the tool-calling stage, evaluating whether the correct tool and arguments are selected, while overlooking errors that arise during post-tool response generation. To address this gap, we introduce ToolHACE, a span-level benchmark for hallucination detection in tool-augmented LLM responses, covering five fine-grained hallucination categories. Through extensive experiments with modern hallucination detectors, we show that post-tool-call hallucinations are widespread and remain challenging to detect. Our results further demonstrate that effective detection requires training on specialized tool-augmented corpora, while transfer from tool-agnostic hallucination datasets performs poorly in this setting. These findings highlight the need for dedicated benchmarks and models for reliable hallucination detection in tool-augmented language systems.

title: Who is the 'I' in AI? Establishing Decentralized Identity and Accountability for Autonomous Agents
abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous AI agents in decentralized ecosystems challenges existing identity paradigms. While human identity is traditionally anchored in biological and/or self-asserted attributes and government credentials, AI agents lack a standardized definition of selfhood, creating critical gaps in trust and accountability. This paper introduces a novel framework for establishing Decentralized AI Identity rooted in Self-sovereign identity (SSI) principles. We propose a formal model that clearly distinguishes human users and AI agents, enabling distinct verification logic for each class while maintaining a unified identity calculus. The central to our contribution is the ABCD Framework, a multi-layered approach to agent identification and verification: (A) Algorithmic Fingerprint, which binds the identity to static model architectures and provenance; (B) Behavioural Fingerprint, which verifies dynamic performance metrics over time; (C) Cryptographic Identity, which anchors the agent via Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and (D) Delegation, which cryptographically binds agent actions to respective human accountability. By orthogonalizing these dimensions, we model how systems can enforce granular trust policies ranging from simple authentication to complex liability assignment, thereby solving the black box identity problem in the autonomous economic activities of AI agents.

title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Frank--Wolfe for Nonlinear Variational Inequalities on Polytopes
abstract: We consider the Frank--Wolfe algorithm for solving variational inequalities over compact polytopes under a monotone $C^1$ operator $Φ$. The linear minimization oracle returns vertices, and we assume a coercivity condition on the Jacobian of $Φ$ at a solution. We prove last-iterate convergence to the unique solution at rate $O(k^{-\min\{α,1\}})$ for step sizes $γ_k=α/(k+β)$ with $β\geqα>0$. The bound holds uniformly over starting points and vertex tie-breaking. In particular, both $1/(k+1)$ and $2/(k+2)$ give $O(k^{-1})$ distance. A matching lower bound shows that this distance guarantee is worst-case order-optimal among prescribed admissible step-size schedules. We also obtain rates $O(k^{-\min\{α,1\}})$ for the Frank--Wolfe gap and $O(k^{-\min\{α,2\}})$ for the dual gap. These yield $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ and $O(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$ calls to each oracle for sustained gap accuracy $\varepsilon$ when $α\geq1$ and $α\geq2$, respectively, with instance-dependent constants. We also treat more general prescribed step-size schedules.

title: EgoProbe: Benchmarking Long-Range and Exact Memory in Streaming Egocentric Videos
abstract: Egocentric video provides a continuous first-person record of everyday activities, making it a natural foundation for wearable AI assistants. Unlike offline video understanding, streaming systems must process observations as they arrive, while queries may refer to experiences from the distant past. Recent work has begun to explore whether information can be recalled across long temporal gaps. Yet remembering how far is only part of the challenge: recurring objects, actions, and locations also require models to remember exactly which detail belongs to which event. We introduce EgoProbe, a benchmark that evaluates streaming egocentric memory along these two complementary dimensions: long-range retention, i.e., how far, and event-specific recall under interference, i.e., how exact. Built on long-form egocentric videos, EgoProbe uses an event-grounded data engine to extend recall intervals, identify related events, and construct event-grounded distractors, followed by human verification. It contains two subsets: EgoProbe-Base, which evaluates long-range recall without intervening related events, and EgoProbe-Echo, which challenges models with similar intervening events and event-grounded distractors. EgoProbe-Echo adopts coarse-to-fine multi-turn probing: the first turn evaluates coarse-grained event recall, while the second tests whether the model can retrieve the target-specific detail associated with the designated event. Extensive evaluation across diverse models reveals substantial limitations in long-range recall, with further challenges in recovering target-event details among related experiences. Even when models correctly answer coarse-grained questions, they often fail to recall the specific details of the designated event. EgoProbe exposes this underexplored failure mode and provides a testbed for advancing long-range and exact memory in streaming egocentric video understanding.

title: Non-branching properties of Regular Lagrangian Flows and well posedness of the continuity equation in the class of nonnegative solutions
abstract: In this paper we deal with the theory of Regular Lagrangian Flows, as initiated in [29] and axiomatized in [2]. In the first part of the paper we show in Theorem 4.3 (see also Corollary 4.5) that the decomposition of $\mathcal{L}^{1+d}$-almost all the space time in a family of (essentially) disjoint characteristics, the technique at the basis of the well posedness in [1] (for planar, divergence-free and autonomous vector fields), and in [13] (for vector fields having a suitable regularity in space, including BV vector fields) is not only sufficient for well posedness, but also necessary. This shows that in many cases the typical uniqueness statement of the DiPerna-Lions theory, namely that the path $\mathbb{X}(\cdot,x)$ is (essentially) unique given the initial position $x$, can, as in the classical theory, be strengthened by saying that the paths $\mathbb{X}(\cdot,x)$ (essentially) do not branch. As the simple Example 1.1 shows, when we consider vector fields with singular divergence well posedness results may hold only for solutions that do not change sign. In the second part of the paper we revisit [8,9] obtaining a well posedness result for special vector fields of bounded deformation and nonnegative solutions, under a mild regularity assumption (5.3) with respect to the time variable, weaker than the space-time $SBD$ regularity assumption made in [9] for nearly incompressible vector fields. Finally, we revisit carefully the constructions of Section 9 of [13], to see how they provide existence and uniqueness for (1.2) assuming $BV$ regularity in space, in the class of nonnegative bounded solutions.

title: EvoQuantLab: Training-Free Dual-Loop Evolution for Auditable Quantitative Research
abstract: Automated alpha factor discovery is critical for modern quantitative research. While large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been integrated into quantitative workflows, existing agent-based approaches remain highly susceptible to severe backtest overfitting. To address this challenge, we propose EvoQuantLab, a training-free, dual-loop self-evolving framework for robust factor discovery. Instead of relying entirely on LLM generation, EvoQuantLab deploys an inner genetic-programming (GP) loop that dramatically improves token efficiency while evolving typed factor expressions under structural and diversity constraints. An outer diagnosis loop then systematically audits evidence across cycles to drive protocol-level improvements. Furthermore, our evaluation pipeline applies multi-metric validation to rigorously filter out spurious factors before deployment. Extensive out-of-sample experiments across both daily and hourly frequencies -- covering equities and cryptocurrency -- demonstrate the robustness of EvoQuantLab. Specifically, on daily CSI 500 and S&P 500 tasks, EvoQuantLab achieves leading annualized returns of 18.34% and 21.30%, consistently outperforming existing agent baselines. On high-turnover hourly cryptocurrency data, EvoQuantLab delivers a 37.91% annualized return while effectively avoiding execution collapse.

title: SonicWorld: Source-Centric Latent Dynamics for Spatial Audio Reasoning
abstract: Dynamic spatial audio reasoning requires a model to associate changing acoustic observations with the correct source and recover its spatial state at a queried time or interval, a challenge intensified by overlapping speech and source motion. To study this problem, we introduce Sonic-Bench, comprising 2.8K first-order Ambisonics clips and 28.8K target-specific question-answer pairs across 480 simulated indoor scenes. The benchmark covers localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in single- and dual-source settings. We further propose SonicWorld, which integrates physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent source states through learned transitions and recurrent updates, and projects them into an Omni LLM for spatial reasoning. Compared with Spatial-Omni on the Sonic-Bench test split, SonicWorld improves direction accuracy from 31.98% to 34.69% and reduces azimuth error from 57.22° to 48.01°. In zero-shot transfer to Spatial LibriSpeech, SonicWorld retains strong localization performance, achieving 73.98% direction accuracy and 19.29° azimuth error, compared with 27.14% and 70.74° for Spatial-Omni.

title: Masked Attention Pooling Is Invariant to Padding and Permutation: A Formal Proof in Lean
abstract: Attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) pools a variable-size bag of instance embeddings into one vector. In batched training, bags are padded to a common length, and the pooled output is expected not to depend on how much padding was added or on the order in which instances are stored. This expectation holds only if padded rows are removed from both the numerator and the softmax normalizer. Common implementation idioms meet it only under side conditions. Zeroing padded features alone does not work. Masking logits with $-\infty$ fails on empty bags and on nonfinite padding. Masking with a large negative constant is exact only after floating-point underflow. We define masked attention pooling with a guarded normalizer and prove in Lean 4 with mathlib that it is invariant under any bijective reindexing of rows and under appending any finite number of masked rows with arbitrary real features and logits. We also prove that values at masked positions are irrelevant and that an all-masked bag maps to zero. The theorems hold for arbitrary finite index types and feature dimensions. Using the jax-lean certificate pipeline, we connect these theorems to the Jaxpr traced from the JAX kernel itself. Lean checks translation certificates for two concrete shapes, identifies the generated functions with the generic specification, and transfers both invariances to the imported Jaxpr's real-arithmetic semantics. All audited theorems depend only on Lean's three standard axioms. The results concern ideal real arithmetic. Floating-point execution, XLA, and the JAX tracer and importer remain outside the proof.

title: LOCAL LLL in $\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n)$ Rounds
abstract: We provide a $\operatorname{poly}(\log\log n)$-round randomized LOCAL algorithm for the constructive Lovász Local Lemma with polynomial criterion $pd^{c} < 1$, for a sufficiently large constant $c$. The best previous general round complexity was $\widetilde O(\log n)$. The key ingredient is a local reduction that amplifies the LLL probability exponent quadratically, while increasing the dependency radius only by a constant factor.

title: Charged Lepton Flavor Violation: A Theory Overview
abstract: We present a theory-oriented overview of the significance of charged-lepton flavor violation -- one of the cleanest windows onto physics beyond the Standard Model. We also summarize the current experimental landscape and illustrate how different measurements can diagnose the underlying new physics.

title: Chow polynomials and chain polynomials of matroids are not log-concave
abstract: The Hilbert--Poincaré series of the Chow rings of the toric varieties of matroids, often called the \emph{Chow polynomials}, and the $f$-polynomial of their boundary complexes, called the \emph{chain polynomials}, have been conjectured to only have real zeros. We construct several explicit infinite families of matroids from finite geometries, whose multichain counts fail to be log-concave. They share a common geometric construction called \emph{hyperplane coalescence}, together with several classical operations in projective geometry and combinatorial designs. This induces failures of log-concavity for Chow, augmented Chow, chain, and $h$-polynomials of several explicit infinite families of matroids, disproving the real-rootedness conjectures of Ferroni--Schröter, Huh--Stevens, and Athanasiadis--Kalampogia-Evangelinou from the lowest possible ranks. As an application of the same mechanism, we also give counterexamples to the log-concavity of $h$-polynomials of graph associahedra, answering in the negative a question of Sack.

title: JWST Imaging of Edge-on Protoplanetary Disks. V. Flux Ratio Reversal and Disk-edge Structure in the Flying Saucer
abstract: We present near- and mid-infrared broadband imaging observations of the edge-on protoplanetary disk 2MASS J16281370-2431391, a.k.a. the 'Flying Saucer', obtained with NIRCam and MIRI on board JWST. These data are combined with archival optical and near-IR broadband imaging from HST, millimeter dust continuum emission from ALMA, and optical lightcurves from the K2 and TESS for a comprehensive multi-wavelength study. The JWST observations reveal a reversal of the flux ratio between the two reflection nebulae at near-infrared wavelengths (2-3 $μm$), which can be explained by a misaligned inner disk. For the first time, JWST reveals the bright lining along the disk edge at 2 and 3 $μm$, arising from forward scattering of background photons by dust grains near the $τ\approx 1$ layer. By combining the dust lane thickness measured with HST and JWST, we find the dust grains up to at least $\sim$3$μ$m are vertically mixed throughout the disk and have undergone significant growth. In addition, comparison of earlier HST/NICMOS J and K band images with those from JWST/NIRCam reveals variability in the scattered-light morphology, as well as measurable proper motion of the system with respect to the background stars, confirming that the Flying Saucer is co-moving with the young star population of $ρ$ Ophiuchi.

title: Cyclotomic Structure and Exact Recurrences in Floquet Many-Body Quantum Dynamics
abstract: Periodically driven quantum systems exhibit a wide range of complex dynamics, including chaos. Yet, at special parameter values, their evolution can recur exactly. Several quantum protocols have recently been proposed that exploit exact Floquet recurrences to demonstrate genuine quantum advantage. Such recurrences can be studied through the arithmetic structure of the Floquet unitary. In this work, we establish a necessary and sufficient arithmetic criterion for exact recurrence and determine the minimal recurrence period when one exists. Because recurrence is a global property of the unitary, it holds for every initial state. Applying our framework requires only knowledge of the number field associated with the Hamiltonian parameters. We demonstrate the method using the kicked Ising chain, establishing exact recurrences in both Clifford and non-Clifford regimes. We further show that, in the recurrent non-Clifford regime, magic--a resource for quantum computation--is generated at intermediate times and undergoes exact periodic revivals enforced by the recurrence of the full Floquet unitary. By connecting number theory, quantum many-body dynamics, and quantum information, our work shows that exact recurrence extends beyond Clifford circuits and opens new avenues for magic generation and quantum hardware benchmarking.

title: Probability generating functions for epidemiological time series
abstract: Probability generating functions (PGFs) are a fundamental tool in mathematical epidemiology to characterize the stochastic evolution of epidemics via branching process theory. However, they are rarely used as operational tools in real-time during an outbreak, the main barrier being a lack of a systematic, computational methodology to describe epidemiological time series, such as cases or hospital admissions over time. Here, we introduce a general and computationally efficient framework for outbreak analytics based on PGFs. We first develop a method to encode joint distributions of incidences and their noisy measurements by realistic surveillance systems. Then, by transforming PGFs to cumulant generating functions (CGFs), we enable efficient evaluation of these joint distributions. We demonstrate the practicality of our approach for Bayesian inference and short-term forecasts, offering a significant computational advantage over simulation-based methods. Altogether, our framework operationalizes generating functions and paves the way for their broader adoption in computational epidemiology.

title: (Sharp arithmetic) localization beyond transversality
abstract: We prove sharp arithmetic localization for one-dimensional quasiperiodic potentials with jump discontinuities, beyond uniform transversality. Our results include every non-constant $C^1$ monotone sampling function, even with arbitrarily large flat regions, and also certain non-monotone potentials. A key new mechanism is a symbolic unique-continuation principle: first-return words to the region where $f'>0$ have no common Dirichlet resonance, forcing eigenfunction mass to transfer away from flat or negatively sloped regions and recovering quantitative monotonicity of finite-volume eigenvalue branches.

title: The nearby Type II supernova 2024ggi beyond 600 days: circumstellar interaction and dust formation
abstract: The Type II SN 2024ggi is one of the nearest core-collapse SNe to have exploded in recent decades. Its proximity has enabled extensive multiwavelength monitoring from early times through the nebular phase. Signatures of late-time interaction between the SN ejecta and hydrogen-rich circumstellar material (CSM) have recently been reported. Here we extend its study using late-time optical photometry and spectroscopy from 570 to 820 d after explosion. We investigate the emergence and evolution of late-time ejecta-CSM interaction and constrain the geometry of the interaction region and the properties of newly formed dust. Comparisons with other interacting SNe II and with synthetic spectra are presented. We model the H$α$ profile with the Monte Carlo radiative-transfer code Damocles, including both gas and dust components. Spectroscopic signatures of interaction precede the photometric flattening. The spectra evolve from ejecta-dominated to interaction-dominated as H$α$ develops a broad, boxy profile. The optical light curves subsequently flatten relative to the $^{56}$Co decay rate at approximately 650-670 d. The emission lines show a systematic blue-to-red asymmetry that requires a dust component newly formed within the ejecta. The inferred dust mass formed in the ejecta is $10^{-6}-10^{-5}$ M$_\odot$ if the grains are amorphous carbon or a carbon-silicate mixture, but can reach up to $10^{-3}$ M$_\odot$ for pure silicates.

title: MARS: Systematic Multi-Level Acceleration for World Action Models
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising alternative for embodied intelligence by jointly predicting future world states and robot actions. However, their heavy visual encoding and iterative generative inference incur substantial latency, limiting their applicability to high-frequency closed-loop control. Existing training-free acceleration methods typically optimize a single stage, yielding limited speedups or degraded control under aggressive reuse. In this work, we systematically profile the inference overhead of WAMs and observe abundant redundancy across Transformer computation, diffusion denoising, and consecutive policy queries. However, the safe removal of such redundancy depends strongly on its impact on action prediction and control sensitivity. Based on these observations, we introduce \textbf{MARS}, a training-free and plug-and-play framework for multi-level WAM acceleration. MARS selectively removes low-impact attention computation, adaptively accelerates diffusion inference according to motion granularity, and speculatively reuses predicted future visual representations across consecutive queries with online verification. Together, these complementary mechanisms provide remarkable acceleration while limiting approximation error. Extensive experiments across LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and RoboCasa show that MARS achieves up to $4.00\times$, $3.94\times$, and $2.10\times$ end-to-end speedups, respectively, while maintaining task success rate close to the original policy. Moreover, MARS generalizes across different model backbones and across simulation and real-robot experiments, substantially improving the efficiency--performance trade-off of WAM inference. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MARS.

title: Analytical and numerical periodic homogenization of Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman and Isaacs equations in a $W^{2,p}$ Cordes framework
abstract: We study periodic homogenization of fully-nonlinear second-order Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman and Isaacs equations subject to a homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition and the numerical approximation of the effective Hamiltonian, where the diffusion matrix is assumed to satisfy the Cordes condition. In the first part, assuming the Cordes parameter is sufficiently large, we show existence and uniqueness of $W^{2,p}$ solutions to the true cell problem, prove homogenization under minimal regularity assumptions, and establish a quantitative homogenization result. In the second part, we propose and rigorously analyze $W^{2,p}$-conforming and mixed finite element methods for the approximation of the corrector, which are then used in the approximation of the effective Hamiltonian. The key tool used throughout this work is Campanato's concept of near operators.

title: OpenDGO: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Organizations Across Diverse Application Domains
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems are increasingly applied across diverse domains, yet different applications require different forms of agent organization. Existing studies typically adopt predefined organizations, such as Star, Chain, and Tree, or learn communication graphs to improve performance on specific tasks. However, these methods are largely designed and evaluated within a limited set of application domains, providing little understanding of whether an organization effective in one domain remains suitable for others with different collaboration requirements. We present \textbf{OpenDGO}, a controlled benchmark and analysis framework covering six real-world domains and three collaboration settings: Sequential Dependency, Parallel Decomposition, and Information Integration. Under matched tasks, agents, tools, and resource limits, OpenDGO compares fixed and learned organizations while separately examining communication graphs, role assignments, input assignments, resource budgets, and component failures. Our results show that there is no ``one-organization-for-all'' solution: preferred organizations vary across applications, and even the same communication graph can yield different outcomes under different role and input assignments. These findings highlight the need for application-dependent organization design, aiming to understand \emph{which organization is suitable for a given application, under what conditions, and why}.

title: Distribution of central values of Hecke $L$-functions of $n$-th order characters
abstract: We prove a one-sided central limit theorem for $\log |L(\tfrac 12,χ)|$ in a thin family of $n$-th order Hecke characters, for $n \geq 3$. The proof combines the method of Radziwiłł and Soundararajan with a recent asymptotic formula of Diaconu, Ion, Paşol, and Popa for the twisted second moment with a power-saving error term. We also obtain upper bounds of the conjectured order of magnitude for the $2k$-th moments for $0< k< 1$.

title: On the Computational Complexity of Blind Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: Can quantum advantages in computational efficiency coexist with quantum advantages in privacy? In this paper, we construct and use MasonQ, a universal brickwork transpiler, to answer this question with a resounding yes.
