title: Computing All-Pairs Shortest Communication Time Paths for Periodically Varying Satellite Networks
abstract: We address the problem of designing an efficient algorithm for computing the all-pairs shortest-time paths in time-varying networks, specifically targeting the dynamic topological characteristics of low earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations. We model such temporal graphs as $G = (V, E_t)$, where $V=\{1, 2,\ldots , n\}$ is the set of $n$ vertices in the graph, and $E_t$ is the set of $M$ time-varying edges considered over a total time window of size $T = Mτ$, $τ$ being the duration of each interval in that time window. For such a network, our algorithm finds the all-pair shortest paths in $O(M^2n^3)$-time. A key advantage of our approach is its computational structure, which mirrors two matrix multiplication steps, first in the forward direction and then in the backward direction. This structure of the algorithm makes it exceptionally suitable for parallelization on SIMD architectures like GPUs, thereby offering a significant speedup over traditional shortest-path algorithms and enabling efficient, network-wide message routing in rapidly changing LEO satellite constellations.

title: FINESSE: A Versatile Beamline for Fundamental Interactions with Neutrons at the European Spallation SourcE
abstract: FINESSE (A Versatile Beamline for \textbf{F}undamental \textbf{I}nteractions with \textbf{N}eutrons at the \textbf{E}uropean \textbf{S}pallation \textbf{S}ourc\textbf{E}) is a proposed versatile beamline for fundamental interactions with neutrons at the European Spallation Source. Building on the HIBEAM design studies, FINESSE extends the original concept into a dual-guide beamline capable of operating either in a high-flux configuration or in a low-background configuration within a single ESS beam port. The high-flux branch is optimized for rare-process searches, including neutron--antineutron oscillations, neutron--sterile-neutron transitions, axion-like-particle searches, neutron charge measurements, and rare neutron decays. The low-background branch is designed for precision measurements requiring strong suppression of prompt and line-of-sight backgrounds, with a cryogenic neutron electric-dipole-moment experiment used as a benchmark case. A baseline exchangeable-guide concept has been developed in which only short guide sections inside the ESS bunker are exchanged, while the upstream extraction system and chopper positions remain fixed. A staged implementation, Short FINESSE, would use the upstream section of the high-flux beamline together with a compact magnetically controlled experimental region, enabling an early physics and R\&D programme before completion of the full facility. This paper summarizes the scientific case, beamline concept, guide simulations, chopper and timing system, magnetic-field control, detector developments, and staged implementation strategy. FINESSE would establish a long-term particle-physics infrastructure at ESS, providing a beamline for both discovery-driven searches and precision neutron measurements throughout the lifetime of the facility.

title: VulnBump: A Benchmark for Fixing Vulnerable Dependencies in Real Projects While Keeping the Build and Tests Green
abstract: Software composition analysis (SCA) tools report far more vulnerable dependencies than teams fix: in Snyk Open Source production data, 94% of vulnerability findings have a known fixed version, yet only about 10% are resolved. Agentic coding tools could close this gap, but no benchmark evaluates them on vulnerability-driven upgrades in real, runnable projects across ecosystems, verified independently of the agent. We present VulnBump: 307 upgrade tasks covering 2,066 fixable vulnerabilities in 43 repositories across six package managers, matched to Snyk Open Source production vulnerability distributions. An upgrade passes only if, in a fresh container, dependencies resolve, a rescan shows the targeted vulnerabilities fixed, the project builds, and every previously passing test still passes. A non-agentic baseline that only applies Snyk's recommended version passes 46.9% of upgrades; with the same model (Claude Sonnet 5.5), Snyk's Evo Remediation Agent passes 90.2%, Claude Code + Snyk scan 77.5% and Claude Code unaided 59.6%. The agents fail in opposite ways: Claude Code mostly leaves the vulnerability in place, whereas most of Evo Remediation Agent's failures break the build or tests. An SCA scanner is a key tool for agents: Snyk's guidance raises Claude Code's PASS rate by 17.9 percentage points; without it, Claude Code often settles on a still-vulnerable version. Yet knowing the target is not enough: given the same Snyk findings, Evo Remediation Agent's purpose-built harness passes 12.7 points more than Claude Code + Snyk scan. Major framework migrations remain hard for all harnesses. Because the agents keep projects working at similar rates, evaluating remediation quality in dependency upgrades requires verifying the fix, the build and the tests together.

title: PIG: Parallel Inconsistency Guidance for Accelerating Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by decoding multiple masked positions per forward pass. However, accuracy is known to drop when parallel decoding trajectories deviate from their sequential counterparts, which are slow and expensive "oracles" that adhere to the joint distribution of language. In this paper, we propose Parallel Inconsistency Guidance (PIG), a new paradigm that uses a trained auxiliary model to directly estimate the inconsistency between parallel and sequential generation from a single model forward pass. During inference, masked positions are traversed by decreasing confidence, and tokens are added to the parallel decode set one-at-a-time until the total estimated inconsistency between the parallel and sequential generation exceeds a threshold. Surprisingly, it suffices to train a lightweight ~2M parameter auxiliary model on a small mixture drawn from OpenCoder, GSM8K-train, MATH-train, and MBPP-train. For LLaDA-8B Instruct and NemotronDiffusion-3B Instruct, PIG extends the accuracy-TPF frontier on GSM8K, MATH500, MBPP, HumanEval, and MMLU, when compared to the industry standard Fast-dLLM and measures favorably on LLaDA-8B Instruct against DAPD, KLASS, EB-sampler, and other learned unmasking policies.

title: What Makes a Latent Space Shared? Direct and Recoverable Compatibility in Motion VAEs
abstract: A shared latent space is often assumed to make representations from different schemas directly interchangeable, yet sharing parameters, dimensionality, or a prior does not determine how corresponding instances are expressed in latent coordinates. We show that this assumption conflates recoverable correspondence, direct compatibility, and decoder reuse. In a controlled multi-schema motion VAE on HumanML3D, even identical inputs yield only $5.9$--$17.7\%$ raw Recall@1 and $0.221$--$0.484$ paired-token cosine, despite correspondence being almost perfectly recoverable after linear calibration. Cycle consistency strengthens recoverability but still leaves direct retrieval and token agreement near zero. In contrast, only $64$ paired clips raise raw Recall@1 to $88.4$--$90.3\%$ and token cosine to approximately $0.82$, making most post-hoc alignment unnecessary, although crossed decoding remains substantially worse than native reconstruction. We further find that reducing measured marginal discrepancy does not imply schema invariance. These results show that a shared backbone or prior does not ensure directly compatible latent coordinates, while limited paired correspondence can substantially improve direct compatibility in the tested setting.

title: Ultraviolet Reflected-Light Spectroscopy of Modern Earth Analogs with Starshade Observations
abstract: Characterizing rocky, habitable zone planets in reflected light is a key science objective for future direct imaging missions, and the ultraviolet (UV) is uniquely suited for supporting the characterization of Earth-like atmospheres. The Hartley-Huggins ozone band at $0.25 ~μ\mathrm{m}$ remains detectable at low spectral resolution down to $0.1\%$ PAL $\mathrm{O}_2$, providing a sensitive proxy for oxygen-bearing chemistry even for Proterozoic-like atmospheres where the visible and near-infrared $\mathrm{O}_2$ features become inaccessible. This work uses an end-to-end framework for UV starshade spectroscopy of modern Earth analogs that integrates high-fidelity observation simulation, conservative post-processing, and Bayesian spectral retrieval to quantify ozone detection significance. The framework is applied across 108 simulated scenes spanning a range of planet phase angles, system inclinations, and exozodiacal dust densities. The results establish that robust ozone detection with UV-only, $R=7$ reflected light spectroscopy requires a photometric $\mathrm{SNR} \sim 30$. UV starshade observations with the Habitable Worlds Observatory achieve this threshold within 3-day integrations for solar-type systems at 10 parsecs with inclinations up to $60^\circ$ at favorable phases ($\leq 90^\circ$). Above this SNR threshold, ozone detections are robust to systematic bias from imperfect exozodi calibration within $\sim30\%$, and the median retrieved ozone abundance remains accurate to within one order of magnitude of the true value.

title: Get In, Decide, Prove: A Merchant-Side Readiness Benchmark for Agentic Commerce
abstract: AI agents now browse and buy on people's behalf, and benchmarks measure how well the agents perform. Far less is known about the other side of the transaction: whether a merchant's website lets an agent in, publishes terms precise enough to decide a purchase, and leaves evidence of what was agreed. This paper presents a merchant-side benchmark built on those three questions and reports a pilot of it. The central measurement, decision sufficiency, rates each criterion of a concrete buyer mandate (total cost, cancellation or return terms, service date, variant identity) as determinate, indeterminate, or unknown from the merchant's own published evidence. Readiness scores carry their evidence coverage and missingness bounds; access is reported separately for a declared bot, a declared headless browser, and a user-present browser; and each observed term is mapped to the RAILS admissibility class of the evidence that could support it in a dispute. Four large merchants received the full assessment: three refused the declared profiles at their offer pages, and no mandate could be confirmed as met, because each merchant left a total or a refund term undetermined. An access census of 555 sites of merchants that two payment processors publicly name as clients found the home page unreadable to both declared profiles at 105 sites (18.9%). A declared assessment of 330 merchants, scored by deterministic rules without a rater, found that evidence coverage rather than the score decides who can be ranked: 115 merchants (35%) reached the ranking threshold, rankable profiles scored a median of 89 to 90, and material terms was the one pillar well below the others, because the all-in total was decidable at 18 merchants. The pilot shows that the measurements can be taken; it does not validate them or rank merchants, and the weights and the projected clearing band await validation against outcomes.

title: EPOCH: Coverage-Aware Evolution with Experiential Preference Optimization for LLM-based Automated Heuristic Design
abstract: LLM-based automated heuristic design (AHD) discovers heuristics for combinatorial optimization problems (COPs), where an LLM generates candidates in an evolutionary search. Existing frameworks freeze the generator or fine-tune it on a scalar fitness signal hiding which instances each heuristic covers. Reflection-based frameworks improve heuristics with natural-language feedback, but it stays in the prompt and never reaches the generator's weights. We propose EPOCH, which makes instance coverage the objective of the evolutionary search and fine-tunes the generator to internalize reflection. Parent selection, operator allocation, and stagnation recovery all optimize how well the heuristics jointly cover the training instances, so the search returns a complementary heuristic ensemble. The generator learns from its own search by experiential preference optimization. A teacher LLM returns a natural-language insight on the generated heuristics, and the generator produces new heuristics with this insight. These improvements join the preference pairs for direct preference optimization (DPO). Since DPO only teaches the generator to rank these improvements, a reflective self-distillation (RSD) term makes it more likely to generate them on its own, and the gains accumulate over the long horizon of the search. Across COPs and open-source LLM backbones, EPOCH's heuristic ensembles outperform inference-only and fine-tuned baselines and generalize across problem scales.

title: What Is the Cost of a Handover Interruption? Rethinking 5G Mobility for Aerial Vehicles
abstract: Low-altitude aviation is moving toward large-scale operations increasingly dependent on 5G cellular connectivity. However, 5G mobility remains blind to the operational risk of its decisions: the same interruption may be harmless in cruise over an empty field but critical near obstacles, crowds or other aircraft. Although 5G already provides mechanisms to obtain location, population density, and radio conditions, mobility decisions do not translate this information into an operational risk metric. We propose Risk-Aware Mobility (RAM), which maps predicted communication disruptions to an operational-risk proxy using information staleness, position uncertainty, and operational context, and exposes this risk to existing mobility mechanisms. In a dense São Paulo deployment with 188 licensed 5G sectors, risk-aware handover timing reduces the mean operational-risk proxy by 45\% relative to conventional A3 without degrading serving-link quality. These results motivate shifting 5G mobility from optimizing handover performance to managing the operational risk of mobility decisions. Beyond handover timing, this perspective raises a broader question: which cells should serve aerial operations when connectivity is evaluated by operational risk rather than radio performance alone?

title: Robustly Reliable Learning for Regression
abstract: We introduce the problem of robustly reliable learning for the regression setting in adversarial environments. Given a test point $x_{test}$, a training dataset $S$ of $n$ data points, a corruption budget $b \ll n$, and a real-valued hypothesis class $\mathcal H$, our goal is to output the optimal prediction range $I^*_{x_{test}}(S, b)$, such that any $L$-Lipschitz predictor consistent with all but at most $b$ points in $S$ must predict a value $h(x_{test}) \in I$. We then instantiate the analysis for $L$-Lipschitz hypothesis classes, a natural and widely studied class in the regression setting, focusing on two key scenarios. First, for the restricted case where the corrupted dataset is guaranteed to be $L$-Lipschitz consistent, we propose a simple and efficient $b^{th}$-best heuristic algorithm and prove its correctness in computing the tightest possible range $I^*_{x_{test}}(S, b)$. We then establish its computational complexity of $O(n)$ and show that it is computationally optimal in this scenario. Building on this foundation, we address the general scenario where the dataset $S$ is no longer $L$-Lipschitz consistent. We demonstrate that computing the optimal range in this setting reduces to analyzing a violation graph, which models the pairwise $L$-Lipschitz violations among data points. By leveraging the structural properties of this graph's kernel, we propose a Fixed-Parameter Tractable (FPT) algorithm that computes the exact optimal range in $O(n^2 + b^4)$ time. Furthermore, under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), we establish a computational lower bound of $Ω(n^{2 - o(1)})$, proving that our algorithm is computationally optimal. Finally, we discuss open directions for the problem of robustly reliable learning for regression.

title: Mitigating Black-Box Score-Based Query Attacks via Gradient Confusion
abstract: Score-based black-box adversarial attacks pose a serious threat to deployed machine learning systems by exploiting repeated model queries to craft adversarial examples, requiring neither access to model parameters nor architecture. Existing defenses predominantly rely on stochastic output perturbations, which fail to prevent determined attackers from recovering stable gradient estimates by increasing query budgets or averaging over randomness. In this work, we propose the Gradient Confusion Defense (GCD), a retraining-free, deterministic test-time wrapper that actively shapes the probability vector returned to querying adversaries. By solving a constrained optimization problem grounded in the model's Jacobian, GCD aligns the exposed logit-gradient with a target confusion direction that is maximally misaligned with the true adversarial loss gradient---increasing the query complexity of attacks without sacrificing predictive utility or top-1 accuracy. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating that GCD provably slows gradient-estimation-based attacks and induces systematic accept/reject errors in random search-based attacks, with the confusion effect amplifying as the fraction of defended queries increases. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across multiple architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16) and four state-of-the-art attacks confirm these predictions: GCD achieves state-of-the-art robustness, while incurring zero clean accuracy degradation. %Crucially, unlike randomization-based defenses, GCD's deterministic structure provides resilience against adaptive attacks that exploit stochasticity, making it well-suited for security-critical deployment settings.

title: Variable Input Masked Autoencoders for Wrist-Worn Accelerometry
abstract: Large-scale repositories of wearable sensor data have enabled the development of foundation models for human activities and behavior. However, existing models are pretrained using fixed input durations and sampling rates, despite substantial heterogeneity in recording conditions, downstream tasks, and deployment constraints. We introduce VarMAE, a variable input masked autoencoder that learns a single representation across sampling rates and temporal contexts. During pretraining we construct two views of the same signal: a long duration high frequency view, and a short duration lower frequency view, obtained via random cropping and downsampling. We perform masked reconstruction within each view and introduce a cross-resolution masked reconstruction objective that uses visible tokens from the long view to predict masked tokens from the short view. Cropping and downsampling impose complementary information bottlenecks, encouraging the model to learn representations that remain effective across input durations and sampling rate changes. We pretrain VarMAE on the large-scale NHANES dataset, producing a single pretrained encoder matching or outperforming controlled foundation model baselines on eight benchmark datasets. With only 3.82M parameters, VarMAE is parameter efficient and shows that a single foundation model can achieve broad transfer capabilities across sensing configurations.

title: Measure Neural Mappings
abstract: We introduce and define measure neural mappings (MNMs), which combine measure-dependent neural transport with ensemble consistency for learning operators on probability measures. Ensemble consistency requires outputs from growing ensembles sampled from an input law to converge to the specified population output in probability. We establish quantitative continuum limits for attention on noncompact laws under strong sub-Gaussian and tail-integrability assumptions. These laws accommodate unbounded state spaces in scientific machine learning, including Bayesian inference and uncertainty quantification. For fixed self-attention transformers, the expected output Wasserstein error is bounded by the empirical input Wasserstein error plus an additional $N^{-1/2}$ attention term. These self-attention transformers are MNMs under the stated assumptions: pre-norm architectures follow from compact stability after normalization, while post-norm architectures are covered under the stated tail conditions. We prove corresponding cross-attention estimates and extend the results to multihead attention and grouped transformer evaluation, with convergence as the group size grows. For Set Transformers viewed as measure-to-vector mappings, we obtain an $N^{-1/2}$ bound on the expected Euclidean output error under the stated assumptions. Experiments on seven operators in dimensions $d=1,2,3,5,10$ support the predicted particle-count dependence, using one-dimensional Wasserstein computations and Sinkhorn approximations in higher dimensions. The observed Wasserstein and sliced Wasserstein decay rates are close to their respective theoretical sampling benchmarks.

title: Direct Electromechanical Actuation of the Shift Drum in Non-Synchronized Motorcycle Transmissions: From Actuator Sizing and Electronics Design to Closed-Loop Position Control
abstract: This thesis presents the direct electromechanical actuation of the shift drum in a non-synchronized motorcycle transmission. A DC motor drives the shift drum through a self-locking worm gear, so the entire foot shift mechanism is eliminated. As a reference, 84 manual gear changes of a large-displacement series-production motorcycle were measured on a chassis dynamometer; the mean shift time is 80 ms for upshifts and 92 ms for downshifts. The system design covers the complete chain from the mechanics to the software. The actuator motor is sized from inertia, friction and gear ratio. A dedicated shift controller is developed with supply filtering, signal conditioning for the position sensor and the incremental encoder, an H-bridge motor driver and a custom circuit board based on a SAMD21 microcontroller. The embedded firmware implements position control of the shift drum with a proportional controller, without inner speed or current loops. On a gearbox test rig, a gear change is completed in less than 80 ms without overshoot in a single measurement, below the mean of the manual reference shifts. The analysis reveals a trade-off in the choice of the worm gear ratio: at a ratio of 30, about 93% of the motor torque is needed to accelerate the motor shaft and the worm. A ratio of about 8 halves the required torque, but the worm gear then loses its self-locking. The measured shift times are published as an open dataset.

title: Beyond periodicity: Fourier methods for optimal control
abstract: Fourier-based spectral methods provide compact global approximations, permit simple differentiation and integration, and achieve spectral convergence for smooth periodic functions. Their use in finite-horizon optimal control problems (OCPs) is nevertheless challenged by the generally nonperiodic state and control trajectories: endpoint mismatch induces artificial discontinuities and can destroy spectral convergence. Leveraging Eckhoff-type endpoint-correction techniques, we develop a Fourier-based spectral framework for OCPs with possibly nonlinear dynamics and constraints. The correction improves convergence without enlarging the set of decision variables, yielding an efficient finite-dimensional numerical method. Furthermore, we formulate selected dynamics and obstacle-avoidance constraints through Sobolev residual bounds, which incorporate information about the residuals over the entire time horizon and improve constraint satisfaction. Numerical experiments on benchmark problems demonstrate competitive computational performance, lower residual errors, and improved solution accuracy.

title: Cross-Market Meta-Learning for Electricity Price Forecasting
abstract: Day-ahead (DA) electricity price forecasting is usually posed per market, with a separate model fitted to each grid's own history. This caps accuracy: statistical and tree-based baselines saturate, while higher-capacity sequence models need more training data than a single market's few years of hourly prices can supply. Such methods also treat each node as an independent series, discarding the spatial dependencies induced by network topology and congestion. Because price formation across independent system operators (ISOs) is driven by shared physics and largely common market design, we instead treat cross-market history as a pretraining corpus. We present MetaGrid, a topology-aware transformer, meta-trained across markets so that a single zone-count-independent parameter set adapts to an unseen grid. On a leak-free benchmark of five U.S. ISOs, where every model receives the same prices, DA load forecasts and calendar features, MetaGrid attains the lowest average MAE, improving on the best baseline by 3.1\% and on the same architecture trained from scratch by 7.7\%.

title: Hanslick's Musical Formalism as a Mathematical Structure - Examining meaning in Music through the Lens of Category Theory
abstract: We investigate Eduard Hanslicks formalist aesthetics through the prism of Category Theory

title: A characterization of central extensions relative to n-nilpotent objects
abstract: We characterize the central extensions, in the sense of the categorical theory of central extensions of Janelidze and Kelly, relative to the Birkhoff subcategory of $n$-nilpotent objects of a semi-abelian and algebraically coherent category. An extension $f \colon A \to B$ with kernel $K$ turns out to be central precisely when the iterated Huq commutator $[A,[A,\dots,[A,K]\dots]]$, with $n$ occurrences of $A$, vanishes. For $n=2$ this condition reads $[A,[K,A]] = 0$, that is, $[K,A]$ is a central subobject of $A$. In the special case of groups this description was obtained by Everaert and the first author. The present proof is categorical, and applies in particular to Lie algebras, to crossed modules, to cocommutative Hopf algebras over a field, and to any category of interest.

title: Intermittency in the Multiphase ISM --- II. Non-Gaussian Dust Polarization and Foreground Variance
abstract: Interstellar turbulence produces non-Gaussian polarized Galactic dust emission whose higher-order statistics depend on thermal phase and turbulent forcing. We synthesize optically thin dust polarization from three thermally multiphase diffuse interstellar medium (ISM) simulations with compressive, mixed, and solenoidal forcing. We characterize the resulting non-Gaussian structure in the warm, unstable, and cold phases using $E$- and $B$-mode spectra, one-point distributions, scale-dependent increments, and Minkowski functionals. Both $E$ and $B$ modes are intermittent. Warm-phase emission remains closest to Gaussian, whereas cold gas shows flatter intermediate-scale spectra, broader non-Gaussian tails, and the strongest departures from Gaussian morphology. Compressive forcing generally produces the strongest projected intermittency, particularly in the cold phase and total emission, while mixed and solenoidal forcing show weaker signatures. These higher-order structures also enhance spatial fluctuations in polarized dust power: Gaussian fields matched to the same two-point covariance underestimate the region-to-region scatter by factors of up to $\sim2.6$. Our results show that thermal phase and turbulent forcing regulate not only the mean polarized dust spectrum but also the field-to-field distribution of foreground power, with implications for modeling Galactic foreground in CMB polarization measurements.

title: Learning to Play: Reinforcement Learning and Games
abstract: Amazing breakthroughs in reinforcement learning have taken place. Computers teach themselves to play Chess and Go and beat world champions. There is talk about expanding application areas towards general artificial intelligence (AI). The breakthroughs in Backgammon, Checkers, Chess, Atari, Go, Poker, and StarCraft have shown that we can build machines that exhibit intelligent game playing of the highest level. These successes have been widely publicized in the media, and inspire AI entrepreneurs and scientists alike. Reinforcement learning in games has become a mainstream AI research topic. It is a broad topic, and the successes build on a range of diverse techniques, from exact planning algorithms, to adaptive sampling, deep function approximation, and ingenious self-play methods. Perhaps because of the breadth of these technologies, or because of the recency of the breakthroughs, there are few books that explain these methods in depth. This book covers all methods in one comprehensive volume, explaining the latest research, bringing you as close as possible to working implementations, with many references to the original research papers. The programming examples in this book are in Python, the language in which most current reinforcement learning research is conducted. We help you to get started with machine learning frameworks such as Gym, TensorFlow, and Keras, and provide exercises to help understand how AI is learning to play.

title: A Method for Exact Enforcement of Boundary Conditions on General Curved Triangular Domains: Algorithm and Application to Scientific Machine Learning
abstract: We present a method for enforcing exactly Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin conditions on general triangular domains with arbitrarily curved boundaries. The algorithmic constructions developed here complements those in a previous work for general quadrilateral domains. Our method combines (i) the exact mapping between a general curved triangular domain and the standard triangle, (ii) TFC constrained expressions, and (iii) Barnhill transfinite interpolations, to provide explicit closed-form trial ansatze that mathematically satisfy the imposed boundary conditions exactly. Corner compatibility induced by the boundary conditions is pivotal, and enforcing exactly the imposed boundary conditions hinges on the exact enforcement of the induced compatibility constraints. The corner compatibility associated with the acute vertices of the standard triangle and the coupling between gradient components when the hypotenuse corresponds to a Neumann/Robin boundary pose particular challenges. Two strategies are critical to resolving these issues, by reformulating conditional corner constraints into equivalent unconditional forms and by introducing a separate TFC-style auxiliary edge construction together with an associated linear solve on the hypotenuse. We analyze the corner compatibility constraints and present formulations for the general form of functions that exactly satisfy the imposed Dirichlet, Neumann, or Robin conditions on curved triangular domains. The proposed method has been implemented using extreme learning machine type randomized neural networks for solving PDE problems. We present ample numerical experiments with linear/nonlinear PDE problems on a variety of domains with complex boundary geometries. Numerical results show that the current method has enforced the Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin conditions on curved domain boundaries to the machine precision.

title: Towards a Characterization of Matrix Monotonicity via Radial Convexity
abstract: The theory of matrix monotone functions of finite degree depends subtly on the matrix size. Motivated by this phenomenon, we introduce radial convexity of metrics with respect to matrix orders on the cone of positive definite matrices. We establish radial convexity of several natural metrics with respect to the Loewner order and then focus on the Frobenius norm. Using the Daleckii-Krein formula, we relate radial convexity to the positivity of the Hadamard square of the corresponding Loewner matrix. This leads us to conjecture that radial convexity of order $n$ is equivalent to matrix monotonicity of degree $n$, and we prove this equivalence in degree $2$. We further provide evidence in higher dimensions, obtain a characterization in degree $3$, and discuss extensions of our results to arbitrary unitarily invariant norms.

title: The rational homology of independence complexes of Kneser graphs on triples
abstract: The independence complex of the Kneser graph $\KG(n,k)$ is the simplicial complex of pairwise intersecting families of $n$-subsets of $[2n+k]$; equivalently, it is a Vietoris--Rips complex of the $n$-subsets of $[2n+k]$ under the symmetric-difference metric. Feng and Wang asked whether, for $n=3$, its reduced homology is nontrivial only in dimensions $6$ and $9$, and conjectured the rank in dimension $9$. We answer the question affirmatively over the rationals and determine all the associated Betti numbers. For every $k\ge0$, the only nonzero reduced Betti numbers using rationals of $\Ind(\KG(3,k))$ are \[ β_6=\binom{k+5}{7}+29\binom{k+6}{7} \qquad\text{and}\qquad β_9=\binom{k+6}{6}. \] The proof uses an inductive decomposition based on a simplicial retraction and Barmak's star clusters, Dowker duality together with Jonsson's computation of the homology of complexes of graphs with bounded covering number, and a relative Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence which reduces the problem to the six-element sets.

title: A Controlled Null Result for Per-Gate Riemannian Optimization in VQE
abstract: Parametrized gates in a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) live on a product of unitary groups, which makes Riemannian optimization a natural candidate for improving training. We test this candidate in the clean per-gate setting: each single-qubit gate is optimized directly on U (2) and compared with Adam on an unconstrained Euler-angle chart representing the same physical gate, initialized from the same unitaries and tuned with a separate learning-rate sweep. On a validated hydrogen-chain benchmark, we find no measurable practical advantage from the Riemannian machinery. The direct manifold optimizer and the Euler-coordinate baseline are interleaved in final error and success rate; the classical coordinate baseline is not slower in iterations on the successful cells; and the choices of Riemannian metric, retraction, and momentum vector transport do not change the conclusion. We also identify four failure modes that can manufacture an apparent positive result: a trivial product-state benchmark, a projected-matrix Adam baseline that discards most of its own step, a non-unitary inherited Cayley retraction that lets the reported energy pass below the variational minimum, and a learning-rate grid whose optimum sits at its boundary. Each failure mode produced a plausible multi-seed result in our own workflow before being caught. The practical output of this paper is therefore a controlled null result and a validation checklist for VQE optimizer comparisons.

title: Model-Based Cortisol Replacement Strategies for Patients With Adrenal Insufficiency
abstract: Cortisol is an essential hormone secreted by the adrenal glands. Abnormally low level of cortisol is referred to as adrenal insufficiency. This paper focuses on devising treatment strategies for patients suffering from adrenal insufficiency using a model-based approach. Two conditions of adrenal insufficiency are analysed. They are hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) and adrenal gland disorders. The hypothalamus, pituitary, and adrenal glands constitute the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which regulates stress and maintains physiological homeostasis through cortisol secretion. A comparative analysis of the existing mathematical models of the HPA axis is conducted. Based on this analysis, a novel model of the HPA axis is proposed that incorporates endogenous circadian rhythm. This proposed model is used to design effective cortisol replacement strategies. In addition, hydrocortisone replacement therapies are proposed and validated with clinical data from the literature. The results presented in this paper are applicable to patient-specific treatment strategies for individuals with adrenal insufficiency.

title: JustOPD: On-Policy Distillation from Autoregressive to Diffusion Language Models
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach for large language models (LLMs) that enables a student model to learn a teacher model's distribution from sequences sampled from the student's own policy. Despite its promising capability, OPD for diffusion language models (DLMs) remains underexplored and existing studies primarily focuses on DLM-to-DLM distillation. The limited availability of strong teacher DLMs and the flexible generation order of DLMs impose additional technical challenges as well. However, it remains unclear how to effectively distill knowledge from a strong autoregressive language model (ARM) into a weaker DLM, given the mismatch between the left-to-right decoding of ARMs and the flexible decoding order of DLMs. Inspired by Ni et al. (2026), we propose JustOPD, an ARM-to-DLM on-policy distillation method that uses autoregressive rollouts during training to align the student's generation process with the ARM teacher's left-to-right decoding. This alignment enables effective distillation from ARM teachers while preserving the DLM's flexible generation-order capability at inference time. Experiments using Qwen3-14B as the teacher and Dream-7B as the student demonstrate that JustOPD consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance over the base DLM across multiple divergence choices.

title: Fresnel scattering for open waveguide networks
abstract: This paper concerns the Helmholtz scattering problem for open waveguide networks, extending the analysis from [arXiv:2302.04353, arXiv:2310.05816, arXiv:2401.04674] to plane-wave incident data. We first reduce the problem to a Fredholm second-kind integral equation on an infinite interface. This produces an integral representation of the solution to the original scattering problem, which is then used to obtain detailed asymptotic estimates of the solution at infinity. To leading order and away from the waveguides, the scattered field is itself a plane wave. Its amplitude and phase shift exhibit a jump across a critical polar angle depending on the direction of the incident plane-wave. Our estimates also imply that the scattered field is outgoing in a weak sense, allowing us to establish a uniqueness result. We conclude by calculating the waveguide-mode contributions to the scattered field in a perturbative regime.

title: Learning to Detect Shifts in Unstructured Data Streams via Monitoring-by-Betting
abstract: Continuous monitoring of generative AI systems requires detecting distribution shifts in the unstructured data they ingest and generate. Existing monitoring methods typically control false alarms by requiring the discrepancy measure used to detect shifts to be *pre-specified*. However, for unstructured data, pre-specification creates a sensitivity--breadth trade-off: a narrowly defined measure is sensitive to the anticipated shift but may miss unexpected changes, whereas a broadly defined measure may detect a wider range of shifts but with reduced sensitivity. Although adaptively hypothesizing the shift direction can overcome this limitation, such data-dependent adaptation generally invalidates conventional false-alarm guarantees. We reconcile adaptivity with statistical validity through testing-by-betting, reframing sequential changepoint detection as a betting game in which the bettor continually updates its hypothesized shift direction, or witness function, as new observations arrive. We introduce *asymptotic e-detectors*, which approximate the pre-change distribution using a calibration set of size $m$, and prove that they asymptotically control the average run length to a false alarm as $m$ increases. Empirically, calibration sets as small as $m=30$ provide effective control. We then develop adaptive monitoring strategies ranging from black-box bettors that learn from embeddings to interpretable bettors based on LLM-proposed concepts. Across three real-world datasets, including data from a clinical AI scribe deployment, adaptive monitors detect shifts faster than fixed monitors at the same false-alarm level. Further, when the true shifts are sparse and interpretable, LLM-concept monitors provide the fastest and most interpretable detection, while also guiding root-cause diagnosis for complex shifts.

title: Steiner Minimal Trees in the Gromov--Hausdorff Space and in Gromov--Hausdorff Clouds
abstract: We prove the existence of Steiner minimal trees spanning a finite family of metric spaces in two cases of the Gromov--Hausdorff theory. In the compact Gromov--Hausdorff space $\mathcal{M}$, every finite family of nonempty compact metric spaces is spanned by a shortest Steiner minimal tree whose Steiner vertices are again nonempty compact metric spaces. In a fixed Gromov--Hausdorff cloud $\mathcal{C}$, every finite family of proper, isometrically cobounded spaces admits a finite-length Steiner minimal tree all of whose vertices remain in $\mathcal{C}$. The compact case uses compact replacement through distance profiles and the Hausdorff hyperspace, and the cloud case uses pointed ultralimits.

title: Generalizable field of view extension for diffusion MRI via conditional flow matching
abstract: Incomplete field-of-view (FOV) diffusion MRI (dMRI) acquisitions compromise whole-brain white matter analysis by excluding brain regions from tractography and connectivity studies. While deep generative models for dMRI FOV extension have been proposed, their generalizability remains limited by the acquisition-dependent nature of dMRI, where signal intensity varies with b-value, gradient direction, and scanner protocol, and the inherent 4D complexity of the data, making it difficult to train models that transfer across sites or acquisition schemes without retraining. We propose a flow-matching generative model that extends the dMRI FOV in both the superior and inferior directions by predicting apparent diffusion coefficients (ADC) in six directions, conditioned on the two nearest acquired slices and the full-FOV T1w image to enforce both local diffusion continuity and anatomical consistency. The ADC representation decouples the model from acquisition-specific b-values and gradient directions, providing a middle-ground across protocols. The model was trained on 3,103 subjects (5,105 sessions) across five different datasets spanning diverse acquisition schemes (b = 500 and 1000 s/mm$^2$; 21--192 gradient directions), four single-shell (b = 1000) and one multi-shell (b = 500/1000). Evaluated on 299 subjects across five independent datasets spanning b = 750--1500 s/mm$^2$ and 32--90 gradient directions, with single- and multi-shell schemes unseen during training, the proposed method achieves significantly improved bundle Dice score on downstream tractography (p < 0.01).

title: Evaluating Temporal Reasoning in Large Language Models: Event Temporal Relation Extraction with Allen's Interval Algebra, Logical Consistency, and Relative Time in Narratives
abstract: Understanding a narrative means knowing how every event relates in time to every other, yet large language models (LLMs) are mostly tested on isolated event pairs or coarse labels. We ask five LLMs to reconstruct the complete network of Allen's 13 interval relations for 360 English narratives whose events are placed relative to one another rather than by dates, and evaluate the outputs under a pre-registered protocol for agreement with our gold annotations, converse consistency and logical satisfiability. End to end, the best model clearly beats trivial baselines on macro-F1, our primary metric, yet under our pre-registered parser no model matches the accuracy of always answering "before", which the skewed labels inflate. Most of that accuracy gap is a parsing artifact: formatting errors in large matrices cost whole rows, and a post hoc parser that recovers the determined cells of malformed rows raises coverage from 0.60 to 0.84 and closes the gap to the baseline for the best model. On the cells they do answer, models recover precedence and containment but rarely overlap, and they fail most on flashbacks, where both the narration and the event list present the later event first. Logical consistency varies widely yet says little about agreement with gold: enforcing it raises accuracy mainly by filling empty cells, and is beaten there by the trivial control of guessing the majority label. Reliable structured output and robust handling of relative time are prerequisites for temporal reasoning over whole narratives.

title: Overlap, Not Moments: Finite-Sample Theory for Bridge Sampling
abstract: Bridge sampling estimates of marginal likelihoods are routinely reported with a delta-method Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE). Existing theory is asymptotic and cannot say whether a given run is long enough to trust the estimate or its MCSE. We give finite-sample answers. The optimal bridge estimator fits a logistic regression that separates posterior from proposal draws, and its accuracy is governed by their overlap, within a factor of two of the classification's Bayes error. Because the estimating function is a sum of bounded terms, no moment conditions are needed, and all bounds hold uniformly over targets, proposals and dimensions. A number of draws inversely proportional to the overlap suffices and is necessary in the worst case, paralleling the exponential-in-Kullback--Leibler requirement of importance sampling. A Berry--Esseen bound with an explicit constant holds at the optimal rate, and the MCSE is accurate once the effective overlap is large; it is estimated at no cost. For Markov chain draws, the required sample size grows in proportion to the sampler's relaxation time, unavoidably in the worst case. The estimated bridge, the fixed-point iteration and the fitted proposal matter only at second order, and we give free diagnostics for sampler failure and misestimated autocorrelation.

title: Event-Centric Earthquake Monitoring with a Multi-Station Transformer
abstract: Earthquake catalogs underpin studies such as fault structure, earthquake processes and seismic hazard, and their value depends on being both complete and reliable. Machine learning has improved individual tasks of earthquake monitoring, but processing stations independently discards the consistency of arrivals across the network, and running tasks in sequence fragments the information describing each earthquake. We present EQNet2, a geometry-aware multi-station Transformer that jointly predicts phase arrivals, first-motion polarities, source location and magnitude, and the association of arrivals into events. On a Northern California test dataset and on continuous waveforms from Ridgecrest and the San Francisco Bay Area, EQNet2 recovers more weak arrivals, produces fewer false detections, and associates more picks into located events. Its learned attention links information across stations along time--distance patterns consistent with seismic moveout. As seismic networks grow denser, exploiting multi-station coherence and event-centric prediction offers a path to more complete and reliable catalogs.

title: Purely non-free actions on Riemann surfaces
abstract: A group of conformal automorphisms of a Riemann surface is said to act purely non-free, or to produce a gpnf-action, if each of its finite-order elements has fixed points. It is known that every finite group admits a gpnf-action on a suitable closed Riemann surface of genus at least two. If $G$ is an infinite countable group, and $X$ is an infinite-type orientable surface, without planar ends and whose space of ends is self-similar, then we observe that there is a Riemann surface structure on $X$ admitting a gpnf-action by $G$. We obtain upper bounds for those finite groups producing a gpnf-action on a closed Riemann surface of genus $g \geq 2$. If $G$ is a finite group, then its purely non-free genus $σ^{pnf}_{hyp}(G)$ is the minimum genus of at least two of a closed Riemann surface admitting a gpnf-action by $G$. This parameter is already known for cyclic, abelian non-cyclic groups, ${\mathcal A}_{4}$, ${\mathcal A}_{5}$ and ${\mathfrak S}_{4}$. For general $G$, we provide the value of $σ^{pnf}_{hyp}(G)$, correcting a previous statement on this value. In particular, we observe that every genus is the purely non-free genus of some group. As an application, we describe the minimal purely non-free actions for the family of metacyclic groups $G^{0}_{s}(n)=\langle x,y: x^{n}=y^{2}=1, yxy=x^{s}\rangle,$ where $n \geq 3$ and $2 \leq s \leq n-1$ is such that $s^{2} \equiv 1 \mod(n)$.

title: Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions
abstract: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94 GB/s on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In Node 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6x compared with Node 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.

title: Cross-View Time-Frequency Diffusion for Extreme-Aware Time-Series Generation
abstract: Generating realistic time-series requires faithfully reproducing rare but high-impact extreme events. Existing approaches often rely on specialized representations or extreme-focused training objectives, which may restrict the diversity of captured extremes or compromise overall distributional fidelity. We propose Cross-View Time-Frequency Diffusion (CrossTF), a framework that exploits discrepancies between time- and frequency-view denoisers for extreme-aware time-series generation. Our key empirical finding is extreme-sensitive cross-view asymmetry: moving along the direction connecting the two views' clean-sample estimates substantially changes extreme fidelity while having limited effects on overall generation quality. We further identify a late-stage cross-view window in which this discrepancy stabilizes and cross-view adjustments have a particularly strong effect on extreme fidelity. These findings motivate a staged optimization strategy in CrossTF: after training and freezing both denoisers, it only needs to learn step-specific fusion parameters within this window using an Extreme Value Theory-based objective under an energy-distance constraint. This formulation supports interpolation between and extrapolation beyond the view-specific estimates while limiting degradation in overall generation quality. Extensive experiments on seven real-world datasets against 11 baselines show that CrossTF improves extreme fidelity by 26.1% and overall performance by 7.4% relative to the strongest baselines. These results highlight cross-view discrepancy as an effective basis for low-dimensional optimization in extreme-aware time-series generation.

title: Group gradings, graded identities and central polynomials of algebras with almost polynomial $δ$-growth
abstract: The finite-dimensional $F$-algebras $D=F(e_{11}+e_{33})+Fe_{22}+Fe_{12}+Fe_{13}+Fe_{23} \subseteq UT_3$ and $D_0=Fe_{22}+Fe_{33}+Fe_{12}+Fe_{13}+Fe_{14}+Fe_{23}+Fe_{24}+Fe_{34} \subseteq UT_4$ occupy a distinguished position in the theory of central polynomials. Together with the infinite-dimensional Grassmann algebra, these algebras generate the only varieties of almost polynomial growth of proper central codimensions. We determine finite generating sets for their $T$-spaces of central polynomials and compute their central and proper central codimensions. We also prove that every group grading on $D_0$ is isomorphic to an elementary grading and determine the identities and codimensions associated with all its $\mathbb{Z}_2$-gradings.

title: Position: Beyond Training Time, Test-Time Coordination is Essential for Cooperative MARL
abstract: We argue that cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) should treat test-time coordination as part of the problem definition rather than a deployment artifact. Our focus is on long-horizon, centrally monitored cooperative systems such as warehouse robotics, automated storage-and-retrieval systems, and cloud-resource scheduling, where teams share a reward, operate under shifting objectives, and already run with global telemetry at deployment. The dominant paradigm in this regime, centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), uses global information only during training and provides no coordination channel at execution. This is sufficient when agents are weakly coupled or the environment is stationary, but it fails when the team must realign after conditions change. The limitation is structural rather than algorithmic, and more training cannot add a channel that does not exist at execution time. We call this the recoverability gap. To address it, we name the underexplored design space of intermittent test-time coordination as centralized training with mixed execution (CTME), in which a coordinator observes global state and emits high-level signals while agents act locally. CTME is not a particular learning algorithm, but a cooperative MARL problem setting that makes test-time information structure explicit. It specifies team-level information, high-level signals, and update frequency after training, with CTDE recovered as a limit case. We do not argue that CTDE is obsolete. We argue that removing the test-time channel is a modeling choice, not a necessity, and the wrong default when global telemetry is available and teams must recover from drift.

title: Agency as a New Organizing Abstraction for Computer Science
abstract: Advances in large-scale machine learning have enabled agentic AI systems: persistent, autonomous computational entities that pursue goals, initiate actions, and interact with open environments. These systems are often framed as applications of foundation models. We argue that this framing is incomplete: agency is also a candidate new organizing abstraction for computer science. What is new is not the concept of an agent, nor runtime policy generation per se, but its general-purpose, open-ended form, in which systems can synthesize courses of action from goals, observations, and memory, over tools and environments for which no complete task-specific model was specified in advance. Thus agency becomes a systems-level abstraction as well as an AI modeling concept. Where the process abstraction organizes computation around executing programs, agency organizes it around pursuing goals under bounded resources: a process executes a program; an agent pursues a goal. From this perspective, the recurring failures of deployed agentic systems (runaway resource consumption, behavior redirected by adversarial content, opaque continuous operation) are symptoms of structural abstraction gaps, not isolated engineering defects. We examine these gaps across six dimensions (execution, interfaces, correctness, oversight, coordination, and persistence) and argue that closing them requires coordinated advances in systems,

title: On the generators of separable unital C*-algebras
abstract: Let $A$ be a separable unital $\mathrm C^*$-algebra with nonempty tracial state space and strict comparison by ordinary tracial states. If $\mathcal Z$ embeds unitally into $A$, then $A$ is singly generated. In particular, every simple separable unital $\mathrm C^*$-algebra $A$ with $\mathrm T(A)\ne\varnothing$ and strict comparison is singly generated.

title: Bottlenecked semantic compression by representation reconstruction
abstract: Vision Transformers incur high computational costs when processing long visual token sequences. Existing reduction methods typically rank tokens independently and discard those deemed unimportant or redundant. We propose a reconstruction-guided framework for visual token condensation (ReConV), which summarizes the complete visual sequence with a compact Summary Bank (SMB) and retains tokens whose information is not adequately captured by the SMB, as indicated by their reconstruction residuals. At each compression layer, a lightweight position-conditioned decoder reconstructs the current tokens, leaving shared information compressed in the SMB while explicitly preserving poorly reconstructed details. Experiments on image classification and multimodal understanding demonstrate favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs: ReConV surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48\% fewer GMACs on ImageNet and enables reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference. Code is available at TokenDrop.

title: A complete forward projection algorithm through cylindrical and spherical refractive windows
abstract: Cylindrical or spherical windows often appear in experiments and real applications. Measuring through those windows requires projecting 3D points to pixels, which is different to compute due to refraction. A point may have multiple projected images but cannot be efficiently determine with the existing projection algorithms. Using the ray's conserved momenta, we reduce this projection to closed-form equations with a concave structure. As a result, we can successfully determine whether a 3D point has a single projection or multiple and compute those locations. In simulations, with one single search, we can recover images that iterative methods miss even with many restarts. A wand calibration based on it can reach the precision limit set by image noise, enabling accurate 3D particle tracking in a swirling flow through cylinder windows. This algorithm shows how to predict visibility and multiple images through curved windows, shedding light for 3D pipe flow measurements, accurate underwater reconstruction, and many real applications.

title: Simulation and Deep Learning Inversion for Full-sky Energetic Neutral Atom Imaging at the Heliospheric Boundary
abstract: The distribution of energetic neutral atom (ENA) differential flux density at the heliospheric boundary is the key to revealing the interaction mechanism between the solar wind and the interstellar medium. The Helios ENA Rapid Mapper (HERMA) is a pre-research project for a new ENA detection concept and technical principle, which is designed to provide technical support for refined detection with its advantages of wide energy range coverage and high spatial resolution. To verify the high spatiotemporal resolution rapid imaging capability of the HERMA, this study restored the particle response characteristics of the HERMA (spatial modulation grid + 256-pixel linear array silicon detector) based on Geant4 simulation, and we compared the performance of the traditional inversion algorithm with the convolutional neural network (CNN) inversion algorithm using INCA data as the benchmark. The results show that under different sampling times, the source distribution inverted by the CNN algorithm has a higher degree of agreement with the ideally expected distribution, and the CNN algorithm exhibits better stability and accuracy than the traditional algorithm under the conditions of low signal-to-noise ratio and short staring time. This study provides core technical support for the engineering verification and on-orbit application of the HERMA instrument, fills the technical gap in wide-energy-range and high-resolution ENA detection, and helps to deepen the research on the interaction mechanism between the solar wind and the interstellar medium at the heliospheric boundary.

title: Henrietta Leavitt's classical Cepheid relation
abstract: The Leavitt & Pickering (1912) mean period-magnitude relation for SMC Cepheids exhibits correlated residuals relative to modern Gaia $B_G$ and Johnson $V$ photometry ($r_{δV/δL12}\approx0.76$). Therefore dispersion inherent to Leavitt's photographic photometry relation is not solely random scatter ($σ_{L12,B_G,V}=0.22\pm0.03,0.25\pm0.04,0.20\pm0^{m}.03$), and is potentially consistent with the partial encoding of combined effects from the elongated SMC, classical Cepheid instability strip, differential reddening, etc. OGLE data indicate that $\gtrsim870$ SMC variables identified by Leavitt (1908, Table 2) are classical Cepheids ($\gtrsim 90$ %), and the preliminary unphased Table 2 photometry likewise features correlated residuals relative to contemporary observations ($r_{δB_G/δL08-T2}\approx0.54$). Table 6 data in Leavitt (1908, $n=16$) define a highly linear Leavitt law over an extensive baseline ($r\approx-0.98$), but constitute a smaller sample than the later 1912 work ($n=25$).

title: Dynamic Run-Out Pricing for Perishable Goods
abstract: I study a dynamic pricing problem in which a seller with limited inventory must sequentially price a perishable product for arriving customers with heterogeneous valuations. The key difficulty lies in balancing immediate sales against future opportunities under capacity constraints and stochastic customer valuations. I propose a simple, interpretable, and asymptotically optimal dynamic pricing algorithm, called Dynamic Run-Out Pricing (DROP), that adjusts prices in real time based on current inventory and anticipated future demand. Under the assumption that customers' valuations follow bounded or exponential distributions, our theoretical results show that DROP's expected revenue converges to the optimal revenue as market size grows. Unlike traditional notions of near-optimality, where the ratio of the algorithm's revenue to the optimal revenue converges to 1, I show that the absolute difference between the two revenues converges to 0 as the market size increases, underscoring the algorithm's effectiveness. Furthermore, I extend our analysis to heavy-tailed valuation distributions, specifically the Pareto distribution, where standard run-out heuristics severely underprice inventory by ignoring the value of waiting for extreme valuations. To correct this, I introduce the Tail-Aware DROP (TA-DROP) heuristic, which intentionally inflates prices to protect inventory, and I prove that it restores asymptotic optimality with a strict polynomial convergence rate.

title: High-Resolution X-ray Spectro-Microscopy of Au Microcrystallites
abstract: Understanding the functionalities of heterogeneous catalysts requires high-resolution nanoscale chemical imaging tools. X-ray spectro-ptychography offers this capability by enabling X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) based amplitude and phase contrasts imaging with high spatial resolution. However, such demonstrations at energies above 10 keV, such as the Au L-edges, remain limited due to weak X-ray absorption cross-sections and correspondingly, low signal levels. Here, multimodal spectro-microscopy has been performed on Au microcrystallites that host both conventional face-centered cubic (fcc) and unconventional non-cubic lattices, particularly important for catalysis. Amplitude and phase contrasts across the $\mathrm{L}_3$ edge are resolved on thin Au crystallites (150 nm to 1.71 $μ\mathrm{m}$) with 45 nm spatial resolution. The resulting XANES spectra exhibit excellent agreement with standard transmission and fluorescence contrasts, while providing complementary chemical insights with improved spatial resolution. Quantitative retrieval of anomalous phase variations ~12 keV further demonstrates the suitability of this method for high-resolution chemical imaging across a wide range of functional materials.

title: Why Agentic Workflows Fail: A Taxonomy Derived from Literature and Empirical Data
abstract: Agentic workflows combine large language models with planning, memory, tools, execution environments, and iterative feedback. Their failures are difficult to diagnose because the same user-visible symptom may originate from model behavior, workflow orchestration, external tools, infrastructure, or their interaction. This paper presents a source-aware taxonomy of agentic workflow failures and applies it to evidence from academic literature and GitHub. The taxonomy combines source attribution with three empirical dimensions: a concrete failure-type dictionary, workflow-stage localization, and agent-capability localization. Its central structure is a two-axis localization matrix: workflow stages form the horizontal process axis and agent capabilities form the vertical functional axis. This design moves beyond taxonomies that mainly classify final failure manifestations by localizing intermediate process states inside agent operation. Our empirical comparison shows that literature-derived failures emphasize planning, reasoning, learning, perception, and knowledge-related mechanisms, whereas GitHub-derived failures concentrate on execution-stage, actuation-related, tool, API, and infrastructure failures. The dominant hotspot is iterative execution and actuation. These findings indicate that agentic workflow reliability should be treated as a systems problem rather than only a model-output problem. The taxonomy provides a basis for structured evaluation, root cause analysis, failure injection, and engineering triage.

title: ClearNav: Perception-Aligned Quadrotor Flight Using Differential-Physics
abstract: Autonomous quadrotor flight in cluttered environment is an key capability for tasks like inspection and search. Navigation policies trained in simulation and transferred to hardware can fly at high speed in open space, but they can still collide as obstacle clearance shrinks. We attribute most of these collisions to a single mechanism, namely motion in directions the onboard camera does not observe. Heading that is not aligned with the direction of travel and lateral excursion during obstacle avoidance both carry the vehicle toward obstacles outside its field of view. We introduce ClearNav, a navigation policy trained with two reward terms that constrain motion to the observed direction, a forward-looking heading target and a penalty on lateral velocity. A third term penalizes speed near obstacles so that an obstacle entering the field of view remains avoidable. In simulation, across 18 held-out scenarios with 2304 paired flights per policy unseen in training, ClearNav improves success by 6.8 points, cuts the collision rate by 65% relative to the state of the arts, and flies at maximum 5m/s. For the proximity term alone under matched commanded speeds, the collision reduction still holds at 70%. The effect is significant on static scenes and consistent in direction on moving obstacles, though not significant there at the suite level, showing that safer flight in clutter is possible even on the limited sensors and compute of small drones. We also validate our navigation policy in a real-world cluttered environment, showing that it enables the quadrotor to navigate through the cluttered environment successfully and safely.

title: Thin matrix products up to D <= N^0.172 and lossless reductions for 3SUM, Exact Triangle and APSP, with 3SUM over abelian groups and a dichotomy for coordinatewise problems
abstract: Alman and Vassilevska Williams (arXiv:2610.06783) gave the first polynomial improvements over the textbook algorithms for 3SUM and APSP: deterministic algorithms with exponents 1.9992 for 3SUM, 2.9983 for Exact Triangle and 2.99942 for APSP. Their algorithm has two steps: a matrix theorem, computing N^2/sqrt(D) prescribed entries of the product of an N x D and a D x N integer matrix in time N^2/D^gamma, gamma > 0, when D <= N^eps, for every eps < 0.1204; and reductions from the three problems to the lopsided sparse triangle problem. We improve both. With Schönhage's five-term partial-product tensor, the matrix theorem holds for every eps < 0.172. The preprint's reductions keep a quarter of the matrix theorem's saving for 3SUM and a half for Exact Triangle and APSP; ours keep all of it, by calling the counting version of the triangle problem adaptively and building composite moduli one prime at a time. Together this gives deterministic 3SUM in n^{1.9945+o(1)}, and Exact Triangle, (min,+)-product and APSP in n^{2.9945+o(1)}. We also improve on the preprint's proof sketch for 3XOR and solve it deterministically in O(n^{1.99451}). Which other problems on three lists does the method make truly subquadratic? It solves 3SUM over F_p^d for every fixed prime p with 3XOR's exponents, and over every finite abelian group of exponent p^2, such as Z_4^d, in O(n^{1.99726}). For coordinatewise problems with a fixed relation P on every coordinate triple, a certified exhaustive computation shows that every Boolean P, and every functional P over three letters, either is the solution set of an equation over Z, F_2 or F_3, and the problem is then truly subquadratic, or has a gadget for Orthogonal Vectors, and the problem is then hard under the Orthogonal Vectors hypothesis. Over four letters, just four functional relations, up to symmetry, satisfy neither condition.

title: Optimal Gating for Dead-Time-Constrained Single-Photon Detectors
abstract: We develop a Fisher-information framework for optimizing single-photon detector gating in periodic experiments, in contrast to previous more empirical or heuristic gating choices. After each photon detection, such a detector is insensitive for a dead time, so that an early background detection can obscure a later signal. Gating preserves availability for informative photons by selectively deactivating the detector. In our high-pile-up simulation of distance-attenuated lidar, our practical data-independent gating design reduces the worst-case asymptotic range variance by more than half relative to the free-running acquisition (which does not use any gating). More generally, we characterize achievable detector-active frequencies as a convex polytope and construct an adaptive rule that asymptotically attains an optimal "oracle" design without prior knowledge of the physical parameters. We also derive practical criteria that quantify the potential gains of gating and/or photon attenuation over unattenuated free-running acquisition.

title: MIRROR: Reflecting Hidden Symmetries from Offline Robot Interaction Data
abstract: Symmetry-aware robot policy learning requires coupled observation-action transformations. For pixel observations, even simple physical symmetries can induce complex, viewpoint-dependent image transformations that are difficult to specify by hand. Existing symmetry-aware methods often rely on representations with predefined transformations, requiring preprocessing tailored to the sensing setup and task. We introduce MIRROR, a framework that learns how a known symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) from offline interaction data. MIRROR couples these transformations through adversarial tuple matching over one-step transition tuples, while explicit group-consistency regularization penalizes violations of the group-operation axioms. On four Robosuite tabletop manipulation tasks, MIRROR achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 61% reduction in compatibility error (which measures consistency under transformation composition) relative to an adapted LaLiGAN baseline. Using the learned transformations in frame-averaged behavior cloning (BC) yields higher mean success rates than vanilla BC on all four tasks, increasing average success from 80.48% to 85.12%, with per-task gains up to 9.66 percentage points. We also repeat symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation with heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, then deploy the resulting policy zero-shot on a real Kinova GEN3 arm. Project page: https://pomdp-mirror.github.io.

title: Internal Nucleon Properties and the Equation of State of Ultra-Dense Matter
abstract: The question of the link between the nucleon properties and the equation of state of ultra-dense matter, both being composed of quarks and gluons, is investigated by adopting a soliton model to describe internal nucleon properties and a direct mapping between nucleon and quark matter to obtain the equation of state of ultra-dense matter. We compare $π+ω$ and $π+ω+ρ$ soliton models and analyze the presence of a pressure singularity at the nucleon center due to the $ρ$ field. This singularity impacts the equation of state in ultra-dense matter. Only the pressure derived from the canonical energy-momentum tensor has a singularity, while the Belinfante pseudo-gauge transformation of the energy-momentum tensor generates an internal pressure without a singularity. We then investigate predictions for the equation of state of ultra-dense matter based on different prescriptions for the nucleon pressure. It is shown that none of the prescriptions agree with the thermodynamical pressure defined in uniform matter. The mismatch between any equation of state and the thermodynamical one questions the simplicity of the direct mapping between finite-size nucleon properties and uniform matter as well as the role of the nucleon surface in the internal energy density and the pressure.

title: On Making $\mathrm{SE}(2)$-Invariant Networks Optimal
abstract: Respecting a-priori known symmetries of underlying data is a key principle in designing efficient neural architectures. Convolutional neural networks are a canonical example, encoding translation equivariance. Extending this inductive bias to richer symmetry groups such as $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ in the most effective way possible is an ongoing architectural and computational challenge. Building on classical invariant theory, we derive invariant feature maps that are provably optimal: minimal and information-preserving with respect to the symmetry group. Our construction is designed to integrate seamlessly into standard architectures, requiring no modification to nonlinearities or normalization layers. As a concrete implementation, we introduce a plug-and-play module for convolutional neural networks that enforces $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ invariance, capturing both translations and rotations within standard architectures. The resulting models are both efficient and expressive. Experiments show competitive or improved accuracy compared to state-of-the-art equivariant methods at significantly lower computational cost. Finally, we provide a theoretical and empirical analysis of the relationship between equivariance and invariance, offering insight into their roles in controlling robustness and flexibility.

title: When Sparsity Breaks Connectivity: Functional Reachability and Guided Topology Dynamics in Extreme Sparse Training
abstract: Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) periodically prunes and regrows connections, inducing a discrete dynamical mechanism over network topologies. At extreme sparsity ($\ge 99\%$), this dynamic tends to destroy input-output information pathways, and performance with standard magnitude/random updates degrades sharply. We formalize forward, backward, and functional reachability on layered sparse graphs, derive closed-form expectations for reachable neurons and edges, and show that Monte Carlo realizations match the theory. Guided by this reachability-based structure, we bias pruning toward non-functional edges and regrowth toward functionally consistent candidates. We introduce this reachability-driven modification of topology evolution as Reachability-guided in DST, referred to as guided DST. On CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet, guided DST recovers large accuracy gaps versus unguided DST (up to $+14.4$ points at $99.9\%$ sparsity on CIFAR-100), and on MLP-Mixer guided DST remains trainable at $99.99\%$ sparsity while unguided random regrowth degrades sharply. These results cast extreme-sparse training as a connectivity-preserving dynamical process. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/mzjaworski/ea_dst.

title: Reinforcement Learning In Partially Verifiable Environments for Colon Cancer Treatment Planning
abstract: Clinical decision-making is a sequential process of information collection, clinical inference, and forecasting under partial observability, often without a uniquely correct treatment decision. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong medical question-answering capabilities but extending these advances to clinical reasoning remains challenging because many clinical tasks are only partially verifiable. Recent clinical reinforcement learning (RL) work has therefore largely focused on diagnostic endpoints, where correctness can be more directly verified. Oncology treatment decision making is a particularly challenging instance of this problem that extends beyond medical question-answering in which multiple decision trajectories can be clinically defensible for the same partially observed patient state. We formulate oncology treatment planning as an interactive RL problem under partial observability and construct patient-specific, process-aware rewards from decision processes observed in real world clinical records. The agent must learn to sequentially acquire information from a structured patient representation before committing to a first-line treatment recommendation, and is evaluated on information gathering, treatment selection, and reasoning alignment. Using GRPO and GDPO to optimize Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct within this environment, RL substantially improves the base policy beyond frontier model capabilities. The GDPO-trained policy increases Mean@3 scalar clinical reward by $79.60\%$ over base Llama and exceeds GPT-5.2 by $18.82\%$ under the same interactive environment, while reducing query count during training. Overall, our results show that patient-specific, partially verifiable rewards can provide an effective learning signal for interactive clinical RL when both the patient state and the underlying clinical decision process are only partially observed.

title: Smoothness Ranks Skill, Not Success: An Audit of Published Trajectory-Smoothness Curation Metrics Under Episode-Length Controls
abstract: Trajectory smoothness has been proposed as a cheap, training-free signal for curating imitation-learning demonstrations, most recently by rinse, which introduces Spectral Arc Length (SAL) and a contact-aware Trajectory-Envelope Distance (TED). We test whether these published metrics survive episode-length controls on real robomimic data. On can/mh, SAL separates better from worse operators with AUROC 0.952, but episode length alone achieves 0.957, and inside a duration-matched band SAL falls to 0.628 while raw mean jerk, the baseline rinse argues against, rises to 0.896. The confound replicates on square/mh. On can/mg, where every episode is exactly 150 steps, SAL is at chance (0.454) and TED is inverted (0.376) against task success, while jerk reaches 0.706. Training GMM behavior-cloning policies on each metric's curated subset (10 seeds), curating by TED costs roughly a third of downstream success relative to random selection of the same size (0.240 vs. 0.360, p=0.0001, surviving Bonferroni correction), while SAL and jerk are indistinguishable from not curating.
