Under a diffusion policy TED still ranks worst, though its deficit is not resolvable at five seeds, and jerk becomes significantly better than both baselines, so the curation decision does not transfer unchanged across the two policy configurations we tested. Inspecting trajectories shows why TED inverts: successful manipulation requires sustained high-deviation motion through contact, while failure is low-amplitude hovering that a smoothed envelope follows closely.

title: KINTORA: a semi-Lagrangian discontinuous Galerkin drift-kinetic, unstructured mesh tokamak solver
abstract: Continuum gyrokinetic codes use structured, field-aligned grids on nested flux surfaces; particle-in-cell codes support unstructured meshes and open field lines but carry a statistical noise floor. We present a continuum drift-kinetic solver that occupies neither position: a semi-Lagrangian discontinuous Galerkin discretization on unstructured triangular poloidal planes extruded toroidally, whose parallel advance is a map along the exact field line in the flux-coordinate independent manner, so the mesh is never aligned with the field, with adiabatic electrons and a long-wavelength polarization field solve. Every operator is verified against an independently computed reference, from Landau damping to the geodesic-acoustic root and a linear ion-temperature-gradient eigenvalue problem, every measured rate within 4% except the geodesic-acoustic damping, within 12%. A linear toroidal ion-temperature-gradient demonstration on a canonical-Maxwellian equilibrium recovers a radially coherent mode whose growth rate, 0.065 c_s/a, is stationary in time. The collisionless zonal-flow residual is the one measurement still moving: it rises with poloidal refinement from 0.72 to 0.87 of the model's own orbit-quadrature prediction for the measured observable and has not converged. The solver is fully device resident, and every result is reproduced between CPU and GPU builds and across MPI process counts. The code, the data behind every table and an artifact description are in a public repository.

title: Monarch-Muon: Structure-Aware Muon for Fast and Memory-Efficient Pretraining
abstract: Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch-Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch-Muon improves over Monarch-AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch-Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

title: Optimal Planar $k$ Nearest Neighbors Queries for Additively Weighted Euclidean Distances and Convex Metrics
abstract: Given a set $P$ of $n$ point sites in the plane, the $k$ nearest neighbors problem is to build a data structure that, for a query point $v$ and a query integer $k$, reports the $k$ nearest point sites of $v$ in $P$ efficiently. For the Euclidean metric, after four decades of efforts, an optimal data structure has been developed with $O(n)$ space, $O(\log n+k)$ query time and $O(n\log n)$ preprocessing time [Mat92b, Cha00, AC09, CT16]. In contrast, for a family of distance functions, the state-of-the-art data structure [AES99, KMR+20, Liu22] attains $O(n\log\log n)$ space, $O(\log n+k)$ query time and expected $O(n\log n)$ preprocessing time. An open question is the existence of an optimal data structure with $O(n)$ space and $O(\log n + k)$ query time for distance functions more general than the Euclidean metric. Such an optimal data structure also remains unknown for non-point sites in the Euclidean metric, even for disk sites or, more generally, additively weighted Euclidean distances. We develop an optimal $k$-nearest-neighbors data structure for additively weighted Euclidean distances with $O(n)$ space, $O(\log n + k)$ query time and expected $O(n\log n)$ preprocessing time. Since this data structure can be adjusted to disk sites, it serves as an initial result toward optimality for non-point sites. We also adapt our data structure to point sites under a family of convex metrics, including commonly used $L_p$ metrics and uniform orientation metrics. The data structure can be further extended to distance functions that satisfy certain axioms. Thus, we demonstrate the existence of optimal $k$-nearest-neighbors data structures for distance functions more general than point sites in the Euclidean metric. Our main technical advance is to generalize Matoušek's shallow partition theorem for hyperplanes [Mat92b] to these settings, while achieving a logarithmic crossing number.

title: VeriRouter: Towards Verifiable LLM Routing
abstract: Large language model (LLM) routers are increasingly deployed to optimize quality, latency, and cost through dynamic model selection and request rewriting. However, a compromised router can cause ineligible selection on the control plane, unendorsed rewriting or unfaithful relay on the data plane, undermining LLM routing integrity. We present VeriRouter, a verifiable LLM routing framework. Under an endorsed public context binding a private semantic index and rewrite banks, VeriRouter combines ZK proofs with a provider-issued serving certificate to establish integrity across both planes while keeping the router's private routing assets hidden from clients. For model selection, we design an efficient ZK proof for semantic search. For rewriting, local checks enforce message preservation and additions from committed banks. On real-world workloads, VeriRouter's model-selection and rewrite proofs average 21.92~s and 4.24~s, yielding 1,307$\times$ and 101$\times$ speedups over the fastest completing baselines. Relative to serving without verification, VeriRouter adds only 4.08 s under per-turn selection and 0.11 s under session-pinned selection.

title: Plane Cremona maps preserving a Euclidean volume form
abstract: We give a presentation by generators and relations of the group of birational transformations of the plane preserving a differential form with poles along a triple line. This group strictly contains the automorphism group of the affine plane.

title: What Does 2D Coronal Seismology Measure?
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) coronal seismology based on coronagraphic imaging spectroscopy has emerged as a promising method for mapping the coronal magnetic field, but the physical meaning of its inferred quantities under optically thin line-of-sight (LOS) integration remains uncertain. We investigate this problem by synthesizing coronagraphic observables from a global wave-driven magnetohydrodynamic model with a long LOS extent and a structured corona, and by applying the same analysis procedures used for observations. We compare the diagnosed density, wave propagation direction, phase speed, and magnetic-field strength with different LOS-weighted reference quantities from the model. We find that the measured density and the wave propagation direction are both well represented by LOS emissivity-weighted quantities. In contrast, the phase speed is not controlled by emissivity weighting alone: the LOS distribution of wave velocity amplitude also plays an important role. As a result, the inferred magnetic field is better represented by combining the emissivity-weighted density with an amplitude-dependent effective speed. Emissivity weighting nevertheless remains a reasonable approximation, and a useful baseline, over much of the field of view, especially where the LOS does not cross strongly structured plasma-sheet-like regions. These results clarify the physical interpretation of 2D coronal seismology and provide guidance for future coronal magnetic-field tomography and model-constrained applications.

title: World-T3: Test-Time Training as Persistent Memory for Real-Time Video World Models
abstract: Recent advances in video world models have enabled plausible interactive environments, yet long-horizon generation places a fundamental demand on visual memory: the previously observed world must remain consistent as the model continues to generate. Existing autoregressive approaches often implicitly rely on the generative model itself to retain such information, leading to spatial memory decay beyond the active context. We introduce World-T3, a camera-controlled video world model with a test-time training memory that consolidates past observations into dedicated model parameters. To robustly update this memory, we propose a recursive least-squares rule that incrementally absorbs novel visual features via online pose-keyed memory updates. Our TTT memory reads out previously observed scene features from the fast-weight state by camera pose, enabling consistent generation with constant storage and per-step computation regardless of rollout length. To facilitate real-time interactive generation with this robust memory, we further distill the autoregressive model into a few-step generator via dual-teacher distribution matching. On a long-horizon revisit benchmark, World-T3 raises revisit PSNR from 13.52 to 18.31 dB and reduces absolute rotation error from 3.344 to 1.075 relative to the strongest baseline on both metrics, while sustaining 20.6 FPS at 1280 x 704 on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU.

title: Model theory of quasitracial $\mathrm{AW}^*$-algebras and the absoluteness of monotone completeness
abstract: We examine various applications of logic to $\mathrm{AW}^*$-algebras, particularly the monotone completeness conjecture. We develop a model theory for $\mathrm{AW}^*$-algebras equipped with a faithful normalized quasitrace. Using this language, we provide a separable coding which allows us to reduce the finite case of the monotone completeness conjecture to monotone sequential completeness of $\mathrm{II}_1$ $\mathrm{AW}^*$-factors. Combining an explicit recursive axiomatization with the completeness theorem for continuous logic, we show that this case of the conjecture, and Kaplansky's problem whether every $\mathrm{AW}^*$-factor of type $\mathrm{II}_1$ is a von Neumann algebra, are each equivalent in ZFC to a $Π^0_2$ sentence of arithmetic, so that their answers are the same in every $ω$-model of ZFC. We also consider real $\mathrm{AW}^*$-algebras. Here the Baer-$*$-ring notion of an abelian projection must be distinguished from commutativity; following the real-operator-algebra terminology we call the former semi-abelian. Handelman's matrix theorem implies that a real $\mathrm{AW}^*$-algebra with no nonzero central semi-abelian projection has $\mathrm{AW}^*$ complexification. We answer a number of other open problems in real $\mathrm{AW}^*$-algebras.

title: SchemaWeaver: Accelerating On-Device Mobile Agentic AI via Schema-Guided Parallel LLM Decoding
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices can act as agents that call external software tools to complete complex tasks, but the major challenge of supporting on-device mobile agentic AI with LLMs is the long latency of LLM tool calling on mobile devices. In particular, the decode phase is the main contributor of such long latency, but is hard to speed up on mobile processors as it is bound by memory bandwidth rather than compute power. To address this limitation, in this paper we present SchemaWeaver, a new on-device mobile agentic AI technique that enforces schema-guided parallel decoding in the decode phase of LLM tool calling, to reduce its latency by producing multiple tokens in each decode pass. SchemaWeaver can be generically applied to the LLM inference engine on mobile devices without involving any training efforts or changes on LLMs, and our experiment results on major mobile SoCs and LLM families show that SchemaWeaver can reduce the LLM tool calling latency by up to 3.9 times, compared to the competitive baselines.

title: Type I-II/II-I vortices from dimension-six self-interaction
abstract: We show that adding a dimension-six self-interaction to the Abelian-Higgs or Ginzburg Landau model results in a remarkable and rich structure of multi-vortex solutions. Besides the standard type I (attractive) and type II (repulsive) regimes, separated by the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfeld limit (BPS), we identify two new possibilities: type I-II vortices, which attract at short distances and repel at long distances; and type II-I vortices, with the opposite behaviour. Specifically, within the type II-I regime, multi-vortex solutions form chunks of the Abrikosov lattice or clusters. Conversely, in the I-II regime, axially symmetric multi-vortices are stable; nevertheless, depending on the model parameters and topological charge (winding number), they can be either the ground state or not.

title: Evading the Swampland de Sitter Obstruction via Thermodynamic Duality-Induced Horizon Corrections in Unimodular Gravity
abstract: We investigate the early-universe cosmological implications of Unimodular Gravity coupled to Power-Law Nonlinear Electrodynamics in the presence of quantum-corrected horizon thermodynamics derived from the principle of thermodynamic duality. By incorporating both logarithmic and inverse-area corrections to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, we derive modified Friedmann equations exhibiting novel $H^4$ and $H^6$ terms that represent genuine quantum gravity effects. We demonstrate that these higher-order corrections become dynamically significant in the high-energy regime of cosmic inflation, naturally modifying the slow-roll dynamics without requiring a fundamental inflaton potential. A comprehensive phase-space analysis reveals that the quantum corrections drive early-time de Sitter-like attractors, providing a robust mechanism for sustained inflationary expansion. Confronting the model with the Swampland program, we show that the correction factor $\mathcal{F}(H)$ modifies the effective slow-roll parameters, enabling the model to satisfy the Swampland de Sitter and Distance conjectures during the inflationary epoch. We calculate the inflationary observables, including the spectral index $n_s$ and the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$, and demonstrate that the model's predictions are in excellent agreement with the Planck 2018 observational constraints. Our results suggest that thermodynamic duality-induced horizon corrections offer a viable and testable pathway for realizing successful inflation within a well-motivated quantum-gravitational framework.

title: Large Language Models Extend Known Research But Do Not Create New Research Directions
abstract: The success of autonomous research systems relies on the quality of the scientific hypotheses they generate. Recent studies report that human reviewers often rate LLM-generated ideas as more novel than those from human experts, raising hope that AI can accelerate scientific discovery. Yet it is unclear whether these models can do more than extend existing knowledge. Can LLMs drive genuine innovation by revealing new research directions, or are they limited to repeating and recombining what science already knows? This unresolved question lies at the heart of discussions about AI and the future of science. To address this, we distinguish two types of novelty: distance, which measures how far a hypothesis lies from existing work, and direction, which captures whether the hypothesis pursues new lines of inquiry beyond those already present. These two measures diverge sharply for LLM-generated work. We represent scientific papers in a shared conceptual space using a pretrained scientific-paper embedding model. Within this space, we embed 26.9 million human-authored papers across 1,325 research topics in six natural-science fields and 524,308 LLM-generated hypotheses from eight models. Distance is measured using existing metrics. To quantify direction, we introduce the orthogonal novelty score (ONS). LLMs consistently generate ideas more distant from existing work than human-authored papers, up to 16\% further when the LLM is given the papers farthest from the centre of the topic. However, LLM hypotheses have a 15--23\% lower median ONS than published papers from the same topic. Thus, LLMs move further from what is already known, but remain within established directions. This pattern persists across changes in various configurations. As a result, LLMs excel at extending the frontier but the creation of new directions is still led by human scientists.

title: Know-Thy-Not: Training-Free Targeted Negation in Dual-Encoder Vision-Language Models
abstract: Dual-encoder vision-language models systematically fail at negation, scoring ''a cat without a dog'' nearly identically to ''a cat with a dog.'' We show that this failure is inherent to the single-embedding framework. Under contrastive training, single-embedding methods can at best ignore the negated concept (dilution) but never penalize its presence (rejection). We propose Know-Thy-Not (KTN), a training-free method that introduces an image-side rejection dimension to penalize the negated concept directly in the visual representation. We also introduce COCO-Confusion, the first benchmark requiring genuine rejection to succeed. Across 9 backbones, KTN improves COCO-Confusion mAP by up to +25.6 over vanilla VLMs and +9.6 over the strongest existing method.

title: Linear Laurent phenomenon algebras are of finite type
abstract: Laurent phenomenon algebras generalise cluster algebras by allowing irreducible exchange polynomials in place of binomials. Lam and Pylyavskyy proved finite type for those arising from graphs and conjectured that the same holds for every Laurent phenomenon algebra admitting a linear seed. We prove this conjecture over an arbitrary unique factorisation domain. Our proof constructs a nonzero element of the upper algebra divisible by every cluster variable. Comparing noninitial cluster variables with the prime factors of this element in the initial Laurent ring bounds the number of cluster variable classes and yields a finite normalised mutation pattern.

title: Spectral Self-Concordant Barriers: A Proof of a Conjecture by Tunçel
abstract: Let $Q \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a open, convex, and symmetric set and let $f:Q \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a $\vartheta$-self-concordant barrier function, that is also symmetric. We show the associated spectral function $F(X)= \mathcal{O}^2 (f \circ λ)(X)$ is a $\mathcal{O}^2\vartheta$-self-concordant function, where $\mathcal{O} = 8\max\{1+3\vartheta, 12\}$, on the domain of all $n \times n$ symmetric matrices $X$, with eigenvalues $λ(X) \in Q$. This generalizes the relationship between the standard logarithmic barriers $-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i$ and $-\log \det X$ and gives a solution to a conjecture by L.~Tunçel, 1995.

title: A Stochastic Growth Model for Online Platforms
abstract: We investigate the growth trajectory of online platforms operating as market makers in two-sided matching markets. Their expansion, often referred to as the ``chicken-and-egg dilemma'' in the literature, poses an inherent challenge: service providers find value in joining the platform because of the presence of customers, while customers are drawn to the platform by the availability of service providers. Much of the existing literature addresses this expansion challenge through either a static market-clearing lens or aggregate dynamic models, emphasizing how network externalities shape a platform's growth trajectory and equilibrium size. These approaches do not fully capture how gradual growth must be implemented through server-level admission, assignment, and compensation decisions. Embedded in this growth process are intertemporal participation constraints that the platform must satisfy to attract and retain forward-looking servers. To explicitly account for the stochastic dynamics of a platform's gradual growth, we model the system as a Markov process. Potential servers and customers arrive according to Poisson processes, and customer demand is non-decreasing in the number of active servers. Under mild conditions, we characterize the platform's optimal admission, assignment, and compensation policies. The platform admits servers at the maximum feasible rate until it reaches an endogenous target size, which can be smaller than the static market-clearing optimum. In the baseline model, seniority-based compensation acts as an operational substitute for financially subsidized growth: instead of using upfront subsidies to induce early server participation, the platform uses future cash flows to reward early servers for joining when demand is limited and for helping the platform reach later, higher-demand states.

title: The belief-action gap in language model agents
abstract: Language model (LM) agents can fail for different reasons, requiring different explanations and interventions. We study how state beliefs, action values, and action preferences interact as LM agents reason and commit to decisions in text-rendered grid worlds. We estimate task-relevant beliefs using report-based and representation-based probes, and action values using inverse reinforcement learning. We find that task-relevant state and value information is often represented more reliably than it is reflected in behaviour. Tracking action preferences throughout reasoning further shows that decisions sharpen around a commitment point and reported belief uncertainty decreases near commitment, although individual belief changes do not consistently explain shifts in action preference. Finally, forced actions follow reasoning prefixes from other decisions when transplanted, whereas the tested reasoning-window activation edits provide limited control over the action. Together, these results suggest that some failures arise not from missing task-relevant information, but from how available information is translated into action. Our measurements distinguish information availability from belief-action consistency without by themselves identifying the cause of each failure. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/belief-action-gap-F745/

title: When Is RTL Better? Auditing Evaluation Stability with Tool-Grounded Requirement Profiles
abstract: RTL-generation studies increasingly report functional correctness and post-synthesis quality, yet the evaluator itself is rarely treated as an experimental variable. A candidate can appear better when a security rule, protocol obligation, target context, feasibility gate, uncertainty policy, or provenance constraint is omitted. We introduce tool-grounded requirement profiles: machine-readable contracts binding each requirement's meaning to its executable evidence and comparison rule, together with cross-requirement gates, uncertainty handling, and provenance. We audit evaluator stability by freezing candidate pairs and perturbing only their evaluation profile. In a preregistered controlled pilot with six designs, twelve pairs, three requirement families, six evaluator conditions, and 72 decisions, a generic cell-count evaluator reports unsupported improvement for 6/12 pairs (50%; Wilson 95% interval 25.4 to 74.6%; design-cluster bootstrap interval 25 to 75%). The matched evaluator detects all twelve injected regressions, whereas syntax, generic synthesis, context mismatch, and gate ablation each lose the required distinction for 12/12 pairs. In a separately frozen external validation of all 290 public RTLLM v1.1 text-only candidates, 81/215 evaluable comparisons (37.7%; task-cluster 95% interval 24.8 to 51.4%) yield unsupported scalar improvements, including 72 functional-gate reversals. Separately, 26 OpenROAD-flow-scripts runs show why timing context and activity qualification must be part of the contract. The study does not rank generators; it establishes evaluator configuration as a measurable, auditable source of conclusion instability.

title: Einstein Telescope: the triangle in a network and the impact of the relative orientation of detectors
abstract: The geometrical configuration of the Einstein Telescope (ET) gravitational-wave observatory is one the most important design choices to be made for this future scientific facility. Two baseline configurations are currently being considered, a single triangle or 2 distant L-shaped detectors tilted by about $45^{\circ}$. In this document we present a study of the scientific performance of the ET baseline configurations in both stand-alone mode and in the presence of either an L-shaped Cosmic Explorer detector with 40-km long arms located in the United States or the existing LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA network. We also include in the study an alternative ET configuration, which is currently not being considered and consists of a triangle plus a distant L-shaped detector. We find that in stand-alone mode this alternative configuration performs significantly better than the other two in both the compact binary coalescence and stochastic gravitational wave background scientific cases. The differences in performance between the ET configurations are reduced in the presence of the considered, additional non-ET detectors. We also show that the impact of possible correlated noise in co-located detectors on the stochastic gravitational-wave background performance can be addressed with the addition of extra detectors. Finally, we study the impact on the ET scientific performance of the relative orientation of the future detectors in the network. We find that, while the configurations that include a triangular ET detector are basically insensitive to this orientation, a balanced compromise for the ET configuration consisting of two L-shaped detectors could be represented by a tilt angle between the two detectors of about $30^{\circ}$.

title: Distributed quantum phase sensing using an SU(1,1) Perelomov coherent state in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer network
abstract: We present a theoretical study of distributed quantum sensing using a reconfigurable network of $N$ Mach--Zehnder interferometers to simultaneously estimate weighted linear combinations of relative phase shifts. The proposed scheme relies on injecting a Perelomov coherent state, generated from the SU(1,1) group representation, into one port of a passive quantum circuit while the remaining modes are initialized in the vacuum state, thereby establishing non-trivial quantum correlations among the sensors. Based on multi-parameter quantum estimation theory, our analysis shows that this entangled strategy outperforms the standard shot-noise limit and asymptotically achieves the Heisenberg limit. Furthermore, we highlight the crucial role of the first beam splitter's asymmetry; specifically, the optimal transmission coefficient that maximizes sensitivity corresponds to its maximum imbalance. Compared to a separable approach utilizing the same total average photon number, the entangled strategy yields a more efficient use of quantum resources, guaranteeing an accuracy gain between $1$ and $N$. This demonstrates that the entangled strategy is systematically superior to its separable counterpart. Ultimately, these results illustrate the potential of entangled distributed quantum sensor networks for high-precision measurements and provide clear guidelines for optimizing interferometric architectures in quantum metrology.

title: TableVision: Recovering Verified Structure from Historical Tables
abstract: Gaps, skips, and mistakes are the normal state of a historical register: rows go missing, tables cross page breaks, columns slip under wrong names, and column sums disagree with the corresponding row entries. Readers read digits correctly but lose the table structure. On seven clean panels of election returns, the best open-source reader reproduces 99.0\% of the digits but files only 83.7\% of the figures in the correct cells and gets 11 of 30 columns correct. TableVision treats table structure recovery as the problem. On three degraded 1888 pages, Amazon Textract files only 1 of 1494 figures correctly; TableVision correctly files 99.2\%, and all 51 columns its exact-total check releases are correct. A dynamic program cuts a volume into blocks by how many columns sum to their last line; witnesses read the cells; the gate classifies each column as exactly reconciling, flagged as faithful to a page whose arithmetic is wrong, or withheld. A theory of the sum check says which errors it cannot see and why its optimal block is about $θ^{-1/2}$ rows at defect rate $θ$. On 2201 columns of Wisconsin electoral data, the gate accepts 2042, flags 118, and withholds 41; failure rises with column length $R$ as $1-(1-θ)^R$ at 1.1 defects per 1000 cells in general elections; official returns confirm 933 of 934 testable accepted sums and all 35 testable flagged totals; and the deployment added 491\,359 gated precinct rows to a 9.3-million-row dataset. One implication is that the design of the verification block is critical.

title: Formal-Verification-Guided Bayesian Optimization for Non-Intrusive Last-Mile Coverage Closure
abstract: Last-mile functional coverage closure for modern chip designs remains costly because a mature UVM environment exposes many controls while direct hits on the remaining bins are sparse. We present a non-intrusive workflow that closes pre-defined bins in an existing, human-authored functional coverage model; it does not synthesize verification objectives from the design specification. The workflow first uses abstract-syntax-tree (AST) parsing and cone-of-influence (COI) tracing to map each residual target to existing testbench knobs. Under a matched 20-simulation budget, Bayesian optimization (BO) is compared with continued constrained-random verification (CRV) and random search over the same AST/COI-reduced space. Formal reachability then removes only targets supported by complete unreachability proofs, after which retained targets are grouped by formal difficulty and processed by group-specific BO under a second matched 20-simulation budget. Cleanup and grouping never add numerator bins; only simulator coverage artifacts do. On OpenTitan AES, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 241/271 bins; formal cleanup removes two denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 20 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 261/271 raw coverage (96.31%) and 261/269 effective coverage (97.03%). On Entropy Source, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 2117/2277 bins; formal cleanup removes ten denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 93 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 2210/2277 raw coverage (97.06%) and 2210/2267 effective coverage (97.49%). These results characterize the integrated diagnosis-and-search workflow; the present evaluation does not isolate the causal contributions of difficulty classification, policy routing, and post-cleanup BO.

title: Unit-Demand Pricing for Min-Buying Customers
abstract: We study the unit-demand pricing problem under \textit{min-buying} behavior, where customers purchase the lowest-priced item that yields non-negative utility. In contrast to the quasi-linear model, we show that uniform pricing becomes substantially more effective under min-buying. First, we study symmetric environments. We show that for min-buying customers with independent and identically distributed valuations, a uniform price across items is optimal. We then extend this optimality result to all valuations drawn from exchangeable and affiliated distributions. However, uniform pricing is not optimal in all symmetric environments: for min-buying customers we construct an exchangeable and non-affiliated valuation distribution for which the gap between uniform pricing and optimal item pricing is logarithmic in the number of items. This gap is tight and matches the worst-case gap in the quasi-linear setting. Next, we consider asymmetric environments in which valuations are independent but not identically distributed. When these valuations are regular and customers are min-buying, we show that a uniform price guarantees approximately 69.86\% of the optimal item-pricing revenue and this is tight. Overall, our results highlight that the value of non-uniform pricing substantially diminishes, and often disappears entirely, under more conservative demand models in which customers engage in satisficing behaviors such as min-buying.

title: On Sleep-Wake Disorder Identification from Polysomnographic Representations
abstract: Self-supervised polysomnography foundation models (PSG FMs) aim to capture clinically useful information beyond sleep staging, yet are rarely compared with sleep-staging encoders pretrained at comparable scale and modality coverage. Using a common whole-night, missingness-aware state-space downstream modeling framework, we compared frozen representations from prominent large-scale, multi-cohort sleep-stage-supervised encoders and self-supervised PSG FMs for multilabel identification of six sleep-wake and circadian disorder groups in 7,906 PSGs from an unseen registry. Although PSG FMs outperformed an EEG-only, single-cohort supervised baseline, this ordering reversed when supervised pretraining approached comparable scale and modality coverage. Transfer learning from neural sleep scorers achieved higher overall performance while exhibiting greater downstream data efficiency. These findings underscore the need for scale- and modality-matched pretrained supervised baselines when assessing PSG FMs' downstream potential.

title: Crystal growth, magnetic, and transport properties of the candidate altermagnet Cr$_{1/4}$NbS$_{2}$
abstract: Altermagnetism is a rapidly emerging paradigm in condensed matter magnetism, yet the number of experimentally confirmed altermagnetic candidates remains remarkably limited. Cr$_{1/4}$NbS$_2$ has long been theoretically proposed as a promising altermagnet, but there are no reports on experimental investigation of single crystals. Here, we report the successful growth of high-quality single crystals of Cr$_{1/4}$NbS$_2$ and present its structural, thermal, magnetic, and transport properties. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction provides detailed crystallographic information and confirms the hexagonal crystal symmetry ($P6_3/mmc$), one of the criteria for altermagnetic behavior. Resistivity and heat capacity measurements unambiguously identify an antiferromagnetic Néel temperature of $T_N \sim 141$ K. Magnetotransport measurements reveal non-trivial features in the magnetoresistance and Hall response, indicative of quantum diffusive transport phenomena. Cr$_{1/4}$NbS$_2$, synthesized here for the first time in single-crystalline form, therefore serves as an experimental platform for probing the rich spectrum of phenomena predicted for altermagnetic materials.

title: Effect of Spherical Parameter Space on Number of Non-Forgetting Tasks and Capacity of Continual Learning
abstract: We propose a continuous learning formulation for $T$ non-forgetting tasks with the spherical parameter space $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}(\sqrt{d})$ in asymptotic regime $d\rightarrow \infty$. Each task $i$ has an optimum $\bmΘ_i$, minimizing its corresponding loss function $R_i(\bm{w})$ on sphere. We reduce each task $i$ to an acceptable loss region modeled by a geodesic ball $B_{\bmΘ_i}(r_i(d))$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}(\sqrt{d})$ centered at $\bmΘ_i$ with radius $r_i(d)$. To model task dependencies (similarities), task optima $\bmΘ_i$ are distributed by a Neyman-Scott clustered point process $Φ$. Cluster centers $\{\bm{Y}_j\}_{j=1}^{N_p}$ form a homogeneous Poisson point process on sphere, while intra-cluster task optima follow a von Mises-Fisher distribution with mean $\bm{Y}_j$ and concentration $κ$. Each task $t\in \{1, ..., T\}$ learning algorithm is considered to be a channel $Q_{t}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}_t | \bm{w}_{t-1}, \mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bmθ_{1:t-1}), \bmθ_t)$, where $\bm{W}_t$ is the learned parameter of task $t$ and $\mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bmΘ_{1:t-1})=\bigcap_{i=1}^{t-1}B_{\bmΘ_i}(r_i(d))$. Since in continual learning, the learner does not need to reach $\bmΘ_t$ exactly to successfully learn task $t$, to avoid forgetting as well as reliable learning, it only needs for the learned parameter vector $\bm{W}_{t}$ to enter $B_{\bmΘ_t}(r_t(d)) \cap \mathcal{K}_{t-1}(\bmΘ_{1:t-1})$. Using this model, we derive an upper bound on $T$ ensuring $\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{K}_{T}(\bmΘ_{1:T}) \neq \emptyset] \rightarrow 1$ as $d\rightarrow \infty$ and $κ/d \rightarrow α$, where $α>0$ is a constant. Finally, for $T$ tasks sampled uniformly from $Φ$, we derive an upper bound for total information theoretic capacity under the non-forgetting constraint for each task.

title: Norm properties of quantum uniformity measures
abstract: We give a complete classification of the norm properties of quantum uniformity measures, introduced by Bu, Gu, and Jaffe to analytically characterize the Clifford hierarchy. Resolving an open question they posed, we show that quantum uniformity measures define norms precisely for $k=2,3,4$. In particular, we establish the triangle inequality for $k=4$, whereas for every $k\geq5$ it fails in some dimension. The higher-order result is proved using the structure theory of norming systems of linear equations over finite fields. We also study the geometry of quantum uniformity measures, establishing explicit bounds on the modulus of convexity whenever they define norms. Finally, we give a complete classification of the norm properties of matrix-valued Gowers uniformity functionals, showing that only $k=2$ defines a norm.

title: Functional Projection and Complexity Reduction
abstract: Törnquist (arXiv:1310.3250) proved that if there exists a $\boldsymbolΣ^1_2$ maximal almost disjoint (MAD) family, then there exists a $\boldsymbolΠ^1_1$ MAD family. Since then, several other "complexity reduction" proofs have been found for other combinatorial objects, such as maximal independent families or ultrafilters. All of these proofs have relied on $\boldsymbolΠ^1_1$-uniformization, so they did not easily lift to higher projective levels. In this paper, we introduce a principle weaker than Uniformization which we call "Functional Projection", and show that this principle is sufficient for most complexity reduction proofs. On the other hand, we prove that in $L[U]$, the canonical inner model for a measurable cardinal, Functional Projection holds for $\boldsymbolΠ^1_2$ relations. As an immediate corollary, we obtain that in $L[U]$ there are $\boldsymbolΠ^1_2$ witnesses for many combinatorial families.

title: Compositional RL: Evaluating and Training LLMs for Collaborative Reasoning
abstract: Language models are often evaluated alone but increasingly deployed together, routed between, made to debate, ensembled, or collaboratively trained. For a model inside a system, what matters most is not how well it performs on its own, but how much the system gains from its presence. We call this a model's compositional strength and formalize it using the Shapley value of a cooperative game over coalitions of a model pool, and use a model's leave-one-out contribution to the full coalition as a tractable proxy, requiring n+1 rather than 2^n system evaluations. Evaluating individual vs. compositional strengths across five model pools, twelve collaboration methods, and twelve datasets, we find them largely uncorrelated: in 12 of 15 (pool, method-family) settings, individual strength does not translate into compositional advantages, and the coupling is weakest among general-purpose models that practitioners are most likely to deploy. Standalone benchmarks are therefore often poor proxies for models' value in collaborative systems. We then propose compositional reinforcement learning (C-RL), which trains a policy inside a live multi-model system and rewards the outcome produced by the system as a whole, rather than the policy's correctness in isolation. The leave-one-out baseline in Shapley values cancels under a group policy gradient, so this needs no additional rollout cost beyond RL on the collaborative system's outcome and never requires running a coalition without the policy. Across three collaboration protocols and eight tasks spanning reasoning, coding, and scientific discovery, C-RL produces the strongest collaborator in 21 of 24 settings, lifting collaborative performance by +4.0 to +5.4 pts on average (~3x the gain of baselines), up to +13.1 pts.

title: BrowseSafe++: Benchmarking Prompt Injection Detection Across Web Contexts, Languages, and Browser Views
abstract: Browser agents need to make decisions and execute actions on behalf of users while consuming untrusted webpages, creating opportunities for malicious instructions embedded in webpages to redirect legitimate tasks. We introduce BrowseSafe++, which extends BrowseSafe from 14,719 pages to 38,675 pairs of pages. Most of its prompt injections were observed in the wild on production websites. We keep each injection unchanged and rewrite the sensitive parts of the page around it to protect privacy. Each attacked page has a clean copy of the same page as its control. Both are provided as HTML, Markdown, an accessibility tree, and a screenshot. Every pair includes a user task and its expected answer. The benchmark includes twelve types of websites, from news articles to shared documents and forums, with 24 attack types appearing in 18 different locations on a page. We use these paired pages to train BrowseSafe-Guard, two 0.8B-parameter detectors for text and screenshots. Both achieve higher F1 scores than the detector based on frontier models, while keeping false-positive rates on benign pages and inference cost low. BrowseSafe-Adapt revises benchmark injections from browser-agent feedback, and attacks that succeed on only a few percent of tasks when replayed directly reach up to 95.41% success once adapted.

title: Selective Inference for Clustering Under Unknown Covariance
abstract: Unsupervised clustering is widely used to discover underlying group structure, after which researchers often seek to validate these groups via post-hoc hypothesis testing on the population means. However, using the same data both to form clusters and to test for a difference in means inflates the Type I error rate. Recent work in selective inference has proposed solutions when the underlying data are drawn from a multivariate Gaussian distribution with a known covariance matrix or an unknown isotropic covariance matrix. We propose a new selective test for the difference in means between two clusters that provably controls the Type I error rate under an arbitrary unknown covariance matrix. Our test statistic does not require estimating the feature covariance matrix; instead, it leverages a Monte Carlo sampling procedure over the set of orthogonal matrices. We show that this new selective test can be computed efficiently, and we derive closed-form solutions when clusters are formed using k-means or hierarchical clustering. In simulations, we demonstrate that our proposed p-value controls the selective Type I error rate and achieves substantial power, and we illustrate its application on gene expression and drug review data sets.

title: Co-Adaptive Entropy Modeling and Rate-Distortion-Optimal Bit Allocation for Perceptual Audio Coding
abstract: We present a perceptual audio coder in which the entropy-coding model and the bit allocation co-adapt across blocks without model side information. Mantissas are coded by a hybrid of bit packing and arithmetic coding with per-band probability models learned online. Encoder and decoder accumulate identical histograms from decoded blocks and advance the same model state. The model enters bit allocation directly: per-band rate--distortion frontiers combine measured perceptual distortion with entropy-coded rate estimates under the current model, and a dynamic program attains the exact minimum of total objective perceptual distortion for each block's budget under the model's rate estimates, with reservoir carry-over. Under a strict per-block rate, entropy-coding-aware bit allocation lowers this distortion (band noise-to-mask ratio in linear scale) by 15-24% relative to the same solver without it, and co-adaptation removes a further 3-4% (up to 15% on oboe) that a backward-adaptive coder alone cannot realize in one pass; a MUSHRA test at 80 kbps per channel confirms the ranking.

title: Continuity of stable marriage correspondences
abstract: We study a continuum version of the stable marriage problem, in which each agent has a variable mass to be paired to the opposite side. An agent's mass is interpretable as the divisible time of a single atomistic agent, or as a mass of infinitesimal agents of a particular type. Our object of interest is the mapping between the vector of masses to the set of stable matches. As in the canonical stable marriage model, the set of stable matches can be multi-valued, so this mapping is a correspondence. This correspondence is continuous if and only if the stable match is unique, implying that small changes in the masses may cause discontinuous jumps in the set of stable matches.

title: Distilling Text LMs into Speech-to-Speech LMs by Matching Internal Text Predictions
abstract: Text language models (LMs) acquire broad linguistic and factual capabilities through large-scale pretraining, while comparable capabilities remain difficult to learn from speech alone. Recent work has shown that knowledge distillation from pretrained text LMs offers a promising way to transfer their linguistic and factual capabilities to speech models. However, existing distillation approaches have largely focused on speech-input, text-output models. This idea has yet to be explored for {\it speech-to-speech} models, which operate on both speech input and speech output. In this work we introduce a speech-to-speech pretraining method that creates an internal text interface for knowledge transfer while preserving the speech-only input and output. The model first consumes speech context without its transcription, switches to text prediction, and then uses the predicted text to lead future speech generation word by word. It also provides an interface for knowledge distillation: the internal text predictions can be directly distilled from the base text LM. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of text LM distillation to a speech-to-speech LM. Under matched training conditions, the proposed sequence construction substantially improves the generative perplexity of spoken continuations over speech-only and interleaved speech-text models, approaching the performance of a text-leading inner-monologue model with external ASR prompt transcription. More importantly, distillation improves factual performance under both text and speech evaluation, indicating better retention of knowledge from the base text language model.

title: Act4R: Action-conditioned 4D reconstruction for kinematics-free control
abstract: Precise control of movement across various robotic embodiments is a longstanding challenge. Modeling complex robotic structures requires significant time, dedicated sensors, and manual labeling. Recent advancements in 4D representation learning offer an interesting alternative: can we leverage 4D features lifted from 2D observations to densely map a robot's spatial movement based on the action signal? To this end, we propose Act4R, a framework that builds on 3D foundation model to predict a robot's 3D scene flow with any given action. Act4R introduces a Spatial-Action Encoder, which encodes the current 2D robot state and its action signals into embeddings that represent future robot state in 3D. Then, both the current and future spatial embeddings are decoded into point maps to estimate action-conditioned scene flow. To effectively learn the mapping between action and future state, Act4R introduces spatial-action fusion in its transformer-based encoder, and a spatial alignment loss that guides the encoder for future flow prediction. After training on some samples of a given embodiment, Act4R can perform inverse control by optimizing the signal to achieve the desired scene flow. We evaluate Act4R on a public real-world dataset and synthetic data collected in simulator. Experiments on various robotic platforms show that Act4R outperforms the previous SoTA in scene flow prediction. Our method also performs better in inverse control, both on the action accuracy metric and in closed-loop control in simulation.

title: An FPGA-Based Spiking Neural Network for Spatiotemporal Pattern Learning and Classification
abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient spatiotemporal pattern recognition at the edge, but efficient deployment and on-device adaptation require specialized hardware. In this work, we present an FPGA implementation of multilayer SNNs for spatiotemporal pattern classification, in which both inference and training take place on the same hardware. Our design adopts a temporal-forward-only training algorithm that avoids the memory and latency overhead associated with traditional Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT). A mixed-precision scheme balances training stability with resource efficiency, and architectural optimization maximizes hardware and memory utilization. We further identify and resolve hazards that arise when inference and learning share the same memory, including port conflicts between the forward and backward access patterns and read-after-write dependencies in floating-point potential accumulation. Experimental evaluations on MNIST and five multivariate time-series classification datasets demonstrate that, with fully on-chip training, our SNN model achieves accuracy comparable to SNN or LSTM trained with BPTT. Compared to CPU and GPU based implementations, our FPGA design delivers 2.5 to 6 times higher throughput while consuming an order of magnitude less energy per sample.

title: Imaging the topological sign of a Dirac mass with spin-polarized tunneling
abstract: A Dirac mass is characterized not only by its magnitude but also by its sign, which influences the Berry curvature, Hall response, and the propagation direction of chiral boundary modes. However, local spectroscopy of magnetic topological surfaces has so far accessed only the gap magnitude $|M|$. Here we show how the topological sign of $M$ can be determined locally. We first establish the sign information that spin-resolved tunneling can access and the reference required to obtain an absolute Hall sign. Although spin--orbital entanglement generally obscures the relation between measured spin and Dirac pseudospin, crystalline rotation symmetry alleviates this ambiguity at the band edge. On a $C_3$ axis, an axial tip couples to a fully spin-polarized state whose tunneling asymmetry directly reveals the sign of the occupied-band Berry curvature, independent of orbital composition. We further show that the zeroth Landau level provides an independent mass-sign measurement with an unpolarized tip, while opposite domains and their chiral domain-wall modes provide self-consistency checks. These results pave the way for imaging the locations where the topological character changes within a material, rather than merely identifying where a spectral gap appears.

title: Optimal Feature-Based Newsvendor Policies under Censored Demand
abstract: We investigate a newsvendor problem where a decision-maker observes a z-dimensional vector of covariates, and wants to learn how much stock to order given a sample of size n of censored demand data to minimize costs. Demand is censored when insufficient stock is available to meet it, and past stocking quantities are known. We propose a new model-agnostic loss function approach to estimate optimal order quantities using observational data, and characterize the optimal newsvendor policy as the policy that minimizes our proposed loss function. Our method requires only a single estimation step, can be scaled to datasets with hundreds of thousands of data points, and does not suffer from the same instabilities as inverse censoring probability weighting methods. We describe how this loss function can be implemented in linear empirical risk minimization, kernel weights optimization and deep neural network algorithms, and provide excess risk generalization bounds for their out-of-sample performance. Moreover, we show through numerical experiments that our method quickly converges to the optimal policy on synthetic data, and leads to improved performance on real world retail data.

title: Efficient Fréchet Distributional Decoder Alignment for Latent Generative Models
abstract: Fréchet Distributional (FD) objectives provide an effective distribution-level signal for post-training generative models. For latent generative models, however, existing FD-based post-training methods optimize only the latent generator while keeping the decoder frozen: the decoder is trained on reconstruction latents obtained from real images but deployed on generator-produced latents at generation time. When these latent distributions differ, this \textbf{decoder train-generation mismatch} means that the decoder is deployed on inputs drawn from a distribution it was not directly trained on. We introduce \textbf{Fréchet Distributional Decoder Alignment (FDDA)}, an efficient post-training method that freezes the latent generator and directly optimizes the decoder on generation-time latents using an FD objective. A single epoch of FDDA consistently improves gFID and gFDr$^6$ across diverse flow-based and autoregressive latent generative models. Across all 11 evaluated models, FDDA reduces gFDr$^6$ by 34.0-59.6\% from the original pretrained models and provides a further 10.2-57.2\% reduction after generator-side FD post-training. FDDA also reduces total wall-clock time by factors of $3.6\times$-$328.7\times$ relative to generator-side FD post-training across these models. These results show that generator-side post-training alone does not exhaust the benefits of FD optimization, and that further gains can be obtained by adapting the decoder at substantially lower cost.

title: Computed, not Memorized: Bit-Factorized Identifiers for Efficient Generative Retrieval
abstract: Generative retrieval is known for its efficient end-to-end indexing and retrieval. In particular, numeric Document Identifiers (DocIDs) are generally more efficient because they are shorter and generally fixed-length sequences over a small vocabulary, requiring fewer decoding steps during beam search. However, they tend to generalize poorly to unseen documents and must be learned during indexing-stage training. In this paper, we propose a numeric DocID design for generative retrieval that enables better adaptation to unseen documents without retraining. Our DocID design inherits the language model's knowledge: each DocID is a sequence of tokens factorized into bits, and each token is scored as the sum of its bits. Unlike existing numeric DocIDs, whose tokens carry meaning only through embeddings memorized during indexing training, each bit here derives its meaning from the model's representation. Therefore, the DocIDs of unseen documents remain scorable without retraining. Experiments on three benchmarks show that our DocID design substantially improves unseen-document retrieval while maintaining comparable performance on seen documents. It achieves over 20 percentage points higher Hit@10 on unseen documents and up to 7 times lower inference latency than existing numeric DocID designs on NQ320K and TriviaQA, while performing only 3 percentage points below weight-update methods on MS MARCO without additional training. These results show that an appropriate DocID design can heavily reduce retraining costs when adapting generative retrievers to new documents.

title: From Orbit Matching to Docking: A Hierarchical Reinforcement-Learning Approach to Multiphase Rendezvous Trajectory Design
abstract: As the complexity of space missions increases, autonomous spacecraft guidance must accommodate transitions between mission phases with distinct dynamics, objectives, and constraints. Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) are particularly challenging because they span multiple operating regimes, from orbital-scale matching and far-range approach to close-range maneuvering and terminal docking. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches generally address only a subset of this sequence or rely on manually defined switching conditions between controllers. This study presents a hierarchical reinforcement-learning framework for autonomous, three-degree-of-freedom RPO that spans the complete trajectory from orbit matching to docking. Five specialized policies are trained for orbit matching, far-range approach, mid-range approach, close-range approach, and docking. A learned high-level manager policy then selects among these phase-specific controllers based on the evolving spacecraft state. The hierarchical approach is evaluated over the full end-to-end rendezvous sequence and compared with a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic to assess trajectory performance and transition behavior. Training and inference metrics are also analyzed for the individual phase policies and the complete hierarchical system.

title: Assessing the Performance of AI Models in Misinformation Detection Using Predefined Social Noise Constructs
abstract: Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated content that often obscure meaningful discourse, a phenomenon conceptualized as social noise. While existing misinformation detection methods primarily focus on factual verification, they largely overlook the role of social noise in amplifying misinformation. This study assesses the performance of six text-based models and a graph neural network (GNN) in mitigating the effects of misinformation using predefined social noise constructs. The dataset consists of 500,000 tweets collected from the X platform using the Ukraine hashtag during the Russia-Ukraine conflict from March 2024 to March 2025. Advanced machine learning models achieve strong performance, with accuracies ranging from 79.94% to 97.17%. RoBERTa demonstrates the highest performance, with an accuracy of 97.17%, Cohen's kappa of 0.9660, MCC of 0.9660, and AUC of 0.9977. The GNN achieves an accuracy of 64.52% and an AUC of 0.899, demonstrating performance above random-chance classification by exploiting the relational structure between tweets. All text-based models achieve kappa values greater than 0.75, indicating substantial overall agreement. Explainable AI analysis using LIME reveals that 89.6% of predictive weight is attributed to contextual features rather than isolated keywords. The findings highlight that integrating social noise into AI pipelines enhances misinformation detection and supports more effective mitigation strategies in large-scale social media environments.

title: Time-Domain Observables for Resonant Scattering in Quantum Simulations of Lattice Gauge Theory
abstract: Quantum computing may allow unprecedented access to nonequilibrium quantum dynamics, including problems of interest in particle physics, like the real-time development of scattering processes. Although fault-tolerant simulations at scale are still in the future, recent advancements toward early fault-tolerant simulations motivate building increasingly elaborate benchmark problems in order to assess state-of-the-art capabilities and test new algorithms and observables. In this work, we study glueball scattering on a line-of-plaquettes lattice in pure $SU(3)$ lattice gauge theory. We characterize scattering of the lowest-energy glueball states using classical exact diagonalization methods, identifying the continuum resonance structure using real-time simulations and approximate analytic methods, and we propose time-domain observables for extracting properties of the resonance from quantum simulations. We furthermore construct a toy model that shares the spectral features of the lattice gauge theory and demonstrate extraction of the observables. Feasibility on near-term hardware is demonstrated through simulation of a resonant collision of this toy model on Quantinuum System Model $\texttt{H2-2}$, with a 14-plaquette chain encoded in 28 qubits. The Trotterized circuit after optimization and compression requires $\sim 25n$ entangling gates for $n$ Trotter steps.

title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents
abstract: Multi-agent systems promise a new axis for scaling inference: rather than having one agent think longer or sample more attempts, a task is split across many agents that work in parallel and coordinate. However, in practice, more agents can easily produce duplicate work, coordination failures, and higher costs. We therefore formulate team design as a compute allocation problem: starting from a solo agent, where should additional inference compute go to reach the reward-cost Pareto frontier? We build a minimal multi-agent harness from the ground up and trace this frontier by varying, one at a time, the workflow stage at which a lead delegates to its workers (planning, implementation, or verification), the models that form the team, and the number of workers. On ProgramBench, teams outperform solo agents but cost three to seven times as much. With the right compute allocation, however, a heterogeneous 17-agent team comes within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost. This efficiency stems from three findings. First, planning is the most valuable use of workers: in a homogeneous team whose lead decides how many workers to spawn, a lead that delegates only planning to its workers, and then implements and verifies the code itself, matches the reward of a lead that delegates to workers throughout planning, implementation, and verification, at half the cost. Second, cheap models pay off as planners but not as implementers: a strong lead with cheap planners recovers 47.5% of the reward gain of an all-strong team for only 13.9% of its additional cost, whereas cheap implementers lower reward. Third, planners keep improving reward as the team grows, whereas implementers and verifiers plateau beyond four workers. Together, our results offer a guide to spending an agent budget where it counts, given the task, cost, and latency constraints a user has.

title: Compactness of Cone Yang-Mills Connections
abstract: We consider the cone Yang-Mills functional recently introduced by Tseng and Zhou. This functional generalizes the Yang-Mills functional by coupling it to a closed 2-form which can represent a geometric structure of interest, e.g. a symplectic form or Ricci form. While the perspective of dimensional reduction is not always possible, we show that a cone Yang-Mills field is always locally the dimensional reduction of a pure Yang-Mills field. We then prove a monotonicity formula and use the dimensional reduction framework to prove an $ε$-regularity theorem in two ways. Finally, we prove a compactness theorem for sequences of cone Yang-Mills connections with bounded action and $L^p$-bounded Higgs fields. Away from a singular set of codimension at least 4 and after suitable bundle identifications, the sequence subconverges in the $C^\infty_{\operatorname{loc}}$-topology.

title: REA: From Correct LLM Judgments to Safe Decision Delivery
abstract: Generative safety guards must classify requests correctly and return outputs that applications can parse. Reasoning guards can improve classification accuracy while producing outputs that applications cannot parse. When applications cannot extract a correct prediction, fallback handling can allow harmful requests or block safe ones. We introduce Resolve--Express--Act (REA), a framework that traces judgments through parsing and fallback to application actions. Experiments on classifiers and safety guards show that correct predictions can appear in incorrectly formatted outputs. Parsing the safety verdict preserves the reasoning guard's accuracy advantage, while stricter explanation requirements reject additional correct predictions. Accepting formatting variations recovers most rejected correct predictions. Held-out tests confirm that output requirements and generation limits affect whether correct predictions can be parsed. In our fail-open replay, matching the parser to the output and fixing formatting reduced the fraction of harmful requests allowed despite correct guard judgments from 95.5% to 0%. A fixed-output comparison shows that model-based extraction can preserve guard verdicts, but is not automatically reliable; deterministic normalization already repairs the observed native-format failures. Fallback replay shows that the same correct prediction can lead to different safety actions depending on the parser and fallback policy, including allowing requests the guard correctly identifies as harmful.

title: HoOPOE: A Holography-Optimized Perceptual ObjectivE function
abstract: Holographic devices must reconstruct an entire light field given a finite number of spatial light modulator (SLM) pixels, and must do so using scalar-wave diffraction from coherent illumination alone. As a result, computer-generated holography (CGH) often has speckling artifacts. We propose HoOPOE (Holography-Optimized Perceptual ObjectivE function), a CGH-specific, perceptually-aware loss function that hides speckles from human vision. HoOPOE is effective for CGH optimizations because it accounts for the human visual system's sensitivity to spatio-temporal frequencies and color, and its parameters are tuned to maximize its performance as a loss function for CGH. We use HoOPOE to generate holograms for mesh-derived focal stacks. We then conduct a user study to benchmark HoOPOE-generated holograms against existing loss functions. HoOPOE yields the most visually pleasing results; users prefer HoOPOE 68% of the time over the next best objective function on average.

title: Mathematical framework for simulation of non-perturbative cavity optomechanics with plate-like dielectrics
abstract: Cavity optomechanical models typically treat a sensor either as a perturbative polarizable object in a pre-existing optical field, or solve the field at a fixed equilibrium and linearize in a fixed optical-mode basis. Neither self-consistently determines the spatially resolved cavity field, the optical force, the mechanical equilibrium, and the back-action when a finite-thickness dielectric plate intercepts the entire optical mode and restructures the intracavity field. In this companion paper to [1], we develop that treatment by extending the vacuum two-photon formalism to finite-thickness planar dielectrics, incorporating their Fresnel reflection, internal propagation, optical forces, and mechanical back-action directly into the field equations. We derive the carrier and sideband transfer functions needed to describe the coupled optical-mechanical system, including optomechanical cooling and the response to external perturbations. The result is a systematic starting point for calculating detector response and noise budgets for cavity experiments with intracavity dielectrics, including gravitational wave detectors deploying levitated sensors.

title: $a$-Numbers, higher Cartier ranks and maximality of van der Geer-van der Vlugt curves
abstract:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $C_R$ be the van der Geer-van der Vlugt curve $y^p-y=xR(x)$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$, where $R(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{h}a_ix^{p^i}$ is an additive polynomial of degree $p^h$. We determine the image and the rank of every power of the Cartier operator $\Cart$ on $H^0(C_R,\Omg)$. For $1\le r\le h-1$ the image of $\Cart^r$ is spanned by an explicit set of monomial differentials that does not depend on $R$, and $ank(\Cart^r)=p^{h-r-1} inom{p+r}{r+2}$. The last iterate detects the linear coefficient: $ank(\Cart^h)=0$ if $a_0=0$ and $ank(\Cart^h)= inom{(p-1)/2+h}{h+1}$ if $a_0
eq0$, so the nilpotency index of $\Cart$ is $h$ or $h+1$. Hence, for $h\ge2$, the loci $a_0=0$ and $a_0
e0$ have the same $a$-number, which is the largest $a$-number of a one-point Artin-Schreier curve with pole order $p^h+1$, but they share no Ekedahl-Oort type. Over finite fields we deduce that a curve over $\F_{p^{2n}}$ that is geometrically isomorphic to $C_R$ can be $\F_{p^{2n}}$-maximal or $\F_{p^{2n}}$-minimal only if $n\ge h$, and only if $n\ge h+1$ when $a_0
eq0$. Explicit examples show that the second bound is attained for $(p,h)=(3,1)$, $(3,2)$ and $(5,2)$.

title: Balancing cost and demand in a smart grid - a mean-field game analysis
abstract: In a smart grid, consumers can also play the role of producers and sellers of energy. Therefore, the control of a smart grid over time becomes a dynamic game with a large number of small players and one or several large players. This is much more complicated than the control of an energy system with a single producer. The framework of mean-field games with common noise allows the transformation of such a complicated model into a control problem for a typical prosumer (producer and consumer in one) optimizing his behavior against a flow of other such prosumers. In our model, we introduce 2 decision variables for such a controller: one describing the amount of electric energy bought from the grid (or sold to it), and the second one describing the charging rate for our battery. The cost function is designed to satisfy two goals: satisfying the demand of the consumer (a single home) and minimizing the payment for energy. Players are allowed to sell/buy energy from the grid. Common noise is hidden in price volatility and sun irradiance, which influence all the players. We compute the optimal controls for our model and simulate solutions on real data. The novelty of our construction, compared to other works on smart grid control, lies in combining the minimization of the cost of energy and sustaining some level of demand satisfaction. We analyze the impact of battery usage on achieving a balance between these two criteria. We also take into account that the smart grid is only part of the energy market, which makes consumer strategies dependent on energy consumption outside the grid.

title: Energy-Efficient RF Chain Activation for Uplink mmWave Cell-Free Massive MIMO Systems: A Minimum-Cost Maximum-Flow Approach
abstract: With the incessant demand for green and sustainable communications, energy efficiency (EE) has become a cornerstone of sixth-generation (6G) network design, especially for cell-free millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, which can achieve significant throughput gains by leveraging large-scale antenna arrays. Adaptive radio frequency (RF) chain activation (ARFA) is a key technique for reducing power consumption without severely degrading the achievable rate, thereby enhancing the total EE of 6G MIMO systems. In this paper, we propose a minimum-cost maximum-flow (MCMF)-based ARFA scheme to reduce unnecessary power consumption and maximize the total EE of uplink mmWave cell-free massive MIMO systems. Simulation results indicate that the proposed approach can significantly improve the total EE while maintaining a relatively high achievable rate and acceptable computational complexity.

title: Limit Theorems for the Complete Feedback Card Guessing Game
abstract: We study the optimal score $T_{n,m}$ in a complete feedback card guessing game. The deck has $n$ types and $m$ cards of each type. Its predictable compensator $S_{n,m}$ is the sum of the conditional success probabilities. We prove that Var$(S_{n,m})\leq C((\log\log n)^2+m/\log n)$, uniformly in $m$ for large $n$. This bound yields a central limit theorem for every sequence $m=m_n\geq1$ as $n\to\infty$. The score variance is asymptotic to its mean. We also give uniform Kolmogorov bounds using the conditional Bernoulli moments. For $m,n\to\infty$, the excess mean is asymptotic to $(\log n)\log\min\{m,\log n\}+(π/\sqrt2)\sqrt{m\log n}$. The two contributions balance at $m\asymp(\log n)(\log\log n)^2$. The variance proof uses reversed occupancy hitting times. Discrete hypergeometric tail estimates control their fluctuations in the large-deviation, Gaussian, and saturation regimes. For fixed $n$, we also show that the compensator has a Brownian-bridge functional limit as $m\to\infty$.

title: Resonant JPZ algebras and 3D Chern--Simons gravity
abstract: In this work we construct three-dimensional Chern--Simons gravity theories for the six resonant $JPZ$ algebras generated by the Lorentz generators $J_a$, translations $P_a$, and an additional Lorentz-like generator $Z_a$. The resonance condition together with the Jacobi identities leaves precisely six configurations arising from the semigroup expansions. Our main result is that three of them, $B_4$, $\widetilde C_4$, and $C_4$, are isomorphic to $iso(2,1)\oplus so(2,1)$, although they yield different gravitational realizations when we keep the original $JPZ$ field identification fixed. For each case $JPZ$, we determine the invariant tensors, gauge curvatures, Chern--Simons action, field equations, and the corresponding maximal-rank coupling sectors. The field equations can be written in the compact form $Ω_σ\mathbf F=0$, which makes explicit how the additional field $h^a$ contributes to the curvature, torsion, and the remaining gauge-curvature components. We use the direct-sum isomorphisms to classify the local metric sectors and to relate them to known global and asymptotic solutions, while keeping the gravitational interpretation tied to the original $(ω,e,h)$ fields.

title: Designing Independent Variation: A Guided Iteration Methodology for Price Experiments in Short, Correlated Panels
abstract: Estimation error in short, correlated pricing panels is dominated by trajectory dispersion rather than sampling noise, creating an identification shortfall that only independently assigned variation can resolve. We propose a guided iteration methodology to decide how much variation to generate, where, and for how long: a cyclic price-perturbation scheme under a revenue-at-risk budget, framed as variance minimization over design-specific error covariances, analogous to portfolio selection. We establish four key results: (1) a closed-form minimum-variance combination rule; (2) proof that a convex cost of intensity yields an interior, spread-out allocation, whereas under a concave tolerable-volume-loss cost, concentrating intensity into fewer perturbations pays off only with heterogeneous candidates, priced-in fixed costs, or perturbations beyond the cost curve's inflection point; (3) a discounted recursion yielding a data-dependent exit timeline from the experimentation zone; and (4) an application to Dominick's retail data, in which about five designed independent units match the precision of approximately 700 passive equivalents in the anchor category, while a fast proxy across ten categories achieves a median 97% variance reduction relative to passive panels. Sixteen comparisons (eleven pre-specified) support the theory: greedy selection achieves 90-93% of the global optimum across more than fifty exhaustively verifiable instances, and the recursion reaches its predicted 90%-of-steady-state benchmark two cycles early, though a parametric bootstrap indicates that its delta-method interval understates the right-tail risk. Boundary conditions show that regularized covariance estimators extend plug-in noise tolerance from 29% to beyond 50%, submodularity holds up to a clear curvature threshold, and a shared shock imposes a fundamental precision floor.

title: Cyclic reflections and the flip equation for the graded Grothendieck-Teichmüller group
abstract: Furusho, Hirose and Komiyama reformulated the pentagon equation using an involution called the flip, which led to a new characterisation of the graded Grothendieck-Teichmüller group $\mathsf{GRT}_1$. We show that the flip is a reflection in the cyclic structure of the operad of framed Drinfeld-Kohno Lie algebras, with the framings removed. Applying the reflection twice to the pentagon gives the two-cycle relation for every Drinfeld associator. This relation is precisely the condition for cyclic compatibility on the associativity morphism, giving a new proof that $\mathsf{GRT}_1$ acts by cyclic automorphisms of parenthesized ribbon chord diagrams.

title: Structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics for partial differential equations
abstract: Machine learning surrogates of partial differential equations (PDEs) are commonly trained on data generated by numerical solvers. Therefore, the training data obey not the PDE but the modified equation of the numerical scheme, and the test loss, computed on data from the same solver, cannot distinguish a model that learned the physics from one that learned the discretization error. Here, we show that the difference is nevertheless visible in the trained model. We propose a suite of structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics, simple scores that measure whether a learned model respects one known property of the physics, such as a conserved quantity, a symmetry or a Hamiltonian structure, without access to the training data or the governing equation. Over five systems, the diagnostics track the error with respect to the true dynamics with a rank correlation of up to $0.94$, while the test loss is uncorrelated or anti-correlated with it. For the Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries and Navier-Stokes equations, the diagnostics separate numerical schemes that the test loss ranks as equivalent, including schemes of the same order. order.

title: Fundamental Limits of Prescribed-Time Regulation: Gain Budgets, Accuracy Frontiers, and Arrival Costs
abstract: Prescribed-time controllers drive the state to the origin at a time $T$ chosen in advance, with gains that grow without bound as $t$ approaches $T$. This paper shows the growth is a necessity and computes the exact price of avoiding it. The starting point is a simple estimate: any trajectory with $\|\dot z(t)\|\le L(t)\|z(t)\|$ satisfies $\|z(t)\|\ge\|z(0)\|e^{-\int_0^t L}$. From this: a gain profile $L$ supports exact prescribed-time convergence, over the unrestricted class of closed-loop vector fields admitting it, if and only if its integral over $[0,T)$ is infinite; so every design must either use an envelope of infinite integral or violate the linear growth bound at the origin, as finite-time and fixed-time designs do. Under a finite gain budget $\mathcal B=\int_0^T L$ the best worst-case contraction over the class is exactly $e^{-\mathcal B}$, a floor valid for every plant, and a finite-budget trajectory converges to a definite point away from the origin. A comparison lemma then carries the theory beyond linear growth: for envelopes $\|\dot z\|\le L(t)\,ω(\|z\|)$, first arrival at the origin requires budget at least $\int_0^{\|z_0\|}du/ω(u)$; arrival is impossible whenever this integral diverges, and when it is finite it is the exact threshold, attained inside the class. The classical settling expressions of finite-time control reappear as hitting-time floors, and the known fixed-time condition is the two-ended convergence of the same integral.
