Geometric analysis further supports this pattern: evil vectors from the two high-resource languages are closely aligned, whereas low-resource vectors align only weakly with this shared direction. These results suggest that a shared cross-lingual evil direction exists and, once reliably extracted from a high-resource language, can be reused to steer behavior in low-resource languages without additional per-language data collection.

title: Agentic Robot Creation through Generation, Verification, and Revision
abstract: Can an AI agent turn high-level user intent into a functioning robot and teach it how to behave? We study this question from two complementary aspects: embodiment and behavior creation. For embodiment creation, we investigate how well current multimodal models capture mechanical requirements, and introduce computational metrics for evaluating generated designs before fabrication. For behavior creation, we present Roboforge, an agentic framework that turns task specifications into executable policies through motion generation, policy learning, and execution-grounded revision. Given a robot embodiment and task, the agent generates a reference motion, configures the learning objective, and trains a policy. Crucially, motion remains in the loop: rollout feedback can revise the reference motion, reward, or both. We evaluate a generated embodiment across multiple MLLMs and behavior creation across four diverse robots against reward-refinement and one-shot motion baselines. Our computational metrics expose recurring mechanical failures in generated designs, while behavior experiments show that execution-grounded refinement improves task-level behavior and execution quality. Finally, we fabricate an agent-generated Gorilla and directly deploy learned behaviors on the physical robot.

title: Diagnose-to-Generate: Eliminating Structural Distortions in Flow Models via Patch-Level Grounded Alignment
abstract: Flow-based image generators achieve strong semantic synthesis but still produce localized structural distortions, such as malformed hands and limbs. Existing post-training methods typically optimize global scalar rewards, which provide weak spatial credit assignment and may alter well-formed regions while correcting local defects. We present \textit{Diagnose-to-Generate (D2G)}, a grounded alignment framework that separates visual diagnosis from generative optimization. We construct \textbf{Achilles-600K}, a region-annotated dataset for structural anomalies, and train \textbf{ARGUS} through supervised cold-start and Region-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization to predict anomaly categories and bounding boxes. These diagnoses are converted into confidence-weighted spatial rewards for our \textbf{Patch-level Flow-GRPO}. We further identify that global stochastic exploration can shift semantic regions across group rollouts, making patch-wise relative advantages spatially inconsistent. Our \textbf{Trajectory-Preserving Stochastic Sampling (TPSS)} anchors early denoising with deterministic ODE trajectories and introduces stochasticity only at later steps, thereby limiting intra-group spatial drift while retaining local exploration. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev and SD3.5 show improved structural fidelity with preserved FID and CLIP scores. Consistent gains under HumanRefiner, zero-shot GPT-4.1, and blinded human evaluation further demonstrate that the improvements extend beyond the training reward model.

title: Dynamics of low energy wave packets in the one-dimensional quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet
abstract: Spin wave theory plays a central role in the analysis of low-energy properties of the quantum ferromagnetic Heisenberg model. In this work, we present a first step towards a rigorous justification of this approximation in the context of quantum dynamics in one dimension. According to spin wave theory, the evolution of a spin wave state should be well approximated by its free evolution with the appropriate energy of free quasiparticles called magnons. Our main result establishes this idea rigorously for a class of spin wave packets. We focus on spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ systems, and consider wave packets composed of two magnons. We argue our result is optimal with respect to the timescales.

title: The chromatic number of $G$-stable Kneser graphs
abstract: Extending the notions of Kneser graphs and Schrijver graphs, we define the $G$-stable Kneser graph $KG(G,k)$ (where $k\geq 2$ and $G$ is a graph on $n\geq 2k$ vertices) as the graph whose vertices are the $k$-element independent sets in $G$ and whose edges join pairs of disjoint independent sets. The well-known result of Lovász on the chromatic number of Kneser graphs implies that $χ(KG(G,k)) \leq n-2k+2$ for any $G$. We call $G$ $k$-tight if equality holds, and we study the following question: Which graphs are $k$-tight? A result of Daneshpajouh et al.\ implies a characterization of $2$-tight graphs. We prove a necessary condition for a graph to be $k$-tight for $k\geq 3$ which extends this characterization, and we conjecture it to be sufficient. Another result gives a lower bound to the chromatic number of the $G$-stable Kneser graphs when $G$ is a disjoint union of cycles. We use this result to give a short proof of the fact that $4$-regular graphs on $3k$ vertices consisting of two vertex-disjoint cycles and $k$ cycles of length $3$ admit an independent set of size $k$.

title: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics
abstract: Microscopic simulations resolve spatial patterns but are feasible only over small domains and short timescales, whereas bulk descriptions erase those patterns through spatial averaging. Mesoscopic fields preserve this spatial organisation, but their effective equations are known only for selected microscopic systems and scaling limits. We introduce Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics (DeepMesoD), which uses neural networks to learn an effective mesoscopic field equation from microscopic trajectories at a prescribed coarse-graining scale. For the nonconserved dissipative dynamics studied here, DeepMesoD learns the free-energy functional with a spatial interaction kernel and a state-dependent dissipation operator constrained by the fluctuation-dissipation relation. We first validate the construction in the Ising-Kac model, where the learned mesoscopic equation recovers the known hydrodynamic limit and rollouts remain stable far beyond the training horizon. We then treat two systems without closed-form mesoscopic descriptions. For a two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet governed by atomistic spin dynamics, DeepMesoD learns a mesoscopic model whose predictions match atomistic references up to 1 ns, and a rollout with an unseen initial condition remains bounded up to 25 ns. For layered CrBr$_3$, the learned kernel captures the suppression and sign reversal of interlayer coupling at a stacking fault whose location and strength are not supplied as inputs. Controlled changes to the learned interaction show how fault number and placement shape multistep magnetic responses, complementing our magneto-photoluminescence measurements. Across the two atomistic systems, DeepMesoD achieves a three-to-four-order-of-magnitude reduction in wall-clock time compared with atomistic spin dynamics.

title: Compositional Information Geometry of Probabilistic Programs
abstract: We study the compositional, intensional information geometry of probabilistic programs. For a first-order probabilistic programming language with finite random variables, we construct a contravariant lax monoidal functor that, for a program of type $X \to Y$, pulls back a (degenerate) Riemannian metric on $Y$ to $X$. It specialises to the Fisher metric in the case of standard statistical models and to ordinary pullback in the case of deterministic programs. We further justify this construction in two ways. First, we show that this functor arises as a pullback of geometry from a universal space of programs over a type $Y$ with a fixed trace space. Second, we show that it is a special case of a more general pullback construction over weighted measures. Our compositional geometry depends on the presentation of the program, and we study how it relates to the (non-compositional) geometry of the realised measures by establishing a three-level inequality relating our score-velocity metric for the program, the program's corresponding output-conditioned metric, and the standard Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric of the realised family. Finally, we show how the theory can be extended to accommodate continuous random variables using diffeological quasi-Borel spaces. We also discuss several concrete directions for future work.

title: Path Length Existence Problems in Bounded-Treewidth Probabilistic Graphs
abstract: We consider the problem of computing the probability of existence of a source-to-target path or walk satisfying a given length constraint in an input probabilistic graph. The length constraints we consider can require the length to be at least $\ell$, at most $\ell$, or exactly $\ell$, for $\ell$ a target length given as input. The probabilistic graphs that we consider are directed graphs where each edge is annotated with an independent probability of existence. As this task is generally intractable (#P-hard), we aim for algorithms applying to input graphs that are assumed to be of bounded treewidth. We classify the complexity landscape of these problems: - We give an XP algorithm parameterised by treewidth to compute the probability that an input probabilistic graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length $\geq \ell$, and do the same for a path/walk of length $\leq \ell$. - We show that the four problems mentioned in the last item are W[1]-hard parameterised by pathwidth (hence not FPT under the standard assumption that FPT$\neq$W[1]). This is in contrast to the case of non-probabilistic graphs, where the corresponding problems were known to be FPT parameterised by treewidth; and to the connectivity problem (and more generally MSO evaluation) on probabilistic graphs, where the same was known. - Surprisingly, we show that it is #P-hard to compute the probability that an input graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length exactly $\ell$, even on graphs of pathwidth $2$. By contrast, all our problems are tractable on graphs of treewidth $1$. - Last, we investigate the complexity of our problems when the edges can carry weights. This causes all our problems to become #P-hard already on pathwidth-2 graphs, and causes specifically the ``exactly $\ell$'' walk problem to be #P-hard even on pathwidth-1 graphs.

title: Multiplicity One for Five Strongly Tempered Spherical Varieties
abstract: Let $F$ be a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic zero. We prove multiplicity one for every irreducible smooth admissible representation in the split forms of Wan-Zhang Models 6-10. Combining the Gelfand-Kazhdan method with nilpotent-wavefront restrictions on Bernstein-finite equivariant distributions, we establish the required symmetries through rational orbit analysis, parabolic descent, stabilizer characters, and conormal arguments. The type-$D_6$ analysis treats both the vector-similitude group of Model 9 and the semispin form arising in the exceptional $E_7$ model. For Model 10, the distribution theorem gives a product bound for periods; the individual multiplicity bound follows from Langlands classification and a vanishing theorem for standard modules induced from nongeneric tempered data on the maximal $E_6$ Levi.

title: Size, atmospheric, and ring constraints on the large Kuiper belt object (55565) Aya from a stellar occultation
abstract: We aim to constrain the projected size, geometric albedo, possible atmosphere, and possible ring material of the mid-sized trans-Neptunian object (55565) Aya from the stellar occultation of 2024 May 10 (UT). We observed the event from three Japanese sites with high-cadence optical imaging. We combined one positive occultation chord with an informative prior on the shadow centre derived from orbital and astrometric uncertainties, and inferred the body radius with Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo modelling. We constrained a possible atmosphere by fitting refraction models for pure CH$_4$, N$_2$, and CO atmospheres to multi-band light curves, and searched for ring-like extinction signatures in unbinned and binned high-time-resolution photometry. We derive an equivalent radius, i.e., the radius of the circle fitted to the projected shadow, of $r=401^{+28}_{-40}$ km for Aya, corresponding to a geometric albedo of $p_V=0.101^{+0.023}_{-0.013}$. This estimate is insensitive to the adopted ephemeris solution and is consistent with an ephemeris-independent analysis that makes no assumption about the position of the shadow centre. We obtain 3$σ$ upper limits on the atmospheric surface pressure of $p_0=60$, 90, and 80 nbar for pure CH$_4$, N$_2$, and CO compositions, respectively. No significant ring-like extinction is detected over projected distances of about 430-8060 km sampled by the three stations, and our most sensitive data exclude dense narrow features with apparent opacity $p'\gtrsim0.1$ and radial widths of a few kilometres or larger over $\sim3r$-$14r$. This is the first stellar occultation by Aya ever observed. In addition to constraining Aya's size and albedo and finding no ring-like extinction, we place a stringent atmospheric upper limit that supports diversity in atmospheric states among similarly sized trans-Neptunian objects.

title: Metaplectic-c prequantizations and the Einstein--Brillouin--Keller quantizability condition
abstract: We show that every symplectic manifold admits a symplectic form whose metaplectic-c prequantizations give quantizability conditions on all its Lagrangian submanifolds. Metaplectic-c prequantizations descend to prequantizations over the Lagrangian Grassmannian bundle that are fibrewise flat with holonomies primitive fourth roots of unity on the generators of the fundamental groups. This fibrewise holonomy is consistently interpreted as that of both Leray two-orientations and normalized Blattner--Kostant--Sternberg half-forms. The prequantizations pull back to flat circle bundles on each Lagrangian submanifold whose holonomy character defines a quantizability condition. The first and second Stiefel--Whitney classes are identified as splitting obstructions to the Lagrangianwise holonomies. These holonomies split into a product of holonomies on any orientable Lagrangian submanifold, and split consistently for all Lagrangian submanifolds of a manifold with metaplectic structure. When the first Chern class vanishes, the holonomy splits into the Bohr--Sommerfeld factor and a quarter phase Maslov correction, recovering the classical Einstein--Brillouin--Keller condition. We develop the underlying obstruction theory for circle extensions associated to general Lie group double coverings with first hypercohomology groupoids.

title: The logarithmic exponent of the Ramsey number $r(4,t)$
abstract: We prove that $r(4,t) \ge \frac{t^3}{(\log t)^{2+o(1)}}$. This improves the lower bound of Mattheus and Verstraëte (Ann. of Math., 2024) by a factor of $(\log t)^{2-o(1)}$.

title: Provable Method of Moments for Cryo-EM
abstract: We study the recovery of a three-dimensional volume in single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) from noisy tomographic projections acquired at unknown viewing rotations, drawn independently and uniformly from $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. We show that, in a spherical-shell representation satisfying an explicit shell-separation condition, the first three moments generically determine the underlying real volume up to its intrinsic global $\mathrm{O}(3)$ ambiguity. The proof is constructive and yields a frequency-marching procedure that successively recovers the volume. Consequently, consistent recovery in the high-noise regime has sample complexity $n=ω(σ^6)$, where $n$ is the number of observations and $σ^2$ is the noise variance. Numerical experiments validate the constructive recovery scheme under finite sampling and additive noise, and indicate that direct third-moment optimization can succeed beyond the structural assumptions required by the constructive proof.

title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.

title: Swiss4Arg: A Parallel Dataset for Multilingual Argument Mining across Swiss National Languages
abstract: We present Swiss4Arg, a multilingual dataset for argument mining based on official Swiss voting brochures, covering all four national languages: German, French, Italian, and Romansh (a Romance minority language exclusively spoken in Switzerland). The brochures contain explicitly formulated arguments systematically organized into pro and con sections, resulting in a cross-lingually aligned resource with balanced argumentative stance. We create a dataset that comprises 53 federal voting issues collected between 2019 and 2025, annotated for argument components (major claims, claims, premises, and non-argumentative units) and relations (support and attack) by three native speakers per language. Inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's alpha) reaches 0.548 for component classification and 0.623 for relation and target classification, computed jointly across all annotators on the parallel data. We release both adjudicated labels and individual annotator annotations, enabling analyses of disagreement and cross-linguistic variation, and provide baseline results using GPT-5.4 and SwissBERT. Swiss4Arg establishes a novel benchmark for multilingual argument mining, with a particular focus on cross-lingual comparability and low-resource settings such as Romansh. The dataset and code are publicly available at https://anonymous-hf.up.railway.app/a/gozw0nion72y/ (HuggingFace) and https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MultiVote-03BD/ (GitHub).

title: Interaction-as-a-Judge
abstract: Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.

title: Cumulus parameterization controls simulated rainfall more than microphysics, but not at heavy thresholds: a 3 * 2 factorial WRF study over the Western Himalaya
abstract: Rainfall forecasts over the Western Himalaya remain poor, and the relative contributions of the cumulus and microphysics parameterizations to that error are not well constrained.

title: The Maximum Nonlinearity of 8-variable Balanced Boolean Functions is 116
abstract: Does there exist an 8-variable balanced Boolean function with nonlinearity 118? This is a famous and long-standing open problem in Boolean functions. In this paper, we give a negative answer to this open problem, and prove that the maximum nonlinearity of balanced Boolean functions in 8 variables is 116, establishing the 8-variable instance of Dobbertin's conjectured recursion for the minimum Walsh peak of balanced functions. Equivalently, the covering radius of the Reed--Muller code RM(1,8) in 0-resilient Boolean functions is 116. We deduce the result by obtaining a quadratic form of polar rank 6, and reducing the problem to the existence of a 6-variable Boolean function with nonlinearity greater than 26 whose Hamming distance to a bent function is between 4 and 6.

title: Evaluating the Causal Faithfulness of SHAP as a Candidate Attribution Method for SAE Features
abstract: Sparse autoencoders decompose language model representations into interpretable features, but feature interpretation in this literature remains predominantly correlational. Attribution methods offer more direct estimates of feature influence, yet their faithfulness to actual causal effects has not been systematically evaluated in the SAE setting. We apply SHAP-based attribution to SAE latent features and evaluate it against direct causal intervention, using sentiment classification on SST-2 with GPT-2 Small and a 32,768-feature layer-7 SAE as a testbed. We compare SHAP to Integrated Gradients, Gradient$\times$Input, and probe-weight baselines across linear and MLP probe arms, scoring each against feature ablation and activation steering measured through the language model's own logit difference. Most faithfulness associations we measure do not survive multiple-comparison correction, and attribution methods that agree strongly with one another ($ρ= 0.42$--$0.80$) agree poorly with measured causal effects, indicating that inter-method agreement is not evidence of causal faithfulness. Two effects hold under control. First, local per-example attribution retains a directional advantage over global averaged attribution, while its apparent importance advantage is explained by feature activity rather than superior causal ranking. Second, under known-ground-truth minimal pairs, attribution recovers inserted sentiment signal well above chance (AUROC $0.792$) but fails to localize deletions (AUROC $0.520$), suggesting that these methods detect the presence of a feature's influence more reliably than its absence. We argue that importance faithfulness and directional faithfulness are separable properties requiring separate evaluation, and that attribution agreement should not substitute for causal validation.

title: Towards Virtual Networking for a Time-Triggered Hypervisor
abstract: Virtualization enables mixed-criticality applications to run on shared hardware by isolating them within separate virtual machines (VMs). However, achieving end-to-end timing guarantees for critical tasks hosted on virtual CPUs (VCPUs) without relying on static partitioning is hard. A possible solution is a time-triggered hypervisor that dispatches VMs' VCPUs to processor cores according to a predetermined global schedule. A global schedule includes the computation, the network, and the virtualization layer to provide end-to-end timing guarantees across hosts and VMs during design time. In this work, we propose a VirtIO-based virtual network that realizes IEEE 802.1Qbv quasi-compliant inter-VM communication, providing predictable timing for critical messages exchanged between time-triggered VMs. We present our VirtIO-based virtual network architecture and derive network-level scheduling constraints that emerge from the properties of the proposed solution. We implement the proposed design in the ACRN hypervisor and evaluate the end-to-end latency of critical traffic in a loaded network, demonstrating that our time-triggered VirtIO-net prototype provides predictable end-to-end latency under load.

title: PaceReasoner: Label-Free Learning to Answer Briefly from Long Reasoning
abstract: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. Both modes share a trainable policy, creating a need for reliable supervision, sufficient SHORT training samples, and continued LONG responses to guide learning. PaceReasoner combines all-response and LONG-only answer consensus through progressive, confidence-weighted supervision. A behavior reward gradually shifts from encouraging SHORT exploration to rewarding agreement with LONG answers, while a ratio controller regulates the balance between modes. Across three model backbones and four benchmarks, PaceReasoner improves average SHORT accuracy over the baselines by 7.4--13.5 percentage points, with fewer than 25 reasoning tokens per response on average. Ablations support the key components, and cross-dataset results demonstrate transfer beyond the adaptation set.

title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
abstract: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models couples structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, share-question, sliding-window, block-sparse) with multi-node context parallelism, making the mask a dominant bottleneck. FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask compresses them from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ via four query-axis boundary vectors, covering broad structured patterns. Implemented for Ampere GPUs, it neither exploits FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline on Hopper nor supports distribution. The column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis interval boundaries. Under any multi-chunk context-parallel assignment, it reduces per-rank mask localization to a provably zero-communication \emph{clip--shift--max} on the boundary vectors, compatible with the single-GPU kernel. FlashMask-3 introduces a mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization atop FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA pipeline, plus a mask-aware distributed extension: zero-communication mask localization, a sparsity-aware load balancer (HCC-IPO), and a mask-aware compute-communication overlap with mask-driven communication pruning, whose forward all-gather uses topology-aware hierarchical routing. On a single H100 across 12 masks at 4K--128K context, it improves achieved TFLOPs over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45--141%, 34--71%, and 2--44%. At context-parallel degrees 4--32 with 8K sequence per device, it attains 31--75% compute-communication overlap efficiency and improves throughput over Megatron-Core CP ring, Megatron-Core CP all-gather, and MagiAttention by $1.80\times$--$3.71\times$, $1.71\times$--$2.92\times$, and $1.09\times$--$1.46\times$. In end-to-end training of a 118B-A14B MoE at 128K on 128 H100 GPUs, it raises throughput by 7.3--11.0% over a Dual Chunk all-gather baseline, with attention forward+backward 24.5--44.9% faster.

title: Visual Dependence Does Not Imply Answerability: A Systematic Analysis of Answerability Signals in Frozen InstructBLIP
abstract: Visual question answering models often produce plausible responses even when the available visual evidence is insufficient to support a valid answer. Although prior work has introduced benchmarks and abstention mechanisms for unanswerable visual questions, it remains unclear which signals derived from a frozen vision-language model reliably indicate answerability on unseen image-question pairs. We systematically evaluate answerability signals on a stratified 10K subset of UNK-VQA using frozen InstructBLIP, covering predictive uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, visual grounding, visual dependence, internal representations, and learned probes. Answerability discrimination remains weak, with test AUROC largely confined to 0.50-0.54. CLIP alignment yields the highest point estimate but does not significantly outperform generation confidence under paired bootstrap analysis. Targeted removal of question-relevant visual evidence causes substantially larger changes in answer confidence than same-size random masking, yet intervention sensitivity provides essentially no answerability discrimination. Increasing probe capacity, combining multiple signals, and adding reason-aware supervision do not provide robust improvements, while post-freeze cross-validation yields similarly weak discrimination. Selective-answering analysis shows limited usable coverage under low-risk operating criteria. Failure-mode analysis shows that the relative utility of individual signals varies across perturbation mechanisms. Taken together, these results show that, on our UNK-VQA subset with frozen InstructBLIP, visual dependence, uncertainty, semantic alignment, and static representations are not robust standalone proxies for answerability. Our findings emphasize the need to distinguish a model's reliance on visual evidence from whether that evidence is sufficient to support an answer.

title: DriveWLA: Unifying Future Dynamics and Scene Semantics through World-Language-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and world models have demonstrated strong capabilities in semantic understanding and future scene evolution for autonomous driving. However, effectively integrating both capabilities for trajectory generation remains challenging. In this work, we propose DriveWLA, a unified World-Language-Action model based on Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that jointly models semantic understanding, future scene dynamics, and trajectory generation. DriveWLA consists of three experts: a World Expert for future prediction, a Language Expert for semantic understanding, and an Action Expert for trajectory generation. We further introduce Cross-Expert Attention, which enables controlled information flow across experts while aligning semantic and dynamic representations. To improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning, we apply Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning post-training to refine the Action Expert. Extensive experiments show that DriveWLA achieves superior performance in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. DriveWLA achieves 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, demonstrating strong performance among VLM-based and world-model-based planners. Without specific fine-tuning, DriveWLA further demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive. These results validate the effectiveness of our unified World-Language-Action modeling, establishing DriveWLA as a generalizable framework for autonomous driving.

title: Stable-Plastic Subspace Construction for Differentially Private Continual LoRA
abstract: Continual learning (CL) adapts pretrained models to a sequence of tasks while retaining knowledge acquired from earlier tasks. When task data are sensitive, differential privacy (DP) provides record-level protection, but maintaining both adaptation and retention under privacy constraints remains challenging. We study this problem in continual low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and observe that: 1) private training increases forgetting primarily during subsequent adaptation rather than initial task acquisition; 2) jointly perturbing both LoRA factors introduces a non-negligible bilinear noise interaction; and 3) DP aggravates the stability-plasticity dilemma, hindering both knowledge retention and adaptation to new tasks. Based on these observations, we propose DP-SPA, which constructs a stable subspace from previously privatized updates and a plastic subspace from pretrained weights within its orthogonal complement. The method fixes these bases and privately optimizes only the LoRA factor, eliminating the bilinear noise interaction within each step. Before merging each task update, it rescales stable-direction coefficients using historical and current update energies. We establish a privacy guarantee and show that recalibration does not increase historical overlap and tightens a conditional upper bound on old-task loss increase. Experiments across five datasets, eight settings, and multiple privacy budgets show that DP-SPA improves average accuracy and reduces forgetting compared with the evaluated baselines.

title: Content-Edited Layout Generation for Graphic Design
abstract: In this paper, we formulate a novel form of conditional layout generation for graphic design, termed content-edited layout generation(CELG). CELG extends conventional content-aware layout generation (CLG), which generates a foreground layout for a fixed background image. The key distinction is that CELG treats the input image as an editable visual asset and, conditioned on a textual design intention and a foreground requirement that may be empty, produces an adapted background together with its layout. To study this task, we introduce Search-Compare-Edit(SCE), a data construction framework that supplies the paired supervision missing from existing design datasets. Starting from professional design canvases and their layouts, SCE synthesizes plausible pre-edit source images and corresponding editing instructions, yielding InstructEdit, a dataset of aligned source images, target canvases, instructions, and layouts. Based on the generated data, we train a two-flow multimodal flow matching model that couples a pretrained image editor with a layout flow transformer, enabling background editing and layout generation simultaneously within a unified framework that more closely reflects real-world design workflows. Our experiments systematically demonstrate the value of CELG as a distinct task and the performance advantages of the proposed model.

title: Non-Contiguous Channel Allocation in Multi-Beam Satellites: Formulations, Upper Bounds and Cooperative Matheuristics
abstract: Demand for wireless communication is growing, and commercial satellite services are expanding with it, increasing pressure on a finite radio spectrum. Allocation efficiency directly limits how many users a satellite can serve. We study how to assign frequency sub-channels to the carriers of a multi-beam satellite, maximising the total priority of admitted carriers while keeping each within its interference tolerance. Earlier work on this interference-limited channel allocation problem placed each carrier in a single continuous frequency block. Removing this restriction can admit more carriers, but a direct integer programming model cannot solve the largest test problems in practical time, so new methods are needed. We prove the problem computationally hard, reformulate it around how carriers share sub-channels, and derive three bounds on the optimum. We develop heuristics, including matheuristics combining local search with optimisation models, and an orchestrated portfolio that schedules them, recombines their solutions and stops early once its result is proven optimal or no longer improves. On 24 problems with up to 500 carriers, the best heuristics come within about 1% of the best known solution on average. The portfolio matches or exceeds the best heuristic for each problem on 23 of 24 with equal weights and 22 with priority weights, and is up to about 5% better on larger, more congested problems. It requires about a quarter of the time to run every heuristic and keep the best, and under half that of its heuristics run in a fixed order, which return slightly worse solutions on average.

title: SpecCloak: Probing Harmful Code Generation through Engineering Specifications
abstract: The code generation capabilities of large language models (LLMs) can equally be misused to implement harmful functionality, underscoring the need to understand their safety behavior in response to programming requests. While request phrasing is known to influence refusal, it remains unclear whether the form in which coding task requirements are stated affects the refusal process for malicious code generation. We introduce PseudoSpec, a template that organizes functional requirements as engineering specifications, and investigate its effects through controlled comparisons, representation analysis, and activation interventions. Across five open-weight models, removing explicit risk keywords only partially reduces refusal, whereas specification prompting substantially lowers refusal even when these keywords are retained. This reduction accompanies consistent shifts toward code-output-related representations, and interventions along condition-difference directions alter refusal behavior. Output analysis further distinguishes code-related responses from generation degeneration. Building on these findings, we propose SpecCloak, a black-box red-teaming framework combining PseudoSpec with discriminator-guided optimization, achieving an average execution-verified attack success rate of 28.91\% across eight target models on RedCode-Gen. We also introduce SpecReveal, a defense prototype combining natural-language intent reconstruction with dual-view detection without target-model fine-tuning. It achieves a 96.88\% attack detection rate in a separate prompt-detection evaluation, with false positives assessed on benign programming and specification-style inputs. These results connect specification-induced response differences to practical security consequences and identify intent reconstruction as a complementary detection approach.

title: Text-Only vs. Image-Aware VLM Judges for Manga Translation Evaluation
abstract: In manga translation, visual context outside speech-bubble text, including speaker identities, referents, and scene tone, is depicted in page images, making it natural to refer to images during translation evaluation. However, most conventional manga translation evaluations rely solely on text-only automatic metrics, leaving the impact of image input insufficiently explored. We propose a practical validation framework that employs the same vision-language model (VLM) as both a text-only judge (TOJ) and an image-aware judge (IAJ) to investigate evaluation divergences associated with image-aware evaluation procedures. We use a Japanese-English manga dataset of official translations aligned at the page and speech-bubble levels. First, adding page images to TOJ improved the primary VLM's detection of deliberately injected, visually dependent degradations. Second, we analyzed evaluation divergences between TOJ and IAJ, finding different error counts and error-category distributions. Human verification did not reveal a consistent preference between TOJ and IAJ.

title: Geometry and barycenters in large $\CAT(κ)$ spaces
abstract: We study the geometry and resulting properties of Fréchet functions and barycenters in metric spaces with curvature bounded above by a positive constant in the sense of Alexandrov. Existing results typically rely on the assumption that the support is small enough that the squared distance, and thus the Fréchet function, is strongly geodesically convex. We work in the sharper regime where existence and uniqueness of the barycenter are guaranteed, but where convexity typically fails. We develop new geometric properties of these spaces, including a quantitative four-point inequality and a geodesic stability result. Using these tools, we establish new finite sample error bounds for two statistical estimators: the empirical barycenter and the iterated barycenter, as well as new results on sparse representations and approximations of barycenters.

title: Jumbled Simon's Equivalence and Embeddings
abstract: \emph{Jumbled scattered factors} are a generalisation of scattered factors (or subsequences) where a jumbled scattered factor is obtained from another word by deleting and rearranging letters. For limiting the number of rearrangements, we distinguish $\ell$-jumbled scattered factors where $\ell$ limits the number of letters that may occur rearranged. For instance, $\mathtt{car}$, $\mathtt{start}$, $\mathtt{rat}, \mathtt{cat}$ are jumbled scattered factors of $\mathtt{abstract}$ even though $\mathtt{car}$, $\mathtt{start}$ and $\mathtt{cat}$ are no scattered factors and each need one jumble. An example for a jumbled scattered factor with $2$ jumbles is $\mathtt{tatar}$. In this work, we investigate two problems on jumbled scattered factors from an algorithmic perspective. First, we give algorithms for testing jumbled Simon's equivalence where two words are equivalent if they share the same $\ell$-jumbled scattered factors up to length $k$. Second, we investigate how to count the possible occurrences of a jumbled scattered factor -- the jumbled binomial coefficient. After defining the jumbled binomial coefficient, we study jumbled embeddings and factorisations of such as well.

title: Routing Optimality for Demand Graphs of Matching Number at Most Two
abstract: We prove that network coding and fractional routing have the same capacity region in undirected networks whose demand graph has matching number at most two, that is, when no three demand edges have pairwise disjoint endpoints. The metric-packing reduction of Liu et al. reduces this problem to a distance-weighted communication inequality on the fixed graph $Γ_{3,3}$. We first prove two entropy inequalities for sessions between designated terminal pairs on $Γ_{3,3}$. We then extend this result to sessions with arbitrary endpoints to obtain the distance-weighted communication bound required by the reduction. The proof combines conditional entropy inequalities with two graph contractions and an information inequality for deterministic interaction. Combining this inequality with the existing reduction establishes routing optimality for this class of demand graphs.

title: Multi-Agent Path Planning via Compatible Encounter-Space Allocation in Crowded Spaces Dynamically Occupied by Work Activities
abstract: Lifelong multiagent path planning on construction floors must accommodate continually changing goals and work occupancy. Existing planners can update paths and timing online, but work motion space coupling changes the spatial basis of unfinished encounters, while rerouting affects later encounters. Planning must therefore construct and maintain local encounter possibility. We propose Width based Planning with Compatible Encounter Space Allocation (WP), which constructs shared passage relationships from actual encounter demands and real time widths. Shared channels, ordered anchors, and urgency based updates coordinate successive encounters while retaining individual greedy motion between them. A necessary and sufficient width condition for fixed-point position exchange and a necessary directional condition for composite exchange provide geometric grounds for channel construction and encounter relocation. In crowded floor computational experiments, WP maintained route continuation after occupancy changes and enabled multi agent clearing, with infrequent, brief near stops. Complete run comparisons with four methods showed 25.2% to 52.2% more mean goal arrivals than the best baseline at each configuration of 5 to 10 agents, with lower mean computation time than the rolling horizon K_CBS adaptation. The contribution is a planning principle that constructs and continuously maintains local passage relationships from real time space, unifying shared spatial allocation and conditional local clearing to extend lifelong planning to work motion space coupling.

title: NBCLT: Parameter-Agnostic Norm-Ball Clipped Local Training
abstract: Distributed learning with multiple local steps reduces communication but aggravates drift, and its practical performance often depends on carefully tuned hyperparameters under heterogeneous data and communication constraints. At the same time, recent Muon-type optimizers suggest that constraining updates within suitable norm balls provides a simple way to encode geometric priors into optimization. In this work, we propose NBCLT (Norm-Ball Clipped Local Training), a unified local-training framework for both federated learning (FL) and decentralized learning (DL). NBCLT combines a predict-and-correct local update rule with Euclidean projections onto flexible norm balls, thereby performing norm-ball clipping under flexible update geometries while retaining a simple implementation. In FL, its problem-parameter-free regime achieves $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-2})$ communication complexity and $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$ total stochastic-gradient complexity without assuming bounded heterogeneity, when the per-round local-computation budget is scaled appropriately with the horizon. In DL, NBCLT is compatible with both static and time-varying mixing and preserves these accuracy exponents under the analogous computation scaling, up to fixed network constants and an additive initialization cost.

title: LinMorph: Learning to Morph Weights for Efficient Video DiT Linearization
abstract: Post-hoc linearization is an attractive way to accelerate pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers (Video DiTs), yet existing methods largely treat the quality loss induced by attention replacement as a recovery problem. We show that a more fundamental bottleneck lies upstream: \emph{initialization}. Random initialization discards pretrained knowledge, whereas manual weight reuse transfers it through rigid and incomplete source--target correspondences. We introduce \textbf{LinMorph}, which recasts Video DiT linearization as a learnable softmax-to-linear weight transformation problem. Instead of copying predefined counterparts, LinMorph learns a cross-parameter morphism that lets each target Gated DeltaNet (GDN) parameter draw jointly from pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including for parameters with no direct softmax counterpart. A single morphism is shared across layers and learned through local teacher alignment, while producing layer-specific initializations from their respective pretrained weights. The resulting weights are then materialized as independent GDN modules for progressive distillation and joint recovery.Since the morphism operates in weight space rather than token space, it can be learned on short, low-resolution clips and directly reused at larger video scales. Across pretrained Video DiTs, LinMorph enables markedly faster recovery and better final generation quality than random initialization and heuristic weight reuse. Results show that efficient linearization depends not only on how a converted model is recovered, but critically on how pretrained knowledge is transferred before recovery. Project page: https://lonelyling.github.io/LinMorph.

title: On integrability of local utility maximizing strategies
abstract: In stochastic control problems involving optimal portfolio choice, one often seeks an optimizer of some local criterion (dynamic programming value function) generated by some global criterion (e.g., expected utility). The local optimizer then typically acts as a stochastic integrand with respect to some multivariate stochastic process (e.g., asset prices). This paper takes a closer look at local criteria in the form of ``local expected utility''. Since the existence of the local optimizer can be established under very mild conditions, it is crucial to understand under what circumstances the local optimizer has good integrability properties. It is shown that the reasonable asymptotic elasticity condition of Kramkov and Schachermayer (1999) applied to the local utility function plays a key role in this context.

title: Safe Unicycle Navigation Among Multiple Obstacles Under Bounded Disturbances: A Learning-Augmented CLF-CBF Approach (Extended Version)
abstract: This paper presents a robust control framework for safe navigation of a unicycle robot to a goal among multiple static obstacles under an unknown, time-varying disturbance. The controller solves a single real-time quadratic program (QP) that combines a goal-reaching term with one safety term per obstacle. The goal-reaching term is a cross-track control Lyapunov function built from body-frame tracking errors rather than a bearing angle, which keeps its Lie derivatives bounded everywhere, including the goal. Safety is encoded using robust control barrier functions, one per obstacle, each tightened by a closed-form, state-dependent disturbance bound. When stabilization and safety conflict, a slack variable relaxes only the convergence requirement, so that the safety constraints remain strictly enforced. Whenever the QP is feasible, the robust barrier constraints guarantee forward invariance of every obstacle's safe set under all admissible disturbances. Complementing this safety guarantee, a Lyapunov analysis yields an explicit ultimate bound on the distance to the goal. A learning-augmented variant replaces the fixed objective with a reinforcement-learning reference, which accelerates convergence when multiple constraints are simultaneously active. We further derive the obstacle separation below which the gap between two obstacles becomes too narrow to pass through under the robust constraints. For such gaps, a learned virtual goal for the Lyapunov function steers the robot around the obstacles without compromising safety. Simulations, a Monte Carlo study, and a comparison against a sampled-data robust baseline support the theoretical results.

title: Batch-Paced: Fixed-Budget Batch Decoding in Discrete Diffusion Language Models
abstract: As generative language models become more capable and widely used, inference demand grows, making efficient serving increasingly important. Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer a promising path to more efficient inference through parallel token generation. Prior dLLM decoding methods, however, focus on improving inference efficiency for individual sequences. We formulate fixed-budget dLLM batch decoding and introduce Batch-Paced, a training-free method that jointly optimizes the allocation of decoding compute across requests to improve overall batch quality. Across two dLLM backbones, five benchmarks and their representative mixtures, Batch-Paced improves batch performance under matched budgets; gains generally grow with batch size and largely persist across decoding configurations. Analysis of requests' decoding trajectories suggests that these gains arise largely by raising the committed-token confidence of lower-confidence requests. We further show that Batch-Paced's batch decode time remains competitive and that adding a decoding-depth allowance during Batch-Paced decoding can shorten it further at a modest performance cost.

title: A Photonic Integrated Light Generation, Control, and Delivery Engine for Creating Cold Atoms
abstract: The creation of cold atoms underpins quantum sensing and precision metrology, computing, timekeeping, and fundamental science experiments. Miniaturizing the lasers and optical infrastructure, which occupy over 80% of the volume of these experiments, through photonic integration could improve robustness, reliability, and manufacturability while reducing cost and enabling portable space-based precision measurements and quantum tools for non-experts. Yet, there has been limited progress towards integration of the laser and optical infrastructure required to generate cold atoms onto a single chip. We demonstrate a photonic engine that generates, controls, and delivers precision light to create cold atoms in a rubidium 3-dimensional magneto-optical trap (3D-MOT). We integrate on a single chip two frequency-agile self-injection-locked lasers, laser frequency and intensity control, passive beam combining and splitting, signal monitoring, and high-efficiency beam delivery to a rubidium vapor cell. The integrated engine is shown to support multiple functions required for generating cold atoms including stable generation of low-noise cooling and repump light, frequency control for atom spectroscopy and stabilization, real-time laser monitoring, routing for laser offset locking, optical power modulation, and large-area three-beam delivery of 3 mW to the physics package. Fully electrically controlled, the engine enables sustained 3D-MOT operation, trapping more than 1 million atoms at an average temperature of 350 uK and supporting atom-number and temperature measurements. These results demonstrate the first single-chip integration of light generation, control, and delivery for cold-atom generation, offering a path toward smaller, more robust, and manufacturable cold-atom systems for applications including cold-atom clocks and sensors.

title: Rattling Resonant Chains with Dynamical Tides and Parametric Resonance Passage
abstract: Close-in sub-Neptunes are born in mean-motion resonant chains that break apart on a timescale of $\sim$100 Myr. If the chains are first ''rattled'' --- have their free eccentricities excited to a few percent --- then breaking occurs on the required timescale. We propose that chains are rattled by internal oscillations tidally driven by the star in the innermost planet. Unlike other proposals, there is no need to invoke any reservoir of planetesimals or external perturbers --- the chain unravels from within. We develop a Hamiltonian theory (and an accompanying toy model) which predicts a parametric instability whereby chain librations exponentially amplify when the tidal forcing frequency equals the sum of the internal mode frequency and the chain libration frequency. We also introduce a new eigenmode solver for rotating planets, $\texttt{MAQAM}$, that in combination with the evolutionary code $\texttt{ORCHARD}$ enables us to track the frequency evolution of pressure, gravity, and inertial modes in cooling sub-Neptunes. Inertial modes in the gas envelope and fluid mantle can evolve to become momentarily parametrically resonant. Passage through a single parametric resonance can raise the free eccentricities in the chain to a few percent within a few tens of Myrs.

title: Conformal soft modes at elastic instabilities
abstract: In case a crystal is close to a continuous elastic phase transition, pronounced critical fluctuations emerge. We show that on the level of linear elasticity theory the displacement vector for these critical modes obeys a condition reminiscent of the conformal Killing equation. For an isostructural instability, four critical modes arise corresponding to one dilation and three special conformal transformations. At crystal symmetry-breaking instabilities, the critical fluctuations include a continuum of modes even for crystals with finite size. For certain cases, these comprise the conformal transformations associated with two-dimensional Minkowski space. These results have implications for critical elastic phenomena as well as for extremal mechanical metamaterials.

title: A breath of fresh air: Oxygen enhancement from silicate sublimation during early protostellar evolution
abstract: Recently, an analog to the t = 0 moment of our Solar System's meteoritic record was identified for the first time around the Class I protostar HOPS-315. Crystalline silicates were found to recondense from SiO gas that cools as it advects upward from a hot thermostat region in the inner midplane. This t=0 moment may be associated with the formation of the first planetesimals in this disk. We explore whether HOPS-68, a Class I protostar with similar properties and system geometries, is engaged in such refractory recondensation as well. A detection of cooler gas-phase SiO in absorption above a hot disk midplane would allow us to achieve this goal, thanks to a previous detection of crystalline silicates. HOPS-68 was observed with the JWST MIRI and NIRSpec, showing multiple bands of molecular absorption. We use local thermal equilibrium slab models to measure the temperature, column density, velocity, and radial location of these bands. The molecular absorption bands of gaseous SiO, H2O, CO2, and 13CO trace a warm molecular inversion layer (300-500 K) at mid-altitudes above the hot disk midplane from 0.3-16 AU, which is consistently blue-shifted with respect to the system velocity by 33-53 km/s. Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations of HOPS-68 kinematically resolve an SiO-rich jet and wind. We confirm that HOPS-68, like HOPS-315, is undergoing an epoch analogous to the t=0 moment in the Solar System's planet formation timeline. The detected warm molecular layer traces the base of a disk wind, which carries sublimated material from the thermostat region near 2 AU up into the outer disk. As for HOPS-315, the molecular layer in the inner few AU of HOPS-68 is enhanced in bulk oxygen as a result of this sublimation. Since HOPS-68 is less evolved than HOPS-315, this may indicate a prolonged epoch in protostellar evolution in which such oxygen enhancement occurs.

title: WoVR+: World Model as Reliable Simulator for Versatile VLA Policy Optimization with RL
abstract: Action-conditioned world models can reduce costly real-robot interaction in reinforcement learning for Vision-Language-Action models (VLA-RL), but hallucinations can mislead policy optimization. Extending them to richer VLA interfaces and long-horizon tasks raises challenges in spatiotemporal and cross-modal consistency, exploration-reliability balance in RL, and compounding rollout errors. We present WoVR+, extending WoVR's hallucination-aware WM-RL framework by redesigning the learned environment and imagined interaction protocol: A VLA-interface-aligned world model provides multi-view prediction and proprioceptive updates while mitigating hallucinations. Chunk-wise noise preserves flow-based policy exploration while limiting prediction-degrading action jitter. For long-horizon tasks, stage-local imagined training combines stage-entry resets, stage-specific rewards, local horizons, and controllable sampling to shorten generated prefixes and balance training across stages. WoVR+ improves success over SFT by 21.09% and 16.7% on RoboTwin and 6 real-robot tasks. Long-horizon phone-packaging success rises from 30% to 75%. Videos are available at https://youmo445.github.io/WoVR_Plus.github.io/.

title: Dynamical BEC formation and vanishing entropy for trapped bosons in non-relativistic QED via nonlinear resonance cascades
abstract: The dynamical formation of a complete Bose-Einstein condensate and the asymptotic purification of trapped bosons coupled to a quantized radiation field are rigorously established. By tracking the macroscopic one-particle density matrix $κ_T$ through a nonlinear resonance cascade, it is demonstrated that radiative relaxation irreversibly depletes all excited trap modes, even when the initial macroscopic state $κ_0$ is genuinely mixed. Here $κ_T$ is an average, with respect to a de Finetti measure $μ_0$, over mean-field particle-field orbits, so that the mixedness of $κ_0$ reflects a statistical ensemble of orbits. Under the assumptions of a non-vanishing initial ground state component and strictly positive downward Fermi-Golden-Rule rates, strong trace-norm convergence to a pure condensate is proven, $$ \lim_{T\to\infty} \| κ_T-|χ_0\rangle\langleχ_0| \|_{\mathfrak{S}_1(\mathfrak{h})} = 0 \, . $$ Furthermore, the von Neumann entropy of the macroscopic one-particle density matrix is shown to vanish asymptotically, $$ \lim_{T\to\infty}S[κ_T]=0 \, , $$ without any claim of monotonicity in $T$. Thus, any initially mixed, positive-entropy state ($0<S[κ_0]<\infty$) is purified to the ground state $|χ_0\rangle\langleχ_0|$. For the proof, we derive the Hartree hierarchy of the coupled system of bosons and photons from the finite-$N$ BBGKY hierarchy of the microscopic quantum many-body system, establishing trace-norm convergence in the mean-field limit as $N\to\infty$. The limits are taken successively; first $N\to\infty$, then the weak-coupling limit, and finally $T\to\infty$. Although the global particle-field evolution remains unitary, the macroscopic one-particle state converges to a pure state as energy and correlations are continuously radiated into the dispersive field.

title: Free-support Wasserstein Resampling in Sequential Monte Carlo
abstract: In modern sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) applications, such as diffusion model samplers, propagating a particle is expensive, so only a few particles can be afforded. In this regime, each resampling step decides which regions of the state space survive, so a better resampling scheme is worth extra computation. However, classical resampling methods only replicate existing particles and suffer from sample impoverishment, especially when the particle size is small relative to the dimension. To create new particles, we relax the unbiasedness of resampling and control the mean squared error via a Wasserstein criterion. Specifically, we propose Wasserstein-Dirichlet resampling (WDR), which constructs an equal-weight measure that optimally approximates the weighted particle distribution by solving a free-support Wasserstein barycenter problem. We then randomize the resulting optimal coupling by Dirichlet mixing. Theoretically, we provide non-asymptotic mean squared error bounds that quantify the bias-variance trade-off and show that the rate depends on the intrinsic dimension. A truncated variant preserves high-weight particles while applying WDR to the remaining mass, targeting mild weight degeneracy. Experiments on state-space models and conditional image generation demonstrate that WDR consistently improves estimation accuracy, stability, and sample diversity. The improvements persist at matched wall-clock cost when the propagation cost dominates.

title: Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions
abstract: Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss. Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1/M. We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control.

title: CineMem: Attention-Aligned Fine-grained Memory Retrieval for Multi-Shot Long Video Generation
abstract: Autoregressive video generation relies on memory retrieval to model long-range dependencies. This capability becomes particularly critical for multi-shot generation, where models must reconcile substantial visual changes across shot transitions with persistent semantic continuity. Existing methods tend to perform memory retrieval at the frame level and share the same historical context across all query tokens, overlooking the heterogeneous information needs and leading to redundant retrieval and inefficient use of historical memory. To bridge this gap, we introduce CineMem, an attention-aligned fine-grained memory retrieval framework that combines online memory organization with query-adaptive retrieval for autoregressive multi-shot video generation. Specifically, guided by intrinsic memory-access patterns revealed through attention analysis, we propose an online-clustered KV cache as a memory organization strategy over all historical tokens, enabling semantic-aware memory grouping and more precise retrieval. In addition, we introduce a query-level retrieval mechanism that provides broader access to historical information under a fixed retrieval budget, thereby improving long-term memory utilization. Together, these designs enable the multi-shot video generator to preserve long-range consistency across shot transitions, particularly in revisitation scenarios, while approximating full-memory access under a constrained memory budget. To facilitate evaluation, we further introduce a suite of task-specific, VLM-assisted metrics for faithful inter-shot consistency assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.

title: GLST: Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition Framework for Online Chained-Goal Navigation
abstract: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memory-decomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Real-robot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework.

title: Learning How to Remember: Memory Modality Selection for GUI Agents
abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have substantially improved the capabilities of GUI agents, while memory augmentation has emerged as a promising approach for reusing knowledge from past interactions. However, existing memory augmented GUI agents typically adopt a fixed representation strategy, providing retrieved experience as a static modality. It remains unclear whether a single memory modality is consistently optimal, or how modality preference changes across interaction steps. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of memory modality in VLM based GUI agents. Across GUI benchmarks, we find that the preferred memory representation is strongly step dependent. Motivated by the finding, we introduce \textbf{SwitchMem}, a routing framework that dynamically selects between textual and visual memory representations at each step. Across three GUI benchmarks, SwitchMem outperforms memory augmented baselines that rely on static memory representations. Our findings validate our claim that memory modality is a step dependent decision rather than a fixed design choice. Code and project resources are available at https://txxnrd.github.io/switchmem

title: Enforcing a Strict Safety Margin in LLM Text Generation via Barrier Lyapunov Control
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed without formal guarantees against toxic text generation. Existing control barrier function (CBF) based safety filters can keep the generation trajectory within a toxicity-free region, but do not enforce a positive distance from its boundary, allowing formally safe trajectories to approach the toxicity threshold arbitrarily closely and leaving little buffer against modelling errors or disturbances. We address this limitation with a Barrier Lyapunov Function (BLF) safety filter that enforces a prescribed clearance margin throughout generation while retaining the continuous-time transformer dynamics, including feedforward layers. The resulting safe input set is a half-space defined by a constraint affine in the control input, and is non-empty under certified surjectivity and classifier-nondegeneracy conditions. For margin-compatible initial conditions we prove that the clearance margin is never violated and that the prescribed clearance is restored exponentially, yielding an explicit clearance floor, and show that, as the margin vanishes, the admissible trajectories satisfy the exponential second-order CBF condition. We further derive an explicitly computable sufficient disturbance budget under which the clearance guarantee degrades gracefully. Simulations on a small transformer illustrate the resulting improvement in safety clearance.

title: Locomotion with Online Awareness of Dynamics for Precision Footholds
abstract: Unknown payloads alter robot dynamics and make precise contact execution difficult when foothold margins are small. We present LOAD, a perceptive locomotion framework that combines explicit inertial estimates with implicit dynamics features for narrow-beam traversal. Separate recurrent modules infer torso inertial changes and task-relevant history from proprioception, while a height-map teacher is distilled into a depth-based student. We extensively evaluate LOAD and its variants in simulation and on hardware across beam widths and payload configurations. The results show that implicit dynamics features accelerate training, while explicit inertial estimation further improves traversal success; combining both enables LOAD to approach the performance of a privileged policy supplied with ground-truth inertial parameters. Hardware experiments demonstrate traversal with unilateral payloads of 6 kg on a 10 cm beam and 9 kg on a 15 cm beam, and an evenly distributed 11 kg payload on a 15 cm beam. These results support combining physical estimates and history features for precision locomotion under unknown loads.

title: Radiation limits on amino acid preservation and chiral measurement at Oxia Planum
abstract: Amino acid enantiomeric excess (EE) is a potential biosignature, but its measurement requires sufficient surviving material as well as preserved chirality. We derive a criterion that separates abundance-limited from racemization-limited preservation and apply it to the Mars Organic Molecule Analyzer (MOMA) on the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover. The model combines cosmic-ray and radiogenic doses with laboratory destruction kinetics and assumed ratios of interconversion to destruction rates. For an initially homochiral population of 1000~ppmw, the surviving EE is 58\% or 25\% when the total abundance reaches 1~ppmw for rate ratios of 0.04 or 0.10, respectively. This abundance criterion does not ensure that both enantiomers can be quantified. Applying provisional estimates of 1~ppmw per enantiomer and 10\% EE, serine at 2~m requires initial concentrations of 340 and 960~ppmw after cosmic-ray exposures of $10^{7}$ and $10^{8}$~yr, respectively, under transferred fused-silica--perchlorate kinetics and a 1.57-MGy radiogenic dose. These concentrations exceed measured meteoritic serine abundances, but do not predict the initial Oxia inventory. For organics retained in a closed host since deposition 3.9~Ga ago, the modeled radiogenic dose is 1.6--5.6~MGy across the adopted compositions. In the lower-dose case, drilling to 2~m reduces the total dose by only a factor of 1.5 after $10^{7}$~yr. The boundaries depend on mineral kinetics and organic residence time; they distinguish preserved chirality from a measurable excess.

title: Real-time monitoring of LHCb beam spot properties based on FPGA hit reconstruction
abstract: We present a real-time trackless method to monitor the centre of the LHCb luminous region and the relative alignment of the two halves of the LHCb Vertex Locator, using cluster counts accumulated in selected regions of the detector and processed in firmware. A Principal Component Analysis performed on simulated data yields a set of weight vectors that reduce the position estimators to scalar products of the counter rates, executable with negligible computational overhead. With pp collision data from 2024, the transverse position of the luminous region is reconstructed with a statistical precision of approximately 4 micrometre per coordinate in a 90 millisecond accumulation window. A measurement of the longitudinal centre is demonstrated with a statistical precision of a few millimetres in simulated studies. The introduction of run-time configurable firmware counters has been studied in simulation to improve the transverse and longitudinal resolutions by a factor of three with respect to the fixed-geometry baseline.

title: HierarchiRetina: A Diabetic Retinopathy Screening and Grading Cascade with Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Lesion Segmentation
abstract: Clinical screening for diabetic retinopathy proceeds in stages, yet most automated systems grade fundus images with a single black-box network. Three gaps remain: (i) lesions differ widely in size and contrast, but segmenters typically apply the same blocks to all; (ii) ungradable images are usually excluded or treated as an extra class, and lesion-aware graders seldom test whether lesions drive the grade; (iii) staged systems often report each stage only on the images reaching it, leaving propagated errors unmeasured. HierarchiRetina, a screening, segmentation and grading cascade with inspectable stage outputs, addresses each gap. First, HSMoE-AUNet is a U-Net whose skip, bottleneck and decoder blocks are sparse mixtures of heterogeneous experts, with lesion-matched types, counts and losses; SwinHRUNetPP, a dual-encoder vessel segmenter, uses a field-of-view-restricted loss. Second, LG-DRG separates gradability from ordinal severity and lets lesion masks query the image through gated cross-attention. Third, an end-to-end evaluation counts screening misses as errors and traces each error to its stage. Pooled Dice ranged from 0.184 (microaneurysms) to 0.579 (exudates); vessel Dice was 0.731. On 58,689 held-out images from six datasets, end-to-end quadratic weighted kappa was 0.804, with referral sensitivity 0.832 at specificity 0.947, and the screening gate caused 66% of errors. In ablations, the grade ignored the masks, even with the cross-attention gate started open. On all 4,105 official DDR test images, six-class accuracy was 85.6%, above the best published six-class result we found (83.8%). Staged screening systems should be evaluated end-to-end, with stage attribution and mask ablation, before clinical deployment.

title: Chordal Codes: Code Construction and Efficient Gaussian-Elimination Decoding
abstract: Maximum-likelihood decoding of linear codes over erasure channels can be considered as solving a linear system of a column submatrix of the parity-check matrix. In practice, Gaussian elimination is usually applied, and its computational cost depends on the structure of the matrix, especially the sparsity and the fill-in generated during the elimination. The \emph{chordal graph}, or \emph{triangulated graph}, first introduced by C. Berge, has a so-called \emph{perfect elimination ordering}, indicating that if the primal graph of a matrix is a chordal graph, then there exists a perfect elimination ordering such that a special class of fill-in under Gaussian elimination following this ordering will be avoided. In this paper, we introduce \emph{chordal codes}, i.e., codes equipped with parity-check matrices such that the primal graphs of the parity-check matrices are chordal. We prove that, for a chordal code, the decoding submatrix associated with any erasure pattern retains a chordal primal graph. So, the complexity of chordal elimination (Gaussian elimination following the perfect elimination ordering applied to the chordal code decoding) will be smaller than decoding a random code by Gaussian elimination. Also, we provide an upper bound on the complexity of chordal elimination.

title: Provenance and Authorization in Autobiographical Language Models
abstract: Autobiographical language models may draw on archives containing observations, quotations, emotional reports, and earlier model outputs. Cryptographic authentication can preserve an archive while leaving these sources semantically conflated. We formulate this gap as a computer-security problem: narrative content must not silently become consent or alter an authorized decision rule. We define typed records, authenticated attestations, a separate policy channel, and admissible views. Under explicit assumptions, we give a standard integrity reduction and a noninterference argument, characterize the information required by exact decision-preserving summaries, and show why passive history and fixed-point convergence need not identify a preferred action. Alpay Algebra supplies a comparative language for iterative memory without being a premise of the proofs. Sociology of religious affiliation, source-monitoring psychology, and self-determination theory motivate distinctions in a bounded Latter-day Saint vignette. A separate, reproducible pilot uses a frozen public language model on 32 wholly synthetic cases across 576 paired conditions. It compares flattened records, source labels, and an explicit admission gate under contradictory summary repetition. The study concerns computational attribution and authorization, not the motives or psychology of the people in the vignette.

title: PUGS: Physics-Guided Uncertainty Modeling for Underwater Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides an efficient framework for dynamic scene reconstruction. Most existing approaches model scene dynamics with deterministic deformation fields, assuming each Gaussian follows a distinct geometric trajectory over time.
