We evaluated the angular resolution measure (ARM) and the energy reconstruction error as functions of electronic noise, pixel pitch, and the recombination correction method. An electronic noise level of 4 keV and a pixel pitch of 1 mm yield an ARM (FWHM) of about 3 degrees at 1332.5 keV and an energy reconstruction error better than 4\% for incident energies of 1173.2 keV and above. Recombination correction using both scintillation light and charge signals improves the ARM and the energy error by factors of 1.7--2.3 and 2.2--5.4, respectively, compared to the charge-only correction, although the uncertainty of the recombination-fluctuation model remains. Since this simulation relies on idealized assumptions such as the use of the Monte Carlo truth in the event reconstruction, these values represent the best cases achievable under these detector conditions; nevertheless, they show that a large-scale LArTPC is a promising Compton camera for cosmic MeV gamma-ray observations.

title: A CaLLM Judge is a Better Judge: Mitigating Bias in LLM-as-a-judge
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to predict which of two candidate answers a human evaluator would prefer, providing a scalable alternative when human evaluation is too costly. Unfortunately, LLM judgments can exhibit systematic biases. Prior work has documented position, verbosity or model family of the candidate answers influencing the judge decision rather than their quality, while additional biases may remain undocumented. $\textit{Multicalibration}$ provides a natural framework to address this problem: each bias corresponds to miscalibration on an identifiable group, $\textit{e.g.}$, family bias manifests as overconfidence in answers generated by models belonging to the same family of the judge. The challenge is to fix miscalibration simultaneously across many, potentially unknown groups. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{CaLLM}$, a post hoc framework that multicalibrates an LLM judge, thereby bounding all such biases simultaneously. We prove that $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ bounds the bias of every group whose error structure is captured by an available representation, and that augmenting it with explicit bias groups further reduces the residual bias. We then derive theoretical conditions under which $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ improves the judge's accuracy, rather than trading it for calibration. Finally, we evaluate $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ across pairwise preference benchmarks, showing that it reduces the multicalibration error on both specified and unspecified bias groups, while improving predictive performance of the judge.

title: Interpreting Paper-to-Patent Citations in AI-Related PMC Articles
abstract: Paper-to-patent citations connect scientific and technological documents, but their interpretability depends on how patents are used in the citing text. This study examines citation contexts and paper-level outcome associations in AI-related articles in PubMed Central (PMC). Screening 189,073 articles identified 746 with explicitly tagged patent references (0.395%), including 713 with 1,544 identifiable in-text patent-citation instances. Three large language models classified these instances by represented content, motivation, textual position, and evaluative stance. Regression models examined associations among these dimensions, and propensity-score-matched regressions compared patent-citing papers with XML-screened controls. Background-oriented citations were predominantly neutral and introductory, whereas adoption-oriented citations were more closely associated with methodological positions and supportive evaluations. These patterns suggest heuristic configurations of contextualization, operationalization, and problematization, although classification overlap and exclusion of rare categories limit their interpretation. In matched samples, the patent-citing indicator was associated with lower scholarly-citation measures and more citations received from patents. These associations are observational, not causal. Together, these findings show that paper-to-patent citations encode heterogeneous forms of engagement with patented technology and should be interpreted as selective bibliographic signals rather than direct indicators of technology-to-science knowledge transfer or research value.

title: SYNPRED: A Synergistic Approach to Multimodal Learning for Clinical Prediction
abstract: Multimodal medical data captures complementary aspects of disease. It provides a comprehensive basis for diagnosis and the identification of biological associations linked to progression or treatment response. Established contrastive learning approaches exploit shared information across modalities, but fall short in exploiting complementary, modality-specific signals relevant for a task. Here, we propose a synergistic multimodal variational autoencoder (VAE) framework that separates task-relevant unimodal and multimodal information from instance-specific variation task-irrelevant, allowing complementary signals across modalities to be leveraged for prediction. The method yields benefits even if modalities are missing at test time. We evaluate the method on a treatment response prediction task using medical imaging and RNA data. Empirical comparison with alignment-based and multimodal VAE state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates improved multimodal prediction performance, and consistent benefits for prediction from a single modality after multimodal training. The full code can be found here: https://github.com/cirmuw/SYNPRED.

title: Dynamical and thermal evolution of localized reconnecting current sheets under varying guide-fields in the solar corona
abstract: Although magnetic reconnection in coronal current sheets (CSs) is a fundamental energy release mechanism in the solar corona, the role of guide-fields in governing its formation and self-consistent evolution is not fully understood. Through 2.5D resistive magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations, we investigate how guide-fields affect the formation and evolution of a localized reconnecting coronal CS. Strong guide-fields prevent oppositely directed field lines from approaching sufficiently to form a CS, delaying and suppressing its subsequent evolution. The reconnection rate exhibits a rising phase resembling a power-law, with exponent $δ_1$ decreasing with rising guide-fields, indicating slower temporal growth of the reconnection rate. The aspect ratio of the CS follows a similar power-law trend with the exponent $α_1$ decreasing with rising guide-fields. A subsequent slower growth phase of the reconnection rate shows a power-law exponent $δ_2$ that increases with rising guide-fields, as does the corresponding aspect-ratio exponent $α_2$. As the CS evolves, the latter phase is achieved due to a sharp decremental transition of the guide-field within the CS after a time when the increasing inflows are inefficiently resisted by the guide-field itself. In the reconnection regime during prior phases, the power-law exponents of the maximum temperature and the outflow velocities also decrease with rising guide-fields demonstrating that stronger guide-fields suppress the growth of these indicators also. This study suggests that a self-consistently formed CS displays phases of efficient and inefficient quenching of the reconnection mechanism, promoted by non-zero guide-fields. We also quantify this behavior for indicators of the reconnection process and discuss their applicability to observations of apparent CSs and probing background coronal conditions.

title: Kantowski Sachs Cosmological Model with Radiation and Generalized Chaplygin Gas
abstract: In the present paper we study the evolution of a homogeneous and anisotropic Kantowski Sachs cosmological model coupled with radiation and a generalized Chaplygin gas. Our main objective is verifying if this model evolves to a homogeneous and isotropic Friedmann Robertson Walker cosmological model, which is the more accepted model to describe our present Universe. If this is the case, we may imagine that the Kantowski Sachs cosmological model could had been an early stage of our Universe.

title: When Missingness Follows the Graph: Beyond Feature Propagation for Missing Features
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) commonly assume that node features are fully observed, despite missing features being pervasive in real-world applications. By leveraging the dependence between node features and graph structure, existing graph-specific methods handle missingness by propagating observed feature values along graph edges. However, these methods have mainly been evaluated in overly optimistic settings, where feature entries are removed independently and uniformly across the graph. This overlooks realistic scenarios in which missingness propagates among connected nodes, as can occur during localized sensing failures in sensor networks. We formalize this complementary notion as graph-structured mask dependence, where the joint distribution of missingness indicators is shaped by the graph, and introduce a controlled mechanism that instantiates this setting. We study propagation-based methods theoretically and empirically in this setting, showing that their effectiveness changes substantially compared with the uniformly random regime. Motivated by this limitation, we propose PEMix, designed to remain effective under challenging graph-structured missingness. Rather than propagating observed values, PEMix uses global structural representations to condition a probabilistic model of incomplete node features before message passing. Experiments under controlled graph-structured missingness and naturally occurring missingness show that PEMix remains robust across complex missingness regimes, with particularly strong performance as missingness becomes severe.

title: 3D Global Climate Simulations of Synthetic Mars Warming
abstract: Artificial warming via engineered aerosols presents a novel pathway to bypass volatile scarcity on modern Mars. Utilizing the Generic Planetary Climate Model, we evaluate the physical feasibility of aerosol-induced terraforming over a full Martian year (669 Sols). Unlike previous approaches that added aerosols to background dust or assumed continuous nanoparticle injection, we simulate the complete substitution of natural dust with a single-injection profile of radiatively active aluminium nanoparticles without continuous dumping. This tests whether initial infrared greenhouse forcing can overcome the severe ice-albedo cooling induced by a massive regional water-ice sheet ($3400 \text{ kg/m}^2$) localized in the Hellas Basin. Comparing this scenario against an unperturbed control run, we analyze surface temperature dynamics, sublimation fluxes, and water vapour concentration. Our 3D global climate simulations quantify the radiative-dynamical feedback thresholds and determine whether engineered aerosol forcing can trigger a self-sustaining water-vapour greenhouse effect or remains fundamentally limited by regional ice-albedo suppression in Hellas.

title: Sense-Making phase transition framework for Affect
abstract: Contemporary accounts of affect emphasize different perspectives, ranging from the regulation of bodily states in allostatic approaches to the relational and sense-making character stressed by enactive theories. Here, we show that affect can be made explicit within the sense-making phase transition framework previously introduced for the perception of an inner sensation. Within this same formal structure, each stable minimum of the sense-making potential defines an affective state: its position determines valence, while its depth determines arousal. Affect therefore is not introduced as an independent ingredient, but emerges as the associated state in the valence-arousal space, providing a link between allostatic and enactive approaches to affect. This formulation distinguishes valence intensity from arousal, allows for dominant and secondary affective states, and naturally accommodates mixed-valence configurations beyond a strictly bipolar description. Revisiting representative landscapes of the model, we show how neutral, uncertain, polarized, and mixed-valence regimes arise as a function of contextual sensory information, learned historical evaluation, and externally supplied information. We further show that the resulting valence-arousal relation provides a theoretical basis for the upper-open V-shaped organization discussed in the affect literature, while also opening a natural route toward a dynamical description of affect and emotions.

title: Chirality Inversion and Giant Optical Activity in Scalable Self-Assembled Metamaterials
abstract: Chiral materials manipulate light in ways that hold promise for sensing, imaging, and photonics, but producing such materials with strong and reproducible optical activity at large scale remains challenging. Here, we develop a scalable strategy to assemble hierarchical helicoidal metamaterials from metallic nanoparticles and chitin nanocrystals, a biosourced polysaccharide. Spontaneous co-assembly produces ordered chiral structures with strong plasmonic optical activity, reaching a dissymmetry factor of 0.55. The unprecedented ability to vary the helicoidal pitch allows control of the optical response, enabling inversion of optical handedness without changing the handedness of the template, effectively decoupling geometrical chirality from optical chirality. Remarkably, the gold nanoparticles can also be recovered from dry films and redispersed as colloids, introducing an appealing circularity concept for sustainable chiral plasmonic materials.

title: Density of polynomials whose Aron--Berner extensions attain their norms
abstract: We establish a polynomial analogue of Lindenstrauss' theorem in full generality. More precisely, we prove that, for every real or complex Banach space X and every positive integer n, the n-homogeneous scalar-valued polynomials whose Aron-Berner extensions to the bidual X** attain their norms form a dense subset of the space of continuous n-homogeneous polynomials on X. This resolves a problem posed by Aron, Garcia and Maestre in 2003, extending their result for quadratic polynomials to arbitrary degrees without imposing any structural assumptions on the underlying Banach space. We further establish the corresponding theorem for vector-valued polynomials with arbitrary Banach space codomains. Our approach relies on a new perturbation scheme based on averaged linear contractions, which provides simultaneous control of the multilinear variables and yields norm attainment through iterated limits in the bidual.

title: ForeTac: Predictive Contact Guidance for Generative Robot Policies
abstract: In contact-rich manipulation, actions that appear equally plausible from vision can produce different contact outcomes, while reactive control based on current tactile feedback may respond too late to prevent failure. We present ForeTac, a predictive contact-guidance framework organized as a represent-predict-evaluate-guide loop. ForeTac encodes the current tactile state, predicts future tactile latent trajectories conditioned on candidate action sequences, and evaluates each predicted trajectory with a contact-quality objective learned from successful and failed physical interactions. At inference, gradients of this objective are backpropagated through the tactile predictor to guide action generation before execution while keeping all model parameters frozen. We evaluate ForeTac on four real-robot tasks (planar and curved-surface wiping, card swiping, and fragile-object grasping) with diffusion and flow-matching policies. Compared with vision-only Diffusion Policy, ForeTac improves the average task success rate (SR) from 36.3% to 71.3% and the average contact success rate (CSR) from 20.0% to 66.3% across these tasks, and yields gains in both metrics with a flow-matching policy. Component analyses support the learned tactile representation, action-conditioned foresight, and generation-time gradient guidance, while predicted tactile latent trajectories preserve contact-quality ordering. Project page: https://foretac.github.io/.

title: Certifying Almost-Sure Reachability in Unknown MDPs
abstract: {\em Specification-Guided Reinforcement Learning (RL)} has largely concerned itself with \emph{learning} an optimal policy against a formal specification in an unknown {\em Markov Decision Process (MDP)}. We take up the dual question. Given a policy already in hand, can one \emph{verify} that it is correct against a formal specification in an unknown MDP, using sampling access alone? Such a question arises naturally in safety-critical systems. We investigate it for the {\em almost-sure reachability property}, whose correctness is witnessed by a {\em ranking supermartingale (RSM)} certificate. Our first finding is negative. In the absence of any further information about the MDP, one can neither learn such a certificate nor verify a candidate one with probabilistic guarantees. On the positive side, we show that, under a mild restriction, a known lower bound $p_{\min}$ on nonzero transition probabilities, a correct certificate \emph{can} be learned with PAC-style guarantees. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of learning and verifying certificates for almost-sure reachability in unknown MDPs from sampling access alone. Finally, our experiments show that the $p_{\min}$-based sufficient condition, while sound, is conservative: the learned certificate often remains valid on the true MDP even when the condition fails.

title: Self-Supervised Source-Filter Model of Speech Production
abstract: Deep learning models of speech seldom represent the source-filter process by which speech is produced, relying instead on latent features with no physical correspondence to articulation or phonation. We propose SoFilNet, a self-supervised, differentiable Source-Filter Network that estimates the parameters of speech production directly from the raw waveform: a source, specified by fundamental frequency (F0), voicing and the aperiodicity of five frequency bands, and a filter, specified by ordered formant poles, additional poles that shape the rest of the spectral envelope, and antiresonance zeros. The model is trained only to reconstruct the input speech; no formant or pitch annotation is used. Since per-bin spectral losses favor blurred spectra wherever the model is uncertain, we train F0 and voicing against autocorrelation pseudo-labels refined with the model's own filter, aperiodicity against the periodic fraction of each band, and formant sharpness against spectral contrast. On VTR-FORMANTS, the estimated formants attain the lowest mean error among the reported methods, including supervised trackers, and on the unseen PTDB-TUG corpus the F0 frame error matches the best classical tracker and is lower than that of all learned trackers. The parameters are also consistent with speech production theory: aperiodicity rises with frequency and orders phone classes by the turbulence of their excitation, and the zeros deepen on nasal consonants, the lower one rising with place of articulation.

title: Narrative Lookahead in LLMs: Event-Level Decodability, Predictive Advantage, and Steering
abstract: Do language models carry information about narrative events before writing them, and how far ahead? We examine narrative lookahead through salient, state-changing events rather than tokens or response-level attributes. We extract 23,355 LLM-annotated events from 2,000 stories generated by four open-weight LLMs, labeling them along three nonexclusive dimensions of change: within agents, between agents, and in the story world, with human validation on a subset. Event segmentation and plot-independent labels enable comparisons across stories at horizons measured in events rather than in tokens. At event ends, we probe hidden states for upcoming event types and compare predictions with text-only predictors using matched prefixes. Across four models, future event types are decodable above prevalence baselines for at least four subsequent events, but probes significantly outperform both primary text-only predictors only for the next event. In exploratory steering with OLMo-3.1-32B, a probe-derived direction shifts the proportion of the target event type in both intended directions at higher strengths. Our event-level approach links the prediction of future narrative developments to interventions that reshape subsequent event composition.

title: Cheap, Consistent, Calibrated, but Biased? Typed Decision Models as Judges
abstract: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability for each allowed answer instead of generating text, which makes them candidates for cheaply replacing LLM judges that compare two answers. Whether they share the biases of LLM judges is untested. We run the CALM benchmark's bias tests on eight TDMs and seven LLM judges of 2024 and 2026. Every TDM is biased, in three to eight of twelve tests. Emotional tone affects them most, and rewriting the better answer in such a tone lowers the accuracy of a typical TDM from 99% to 42%. TDMs are more biased than 2026 LLM judges. All eight change verdicts when the answers swap places, which the 2026 LLM judges hardly do, and several side with an answer that most people allegedly prefer or that a famous model allegedly wrote. Yet both kinds of judge are tripped up by the same prompts. The TDMs' probabilities show that most tests mainly flip verdicts the TDM was unsure of, and that good calibration does not protect against bias. As TDMs are more consistent and 37 times cheaper than 2026 LLM judges, our results suggest they can be attractive judges if their biases are tested for the task.

title: MARTS: A Modular Agricultural Robot for Targeted Spraying of Diseased Tomato Plants in Greenhouses
abstract: Broadcast spraying remains the dominant method of disease control in greenhouse tomato production, yet it treats healthy and diseased tissue alike, exposes workers to hazardous aerosols, and depends on operator skill. This paper presents MARTS (Modular Agricultural Robot for Targeted Spraying), a low-cost robotic platform that closes the loop from plant-level disease detection to leaf-localised spray delivery in commercial greenhouses. MARTS integrates a Clearpath Husky A200 mobile base, a UR5 manipulator, a novel modular spraying end-effector built around a single 12 V micro-diaphragm pump, and a wrist-mounted Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D camera. Disease detection reuses our previously published Tomato Leaf Disease Vision Language Model (TLDVLM; Grounding DINO, SAM-2 and LoRA-tuned BLIP-2, 97.27% accuracy over 10 classes); this work focuses on actuation, control and system integration. A ROS pipeline lifts detections into 3D targets, generates collision-aware nozzle poses at a 120 mm stand-off using fitted leaf normals, and scales pump pulse duration to lesion area. Water-sensitive paper calibration showed a linear pulse-volume relationship (R^2 = 0.994). In MuJoCo simulation, an adaptive base-repositioning strategy achieved 100% coverage of 18 waypoints with a maximum orientation error of 1.1 deg. Deployed at the SILAL commercial greenhouse (Al Ain, UAE) on cherry tomatoes under natural infection, MARTS treated 312 diseased leaves in 12 autonomous trials with 92.4% targeting success, 18.7 mm mean spray-centre error, 6.1% adjacent-leaf overspray, and a 71% reduction in pesticide volume versus broadcast spraying. Mean cycle time was 4.8 s per leaf, and the spraying subsystem costs USD 412, 6-10x lower than comparable systems, showing that accurate leaf-level targeting is achievable on commodity hardware.

title: Local error correction prolongs time-crystalline memory
abstract: Discrete time crystals are non-equilibrium phases of matter with spatiotemporal order and a response that breaks the time-translation symmetry of a periodic external drive. Interactions, spatial disorder and correlated random driving can in theory stabilize this order. In experiments, however, coupling to the environment limits the time crystal lifetime. Here we use stochastic local bit-flip error correction to prolong the time-crystalline response of a driven, spatially disordered two-dimensional Ising model on a superconducting quantum processor, using a repetition code with distances three and five on a honeycomb lattice with up to 68 physical qubits. Even though ancilla qubits, midcircuit syndrome measurements and decoding increase the required quantum and classical resources, the stochastic drive increases the memory decay time by a factor of up to two. At late times we observe that recovery stabilizes spatial order across the lattice. The spin-configuration distributions explain this separation, as recovery suppresses disagreeing bonds while broadening occupies completely reversed states. Syndrome measurements without correction accelerate the memory decay, demonstrating the importance of conditional correction. Our results show that local bit-flip error correction can preserve time-crystalline memory over more drive cycles than the bare dynamics.

title: H-DDCM: Hadamard Codebooks for Fast Generative Image and Video Compression
abstract: Training-free diffusion-based compression methods repurpose the generative priors of a diffusion or a flow model to compress data without retraining them as task-specific codecs. Recent codebook-based approaches such as Turbo-DDCM achieve strong perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates, but their reliance on dense Gaussian codebooks remains costly in both memory and computation, and scales poorly with the large latent dimensions of modern image and video generators. Their combinatorial bitstream encoding further becomes computationally heavy at this scale. We introduce H-DDCM, a scalable generative compression framework that replaces Gaussian codebooks with implicit randomized Hadamard dictionaries. The fast Walsh-Hadamard transform allows for implicitly synthesizing full-dimensional dictionaries with $O(d \log d)$ compute for projection and reconstruction and $O(d)$ memory, without materializing the full-dimensional dictionary. We further introduce an efficient table-free lexicographic coding scheme that makes combinatorial encoding practical at larger dimensions. Beyond images, we adapt the framework to an autoregressive video flow model and develop a streaming compression scheme that periodically re-encodes recently reconstructed frames into a fresh KV-cache prefix, preserving temporal context across segments at no additional transmitted bits. This enables long-form, close to real-time generative video compression on a single GPU. Across image and video benchmarks, H-DDCM achieves competitive rate-distortion-perception performance while substantially reducing the memory and computational overhead of codebook-based training-free generative compression.

title: Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action: Routing New Information to LLM Decisions Already Made
abstract: Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the moment it is made; the action it commits to is latent, carried out later, in a changing world. We therefore introduce a timestamp theory of decision validity and a decision ledger that realises it. Six timestamps define a decision; a freshness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence guarantees at action time, placing the remaining risk in information published afterwards. Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities: routing, which delivers that information to affected decisions before their revision deadlines, and temporal judgment, which reads it for the time of action. The ledger is persistent state holding each decision's times, evidence and background knowledge, indexed by watch conditions written at decision time. Controlled decision streams with exact labels confirm four predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to frontier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on decisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows routing; the ledger's index sets what routing reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect dependencies at low exposure; and the remaining errors concern when a change takes effect. Freshness makes a decision right when it is made; routing and temporal judgment keep it right when it is carried out.

title: Monitoring latent reasoning in looped language models
abstract: Looped language models (LMs) reuse one block of layers several times per token generation, promising more latent computation at no additional storage cost. Despite their rising popularity, the analysis of looped LMs is still in its infancy: little is known about whether the iterative transformations actually improve their capabilities, or whether these models remain stable under prompt perturbation. We construct an inspection protocol rooted in Mechanistic Interpretability comprising five diverse lenses. We apply it to examine eight looped LMs from four families. Models differ in many aspects but the key one is whether the prompt is transmitted only within the looped state (carry loops: Ouro, LoopUS) or re-supplied at every iteration (re-read loops: Parcae, and Rec-OLMo & Huginn from the Raven family). The results of our study provide valuable insights concerning safety and efficient use of looped language models.

title: Organisation and aggregation of calcium carbonate ions in water via molecular simulation
abstract: Crystallisation of calcium carbonate (CaCO$_3$) in aqueous solutions is essential for carbon dioxide sequestration and the sustainable production of calcium carbonate materials, which are widely used in industry and increasingly explored for novel applications. While crystallisation is often analysed within the framework of classical nucleation theory, CaCO$_3$ and other ionic crystals often form through amorphous precursor phases, motivating the need for alternative descriptions. In this work, we investigate the relationship between the formation of the first CaCO$_3$ coordination sphere, a fundamental unit of local ordering, and ionic aggregation using two complementary simulation approaches: on-the-fly probability-enhanced sampling (OPES) and asynchronous and infinite-swap replica exchange transition interface sampling ($\infty$RETIS). OPES was used to explore free-energy landscapes, whereas $\infty$RETIS was used to determine reaction kinetics. We studied systems at two levels of supersaturation, between which the formation of the first coordination sphere exhibited distinct kinetic behaviour. These differences were found to be linked to concentration-dependent ionic aggregation. At lower concentration, aggregation remains limited, whereas higher concentration promotes extensive spinodal-like aggregation. For both concentrations, the first coordination sphere forms within the pre-formed clusters through one of two distinct pathways: either within a cluster close to the minimum size required for its formation, or within larger amorphous aggregates whose size and structure depend on concentration. The coexistence of these pathways at both levels of supersaturation reveals the multifaceted nature of early-stage CaCO$_3$ crystallisation and highlights the importance of differentiating ionic aggregation and organisation.

title: Extensions of Operator Systems, Hyperrigidity and Quantum Double Suspension
abstract: We introduce a class of extensions of unital operator systems satisfying a certain Toeplitz type property. We show that these extensions induce corresponding extensions of the $C^*$-algebras they generate. We prove that hyperrigidity is preserved under these extensions, yielding new examples through iteration. We introduce the quantum double suspension of operator systems as a special class of these extensions and show that its iterates yield the Hong-Szymański quantum double suspensions at the $C^*$-algebra level, encompassing, in particular, the Vaksman-Soibelman quantum spheres. We construct hyperrigid operator systems underlying these quantum spheres. As a further application, we show that every counterexample to Arveson's hyperrigidity conjecture gives rise to a sequence of counterexamples. We identify the $C^*$-envelopes of these extensions and use this identification to obtain a $K$-theoretic condition ensuring that each such sequence contains infinitely many pairwise non-isomorphic counterexamples. We also observe that the validity of the conjecture in the commutative setting is linked to its validity for an infinite family of noncommutative operator systems obtained through successive extensions. Finally, we compute the propagation number, an invariant of operator systems introduced by Connes and van Suijlekom, for these extensions.

title: Distance Prediction for Quantum Codes
abstract: The distance of a quantum code is a fundamental metric that dictates its error-correction capability. While quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) families such as Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes offer a promising pathway to low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computing, computing their distance is challenging. Current exact solvers and even search heuristics that provide a distance upper bound suffer from severe computational bottlenecks, restricting the discovery of optimal codes. In this paper, we construct a dataset of BB codes with corresponding distance upper bounds obtained through high-budget heuristic searches. We introduce BB-Net, an attention-based neural network architecture for predicting the distance of BB codes. It achieves 96.39% accuracy on the reference distances in the test set, compared with 94.86% for state-of-the-art heuristics with a budget of up to $10^{4}$ times more computational runtime. On a subset with certified exact distances, BB-Net achieves 98.94%. By relieving the distance-calculation bottleneck, BB-Net enables faster screening of large code spaces, particularly in ML-driven search pipelines, and thereby can accelerate the discovery of novel quantum error-correcting codes, an important capability for advancing scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/NadavSc/BBNet

title: Spectrally enhanced gravitational redshift signals in photonic interferometry
abstract: Quantum mechanics and general relativity are remarkably successful, yet their joint predictions remain beyond direct experimental reach. Photonic interferometers operating in a gravitational field offer a promising route to test this regime: gravitational redshift differentiates photon propagation between vertically separated arms, leading to a predicted phase shift and reduction in interference visibility. These effects are minute on laboratory scales, motivating existing proposals to consider large interferometer areas to accumulate them geometrically. Indeed, such schemes typically require kilometre-scale optical paths to produce appreciable interferometric signals. Here, we propose a strategy that replaces geometric accumulation with spectral enhancement by coupling the two interferometer arms to optical scatterers based on ultranarrow atomic transitions. These transitions serve as local spectral references: gravitational redshift changes the photon's detuning from each resonance, producing large differences in reflection amplitude and hence substantial visibility loss and interferometric phase shift already for centimetre-scale height differences. We quantify the experimental requirements and assess the feasibility of implementation with current or near-term technology. Our proposal thus opens a route to tabletop optical tests of the interplay between quantum mechanics and general relativity.

title: Excess inertia of finite metric spaces
abstract: This paper classifies the possible inertias that are realized by an excess matrix of a finite metric space with at most nine points. For the classification, we make use of relationships between finite metric spaces and non-obtuse and acute sets in classical geometry. As an application, we prove that the small-scale limit of the magnitude function of any six-point metric space is at least one whenever this limit exists.

title: Human-Inspired Asymmetric Collaboration for Dual-Student Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Dual-student learning enriches predictive diversity in SSMIS by introducing a strongly augmented view alongside a weakly augmented view. Insufficient strong augmentation may homogenize the students, whereas excessive augmentation can corrupt anatomical evidence and destabilize collaboration. This challenge echoes feedback-regulated human instruction, where learners receive differentiated tasks and the task difficulty is continually adjusted according to their evolving responses. Inspired by these, we propose Human-Inspired Asymmetric Collaboration (HAC), a closed-loop dual-student framework that maintains weak--strong learning through adaptive difficulty calibration and geometry preservation. Specifically, Reinforcement-guided Difficulty Calibration (RDC) formulates strong-augmentation control as a window-level reinforcement learning process, using augmentation history, realized perturbations, and training responses to dynamically adjust the augmentation magnitude, operation number, and magnitude range. Meanwhile, the Gramian Geometry Preservation Constraint (G2PC) preserves the early-stage three-branch geometry through global volume and pairwise area constraints, preventing shared supervision from homogenizing the two students. Comprehensive evaluations across LA, Pancreas, and BraTS-2019 validate both the segmentation effectiveness and capability-aware difficulty calibration of HAC.

title: MATISSE unveils a dusty disc in the interior of EP Aquarii. First evidence of a misaligned hierarchical triple system with a central AGB star?
abstract: Aims. We have mapped the dust and molecular gas emission distributions in the vicinity (a few stellar radii) of the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star EP\,Aquarii, with a previously reported stellar companion at $\sim$50\,au, to search for binary-induced asymmetries. Methods. We present an analysis of new high-angular-resolution ($\gtrsim$4\,mas) images obtained with MATISSE (in the wavelength range $\sim$3--8\,\mum) as well as archival high-angular-resolution ($\gtrsim$20\,mas) ALMA $\rm^{12}$CO\,(c$J$=2-1) line and continuum emission observations ($\sim$230\,GHz), to study the circumstellar morphology and kinematics of the molecular gas on these spatial scales. Results. The MATISSE images display a bright central source and two slightly extended emission features ("blobs") located on opposite sides of the AGB star (at radial distances of $\sim$4--10\,au). These structures are consistent with previous mid-infrared interferometric observations, suggesting stability over decades. The central source is elongated along the direction defined by the blobs, in both the MATISSE and ALMA continuum images. The ALMA $\rm^{12}$CO\,($J$=2-1) maps display an asymmetric inner wind with a velocity gradient. Conclusions. The observations are consistent with an edge-on dusty equatorial overdensity (disc-like), hinting the presence of a close ($\lesssim$4\,au) companion. The inferred symmetry axis is almost perpendicular to the CO velocity gradient and the orbital plane proposed for the distant ($\sim$50\,au) companion. EP\,Aqr may represent the first misaligned hierarchical triple system with a central AGB star.

title: SkipWorld: Latent Skip Planning with Distilled World Models for Efficient Visual Navigation
abstract: World-model-based visual navigation enables action planning by predicting future states under candidate trajectories. However, long-horizon rollout remains challenging: models are often trained with ground-truth visual histories but deployed in closed-loop prediction, and evaluating many candidates with step-by-step rollout is computationally expensive. We propose SkipWorld, a latent skip planning framework for efficient visual navigation. SkipWorld introduces three components: (i) Latent AutoRoll, which trains a world model to recursively roll out future states in latent space, reducing the mismatch between training and closed-loop inference; (ii) SkipDistill, which distills the latent autoregressive model into a skip world model that directly predicts long-stride future latent states; and (iii) Skip-then-Refine Planning, a dual-model coarse-to-fine planner that first filters candidate trajectories with the skip model and then reranks selected candidates with the stronger autoregressive model. This design preserves accurate trajectory evaluation while reducing redundant rollout computation. Experiments on RECON, HuRoN, SCAND, and TartanDrive show that, compared with NWM, SkipWorld reduces the average ATE by 4.2% and RPE by 2.7%, while decreasing planning time by 62.4% with a 2.7-fold speedup.

title: FPGA Based Design And Implementation of Neural Network Compensators for Nanocrystalline MEMS Pressure Sensor
abstract: In this paper the effects of nonlinearity and temperature of nanocrystalline MEMS pressure sensor have been compensated using neural network algorithm which has been implemented on a FPGA chip. The neural network employs back propagation algorithm to train the multilayer perceptron feed forward network that causes an error reduction due to temperature upto the level of 98%. It is realized on FPGA with pipelined architecture for parallel and fast sensing operation. The pressure sensor along with the FPGA based compensation results in an intelligent sensor system capable of high speed and accurate pressure measurement which has been tested for a typical biomedical application.

title: Local-resolvent formulation and assessment of linear-scaling Kohn-Sham calculations
abstract: Kohn-Sham density-functional theory is expensive because it needs orbitals that extend over the whole system. For insulators this can be avoided by using only the diagonal of the one-electron resolvent, $g(\mathbf{r},z)=\langle\mathbf{r}|(z-\hat h)^{-1}|\mathbf{r}\rangle$, at a few complex energies $z$. We call the scheme local-resolvent density-functional theory (LRes-DFT). The density and the band energy are linear in $g$, so neither orbitals nor a kinetic-energy functional are needed. The complex energies are $M$ equally spaced points on a circle that encloses the occupied levels, offset by half a spacing so that no point lies on the real axis. Summing the resolvent over them is equivalent to occupying each level with $1/(1+u^M)$, where $u$ is the level's energy measured from the circle's center in units of its radius. This is a smooth step that is near 1 inside the circle and near 0 outside, and it stays between 0 and 1 for every $M$. If the circle moves with the chemical potential, forces at fixed electron number are exact. Gauss-Legendre and Zolotarev rules need fewer points when the gap is small. In three dimensions we use eigenpairs of small windows around each molecule instead of resolvents. This is divide-and-conquer (DC) with a different occupation function, and it is as accurate as DC with Fermi-Dirac occupations. For H$_2$ molecular crystals of up to 1024 electrons it agrees with Kohn-Sham to $2.5\times10^{-7}$ Ha per electron. On one core it is slower than dense diagonalization below about 500 electrons and 3.5 times faster at 1024 electrons. It loses accuracy for disordered or compressed systems and for diffuse basis functions.

title: Preliminary Exploration of Large Models Based on Self-Supervised Learning for Health Monitoring of Power Electronic Converters
abstract: Current artificial intelligence (AI) methods for power electronics converters make limited use of the abundant unlabeled data generated during real-world operation. This underexplored resource holds significant potential for advancing model performance. To address this gap, this paper presents PE-TSFM, a time-series foundation model tailored for power module health monitoring. The model adopts the PatchTST architecture combined with self-supervised learning and is trained on more than 143 million timestamps, where over 98\% of this training data is unlabeled and collected directly from an operating traction converter. In degradation classification tasks, PE-TSFM achieves an accuracy of 87\%, considerably surpassing five conventional time-series AI models whose performance ranges from 27\% to 45\%. These results demonstrate the model's strong few-shot learning capability and generalization across different operating conditions. This work promotes a shift from narrowly focused models in power electronics toward unified, scalable foundation models that can unlock value from large-scale unlabeled operational data.

title: Revisiting Error Feedback for Model Quantization
abstract: We study causal error-feedback coefficients as design variables for model quantization. Modeling instantaneous quantization errors as independent, zero-mean variables with a common fixed variance, we formulated a metric-dependent trace problem for designing feedback coefficients. The formulation resembles fixed-order GPTQ/LDLQ feedback and supports Jacobian-aware designs that account for downstream error propagation. For a positive-definite metric $\boldsymbol{H}$, we prove that the joint rotation-feedback trace minimum is $n\det(\boldsymbol{H})^{1/n}$ and present an attaining pair using the geometric mean decomposition. Experiments on synthetic networks, trained MLPs, and language models show benefits from downstream-sensitive feedback, but also reveal that trace optimality need not improve finite-level performance. Small QAT experiments further illustrate direct loss-driven feedback tuning with fixed or trainable network weights.

title: SparPR: Runtime KV-Cache Recovery for Resource-Constrained LLM Inference on Consumer Hardware
abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on consumer hardware is bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with every decoded token and quickly exhausts the memory and bandwidth of a single consumer GPU. We present SparPR (Sparse Partial Recomputation), a runtime KV-cache recovery mechanism that does not modify model weights and requires no offline training. SparPR couples three online decisions: Query-Aware key-block selection scores historical blocks against the current query; dynamic budget control estimates per-block copy and recompute costs to decide how many blocks to retain; and on-demand local recomputation with cost-aware fallback merges retained blocks into continuous spans and switches between sparse recomputation and full recovery according to a runtime cost comparison. Implemented on FlexGen/FlexLLMGen, SparPR is evaluated on a single consumer laptop (RTX 3070 Ti 8GB, Ryzen 9 6900HX, 16GB RAM). It cuts end-to-end latency by 31%, 52%, and 63% at 1k, 2k, and 4k prompt tokens respectively, with 1.4x-2.7x higher throughput, and completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes where the FlexGen baseline times out. Under a fixed cache budget, SparPR retains a Needle Accuracy that stays well above StreamingLLM and H2O at every keep ratio, and ablation studies confirm that the three mechanisms act jointly.

title: Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations by Correcting Modality Misrouting in Omnimodal LLMs
abstract: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs) are susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations under audio-visual interference. We find that, for a substantial fraction of incorrect joint predictions, the question-relevant unimodal branch can still recover the correct answer, suggesting that task-relevant evidence can remain recoverable from the relevant modality even when it is not reflected in the joint prediction. We refer to this recoverable failure pattern as \emph{modality misrouting}. We propose CaRe (Conflict-aware Residual Intervention), a training-free inference-time method for identifying and correcting modality misrouting. CaRe uses a text-only modality probe to identify a candidate modality-specific counterfactual branch, and flags potential misrouting when its prediction conflicts with the original joint prediction. For such cases, CaRe computes a residual direction from the discrepancy between the counterfactual and fused representations and uses it to steer the original multimodal state toward the relevant modality evidence, while retaining both modalities in the original audio-visual inference path. The intervention strength is adapted based on the confidence of the counterfactual branch. Experiments on CMM and AVHBench across two OLLMs show that CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time hallucination-mitigation baselines.

title: FlowCred: Hierarchical Credit Assignment and Functional Coordination for Joint Text-to-Video Post-Training
abstract: Prompt optimization and generator post-training are two complementary ways to improve text-to-video (T2V) generation, and recent systems increasingly train both modules jointly. However, optimizing a prompt policy and a video generator from the same terminal reward creates two ambiguities: prompt quality is confounded with stochastic generation, and the two modules may realize overlapping local improvements. We introduce FlowCred, a two-level framework for joint T2V post-training. First, hierarchical credit assignment uses matched prompt-seed rollout grids to separate prompt-level credit from prompt-conditioned generator residuals under shared randomness. Second, functional coordination probes alternative current-policy prompts at states from actual generation trajectories, providing generator-aware evidence for prompt optimization while selectively attenuating generator updates already supported by conditioning changes. Across multiple T2V benchmarks, FlowCred consistently improves matched joint-training baselines. On LTX-2.5, FlowCred improves a strictly matched joint-training control from 61.47 to 64.46 on T2V-CompBench and from 55.58 to 58.08 on StoryEval, without increasing decoded-video or reward-model-call budgets. Factorial and realized-update analyses show complementary contributions from prompt shaping and generator routing, while human evaluation and transfer across backbones and updater families provide further supporting evidence.

title: RadixFlow: Filling Execution Bubbles in Prefix-Cached Hybrid LLM Serving
abstract: Prefix reuse improves LLM inference by sharing the KV cache of common prompt prefixes. This helps only if the scheduler can execute a matched branch in the current worker round. Schedulers assume that a matched prefix is ready, which holds for full attention but fails for hybrid LLMs. There, a branch (the consumer) may need recurrent state that another branch (the producer) is still computing in the same round. The native scheduler stops its waiting-queue scan at this blocked consumer, and the resulting head-of-line blocking creates \emph{execution bubbles}: idle batch slots that independent work could fill. We introduce RadixFlow, which decouples prefix matching from state readiness. Its state-ready traversal turns a global scan barrier into a local wait: only the consumer is blocked until the next round, while feasible independent branches keep filling the batch under the native state check. On five hybrid models, RadixFlow lowers mean latency by 3\% to 24\% and worker rounds by 11\% to 44\% at almost unchanged reuse. On the larger Qwen3.5 models, ablations show that most of the gain comes from traversal, which adds little on a full-attention control. Heavier rounds limit how much of this saving reaches latency.

title: A Better-than-2 Approximation for k-Median Part I: The Power of General Bids
abstract: The Greedy algorithm of Jain, Mahdian, Markakis, Saberi, and Vazirani was the best Lagrangian-multiplier-preserving (LMP) approximation algorithm for facility location, and thus the engine behind the best $k$-median guarantees, for over two decades. Its $2$-LMP guarantee was only recently broken by a small amount ($(2-η)$-LMP where $η\approx 2.25 \cdot 10^{-7}$) through local-search post-processing. That analysis relies on the structure of worst-case instances, and it appears difficult to obtain substantial further improvements along those lines. We take a different approach and change the algorithm itself: we introduce general bidding functions, replacing the classical linear bid with a richer family of rules and prove a polynomial-time $1.95$-LMP approximation, a large improvement over the long-standing factor of~$2$. We further show that these generalized bidding rules can be made smooth (log-adaptive), building on the recent framework developed for the classical Greedy algorithm by Cohen-Addad, Grandoni, Lee, Schwiegelshohn, and Svensson. This yields a polynomial-time $1.95$-approximation that opens $k+O_\varepsilon(\log n)$ centers. Combined with a $(1.89+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for stable instances in our companion work \cite{stableinstances}, we achieve a better-than-2 approximation for the $k$-median problem in polynomial-time.

title: Linking Horizontal and Vertical Submesoscale Lagrangian Dynamics South of the Ibiza Channel
abstract: Fronts, eddies, jets, and meanders populate the ocean surface and play a key role in organizing transport and mixing across a wide range of scales. From a Lagrangian perspective, frontal structures are conveniently detected as surface filaments that act as barriers to horizontal transport. However, the degree to which these structures maintain coherence below the surface and the relationship between horizontal and vertical motions in their vicinity remain poorly understood. Here we analyze two such filaments in the western Mediterranean Sea, south of the Ibiza Channel, using a high-resolution ocean simulation and Lagrangian diagnostics specifically designed to characterize submesoscale transport. Backward Finite-Size Lyapunov Exponents (FSLE) computed at successive depths reveal nearly vertical, curtain-like structures extending several tens of meters into the water column, with intensity decreasing with depth. Vertical-velocity sections across the filaments show coherent downward motion aligned with the filament cores, while Lagrangian trajectories indicate rapid horizontal convergence of fluid particles accompanied by sustained downward displacement. The barrier effect of Lagrangian Coherent Structures (LCSs) is commonly associated with persistent dynamical features of large-scale flows. Here, however, we demonstrate that FSLE filaments generated by rapidly fluctuating submesoscale dynamics can also act as effective transport barriers. The results demonstrate that the surface signatures of Lagrangian filaments identified through FSLE techniques correspond to three-dimensional transport structures that regulate both lateral aggregation and vertical connectivity in the upper ocean.

title: Low-frequency spectra and scattering of pulsars towards the Gum Nebula with the MWA
abstract: Context. The Gum Nebula is a nearby ionised complex with sight-line-dependent pulsar propagation. Aims. We test whether a smooth ionised structure can explain low-frequency spectral turnovers and pulse broadening, or whether smaller-scale material is required. Methods. We analysed Murchison Widefield Array observations of six pulsars at 80--240 MHz, combining sub-band flux densities with literature data. We compared power-law, free--free absorption (FFA), and turnover-constrained broken-power-law (BPL) spectra, and modelled scattering through pulse-profile convolution. PSR J0820-4114 and the Vela pulsar were fitted jointly across frequency. Results. All six spectra depart from a single power law. FFA is favoured for PSRs J0737-3039A and J0820-4114, and BPL for J0742-2822 and J0835-4510; the other two classifications depend on assumed error floors. Conditional FFA solutions imply emission measures of $10^4$--$10^5$ pc cm$^{-6}$ for electron temperatures of $3\times10^3$--$10^4$ K, far exceeding smooth-shell expectations. PSRs J0737-3039A and J0837-4135 have scattering laws consistent with $τ_{\rm sc}\proptoν^{-4}$. We obtain $α_{\rm sc}=-3.07\pm0.11$ for J0742-2822 and $-1.59\pm0.44$ for J0820-4114 using a joint two-component model. The Vela pulsar is best described by an effective thick-screen model with $α_{\rm sc}\simeq-2.74$. Neither tested Galactic electron-density model reproduces both independent distances and low-frequency scattering uniformly. Conclusions. The results favour a structured Gum--Vela magneto-ionic environment in which neighbouring sight lines probe different absorbing and scattering material; these effects need not arise in the same plasma component.

title: Walk Like This: Stylized Locomotion for Physics-Based Characters through Example-Driven Diffusion
abstract: We present a real-time framework for expressive legged locomotion that enables independent control over velocity and style. Unlike existing data-driven controllers, which typically require explicit style labels for training, our method efficiently leverages large-scale unstructured motion data and generalizes to unseen styles. We disentangle style from functional locomotion through a tailored sampling strategy used to train a style encoder whose output conditions an autoregressive diffusion model. During inference, the user provides a style reference clip and a joystick velocity command. The diffusion model then generates a kinematic reference tracked by a reinforcement learning controller. To improve user controllability and stylization strength, we propose an attention biasing mechanism and a velocity command correction strategy. We demonstrate our method on a physics-based humanoid character in simulation and on a physical robot, showcasing robust real-time control and continuous style modulation. The results can be best seen in our supplemental video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=roFnS6N7nJ4).

title: Topological entropy of saturated sets for Lorenz attractors
abstract: We study the topological entropy of saturated sets for continuous flows, with emphasis on singular hyperbolic dynamics. For a $C^r$-generic ($r \geq 2$) vector field $X$ carrying a geometric Lorenz attractor $Λ$, we prove that for every nonempty compact connected set $\mathcal{K} \subseteq \mathcal{M}(Φ,Λ)$ and every open set $U \subseteq M$ with $U \cap Λ\neq \emptyset$, $h_{\mathrm{top}}(Φ,G_{\mathcal{K}}(Φ) \cap \operatorname{Trans}(Φ,Λ) \cap U)=\inf_{μ\in \mathcal{K}} h_μ(ϕ_1)$, where $Φ=(ϕ_t)_{t \in \mathbb{R}}$ is the flow induced by $X$ and $\operatorname{Trans}(Φ,Λ)$ denotes the set of points whose positive orbits are dense in $Λ$. The same formula holds $C^1$-generically for singular hyperbolic attractors. In contrast with the uniformly hyperbolic case, we also prove that, for vector fields in a dense subset of $\mathcal{X}^r(M^3)$, geometric Lorenz attractors admit a positive-entropy invariant measure with no generic points. An analogous conclusion holds for vector fields in a dense subset of $\mathcal{X}^1(M)$ whose non-trivial singular hyperbolic attractors contain singularities and satisfy $\dim E^{cu}=2$. These examples show that the discrete-time saturated entropy theory does not extend directly to singular flows.

title: Standard identities for polynomial vector fields
abstract: Let $W_n$ be the Lie algebra of polynomial vector fields in $n$ variables over a field of characteristic zero, and let $s_k$ denote the alternating sum of compositions of $k$ vector fields. The identity $s_{n^2+2n-1}=0$ has been asserted for arbitrary $n$. We give an explicit counterexample in dimension five, verified by an exact integer computation of a $34$-commutator. Together with the known vanishing of $s_{35}$, this shows that $35$ is the least degree of a standard identity on $W_5$. We then prove that $s_{n^2+2n-1}=0$ for every even $n\geq2$. The proof uses Lie algebra homology with coefficients in the polynomial algebra modulo constants and a lemma on invariant tensors. We describe the computation and provide the source code and verification results.

title: Reverse Translation and Convolution Estimates in the Framework of the Mehler-Fock Transform
abstract: In this paper, reverse translation and convolution estimates in the frame of $μ^{th}$ order Mehler-Fock transform are obtained. Continuity properties of these operators on the test function space $\mathfrak{H}_{l,r,n}$ have been discussed. Moreover, Sobolev space $S_{r,p}^{N,α}$ has been introduced and again continuity properties of these operators in this Sobolev space have been discussed.

title: Attacking Only Half the Data: Two-Sided Evaluation of AI-Text Detector Robustness
abstract: We investigate the robustness of widely used AI text detectors under attacks applied to both human and machine text. Prior evaluations typically attack only machine text, overlooking that human text is routinely modified through grammar correction, formatting, or invisible character insertion. We introduce a two-sided protocol that applies attacks to both classes. Across two corpora and nine detectors, reported AUROC gains vanish under two-sided evaluation, with attacked human text misclassified at rates up to 100%. While simple preprocessing reverses character-level attacks, word-level synonym substitution remains effective meaning-preserving, and irreversible.

title: Alternating Hamilton Paths and Cycles in Poset Products
abstract: We study alternating Hamilton paths and cycles in the comparability graphs of finite posets. We prove that if a finite poset $P$ with at least two elements admits an alternating Hamilton path, then $P\times B_r$ admits an alternating Hamilton cycle for every $r\ge2$, where $B_r$ is the Boolean lattice. As a corollary, we settle a conjecture of Katona [Discrete Appl. Math., 2013]. Furthermore, we characterize the divisor lattices admitting alternating Hamilton paths and cycles.

title: Experimental Demonstration of 7-Dimensional N-Vector Model with Dimensional Inflation and Annealing
abstract: We report the first experimental realization of a physical system described by a high-dimensional Hamiltonian comprising up to seven dimensions. Our setup is based on a holographic optical computer, which realizes a dimensional inflation by spatial and temporal multiplexing of lower dimensional systems. We demonstrate an $N$-vector model, with applications in field theory and computing. The approach is scalable and enables table-top implementation of high-dimensional theoretical models, and novel methods for combinatorial optimization. We experimentally demonstrate dimensional annealing: by dynamically reducing the number of dimensions, the ground state of an Ising model is found in complex graphs by an adiabatic evolution from high-dimensional spaces.

title: Learning a Group Element from Its Action: Galois Correspondences, Optimal ERM, and an Abel-Ruffini Threshold for the Natarajan Dimension
abstract: We study learning an unknown element $g$ of a group acting with finite orbits on a countable set, from examples $(x,gx)$. After a sample on $A$, the consistent hypotheses are the restrictions of a coset of the pointwise stabilizer of $A$, and the sample forces exactly the labels of points this stabilizer fixes; for a Galois group, they form the field generated by the data. Through this correspondence, multiclass dimensions become group invariants: the DS and graph dimensions equal the height, the Littlestone dimension the longest irredundant sequence length, and the teaching dimension the minimal base size. Among deterministic learners, symmetry makes empirical risk minimization optimal: on nondegenerate classes every consistent learner, whatever its tie-breaking, attains the optimal realizable sample complexity up to constant factors, and every consistent online learner the optimal mistake bound. Agnostically, every ERM's sample complexity exceeds the known lower bound by at most the DS-to-Natarajan ratio, up to constants. For finite Galois extensions of countable fields, the Natarajan dimension equals a group invariant, the coset-cube number, which is at least the number of complemented factors of any chief series of any subgroup. Hence the dimensions coincide for every solvable Galois group, while for the groups $A_5$ and $S_5$ of the quintic they are $2<3$ and $3<4$, and $A_5$ is the smallest group with a gap. For the Galois group $S_n$ of the general equation of degree $n$, they coincide exactly when $n\le 4$, i.e., in characteristic zero, exactly when the equation is solvable by radicals; the implication is one-way, as the simple group $\mathrm{PSL}(2,8)$ has no gap. For linear, orthogonal and unitary maps of $\mathbb R^d$ or $\mathbb C^d$ both dimensions equal $d$, and a two-fibered pseudo-cube is a disjoint union of Natarajan cubes exactly when its monodromy group is abelian.

title: When Do Learned Blocks Preserve Causal Meaning? Block Identifiability and Constructive Causal Abstractions
abstract: Standard identifiability theory assumes one-dimensional latent factors, but learned representations can encode latent information across multidimensional blocks whose internal coordinates are not uniquely determined. When such blocks are used to represent and intervene on higher-level concepts, it is unclear whether their causal meaning survives the transformations left unresolved by block-identifiability. We connect block-identifiability to constructive causal abstraction. We show that block-diagonal invertible transformations followed by compatible coordinate permutations form the maximal class that preserves every constructive causal abstraction built on those blocks. This guarantee assumes that the correspondence between blocks and concepts is updated with the representation. A small synthetic experiment with additive autoencoders shows that high-level interventions can be transferred between independently learned representations while approximately preserving their intended effects.

title: UQ-ACE: Stability-Aware Counterfactual Controller Tuning via Bayesian SINDy
abstract: Retuning feedback controllers in critical processes is challenging when experiments are costly, open-loop excitation is infeasible, and candidate controllers must be screened before deployment. The existing Adaptive Sampling for Counterfactual Explanations (ACE) method provides a sample-efficient approach for finding minimal controller-parameter changes that recover prescribed closed-loop performance, but it does not explicitly account for stability of candidate controllers proposed during the search, which may be destabilizing under plant uncertainty. This paper introduces UQ-ACE, a stability-aware retuning method based on Bayesian SINDy. In UQ-ACE, closed-loop trajectories are used to infer a posterior distribution over local dynamical models, from which candidate controllers are screened for stability before implementation. Extensive simulations show that UQ-ACE achieves valid retunings with few closed-loop experiments while preventing deployment of unstable candidates.

title: Fan Out or Relay? Ownership-Aware Routing for LLM Agents Querying Siloed Tables
abstract: Inside organizations, a question's data often sit with several owners, who query their own tables but never hand them over. An LLM coordinator can fan out, sending the question to every owner at once, or relay, querying owners in turn and reusing earlier rows. We show that neither is safe in advance, because data ownership decides which one is right. Across thirteen settings on PeopleJoin and BIRD with three model families, fan-out is more accurate in twelve on questions one owner can answer, yet answers at most 4.3% of those joining two owners' tables. The flip follows ownership, not query shape: on BIRD two-table joins, fan-out answers 32-44% when one owner holds both and 1-4% otherwise. Relay wins by conditioning on returned rows, and hiding them from an otherwise identical planner cuts two-owner accuracy from 23.2% to 5.1%. Since ownership is public, we propose Ownership-Aware Routing (OAR), which drafts a schema-only SQL query, counts the owners whose tables it joins, and routes the question before any private row is read. In ten settings OAR is never significantly less accurate than the best fixed protocol, and beats every fixed protocol on PeopleJoin, by up to 9.3 points on held-out organizations.

title: When and How Order-Flow Interventions Work After Dealers Adapt
abstract: Learning dealer agents can settle on persistently wide quotes, raising what customers pay to trade. A venue can route more orders to tighter quotes, but a wide quote may reflect real risk, and once dealers adapt, an end-to-end comparison cannot show why a rule works: because it intervenes more, picks better moments, is announced in advance, or rewards the right quote. We propose SOFA (State-aligned Order-Flow Allocation), a public order-flow contract with three parts: a State Scorer ranks market states from lagged public data, a Commitment Scheduler announces a budgeted intervention strength before dealers quote, and a Quote-to-Flow Allocator shifts a bounded share of fixed customer demand toward tighter quotes. Our paired re-adaptation protocol gives competing rules the same intervention strengths, only re-timed, lets dealers re-adapt to each rule from a shared checkpoint, and breaks one link at a time. Across 20 independently trained dealer populations in an ABIDES market, concentrating the intervention in states that the score ranks as low-risk lowers low-risk execution cost relative to random timing in every population, by 0.040 tick on average, while a stale announcement or a broken quote-to-flow link raises this cost. In the primary setting the gain comes at the expense of high-risk trades, whose costs rise, so state alignment pays off only for a venue that weighs low-risk costs more than 1.38 times as heavily as high-risk costs. Our code is available at https://github.com/moderncavemann/state-aligned-order-flow-contracts.

title: Claim Framing as a Driver of LLM Sycophancy
abstract: Sycophancy in Large Language Models, the tendency to align responses with user preferences over ground truth, has largely been studied using questions without a clear ground truth and with a single, plainly stated user opinion. We present a systematic study of which framings of a user's claim trigger sycophancy in factual question answering, where every answer is objectively verifiable without extra context. Evaluating 14 models on 42K questions, we express correct and incorrect user opinions through various claim framings over 8 dimensions and 21 types, and measure a broad set of opinion-driven behaviors. We find that all models are susceptible to user opinions regardless of size. Models are most influenced by how confidently an opinion is stated, whom it is attributed to, and whether it is presented as shared between the user and the model. In contrast to prior work, framings based on the user's expertise, authority over the model, or social pressure matter little in our factual setting. Larger models resist incorrect opinions better but are no better at recovering from their own errors. Our results call for sycophancy evaluations that probe how an opinion is framed, not merely whether one is present, and that measure multiple behaviors beyond a single flip rate.

title: Force Sensor-Based Picking Pattern Analysis and Two-Jaw Gripper Design for Cherry Tomato Robotic Harvesting in Greenhouse
abstract: Robotic harvesting of cherry tomatoes in greenhouses remains challenging due to dense fruit clusters, delicate skin, and the need for gentle yet effective detachment. This study presents a force-data-driven framework for autonomous cherry tomato harvesting that integrates six-axis force/torque sensing, a bio-inspired compliant gripper, and deployment on a mobile robotic platform. A wearable ATI six-axis force/torque sensor mounted on the index finger captured kinetic signatures of three elemental picking patterns (gripping, twisting, and lateral pulling) across 150 manual trials (50 per pattern) in laboratory and greenhouse settings. Gripping required a peak normal force of 3.92 and 0.45 N, twisting produced a dominant torque of 19.20 2.10 Nmm about the pedicel axis with minimal truss disturbance, and pure lateral pulling alone was insufficient for reliable detachment. These measurements informed a novel fingertip-localised Finray gripper, with compliant TPU 95A Finray geometry restricted to the fruit-contact region and a rigid PLA body, emulating the dual-stiffness human fingertip. A Dynamixel XM430-W350 servomotor under current-based torque control applies the measured gripping force and a 45° wrist twist. Finite element analysis showed a maximum von Mises stress of 0.24 MPa under the 3.92 N load, below the bruising threshold of cherry tomato skin. Integrated on a UR5 arm and Clearpath Husky A200 base, the system was validated in NVIDIA Isaac Sim and in 50 autonomous trials at the SILAL commercial greenhouse, Abu Dhabi, UAE. The hybrid grip-twist-pull strategy achieved an 86.0% picking success rate, 2.3% fruit damage, and an 8.4 s cycle time per fruit, outperforming vacuum (66.3%), rotating (70.1%), clamping (76.0%), and suction-cutting (52.4%) end-effectors. These results demonstrate preliminary feasibility under the tested facility and cultivar conditions

title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Zero-Shot Human-Object Interaction
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong zero-shot reasoning across diverse domains, but their potential for Human-Object Interaction (HOI) remains unexplored. Unlike traditional HOI approaches that rely on extensive labeled datasets and fixed interaction taxonomies, MLLMs offer flexible reasoning, making them well-suited for dynamic, real-world scenarios. In this work, we present the first systematic study of MLLMs for HOI recognition and detection within a pipeline that combines an external object detector for entity localization with zero-shot multimodal reasoning for interaction understanding. We introduce a benchmark framework for principled zero-shot evaluation, consisting of (i) a unified taxonomy of zero-shot prompting strategies, and (ii) a methodology that transforms token-level logits into interaction scores, enabling fair comparison with specialized HOI models under standard metrics. To support prompt-based evaluation, we additionally construct new question-answer annotations for standard HOI datasets, transforming them into a format suitable for MLLMs. Building on this, we propose two visual prompting strategies, namely Objects as Context and Black Other Objects, that guide MLLMs to target objects while preserving scene context. Experiments on HICO, HICO-DET, and V-COCO demonstrate state-of-the-art zero-shot performance, achieving 53.50 mAP on HICO and 23.69 mAP on HICO-DET. Overall, our work provides a principled benchmarking framework for MLLMs in HOI, opening the door to new models and datasets and enabling flexible open-world interaction understanding.

title: LoOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Looped Teachers
abstract: On-policy self-distillation improves a model using guidance from the model itself, but it still requires a teacher that provides more useful predictions than the student. Existing approaches obtain such guidance by giving the teacher additional context or instructions. We ask whether it can instead come from changing how the same model uses its own layers. To address this, we introduce LoOPSD, which searches over a model's layer execution order to construct a stronger teacher and distills its advantage into the student. Specifically, we keep the model weights unchanged while searching for layers to repeat, and use the resulting teacher's predictions on student-generated prefixes to guide learning. We then alternate search and distillation, rebuilding the teacher from the updated student in each round so that the student progressively absorbs the gains from alternative layer execution. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show improvements across models. On GSM8K with a 400-token thinking budget, LoOPSD raises Qwen3-1.7B accuracy from 42.30% to 79.61%; subsequent distillation rounds yield further gains beyond the first round. Together, these findings show that by searching layer execution to construct teachers, we can turn a model's additional computation into improved student capabilities, opening a new avenue for self-distillation to derive supervision from the model's own computation.

title: RESTA: Time-Scaling Augmentation for Data-Efficient Robot Imitation Learning
abstract: Robot manipulation policies trained through imitation learning commonly rely on costly demonstrations recorded in one task direction and at one temporal resolution. We propose Reversal and Stride-based Trajectory Augmentation (RESTA), which exploits time-scaling data augmentation to improve data efficiency through trajectory reversal and temporal resampling. Trajectory-reversal augmentation reverses and relabels demonstrations between paired tasks with opposite objectives, reusing recorded rollouts without additional environment interaction. Because contact-rich manipulation is not exactly reversible, we treat reversal as an approximate paired-task prior rather than a physical symmetry. Temporal-stride augmentation varies observation and action sampling strides and conditions the policy on the resulting offsets, enabling fixed or randomized temporal schedules. Experiments across 16 paired bimanual manipulation tasks show that trajectory reversal is particularly effective in the low-data regime and that temporal-stride augmentation improves success under randomized temporal schedules. With 25 and 50 independently collected demonstrations per task, RESTA achieves 78.4% and 85.2% average success, respectively, matching or exceeding baselines trained with twice as many demonstrations (77.3% and 85.4%). These results show that RESTA can improve data efficiency in robot imitation learning.

title: Random Probing for Structural Self-Interactions in Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) fundamentally lack the ability to capture structural properties defined by node self-interactions, such as cycle counts, subgraph centrality, and heat kernel signatures. Existing solutions often rely on computationally expensive higher-order architectures or hand-crafted features. In this work, we introduce DIAL, a message-passing layer that gives nodes access to graph structure through the diagonal of graph-derived operators. Our approach uses randomized probing to provide nodes with learnable, permutation equivariant access to diagonal entries. We prove that our approach can express important structural features, including cycle counts, subgraph centrality, and heat kernel signatures. The proposed method can be integrated directly into message passing layers. Experiments on molecular property prediction, cycle counting, and pattern detection demonstrate the effectiveness of DIAL across a range of graph learning tasks.

title: Soliduzz: Finding Miscompilations in Smart-Contract Compilers with Assertion-Driven Equivalence Oracles
abstract: Smart contracts compiled to the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) can manage high-value assets and are difficult to patch after deployment. Compiler miscompilations are therefore especially dangerous: compilation succeeds, but the generated bytecode does not preserve the semantics of the source program. Existing smart-contract compiler fuzzers either focus on robustness failures or rely on differential oracles that compare compiler configurations.
