On the seller side, honest sellers join voluntarily whenever the price premium exceeds the fee. Lock-in and a critical mass for diffusion, however, call for fee governance and support for entry.

title: Orbital Angular Momentum Transfer and Beam-Quality Limits in Fork-Grating Electron Diffraction
abstract: We analyze fork-grating generation of electron vortex beams beyond the ideal single-mode approximation. The incident beam is described as a paraxial Gaussian ensemble with finite transverse momentum spread and a first electromagnetic Hartree phase accumulated before the grating. Within Fresnel propagation we derive an analytical expression for each diffraction order and determine the corresponding orbital-angular-momentum statistics. The mean OAM of a selected order remains fixed by the topological rule, $\langle L_z\rangle_m=mp\hbar$, while its variance is set by the residual transverse momentum spread of the beam prepared at the grating. For the Gaussian mixture, the transverse purity is $\mathcal P_{\perp,m}=[1+2(ΔL_{z,m}/\hbar)^2]^{-1}$. The observed annular profile is governed by a separate propagation-dependent blurring scale, so a beam can retain well-defined mean OAM while having low transverse purity or a partially filled vortex minimum. Within the radial phase-screen approximation, the Hartree self-field modifies the propagated profile while preserving the full-plane OAM moments and transverse purity.

title: Ramsey properties of trees and $C$-relations via the partite construction
abstract: Finite convexly ordered binary branching $C$-relations have been viewed as a notable exception to the broad applicability of the partite construction in structural Ramsey theory. The absence of a proof of their Ramsey property by the partite construction was noted by Bodirsky in his 2015 survey and pointed out again by Hubička and Konečný in their 2026 survey. We overcome this limitation by giving proofs based on the partite construction of the known Ramsey properties of the class $\mathcal{CT}$ of finite convexly ordered treeable meet semilattices and of the classes of finite convexly ordered $C$-relations with arbitrary branching and with binary branching. Our proofs do not rely on Milliken's tree theorem. The key is to expand $\mathcal{CT}$ by level predicates and a predecessor function so that the locally finite subclass method applies. We then transfer the resulting Ramsey witnesses to the corresponding reduct classes and to the classes of convexly ordered $C$-relations.

title: Doubly commuting invariant and co-invariant subspaces
abstract: Given complex separable Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}_i$ and bounded operators $T_i$ on $\mathcal{H}_i$, for $i=1,\ldots,n$, we consider the tensor product space $\mathfrak{H}:=\mathcal{H}_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathcal{H}_n$ and a tuple $(\tilde{T}_1,\ldots,\tilde{T}_n)$ on $\mathfrak{H}$ where \[\tilde{T}_i=I_{\mathcal{H}_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes I_{\mathcal{H}_{i-1}}\otimes T_i\otimes I_{\mathcal{H}_{i+1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes I_{\mathcal{H}_n}.\] A closed jointly $(\tilde{T}_1,\ldots,\tilde{T}_n)$-invariant subspace $\mathfrak{M}$ of $\mathfrak{H}$ is said to be doubly commuting if the tuple $(\tilde{T}_1|_{\mathfrak{M}},\ldots,\tilde{T}_n|_{\mathfrak{M}})$ is doubly commuting. In this paper, we show that if the hereditary polynomials in each $T_i$ are dense in $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_i)$ with respect to the weak operator topology for $i=1,\ldots,n$, then doubly commuting jointly $(\tilde{T}_1,\ldots,\tilde{T}_n)$-invariant subspaces $\mathfrak{M}$ of $\mathfrak{H}$ are characterized in the form \[\mathcal{M}_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\mathcal{M}_n,\] where $\mathcal{M}_i\subseteq\mathcal{H}_i$ is $T_i$-invariant, for each $i=1,\ldots,n$. As applications, we provide a unified framework for understanding and characterizing doubly commuting quotient modules of weighted Bergman spaces over the open unit polydisc, doubly commuting quotient modules of tensor products of complete Nevanlinna-Pick spaces, and doubly commuting invariant and co-invariant subspaces of certain operators acting on tensor products of de Branges-Rovnyak spaces $H(b)$ associated with both extreme and nonextreme points $b$. This recovers, through a different approach, the known characterizations of doubly commuting quotient modules of the Hardy space over the open unit polydisc and doubly commuting submodules of Jordan blocks of Hardy space over the open unit polydisc.

title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting: Continual Learning for Radar Waveform Classification
abstract: Automated radar waveform recognition classifies the waveform and modulation type of a received signal. As new waveform variants appear over time, a deployed classifier must learn them without retraining from scratch. Catastrophic Forgetting occurs when learning new waveforms overwrites prior knowledge. Continual Learning (CL) methods tackle this challenge, but prior radar studies only evaluate a few methods on narrow benchmarks. Practitioners lack evidence on which method to deploy or which mechanisms are effective. This work presents the first large-scale benchmark of continual learning for radar waveform recognition. Eighteen CL methods are evaluated on a sequential ten-task problem, drawn from four public datasets spanning 54 waveforms, under task- and class-incremental (TIL, CIL) settings and single- and multi-epoch regimes. Methods that retain data from old tasks lead both TIL and CIL settings. Plain replay alone closes 77-88% of the gap between the lower and upper practical limits under TIL, but only 46-55% under CIL. The internal mechanisms of the leading methods are ablated and statistically tested to identify effective mechanisms. Each ablation is paired against its full method over n=6 training seeds, topped up to n=12 when inconclusive, and p-values are Holm-Bonferroni corrected within each method's family. Ablation results show that several mechanisms confer smaller but statistically significant gains. Combining these mechanisms improves the leading F1 score by 3.4-5.5% and 2.7-4.9% under TIL and CIL, respectively, and the combined models exceed every benchmarked method in both settings for all SNRs. These results give researchers of radar waveform classification systems a mechanism-level basis for design.

title: Impact of Security Modeling Fidelity on Hyperscale Data Center Hosting Capacity Assessment
abstract: This paper assesses hyperscale data center hosting capacity in transmission grids. Hosting capacity (HC) analysis quantifies the maximum additional load a bus can accommodate without violating operational constraints. This paper defines data center HC as the maximum time-invariant active power demand at a single target bus over a 24-hour peak-day horizon, and evaluates it under four models of increasing fidelity (i.e., the extent to which the model enforces real-world operational security requirements) on the modified IEEE 24-bus system: (i) DC optimal power flow (DC-OPF) without unit commitment (UC), (ii) basic SCUC (security-constrained unit commitment) without reliability constraints, (iii) SCUC with spinning reserve, and (iv) N-SCUC with both reserve and branch-contingency security. Comparing these models quantifies the impact of unit commitment, reserve requirements, and N-1 security on bus-level HC estimates. The N-SCUC yields an average HC of 444 MW; omitting N-1 security raises this to 532 MW, a 19.8% overestimation. The DC-OPF and basic SCUC models further overestimate HC, indicating a trade-off between model complexity and estimation accuracy.

title: Tanchun: Robust Flow-Based HTTP(S) DDoS Detection via Behavioral Attribute Guidance
abstract: HTTP(S) DDoS attacks have surged in frequency and scale, posing a significant threat to network security. Flow-based detection is a promising solution for large-scale HTTP(S) DDoS detection due to its decryption-free operation and scalability. However, the coarse-grained numerical statistics in flow data limit accurate attack detection and lack robustness when benign and attack traffic patterns drift over time. In this paper, we present Tanchun, a drift-aware flow-based HTTP(S) DDoS detection system that relies solely on decryption-free flow data. Specifically, Tanchun groups flows by IP-pair and aggregates them over consecutive time slots into behavior sequences, capturing temporal access patterns to compensate for the limited information in individual flows. It further abstracts these sequences into human-understandable behavioral attributes that capture stable behavioral semantics. Tanchun then aligns behavior sequences with their corresponding behavioral attributes to guide representation learning, enabling robust detection under traffic drift. We evaluate Tanchun across diverse HTTP(S) DDoS scenarios. Tanchun achieves the best overall performance, with an average F1-score of 0.988, and outperforms the second-best method by 5.3\% and 9.6\% under benign-traffic and attack-traffic drift, respectively. Experiments on real-world traffic traces further demonstrate its practical effectiveness.

title: Multi-Stream Residual Computation in Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Diffusion language models reconstruct masked tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to autoregressive generation. Yet their Transformer backbones typically carry visible evidence and evolving masked predictions through a single residual stream. We equip masked diffusion models with multiple residual streams that persist through depth and adaptive routing between them, then investigate how they support these complementary roles. On the pretraining task, two streams reduce reconstruction perplexity by 5.71% on validation data and 5.13% on average across external corpora compared with standard residual connections. We observe that, without predefined roles, visible and masked positions learn distinct routing patterns. Causal interventions show that this distinction organizes read and write routing, while token-specific write strength remains important within each role. Guided by these findings, a model trained with role-conditioned routing recovers half the validation gain from adding a second stream. State interventions explain the benefit of the additional stream: it preserves early token representations for later reuse while evidence accumulates at masked positions. This mechanism recurs at a larger model scale, showing how persistent streams support context preservation alongside prediction refinement.

title: Prompt-Injection Probes Learn the Conversation, Not Just the Injection
abstract: Linear probes on a model's hidden states are used as cheap monitors for indirect prompt injection: they screen the tool outputs an agent reads and send suspicious ones to a slower second check, so every false alarm has a cost. But a probe learns whatever separates its training examples. The standard evaluation of injection probes can be passed without the model: conversation position and text lengths alone reach 0.91-0.98 AUROC. When each attack is compared with the same conversation without the injection, or with harmless text formatted like an injection, standard probes flag most of these harmless cases. We add such cases to the training data as matched negatives. Across six open models, in applications seen during training and at the default threshold, changing only the training data cuts false alarms on injection-free conversations from 41-80% to 4-27%, and on harmless look-alikes from 92-98% to 3-16%. With a threshold set on normal traffic, our probe still catches a median 95% of the attacks that fooled the agent (91% without our data). In new applications, false alarms stay low, but detection depends on the model and on how the threshold is set. The same data also helps a text-only filter.

title: Full classification of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear generalized Hadamard codes
abstract: The $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-additive codes are subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}^n$. A $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-linear generalized Hadamard (GH) code is a GH code over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ which is the Gray map image of a $\mathbb{Z}_{p^s}$-additive code. A recursive construction gives such codes $H_p^{t_1,\dots,t_s}$, of type $(n;t_1,\dots,t_s)$ and length $p^t$, and a partial classification of them is known. In this paper, we complete the classification of these codes for every prime $p$. The main tool is the derived code, obtained by puncturing the code outside a block of coordinates determined by its kernel. For a nonlinear code $H_p^{t_1,\dots,t_s}$ with $t_1\geq2$, the derived code is a $\mathbb{Z}_{p^{s-1}}$-linear GH code of the same family, although the mechanism for odd $p$ differs from the binary one. As a consequence, for $t\geq3$, there are $\mathcal P(t+1)-\mathcal P(t)$ nonequivalent such codes of length $p^t$ if $p$ is odd, and $\mathcal P(t+1)-\mathcal P(t)-1$ if $p=2$, where $\mathcal P(n)$ is the number of partitions of $n$. In particular, this completes the classification of the $\mathbb{Z}_{2^s}$-linear Hadamard codes. We also prove a conjecture on the codes with $t_1\geq2$ and $t_s=0$.

title: Graph-free Retrieval with Graph-Modified Embeddings
abstract: Dense vector retrieval can miss evidence connected through intermediate entities, while direct graph retrieval requires access to the graph at query time. We compare five offline graph-based embedding transformations and strategies for using the resulting graph-modified embeddings alongside the originals, without query-time graph access. On a synthetic professional-network benchmark with complete supporting-evidence sets, direct replacement of the original embeddings reduces evidence recovery. Multi-stage strategies improve recovery by using graph-modified embeddings to guide the search while retaining the originals for semantic relevance. On questions requiring linked facts or comparisons among candidates, the strongest configuration improves recovery by up to 25.9% relative to plain vector retrieval. It also matches baseline recovery with 40% fewer returned nodes. Controls confirm that graph information contributes beyond multi-stage retrieval alone. Across the tested methods, retrieval performance depends more on how graph-modified embeddings are used than on how they are produced.

title: Curie-Weiss cell fluid model: Fitting to experimental critical-point data
abstract: We examine how the Curie--Weiss cell fluid model can be quantitatively related to real fluids by determining its microscopic parameters from experimental critical-point data for water, carbon dioxide, and three polyol ester lubricants (POE5, POE7, and POE9). The microscopic parameters of the model are determined from the experimental values of the critical temperature and critical density: the global attraction coupling constant is fixed by the critical temperature, and the cell volume by the critical density. The critical pressure then follows as an independent model prediction, deviating from experimental values by 10--41$\%$ across the studied substances. Varying the ratio of local repulsion to global attraction $f=J_2/J_1$ over a wide range has only a weak effect on this deviation. For $f\geq1$, the model's critical compressibility factor lays within a narrow range $Z_c\approx0.382-0.386$, remaining close to the mean-field van der Waals value $Z_c=3/8=0.375$ and consistently overestimating experimental values. The best agreement with experiment is obtained for the polyol ester lubricants and improves along the POE5--POE7--POE9 series with increasing molar mass, suggesting that multiple-occupancy cell fluid models are well suited to systems of large molecules, particularly soft-matter systems with bounded interaction potentials. We further show that generalizing the model by introducing a temperature- and phase-dependent effective attraction allows it to describe a triple point and to reproduce the broad range of critical-to-triple temperature ratios $T_c/T_{\mathrm{tr}}$ characteristic of real fluids.

title: Not All Drift Is a Mechanism: Tracing Prompt Adaptation in LLMs
abstract: Prompt-based adaptation offers several ways to specialize a frozen language model, ranging from natural-language prompt optimization to learned continuous prompts. These methods are usually compared through downstream performance, although similar outputs need not arise from similar internal computations. We study how discrete prompt optimization, prompt tuning, and prefix tuning alter the processing of dense and mixture-of-experts language models. Our analysis shows that the location of the adaptation predicts how task information is carried to the output: optimized text primarily changes response construction, input-level prompts write their influence into content representations, and layer-wise prefixes maintain direct control through attention. In MoE models, these differences further induce distinct expert-routing patterns. At the same time, common representation-level measurements respond strongly to generic context changes and do not reliably distinguish useful adaptations from matched placebos. We argue that understanding prompt adaptation requires separating representation drift from the part of that drift that is aligned with, and causally used by, the model's task computation. This perspective provides practical guidance for selecting, evaluating, and interpreting prompt adaptation methods.

title: Scalar curvature rigidity of small spherical caps with arbitrary fill-ins
abstract: We prove an analogue of Min-Oo's conjecture for sufficiently small spherical caps in the unit round sphere. For every dimension $n\ge3$, there exists $r_*(n)>0$ such that the following holds for every round cap of radius $0<r\le r_*(n)$: any smooth compact connected oriented Riemannian fill-in with the same intrinsic boundary metric and with scalar curvature and outward boundary mean curvature at least those of the cap is isometric to the cap.

title: Revisiting the Estimation of Unigram Surprisal in Computational Psycholinguistics
abstract: Contextual and unigram surprisal are standard predictors of reading time in computational psycholinguistics. While contextual surprisal is typically derived from neural language models, unigram surprisal is usually obtained from independent corpus counts. Although both quantities are deterministic functionals of a single underlying distribution---capturing conditional and marginal structure respectively---this practice breaks their probabilistic link and may introduce estimation error from the mismatch. We propose three principles for estimating unigram surprisal in psycholinguistic research, including the requirement that both quantities be derived from the same language model. We operationalize this principle by introducing a Monte Carlo estimator of unigram surprisal from a language model, along with a marginalized variant that has lower variance empirically. When unigram surprisal is re-estimated under this unified framework, we find evidence that predictors change in their predictive contribution to reading time. We also confirm prior findings that frequency can be a stronger predictor of processing effort than contextual surprisal under this unified framework.

title: Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. In this paper, we present the first independent reproduction of five factuality alignment methods, which span on-policy RL (PPO, GRPO, and Dr.~GRPO) and offline preference optimization (DPO and KTO), and compare them on a common benchmark with common evaluation metrics. We found that none of these methods reproduces in full, and on the common benchmark none of the methods significantly outperforms the base model. On closer inspection, the rewards optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality and relevance, whereas the choice between on-policy and offline training matters little. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics and benchmarks are also part of the problem since they do not measure relevance of text to the prompt. Since there is no ground truth associated with the prompts, the reliance on LLM judges and retrieval for verification also makes the evaluation fragile. We release our code, data, and checkpoints.

title: A parity constraint on the topological numbers of self-complementary triply-periodic surfaces
abstract: The stability zone of Novikov's problem of planar sections of triply periodic surfaces are labeled by indivisible triples of integers, which we call the soul of the zone. Which triples may occur is not known. We show that, if a Morse function $f$ on $\mathbb T^3$ admits a translation $τ(x)=x+v$ with $f\circτ=-f$, so that the sets $\{f<0\}$ and $\{f>0\}$ are congruent, then in the generic genus-$3$ situation every topological number $L$ satisfies $\langle L,2v\rangle\equiv1\pmod2$. The mechanism is that the electron/hole type of a null-homologous closed trajectory is invariant under the period lattice and is reversed by $τ$. For $f=\cos2πx+\cos2πy+\cos2πz$ and the $μ$-cube, this means that the sum of the components of each soul is odd.

title: Resource-Efficient 3D Shape and Orientation Estimation of Road Users using Roadside RGB Camera and 3D Radar
abstract: End-to-end deep learning pipelines for camera-radar 3D object detection are well established in driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles; however, adapting them to roadside-mounted infrastructure presents significant challenges. On vehicles, sensor heights, pitch angles, and relative geometries remain largely uniform, allowing end-to-end models to generalize effectively. On the contrary, roadside sensor installations vary drastically in height, tilt, and field of view across locations, rendering end-to-end models prone to failure and difficult to adapt without massive location-specific datasets. Hence, instead of designing a complex end-to-end pipeline for direct 3D bounding box estimation, a low-cost, resource-efficient two-stage approach is proposed for real-time 3D shape and orientation estimation. The first stage utilizes any off-the-shelf, state-of-the-art method to extract 2D camera bounding boxes and associated 3D radar points for each road user. The proposed second stage then processes these inputs to construct 3D oriented bounding boxes where radar data determines 3D position, predefined templates define size for each road user, and a tiny neural network predicts a site-specific and optimized yaw angle. The algorithm is successfully validated at a curved road with a junction for pedestrians, bicycles, and cars, where it achieves 25 frames per second on an NVIDIA Jetson ORIN for real-time applications.

title: The role of dependency range in thermally coupled superconducting networks
abstract: Interdependent networks can be highly fragile because dependency links amplify local failures into cascades that trigger global collapse. Much of the theoretical understanding comes from geometric network models, where dependency range is imposed externally and coupling strength is distance independent, and it is unclear how these insights apply to real materials, where interdependence arises from physical transport. Here we study thermally coupled amorphous superconducting networks, in which dependencies emerge from current redistribution and heat-mediated interactions governed by thermal diffusivity. Using an experimentally calibrated model of resistively shunted Josephson junctions, we show the system reproduces the three canonical transition regimes: continuous, nucleation-dominated, and mixed-order. However, because heat-driven dependency simultaneously broadens and weakens with distance, long-range thermal coupling can stabilize the superconducting phase upon heating, in contrast with its destabilizing role in geometric models. Cascades are anisotropic, with one-dimensional front propagation. These results offer an experimentally testable perspective complementing the geometric framework.

title: Low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations
abstract: In this work, we develop low-cost non-iterative Sylvester solvers for dynamical low-rank approximation of reaction-diffusion equations and incorporate them into a basis-update \& Galerkin mass-lumped finite element method (\mbox{BUG-MLFEM}). By incorporating mass lumping via Gauss-Lobatto quadrature, the spatial discretization yields a matrix differential equation equipped with diagonal positive-definite mass matrices. We establish the weighted dynamical low-rank approximation (WDLRA) within the Galerkin framework of the MLFEM system, proving the theoretical equivalence between the BUG integrator and MLFEM on low-rank subspaces, which guarantees the discrete well-posedness of the implicit BUG steps. To overcome the severe computational bottleneck of standard $O(m^3+n^3)$ Sylvester solvers, we develop tailored, low-cost non-iterative solvers that exploit the inherent sparse-by-small algebraic structure. Under Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions (BCs), the large coefficient matrices are banded, enabling efficient diagonalization of the small $r \times r$ factor matrix and reducing the per-step computational complexity to $O((m+n)r^2)$ and storage to $O((m+n)r)$. For periodic BCs, we combine this diagonalization strategy with a rank-2 Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury update to handle wrap-around corner entries at negligible additional cost. Numerical experiments demonstrate first-order temporal and $(k+1)$th-order spatial convergence of the proposed BUG-MLFEM in the discrete $L^2$ norm, where $k$ denotes the polynomial degree of the finite element space, together with significant computational speedups over existing low-rank integrators.

title: Agaram 2.5B: The First Tamil-First Language Model Trained from Scratch with Tool Calling. A Playbook for Under-Represented Languages
abstract: We trained Agaram 2.5B, a 2.5-billion-parameter Tamil-English language model, from scratch on about 50 billion tokens (58% Tamil, the rest English, math, code and parallel text) on one node of eight H100 GPUs in about six days, with a new tokenizer that, unlike our first model's, keeps line breaks. Supervised fine-tuning on 134,428 conversations, whose replies an open-weight teacher model wrote, and three short targeted rounds turned it into a chat model that answers in Tamil script, romanized Tamil (Tanglish) and English and can call tools: on 25 tool prompts whose schemas appear in training it picks the right tool 23 times and gives exactly the expected arguments 13 times. The released model translates better than Sarvam-1, a 2B Indic base model, in all six FLORES and IN22 directions (FLORES chrF 54.3 into Tamil and 55.2 into English, against 49.2 and 44.2), and nearly doubles its base model on native-Tamil IndicIFEval (19.3% from 10.0%). It is weak on knowledge: reading-comprehension and knowledge benchmarks sit near chance, and on 50 held-out everyday questions written by one native speaker, one LLM judge rated 46% of its replies usable (22-24 of 50 over three passes; 95% interval for 23 of 50, 33-60%), with nearly every failure a wrong fact. Our two further SFT experiments changed answer format but not the knowledge measures. We also describe our first model, Agaram 1.5B, whose failures shaped the choices here; how the judge's scores varied between passes on identical replies; and, item by item, what the targeted rounds trained against and where frontier-model text entered the data. The project ran on compute credits and our own funds, about USD 13,300 across both models; the weights are released (licence to be announced after legal review), with GGUF files for llama.cpp, at https://huggingface.co/murai-labs/agaram-2.5b-instruct; code at https://github.com/Murai-Labs/Agaram2.5b

title: Spectral Theory of an Exactly Solvable Quantum-Optical Oscillator
abstract: We study a one-dimensional single-excitation model of a scalar photon field coupled to a continuum of two-level atoms with quadratic density. The resulting matrix Hamiltonian has an unbounded spatially varying coupling and is not semibounded. We prove that it is essentially self-adjoint and determine its spectrum explicitly. The continuous spectrum is the half-line $(-\infty,Ω]$, where $Ω$ is the atomic resonance frequency, while the spectrum above $Ω$ consists of a strictly increasing sequence of simple eigenvalues. These eigenvalues are characterized by the interlaced zeros of the Airy function and its derivative and satisfy \begin{align*} ω_n = \left(\frac{3πg n}{4}\right)^{1/2} + \fracΩ{4} + O(n^{-1/2}). \end{align*} The analysis is based on a nonlinear spectral reduction that yields a confining massless relativistic oscillator above $Ω$ and an inverted oscillator below $Ω$.

title: Augmenting Real-time Visualization in Minimally Invasive Surgery with Particle Filtering and Depth-Aware Occlusion Handling
abstract: We present a real-time, hybrid framework for occlusion handling and depth-aware tracking in minimally invasive surgeries (MIS). Occlusions caused by surgical instruments often obscure the region of interest (ROI), affecting surgical precision. To address this, our approach integrates enhanced You Only Look Once (YOLO) based detection, Particle Filtering (PF), and monocular depth estimation using Multiple Depth Estimation Accuracy with Single Network (MiDaS). Occlusion is detected using a distance-based threshold between instruments and ROI. Experimental results demonstrate robust instrument detection with a confidence score of 0.85, effective occlusion event handling, and accurate depth prediction with an MAE of 0.34 cm and RMSE of 0.53 cm. Independent phantom-based validation against stereo depth measurements yielded an MAE of 0.65 cm and RMSE of 0.66 cm. The framework further achieved an occlusion detection accuracy of 81.95\% while maintaining real-time performance at 38.7 FPS. Preliminary surgeon feedback indicates that the proposed visualization framework is clinically relevant and holds promise for future intraoperative image-guided navigation and decision support in MIS.

title: Curvature measures and volume preserving flows in h-convex geometry
abstract: In this paper, we introduce a concept of modified curvature measures for h-convex domains in hyperbolic space and prove a shifted version of the generalized Alexandrov theorem, which characterizes geodesic balls in hyperbolic space via modified curvature measures. This result generalizes the classical work of Kohlmann (1998). We further investigate a volume-preserving shifted $α$-Gauss curvature flow for strictly h-convex hypersurfaces in hyperbolic space and prove that for any $α>0$ the solution exists for all time and converges smoothly to a geodesic sphere. The theory of modified curvature measures developed in the first part serves as a key ingredient in characterizing the Hausdorff limit shape of the flow.

title: Receiver Decides Agent-to-Agent Negotiations
abstract: When one language-model agent asks another for money, which of the two decides how much changes hands? We ran a round-robin tournament of 1,049 negotiations among fifteen agents. In each game a requester tries to raise money from a holder that has been told to keep a $100 endowment. Knowing which agent holds the money explains 47% of the variance in the amount transferred; knowing which agent asks explains 2%. Dropping the most extreme agents narrows the split to 22% against 4%. Changing the requester's appeal from one named person to a group changed what requesters wrote, but the amounts transferred under the two framings are statistically equivalent. The holders that lose least are the ones that turn down the opening request, and their turn-1 refusal rate ranks them by total losses (Spearman correlation = -0.73). Training moves this behaviour in both directions. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on a persuasion corpus with almost no refusals raised what it gave away as a holder from 12% to 84% of the endowment. Distilling two never-losing holders into a 4B student cut its losses from 95% to 1%. Evaluations of agents that hold resources should test them in the holder role, including after persuasion fine-tuning.

title: CALM: Decentralized Control of Cooperative Aerial Manipulation with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Cooperative aerial manipulation is difficult under wind, payload motion, and noisy goal broadcasts because multiple Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are coupled through a shared payload. We present CALM (Cooperative Aerial Learned Manipulation), a decentralized controller for aerial manipulators carrying a basket while tracking a moving ground robot. CALM combines a parameter-shared Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) policy, trained using Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO), with goal estimation, per-UAV Extended State Observers (ESOs), basket-mass estimation, and anticipatory formation-yaw feedforward. The anticipatory formation-yaw feedforward uses estimated goal motion to rotate the formation before position error develops, reducing basket-yaw lag without adding net commanded force. A disturbance-conditioned critic supports centralized training while execution remains decentralized. Across held-out trajectories, CALM achieves lower mean position and orientation errors than all evaluated baselines, including the matched arm baseline (7.68 versus 10.95 cm and 3.3 versus 4.7$^\circ$), the cable-suspended realization, and two model-based controllers. Under unseen full-information-path degradation, CALM remains statistically comparable or superior to the arm baseline. Videos are available at https://petreric.github.io/CALM/.

title: Evidence-Governed Deployment Readiness for Networked Agents on Industrial OT Infrastructure
abstract: Deploying a workload on a cyber-secure industrial operational-technology (OT) network requires many cross-layer prerequisites to hold at once, including persistent addressing, name resolution, time synchronization, certificate trust, proxy traversal, and reachable industrial-protocol endpoints. These are owned by different teams, yet current tools treat pre-deployment checking, fault attribution, remediation, and ongoing compliance as separate problems, so evidence is rarely reused across stages. As edge platforms come to host self-adapting agents on shared infrastructure, this fragmentation becomes a governance problem. All four stages ask one question: do a workload's requirements hold on a given network? We present an evidence-governed framework that answers it through a single reference, a versioned network-intent artifact specifying a workload's cross-layer requirements for a specific release. A coverage-driven test loop attaches tested evidence to each requirement before deployment. At a site, readiness is reported as ready, not ready, or undecidable, separating untested requirements from genuine failures; a repair step proposes fixes that preserve co-located workloads; and a drift-watch component re-evaluates the site on change, extending assurance across the workload's lifetime. A multi-workload OPC UA commissioning case illustrates all four stages. By detecting runtime deviations and suspending an agent's guarantees until a refreshed artifact is registered, the framework grounds auditable governance for adapting agent collectives on shared industrial infrastructure.

title: Reliable Memory from Unstable Growth: Curating Self-Written Agent Playbooks with Randomized Experiments
abstract: Persistent textual memory lets language-model agents reuse lessons from past tasks to improve on future multi-step tasks without retraining. Systems such as ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet keep it as a playbook: lessons the agent writes after each task and reads in its prompt. A key challenge is to decide which lessons improve later tasks. Current systems leave the decision to the agent itself, which makes performance unstable: the same procedure can write a playbook that helps or one that falls up to 69.6 points below no playbook. These findings motivate valuing lessons by their measured effect on task success rather than by the agent's judgment. We propose Randomized Block Curation (RBC), which measures this effect with a randomized experiment on practice tasks. It groups related lessons into blocks large enough to move success measurably and, on each practice task, includes or leaves out every block at random. Random inclusion makes tasks with and without a block comparable, so the gap in their success estimates the block's effect. RBC keeps the blocks that help and, since the same procedure can write a helpful or a harmful playbook, grows several and serves whichever curated, whole or no playbook scores best on fresh practice episodes. Across two memory systems, three models and three benchmarks, RBC raises average success to 66.9, against 55.5 with the whole playbook, 54.1 with no playbook and 53.8 when the agent's own judgment picks the lessons to keep.

title: Adaptive Variance-Reduced Stochastic Sequential (Quadratic Constrained) Quadratic Programming
abstract: In this paper, we propose an adaptive variance-reduced stochastic sequential (quadratic constrained) quadratic programming (AVR-SS(QC)QP) method for nonlinear constrained optimization. The framework integrates SPIDER-based variance reduction, stochastic quasi-Newton curvature information, merit-function globalization, and adaptive switching between stochastic SQP and SQCQP models. The switching mechanism is governed by a relative constraint model curvature indicator that measures the second-order constraint information neglected by the linearized SQP model. A smoothed hysteresis rule ac?tivates the SQCQP model only when the relative constraint curvature is significant. An exact L1 merit function with Armijo backtracking globalizes the resulting directions, while a coupled stochastic Lyapunov analysis controls the interaction between gradient-estimation error and optimization progress. Under standard smoothness, sampling, regularity, and second-order conditions, we establish almost-sure consistency of the variance-reduced gradient estimator and global convergence of the KKT residual. We further show that, near regular KKT points, the curvature indicator vanishes and the method eventually selects the computationally cheaper SQP model. Numerical experiments on a sparse principal component analysis problem illustrate the practical be?havior of the proposed framework.

title: Delving into the depths of NGC 3783 with XRISM VI. Evidence for a failed wind based on Fe xxv absorption line variability
abstract: NGC 3783 exhibits a prominent Fe XXV absorption trough in the time-averaged XRISM/Resolve spectrum. To investigate its short-term variability, we present a time-resolved analysis of the Fe XXV absorption line during the continuous 10-day observation. We divided the resolved absorption profile into five fixed velocity intervals and measured their normalized equivalent widths in 19 time-resolved spectra. Three velocity intervals exhibit significant equivalent-width (EW) variability. Two velocity intervals respond differently to low- and high-flux states with less emission line contamination. The time-dependent photoionisation modelling is unable to reproduce the most significant observed EW variation ($3.5 \, σ$), possibly owing to uncertainties in the assumed initial equilibrium state, which prevent a precise density measurement. Instead, using photoionisation calculations and assuming the high-density limit, we derive approximate constraints on the ionisation parameters of the two relevant components. The low-velocity component (-320 to -680 km/s) shows a delayed inverse response, indicating a high ionisation parameter, while its relatively short lag timescale indicates a relatively high density and a distance upper limit of 0.05 pc. In contrast, the high-velocity component (-680 to -1040 km/s) manifests a positive response with a longer lag to the ionising continuum, implying a relatively low ionisation parameter. This component appears to be less dense, with an inferred distance upper limit of 0.25 pc. The low-velocity component is consistent with a failed wind, as its outflow velocity is below the local escape velocity, whereas the high-velocity component lies near the escape threshold. Together with the lower-ionisation failed wind detected in 2001, this supports a multiphase failed-wind scenario in the unobscured state of NGC~3783 over more than two decades.

title: FedGraph: Defending Federated Large Language Model Fine-Tuning Against Backdoor Attacks via Graph-Based Aggregation
abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) allows multiple clients to collaboratively adapt models without sharing raw data, offering strong privacy benefits. However, this setting is highly vulnerable to backdoor attacks, in which malicious clients manipulate their updates to induce targeted behaviors while maintaining normal performance on benign inputs. In this work, we make a key observation specific to federated LLM fine-tuning: malicious clients tend to exhibit strong consistency in their model updates, whereas benign clients produce more diverse and dispersed updates. This structural difference is not well captured by existing defense methods, which typically rely on direct anomaly detection in high-dimensional parameter space and therefore struggle in the presence of entangled LLM updates. Motivated by this observation, we propose FedGraph, a graph-based aggregation framework that explicitly models relationships among client updates. By representing clients as nodes in a dynamically constructed graph and extracting structural features that characterize their relative positions and interactions, FedGraph derives compact client representations that effectively separate malicious and benign behaviors. These representations are then used to identify and suppress malicious contributions during aggregation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedGraph significantly improves backdoor defense. It consistently reduces attack success rates to below 10% while achieving high detection accuracy (95.5% on average) and a low false positive rate (2.33%), substantially outperforming existing federated learning defenses.

title: On Permutations Whose Adjacent-Sum Reciprocals Sum to One
abstract: In this paper, we give a constructive proof that for any integer n>7 (resp. n>6), the numbers 1,2,...,n can be arranged in a circle (resp. in a line) such that the sum of the reciprocals of all adjacent sums equals 1. The above conjecture was originally posed by Zhi-Wei Sun. Partitioning the integers according to n mod 12 into nine residue classes, we prove a recursive proposition and inductively construct new examples. Main lemmas and propositions in introduction are proved in Section 2. The rest of the cases are handled by explicit constructions in appendix.

title: Counterexamples to prescribed scalar curvature in the null case
abstract: We construct smooth functions on the flat torus $\mathbb{T}^{n\ge5}$ that change sign and have negative mean but cannot be realized as the scalar curvature of any metric in the given conformal class.

title: Algebraic Direct Sums and Generalized Drazin Invertibility
abstract: Let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on a complex Banach space $X$. We prove that the algebraic decomposition \[ X=\K(T)\oplus \Hq(T) \] forces both summands to be closed and hence characterizes generalized Drazin invertibility. This improves the classical characterizations of Mbekhta~\resultcite{Theorem~1.6}{MbekhtaKato}, Schmoeger~\resultcite{Theorem~4}{Schmoeger}, and Dajić and Koliha~\resultcite{Theorem~6.7}{DajicKoliha}, by removing their closedness assumptions. We also show that $T$ is generalized Drazin invertible if and only if \[ \dim\bigl(\K(T)\cap \Hq(T)\bigr)<\infty \quad\text{and}\quad \codim\bigl(\K(T)+\Hq(T)\bigr)<\infty. \] For ordinary Drazin invertibility, we obtain analogous finite-defect characterizations involving the hyperkernel and the hyperrange. We also give a characterization using pointwise nilpotence on an invariant summand. Finally, we consider arbitrary invariant algebraic decompositions and give a counterexample when the inverse of the restriction to one summand is not assumed bounded.

title: Principled Design of Expected Improvement for Continuous Simulation Optimization
abstract: Expected improvement based on stochastic kriging (SK) surrogate is widely used in continuous simulation optimization, but unknown heteroscedastic noise makes three basic design choices consequential: the incumbent to define improvement, replication allocation, and final recommendation. Existing methods typically either assume the noise levels are known or choose these components separately through heuristic rules or empirical calibration. We instead derive a high-probability upper bound on the simple regret and systematically choose the three components within general rule classes to tighten this bound. We first establish a finite-sample confidence bound for the SK predictor as a foundation for the three design choices. Within general posterior-quantile rule classes, tightening the regret certificate selects a lower-quantile incumbent and an upper-quantile recommendation among sampled designs. The opposing quantiles reflect the different roles of exploratory experiments and the final implemented decision. Under mild conditions satisfied by common kernels, minimizing a tractable kernel-specific bound yields a logarithmic replication order. Based on these design choices, the resulting simple regret matches the existing results under known homoscedastic noise up to logarithmic factors. To our knowledge, this is the first simple-regret guarantee of this form for a continuous-domain EI-type simulation optimization method that learns unknown heteroscedastic variances through replications.

title: How Well Do LLMs Perform in Peer Review? Evidence from Finance and Accounting
abstract: Referees increasingly use large language models (LLMs), while finance and accounting journals disagree about whether to allow it. We ask which part of a referee's job the models can do. GPT-4o, whose training data end before the 2024 conference season, referees the papers presented at the 2024 AFA and NBER finance meetings, and we compare its verdicts with publication in the top-three finance journals over the next two years. Papers the model scores one standard deviation higher are 44\% more likely to be published, net of author reputation. The result is not driven by look-ahead bias, as the model does not recall the outcomes. The information comes from its judgements of correctness and exposition. Its judgements of originality and significance carry none, and a referee guide that stresses importance does not help. The split between correctness and contribution holds for accounting papers and for a newer model, GPT-5. LLMs can check whether research is right, but not whether it matters. The technical check can go to the model, while the judgement of contribution stays with people.

title: Stability of the Markov-Krein Transform Under Classical Convolutions
abstract: We prove that, for every $c>0$, the image of the generalized Markov-Krein transform on probability measures with finite logarithmic moment is closed under classical additive convolution and under the Mellin convolution. This resolves the positivity conjecture for the additive high-temperature convolution, a one-parameter interpolation between classical and free convolution arising in random matrix theory and representation theory in the regime $N\to\infty, Nβ_N/2\to c$. Our proof relies on a convolution theorem for universally prestarlike functions.

title: Connection between MP and DPP for Mean-Field Stochastic Optimal Control Problems
abstract: This paper deals with the optimal control problem for the general mean-field stochastic differential equations, in which the coefficients depend on both the state process as well as on its law. We focus on the connection between the general maximum principle and the dynamic programming principle for such a control problem. We establish the relationship between the value function of the mean-field optimal control problem and the adjoint equations in the maximum principle. We also give a general mean-field stochastic verification theorem. Some examples are solved explicitly to illustrate our results.

title: STAMP as a topology-aware molecular language for fragment-level learning and editing
abstract: Molecular fragments provide chemically meaningful units, but existing molecular languages rarely make their locations and connections explicit for editing. Here we introduce STAMP (Sequential Tree Attachment-based Motif-Preserving representation), a topology-aware molecular language that connects fragment-level representation learning with precise structural editing. STAMP separately encodes motif identity, attachment sites and tree topology, making fragments reusable across contexts and subtrees directly accessible. Learned representations capture motif similarity and recurring transformations, and lower activity-cliff prediction error on 23 of 30 targets versus a matched SMILES encoder. Compatible subtree operations support scaffold-preserving optimization, ranking first among six methods on 15 of 23 benchmark objectives. A deterministic compiler enables frozen language models to act on indexed fragments, improving molecular editing, optimization, transformation transfer and change identification by 9 to 56 percentage points over plain SMILES. Together, these results establish an executable molecular language in which learned chemical units remain directly operable during design.

title: Estimating Surprisal from the Speech Signal
abstract: Although language is predominantly spoken, empirical tests of surprisal theory rely almost entirely on written text. In practice, surprisal is estimated using language models (LMs) trained on text and applied to transcriptions, creating a text bottleneck that limits evaluation of the theory in the spoken modality. We remove this bottleneck by estimating surprisal directly from the speech signal using a speech LM. This raises a key question: should surprisal be defined over realization-specific acoustic inputs or over abstract linguistic units? Since a single unit can have many distinct acoustic realizations, each assigned a different probability by the model, defining surprisal over abstract units is difficult. To address this, we introduce an importance sampling estimator that approximates the probability of an abstract unit by marginalizing over realizations generated by a text-to-speech model. Using pupillometry data from a listening study, we evaluate surprisal theory in this text-free setting at multiple levels of granularity. Obtaining surprisal from several speech LMs, we consistently find that surprisal estimated via importance sampling better predicts pupil dilation than realization-specific surprisal for words. We also find that surprisal values for sub-lexical units are predictive of pupil dilation. While we find that surprisal can be estimated without recourse to text, and that marginalizing over distinct realizations of words is more predictive of lexical processing effort, surprisal as a whole is not a strong predictor of change in pupil size, regardless of its source.

title: A Central Limit Theorem for High-Temperature SYK Model
abstract: The Sachdev--Ye--Kitaev (SYK) model is a quantum many-body model of Majorana fermions with all-to-all random interactions. It has attracted wide interest in condensed matter and high-energy physics as a solvable model of non-Fermi liquids and holography. Fix an even integer $q\geq4$, and let $Z_N(β)$ be the partition function of the Gaussian $q$-body SYK model. We prove that for all sufficiently small inverse temperatures $β> 0$, there exists $ρ=ρ(β)>0$ such that \[ N^{q/2 -1}(\log Z_N(β)-\mathbb{E}[\log Z_N(β)]) \Longrightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,ρ^2). \] In addition to the mathematical results, we discuss how the proofs were developed and refined through interaction between human researchers and AI, and we describe the subsequent formalization of the main arguments in Lean 4. This work thus serves as a case study of a research workflow that integrates human insight, AI-assisted exploration, iterative proof refinement, and formal verification.

title: Altermagnetic Ground States on the Ammann--Beenker Tiling
abstract: We identify exact altermagnetic ground states of a classical Heisenberg model on a quasicrystal. Considering the Ammann--Beenker tiling as an example, we determine the ground states by exploiting the parity structure of its parent four-dimensional hypercubic lattice. The ground state hosts coplanar altermagnetic order characterized by the preserved spin-group symmetry $[C_{2x}\parallel C_{8z}]$. Without translational symmetry, the momentum-space spin splitting that usually identifies altermagnets is not directly accessible. We instead couple the spins to itinerant electrons and show spin-resolved transport with $g$-wave symmetry, confirming the altermagnetic nature in a nonperiodic system. Our results establish a geometric route to altermagnetic order in quasicrystals, connecting exact magnetic ground states to their spin-resolved transport signatures.

title: Copying Is Not Grounding: Training Faithful Long-Form RAG with Authored-Sentence Credit
abstract: In search engines and assistants, long-form RAG answers can mislead readers with claims their sources do not support. Faithfulness rewards, the share of supported sentences, train models toward fewer such claims. We show that these rewards are hacked by copying. A sentence copied from the passages is supported almost by construction, so trained models learn to copy rather than ground what they write. Common defenses only move the hack: a KL or copy penalty leaves copying in place or trades it for shorter, emptier answers and refusals. GRPO, the standard RL algorithm, makes it worse by giving every sentence its answer's advantage, reinforcing copied and grounded sentences alike. We propose Authored-Sentence Credit (ASC) , which fixes both by moving GRPO's reward and advantage from the answer to the sentence level. The reward credits only sentences that are authored rather than copied, say more than the question, and are supported by the passages. The advantage compares each sentence with every sentence sampled for the question, so one that earns no credit ranks last and is never reinforced. Across four models and two in-domain, three held-out corpora, only ASC lowers the error rate of authored sentences and writes more supported ones in every setting, by 38% and 46% at the median under held-out evaluators, giving readers more grounded information. It takes none of these shortcuts, and two LLM judges comparing whole answers prefer no baseline to the base model but rate ASC's answers on par with it. We conclude that a faithfulness reward should credit what a model writes, not what it copies.

title: PACT: Posture-Aligned Co-Design Technique for Hand Configuration and Retargeting in Multi-Finger Imitation Learning
abstract: The fidelity of teleoperated demonstrations used for imitation learning is determined by how faithfully a robot hand can replicate the operator's posture. The posture retargeting law that the robot will execute is typically selected only once the hardware has been finalized, and conventional hand designs often neglect human-like grasping postures. We introduce PACT, an optimization based on human grasping postures that jointly optimizes the mechanical parameters of a 17-servo robot hand (link lengths, joint offsets, mounting angles, and base placements) and its nonlinear posture retargeter (a linear human-to-robot joint map, per-joint posture-IK weights, and damping). The optimization enforces full-finger correspondence (MCP, PIP, DIP, and tip of each finger) to human poses from the DexYCB dataset, and is constrained by servo interference, assembly clearances, and flat-hand protrusion, so the resulting design can be physically assembled. We fabricate the PACT Hand and validate it through teleoperation experiments and an imitation-learning demonstration. The hand reproduces all human hand keypoints with a kinematic RMSE of 3.9 mm, compared to 12.8 mm for the LEAP Hand baseline, and keeps all fingertips within 10 mm on every grasping posture, while the baseline achieves this for only 21.6% of the poses. Under matched per-joint torque limits, it lifts twice the baseline payload, 2 kg against 1 kg, and deforms a held paper cup seven times less, reaching a deformation level comparable to a human hand. It also achieves an 86% grasping success rate on YCB daily objects, compared to 64% for the baseline. Finally, as a demonstration, an imitation-learning policy trained on demonstrations collected with the PACT Hand achieved a 75% success rate at held-out placements in a can pick-and-place task. Project page: https://pact-hand-2027.github.io

title: An Optical KV Cache Network for Disaggregated LLM Serving
abstract: In disaggregated LLM serving, each request's KV cache moves from a prefill GPU to a decode GPU before the response begins, and a coding-agent turn often moves the KV cache of its whole long context. Behind an oversubscribed packet fabric, this transfer adds to the time to first token (TTFT). An optical circuit switch (OCS) can give every transfer a full-rate circuit for less than an oversubscribed packet fabric costs, but a mechanical OCS needs tens of milliseconds to reconfigure. We hide this delay inside the prefill. A reservation scheduler commits each circuit while the prefill is still computing, so the circuit is ready when the KV cache is, and each GPU reaches the OCS through its own wavelength-multiplexed (WDM) optics on one fiber pair. In simulations of GPU clusters on real serving traces with prefill times measured on H100 GPUs, this optical KV cache network matches 400G packet fabrics with adaptive routing at 0.55 to 0.78 times the cost of a 2:1 fabric and tolerates the 50 ms reconfiguration delay of a 384-port mechanical OCS.

title: The Singularity Has a Distribution: Exact Timing Laws and Detection Limits for a Stochastic Intelligence Explosion
abstract: Automating AI research creates a positive feedback loop between software capability and research effort. We study a stochastic realisation of this loop in which independent, positive, multiplicative improvements arrive at a rate proportional to a power of current capability. Within this model, randomness leaves the deterministic explosion threshold unchanged but replaces the blow-up date by an explicit distribution. For equal-sized improvements the explosion time is a geometrically weighted sum of independent exponentials; its $q$-series representation gives its transforms, moments and tail behaviour, including a two-term small-time asymptotic. For Lomax-distributed improvement sizes the explosion time is exactly Gamma distributed. Self-similarity implies that, with parameters known, the relative uncertainty about the remaining time does not vanish as explosion approaches. We formulate a fixed-sample test between constant and geometrically increasing idea-arrival rates. If the baseline rate and the alternative log-rate increment $\ell$ are known, the minimum sample size at error level $α$ is asymptotic to $(12z_α^2)^{1/3}\ell^{-2/3}$, where $z_α$ is the upper-$α$ standard normal quantile. Uncertainty about the growth exponent near its critical value produces a $1/t$ tail with an explicit constant, and hence an infinite conditional mean waiting time, although explosion is certain given a positive exponent. Separate extensions show that a fixed deployment delay prevents explosion in the specified delayed-feedback models, that power-law diversion of effort shifts the growth threshold, and that in a deterministic oversight race a fixed allocation share does not change the asymptotic regime, except at a critical equality of exponents. Numerical illustrations, which are not empirical forecasts, show how timing and detectability depend on the granularity of improvements.

title: CoTL: Compact Token Learning for 3D Scene Representation
abstract: We present CoTL, a framework that learns a compact set of tokens that preserves scene geometry and appearance from unposed multi-view images. Our encoder compresses the input images into small per-view sets of latent tokens that aggregate information across views to form a view-consistent scene representation. Each additional view expands the representation with only a small, resolution-independent set of tokens, allowing its capacity to grow with the available observations. To force this compact bottleneck to retain sufficient scene information, a query-based Gaussian decoder uses scene-independent queries to attend to the learned tokens and recover an explicit, renderable set of 3D Gaussian primitives. Novel-view rendering supervision trains the compact representation end to end through the reconstructed Gaussian scene. Experiments on RealEstate10K and ACID show that the resulting compact, unstructured token set supports competitive novel-view synthesis and can serve as the latent space of a generative model for 3D Gaussian scene generation. Together, these results show that 3D Gaussian reconstruction is an effective objective for compact scene representation learning and the learned token space provides a basis for broader downstream tasks in 3D vision.

title: Thinker-WM: A Unified World Model with Shared Multimodal Representations for Embodied Intelligence
abstract: World models have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied AI, yet existing systems often remain fragmented in the modalities they model and the functions they support. In particular, visual dynamics, geometric structure, and executable action are commonly coupled through separate interfaces or downstream modules rather than being jointly represented and evolved within a shared dynamics model. In this work, we present Thinker-WM, a unified multimodal world model that jointly models and generates RGB, metric depth, and robot action through a shared intermediate Unified Dynamics Transformer with modality-specific encoders and decoders. The model performs multimodal unification at the representation level: appearance, geometry, and action are transformed into a common dynamic representation and jointly evolved by shared parameters, while their distinct output structures are preserved. The same parameterization supports multiple functions, including joint video-action generation, world prediction, policy inference, action-conditioned generation, video-to-action generation, and inverse dynamics. To examine whether the shared representation captures action-related information, we introduce a lightweight motion probe that shows the frozen visual representation contains recoverable motion information. Thinker-WM is trained on a heterogeneous corpus comprising approximately 20K hours of egocentric video, 10K hours of real-robot data, and 1K hours of simulation data, including approximately 4K hours of real-robot data with aligned depth supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong performance across embodied world-model evaluations. Thinker-WM ranks first on EWMBench, WorldOlympiad and WorldArena, while controlled studies further demonstrate the benefits of action conditioning, geometric interaction, and multi-function training within the shared representation.

title: Substrate-controlled epitaxial-like growth of photochromic yttrium oxyhydride thin films
abstract: Yttrium oxyhydride (YHO) thin films are synthesised by reactive magnetron sputtering of \b{eta}-YHx precursor films onto single-crystalline yttria-stabilised zirconia (YSZ) (111) and (100) substrates at 200 °C, followed by post-deposition oxidation in air. For comparison, reference films are also prepared on amorphous SiO2 and soda-lime glass substrates at both 200 °C and room temperature (RT). The structural (X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy), compositional (elastic recoil detection analysis), and optical properties, including photochromic behaviour, of the films are systematically investigated. The results reveal a strong influence of substrate orientation on the film microstructure and crystallographic texture, leading to epitaxial-like growth with a mosaic spread of ~3-4°. YHO deposited on YSZ(100) exhibits larger crystallite sizes (10-20 nm) than YHO grown on YSZ(111) (~8 nm) and exhibits residual in-plane compressive strain while remaining largely relaxed with respect to the substrate. Compositional analysis revealed that the O/Y and O/H atomic ratios ranged from 0.71 to 0.82 and from 0.33 to 0.44, respectively, for films deposited under optimised conditions. These films exhibit photochromic behaviour under solar simulator illumination, with relative transmittance changes ranging from 7 to 22 % after 10 min of illumination. Despite the pronounced structural differences, the epitaxial-like films show no systematic improvement in photochromic response, indicating that the effect is governed primarily by composition. The study shows that the bleaching time constant increases exponentially with increasing contrast reached during illumination, rather than representing an intrinsic material constant of YHO.

title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
abstract: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.

title: A Three-Axis Rydberg Atomic Receiver Model for Polarization-Based Direction-of-Arrival Sensing
abstract: This paper develops a three-axis Rydberg atomic receiver model for direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation of the radio frequency (RF) signal source. Three nominally orthogonal RF local oscillators (LOs), each assigned a distinct frequency offset, project the weak incident RF field into resolvable complex beat coefficients in the optical readout. A beat-vector observation is obtained by adopting a response calibration mechanism that maps the coefficients onto the three axes of the Cartesian coordinate system. For a known circularly polarised RF signal, this observation induces a direction-dependent Rydberg steering vector, enabling maximum-likelihood DoA estimation. The pro posed procedure translates the Rydberg beat-vector front end into a highly sensitive RF field DoA sensor. Simulation results show that trace-level beat extraction supports the proposed DoA sensing workflow and provides a basis for comparison with a traditional vector antenna (VA) benchmark.

title: FastEEP: Fast Intra-Instance Elastic Scaling for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
abstract: Large-scale expert parallelism (EP) has become the standard deployment configuration for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models in production. Meanwhile, the highly dynamic nature of LLM workloads requires providers to continuously adjust serving capacity to match fluctuating demand. Scaling MoE serving cannot be efficiently achieved by simply adding or removing serving instances; instead, it often requires resizing the EP group within an existing instance, which we refer to as intra-instance scaling.Existing inference engines primarily rely on instance-level scaling, which destroys and reconstructs entire serving instances, incurring substantial scaling overhead. We present FastEEP (Fast Elastic Expert Parallel), a fast intra-instance scaling system for MoE serving based on the principle of Partial Reuse. FastEEP reuses existing runtime state across worker execution, GPU memory, and communication by separating reusable execution structures from the resources activated by the current EP configuration. This separation enables coordinated resource reclamation and reconfiguration while preserving costly-to-reconstruct state, allowing fast EP scaling without full instance teardown and reconstruction. Our evaluation shows that FastEEP achieves 4.5x--11.7x faster scaling than the existing vLLM-based approach across different models, enabling efficient, fine-grained scaling of MoE serving.

title: Giant Graviton Expansions from Symmetric Functions and Free Fermions
abstract: Giant graviton expansions express finite-rank corrections to supersymmetric indices in terms of indices for wrapped D3-branes. We give detailed algebraic proofs of two previously proposed relations for four-dimensional $\mathcal N=4$ $U(N)$ super-Yang--Mills theory. The first is the Gaiotto--Lee single-sum expansion of the full superconformal index, proved by Hall--Littlewood orthogonality and an elementary calculation of operator traces. The second is the symmetric double-sum expansion of the flavored Schur index, proved by factorizing its exact free-fermion mode product. We specify the analytic continuation of the brane indices and justify the sums coefficient by coefficient. The two proofs apply to different expansion prescriptions and do not establish the full three-species expansion of Imamura. We discuss the additional physical and mathematical questions raised by that expansion and by the modular properties of the Schur index.

title: The forward-loop-erased ants walk
abstract: In this paper, we study a new variant of the ants walk: a model of reinforced random walks for the phenomenon of a colony of ants being able to find the shortest path between their nest and a source of food. In this model, the nest and the source of food are two distinguished nodes in a finite graph. The ants perform successive random walks on this graph, started at the nest and stopped when they first hit the food source; the transition probabilities of each random walk depends on the trajectories of the previous ants, through some edge-weights that represent the amount pheromones deposited on each edge. In our new variant of the model, the ant (1) forgets loops made on the way to the food as soon as they are made, and (2) comes back to the nest following this loop-erased version of its forward trajectory, and deposits pheromone on the edges it crosses by doing so (i.e. adds one to these edges' weights). We say that the ants "find the shortest path" if, almost surely as the number of ants tends to infinity, the proportion of ants that travel along a graph-geodesic path from the nest to the food tends to one and the proportion of ants that travel along the remaining edges tends to zero. We are able to prove that this new variant of the model finds the shortest path when the graph distance between the nest and the source is at most 2. The strength of our result is that there is no other assumption on the shape of the graph. We prove this result using stochastic approximation theory, the electrical network method for random walks on weighted graphs, and the theory of weighted uniform spanning trees (WUSTs). In particular, the link with WUSTs is unique to the model studied in this paper due to the way the ant erases loops on the outward journey.

title: HEPTABench: A framework for portable and controlled agentic evaluations in high energy physics
abstract: Quantifying the capability and reliability of agentic systems in high-energy physics (HEP) requires repeated evaluations under controlled configurations. Establishing whether changes to models, tools, or harnesses improve performance also requires these components to be varied independently. We present the High Energy Physics Tool-and-Agent Benchmarking (HEPTABench) framework for portable and controlled evaluations of agentic systems, with separately configurable tasks, scaffolding, models, providers, harnesses, and domain capabilities. The framework combines HEP benchmark tasks and scientific rubrics with experiment execution and versioned tool interfaces. To support inspection, reproducibility, and post-hoc grading, the framework prioritizes recording and reporting complete experiment specifications, agent trajectories, and experiment artifacts. We demonstrate the framework in two benchmark campaigns. The first campaign evaluates a forward long-lived-particle reach calculation across four frontier coding-agent systems, comparing their built-in coding tools with the same tools supplemented by HEP domain tools. We show that including these HEP domain tools improves numerical accuracy and reduces trial-to-trial dispersion for every tested system. In a complementary campaign covering eight symbolic two-body decay tasks, we show that adding symbolic domain tools increases the fraction of successful trials for Claude Haiku 4.5 from $8\%$ to $79\%$, while GPT-5.5 succeeds in every trial with built-in tools alone. Through systematic evaluation of agentic systems, HEPTABench enables the identification of factors that improve the accuracy and reliability of their scientific work.

title: EmoGenie: Benchmarking and Evaluating Expressed and Evoked Emotion in T2I Generation with MLLMs
abstract: Rapid advances in artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) have significantly promoted using text-to-image (T2I) models to generate images with specific affective intentions. However, the emotional effects conveyed by generated images frequently deviate from target expectations, and it remains unclear whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reliably interpret the emotion of AI-generated visual content. Existing affective benchmarks are predominantly built on natural images, while affective studies of generated images have largely focused on emotions expressed in portraits, lacking a unified benchmark for studying the emotions expressed and evoked by generated images. We therefore introduce EmoGenie, a benchmark of emotion for AI-generated images that evaluates capabilities in T2I generation and MLLM understanding across expressed and evoked emotions. It comprises 6,400 images generated by eight T2I models using 800 emotion-targeted prompts, annotated with question-answer (QA) pairs, termed EmoGenie-QA, and continuous human ratings, termed EmoGenie-Assess. EmoGenie-QA contains 90,000 closed-set questions in single-image and image-pair settings, as well as 1,057 open-ended questions for emotion description. EmoGenie-Assess benchmarks continuous affective and aesthetic prediction using 13,175 mean opinion scores (MOSs) aggregated from human ratings in terms of valence, arousal, dominance, and aesthetic quality. We further develop EmoProbe, which combines emotion question answering with response-aligned, dimension-specific regression heads for continuous score prediction. Experimental results show that EmoProbe achieves superior results on emotion-related QA tasks, while its affective and aesthetic predictions correlate better with human ratings, demonstrating its state-of-the-art capabilities of unified coarse-to-fine affective understanding for AI-generated images.

title: Learning Perturbation-Specific Representations through Conditional Energy Prior for Cellular Response Prediction
abstract: AI-based cellular perturbation prediction is essential to accelerate drug discovery and therapeutic identification. However, perturbation-specific signals are generally obscured by cellular complexity, making it difficult for existing methods to correctly capture perturbation effects. To address this problem, we propose PerturbEnergy, which introduces a conditional energy-based prior over perturbation representations. It assigns lower energy (higher probability) to representations compatible with the given perturbation and higher energy to others, thereby explicitly tilting the latent space toward perturbation-preferred regions. Besides, PerturbEnergy can be integrated into autoencoder architectures as we find its Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) is equivalent to the ELBO of the complete autoencoder. We further prove that optimizing PerturbEnergy increases the lower bound on the conditional mutual information between representation and perturbation. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our PerturbEnergy: it improves perturbation recognition especially in latent space with improvement of up to 83.2\%; It also achieves state-of-the-art performance for predicting top-50/100/200 differentially expressed gene(DEG) response and remaining competitive on highly variable gene(HVG) prediction. The code is provided: https://github.com/BlueWhaleLab/PerturbEnergy

title: Kairos: Transactional Security Enforcement at the System Boundary for LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. The reach that gives an agent its utility is equally available to an attacker who can steer it. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. Such mediation faces a structural difficulty. Legitimate work and the first step of an attack often look alike when an individual action is observed, and what separates them lies later in the trace, so a monitor limited to allow and deny is forced to decide before the evidence accumulates. We present Kairos, a reference monitor at the isolation boundary of an unmodified, opaque agent, where a tool call, a shell command, and a script the agent writes all cross the boundary as the same file and network operations, so that confinement holds regardless of the agent's behavior. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively.
