A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmarks and three agent models, Kairos outperforms existing defenses in the trade-off between attack success and utility. In particular, on AgentDojo, it reduces attack success from 47.0\% to 2.7\% while its benign utility stays at the level of the undefended agent.

title: $\mathrm{S}^3$-PnP: Plug-and-Play Denoising for Scientific Imaging with Self-Supervised Score Priors
abstract: Modern image restoration methods increasingly rely on large-scale supervised training, yet clean targets are often prohibitively difficult to obtain in scientific imaging modalities such as hyperspectral imaging (HSI) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Plug-and-play ADMM (PnP-ADMM) with pretrained diffusion priors offers a promising alternative, but the learned prior distribution can mismatch both the target scientific image distribution and the distribution of ADMM denoiser inputs induced by dual feedback. To mitigate these mismatches, we propose $\mathrm{S}^3$-PnP, a self-supervised plug-and-play restoration framework that learns a score prior directly from observation-derived ADMM intermediate states, without clean training targets or externally pretrained weights. Specifically, the learned score corrects the input to the analytical prior update, combining observation-driven corrections with analytical regularization. We further analyze the convergence and reconstruction error of the corrected ADMM algorithm assuming an ideal score and quadratic data fidelity. Experiments on reference-guided HSI restoration, single-image HSI denoising, and MRI denoising demonstrate consistent improvements over competing methods.

title: Teacher-Guided Tool Learning for Small Language Models via Bidirectional KL Constraints
abstract: External tools can extend the capabilities of small language models (SLMs), enabling their deployment in resource constrained environments. However, their limited capabilities make it difficult for SLMs to discover effective tool use behaviors through reinforcement learning alone, while direct teacher supervision suffers from teacher student behavioral distribution mismatch and may propagate erroneous preferences. To address these challenges, we propose Selective Teacher guided Policy Optimization (SeTPO), which coordinates student exploration with selective teacher guidance and persistent demonstration supervision. Specifically, SeTPO incorporates reverse KL derived token level teacher feedback into policy advantages on low reward trajectories, while auxiliary forward KL supervision preserves teacher demonstrated behaviors throughout training. Under an idealized bidirectional KL objective, we theoretically establish that the optimal policy achieves expected reward no lower than the teacher's while retaining a guaranteed fraction of the teacher's probability mass. Extensive experiments on BFCL v4 and API Bank demonstrate that SeTPO achieves superior overall performance over supervised fine tuning, reinforcement learning, and distillation baselines across all three student scales.

title: Constraints on the cosmic reheating history from PTA data
abstract: The cosmic reheating is an important epoch in the very early Universe, and has significant impacts on the primordial black hole (PBH) abundance and the scalar-induced gravitational wave (SIGW) spectrum. The relevant energy scale and the constituents of cosmic medium are encoded in the reheating frequency $f_{\mathrm{reh}}$ and the equation of state parameter $w$. In this work, we perform a full parameter space Bayesian inference, using the NANOGrav 15-yr dataset to constrain the thermal history of reheating. Treating $f_{\mathrm{reh}}$ and $w$ as free parameters, we systematically investigate the Dirac $δ$, narrow and broad log-normal primordial power spectra. Current pulsar timing array data can effectively constrain the peak frequency of the SIGW spectrum as $f_{\rm p}\sim 10^{-7.6}$--$10^{-7.0}$ Hz, along with $f_{\rm reh}\sim 10^{-9.0}$--$10^{-8.3}$ Hz and $w\sim 0.19$--$0.79$ (the $68\%$ confidence level), when the power spectrum has a relatively narrow width $Δ\lesssim 1$. A broader power spectrum introduces a smoothing effect that obscures the characteristic frequency knee in the SIGW spectrum, leading to the loss of information about cosmic reheating. Furthermore, for the Dirac $δ$ and narrow spectra, the PBH masses associated with the SIGWs are anchored at the planetary mass scale around $10^{-6}$--$10^{-4} M_{\odot}$. This establishes a consistent physical framework that naturally bridges the nanohertz gravitational wave background with the dark matter candidates implied by the Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment microlensing events.

title: MFVSR: A Multi-Style and Fine-Grained Benchmark for Video Subtitle Removal
abstract: Video subtitle removal (VSR) is an important video restoration task, yet existing evaluation remains limited by low-resolution datasets, fragmented test sets, and generic video-inpainting protocols that fail to adequately capture localized restoration errors, unintended modifications, temporal instability, and incomplete outputs. In this paper, we introduce MFVSR, a large-scale multi-style benchmark for fine-grained and reliability-aware video subtitle removal evaluation. MFVSR distinguishes itself through three key features: (1) Large-scale and diverse data, comprising 3,000 paired videos from Real-HQ, Real-LQ, and AI-Generated sources, with an auxiliary set of 953 in-the-wild real videos for real-world coverage analysis; (2) Controlled subtitle diversity, spanning 16 languages and four factors covering spatial layout, temporal behavior, visual style, and language mode; (3) Fine-grained evaluation, introducing an information-conditioned, spatially decoupled protocol that separates blind from mask-guided removal and measures Restoration Fidelity, Preservation Fidelity, Temporal Fidelity, coverage, and failures. Experiments on six representative methods reveal substantial discrepancies between local restoration, outside-region preservation, temporal consistency, and full-set reliability that are obscured by conventional full-frame metrics. MFVSR therefore provides a more comprehensive and diagnostic foundation for evaluating and advancing video subtitle removal methods.

title: Readout Scaling Shapes Sparse Feature Recovery
abstract: Readout scaling changes what a sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns, but the benefit of removing it depends on the data. We use readout-canonicalized decision-space (RC-DS) coordinates to remove singular-value gains while preserving retained decision information. At a fixed readout condition number, changing the generating distribution reverses which training coordinates recover known factors best. In our controlled coordinate-matching study, recovery is highest when training restores the space in which the factors were generated. When factors are generated before readout scaling, RC-DS increases mean sparse-factor recovery from 0.506 to 0.913 at condition number 100, compared with centered-logit training under the same budget. An exact wrapper reproduces RC-DS training to numerical precision, isolating training geometry rather than additional information. In neural policies, RC-DS improves mean logit reconstruction under the tested budgets. On three fixed language-model checkpoints, RC-DS has higher mean gain-free reconstruction in all 18 tested task-sparsity settings, while centered-logit SAEs reconstruct output logits better in 17. Small-label-head controls show that longer training reduces the reconstruction gap from 0.0198 to 0.0016. Together, these results show how readout scaling, the data distribution, and training shape sparse learning. RC-DS provides an information-preserving method for studying and controlling the readout's contribution. Separate label-detection and steering tests distinguish these reconstruction effects from task-specific feature usefulness.

title: The group generated by a graph's derangements
abstract: We introduce the leap group of a graph, the subgroup of the symmetric group on the vertex set generated by graph derangements. We summarize historical results on graph derangements, which we call hops, and prove additional existence and complexity results. The leap groups of various canonical graphs are computed, and their behavior under basic graph operations is analyzed. We offer partial results on which groups can appear as leap groups, and study hops and leaps for infinite and directed graphs.

title: Lie groups are countably representable
abstract: We prove that every Lie group can be realized by permutations of a countable set, answering a classical question of Ulam. The key deformation construction originated in an argument produced by OpenAI's GPT 6 Astra during extended mathematical discussions.

title: How Safe Is ChatGPT Health Advice? Evidence from Real User Conversations in Four Global South Countries
abstract: People increasingly bring their health questions to ChatGPT, yet safety evaluations of LLM health advice rest almost entirely on clinician-authored vignettes, synthetic prompts, or simulated user profiles. The gap is widest for the Global South, where concerns about demographic bias and unsafe recommendations are well documented but have never been tested on real usage. We present, to our knowledge, the first demographically grounded safety evaluation of real-world health conversations with ChatGPT. From a consent-based data-donation corpus of 202,590 conversations from 1,252 users in India, Nigeria, Brazil, and Pakistan (December 2022 to February 2026), each linked to self-reported age and gender, we identify 15,555 health conversations, classify their health intent using an LLM classifier adapted from an established taxonomy, and score response safety under both a context-blind and a user-context-aware rubric. Roughly one in five health conversations receives a high-risk rating. Risk concentrates in symptom and condition queries and recurs through identifiable failure modes: unsafe medication or dosage guidance, harmful self-diagnosis, missing safety warnings, encouraging over-reliance on the model, and failure to refer users to professionals. Supplying the user's own accumulated context raises the high-risk share by 13-17 percentage points, and about one in four conversations rated safe in isolation turns out to be unsafe for the specific person asking. Safety evaluations built on synthetic cases are likely to miss these harms.

title: Dynamic viscoelastic membranes
abstract: We rigorously derive a dynamic membrane theory for nonlinear viscoelastic solids with Kelvin-Voigt rheology from the corresponding three-dimensional bulk theory, in the limit of vanishing thickness. The bulk model accounts for inertia, a nonsimple elastic energy depending on the second deformation gradient, and a frame-indifferent dissipation. Orientation preservation is ensured by the energy, while self-interpenetration of the limiting membrane is prevented by a uniform averaged invertibility condition. Our analysis relies on a hyperbolic minimizing movements scheme with two time-scales, which recasts the evolution into a hierarchy of incremental, sequential, and time-delayed problems. For fixed thickness, we prove the existence of solutions to the scheme and their convergence to a weak solution of the continuous-time problem as the time-scales vanish. We then identify the membrane limit at each level of the hierarchy, proving the $Γ$-convergence of the incremental functionals and the convergence of solutions to the sequential and time-delayed problems. Since the constant in the Korn inequality is not uniform in the thickness, these limits rely on estimates for the time derivative of the Cauchy-Green tensor rather than for the velocity gradient. Finally, as the outer time-scale vanishes, the membrane time-delayed solutions converge to a measure-valued solution of the membrane continuous-time problem.

title: Ushering in high angular resolution observatories in the far-infrared: The case for a double-Fourier interferometer
abstract: A far-infrared (far-IR) interferometer from a space-based platform would bring about a transformational improvement in the spatial detail of astronomical observations that are inaccessible from ground-based observatories. This orders-of-magnitude improvement would significantly advance studies of newly formed and mature exoplanetary systems and their potential for supporting life, the earliest stages of star formation, and the evolution of galaxies up to the peak of the Universe's star formation activity and beyond. In this work, we discuss the potential for such an instrument and the science it enables in complement to current long-term plans of the global astronomical community and in preparation for the next generation of observatories. We also outline notable far-IR mission concepts, pathfinder instruments, and technology development platforms that have been studied and developed throughout the past few decades and briefly discuss key enabling technologies.

title: A pedestrian's approach to Bayesian methods for inverse problems
abstract: In the past two decades, the Bayesian approach to inverse problems in infinite dimensional spaces has seen significant developments in theory, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, and in applications. The Bayesian approach in finite dimension produces posterior distributions of finite dimensional random variables. In infinite dimensions, the desired objects are random fields and their laws as measures on Hilbert or Banach spaces. There are many textbooks and tutorials available that explain Bayesian methods and MCMC in finite dimensions. To enter the field of Bayesian inverse problems in infinite dimensions, a newcomer has to engage with a quite diverse and extensive literature. The purpose of this article is to provide a basic path to the subject that is easily accessible to a reader with general knowledge in probability and mathematical analysis. We start with a swift introduction to the finite dimensional case. The infinite dimensional case is introduced for Gaussian priors on Hilbert spaces and Gaussian-type likelihood functions. In this situation, mere continuity of the forward map suffices to prove that the posterior measure is well-defined. We also give some new and simple stability results. Two application examples are elaborated, one finite dimensional, one infinite dimensional.

title: PhonoVoxtLM: Exploring Single-Codebook Phonological Tokens for Speech Understanding and Generation
abstract: We investigate how speech token representations can support both understanding and generation within a unified speech language model. We present PhonoVoxtLM, built on the existing VoxtLM framework using phonological tokens designed to retain linguistic content and prosodic information. The existing tokenizer is jointly trained for speech recognition and resynthesis. Its single-codebook units serve as both speech inputs and generation targets, without additional speech-token prediction modules. Experiments show improvements over HuBERT-based baselines across understanding and generation under different training-data scales. Further comparisons with WavLM-based tokens reveal trade-offs between recognition and synthesis, highlighting the importance of evaluating shared representations across both capabilities. We further extend the framework to spoken question answering through fine-tuning with replay. The adapted model improves answering performance over similarly adapted HuBERT baselines while retaining advantages on the original speech tasks. Our findings support single-codebook representations designed for both content and prosody as a practical choice for unified multitask speech modeling.

title: Continuous-wave 148.4-nm generation in strontium tetraborate for nuclear absorption spectroscopy
abstract: Continuous-wave light near 148.4 nm enables direct absorption spectroscopy of the thorium-229 nuclear transition. We demonstrate single-pass frequency doubling in strontium tetraborate, delivering an estimated 8.1 nW at 920 mW pump power. At this power, oxygen admission leaves a background of 1.22 kHz, corresponding to an estimated signal-to-background ratio of 3.8 x 10^4 after current-integration calibration. Several crystals grown by top-seeded solution growth produce polarization-dependent VUV signals. Temperature scans reveal distinct maxima among specimens cut from one boule and among positions within a specimen. The source sustains operation over 33.3 h. In a separate 3-h record acquired with 1-ms gates, local referencing achieves near-Poisson averaging, reaching a fractional Allan deviation of 3.5 x 10^-5 at 1000 s. These results establish a practical VUV source for stable, long-duration spectroscopy of weak nuclear absorption.

title: Graph Metanetworks for Transformer Based Language Models
abstract: Weight-space learning treats the weights of neural networks as data, processed by other models called metanetworks. A key challenge is that different weights can realize the same function, related by a group of symmetries the metanetwork should respect. While symmetry-aware metanetworks for simple architectures such as MLPs are well developed, a comprehensive treatment of transformers, and in particular transformer-based language models, is still missing. Importantly, their weight space has a richer symmetry group: beyond neuron permutations, attention introduces continuous general-linear symmetries of the attention matrices and permutations of entire heads. Existing methods for transformer weights either capture only part of these symmetries or are restricted to a single, fixed architecture, and none accounts for language-model-specific components such as the token embeddings. Building on graph metanetworks, we propose a graph-based approach that is both symmetry-aware and applicable across depths and widths. We formalize a weight-space symmetry group of complete decoder-only language models and provide a graph construction that is invariant to it. We further introduce two new transformer-population datasets with novel tasks, such as training-corpus prediction and fine-tuning detection, on which our approach notably outperforms existing baselines.

title: Simplifying and Improving On-Policy Distillation for Few-Step Diffusion
abstract: Few-step distillation reduces the sampling cost of diffusion and flow models, but existing approaches often require auxiliary score models or specialized architectures. We show that simple on-policy velocity regression already provides a strong foundation for 4-NFE generation. To represent teacher velocity variation within each coarse transition, we introduce Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that separates local corrections from the student's interval-mean prediction. We further repel the student from weaker teacher predictions, providing a lightweight mechanism for avoiding undesirable modes. The resulting framework, Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD), remains entirely regression-based, requires neither online score estimation nor adversarial training, and leaves the deployed generator unchanged. We evaluate SMD on image generation and editing, 3D generation, video synthesis, and joint audio--video generation, scaling to 33 billion parameters. At 4-NFE, SMD outperforms strong few-step baselines and surpasses multi-step teachers on several benchmarks. It also supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation.

title: EDGE-INFERNO: The chemical signatures of assembly history in reionization fossils
abstract: In galaxies, stellar populations represent a superposition of both in situ and accreted components, tracing internal chemical evolution as well as the histories of merged satellites. We investigate how assembly history shapes the chemical properties of present-day stellar populations in low-mass dwarf galaxies. We analyze a suite of EDGE-INFERNO star-by-star cosmological zoom-in simulations of galaxies with present-day halo mass $\sim1.4\times10^9\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$. We systematically vary galaxy growth while preserving the present-day halo mass, engineering our simulations to span a continuum of assembly histories. Early-forming systems form most of their stars in a single progenitor, with centrally concentrated star formation and a continuous enrichment history. In contrast, our late-forming systems assemble by accretion of multiple progenitors with their own stellar populations, resulting in fragmented star formation across several halos with independent chemical evolution tracks. These regimes produce qualitatively different chemical signatures: single-progenitor systems exhibit connected, well-defined trends in abundance space, while multi-progenitor systems show multiple, distinct stellar populations with limited overlap. We find that metallicity distribution functions provide initial constraints on assembly history for samples of at least $50$-$100$ member stars. Multi-element abundance analysis significantly improves the recovery of distinct components, although robust reconstruction still requires larger samples. Fully separating in situ and accreted populations likely requires kinematic information. Accreted stars can contribute substantially even at high metallicities in multi-progenitor systems, while external enrichment can cause accreted material to follow similar chemical trends as in situ stars, particularly in the single-progenitor regime.

title: Unequal Coherent Ergotropy at Equal Interferometric Visibility and Energy in Quantum-Controlled Interferometers
abstract: The ergotropy, or unitarily extractable work, of a quantum system naturally splits into incoherent and coherent contributions, respectively set by population inversion and coherences in the energy eigenbasis. We show that this split makes the coherent ergotropy of a Mach--Zehnder qubit sensitive to path predictability that the output interference fringes do not reveal. We send the path qubit, prepared as a thermal quantum battery, through two quantum-controlled interferometers built from the same elements, a fixed beam splitter and a beam splitter coherently controlled to be present or absent, differing only in the order in which these two act. The two arrangements share identical visibility, stored energy, and incoherent ergotropy at every point in the parameter space. Yet, for work extracted from the output battery alone, placing the controlled beam splitter first never yields less coherent ergotropy, and at fixed visibility and interferometric phase the difference is governed by the path predictability that this ordering creates. The same expression reappears as a purity deficit on the beam-splitter controller, so the work advantage comes with a Landauer bound on the cost of locally resetting the controller that is never larger at the same temperature. We further examine the effects of decoherence on the battery and consider a relativistic realization in which a Wigner rotation correlates the particle's spin with its path. Tracing out the spin decoheres the battery and allows the two arrangements to exhibit different coherent ergotropies even in regimes where their non-relativistic counterparts coincide. These results show that interference visibility is not a complete measure of the coherence available as work.

title: Tidal Excitation of Relativistic Stars
abstract: How a relativistic star responds to a time-dependent tide has lacked a first-principles counterpart of the Newtonian normal-mode expansion. In general relativity, the tidal field is gauge sensitive, radiative modes are non-Hermitian and incomplete, and the direct and late-time responses are intrinsically nonmodal. In this work we present, to our knowledge, the first causal relativistic theory that treats all of these components on equal footing. We first develop the spectral decomposition of the retarded Green function of the matched stellar interior--Schwarzschild exterior, which classifies four separate regimes in time domain: acausal region, prompt wave, surface-reflected wave, and mode+tail. The prompt signal is identical to that of a Schwarzschild black hole with the same mass, which is combined with the surface-reflected wave to be referred as the "direct part". With the Green function and a complex bilinear form on the full metric--fluid phase space, we decompose the linear response of a nonrotating perfect-fluid star into direct, quasinormal-mode, and late-time-tail sectors. Crucially, every sector admits an explicit first-order driven evolution equation: discrete bilinear projections determine the dynamically evolving quasinormal-mode amplitudes, while continuum projections of the same tidal source onto branch-cut states determine the direct and tail amplitudes. The result is a complete modal--nonmodal decomposition of the spacetime and fluid perturbations, which is physically described by the dynamics of a discrete and a continuous-frequency set of oscillators. We verify the decomposition numerically under generic time-dependent tidal driving and discuss applications to black hole perturbations.

title: Broadband non-thermal emission predictions based on 3D simulations of supernova explosions within active galactic nuclei jets
abstract: Thermonuclear and core-collapse supernovae are statistically expected to happen within extragalactic jets, as these jets cross the inner regions of their host galaxies, and supernova ejecta-jet interactions can potentially lead to strong non-thermal activity. We model the non-thermal emission from a supernova interacting with a jet on kiloparsec scales, using detailed numerical simulations of the interaction. Using a post-processing method, we applied a non-thermal model of the acceleration and transport of electron and their synchrotron and inverse Compton emissions, simplified and tuned for flexibility and computational speed, to the results of a three-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamics simulation of the ejecta of a supernova interacting with an extragalactic jet. For intermediate jet powers, radio, optical and X-ray fluxes from supernova ejecta-jet interactions may be detectable for distances < 100Mpc. The non-thermal luminosity budget and local conditions associated with these interactions could be enough to explain knots seen in kiloparsec scale jets at different energies. These conditions might also be suitable for the production of heavy ultra high-energy cosmic rays, but photon and neutrino generation from hadronic processes would be minor on kiloparsec scales. The leptonic gamma-ray fluxes are modest but might non-negligibly contribute in TeV for the nearest or more powerful jet sources.

title: Experimental Realization of a C-Shunt Flux-Qubit Coupler for Controlled-Z Gates between Transmons
abstract: Fast entangling gates and low-interaction idling require distinct operating conditions in superconducting quantum processors. We experimentally realize a transmon-C-shunt-transmon (TCT) device in which a flux-tunable, three-junction capacitively shunted flux-qubit coupler connects two transmon data qubits. The C-shunt coupler provides a flux-tunable, positively anharmonic spectrum for tailoring the interactions between the data qubits. Conditional Ramsey and swap measurements identify an idle region with near-zero residual ZZ interaction strength and suppressed transverse exchange. At this bias, simultaneous single-qubit interleaved randomized benchmarking yields X-gate fldelities above 99.7%, consistent with individual operation. A 45 ns nonadiabatic controlled-Z (CZ) gate achieves an interleaved randomized benchmarking fldelity estimate of 99.23(15)%. Numerical simulations identify coupler energy relaxation as an important limitation on CZ-gate fldelity and indicate that extending the coupler lifetime can improve gate performance. These results demonstrate the experimental feasibility of C-shunt flux-qubit couplers for combining low-interaction idling with fast entangling operations between transmon qubits.

title: MemoryVLN: From Ego-Aware Memory Representation to Cross-Context Memory Reuse in Vision-Language Navigation
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have shown strong potential for embodied vision-language navigation (VLN), yet their performance degrades on long-horizon trajectories due to context-length limits, redundant historical observations, and unstable spatial alignment across time. These issues make it difficult to both compress long navigation histories and reliably reuse past spatial experience. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{MemoryVLN}, a unified memory-driven navigation system built around memory construction and management. During memory construction, \emph{Long Sequence Compression} employs forgetting-curve-inspired temporal sampling to preserve dense recent evidence and sparse yet representative distant observations under a limited token budget. \emph{Ego-Aware Memory Representation} further integrates 2D semantic tokens, 3D geometric tokens, and 6D agent poses, allowing each memory to encode both what was observed and where it was observed. During memory management, \emph{Hierarchical Memory Bank} maintains in-episode and context-level memories through cross-context warm-start and confidence-controlled write-back. \emph{Memory Enhancement} then retrieves the Top-$K$ relevant memories according to the current navigation state and fuses them with the current visual tokens. Together, these mechanisms transform raw navigation history into compact, spatially grounded, selectively retrievable, and reusable navigation experience. Extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE demonstrate consistent improvements over the state-of-the-art baselines by a substantial margin (i.e., 2\% and 6.5\% in successful rate).

title: RTISSLAM: In-air Imaging Sonar SLAM using a Robust Pose Graph and Occupancy Grid Mapping
abstract: Sonar was one of the first sensors with which mobile robots built maps, and in-air sonar keeps working where cameras and lidar fail, in darkness, smoke, dust and next to glass. Classical sonar SLAM, however, relied on geometric features or occupancy grids built from sparse range readings, and both struggle with the specular reflections that dominate indoor sonar. In this letter, we introduce RTISSLAM, a novel sonar-only SLAM system for an embedded 3D imaging sonar, which combines the robust pose graph of BatSLAM 2.0 as back-end with an occupancy grid as map. Energyscapes from delay-multiply-and-sum beamforming with a range-wise CFAR serve as place descriptors for sequence-verified loop closures, acoustic odometry calibrates the wheel odometry online, recognized revisits are registered metrically, and the grid is stored per keyframe and anchored to the pose-graph nodes, so that it follows every loop closure. In simulated worlds with specular walls, RTISSLAM reduces the trajectory error of the wheel odometry from \SI{8.2}{\meter} to \SI{0.31}{\meter} in an office, while lidar-style grid SLAM on the same sonar data fails.

title: When do lazy and invertible cellular automata generate all cellular automata?
abstract: Let $G$ be a group and let $A$ be a set with at least two elements. A lazy cellular automaton over $A^G$ acts as the identity except at the cells where a fixed pattern occurs, where it replaces the central symbol by a fixed different symbol. Let $M(G;A)$ be the submonoid of $\mathrm{CA}(G;A)$ generated by the lazy and the invertible cellular automata. We study when $M(G;A) = \mathrm{CA}(G;A)$. Since no lazy cellular automaton is surjective, every surjective element of $M(G;A)$ is invertible; hence $M(G;A) \neq \mathrm{CA}(G;A)$ whenever $A$ is infinite or $G$ has an element of infinite order. Moreover, if $|A| = 2$ and $G$ has a quotient isomorphic to the Klein four-group $C_2 \times C_2$, then $M(G;A) \neq \mathrm{CA}(G;A)$. For locally finite $G$, and in particular for finite $G$, these are the only obstructions: we prove that $M(G;A) = \mathrm{CA}(G;A)$ if and only if $3 \leq |A| < \infty$, or $|A| = 2$ and $G$ has no quotient isomorphic to $C_2 \times C_2$.

title: ProTok: Unified Protein Tokenization via Modular Multi-Codebook Quantization
abstract: Protein sequence, structure, and functional annotations each capture complementary aspects of protein biology, yet existing tokenizers encode each modality independently, limiting the expressiveness of discrete protein representations. We present ProTok, a unified protein tokenizer that maps all three modalities into a modular discrete vocabulary via product quantization with per-modality codebook groups and modality dropout. A single ProTok checkpoint supports flexible inference from any modality subset without retraining. On seven StructTokenBench benchmarks spanning 14 tasks and 28 test splits, ProTok achieves an average rank of 1.4 across all structure-only tokenizers, placing first on 21 splits and among the top two on 27 of the 28. These gains come without sacrificing reconstruction: ProTok's tokens reach 0.939 lDDT on CATH 4.2, showing that multi-codebook quantization and multi-modal training yield tokens that are both reconstructable and informative. ProTok's structure tokens further lead all baseline structure tokenizers on zero-shot functional retrieval across CATH, Enzyme Commission, and Gene Ontology label hierarchies. The vocabulary also supports generation: a compact language model trained from scratch over ProTok tokens jointly generates backbone and sequence, with 52% of sampled backbones designable versus 21% for a parameter-matched GeoBPE baseline. ProTok shows that structure, sequence, and function can share one discrete vocabulary, motivating protein language models that reason over a unified token stream.

title: Lifting: Quantum State Discrimination Framework for Mid-Circuit Measurements
abstract: Quantum computing promises new capabilities beyond classical computation. Mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) enable error correction and outcome-dependent control, but their reliability is limited by noise on superconducting hardware. These operations depend on accurate quantum state discrimination (QSD), which assigns measured signals to state labels. Neural network-based (NN-based) QSD improves this assignment, yet its error remains bounded below by the Bayes risk of the available readout distributions. A complementary challenge is state deterioration as successive measurements accumulate and circuit execution advances, making static calibration less representative of the workload. We present Lifting, a QSD framework that addresses both challenges through repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration. Encoding supplies joint in-phase and quadrature (I-Q) readout signals from the target and auxiliary qubits, while contextual calibration trains the decoder for the conditions encountered during execution. Our theoretical analysis shows that retaining additional channels from a fixed joint distribution cannot increase Bayes risk and establishes sufficient conditions for contraction of an overlap-based upper bound. Experiments across three IBM processors evaluate the framework on repeated stabilizer measurement, parity-check, and teleportation workloads.

title: Sign-indefinite transmission conditions and near-zero eigenvalues and resonances
abstract: We consider the linear operator for metamaterial modeling $$L_{c,d }=(χ_{\RE^{3}\backslash\overline Ω}+c)\nabla\!\cdot (χ_{\RE^{3}\backslash\overline Ω}+d)\nabla\,,$$ where the material parameters $c>0$ and $d$ are constant on each connected component of the bounded domain $Ω$, $d$ is negative on at least one component of $Ω$ and transmission boundary conditions hold at the interfaces. It turns out that $L_{c,d }$ has, as in the sign-definite case, an absolutely continuous spectrum equal to $[0,+\infty)$; however, contrary to the latter, it has a non-empty point spectrum; in particular, we find conditions on the parameters so that zero is a threshold eigenvalue. In the case $Ω$ is connected, we study how such a threshold eigenvalue behaves under $\varepsilon$-small analytic perturbations of the parameters. We show that, depending on the position of the number $\frac12\,\frac{1+d(\ve)}{1-d(\ve)}$ relative to the nearest eigenvalue of the Neumann-Poincaré operator of the interface, the zero eigenvalue splits into two branches (analytic in $\varepsilon^{1/2}$), consisting either of two branches of resonances, or of one branch of negative eigenvalues and one of resonances.

title: ReTerm: Recovery Training for Self-Improving Terminal Agents
abstract: Terminal agents have shown strong abilities in complex coding tasks. However, they often struggle to recover from errors during long-running execution (e.g., command errors, faulty implementations), eventually leading to task failures. To this end, we present ReTerm, a self-improving terminal agent trained by learning how to recover from its own failed terminal tasks. To support its training, we construct a customized data pipeline and produce ReTerm-10K, a high-quality dataset that provides effective recovery demonstrations for SFT cold start. Furthermore, we propose ReTerm-GRPO, an online RL algorithm that forks from the agent's own failure states to generate multiple independent self-recovery attempts. By learning from whether these attempts successfully complete the task, the agent self-improves through its own recovery experience. Built on Qwen3.5-9B, our ReTerm-9B achieves 34.8% Pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0, improving over the base model by 14.6 points. Further analysis shows that our method achieves consistently higher recovery rates across diverse error categories compared with standard GRPO training. All code, data and model are released at https://github.com/twothsnd/ReTerm.

title: Physics-Aware Deepfake Detection via Distance-Speech Consistency
abstract: Recent progress in generative models has made talking-head deepfakes highly realistic and easy to create, jeopardizing public trust. However, most audio-visual deepfake detectors rely on lip-speech synchronization and are designed for static, frontal videos, limiting their reliability in dynamic, in-the-wild recordings where the speaker moves and lip cues are degraded or missing. As an alternative, we propose a physics-aware detector for dynamic speaking videos that leverages an acoustic constraint: in real recordings, speech energy varies predictably with speaker-to-camera distance, whereas deepfake generation can break this coupling. Our method combines distance estimates from video with distance-dependent acoustic measures from speech to detect deepfakes. Experiments on in-the-wild benchmarks show that the proposed physical cue is effective in dynamic scenarios, and that it complements lip-sync-based detectors, with a simple ensemble achieving consistent gains across datasets. Codes are available at https://byulharang.github.io/PADD/.

title: SoK: Rethinking Membership Inference in Tabular Machine Learning
abstract: Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) are currently the dominant approach to evaluating privacy in machine learning applications. Despite their significance, several concerns remain unexplored, particularly with regard to tabular data. Existing evaluations focus predominantly on high-dimensional datasets, leaving the privacy behavior of small-to-medium datasets unexplored. In this paper, we present a new taxonomy for MIAs and conduct a comprehensive study of the factors influencing vulnerability. We evaluate four distinct state-of-the-art attacks across diverse tabular datasets and model architectures. Our results show that datasets with higher class granularity and majority class percentage are more susceptible to MIAs. We further demonstrate that advanced MIAs are highly dependent on adversarial knowledge of the target model, while reference model-free attacks often achieve statistically comparable results. Most importantly, we show that records with unique signatures (single-outs) remain highly vulnerable, even when common defenses are applied. These findings indicate that current defenses reduce average leakage, but fail to adequately protect the most sensitive individuals.

title: Deviations to cobimaximal mixing in a 3+1 neutrino scenario
abstract: Cobimaximal mixing remains a viable approximate pattern since the predicted atmospheric angle ($π/4$) and Dirac CP phase ($-π/2$) are compatible with current experimental data at the $3σ$ level. In this work, we investigate how an additional sterile neutrino state breaks the cobimaximal mixing and the underlying $μ-τ$ reflection symmetry in a $3+1$ neutrino scenario. Given the strong constraints already imposed on active-sterile mixings, we examine the resulting restrictions on the model parameter space, assuming a small symmetry breaking induced by the sterile state. We derive predictions for the relevant model parameters, active-sterile mixing angles, and Dirac CP-violating phases, by considering small deviations from the symmetric limit. We also analyze the allowed combinations of Majorana phases through their impact on the effective Majorana mass governing neutrinoless double beta decay. Current experimental limits on this process impose severe constraints on the inverted ordering realization of the $3+1$ scenario, excluding the small breaking regime within the parameter ranges considered. In contrast, the normal ordering case remains viable and predicts values of the effective Majorana mass that lie within the sensitivity reach of upcoming neutrinoless double beta decay experiments.

title: Recalibrating Many Questions with Few Labels: Minimax Rates and Identification Limits
abstract: Many related prediction problems, which we call questions, come with few labels each. What information can be shared across them, and what is actually necessary for good decisions? We answer both for recalibration, motivated by decision models such as Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) that return a probability for any yes/no question a developer writes. A predictor reports a probability $P$ with output law $μ$ on $m$ questions, each with $n$ labels and a nondecreasing map $g_j(p)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid P=p)$; the compound risk is the excess Brier score over the true maps, averaged over questions. Over maps within sup-distance $τ\le 1$ and total variation $V\le 2$ of one nondecreasing shape (fixed effects), the minimax compound risk is $(mn)^{-2/3}+\min\{τ^2,1/n\}+\min\{τ^2,V^2,(V/n)^{2/3}\}$ up to universal constants, for every non-atomic $μ$. A pooled isotonic fit with a per-question correction sized once, on held-out labels of all questions, attains it without knowing $τ$, $V$ or $μ$ ($n\ge 2$, $m\ge 3$); tuning each question on its own labels loses a factor of order $\min\{n,\log(m^2/n)\}$ when the maps differ by constants and $m^2/n$ is large. When the maps are drawn from an unknown prior (random effects), other questions need not identify the Bayes rule. The loss, the identification regret, is at most $2^{-n}$ once the law of a question's data is known, extending a bound of Skibinsky (1968) for coins, and in the worst case at least $β_\star^{-n}/(72\sqrt{n})$ at every finite $m$, where $β_\star\approx 3.583$. Beyond a few labels per question, what cannot be learned is nearly unnecessary. For constant maps (an uninformative predictor) and constant-map priors, the exponential base is exactly $β_\star$, not the 4 suggested by the moment range; for monotone maps it lies in $[2,β_\star]$.

title: Irrational families of Fano weighted complete intersection fourfolds
abstract: We study the irrationality of smooth Fano complete intersection fourfolds in weighted projective spaces, using an atom theoretic approach based solely on Gromov--Witten invariants. We prove symplectic irrationality, and hence irrationality for every smooth member, in a wide range of families for which irrationality was previously known only for very general members.

title: Quantitative Modelling of Solvation in 2D Materials via Alchemical Decoupling and Potential Energy Surfaces
abstract: Understanding why 2D materials remain suspended in solutions is essential to understanding the mechanisms of aggregation and exfoliation. These dynamics have been difficult to model because of the long timescales and large activation energies involved in these simulations. Here we describe an improved strategy for modelling the solvation and stability of 2D materials that uses the Gibbs free energy of solvation to accurately calibrate two disconnected potential energy surfaces for the fully desolvated and fully solvated 2D materials. By joining these surfaces using solvation energy, we obtain predictions for 2D material stability in various solvents that are qualitatively different than prior simulations and that have excellent agreement with experimental results. Our approach predicts a much higher barrier to full desolvation of the material, suggesting that materials that appear to be aggregated in fact still retain monolayers of solvent between adjacent layers of 2D materials. This work provides much needed understanding on the interactions between the solvent and 2D material that can guide future experimental work.

title: Some applications of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis to class groups and small generators of number fields
abstract: We prove an effective version of the Chebotarev density theorem, conditional on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis for the Dedekind zeta function. Drawing on recent breakthroughs of OpenAI and Cureton--Thorner, we make unconditional the Ellenberg--Venkatesh bounds on $\ell$-torsion in class groups of number fields and extend an averaged result of Lemke Oliver--Smith to arbitrary families of degree-$d$-fields. Further applications are given to the least prime splitting and to small generators in number fields.

title: Endochain conditions on modules and $p$-quasi-Frobenius rings
abstract: Analogous to quasi-Frobenius rings, dual rings, and Johns rings, the classes of $p$-quasi-Frobenius rings, $p$-dual rings, $p$-Johns rings are introduced and used to discuss and settle principal analogues of the Faith-Menal, Faith, and FGF conjectures. A chain symmetry theorem establishes that for quasi-injective semi-projective modules with semiprime endomorphism ring, endonoetherianity and endoartinianity are equivalent and force the endomorphism ring to be semisimple artinian. Within this unified setting, it is shown that (1) two-sided $p$-Johns rings are $p$-quasi-Frobenius, giving a principal Faith-Menal analogue, with a counterexample showing that the one-sided hypothesis is insufficient; (2) semiprimary principal right ideal rings that are right injective and right Kasch are $p$-quasi-Frobenius-this affirmatively answers a question of Faith (Q2) in the principal two-sided ideal ring case and settles the principal Faith conjecture, with a counterexample showing the principal right ideal ring to be indispensable; and (3) right $p$-Johns rings that are left CF and left perfect are $p$-quasi-Frobenius, yielding a principal FGF analogue, with a counterexample demonstrating that the hypotheses are essential. Wherever needed, examples are provided to show that various classes introduced are different from the existing classes in the literature.

title: Turán numbers of triangular pyramids
abstract: Let $\TP_k$ denote the triangular pyramid with $k$ layers. For a graph family $\mathcal F$, let $\ex(n,\mathcal F)$ be the maximum number of edges in an $n$-vertex graph containing no member of $\mathcal F$ as a subgraph. For a graph $H$, let $\cJ(H)$ be the family of subgraph-minimal graphs among all such graphs $H-I$, where $I\subseteq V(H)$ is an independent set. For every integer $k\ge4$ and all sufficiently large $n$, we prove that \[ \ex(n,\TP_k)=\max_{0\le m\le n}\{m(n-m)+\ex(m,\cJ(\TP_k))\}+O_k(n)=\left\lfloor n^2/4\right\rfloor+Θ_k(n^{4/3}). \] Moreover, for $k=4$, we characterize all extremal graphs and show that \[ \ex(n,\TP_4)=\max_{0\le m\le n}\bigl\{m(n-m)+\ex\big(m,\cJ(\TP_4)\big)\bigr\} \] for sufficiently large $n$.

title: Task-evoked eye movements as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults
abstract: Objective digital measures of depression severity could complement conventional symptom assessments and facilitate more timely clinical evaluation. Here, we investigated whether task-evoked eye movements provide interpretable behavioral markers of depression severity in adolescents and young adults. In this single-center, cross-sectional study, 155 participants aged 14--20 years completed emotional-spatial free-viewing and memory-guided recall tasks and were stratified by 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. We examined 19 prespecified eye-movement features across six task-informed domains using covariate-adjusted ordinal-trend models. Greater depression severity was associated with lower gaze-allocation entropy (standardized $β=-0.599$), fewer inter-area switches ($β=-0.526$), longer first target-entry latency ($β=0.572$), and lower target dwell proportion ($β=-0.678$; all false-discovery-rate-adjusted $q<0.001$). Emotion-specific attentional-bias measures were not associated with severity, whereas associations involving fixation dispersion weakened after adjustment for anxiety symptoms. In a complementary machine-learning analysis incorporating 44 candidate eye-movement features and demographic covariates, a three-stage cascade classifier achieved the highest four-class stratification performance (accuracy, 0.665; macro-F1, 0.670; area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.869), outperforming single-stage and two-stage approaches. Together, these findings identify altered visual exploration and memory-guided gaze control as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity, rather than generalized negative attentional bias. These results support further prospective evaluation of task-evoked eye tracking as a complementary approach for timely severity assessment and clinical decision support.

title: Steering the Fidelity in State Preparation on Noisy Bosonic Systems with Risk-Seeking Optimization
abstract: In order to execute quantum algorithms on bosonic quantum computers, it is necessary to encode their inputs into a desired target quantum state, with a process called state preparation. In real settings, state preparation methods operate in stochastic scenarios, where the prepared state is represented as a mixed state, that is a probabilistic ensemble of pure states. Therefore, existing state preparation methods optimize a variational ansatz by averaging over all possible sequences of photon loss events contained in the prepared ensemble, yielding an output state which approximates the desired target with a certain average fidelity. Such an approach, however, does not take into account directly the distribution of fidelities across states in the ensemble. In this work, we aim to maximize the fidelity of only a subset of pure states sampled from the prepared ensemble, at the cost of reducing the average fidelity overall. This trade-off is relevant when the goal is to obtain high-fidelity states with a certain probability, rather than maximizing the average fidelity of the prepared ensemble. We borrow and adapt objective functions from risk-sensitive optimization, a framework that optimizes specific characteristics of a distribution rather than only its expectation, and that has been successfully applied in Reinforcement Learning. In the considered experimental settings, our results show that the infidelities of some pure states in the prepared ensemble can be reduced by up to four orders of magnitude when using risk-seeking objectives, compared to those achieved using the standard optimization of the average fidelity. Furthermore, we show that it is possible to control the trade-off between the probability of obtaining high-fidelity states and the lowest infidelity threshold reached, providing the flexibility to select the operating point that best suits a certain application.

title: Viscosity Solutions for Hamilton-Jacobi equations on Separable Banach Spaces
abstract: This work provides a framework to treat optimal control problems on separable Banach spaces in the viscosity sense. First, it extends the notion of $B$-viscosity solutions to the Banach setting and relates the extension to the notions of viscosity solutions used in metric space settings. As the main results, the paper proves a strict comparison principle and characterizes the value function of an optimal control problem as the unique viscosity solution to an infinite-dimensional HJB equation.

title: Judges Follow the Reference: The Derivation Gap in Verifying Tool-Call Arguments
abstract: Tool-call judges evaluate argument values proposed by LLM agents. We find that they accept a correct value less often when their input holds no reference for it, that is, no text that says what the value should be. This happens when the value is a default value from the function schema that the user did not mention, when it has to be inferred, or when the text it comes from was cut from the judge input. We call this drop in acceptance the derivation gap. It appears across all seven judges we evaluate, including System One models CLM and Jev. The gap is not only a truncation artifact: correct default values have the largest gap on a benchmark with no truncation. A controlled source-relocation test shows that judges follow the reference in their input: they favor a visible incorrect value over a correct value whose source is hidden. We introduce DeRef (Derived Reference): a separate model reads the full history without seeing the candidate and writes a reference for the judge. Across three benchmarks, DeRef improves overall argument AUROC for all judges tested. On the controlled test, it raises AUROC from chance or below to between 98.40 and 99.59.

title: Aligning Faithfulness for Theory-Scale Autoformalization
abstract: Autoformalization (AF) requires more than compilation: formal statements must preserve the meaning of their informal sources, a property known as faithfulness. An emerging frontier is the automated evaluation of this property, yet most existing methods operate at the statement level and produce whole-item verdicts, failing to reveal how individual expressions correspond or which contextual interpretations support the judgment. This omission is consequential because AF is inherently theory-scale: target statements derive their meaning from surrounding mathematical material and unstated conventions. We formulate faithfulness evaluation as a context-aware align-then-label problem: identifying phrase-level correspondences between informal and formal statements and assigning a faithfulness label to each under explicitly specified contextual interpretations and assumptions. We also introduce FaithAlign, the first theory-scale faithfulness benchmark comprising 460 items and 4,982 annotated phrase-level links, alongside FaithAlign-Gap, a companion set of 146 items with informal context and assumptions withheld. Each FaithAlign item includes the target statement pair, relevant context, formal dependencies, and, where needed, assumptions specifying one given interpretation. Across 8 models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest defect F1 at 47.8% and identifies all defects in only 4.5% of items with two or more defects. On FaithAlign-Gap, Astra identifies only 28.2% of undecidable items as such. These results show the difficulty of recovering context-dependent correspondences, establishing FaithAlign as a testbed for fine-grained, context-aware faithfulness evaluation.

title: EgoOmniWorld: Unifying Egocentric Understanding via Ego-Action-World Interactions
abstract: Egocentric video understanding spans diverse capabilities, modalities, and evaluation formats, yet these are often studied in isolation despite their tight coupling in real-world interaction. We propose the Ego-Action-World interaction loop as a unifying principle: the wearer perceives the world, forms goals, acts, changes the world, and uses feedback to guide subsequent behavior. Based on this view, we introduce EgoOmniWorld, a benchmark organized around four complementary interaction structures: Node captures ego, action, and world states; Edge captures directed relations among them; Chain captures linked dependencies; and Loop captures feedback-closed interactions. We develop an interaction-first, evidence-grounded data pipeline that extracts structured interactions from egocentric videos, grounds them in visual and auditory evidence, and generates questions according to their interaction structure. Required modalities and single- or multi-turn formats follow naturally from the supporting evidence and dependencies. EgoOmniWorld contains 24,166 QA groups, including 20,284 training and 3,882 test samples. Experiments on representative open- and closed-source multimodal large language models reveal substantial and uneven limitations across interaction structures. Models trained on EgoOmniWorld improve in-domain interaction understanding and generalize to existing egocentric benchmarks. EgoOmniWorld provides a unified foundation for evaluating and advancing egocentric video understanding. Data, code, and models will be released.

title: Macroscopic fluctuation theory of stochastic systems undergoing monitoring
abstract: We develop a macroscopic fluctuation theory for diffusive classical lattice gases subject to continuous coarse-grained monitoring. Treating measurements in the typical-outcome (quenched) regime, we show that observation adds a quadratic confining term to the MFT action that pins the density to its hydrodynamic profile. We derive sufficient conditions under which, in the presence of monitoring, the current large-deviation function remains convex, the additivity principle holds, and dynamical phase transitions are excluded. For particle-hole-symmetric one-dimensional models we find that monitoring suppresses dynamical phase transitions and can change their order from second to first, as we demonstrate in the Katz--Lebowitz--Spohn model. In the strong-measurement limit, we find that the current distribution becomes Gaussian and determine the scaling of its cumulants: they follow simple power laws when the mobility remains nonzero throughout the system, but exhibit anomalous logarithmic scaling when the mobility vanishes at the boundaries.

title: Social Norm Diffusion in Societies: Simple or Complex?
abstract: Social norms are a fundamental component of society, shaping how we communicate, cooperate, and avoid conflict. Despite their ubiquitous presence and profound influence on behaviour, questions remain about how they spread from person to person and whether they are adopted. Using an evolutionary game-theoretic model, we study whether simple or complex contagion processes characterise how social norms spread. Crucially, contagion type is endogenous and emerges from the model. We also vary cultural conformism, the cost of following a norm, and network topology to assess the generality of our results. We show that social norms in our model can spread through simple contagion when a new norm is low in cost and cultural conformism is low, while norms spread through complex contagion when the new norm is costly and cultural conformism is high.

title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 2D
abstract: Two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners with Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW) and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces for high-order finite element methods (FEM) and virtual element methods (VEM) are investigated and applied to the Poisson problem in 2D. The GDSW coarse space is a well-established robust choice for preconditioners in domain decomposition, while the RGDSW coarse space offers a competitive alternative by reducing the coarse problem dimension while maintaining robustness. On the theoretical side, a condition number bound for both preconditioners is proved for conforming $\mathbb{P}_k$ and $\mathbb{Q}_k$ finite element spaces with explicit dependence on the polynomial degree $k$. Through numerical experiments on structured triangular and quadrilateral meshes for FEM and on polygonal meshes for VEM, it is demonstrated that both GDSW and RGDSW maintain scalability properties across polynomial orders up to $k=9$ for selected degrees. The RGDSW approach achieves a reduction in the coarse problem dimension by a factor of approximately three compared to GDSW while maintaining competitive iteration counts.

title: Linking numbers and special differential characters in arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds
abstract: We construct non-holomorphic Siegel modular forms whose coefficients encode linking numbers in arithmetic hyperbolic manifolds of simplest type. Our proofs rely on an improved understanding of the transgression forms appearing in Kudla--Millson theory, and along the way we establish some structural properties including in particular their expected current equations.

title: How Low Can You Go: Fine-Tuning LLMs with Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO)
abstract: Recently, Morris et al. introduced TinyLoRA, a strategy for LLM fine-tuning which introduces arbitrarily few parameters, and demonstrated accuracy improvements using less than $10$ parameters rather than the ${\gtrsim 10,000}$ typically demanded by LoRA-based methods. However, that study continued to use gradient-based local search methods of the kind deployed for training multi-billion parameter LLMs in the first place. This article is predicated on the observation that, in the low dimensional setting, global optimization methods become tractable, unlocking Large language Model Bayesian Optimization (LlMBO). LlMBO is sample-efficient, gradient-free, memory-light, parallelizes across devices without synchronization, and, unlike policy-gradient methods, can optimize greedy-decoding accuracy directly. We describe numerical experiments comparing LlMBO against GRPO on fine-tuning tasks for a variety of models on a math benchmark suite which show that LlMBO can be a suitable alternative in this regime, matching or exceeding GRPO's fine tuning gains, while using a fraction of the compute and memory.

title: Black hole spin-mass correlation and accretion disks at birth stage of dense star clusters
abstract: We review the accretion-driven channel of stellar black-hole growth and spin-up in gaseous star clusters, developed within the framework of our MSCA project "protoBH". Our detailed calculations involving semi-analytic modelling, dynamical and hydrodynamic simulations suggest that the growth and spin-up of initially low-mass stellar black holes is an integral element of the formation process of dense massive star clusters, such as the proto-globular clusters observed at high redshift. The black holes accrete residual gas, remaining from the first star formation event, and form accretion disks generated by gas angular momentum induced by the black-holes' own curved orbits. Assuming initial black hole masses below the pair-instability mass gap $\leq 55\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, the gap gets populated with black-hole masses growing to $\sim 10^2\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, and even reaching several hundred solar masses for sufficiently dense and massive proto-clusters. We predict a consistent spin-mass relation with low black hole spins $\lesssim 0.2$ for low black hole masses $\lesssim 20\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, spanning all intermediate spins for higher masses and saturating to high spins $\gtrsim 0.8$ for high masses $\gtrsim 70\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$. We find evidence in favour of such an accretion-driven subpopulation of black holes in the GWTC-5.0 released by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration.

title: Directed percolation in higher-order social dilemmas
abstract: Multiplayer social dilemmas on hypergraphs show a variety of emergent phenomena, which has been attributed to group interactions. Here we test whether pairwise dynamics can reproduce them as well. We derive the mesoscopic Langevin equation of a testbed model and find the operator content of absorbing phase transitions: a directed-percolation line, a tricritical point, and a first-order region whose spinodal is the explosive transition. In our analysis, three-player games only set the values of the Landau coefficients. We construct a strictly pairwise model with short-lived memory, in which every event involves at most two entities, that reproduces these coefficients term by term and has exactly the same mean-field fixed points. Simulations confirm that the two dynamics share mean-field critical and tricritical scaling and the size of the critical mass, and that a purely three-player game on a two-dimensional triangular lattice lies in the directed-percolation class. For these games, the explosive transition and the critical mass therefore do not require group interactions, and the critical behavior is that of the pairwise theory.

title: The Last Mile of Coding Agents for Long-Document Tasks: An Empirical Study on Clinical Trial Protocol Digitization
abstract: Clinical trial protocols serve as the source of truth for study design, but are mostly written and used as unstructured PDF documents. Digitizing protocols turns static content into structured, machine-readable data that clinical software can analyze, validate, and execute. Coding agents, which select tools, execute code, and revise their approach as they work, are increasingly applied to such long-document tasks, yet it remains unclear how reliably they turn complete documents into accurate structured outputs. We study this question using protocol digitization as a testbed. We introduce TrialPD-Bench, an expert-annotated benchmark of 150 publicly available protocol PDFs spanning four task categories. Beyond final-answer performance, our evaluation measures evidence recall from agent traces, agent behavior, and cost. Across nine proprietary and open-weight models in five coding-agent harnesses, even the strongest agents do not fully solve protocol digitization. Our analysis further shows that agents usually locate the required evidence but fail in the last mile of transcribing and structuring it. We further develop TrialScribe, a domain-specific harness that equips coding agents with task skills and a verification loop. TrialScribe improves a locally served open-weight model by 6.2-59.4 points across eight metrics, enabling it to match or surpass proprietary models such as GPT-5.6-Sol.

title: Towards Safe Autonomy for Computer Use
abstract: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher utility than CaMeL-CUA while keeping the attack success rate at zero.

title: Star spots mimic the proposed abundance signatures of planet formation
abstract: Trends with stellar elemental abundances and condensation temperature have been proposed as a possible tracer of rocky planet formation. Here we present an alternative explanation, where we show that stellar activity (star spots) can also cause apparent abundance changes in refractory elements preferentially over volatile elements. This effect arises naturally from atomic physics: refractory (rocky; high-$T_c$) elements preferentially have low first-ionization potentials, with strong transitions that are most sensitive to the cooler, magnetically-perturbed spot conditions, making any spot-induced change in line strength correlated with $T_c$. We re-examine literature on Sun-like stars in the Solar neighborhood and find that the $\log{R'_{HK}}$ stellar activity indicator is correlated with the so-called $T_c$ slope: the gradient of chemical abundances with respect to condensation temperature. Using 1D LTE Korg.jl simulations of the Sun with spots of varying size and contrast, we show that a wide range of spot configurations can manifest as abundance patterns that mimic a signal of abundance trends with condensation temperature. Finally, we conduct a line-by-line differential analysis of an ambient Solar spectrum relative to a Solar sunspot umbra to represent an extreme case, where we find that elements with high condensation temperature can show a factor of three (0.5 dex) increase. We discuss implications that stellar activity poses for precision spectroscopy, and provide some direction on how this effect might be mitigated.

title: Contactless gait-derived features as candidate digital biomarkers of depression severity in adolescents
abstract: Timely assessment of depression severity in adolescents is essential for guiding clinical care, yet conventional evaluations rely on episodic clinical assessments and symptom rating scales. Contactless gait analysis offers a potentially scalable approach to capturing objective behavioral features associated with depression. Here, we introduce the Long-Distance 3D Adolescent Depression Gait Dataset (LD3D-ADG), comprising depth-sensor gait recordings from 119 adolescents at a single center, including 39 healthy controls, 41 with mild depression, and 39 with moderate-to-severe depression. We developed UMLPA-GCN, a graph convolutional network that models spatiotemporal gait dynamics across three anatomically defined skeletal partitions. In participant-independent five-fold cross-validation, UMLPA-GCN achieved 75.63% classification accuracy, a macro-F1 score of 75.52%, and a macro-area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.839 (95% confidence interval, 0.779--0.899). Class-specific recall was 87.18%, 63.41%, and 76.92% for healthy controls, mild depression, and moderate-to-severe depression, respectively. At the participant level, reduced arm swing, slower pelvic movement, restricted joint range of motion, and greater arm-swing asymmetry were identified as leading potential digital biomarkers contributing to depression severity assessment, associated with higher 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores. These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence for contactless digital depression severity stratification in adolescents. Further external and prospective validation is needed to establish their utility for longitudinal monitoring and timely clinical assessment.

title: The Smart Buildings Challenge: Learning Foundation Models for Real-World Optimization at Scale
abstract: Buildings cause nearly 40\% of carbon emissions in the US. Of total building emissions, HVAC systems are responsible for approximately 40-60\% and account for 15\% of global energy consumption. Despite advances in artificial intelligence, most buildings still operate as inefficiently as they did decades ago. Building optimization, perhaps more so than any other optimization problem, has enormous potential for Machine Learning (ML) driven impact on climate change, in both the short and long term. One of the biggest obstacles for building optimization is the lack of policy transfer. Most building control systems, whether simulation or learning based, don't generalize: they only work well for the building they were developed for, but not for other buildings. To solve this problem, we propose a challenge for the development of building foundation models that easily adapt to new buildings with minimal configuration and thereby enable building optimization to scale across the globe. Participants will build control policies on a set of simulated buildings, and have their policies evaluated on an unseen set of buildings. The buildings vary in size, layout, weather, material properties, and HVAC system. Successful outcomes from this initiative promise a massive leap forward in global sustainability efforts and demonstrate the great potential of ML to combat climate change.

title: Haagerup-Izumi modular data from hyperbolic words: S-fold TQFTs, central charge, torsion and the Bethe vacua
abstract: The modular data of the doubles of the Haagerup--Izumi categories is a grafting of two finite metric groups (conjectured by Evans--Gannon, proved for untwisted categories by Gannon--Schopieray--Yadav). Gang and Kim found non-unitary modular data of this shape in the topological twist of rank-$0$ $S$-fold theories, from the Bethe vacua of an abelianised gauge theory. The aim is to understand rigorously the significance of the handle-gluing and fibering operators, and to construct the Bethe vacua. For every hyperbolic once-punctured-torus monodromy $φ$, a word in $L$ and $R$, the two groups are $A_\mp=\coker(φ\mp1)$, with the torsion linking forms of the mapping tori of $φ$ and $-φ$. Over all words of trace $m^2+2$ these forms reproduce the Evans--Gannon table of Q-systems, one printed entry being corrected, and the distinct modular data in the list of Gannon--Schopieray--Yadav. The Bethe data are given in closed form by the word: the level matrix, the positive vacuum, $c_{\eff}=\#L$, and the handle-gluing values $2^{\#L}λ^{\pm1}|A_-||A_+|$ at the identity classes, $λ$ the stretch factor. Each kernel vector of $φ\mp1$ modulo $|A_\mp|$ at which an explicit trigonometric formula does not vanish gives a solution of the Bethe equations in closed form. Under the half-index dictionary, with the unit in the class of $σV^*$, $c\equiv\#L-6\#R\pmod{24}$.

title: Rapid Mixing of Stereographic MCMC for Heavy-Tailed Sampling
abstract: Sampling from high-dimensional, heavy-tailed distributions is a fundamental challenge in computational statistics, as many standard Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods mix poorly in such settings. Recently, Stereographic MCMC [Yang et al., 2024] and the Sub-Cauchy Projection Sampler [Grazzi et al., 2026] have been shown to perform successfully on such tasks. However, establishing their non-asymptotic convergence properties remains an important open problem. In this work, we fill this gap by establishing non-asymptotic upper bounds on the mixing time of the stereographic projection and sub-Cauchy projection samplers. Our results demonstrate that, under certain conditions on the target and initial distributions, the mixing time is polynomial in dimension for a broad class of distributions, including light- and heavy-tailed cases. Motivated by the theoretical analysis, we further establish a new weighted isoperimetric inequality that extends the classical version for log-concave distributions to the heavy-tailed setting with optimal dimension dependence. The proof techniques provide new insights into the geometric properties of heavy-tailed distributions that govern rapid mixing in high dimensions.

title: Approximating Optimal Policies in Heterogeneous Asynchronous Multi-player Bandits
abstract: Motivated by applications to cognitive radio networks, multi-player multi-armed bandits (MMAB) have attracted considerable attention in recent years. The asynchronous variant, in which players are active only at a fraction of timesteps, better reflects real-world decentralized networks, where devices are not permanently active. Despite its practical relevance, this setting remains relatively understudied. Existing work on asynchronous MMAB has focused on homogeneous players, who share the same activation probability, a setting in which the optimal centralized allocation can be easily characterized. In contrast, efficiently computing the optimal allocation in the heterogeneous setting, where players have different activation probabilities, has remained an open problem. In this work, we investigate this problem and first establish its NP-hardness. We then turn to the greedy algorithm, which runs in polynomial time, and prove that it achieves a $\frac{1}{e}$-approximation of the optimal allocation. Furthermore, when players are processed in decreasing order of their activation probabilities, the approximation guarantee improves to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}$. Overall, our results establish the greedy algorithm as an efficient approximation to the optimal allocation, providing a practical oracle baseline for the design of online algorithms for heterogeneous asynchronous multi-player bandits.

title: A Global View of How LLMs Value Human Time
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as personal assistants; however, little is known about how they capture national-level preferences on a global scale. Given that "time" is a universal and representative concept, we examine LLMs' time preferences by varying only users' country and measuring the compensation LLMs deem appropriate for a 60-minute appointment delay. We then compare LLMs' responses with GDP per capita on Purchasing Power Parity (GDP_PPP), Mean Income, and a literature-based index (Patience Score). Our results across 193 countries and 5 LLMs demonstrate that people's time across the world is evaluated in noticeably different ways among LLMs, as well as varying levels of robustness under prompt variations. LLMs consistently recommend the highest compensation for Europe, but mostly the lowest for Africa. Based on GDP_PPP, LLMs underestimate the value of time for users living in Asia and South America. These findings indicate that geographical patterns are embedded in LLMs and may translate in different treatment in agentic settings.

title: Two For The Price Of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
abstract: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce $\texttt{CACTUS}$, a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights. Compared to LLM-Surgeon which targets the same objective, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ can achieve over an order-of-magnitude speedup.
