A set $S$ is bisimplicial if it is the union of at most two cliques. Recognizing graphs in which every minimal separator is the union of at most $k$ cliques is polynomial-time solvable for $k=1$ and NP-hard for every fixed $k\geq 3$. We settle the remaining case $k=2$ by giving a polynomial-time algorithm to decide whether every minimal separator in a graph is bisimplicial. A set $S$ is triad-free if its independence number $α(S)$ is at most two. Given a graph $G$ and two vertices $u,v$, the problem of finding a $u\hbox{-}v$ separator $S$ with $α(S)\leq k$ had the same complexity gap: it was known to be polynomial-time solvable for $k=1$ and NP-hard for every fixed $k\geq 3$. We resolve the remaining case $k=2$ by giving a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a triad-free $u\hbox{-}v$ separator or determines that none exists.

title: A deep energy method formulation for phase-field modelling of ductile fracture
abstract: This work extends the Deep Energy Method to phase-field modelling of ductile fracture in elasto-plastic solids. Its key contribution is an incremental DEM-based formulation that couples history-dependent J2 plasticity and plasticity-dependent fracture toughness with separate energy-optimised displacement and phase-field representations. The formulation combines the second-order Ambrosio-Tortorelli phase-field fracture model with small-strain J2 plasticity and linear isotropic hardening. A volumetric-deviatoric split defines the elastic crack-driving energy, while accumulated equivalent plastic strain governs the degradation of local fracture toughness. Plastic internal variables are updated locally through radial return. The reduced energy is minimised alternately with respect to the displacement and phase fields, represented by a ReZero residual neural network and spatially localised Gaussian radial basis functions with trainable centres, respectively. This split addresses the diffuse phase-field profiles observed in preliminary calculations with a shared global network. Alternating optimisation is combined with transfer learning to reuse trainable parameters and optimiser states across loading increments, while the converged constitutive history is carried forward separately at quadrature points. The numerical results demonstrate close agreement with finite-element reference solutions in predicting force-displacement responses, energy evolution, plastic deformation and crack propagation. The framework captures the main features of ductile fracture, although accuracy becomes more sensitive to loading increments near abrupt fracture events.

title: Similar Models, Broken Odds: Where Luce's Axiom Fails in Chatbot Arena
abstract: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.

title: Understanding the Complex Morphology of a Coronal Mass Ejection. III: How to Create a Severe Geomagnetic Storm
abstract: On April 21, 2023, a complex filament eruption produced an Earth-directed coronal mass ejection (CME) that triggered the first severe geomagnetic storm of solar cycle 25. The primary objective of this work is to understand the physical origin of the severe impact of this CME on Earth. We explore the CME's complex morphology by simulating the eruption using the thermodynamic magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model CORHEL-CME. We model the pre-eruptive structure as two intertwined magnetic flux ropes and validate the early evolution of the event by comparing synthetic observables generated from the model with extreme-ultraviolet and white-light observations. We then compare the simulated CME structure with in situ measurements. From our analysis, we conclude that the CME merged with a stream interaction region (SIR) before reaching Earth. This interaction compressed the CME sheath, producing a sustained negative $B_n$ component that, together with the associated enhancement in solar wind density and velocity, triggered the geomagnetic storm. The internal configuration of the magnetic flux rope, which also maintained a sustained southward component during its propagation toward Earth, intensified the storm to severe levels. This model-data comparison underscores the power of using MHD simulations, when validated by multi-viewpoint observations, to reveal hidden dynamical processes and improve the understanding and prediction of space weather impacts.

title: Benchmarking 3D Reconstruction for Under-Ice Robotic Perception in Arctic Environments
abstract: As the Arctic transitions toward a seasonally ice-free state, capturing the complex morphology of submerged sea ice is crucial for advancing models of ocean-ice-atmosphere heat exchange and monitoring under-ice habitats. Currently, sub-surface ice mapping is predominantly achieved through acoustic sensors such as multibeam sonar. While sonar provides robust large-scale geometry, it lacks spectral and high-resolution textural information required to record fine morphological features - a critical limitation in under-ice environments, where sparse visual features and degraded sensing conditions challenge the capture of detailed structural and optical surface properties. We present a benchmark for vision-based under-ice 3D reconstruction using real-world data from the MOSAiC expedition and synthetic data generated in an Unreal Engine-based underwater robotics simulator. The benchmark evaluates Structure-From-Motion (SfM) and monocular depth estimation, with quantitative comparison enabled through cross-modal registration to upward-looking multibeam sonar.

title: Global Parameter Identification and Uncertainty Quantification of reduced-order ADM1 using Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Bayesian Inference
abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) models can be challenging to calibrate against real data due to limited practical identifiability, data scarcity, and model complexity. Weighted least squares objective functions and gradient-based solvers using finite differences are often used in literature, but result in suboptimal parameter estimates and large uncertainty bands. This paper identifies the parameters of a reduced-order ADM1 by comparing the frameworks of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) and Bayesian inference (BI), and quantifies uncertainties of parameters and outputs. Multirate experimental data are taken from a lab-scale AD reactor fed with agricultural substrates and operated at organic loading rates of 3$\,$g VS $\mathrm{m^{-3}d^{-1}}$. Global optima are found via global and gradient-based local search algorithms using forward sensitivities. Enhanced scatter search provides the best global search results. These are refined by the Gauss-Newton algorithm as the best local search, which delivers $R^2$ values of 0.95 for acetic acid and 0.77 for biogas production. BI yields substantially narrower uncertainty bands than MLE and avoids the need for a global search by incorporating prior knowledge about parameter distributions. The search space is captured efficiently by log10 scaling of parameters. Algorithmic details on its implications are provided. Despite a high-resolution lab-scale dataset, the ADM1-specific inhibition parameter $K_\mathrm{I,nh3}$ is practically not identifiable with MLE, and shows a low output sensitivity, whereas a parameter for the effective ion concentration shows superb practical identifiabilty at high confidence with both MLE and BI. The present work lays a scalable base for calibration of nonlinear AD models by providing reliable simulations. It thus advances model-based monitoring and control applications of multirate processes such as agricultural AD plants.

title: Maximin share allocations for two types of items
abstract: We study the fair allocation of indivisible items among $n$ agents with additive valuations (or costs) using the fairness notion of maximin share (MMS). Since MMS allocations do not always exist when $n > 2$, one direction in the literature has been to identify special classes of instances in which exact MMS allocations can be guaranteed. We show that, when items can be divided into two types of chores, MMS allocations always exist and can be computed in polynomial time using a novel geometric approach inspired by prior work in job scheduling. We further discuss how our technique extends to instances with two types of goods, as well as mixed instances consisting of one type of objective good and one type of objective chore.

title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Constructing robust GUI agents relies on multimodal visual grounding: the ability to precisely map natural language intents to actionable on-screen components. Despite abundant desktop, web, and mobile benchmarks, high-fidelity resources tailored for diverse environments are surprisingly scarce. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Screen Referring Grounding Dataset (ScreenRef), a comprehensive GUI grounding dataset consisting of GUI screenshots paired with natural language referring expressions and box or point annotations. Spanning desktop, web, and mobile domains, ScreenRef comprises 586K screenshots and over 633K referring expression instances, covering tasks such as text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal scenarios. To boost the model's grounding performance, we propose the Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning (D2RL) method to address the limited generalization of supervised fine-tuning and the sparse reward problem in reinforcement learning. Utilizing ScreenRef, we train Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct via sequential SFT and D2RL training, yielding GroundGUI-8B. GroundGUI-8B achieves 95.2% on ScreenSpot-V2, 63.9% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 65.4% on OSWorld-G, 86.8% on MMBench-GUI L2, and 38.3% on UI-Vision. Among 8B-scale models, it produces substantial gains over models trained on open-source datasets, with performance comparable or even superior to models trained on closed-source data. Code, models, and datasets are available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/GroundGUI.

title: Quasiparticle Modeling of Strongly Magnetized Strange Quark Systems
abstract: We examine spin-polarized Strange Quark Matter and the complex structure of Strange Quark Stars in the existence of a strong magnetic field. Our framework uses a quasiparticle model, en hanced by a QCD-informed effective quark mass dependent on both chemical potential value and magnetic field strength. The resulting Equation of State yields an energy per baryon below the iron limit, supporting the hypothesis that the actual ground state of matter is strange matter. The Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff expressions are solved and find that the maximum stellar mass decreases with the degree of spin polarization, reaching as high as 2.35 Mo with a related radius 12.33 km. Furthermore, the model predictions for mass, radius, and surface redshift are in excel lent conformance to observational limitations for the massive pulsar PSR J0952-0607. These results highlight the crucial role of quasiparticle medium effects and strong magnetic fields in describing dense matter.

title: The Gap Is in the Geometry: A Convergent Meta-Analysis of Multi-Facet Aerial and Remote Sensing Video Understanding
abstract: Aerial and remote sensing video is increasingly evaluated like web video, by posing multiple-choice questions to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) over sampled frames and reporting accuracy. This paper argues that this recipe measures the wrong aspect, and supports the claim with a convergent meta-analysis of a broad set of published results, organized in four evidence tiers, in which a claim becomes a position only when collected evidence agrees. Parameter scale exhibits a median of +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase on aerial benchmarks, far below a human gap of at least 19 points, whereas acquisition conditions control perception, as 315 of 318 evaluations in 19 within-paper contrasts lose accuracy when conditions such as altitude, view, object size or time horizon become harder. No aerial benchmark in the corpus combines video input with per-task human and random baselines, competence collapses from answering to acting in closed-loop navigation, and the same MLLMs score higher on the aerial benchmark than on ground spatial ones, but lower on studies that test cross-view geometry. From these findings the current study derives five falsifiable principles and proposes the AVU-Card, a reporting card for aerial video benchmarks

title: Contextual Credit Policy Optimization
abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning enables large language model agents to learn from sparse outcome rewards in long-horizon tasks. Recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing observation-matched experiences across trajectories. However, identical observations can occur in different contexts, and matched peers are not equally informative for a given decision. Moreover, favorable terminal outcomes can obscure redundant actions or detours within successful trajectories. To address these two challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO). For the first, CCPO weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity, computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, allowing peers from similar contexts to contribute more to a step's baseline. For the second, CCPO pairs historical credit, which compares the realized return against the weighted peer baseline, with future credit, which measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation. A step is thus credited for the progress it makes, not only for its trajectory's eventual outcome. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, enabling CCPO to address these challenges without an auxiliary value critic. Across two Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones (1.5B and 7B), CCPO achieves up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop and outperforms GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points. Ablations show that contextual weighting outperforms uniform weighting, and that historical and future credit serve as complementary learning signals.

title: Neural Supervised Clustering for Learning Individualized Treatment Rules with Many Treatments
abstract: Learning an individualized treatment rule (ITR) with many treatments requires estimating treatment-specific effects from limited observations per arm. Treatments with similar conditional responses can share information, but linear contrast models may miss nonlinear heterogeneity. We propose nonlinear supervised clustering fusion (NSCF), a neural Q-learning framework with a shared nonlinear covariate representation and low-dimensional treatment embeddings. Pairwise fusion groups treatments with similar learned contrasts, yielding an ITR and an interpretable partition. An alternating algorithm combines neural training, embedding fusion, validation-based partition selection, and unpenalized grouped refitting. NSCF lowers regret relative to a strong neural reference in nonlinear exact-sharing simulations; perturbations characterize the limits of hard sharing. In a melanoma xenograft application, NSCF improves average policy value over the neural reference. These results support nonlinear representation learning with supervised treatment fusion when treatment effects exhibit shared structure.

title: A Distinct Type of Standstill in Ultra-Compact White Dwarf Binaries
abstract: AM CVn stars are ultra-compact, semi-detached binaries consisting of a white dwarf primary and a hydrogen-poor secondary. In this work, we analyse the AM CVn-type systems MGAB-V270, ZTF18aaxuusk and ASASSN-19ct, which have similar properties and show unusual post-superoutburst behaviour. We focus on the occurrence of standstill-like phases. In MGAB-V270, superoutbursts are followed by a series of echo outbursts that evolves into a standstill-like phase before the system returns to quiescence. ZTF18aaxuus shows similar post-superoutburst activity, with one echo-outburst series also developing into a standstill-like phase. ASASSN-19ct exhibits comparable echo outbursts but no standstill-like phases. Periodicity analysis using TESS data shows that superhumps can persist during both echo outbursts and standstill-like phases. Although standstills have previously been observed in AM CVn stars, the standstill-like phases we observe appear to represent a distinct phenomenon associated with post-superoutburst activity. We compare our results to other AM CVns that may exhibit similar behaviour.

title: Gravity from generalized entropy
abstract: Gravity from entropy (GfE) identifies its Lagrangian with the geometric quantum relative entropy (GQRE) between the spacetime metric and a metric induced by matter and curvature, treating the metric itself as a quantum operator. We extend this construction to the Tsallis, Rényi, and Sharma-Mittal families, which we call gravity from generalized entropy (GfGE), and determine their common Einstein limit, weak-field spectra, auxiliary-field formulation, and horizon entropy. The entropy choice controls the leading higher-curvature terms and additional modes. We confirm that the linearized GfE spectrum contains a healthy scalar and a Planck-scale tachyonic spin-2 ghost. We identify the conditions that remove this ghost: curvature must enter through its scalar trace, or the entropy generator must be flat to quadratic order at the identity. The latter gives exact general relativity for Tsallis at $q=0$ and ghost-free $f(R,L_m)$ theories for Rényi and Sharma-Mittal. On shell, the auxiliary G-field is proportional to the tensor in Wald's entropy formula. For analytic entropy functions, horizons with a single curvature scale have an area term followed by constant and inverse-area corrections. We also extend the volume-constraint cosmological constant to the full family; its leading entropy dependence is set by the scalar mass. A finite set of entropy-function derivatives controls the leading weak-curvature departures from general relativity.

title: Can $^{225}$Ac be imaged on a long axial field-of-view PET/CT with standard clinical settings?
abstract: Purpose: The $^{225}$Ac decay chain includes $^{209}$Tl, whose prominent 1567 keV gamma line can create electron-positron pairs. We investigated whether a long axial field-of-view (LAFOV) PET/CT can image $^{225}$Ac using standard clinical acquisition and reconstruction methods. Methods: A syringe placed next to a vial (5.89 and 10.29 MBq of $^{225}$Ac activity) and a NEMA IEC body phantom (sphere activity concentration 4.56 kBq mL$^{-1}$) were scanned for 45 and 60 min, respectively, on a Biograph Vision Quadra (Siemens Healthineers). To support our findings, FLUKA simulations scored the annihilation locations around a $^{225}$Ac point source. Results: The contours of the syringe and vial were visible despite high noise, but the NEMA spheres could not be distinguished from the background. As illustrated by the FLUKA simulations, the number of annihilation events decreases exponentially according to the mean free path of the 1567 keV photon in the surrounding medium. Conclusion: A LAFOV PET/CT can detect positrons created by pair production of the main $^{209}$Tl gamma line. However, these positrons are created where the photons interact with the surrounding medium rather than at the location of the $^{209}$Tl decays, which rules out standard PET imaging of $^{225}$Ac.

title: Towards a Data-Centric Understanding of Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been widely applied in embodied agents and robotics for vision tasks. However, MLLMs suffer from limitations in spatial reasoning and perception. Post-training techniques have shown promise for improving these capabilities; yet, there are limited data-driven surveys of such approaches. In this survey, we consider approaches to fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs for spatial reasoning tasks, ranging from supervised to reinforcement learning, with an emphasis on the datasets used. We investigate themes of dataset construction, data modality and annotation, and evaluation of the resulting models. Based on these themes, we categorize research into three groups: dataset design, dataset construction and evaluation. We find four main methods for constructing fixed spatial annotations: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop. We also observe substantial variation in evaluation approaches, including different scoring methods, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types. Finally, we identify opportunities for future research in unified dynamic annotation, efficient spatial reasoning, standardization of evaluation, expanded spatial range, and human-centered spatial interactions.

title: Post-Optimization Subspace Corrections to Quantum Ansätze
abstract: Circuit depth and measurement count are the main limitations for chemical applications of the leading variational quantum algorithms on quantum computers. We show that both resource requirements can be reduced by augmenting adaptive variational quantum algorithms with post-optimization corrective techniques. We focus on two such techniques---Hamiltonian-moment Krylov subspace diagonalization and the identity-augmented quantum self-consistent equation of motion (q-sc-EOM)---applied to optimized ADAPT-VQE states without further ansatz growth or nonlinear optimization. Across molecular systems studied with up to 20 qubits, first-order Krylov correction reduces the optimized iterations (and the corresponding number of adaptive layers) needed to reach the $1.6~\mathrm{m}E_h$ threshold by up to approximately sixfold, with a general trend toward larger reductions at higher determinant Rényi entropy. We also find measurement-cost reductions of up to approximately fortyfold using a suitable resource-cost model. Identity-augmented q-sc-EOM improves molecular potential-energy curves obtained from truncated ADAPT-VQE ansätze with limited expressivity and recovers accuracy from states produced by sampled operator ranking without additional gradient-based operator selection, providing an advantage when small pool gradients make selection measurement intensive. Together, these post-optimization corrections offer routes to improve energy accuracy and reduce adaptive circuit growth in quantum algorithms as quantum hardware advances.

title: A new way integral for the $n$-fold cover of $SL_2$
abstract: Let $π$ be a genuine irreducible cuspidal automorphic representation of the $n$-fold cover $SL_2^{(n)}(\mathbb{A})$ of $SL_2(\mathbb{A})$, $n \geq 3$ odd, and let $τ$ be the genuine representation of $GL_1^{(n)}(\mathbb{A})$ obtained from a unitary Hecke character of $\mathbb{A}^\times$. We prove that, for a certain choice of data, a new way integral for $SL_2^{(n)}(\mathbb{A})$ represents the partial $L$-function $L^S(ns+\tfrac12,π\timesτ)$. The integral is derived from the generalized doubling integral of Cai, Friedberg, Ginzburg and Kaplan, following the idea of Ginzburg and Soudry.

title: Pythia-Contrib: a modular contribution framework for the Pythia 8 event generator
abstract: Pythia is a general-purpose Monte Carlo event generator used in particle, astroparticle, and nuclear physics, by theorists and experimentalists, to simulate particle collisions. Because of the size and diversity of the user community, it is challenging to address all of the needs for new and varied physics models. This paper describes the Pythia-Contrib system, which allows for third-party developers to contribute code to Pythia without introducing external software dependencies to the Pythia code base.

title: Engineering Correlated Transparent Conductors via Metal-Insulator Transition Proximity
abstract: Transparent conductors are key functional materials in modern optoelectronic devices. Their performance is governed by an inherent trade-off between optical transparency and electrical conductivity. Correlated metallic oxides offer an attractive workaround to this compromise, where narrow partially-filled bands provide high conductivity, while the absence of visible-range transitions enables optical transparency. Despite this promise, transparency and conductivity remain coupled through carrier density and electronic coherence. Here, we use proximity to a metal-insulator transition (MIT) as a design principle for engineering this balance in correlated-oxide transparent conductors. Epitaxial Ti-substituted $SrVO_3$ films serve as a model platform where the optical window and metallicity are tuned simultaneously. We demonstrate and explain a systematic broadening of the optical window to regimes relevant for silicon photovoltaics. This gain is counterbalanced by carrier depletion and disorder, which drive the loss of coherent transport near the composition-driven MIT. A Haacke figure-of-merit analysis identifies the optimal composition range near the MIT, where the loss of metallic transport is accompanied by persistent near-Fermi-level spectral weight, indicating disorder-assisted localization together with correlation-driven spectral-weight redistribution. These findings establish proximity to an MIT as a general materials-design strategy, using electronic filling as a tuning knob for the transparency-conductivity balance in correlated-oxide transparent conductors.

title: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows language models to adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information controls their predictions. We study the acquisition and trainability of ICL with a controlled diagnostic that separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt. Across 17 models, about a third prefer the copied answer, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show that models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy improves beyond chance level. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the controlled diagnostic, whereas fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings. The results suggest that ICL is not acquired as a single, uniform capability. Instead, prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer can develop along distinct trajectories.

title: Genesis Steering: Better Activation Steering Through Training Data
abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering, which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on Tülu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from Tülu-3-8B's training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On Tülu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.

title: Sequential RF Fingerprinting for AIS: Rejecting Unknown Vessels and Insider MMSI Spoofs Days After Enrollment
abstract: Any AIS transmitter can claim any vessel's identity (MMSI), because nothing in the protocol authenticates it; only the transmitter's analog hardware reveals who is really sending. We treat AIS traffic as streams of bursts keyed by claimed MMSI and accumulate physical-layer evidence with a sequential test. Each burst is scored by its k-nearest-neighbor distance to enrolled fingerprints in the feature space of a classifier whose weights are fixed after training, calibrated into a tail probability, and accumulated by a geometric-entropy-minimization cumulative-sum (GEM-CUSUM) statistic. The same test rejects unknown transmitters when scored against all enrolled vessels, and exposes insider spoofs when scored against the claimed vessel. A threshold refreshed from genuine traffic alone keeps it at a stated false-alarm rate as fingerprints drift. On AIS in-phase/quadrature (I/Q) recordings captured over 13 days at the Istanbul Strait (Bosphorus), the detector rejects unseen vessels at least 10 days after enrollment. Evaluated over 50-burst trials with every vessel weighted equally, it reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUROC) of 0.956 (95% confidence interval 0.913-0.989), where the best score computed from one burst at a time reaches 0.899. A threshold refreshed from the first quarter of the enrolled vessels' traffic holds 5.3% false alarms (3.0-9.2% across five independently trained encoders) at 88.8% detection. Scored against the claimed MMSI, enrolled transmitters spoofing another vessel are rejected at 0.991, a threat that open-set tests cannot see (AUROC 0.500, chance level). The lightweight Transformer GLFormer, reimplemented from its paper (no code is public) and retrained on the same data, reaches 0.652 in the same detector with its published in-phase input and 0.849 when given the same I/Q input as our encoder.

title: Wetting theorems in capillarity theory
abstract: We prove the uniform convergence of Plateau borders to Plateau singularities in the vanishing-volume limit of a soap film model based on capillarity theory. The results are formulated in the context a new type of local area minimizer that takes into account how a soap film locally separates its surrounding space.

title: An algebro-geometric approach to profinite iterated monodromy groups
abstract: We carefully construct the profinite iterated monodromy group of a rational map as a quotient of the étale fundamental group of the punctured projective line. In doing so, we prove a number of folklore results regarding profinite IMGs; in particular, their topological generation by inertia concentrated in the post-critical orbit, and their relationship with the discrete iterated monodromy group over $\mathbb{C}$.

title: DecisionRobust: Benchmarking Robustness for JEV Style Decision Models Across Text and Vision
abstract: Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision-making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision-making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/.

title: A combinatorial proof of the Chan--Robbins--Yuen volume formula
abstract: The Chan--Robbins--Yuen polytope $\mathrm{CRY}_{m+1}$ has normalized volume $\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}C_j$, a product of Catalan numbers. Zeilberger proved the formula using the Morris constant-term identity; finding a combinatorial proof remained an open problem. We give such a proof by counting nonnegative integer flows. We add an extra edge from each vertex to a common sink and count flows according to how many of these edges carry positive flow. A double count proves a special case of a recurrence of Morales and Shi and gives these counts in terms of Narayana numbers. Deleting the first vertex then yields the Catalan product. We also give an explicit bijection for the recurrence and prove the corresponding reduction formula posed by Postnikov.

title: DoReMe: Dual optimization of Reconstruction and Motion estimation for self-navigated free-breathing abdominal MRI using Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Purpose: Free-breathing abdominal MRI is limited by respiratory motion, which introduces image artifacts and k-space inconsistencies. Existing reconstruction approaches often depend on pre-estimated motion fields or external respiratory surrogate signals. We propose a coupled reconstruction-motion estimation algorithm for self-navigated free-breathing acquisition, in which motion is represented by compact Gaussian primitives and jointly refined with the image estimates during iterative reconstruction. Methods: An iterative reconstruction that alternates between data consistency updates and motion modelling was proposed. Respiratory motion was represented using Gaussian primitives. A Gaussian splatting was integrated into the reconstruction algorithm. The method was evaluated on self-navigated free-breathing Cartesian gradient-echo (GRE) acquisition in four healthy volunteers, including retrospective scan shortening experiments, and was compared with regularized compressed sensing (CS) reconstruction. Results: Respiratory motion states were reconstructed in approximately 1.5 min. Compared with CS, the proposed method improved visual image quality, particularly in coronal liver views, and better preserved anatomical structures in retrospectively shortened acquisitions. These findings provide proof of concept for the proposed method. Conclusion: The proposed coupled reconstruction-motion estimation algorithm improved visual image quality compared with CS alone. Gaussian primitives provided a compact and sufficiently flexible representation of nonrigid respiratory motion with practical runtime, supporting further scanner integration and validation in larger cohorts.

title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming
abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.

title: Learning in Orbit: Onboard Training and Closed-Loop Attitude Control with a Thermal Segmentation Model on a Spacecraft
abstract: Deep space missions increasingly require spacecraft capable of autonomously operating in environments with communication delays and bandwidth limitations. A key enabler of such autonomy is the ability to run learning-based algorithms directly onboard. In this work, we present a flight deployment on a 6U CubeSat that demonstrates (1) onboard training and inference of a thermal segmentation model on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX GPU in space and (2) closed-loop attitude control using the segmentation model on a real-time, thermal image feed to track the Moon. In addition to this demonstration, we implement ROS 2 Foxy as a data transport middleware and integrate an open-source file system that provides strong data integrity guarantees and self-healing features. Over the course of approximately one year, we performed 12 experiments on the spacecraft, advancing the state of the art in autonomous spacecraft systems by showing how modern learning-based pipelines, commercially available hardware, and open-source software can operate reliably under the compute and environmental constraints of Low Earth Orbit (LEO).

title: PairIT: Autoregressive Transformers for Low-Data Molecule Optimization
abstract: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.

title: Effective Fermion-Photon Vertex in a Rotating Relativistic Medium: Tree-Level Structure
abstract: We study the tree-level fermion-photon effective vertex for on-shell particles in a relativistic environment undergoing rigid rotation at zero temperature. The rotational background breaks translational invariance in the transverse plane and introduces a preferred direction, leading to a distinct decomposition of the vertex into longitudinal and transverse structures with respect to the rotation axis. Using fermion and photon modes constructed in the rotating frame, we derive the corresponding selection rules and show that the energy and the longitudinal component of the momentum are conserved, whereas no independent transverse momentum-conservation condition arises. Instead, the transverse dependence is governed by radial integrals involving three Bessel functions, whose support constrains the magnitudes of the transverse momentum projections. The vertex can be organized in a circular basis for the transverse components and a Cartesian basis along the rotation axis, and expressed in terms of six Dirac structures. Their coefficients define 24 form-factor components associated with the photon-mode components, physical photon states, and spin-dependent structures induced by the rotating background. We also verify current conservation and gauge invariance of the resulting tree-level matrix element under the boundary conditions considered. These results provide the tree-level structure of the fermion-photon interaction in rotating relativistic matter and establish the basis for the study of radiative corrections in vortical backgrounds.

title: Measurements and Analysis of Distortion in Inertial Force Exciters for Flat-Panel Loudspeakers
abstract: Flat-panel loudspeakers are typically driven by dynamic exciters that employ a voice coil coupled to a reaction mass to exert force on the panel. Unlike conventional loudspeakers, where the cone is relatively light weight, heavy panels may require significant exertion from the driver to achieve sound pressure levels required of consumer grade loudspeakers. Overexertion can cause harmonic distortion and reduced sound quality, especially in drivers where the voice coil is not centered in the magnetic field. There are many different exciters available commercially with different power ratings and price points. The frequency response, linearity, total-harmonic distortion (THD), intermodulation distortion (IMD), and force vs. displacement were measured for three types of exciters to determine the consistency of manufacturing and use in panel loudspeakers. These exciters were found to have high variability in all metrics among units of the same type. Distortion metrics such as IMD may be reduced by running impedance sweeps to match exciters with similar response characteristics in multi-actuator panels.

title: Are Broad Mg II Galaxies Fading AGN?
abstract: We analyzed a sample of 494 galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) I-IV that have unusual properties. They display broadened Mg II $λ$2798 line emission, as would be expected of Type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGN). However, they have weak or absent broad Balmer lines though broadened Balmer lines often accompany broadened ultraviolet lines in Type 1 AGN spectra. We performed a spectral decomposition of these "broad Mg II galaxies'' to assess whether they can be considered fading AGN. The Balmer lines are more responsive to changes in the AGN continuum than the Mg II line. As the AGN power source fades, broad H$β$ and then H$α$ will weaken and eventually disappear, leaving broad Mg II as a signpost of a more active past. In support of this interpretation, we found that broad Mg II galaxies have weaker AGN luminosities and lower accretion rates (parameterized by the Eddington ratio) than typical Type 1 quasars from SDSS. The Eddington ratio of broad Mg II galaxies are similar to dim-state changing-look AGN, with an average value $\lesssim$1\%, which is the threshold at which the inner region of a geometrically thin accretion disk is thought to evaporate and be replaced by a geometrically thick radiatively inefficient accretion flow in stellar-mass black holes. Broad Mg II galaxies may represent the penultimate stage in a changing-look AGN sequence prior to the complete disappearance of all broad lines.

title: AdaFrame: Hierarchical Multimodal Deduplication with Adaptive Information Budgeting for Cost-Efficient Video Advertisement Analysis
abstract: Uniform frame sampling for vision-language model (VLM)-based video analysis often floods multimodal backbones with redundant content, while existing keyframe selection methods are typically optimized for human viewing rather than downstream extraction accuracy. We propose AdaFrame, a content-adaptive preprocessing cascade that reduces visual redundancy without sacrificing extraction fidelity. Three progressively finer filters, perceptual hashing, learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS), and CLIP-based semantic clustering, efficiently eliminate redundant frames before costly cross-modal inference. Per-video frame budgets are determined using Intrinsic Semantic Dimensionality (ISD), which estimates each video's semantic complexity through singular value decomposition of its frame embeddings. Experiments on 500 video advertisements from the Pitt Ads Dataset show that AdaFrame reduces the frame count by 48 percent and VLM inference cost by 75 percent compared with uniform sampling, while achieving 86.0 percent topic accuracy, an improvement of 1.6 percentage points, and 79.4 percent sentiment accuracy, an improvement of 7.5 percentage points.

title: CLASHarness: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Conflict in Computer Use via a Controllable and Verifiable Generation Pipeline
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems to automate complex computer-use workflows, yet existing benchmarks mostly assume consistent, cooperative environments. In contrast, real-world collaboration rarely runs on consistent information: peer or sub-agents frequently report outdated states, issue contradictory instructions, or compete over shared permissions and files, forcing agents to check others' outputs and verify ground truth in the environment. Evaluating such conflict resolution remains challenging: manual authoring cannot scale across complex systems, while unconstrained LLM generation produces narrative drift, answer leakage, and unsatisfiable rubrics. We introduce CLASHarness (Conflict-Loaded Agent Scenario Harness), a controllable framework for generating verifiable multi-agent conflicts in computer use, with a benchmark of 600 multi-round tasks. By combining hierarchical scenario planning with an eight-step verified micro-pipeline, CLASHarness pre-commits decisive visual facts before rendering and compiles hybrid code and semantic graders directly from executed reference trajectories, guaranteeing every task is solvable by construction. Evaluating 15 frontier models on CLASHarness reveals three core bottlenecks. First, when sub-agent outputs conflict with the environment, weaker models blindly follow misleading information, whereas stronger models inspect visual evidence to verify ground truth. Second, resolving conflicts is much harder than finding them: while agents can spot inconsistencies, actively fixing system state drops task success significantly. Third, coordination protocols remain a universal bottleneck: even frontier models fail over 58% of closing actions, often forgetting to release shared locks or hand off tasks. CLASHarness provides a scalable, verifiable foundation for building reliable multi-agent systems.

title: Imagining Goals with Geometric Horizon Models for Policy Generalization
abstract: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.

title: Kinetic Equations and Turbulence in Large $N$ Vector and SYK-like Models
abstract: We apply large $N$ expansion techniques to derive kinetic equations for strongly coupled, far-from-equilibrium field theories with $O(N)$ symmetry. For large $N$ vector models, the quasi-classical approximation holds. Incorporating arbitrary momentum-dependent interactions, we show the dynamics obey the standard kinetic equation, with the scattering amplitude given by the retarded propagator of the auxiliary Hubbard-Stratonovich field. This has broad applications to systems like spin wave and Langmuir ion-acoustic turbulence. For large $N$ random coupling (SYK-like) models in $d$ dimensions, leading-order melon diagrams induce order-one propagator renormalization and finite spectral width. The corresponding kinetic equation, unlike those for standard weakly interacting systems, does not have a local-in-time collision integral. We find evidence for a stationary, scale-invariant infrared solution, revealing a potentially novel strong turbulence scaling exponent.

title: Plant Memory: Technical Language Processing and a Verified Maintenance Ontology for Agent-Accessible Failure Knowledge from SAP PM Work Orders
abstract: Maintenance work orders are the largest written record of how industrial equipment fails, yet in most plants they are close to unusable for analysis. Short texts are abbreviated and misspelt, asset identity is buried in free text, work-type labels contradict the work described, and the fields that matter most for reliability (symptom, root cause, action taken) are usually empty. As a result, diagnostic knowledge stays with senior technicians and leaves when they do. We present Plant Memory, a system that applies technical language processing (TLP) to SAP Plant Maintenance (PM) exports and builds an ISO 14224-aligned maintenance ontology in which every extracted statement is a reified fact carrying a confidence score, the evidence it was read from, and a verification state. Extraction is rule-first, with an optional large language model (LLM) acting as a second reader whose disagreements raise a fact's review priority rather than overwrite it. Technicians verify facts through a review queue, answer targeted knowledge-gap questions where failures repeat without a recorded cause, and approve or reject ontology drift proposals when new terms appear. The resulting graph is served to people through a web application and to AI agents through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so both query the same verified knowledge and every answer cites the work orders behind it. On a synthetic 12-month export of 400 work orders from a parboiled-rice plant, rule-based extraction reaches 96.2% component accuracy, 88.9% failure-mode accuracy and 100% root-cause precision at 62% coverage; on 28 diagnostic questions, ranked root causes from the ontology are correct at top-1 in 82.1% of cases against 53.6% for the raw SAP root-cause column.

title: The zeros of point evaluation extremals in Paley-Wiener spaces
abstract: For $1\le p < \infty$, $φ_p$ is the function of minimal $L^p$ norm among all functions $f$ of exponential type at most $π$ for which $f(0)=1$. We start from the ansatz that the positive zeros $τ_n$ of $φ_p$ are close to \(n+1/p-1/2\) and use a weighted convex correction to first place them in an \(\ell^2\)-neighborhood of this sequence. A bootstrap argument then improves this to a {Poincaré asymptotic} expansion of $τ_n-(n+\frac1p-\frac12)$ in terms of odd powers of $(n+\frac1p-\frac12)^{-1}$. We also get precise information about the Fourier transform $\widehatφ_p$, a result that in particular implies that for all integers $n\ge 2$, $\widehatφ_{2n}$ is an integrable function which, when convolved with itself $2n-2$ times, is constant on the interval $[-π,π]$. In particular, we identify the extremizer in an autoconvolution problem posed by B. Green in 2001.

title: TRACER: Trace-Regularized Training Against Indirect Prompt Injection
abstract: Indirect prompt injection uses untrusted retrieved content, tool outputs, or agent messages to override an LLM's intended behavior. We show that defense robustness is channel-conditioned: the same attack succeeds 18% of the time as a follow-up message but 53% when placed in retrieved context. We propose TRACER (Trace-Regularized Adversarial Channel Exposure with Reward-shaping), a channel-aware adversarial training method that samples presentation wrappers and combines an answer-anchored, evidence-gated reward with ATRC, which aligns attacked reasoning with clean evidence when an injection is invalid. On GSM8K with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, TRACER reduces RAG-framed ASR from 65.5% to 6.1% while preserving 78-82% clean accuracy. Joint RAG+tool training achieves 13.9% average ASR across framings at 3B scale, while a single epoch at 7B reaches 9.4%. These results demonstrate that robust defenses must explicitly train and evaluate across deployment channels.

title: CAFE: Confining Feature Distillation to Language-Routed Adapters for Compact Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition
abstract: Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation. We find that this expectation does not hold for two common feature losses in compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR), and analyze why through their gradients. The gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, while that of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a similarity-based loss, is weakly aligned with it. CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) on non-English languages, but at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies (one trained, two probed) all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5% (about 81% by chance). Guided by this diagnosis, we propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation), which confines the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses, addressing the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, CAFE lowers the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, and makes English more stable across checkpoints. At 254M parameters, it trails the 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points and is competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages. We use 564k hours of training data and state-of-the-art models to keep the findings relevant to practice.

title: Student Copula Markov Networks
abstract: This paper extends the applicability of probabilistic graphical models to non Gaussian data. It establishes a characterization of the pairwise Markov property in undirected probabilistic graphical models in terms of copula densities. Building on this characterization, we derive a necessary condition for the pairwise Markov property in Student copula Markov networks. An Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm (ECM) is provided to facilitate the penalized maximum likelihood estimation and graph selection. The performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated through simulation studies, which demonstrate its effectiveness in estimating model parameters and recovering the underlying graph structure.

title: Graph-Based Orchestration of Heterogeneous AI Models: A Control Node Approach to Composite Intelligence
abstract: We present a graph-based framework for Composite AI systems that integrate multiple AI techniques to address complex problems. We describe an architecture using specialized control nodes to orchestrate diverse models including planning, machine learning, constraint programming, and large language models. The system employs directed acyclic graphs and behavior trees to manage model relationships and execution sequencing. Our methodology encompasses data connectors, computational services, and a containerized deployment framework supporting hierarchical, sequential, and concurrent model composition patterns. Through case studies, we demonstrate how this architecture enables the creation of composite systems that leverage the strengths of multiple AI techniques within a unified operational schema, overcoming the limitations of single-model approaches.

title: Carbon-Aware Joint Resource and Energy Scheduling for Cellular Base Stations
abstract: Decarbonizing cellular networks requires coordinating communication-resource and battery operation with time-varying electricity prices and carbon intensity. We jointly optimize base station and battery operation under a carbon-adjusted electricity price and traffic-demand constraints, and solve the mixed-integer nonconvex problem through a two-stage decomposition exact under a minimum-power rule. Using California price and carbon-intensity data, we show that carbon-aware scheduling reduces emissions most when low-price and low-carbon periods are misaligned. Above a carbon price of roughly 100-300 USD/ton, battery operation shifts from cost-driven to carbon-driven, cutting emissions by up to 57.8% relative to a cost-only schedule.

title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models
abstract: How well can a language model turn a large, incomplete and partly contradictory body of documents into a plan when no single correct answer exists? We introduce Mission Analysis (MA)-Bench, built on mission analysis, the first step of military operational planning, in which a staff reads the full situation and states the problem before anyone proposes a solution. Its 10 expert-built scenarios pair synthetic packets of ten to twelve documents with 1,257 expert-written pass/fail requirements, each containing information on their source, question type, and importance level. A reasoning-model judge grades each brief against the requirements without seeing the documents; it grades like a fifth credentialed planner, leaving a four-planner panel's agreement unchanged (Fleiss $κ$ 0.42 to 0.41), and a judge from a second provider reproduces the model ranking (Spearman 0.94). Across twenty frontier and open-weights models the best gets 62% of the rubric items right. Models are strongest on facts stated in the documents (58%) and weakest on judgments that must be inferred (33%), and six failures in ten are omissions rather than errors. MA-Bench grades the determinations, not the prose. We release the packets, rubrics, prompts, scorer and every graded brief with item-level verdicts.

title: Online Tokenization with Optimal Delay in Linear Time
abstract: Tokenization is an essential preprocessing step in almost all large language models (LLMs). One of the most popular frameworks is BPE tokenization, which consists of special token segmentation, pretokenization, and byte-pair encoding (BPE). However, existing algorithms are sequential, with each stage only processing complete output from the previous stage. In order to reduce latency and memory footprints, recent works (Jiang and Gong, ICML 2026) (Li, Yang and Mamouras, ASPLOS 2026) (Mamouras, Li and Yang, PLDI 2026) have initiated the study of online algorithms for subroutines such as pretokenization and BPE with a goal of streaming input to output as the input arrives online. However, the search for efficient online tokenization remains open. In this work, we formalize and resolve online tokenization. We introduce the notion of delay for online tokenization which characterizes the extent to which the algorithm output lags behind the (possibly computationally intractable) optimum. We give a near-linear time algorithm with optimal delay (up to constant factors). We complement this algorithm with a conditional lower bound: unless $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{NP}$, there is no polynomial time algorithm that beats the delay of our algorithm by more than a constant factor. We implement a practical variant for tokenizers from OpenAI's tiktoken and HuggingFace's tokenizers. We obtain a $7.9\times$-$34.8\times$ latency advantage (measured as time to first token) over tiktoken (as well as the recent gigatoken tokenizer) and our implementation maintains approximately constant memory usage independent of input size. Our implementation also achieves a $2.4\times$-$7.0\times$ improvement in throughput over tiktoken and $15.8\times$-$38.1\times$ over tokenizers.

title: Pseudo-relativistic fermions and topological states in zinc-blende semiconductors and their heterostructures (Habilitation thesis)
abstract: Tracing my scientific path from many-body physics in semiconductor nanostructures to topological quantum matter, this Habilitation à diriger des recherches (HDR) memoir presents only part of my research since defending two PhD theses in Toulouse and Nizhny Novgorod in 2011. Focusing on pseudo-relativistic fermions and topological states in zinc-blende semiconductors and their heterostructures, it highlights my independent research program: identifying physical problems, developing predictive theories, and initiating new directions with experimentalists. The first part addresses Kane fermions in bulk HgCdTe: temperature-driven band inversion, domain-wall states, the collapse of Landau levels in crossed electric and magnetic fields, and disorder-induced topological transitions. The second examines pressure-, temperature-, and disorder-driven phase transitions in single and double HgTe quantum wells (QWs), including bilayer-graphene-like semimetals and a two-dimensional higher-order topological insulator (2D HOTI) phase beyond the minimal BHZ model. The third develops three-layer InAs/Ga(In)Sb QWs as a III-V platform for massless Dirac fermions, large-gap quantum spin Hall insulators, 2D HOTI phases, and semimetals with quadratic band touching, and discusses InAs$_{x}$Sb$_{1-x}$/InAs$_{y}$Sb$_{1-y}$ heterostructures as a promising alternative. Several of these predictions are supported by experimental observations, including quantized helical edge transport up to 60 K and the unconventional quantum Hall effect. Defended on March 25, 2026, at the University of Montpellier. Jury: Michel GOIRAN (chair and rapporteur, LNCMI-CNRS, Toulouse); Alexey KAVOKIN (rapporteur, Westlake University, Hangzhou); Robson FERREIRA (rapporteur, LPENS-CNRS, Paris); Alexei BARANOV (member, IES-CNRS, Montpellier); Benoit JOUAULT and Frédéric TEPPE (members, L2C-CNRS, Montpellier).

title: Collective Learning for Unified Robotic Manipulation via Predictive Dynamics Adaptation
abstract: Learning a collective policy for state-based Cartesian manipulation across diverse robotic embodiments presents a fundamental challenge due to embodiment-dependent transition dynamics. Collective learning aggregates multi-robot experience to discover shared task structure, yet naive aggregation can average incompatible action modes when different embodiments realize the same Cartesian command through different transition behavior. This leads to strategy ambiguity and performance collapse on dynamically outlying embodiments. To address this, we propose PACE, a two-stage collective learning framework that separates shared task-space intent from embodiment-dependent transition dynamics. The first stage employs a representation layer pre-trained on offline trajectories to extract task-level context from collective data. The second stage introduces a decision layer equipped with a predictive dynamics adapter. By forcing the latent state to predict future transitions, this adapter acts as a latent regularizer that grounds the policy in the transition behavior of the executing robot while preserving real-time inference without online planning. Evaluations across simulated embodiments demonstrate that our method prevents performance collapse on distinct robots. It achieves over 93\% overall success and 89\% on dynamically out-of-distribution zero-shot simulated robots, outperforming the Transformer behavior cloning (82\%) and diffusion policy baselines (66\%). Physical KUKA deployment further validates the feasibility of the full state-based pipeline under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.

title: Towards Training and Inference of Graph Neural Networks in Graph Databases
abstract: Graph Neural Networks on large graphs commonly rely on in-memory graph storage with ad hoc data processing pipelines for both training and inference. Graph databases provide scalable storage and efficient traversal for graphs that can evolve over time, but their applicability in GNN training and inference are rarely studied. We show that graph DBs can be used in GNN training and inference directly, executing sampling, feature retrieval, and even the full forward pass. We show different GNN training pipelines can perform on-the-fly sampling and retrieval in graph DBs using Cypher. We further provide optimisations that speed up the training process by \~2.5x while maintaining the same accuracy. We illustrate that fully in-DB inference is possible, independent of how the GNNs are trained. Our inference setup can be >10x faster than cold loading the graph into RAM with no extra memory overhead on real-world graphs. Our work lays the foundation for in-graph-DB GNN training and inference.

title: Post-Training, Finetuning, and Steering:A Field Guide for Curating Training Data
abstract: While Vision-Language-Action models have enabled impressive cross-task transfer in zero-shot settings, \emph{adaptation} methods are often necessary to achieve consistent performance on novel tasks. However, even though a wealth of methods for adaptation have been proposed, it is unclear how to choose the best method based on available trajectories. We close this gap by studying the impact of the adaptation method under a variety of common data scenarios: on- and off-policy data, offline vs online adaptation, and whether the data contains optimal or suboptimal trajectories. Our evaluation spans simulated tasks in the LIBERO suite and real tasks on a Franka platform. In the offline data regime, critic-based steering approaches outperform supervised finetuning when failure data is available. However, offline RL techniques for training critic functions fail to outperform simpler Monte-Carlo-based approaches. Finally, in the online setting, critic-based steering is significantly more sample efficient compared to policy-gradient-based finetuning methods, but has a lower performance ceiling than full finetuning.

title: A Sociophysics Approach to Measuring Democracy in the Decision Making of a Group: Three Indices
abstract: A group does not usually consult all its members before every decision. This paper develops a quantitative framework for measuring how widely members are consulted in decision making within a group. Two kinds of records are considered: the number of members consulted for each decision and the number of decisions in which each member is consulted. From these records, two participation indices are defined, and their equality is proved analytically. A third index measures the fraction of decisions for which at least a specified percentage of members are consulted. The distribution of consultation levels is described using a discrete maximum-entropy model from statistical physics. Tail probabilities are used to obtain bounds for the main participation index. This study examines aggregate survey data from two groups. Their observed characteristics are broadly consistent with the patterns found across the full survey. Using binomial and Poisson calculations, the future probability that all members will be consulted for a decision is examined. Inequality in consultation among members is examined through Lorenz curves, the Gini coefficient and a normalised Shannon participation measure. The member-decision structure is represented as a bipartite network. Controlled simulations show that the same overall level of consultation can have different distributions among the members. The framework measures both the overall breadth of consultation and how consultation is distributed among the members. It therefore provides a quantitative sociophysical description of one measurable aspect of democracy in decision making within a group.

title: Demystifying On-Policy Distillation: Where Does the Teacher's Advantage Live?
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly studied as a cheaper alternative to reinforcement learning, yet it remains a form of knowledge distillation (KD) that relies on teacher supervision. We revisit OPD from the KD perspective by asking where the teacher's advantage lies along student-generated trajectories. Controlled token flips at teacher-student disagreements directly measure the accuracy gained from teacher corrections. Single-token flips yield a modest average gain on selected failed trajectories, whereas repeated flips raise accuracy from 28.4% to 74.5%, close to the teacher's 76.9%. Gains continue to accumulate with more flips, but mass- and KL-based selection outperform random flips by 15-18 percentage points at counts of similar magnitude. Selective intervention remains useful after OPD, but greater argmax agreement does not consistently improve accuracy across model pairs. We advocate training schedules that learn more valuable teacher corrections while maintaining distributional stability. Controlled flips and fork-resolution analysis evaluate OPD beyond accuracy by measuring which teacher preferences the student acquires and what further correction can recover.

title: SQuIGGLE: Radio AGN Found Predominantly in Young, Gas-rich Post-starburst Galaxies at z ~ 0.7
abstract: The processes that rapidly quench massive galaxies and maintain their quiescence remain poorly understood. Substantial molecular gas reservoirs can survive this shutdown in post-starburst galaxies, raising the question of what prevents the remaining gas from efficiently forming stars. We present deep, subarcsecond VLA 6 GHz observations of 52 massive SQuIGGLE post-starburst galaxies at $z\sim0.7$ to test the prevalence and mechanical impact of radio activity during the gas-rich post-burst phase. We detect 6 GHz continuum emission in 18/52 galaxies ($\approx$35\%), spanning $\log(L_{1.4\,{\rm GHz}}/{\rm W\,Hz^{-1}})\simeq23.0$--$25.0$ and generally exceeding the contributions expected from ongoing star formation and the fading starburst, favoring an AGN origin. Ancillary data at other wavelengths provide little evidence for a population of luminous, radiatively efficient AGN, suggesting that these sources are instead dominated by comparatively weak, mechanically powered radio AGN. Radio activity is strongly concentrated within the first $\sim$200 Myr post-burst and is predominantly associated with galaxies retaining substantial gas reservoirs. Above a common radio luminosity threshold, the radio detection fraction is enhanced by a factor of $\approx$2.5 relative to the radio AGN candidate fraction in mass- and redshift-matched quiescent LEGA-C galaxies, primarily due to lower power sources. For efficient jet--ISM coupling, the inferred mechanical power could supply the approximate energy required to unbind the molecular gas on timescales comparable to its observed decline. Together, these results identify a population of radiatively inefficient AGN hosted predominantly by young, gas-rich post-starburst galaxies at $z\sim0.7$ and suggest that they may have a role in maintaining inefficient star formation.

title: Physics-based deep learning for non-stationary adaptive multiple suppression
abstract: Surface-related multiple elimination (SRME) is an indispensable processing step in marine seismic exploration, comprising two main components: multiple prediction and adaptive subtraction. While the multiple prediction is theoretically data-driven and relies on the data itself, the adaptive subtraction step requires a fairly subjective manual control. Our approach introduces a purely data-driven and physics-based deep learning (PDL) algorithm for improving the adaptive multiple subtraction to significantly enhanced performance. There are two main innovations in the proposed deep-learning (DL) multiple subtraction approaches: first, being data-driven and self-supervised, which removes the dependence on inflexible label preparation and model training processes; secondly, being governed by the adaptive matching filtering (AMF) equation to guide the training process. The DL module serves as a strong regression filter analogous to the traditionally known AMF. We segment a moderately sized seismic profile and an initial multiple model into a large number of patches using a patching scheme for self-contained training. The number of patches is controlled by the patch size and the shift size to enable a sufficient number of training samples required by mainstream DL platforms. The patching-based self-training and regression approach, PDL, is inherently a non-stationary matching approach that aims to obtain a globally optimal matching from the initial multiple models to the input full wavefield data through iterative patching-based training. It is also closely connected with the non-stationary regression approach, which was developed almost two decades ago. However, the PDL approach achieves even stronger regression performance due to the backpropagation-based optimization mechanism in DL, and has shown significantly improved multiple subtraction performance over a number of examples.

title: Compiling Expert Procedures into Verified Programs: When a Small Model Is Enough
abstract: In procedural tool-use domains, how much of the gap between base models is procedure rather than capability? We build an explicit program from a teacher's traces and run it in front of unchanged small models, including an 8B model. The construction, PLVR , takes the reasoning traces of a teacher, Kimi-K3, clusters their segments to locate recurring operations, has a frontier model author one typed primitive per operation, each run by a small frozen model and assembles the program by A* search over a mined rule library, under a reference-action objective. At inference the program takes one of two forms: for troubleshooting and tool search it produces the chain of thought the student would otherwise generate for itself, and the student acts on it; for multi-turn tool matching the student proposes each action and the program checks, repairs, or retries it before it goes out. On the official tau2-Bench Retail and Telecom test sets and on LiveMCPBench, with three Nemotron base models and the same program for each, the answer depends on the domain. On Telecom, Granite-4.2-8B as the student goes from 43.0% to 91.2% under the program, and every Nemotron student reaches 93.3-94.4%, against at most 58.2% for fine-tuning on the same traces, prompt optimisation of the student, or two token-matched baselines. With Granite-4.2-8B as the student, the program is within 2 to 3 points of the Nemotron students on Telecom and within 3 on Retail, and 3 to 13 points below them on LiveMCPBench: where the domain is procedural an 8B student is enough, and on tool search the student still matters. On Retail and LiveMCPBench the program is competitive with the best baseline. The spread between base models shrinks from about 7 points to about 2, averaged over the suites, with no weights changed.

title: Infrared-Finite Positivity Bounds in 4D Gravity
abstract: We formulate an S-matrix bootstrap in an exactly flat half-space, where boundary reflection provides geometric infrared control for four-dimensional gravity. Under the channel positivity conditions, we obtain an infrared-finite positivity bound on local four-scalar Wilson coefficients that includes a finite gravitational correction of order $G_N$ and is derived from the full UV absorptive spectrum without specifying a UV theory, imposing a spectral ansatz, requiring weak coupling or expanding the spectrum perturbatively. At fixed dimensionless external state parameters, the coefficient of the leading gravitational correction is independent of the EFT scale and requires neither an arbitrary soft resolution scale nor a model-dependent UV scale. Gaussian wave-packet scattering localizes interactions within the flat region and directly probes bulk Wilson coefficients while exponentially suppressing sensitivity to the boundary. Long-range gravitons remain sensitive to the boundary and give a finite contribution. The smearing functional passes numerical positivity tests with general half-space absorptive kernels in both crossed channels. An explicit string example shows how boundary reflection suppresses the collective contribution of string resonances to the absorptive part of the amplitude, connecting infrared control of low-energy scattering to the UV spectrum of quantum gravity in the same dispersion relation. The framework opens a route to infrared-finite constraints on effective interactions across particle physics and gravity.

title: A Systematic Study of Deprecated Android API Usage Updates
abstract: Android Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) continuously evolve, causing existing APIs to become deprecated and requiring developers to migrate their usages to recommended replacements. Although prior studies have proposed automated migration techniques, their effectiveness is often limited by the diversity and contextual complexity of API changes. This paper presents a systematic study of deprecated Android APIs, their recommended replacements, and real-world usage updates performed by developers. Based on an analysis of 1,000 deprecated APIs and 4,336 migration examples collected from GitHub, we identify six migration categories and derive recurring usage-update patterns involving Android-version checks, parameter adaptation, object initialization, data-type conversion, and changes in API interaction mechanisms. To assess their applicability, we augment the zero-shot GUPPY benchmark prompts with the migration category and corresponding usage-update pattern. On 156 benchmark tasks, the pattern-guided prompt improves correct updates from 139 to 147 and performs better in five of the six categories.

title: $L^p_μ$-Normed Spaces of Bounded Multilinear Operator
