To address this problem, we propose a model-based iterative algorithm that integrates optimal user association, decision tree-based selection of sensing RRUs, and fixed-point power allocation. This algorithm is further used to train a graph neural network (GNN) framework, ISAC-GNN, to overcome scalability and computational complexity limitations. Our theoretical analysis ensures performance guarantees, while a semi-supervised training strategy enhances stability and generalization. Simulation results demonstrate that ISAC-GNN reduces inference time by 67% relative to the model-based approach, enabling real-time implementation for ISAC system resource management. In addition, ISAC-GNN allows scalable deployment across various system scenarios without retraining the model.

title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
abstract: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.

title: Divergent Paths: Learning an Outcome-Predictive Representation of LLM Agent Trajectories
abstract: In this work, we reframe agentic trajectories as paths through a shared embedding space of actions and environmental observations. We show that successful and failed rollouts of the same task separate in this space, with simple per-task discriminators predicting held-out rollout outcomes at up to 0.95 AUROC across three agent benchmarks and three policy models. To exploit this signal across tasks, we introduce Precog-RM, a transformer-based model that meta-learns a representation in which outcome prediction can be performed in a few-shot setting. We show that Precog-RM generalizes to unseen tasks and models, and gives confident predictions of trajectory success long before termination. Deployed as an early stopping controller for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Tau2-Bench, Precog-RM cuts training FLOPs by up to 47.3\% while maintaining performance comparable to baseline GRPO.

title: PolyMorph: Learning Locomotion Policy for Cross-Embodiment Adaptation
abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion for legged robots, but learned policies are typically tied to a specific robot morphology and require additional engineering when the number of legs, actuators, or mechanical properties change. We present PolyMorph, a morphology-conditioned framework that learns a single locomotion policy for heterogeneous legged robots. PolyMorph converts each robot's URDF into joint-link modules and combines a recurrent encoder, graph-based Transformer, and per-joint decoder to generate actions across variable leg counts and joint configurations. To improve training stability, PolyMorph uses morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization. We evaluate PolyMorph in simulation across bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphology variants and platforms, and deploy the policy on real quadruped platforms operated in multiple configurations. The results show that a single PolyMorph policy generalizes across diverse robot morphologies without per-robot policy retraining.

title: A quantum probabilistic approach to the emergence of an inflationary Starobinsky Universe
abstract: We propose that the necessary conditions for the existence of inflation could be explained by a quantum probabilistic approach. We interpret physical states $ψ$ obtained via the path integral formulation as probability density amplitudes for the Universe to be measured at a particular geometric configuration. First, we examine the problem of ordering ambiguities in the Wheeler-DeWitt (WDW) equation. We develop a formalism to handle ambiguities in the canonical quantization of a $1d$ minisuperspace by defining ambiguity functions within the WDW equation. We define a Hilbert space inner product for calculating physical observables, and using an argument from the hermiticity of the Hamiltonian, we obtain an expression for its measure $μ$ in addition to constraints on the ambiguity functions. By defining a new quantum state $Ψ=\sqrtμ ψ$ and using the path integral formalism, we are able to resolve ambiguities and prove the theory is universal. We then generalize for any $M$-dimensional minisuperspace system, for which we can prove universality in the semi-classical approximation for a large class of models. We also show that this universality extends to all orders of quantum theory if the target space manifold of the theory is flat. We calculate probability amplitudes for various cosmological scenarios involving Starobinsky inflation. We summarize the Hartle-Hawking no-boundary proposal for GR and we comment on the distinct possibilities of defining a contour of integration: the sign choice of Hartle-Hawking vs that of Linde-Vilenkin. We make an analogous calculation for $R^{2}$ gravity and find that for the Linde- Vilenkin choice it is statistically more likely for the Universe to emerge in its inflationary stage. Finally, we calculate transition amplitudes when the kinetic energy of the inflaton field $ϕ$ takes non-zero values.

title: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control for Robotic Arms: Language-to-Code Decomposition and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation, and code synthesis for language-driven robot control, making execution outcomes traceable to instructions and programs. We compare one-shot generation with ICMC under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo. We then train an open-weight instruction policy by GRPO through a frozen code generator on cube placement onto two- and five-cube letter layouts, averaging the rewards of five programs per instruction. The logged positive-reward rate rose from 31.6% to 35.3% (253/800 to 282/800) between the first and last five training steps. A log audit identifies positive binary labels associated with geometric-failure messages: at least 19 in that run, 18 in the dense-reward run, and 5 in the run with one program per instruction. In one case, all five rewards were 1.0 while the log reports a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance; the verdict came from the program's own output stream. We distinguish logged reward rates from independently verified task success and report descriptive results for each configuration's single training trajectory. We introduce an independent evaluation protocol that checks task completion against fixed specifications, separating robot control from success assessment to support reproducible evaluation.

title: F2A-ObjectNav: An Adaptive Agentic Architecture for Object-Goal Navigation
abstract: Object-goal navigation requires an embodied agent to explore an unfamiliar environment, identify a target object, navigate toward candidate instances, and reliably determine whether the observed object satisfies the mission goal. This work investigates this problem through a two-stage development process. In Stage I, a fixed modular framework is used to examine combinations of exploration, object detection, and target validation methods. The results reveal clear trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, with no single fixed configuration remaining preferable across all evaluated conditions. These observations motivate F2A-ObjectNav (Fixed-to-Adaptive Object-Goal Navigation), an adaptive agentic architecture in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory. The architecture uses event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional semantic guidance while retaining lightweight execution during normal operation. F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated over 25 episodes in each of AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, achieving success rate (SR) / success-weighted path length (SPL) values of 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37, respectively. In addition to task-level metrics, architecture-specific behavioral metrics are used to characterize semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, memory-supported behavior, and decision stability. The results show different patterns of adaptive intervention across the three environments, with higher intervention frequencies observed in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR than in AI2-THOR.

title: Are AI Decision Models Biased? A Case Study of Jev
abstract: Do AI models designed for fast, structured decisions exhibit the cognitive and social biases observed in human judgment? We evaluate Jev, a model described as a System One decision-maker, using 41,500 responses across cognitive reflection tasks, five classical cognitive-bias paradigms, and a pricing experiment testing ethnic and gender bias. At the level of selected answers, the results are largely encouraging. We confirm previous findings that Jev performs extremely well on cognitive reflection problems. We also observe that it generally avoids the characteristic choice patterns associated with several well-documented human biases, and exhibits only small differences among demographic groups in the tested pricing scenario. However, this apparent robustness conceals important vulnerabilities. Its judgments are sensitive to irrelevant numerical information and the ordering of response options. Moreover, several cognitive-bias manipulations substantially affect returned probabilities even when selected answers remain unchanged. Most strikingly, Jev answers a well-known probability problem correctly in every response but violates the same underlying probability rule in every response to an adapted version. We investigate this discrepancy using 15,000 additional responses across 30 conjunction tasks. Jev violates the rule in 54\% of responses, with accuracy varying dramatically across formulations and answer orders. These findings suggest that evaluating decision models solely on familiar benchmarks and selected answers may substantially overstate their reliability in practical applications. They also identify vulnerabilities for developers to address and practical considerations for users integrating such models into automated decision-making systems.

title: Emergent medium-range order in amorphous silicon
abstract: Medium-range order (MRO) is an important feature of amorphous materials, but its nature in terms of atomic arrangement has remained elusive. Here, using large-scale machine-learning-driven atomistic simulations of amorphous silicon, we probe the MRO of this archetypal network glass. By characterizing the structure in three dimensions, we reveal that the symmetry of the atomic arrangement around a central atom shows a crossover as a function of distance. At short distances, the structure is determined by local bonding constraints, which evolve from predominantly tetrahedral environments in low-density amorphous silicon to highly coordinated and strongly disordered local environments in very-high-density amorphous silicon. At larger distances, however, distinct cubic- and octahedral-symmetry patterns emerge in the three-dimensional atomic-density distribution, despite the absence of these symmetries at shorter length scales. We find that this crossover is accompanied by a quasi-periodic spatial organization of the topological rings in the structure. The characteristic spacing between ring centers matches the length scale of the first sharp diffraction peak (FSDP) in the structure factor, establishing a direct connection between this reciprocal-space signature of MRO and its real-space organization. These results demonstrate that the FSDP, the spatial correlation of the rings, and emergent orientational symmetries are not independent manifestations of MRO, but reflect different aspects of a common structural organization. Our findings provide a unified real-space picture of MRO in amorphous silicon and suggest that intermediate-range structural order in network glasses emerges from the interplay between local bonding constraints and extended atomic arrangements driven by efficient packing.

title: Development and characterization of a millimeter-wave circular polarization observation method using a quarter-wave plate with Simons Array
abstract: We have developed and demonstrated a method for measuring circular polarization at 90 GHz by combining a quarter-wave plate (QWP) and a continuously rotating half-wave plate (HWP). While many bolometric experiments at millimeter wavelengths focus on measuring linear polarization, observations of circular polarization in millimeter waves may open a new window into astrophysics and cosmology. We present a novel approach to circular-polarization search using linear-polarization-sensitive detectors by incorporating a QWP in the optics. The Simons Array was originally designed for precise linear polarization measurements, and we subsequently installed a QWP in front of the receiver targeting 90 GHz. The QWP converts incident circular polarization to linear polarization, allowing detection with our detectors. Laboratory measurements demonstrate a QWP conversion efficiency of 99.0%. We apply our method to observations of unpolarized and linearly polarized bright sources, Jupiter and Tau A. Using these observations, we establish the calibration and characterize the instrumental leakages relevant to circular polarization measurements. The measured polarization efficiency adopted for Stokes $V$ is $46\pm2$%, and the measured U-to-V leakage is $-11.7\pm5.1$%. We measure a circular polarization fraction of $V/I=0.78\pm0.42$% for Tau A, showing no significant detection and providing a consistency check of the calibration and systematic-uncertainty treatment. These results establish the instrument response model and calibration parameters used for the companion circular-polarization source search.

title: Percolative MDLA: phase transition and critical behaviour
abstract: In this paper we introduce the model of Percolative MDLA (PMDLA) on $\mathbb{Z}^2$ which engulfs the entire occupied percolation component of each particle that reaches the aggregate. We prove a phase transition of finite time explosion, as a function of the particle density $λ$, where the critical value equals $λ_c=-\log(1-p_c^{\rm site}(\mathbb{Z}^2))$. Below $λ_c$, the process is nonexplosive and has a linear upper bound on its radius. For $2/3<λ<λ_c$, it also has a linear lower bound on the growth rate. Above $λ_c$, an infinite component is swallowed in finite time a.s. At $λ_c$, every update is finite, but the updates accumulate in finite time, causing a blowup. Excluding criticality, the results are generalized to all higher dimensions.

title: MagicGarment: Benchmarking Single-Image Standalone 3D Garment Reconstruction
abstract: Single-image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single-image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment-aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image-to-3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment-focused visual conditioning, while Flow-Time-Route LoRA (FTR-LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow-timestep, token-routing, and expert-load information. Experiments demonstrate MagicGarment's benchmark utility and the effectiveness of garment-aware adaptation. Project page: https://1019538157.github.io/MagicGarment/.

title: Adaptive Observation Control for Active Visual Recognition
abstract: Visual recognition models usually process a fixed view under a fixed computation budget, although images often benefit from different scales and amounts of spatial evidence. Active vision can adapt by observing a coarse scene and then selecting informative fixations, but the public AdaptiveNN-DeiT-S pipeline still fixes both field of view and observation count. We extend this fixed-step recognizer with a controllable observation interface that adapts both the field of view and the number of fixations to the input. Specifically, the model predicts a per-fixation scale that sets its field of view, refines each selected crop with optional scale-gated foveation and a residual high-resolution detail-token branch, and uses label-grounded stop heads for input-dependent early termination. Experiments across fine-grained benchmarks, full ImageNet-1K, and ImageNet-A/R-derived classification splits show that the interface remains competitive with fixed-step references while exposing a controllable observation budget. The same checkpoint enables threshold-controlled accuracy-compute trade-offs without per-threshold retraining. On sequential ImageNet-1K, the learned stop rule outperforms fixed-step truncation of the same checkpoint, sustaining 81.9% top-1 using 2.45 of the four focus steps and exceeding three-step truncation at lower cost. On each benchmark, a variant combining scale control and detail-token fusion achieves the highest accuracy among the tested component-added non-exit variants. Our code is available at https://github.com/GZHU-DVL/LI-Dikai.

title: DAGFormer: Global Topology Prediction for Transformer Cross-Layer Connections
abstract: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.

title: Isometries of Unit Spheres of SFS-Spaces and a Geometric Approach to Tingley's Problem
abstract: We investigate surjective isometries between the unit spheres of facially symmetric spaces and their interaction with the underlying facial structure. It is shown that such isometries preserve the essential geometric relations associated with symmetric faces, orthogonality, and geometric tripotents. In particular, a surjective sphere isometry induces a natural correspondence between the geometric tripotents of the underlying spaces and preserves the principal structural features determined by the Peirce decomposition. These results provide a geometric framework for studying linear extension problems for sphere isometries. As an application, we establish a positive solution of Tingley's problem for finite-dimensional real neutral strongly facially symmetric spaces satisfying the joint Peirce property. We also obtain an extension result for a wider class of real neutral strongly facially symmetric spaces admitting an appropriate approximation by finite-dimensional Peirce subspaces. In these settings, every surjective isometry between unit spheres extends uniquely to a surjective real-linear isometry of the ambient spaces. The results demonstrate that the facial and tripotent structures play a decisive role in the rigidity of spherical isometries.

title: E2DRL: End-to-End Differentiable Reinforcement Learning for 3D Obstacle Avoidance in Quadruped Robots
abstract: Differentiable reinforcement learning shows strong promise for robot policy learning, but its application to legged locomotion has remained limited to blind walking or simulated 2D tasks. Extending it to end-to-end visual obstacle avoidance is challenging because hard collision constraints and early termination upon contact corrupt first-order gradients, trapping optimizers in local minima. We present E2DRL, which addresses this with a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation: penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping to provide the first-order training signals for 3D obstacle avoidance. To realize a deployable perception-control system, a privileged teacher trained via Soft Analytic Policy Optimization (SAPO) in a differentiable simulator is distilled into a recurrent depth-based student via DAgger, then blended with a base locomotion policy using a terrain-aware gating module for deployment. In simulation, E2DRL achieves higher sample efficiency than PPO and demonstrates superior velocity-tracking performance and 3D obstacle-avoidance capability compared with both PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC. We present the first sim-to-real validation of end-to-end differentiable RL for 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.

title: Self-Conditioning Enables Deep Sequential Reasoning in Flow Matching
abstract: Recent work has explored visual reasoning through image generation, where models solve visual-reasoning problems by directly generating solution images. Intuitively, iterative samplers such as flow matching are well suited to this task, since each sampling step may resemble one reasoning step. However, in this work, from a circuit complexity perspective, we show that this intuition is misleading. We prove that as long as the model outputs satisfy certain mild regularity conditions, the trajectory of the vanilla flow-matching sampler can be simulated by a constant number of sequential rounds of parallel model evaluations. Consequently, additional sampling steps cannot increase the expressive power of a constant-depth backbone model under the standard complexity-theoretic model of transformers. We then reveal that self-conditioning, which conditions the model on the previous step's estimate of the final image, plays a previously unrecognized role in removing this bottleneck. Controlled experiments on diverse visual-reasoning tasks show that flow matching with self-conditioning achieves higher accuracy and greater reasoning depth than vanilla flow matching, and its performance improves with more sampling steps. Theoretically, we prove that with self-conditioning, a constant-depth backbone can achieve expressive power equivalent to that of space-bounded Turing machines. Our study suggests a design principle for future visual reasoning research: carry more information between sampling steps, so that additional steps translate into deeper reasoning.

title: Tidal deformability of white dwarfs in Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld gravity
abstract: We compute the static quadrupole Love number $k_2$ and the dimensionless tidal deformability $Λ$ of cold white dwarfs in Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld (EiBI) gravity. Matter couples to the physical metric while perturbation equations are solved in an auxiliary metric, so the physical tidal field near the surface depends on derivatives of the equation of state. This dependence is regular for a surface polytropic index $1<Γ_{\rm env}<3/2$, but not for the $Γ= 5/3$ Chandrasekhar equation of state. The mechanism, an algebraic map between the metric that carries perturbations and the metric that matter feels, is common to Palatini-type theories, so the same type of surface condition should apply to tidal calculations in this wider class. We use thermodynamically consistent envelopes that exactly reach zero enthalpy. At five masses from \(0.6\) to \(1.3\,\Msun\) and five sampled Born-Infeld couplings \(κ\), with $|κ|\le5\times10^6\,\mathrm{m^2}$, the EiBI-GR differences are approximately linear in $κ$. The largest absolute fractional shifts are \(3.89\times 10^{-5}\) in the stellar radius $R$, \(4.09\times 10^{-5}\) in $k_2$, and \(2.36\times 10^{-4}\) in $Λ$. Across nine envelope models, half the spread of each quantity relative to the baseline envelope is at most \(0.0186\) in $R$ and \(0.0857\) in \(k_2\), but only \(3.02\times 10^{-5}\) in \(Λ\) as the changes in \(k_2\) and \(R^5\) largely cancel. A high-precision calculation shows that the envelope dependence of the EiBI-GR difference in \(Λ\) is small. Half the spread of this difference ranges from \(1.067\times 10^{-12}\) to \(6.208\times 10^{-11}\) over the 20 nonzero mass-coupling points.

title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Automated materials discovery requires evaluating large pools of candidate configurations, with density functional theory (DFT) as a major throughput bottleneck. Pretrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate DFT cheaply, but their errors vary by orders of magnitude across configurations, making it difficult to decide when to trust the MLIP predictions and when to fall back to DFT. We frame this decision as a risk-controlled selection problem and solve it within a conformal risk control (CRC) framework. Each configuration is mapped from atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates to a fixed geometric descriptor, which a lightweight predictor uses to estimate an MLIP-DFT disagreement score in energy, average force, and maximum force. CRC then calibrates this score into a selection threshold for DFT labeling such that the MLIP error on the unselected configurations, which keep their MLIP labels, stays below a user-chosen fraction $α$ of the expected error. Under an identical guarantee across eight dataset-MLIP pairs, our predictor routes 7% and 14% fewer configurations to DFT at $α=0.3$ than committee baselines. Because committee disagreement overlooks errors the MLIPs share, our gains are largest when the DFT labels and MLIP training data differ in DFT functional and basis set, and narrow when the two agree. Without model access, the structure-only predictor also ranks errors as well as the target MLIP's latent representation and outperforms widely used descriptors such as Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) and Atom-Centered Symmetry Functions (ACSF).

title: Active Sculpting: morphodynamics of internally stirred active vesicles
abstract: Active flows are often confined by soft, deformable boundaries that they can push against, reshape, and in turn get reorganized by. Motivated by this interplay, we combine theory and numerical simulations to analyze the morphodynamics of an elastic vesicle enclosing a dilute suspension of extensile active particles. We model the two-dimensional vesicle as a weakly extensible elastic ring with bending rigidity, immersed in a Stokesian fluid, and describe the confined active suspension using a kinetic theory. The vesicle and the suspension are coupled hydrodynamically, through the kinematic and dynamic boundary conditions at the interface, and energetically, through a single alignment interaction that simultaneously aligns active particles with the membrane and the membrane with the particles. We show that this interaction reduces to a weak-anchoring boundary condition familiar from passive liquid crystals and derive a closed-form quiescent equilibrium state in which the nematic order in the suspension organizes into a vortex with a +1 defect core. A stability analysis of this state predicts an ordered hierarchy of activity thresholds at which successive shape modes of the vesicle are destabilized, as well as a purely passive, anchoring-driven instability of floppy vesicles. Nonlinear simulations, performed with a volume-conserving immersed boundary method, reveal that each threshold crossing gives rise to a distinct emergent state: a static spindle with boundary-pinned defects, a rotor that tank treads against its own rotation, a fluctuating spinner, and a turbulent state in which the vesicle acts as a self-stirring compartment. Beyond demonstrating how boundary deformability sculpts, and is sculpted by, confined active matter, our results open the door to study hydrodynamic interactions between such active vesicles and to use membrane fluctuations as a probe of activity of suspensions.

title: Collective-flow signatures of bubble nuclei in intermediate-energy projectile fragmentation reactions
abstract: Characterized by central density depletion, bubble nuclei represent an important class of exotic nuclear structures. Collective flow in the $^{40}$Ca+$^{9}$Be projectile fragmentation reaction at 140 MeV/u is investigated using the extended quantum molecular dynamics (EQMD) model with a parameter on of the isoscalar monopole excitation strength $\varepsilon$. The projectile $^{40}Ca$ is initialized as a relaxed ten-$α$ cluster configuration exhibiting a bubble-like density distribution. The results reveal that increasing $\varepsilon$ modifies the density distribution and the size of the depleted central region of bubble, producing pronounced changes in fragment yields and collective flow around $\varepsilon\approx0.5$. Below this value, heavy-fragment production plays a significant role, while the directed flow $v_1$ of protons and neutrons remains predominantly negative, indicating preferential emission toward the target side. Above $\varepsilon\approx0.5$, enhanced expansion of the central low-density region suppresses heavy residues and drives $v_1$ toward positive values. In contrast, preformed $α$ clusters show different responses, reflecting their origin in the initial cluster configuration rather than solely in secondary decay. At low excitation, the cluster flow exhibits a pronounced impact-parameter dependence, whereas stronger excitation weakens cluster binding and suppresses directional anisotropy, driving the flow close to zero. The rapidity slopes of the flow coefficients also vary systematically with $\varepsilon$, tracing changes in emission anisotropy during expansion. These findings extend traditional static descriptions by probing the dynamical evolution of exotic structures in heavy-ion reactions and the contrasting collective-flow behavior of preformed clusters and single nucleons constitutes a sensitive dynamical probe of bubble-like structures.

title: Sharp $L^q$ estimate of adjoint problem and Pucci conjecture
abstract: Let $L$ be a linear second-order elliptic operator satisfying a nondegeneracy condition. We establish sharp $L^q$ estimates for solutions of the adjoint problem associated with $L$ and, by duality, derive sharp $L^p$ estimates for solutions of $Lu = f$. In particular, this confirms a conjecture of Carlo Pucci.

title: Catalan polynomials for the Wishart-Laguerre $β$-ensemble
abstract: By means of $W$-representation, we investigate the Wishart-Laguerre $β$-ensemble and present a compact expression for Catalan polynomials. For a special Nekrasov partition function associated with the Wishart-Laguerre $β$-ensemble, we show that it can be expressed as a exponential form of the special Catalan polynomials. Furthermore, we make a rule to calculate the Catalan polynomials by means of Feynman diagrams and present another expression for Catalan polynomials. We also establish the connection between certain Catalan polynomials and knot theory.

title: Eye, Robot: Learning Expressive Gaze Dynamics via a VLM-Guided Transformer-VAE
abstract: Gaze coordinates attention in human interaction through coupled eye, head, and eyelid motion. A humanoid robot must choose where to look while generating a suitable movement toward that target; fixed tracking rules alone do not model the temporal structure of human gaze. We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot's 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout. At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback. On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline. The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.

title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specific. A data-driven method could instead build a larger symbolic system by aligning and merging existing ones. We target its first, foundational step: matching units across these heterogeneous systems. Our method, SAE-IDF, encodes a symbol in its native context into a sparse code with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), re-weights each dimension by its rarity and matches across systems. On 12 tasks across 6 kinds of symbolic system, SAE-IDF outperforms the same LLM's dense baseline on all tasks with Gemma-2-9B and all but one with Llama-3.1-8B, by up to 45 points, consistently across SAE layers and configurations. SAE-IDF is also interpretable: every dimension of the sparse code has a human-readable meaning, so each match decomposes into named concepts (features). Our work paves the way to a universal symbolic backbone.

title: What Inverse Problems Can Be Solved Using Neural Networks?
abstract: The relationship between classical methods for solving inverse problems and neural network methods is examined. An answer is provided to the question of what inverse problems can be solved using neural networks. The answer is that neural network algorithms can solve only conditionally well-posed problems (well-posed according to Tikhonov). The reason is that the design of standard neural network algorithms violates the well-known Bakushinsky veto from the theory of ill-posed problems. It requires that any method theoretically guaranteeing a stable solution to an ill-posed problem must depend explicitly on the error level of data. The article highlights the distinction between the concept of regularization (RA) in the theory of ill-posed problems and regularization as understood in neural network training, where Bakushinsky's veto is violated. Due to this violation, any changes to the neural network architecture, regularization during training, or training dataset augmentation cannot alter the answer specified above. It is theoretically demonstrated that an ill-posed inverse problem can be solved only by using a parametric set of neural networks that explicitly depend on the known error levels (as parameters) of data. Accordingly, as an alternative to standard neural network algorithms, \neural network based regularization algorithms (NNBRAs) are proposed to solve ill-posed inverse problems. One approach to their construction involves using a regularized dataset. Such a dataset can be generated from perturbed inverse-problem data using a specific base RA explicitly depended on the error level of the data. Test solving the simplest finite-dimensional ill-posed inverse problem demonstrate that the accuracy of the NNBRA approximate solutions is comparable to that of the base RA. At the same time, errors of conventional neural network methods may be unacceptable.

title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
abstract: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable evaluation in Japanese, we carefully localize tau-bench through machine translation, entity adaptation, and human review. During this process, we also uncover and fix two flaws in the original tau-bench: invalid tasks and a score aggregation error that inflates certain models' results. Experiments show that J-tau yields fewer evaluation errors than a naively machine-translated counterpart and that our fixes resolve both flaws.

title: Hardware-friendly Baseband Design and Performance Analysis for LEO Broadband LoS-MIMO Systems
abstract: High-frequency and broadband line-of-sight multiple-input multiple-output (LoS-MIMO) is a key solution for massive space-to-Earth data downlinks. However, in low Earth orbit (LEO) scenarios, it faces spatial rank deficiency from time-frequency coupling correlation and clock deviations from distributed oscillators. This paper establishes a dynamic effective channel throughput (ECT) framework incorporating waterfall characteristics of forward error correction. A hardware-friendly OFDM-based transceiver architecture with subband-adaptive truncation and dynamic timing recovery to achieve robust spatial decoupling is proposed. Through rigorous closed-form derivations, the equivalent signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) under joint errors is quantified, and an optimal scheduling algorithm combining truncation with variable coding and modulation is proposed to maximize ECT. Simulations confirm that the design circumvents outages caused by spatial notches with low complexity, stably enhancing the potential average throughput of a single dual-polarized beam to over 100 Gbps, providing a reliable theoretical foundation and baseband solution for next-generation high-throughput satellites.

title: Synthetic reaction data from transformation rules for graph-to-sequence pretraining in biodegradation pathway prediction
abstract: The scarcity of observed biodegradation reactions constrains the training of product and pathway predictors. We present enviGraph, a framework that generates and curates synthetic reaction data, uses these data to pretrain a graph-to-sequence predictor, and fine-tunes the predictor on observed environmental reactions for product and recursive pathway prediction. Applying inherited environmental transformation rules to structures from PubChem, NORMAN SusDat and EPA DSSTox, followed by curation, produces 776,851 canonical parent-product pairs for pretraining. We compare this dataset with three United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) reaction datasets: USPTO-50K, USPTO-MIT and USPTO-Stereo. We evaluate enviGraph and the sequence-based enviFormer using ten folds split by pathway on the EAWAG Biocatalysis/Biodegradation Database (BBD), regulatory pesticide biodegradation data (Soil) and activated-sludge biodegradation data (Sludge). For both predictors, synthetic pretraining gives the highest BBD mean precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) among the evaluated pretraining datasets for single-generation and multi-generation prediction. enviGraph achieves BBD single-generation PR-AUC of $0.202 \pm 0.050$ with synthetic pretraining, compared with $0.169 \pm 0.065$ for the retrospectively selected strongest USPTO condition, USPTO-Stereo (mean $\pm$ sample standard deviation across folds). Its exact BBD top-1 and top-5 accuracies with synthetic pretraining are 0.355 and 0.594. The strongest USPTO conditions give higher PR-AUC means than synthetic pretraining in most Soil and Sludge comparisons. enviGraph has higher Soil multi-generation PR-AUC means than enviFormer under each of the four main pretraining datasets, and with synthetic pretraining it also leads enviFormer on BBD single-generation PR-AUC and exact top-1 and top-5 accuracy.

title: "The Rose Garden Is a Cemetery": Spatial Dissonance and Divergent Public Experiences of an Indigenous Augmented Reality Tour
abstract: Community-authored augmented reality (AR) can contest dominant heritage narratives by juxtaposing stories with physical surroundings. We examine the Thámien Ohlone AR Tour, developed with members of the Ohlone Native American community at Mission Santa Clara and Santa Clara University. Combining paired pre/post surveys from 57 participants with collaborative thematic analysis, we compare reception among Ohlone community members, university affiliates, and Mission visitors. Spatial dissonance captures felt tensions when AR challenged familiar campus readings or when surroundings conflicted with Ohlone histories the AR affirmed, such as a garden's significance as a burial ground. Cultural frames shaped interpretation; contemporary people and relationships made Ohlone continuance tangible. Participants appreciated the tour and called for permanent physical acknowledgment. We propose staging reflective encounters, clarifying community-authored meanings, and using AR to prototype public acknowledgment and support community-directed advocacy. These findings foreground relationships to land and place, informed by Indigenous scholarship, in designing and evaluating AR.

title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents
abstract: Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically treats complete environmental observations uniformly as world modeling targets, overlooking the varying decision relevance of observation content. We propose DGS-WM (Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training approach for language agents. DGS-WM employs a Decision-Guided Observation Selection component that filters observation units with decision value as world modeling targets based on their support for subsequent policy responses, and a Confidence-Adaptive Weighting component that adaptively adjusts supervision strength according to the model's prediction confidence on selected targets. Together, these components form a decision-aware auxiliary world modeling loss, jointly optimized with the RL loss on the same policy model. Across multiple benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements under different model scales and RL algorithms, demonstrating more stable and effective performance compared to full-observation world modeling methods.

title: Model-Induced Hazard Geometry and Functional Representations in Survival Analysis
abstract: Individualized survival predictions are often summarized by scalar risk scores or event probabilities at selected time horizons, although clinically relevant risk may also differ in its temporal organization. We consider finite-dimensional representations of individual hazard trajectories through interpretable hazard functionals, such as peak timing, cumulative hazard over prespecified intervals, and persistence of elevated risk. A central issue is that the richness of such representations is constrained by the hazard geometry supported by the underlying survival model. We formalize this through model-induced tangent spaces and functional ranks, derive an exact decomposition of model-supported variation into directions retained and lost by a chosen representation, and introduce a model-relative notion of local completeness. We further distinguish intrinsic model capacity from the variation actually activated by covariates. These results motivate a structured extension of AFT time scaling through a positive-affine deformation on the log-time scale, yielding a power-warp mechanism with an additional temporal deformation direction. Combined with a log-logistic reference hazard, this gives a parsimonious likelihood-based working specification for which peak timing and peak height provide complete coordinates over the unimodal regime. We also establish plug-in recovery and asymptotic inference for hazard functionals. Simulations and a lung-cancer application illustrate how model-induced restrictions propagate to hazard-functional representations.

title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
abstract: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.

title: MFSA: A Multi-Format Systolic Array with Native Micro Scaling Support
abstract: AI workloads increasingly employ low-precision formats such as BF16 / FP16, FP8 variants, FP4, Micro Scaling (MX), and INT modes across models, layers, and execution stages to balance accuracy, memory footprint, and throughput, which in turn requires hardware to support these formats in a flexible and efficient way. We present MFSA, a weight-stationary multi-format systolic array that achieves area efficiency through two architectural choices. At the PE level, MFSA uses dot-product-accumulator-based processing elements extended from an existing open-source trans-precision FPU to support reduced-precision formats (FP32/FP16/BF16/CFP8/FP4/INT16/INT8/INT4) with a shared datapath and proportional throughput scaling. At the array level, MFSA employs Online Block-Scale Rebasing (OBSR) for block-scaled formats, which folds each block scale into the running FP32 partial sum at block boundaries without adding a second cross-block accumulator, thereby reducing the additional overhead of block-scaling support. In TSMC 28 nm at 1 GHz, matched-throughput BF16/FP8/FP4 cascaded FMA-PE baselines are 1.5x/2.5x/4.5x larger than the single-format DPA-PE, the gap growing with subword parallelism. A routed 16x16 MFSA reaches a peak 0.5/1/2/4 TOPS of FP32/BF16/FP8/FP4, and OBSR cuts the incremental MX overhead by 64.2% in area and 67.5% in energy versus a naive MX implementation baseline, without hurting the numerical stability on real LLM traces. Adding support for all other formats based on a BF16+CFP8 systolic array costs 25.7% additional area. OBSR also extends to non-power-of-two block scales: folding the fractional part of an E4M3 scale into the MFPE dot product supports NVFP4 alongside OCP MX for 11.8% area and 7.3% power over a CFP8+FP4 base, less than half the cost of a naive implementation.

title: The Big Match under translation-invariant charges
abstract: We study two-player zero-sum stochastic games in which a stream of stage payoffs is evaluated by a translation-invariant charge on the set of stages. Every patient valuation, that is, every diffuse charge that obeys the time value of money principle, is translation-invariant, and by Mertens and Neyman each player has, for every $\varepsilon>0$, a strategy that is $\varepsilon$-optimal for all patient valuations simultaneously. We show that this robustness breaks down for translation-invariant charges. In the Big Match with $0$--$1$ payoffs, whose uniform value is $1/2$, every strategy of Player 1 is worthless: for every strategy of Player 1 and every $δ>0$, Player 2 has a pure reply, and there is a translation-invariant charge under which Player 1's payoff is less than $δ$. Consequently, the Big Match has no value with respect to all translation-invariant charges. This contrasts with finite Markov decision processes, where every stationary Blackwell optimal strategy is optimal for every translation-invariant charge. We pose questions on robust guarantees in general stochastic games and on optimality with respect to a fixed translation-invariant charge.

title: Mapping Arctic Polynyas from Sea Ice Concentration Data Using Hierarchical Partitioning and Differentiated Region Growing: Sensitivity to Threshold and Product Choices
abstract: Accurately delineating Arctic coastal polynyas from sea ice concentration data remains challenging because of complex coastal geometry and spatially heterogeneous ice conditions. We develop a daily sea ice concentration (SIC) mapping framework based on hierarchical partitioning, connected-component analysis, and differentiated region growing for polynya and open-water regions. Applied to September-May ice seasons from 2002/03 to 2024/25, the framework achieves a mean overall accuracy of 96.74% and a mean kappa coefficient of 0.93 in the 63-scene visual assessment. Sensitivity experiments reveal a consistent pattern: the absolute magnitude of SIC-defined polynya extent is strongly configuration-dependent, whereas major temporal features are comparatively more stable. Relative to a 75% upper SIC threshold, seasonal extent integrals differ by 13.48%, 32.47%, and 65.04% at thresholds of 80%, 85%, and 90%, respectively, while the broad interannual structure remains recognizable. The response is also strongly regional and seasonal, with the largest threshold sensitivity in the Central Arctic Ocean, very weak sensitivity in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and greater pan-Arctic curve separation from January onward. At an 80% threshold, product-comparison MAPE is 68.19% between the 6.25 and 25 km products and 11.47% between the 12.5 and 25 km products under their respective comparison periods and reference definitions. Regional product disagreement is likewise heterogeneous. Together, these results show that reproducible long-term polynya monitoring requires a fixed and explicitly documented combination of SIC product, threshold, and spatial classification rules, while broad temporal patterns can remain informative even when absolute extent differs substantially.

title: Sharp radial--angular mixed norm Fourier extension and global stability on spheres
abstract: We study the sharp Fourier extension inequality from $L^2(\mathbb S^{d-1})$ to the radial--angular mixed space $L^q_{\mathrm{rad}}L^2_{\mathrm{ang}}$. Our work is motivated by and builds upon the foundational analysis of Carneiro, Oliveira e Silva and Sousa \cite{COS}, who initiated the sharp mixed-norm spherical restriction problem from the viewpoint of spherical-harmonic decomposition. Their reduction revealed that the extremal problem is governed by a competition among the individual harmonic modes, and their results established degree-zero extremizers in several important ranges of exponents, including even integer exponents and the endpoint case. The present paper addresses this question by establishing a complete modal ordering result. Building on their spherical-harmonic reduction, the sharp-constant problem is reduced to the weighted Bessel moments \[ I_{ν,k}(q) := \int_0^\infty |J_{ν+k}(r)|^q r^{2ν+1-νq}\,dr, \qquad ν:=\frac d2-1. \] For every integer $d\ge2$ and every finite admissible exponent $q>2d/(d-1)$, we prove \[ I_{ν,k}(q)<I_{ν,0}(q), \qquad k\ge1, \] and hence constants are the unique nonzero extremizers of the sharp mixed-norm extension inequality. In dimensions $d\ge3$ we prove the stronger strict ordering \[ I_{ν,0}(q)>I_{ν,1}(q)>I_{ν,2}(q)>\cdots. \] We resolve this difficulty by combining exact Hankel asymptotics with a finite remainder comparison. The modal ordering also yields the optimal quadratic global stability inequality. For every finite admissible $q$, \[ C_{d,q}^2\|f\|_2^2 -\|\widehat{fσ}\|_{L^q_{\mathrm{rad}}L^2_{\mathrm{ang}}}^2 \ge Γ_{d,q}\|f-P_0f\|_2^2, \] with the best possible coefficient. When $d\ge3$, this coefficient is explicitly \[ Γ_{d,q} =(2π)^d \left[ I_{ν,0}(q)^{2/q}-I_{ν,1}(q)^{2/q} \right]. \]

title: Correlation of galactic very-high-energy gamma-ray sources detected by LHAASO with high-energy neutrinos
abstract: We conducted an investigation into the possible correlation between very-high-energy (VHE, $E>$ 0.1 TeV) gamma-ray sources, as identified by the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO), and high-energy neutrino events captured by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. For this analysis, we utilized the First LHAASO catalog, which comprises 90 VHE gamma-ray sources, and the IceCube Event Catalog of Alert Tracks (IceCat-1), which includes 348 track-like neutrino events. Through Monte Carlo simulations, we assessed the correlations between the neutrino events and LHAASO sources, achieving the best p-values of 0.237, 0.312, and 0.115, respectively, for all LHAASO sources, KM2A sources, and WCDA sources. These findings imply that the spatial coincidence between LHAASO sources and neutrino alerts is relatively weak. Furthermore, under the assumption that gamma-rays are exclusively generated through hadronic interactions, we estimated the most optimistic theoretical neutrino fluxes from LHAASO sources and compared them with the IceCube observed fluxes. The results indicate that the majority of these sources are improbable counterparts to the detected neutrinos. In conclusion, LHAASO sources could be potential galactic neutrino emitters but currently do not exhibit compelling evidence, thereby underscoring the necessity for elevated sensitivity levels in forthcoming detection instruments like IceCube-Gen2.

title: AWARE-RG: Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs for Cyber Physical Systems
abstract: Understanding the security posture of cyber physical systems (CPS) requires reasoning across both information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT). However, a security analyst often holds an incomplete, role-specific view of the underlying system which has most likely resulted from their knowledge limited by a need-to-know framework. Such an incomplete view can potentially lead them to incorrectly assess if a cyber attack produces an untoward physical consequence resulting in making uninformed decisions about system resilience. In this work, we present AWARE-RG (Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs), a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop framework that provides an analyst with a role-bounded, need-to-know explanations of resiliency paths in a CPS. The AWARE-RG abstraction structure is derived using Formal Concept Analysis over MITRE ATT&CK for ICS tactics, ordered by the ICS Cyber Kill Chain. For valid attack-fault queries, plan repair and backward means-end analysis identify the missing dependencies, explain why the physical hazard is reachable, and suggest defensive strategies. For invalid attack-fault queries, AWARE-RG localizes the first abstraction level at which the path fails, and reports confirmed blocking conditions as hardening pointers.

title: SPECTRA-VLA: Base-Fine Hyperspectral Token Transfer at Frozen Vision-Language-Action Interfaces
abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.

title: On Global Joint Lower Bounds in Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization
abstract: Recent work has sought to transfer first-order nonconvex optimization guarantees to zeroth-order methods through gradient estimators, typically incurring a factor linear in $d$. \citet{kornowski2024} obtained an $\mathcal{O}(dδ^{-1}ε^{-3})$ oracle complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization and asked whether its dependence on all three parameters is jointly optimal. Although the dimension dependence and the first-order dependence on $(δ,ε)$ are separately known to be unavoidable, a matching zeroth-order lower bound has remained open. We answer this question in the unrestricted full-space setting. For smooth stochastic nonconvex optimization, we establish a scalar-oracle lower bound of $Ω\!\left(dL_0^2\min\{ΔH,L_0^2\}/ε^4\right)$ assuming a smooth, globally lower-bounded population objective and a second-moment bound on sample Lipschitz constants. A smooth reduction then yields a lower bound for Goldstein stationarity, proving the joint minimax optimality of the dependence on $(d,δ,ε)$ under explicit high-dimensional and small-accuracy conditions. Crucially, our results allow algorithms to query arbitrary points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, adaptively select sample-function labels, reuse the same sampled function at any number of locations, and output points without spatial restrictions. Thus, unlike lower bounds based on bounded query regions or fresh evaluation noise, our guarantees apply to a fully adaptive, reusable-sample scalar oracle. We also establish a separate noiseless exact-value lower bound against randomized algorithms, and hence also against deterministic methods. Our proof combines a globally defined sequential nonconvex construction with an exact Gaussian scalar channel, multistage random-field estimates, and an antithetic finite-sample realization that preserves information hardness under adaptive reuse.

title: Calabi metric on the space of k-Hessian potentials
abstract: Let $(X,ω)$ be a compact Kähler manifold of complex dimension $n$, and let $1\leq k\leq n$. We consider the space of smooth $k$-admissible potentials introduced in the study of the Hessian-cscK equation by Guo--Smith--Tong. The complex $k$-Hessian equation identifies this space, modulo constants, with the space of smooth positive densities of fixed total mass. We compute the differential of the Hessian density map and use it to pull back the Fisher--Rao metric. We then show that the square-root Hessian density map \[ φ\longmapsto 2\sqrt{\frac{ω_φ^{k}\wedgeω^{n-k}}{ω^n}} \] is a global Riemannian isometry onto the positive part of the $L^2(X,ω^n)$-sphere of radius $2\sqrt{V}$, where $V=\int_Xω^n$. For $k=n$, this recovers the spherical description of the classical Calabi metric. We also derive the curvature, geodesic and diameter formulas, and prove a quantitative local comparison between adjacent Hessian--Fisher distances.

title: HACHIMI-II: From Role-Play to Learner Behavior Modeling for Faithful Student Simulation
abstract: Simulated students let researchers test tutoring systems and teaching strategies before real learners are available, but only if the simulation reproduces where a particular learner succeeds and fails. The common approach asks a large language model to role-play a student, but a role does not model what this learner knows or will do next, so the model's own competence fills the gap. Simulated students perform at a level set by the model, differ little from one another, and seldom make the real learners' errors. We model the learner's behavior and recast student simulation as third-person prediction of the learner's next action. HACHIMI-II builds a student model from the learner's history, infers the learner's state for the current item or tutor turn, and compiles it into a behavior harness that constrains the next action. On three item-response datasets, the Wasserstein-1 distance between simulated and real student ability is 2.4--8.4$\times$ smaller than that of the strongest baseline. On two dialogue datasets, HACHIMI-II reproduces real student errors with the same knowledge type, locus, and mechanism 1.8--5.1$\times$ more often than the strongest baseline, and ablations trace the gains mainly to the explicit learner state. Predicting the learner makes capable models usable as simulated students.

title: Time-Inconsistent Singular Dividend Control with Regime Switching and Bankruptcy
abstract: This paper studies infinite-horizon equilibrium dividend distribution for a firm whose surplus follows a diffusion under observable Markov regime switching and is absorbed at bankruptcy. Dividend payments are modeled as singular controls, and non-exponential discounting leads to time inconsistency. We formulate equilibrium control laws and establish a verification theorem for a general finite-state model with surplus-dependent coefficients. For a two-state model with constant positive drifts and volatilities and bi-exponential discounting, we prove the existence of a regime-dependent equilibrium barrier policy for arbitrary positive switching intensities. The policy retains surplus below the prevailing regime's threshold and distributes any excess immediately. Numerical experiments examine how shareholder patience and economic conditions affect dividend decisions. Over the parameter ranges considered, greater discount-rate dispersion at a fixed initial average rate raises both barriers, while switching speed can generate nonmonotone responses and reverse their ordering.

title: Accelerating VLA Inference with Perturbation Informed Execution
abstract: Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls. Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections. To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call. Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples. PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.

title: BioPRM: Step-Level Consistency Verification of Biological Protocols
abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) provide fine-grained supervision for assessing intermediate steps in language-model outputs, but their application to biological protocols presents distinct challenges. Protocol validity depends on both the appropriateness of individual operations and their consistency with the experimental objective and surrounding procedure, while experimental outcomes are typically unavailable during verification. We introduce BioPRM, a contextual process reward model for identifying procedural inconsistencies in structured biological protocols. We construct a supervision corpus from SciRecipe and protocols collected from protocols.io and Bio-protocol using LLM-assisted construction and source-specific review by personnel with biological expertise.

title: Weighted composition--differentiation operators on mixed-norm, derivative Hardy and F(p,q,s) spaces
abstract: We study weighted composition--differentiation operators on mixed-norm, derivative Hardy and F(p,q,s) spaces. Explicit dyadic criteria yield boundedness, compactness and two-sided norm and essential-norm estimates, including endpoint and quasi-Banach cases. We also obtain multiplier and approximation results, Schatten criteria on weighted Dirichlet spaces, and exact singular values for monomial weights and linear symbols.

title: Measuring and Reducing Unusable Replies of LLM Agents
abstract: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. We call this property reply usability and measure it with a reader model that takes the requester's position and tests whether the reply can be interpreted from what the requester has seen, is in the requester's language and answers the request. Its agreement with the majority of five annotators lies within the range of the individual annotators. Across eight models from seven families, 54% of 480 replies fail, and the best model still fails on 30%. Failed replies mostly point to material the requester has not seen or use labels that the agent coined during its work. Stating explicit requirements for the reply reduces the failure rate from 0.52 to 0.43 together with errors and omissions, and a secondary model that rewrites the reply reduces it to 0.36, which human annotators confirm in a blind comparison. Reply usability can thus be scored alongside task success and improved with one appended message or one call to a secondary model.

title: Algebraically Integrable Smooth Convex Bodies
abstract: We prove that a convex body with $C^\infty$ boundary in an odd dimension $n\ge3$ is algebraically integrable if and only if it is an ellipsoid. This answers Arnold's problem for smooth convex bodies. Together with Vassiliev's even-dimensional nonexistence theorem, it gives the classification in every dimension $n\ge2$. More generally, in odd dimensions, a convex body with $C^\infty$ semialgebraic boundary is an ellipsoid whenever its section volume function satisfies a joint algebraic relation.

title: Response of Confined Mesoscale Flames to Acoustic Forcing
abstract: Mesoscale combustion plays a vital role in applications ranging from portable power generation to micro-propulsion systems. This study investigates the response of mesoscale flames to upstream acoustic forcing across three characteristic flame regimes: Flames with Repetitive Extinction and Ignition (FREI), Stable Flames (SF), and Propagating Flames (PF). Acoustic forcing is applied over a broad range of pressure intensities at the first harmonic of the combustor tube. At low forcing intensities, all the flame regimes exhibit oscillations at the forcing frequency without qualitative changes in their respective flame behaviours. However, as the acoustic pressure increases, all flame regimes transition to a common unsteady regime characterised by periodic ignition-extinction cycles (resembling FREI) alongside strong oscillations at the forcing frequency. This response is identified as the oscillating FREI (O-FREI) regime, in which increasing forcing intensity leads to a reduction in the mean heat release rate, an amplification of oscillations at the forcing frequency, and a drop in the Strouhal number associated with the ignition-extinction cycle. The response characteristics across all flame regimes are examined in detail and are further complemented using reduced-order mathematical models.

title: C1 Virtual Element Methods for the Optimal Control of Oseen Equations with Stream-Function Formulation
abstract: This work analyzes a $C^1$-conforming virtual element method for the optimal control of generalized Oseen equations, formulated using the stream-function on simply connected polygonal domains. The method is based on a conforming discretization in $H^2$ of arbitrary order $k \ge 2$. The discrete scheme considers an approximation of the state and co-state equations which involves a specifically designed operator for the convective term and a \textit{variational discretization} of the control variable. We derive quasi-optimal a priori error estimates in the $H^1$ and $H^2$-norms for the stream-function, and in the $L^2$-norm for the control, under standard assumptions on the family of polygonal meshes. The proposed method recovers the fluid velocity, vorticity, and pressure using suitable projections. Finally, we report several numerical experiments to support the theoretical findings using different polygonal meshes including the cavity problem. We highlight that this analysis also covers OCPs governed by Brinkman and Stokes equation.

title: Learning When to Trust Medical Knowledge: Regression-Safe Routing for Clinical Reasoning
abstract: Clinical reasoning LLMs need external medical knowledge, but retrieved evidence and reasoning chains can be outdated, poisoned, or hallucinated. Harmful knowledge can cause regression: changing a correct answer into an incorrect one. We construct a medical knowledge-poisoning benchmark covering retrieved evidence and reasoning chains, with seven attack families filtered by a three-judge "subtle-but-wrong" vote and paired clean exams that separate poisoning effects from question difficulty. No fixed knowledge-use strategy is robust across these settings: strong RAG methods trade robustness to poisoned evidence against accuracy when evidence is useful. We formulate knowledge use as per-instance routing and introduce Med-TrustRouter, a lightweight controller that keeps the solver frozen. From leakage-free runtime signals, it estimates each action's expected correctness gain and uncertainty, preserving the base answer unless another action is confidently better. Across seven medical reasoning settings, Med-TrustRouter achieves 78.9 macro and 69.2 worst-case accuracy, matching the strongest competitor on macro accuracy while substantially improving the worst-case floor. Its gains transfer across solvers and evidence judges, unlike a hand-coded router using the same signals. Similar performance across linear, tree, and neural action-value heads suggests that the benefit comes from routing rather than estimator complexity. These results support learning when to trust external knowledge for robust clinical reasoning.

title: The fence conjecture for convex projective polygons
abstract: We prove the fence conjecture of Dumas and Wolf: for a convex projective polygon with at least five vertices, every zero of the Pick differential lies in the interior of the region obtained by cutting off the triangles at consecutive triples of vertices. The proof gives a stronger estimate for arbitrary properly convex domains. In affine-sphere coordinates normalized at a Pick zero, the domain contains the closed disk of radius $2^{-1/4}$ and its closure lies in the open disk of radius $2^{1/4}$, unless it is a rotated square. The proof compares the canonical Monge-Ampère potential of the domain with that of a normalized square. Their third-order contact gives alternating local sign sectors. A planar separation argument and the maximum principle show that the negative sectors belong to four distinct components, each meeting a different side of the square. Rotation gives the inner disk bound, and conormal duality gives the outer bound. Both constants are optimal for the class of properly convex domains normalized at a Pick zero. The argument requires neither boundary smoothness nor any restriction on the multiplicity of the Pick zero.

title: ESL-former: Event Sparse Linear Transformer for FPGA-Accelerated Malware Detection
abstract: Transformer based intrusion detection has shown strong potential for identifying unknown malware variants, but its deployment on resource constrained edge devices remains difficult due to the high computational and memory cost of self attention. This paper presents an event sparse Linear Transformer framework for malware detection on FPGA edge platforms. Instead of relying on an explicit attention matrix, the proposed method derives token and channel importance directly from the accumulated key value state of Linear Transformer. A contribution aware scoring function is introduced to measure the perturbation of each token or kernel channel to the linear attention state, allowing redundant tokens and low contribution channels to be removed without constructing quadratic attention maps. To translate sparsity into practical hardware acceleration, the proposed design further replaces conventional binary mask based execution with a Top K active token buffer and a hardware compaction unit. The selected active tokens and channels are reorganized into dense fixed length data streams, enabling downstream processing elements to execute regular multiply accumulate operations with reduced redundant memory access and control overhead. This design is suitable for low power FPGA based malware detection, where both latency and on chip resource usage are critical. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed sparse Linear Transformer can reduce hardware cost while preserving malware classification accuracy.

title: Invariable Generation of Groups of Homeomorphisms
abstract: We provide a sufficient condition for a group of homeomorphisms of a compact Hausdorff space to be non-invariably generated, generalizing previous results proved using the dynamics of a group's action. We exhibit new applications among Scott-Röver-Nekrashevych groups and among groups of tree automorphism of with (almost) locally prescribed actions.

title: Remarks on prescribed scalar curvature functions
abstract: This short article is devoted to the study of the positive solution of Yamabe-type semi-linear equation with prescribed coefficient on general closed manifolds. Our main result is to provide some sufficient conditions for the existence of the positive solutions and give some examples to show that those conditions are sharp. An application to scalar-flat manifold settles a long standing question in prescribing scalar curvature problem in negative form.

title: Achieving a 0.49 keV threshold in the COSINE-100 dark matter experiment
abstract: The COSINE-100 experiment searched for weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) with NaI(Tl) crystals at the Yangyang Underground Laboratory. Using its full 6-year dataset, we lower the analysis threshold to 0.49 keV. A multi-layer perceptron classifier separates scintillation events from photomultiplier tube noise. It is trained with approximately $3\times10^{6}$ simulated scintillation waveforms per crystal, separately for groups of events with similar numbers of photoelectron clusters. The selection keeps more than 10% of scintillation events at 0.49 keV while limiting noise contamination to below 1%. The selection efficiency is validated with $^{22}$Na-calibration data and internal $^{22}$Na events, and the selection performance is stable over the six years of data taking. With this threshold, the median expected upper limit on the spin-dependent WIMP-proton cross section reaches $1.1\times10^{-36}$ cm$^2$ at a WIMP mass of 2.5 GeV/$c^2$, probing previously unexplored parameter space in the 2.0-2.8 GeV/$c^2$ mass range.

title: Maximum Likelihood Degrees via One-Edge Chordal Completion
abstract: The maximum likelihood degree of a Gaussian graphical model measures the algebraic complexity of its likelihood equations. This paper studies maximum likelihood degrees of Gaussian graphical models through chordal completion. When a graph becomes chordal after one missing edge is added, its maximum likelihood degree is determined by the maximal cliques and clique-tree separators containing that edge. This recovers Uhler's formula for complete bipartite graphs with one part of size two, and extends it to deleted-spine clique books, whose degree is unchanged when a page is thickened to a clique. For several fill edges, the same method gives a product formula when no clique or separator bag contains two fill edges. We also determine four classes of vertices at which clique blow-up preserves the degree. Two follow from known results, and two are established here.

title: SULA: Robust Langevin Sampling via Drift-Diffusion Saturation
abstract: The unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) and its stochastic-gradient variant, SGLD, are workhorses of modern Bayesian machine learning, but can be fragile when faced with a target distribution possessing a non-Lipschitz drift.
